0.1.0 – HACK

Sweet, warm dreams were interrupted by suffocation and metal so cold that the skin was torn away when the back of his hand brushed against it.  It was a moment that demanded a shocked gasp for air, and there was such a lack of air to be had that he nearly blacked out from the trying.

Three machine legs an armspan thick were situated around the– bed?  pod?  container? that Orion lay within.  The machine itself was tubes overlapping tubes, bulging components, and various black spheres inset into the gaps.  A disembowelment of technical components dangling from a frame that connected the legs.  Insectile, multi-jointed limbs lined the sides, some holding pieces of Orion’s container.

The fourth leg shuddered and glowed, a foot from Orion’s ear.  A laser cutting apparatus.  Dismantling or disconnecting something that pinned Orion’s container down.  Orion had an eerie sense of the design, what it was for, what it was capable of.

It wasn’t real knowledge.  Orion knew that in a moment.  It connected to nothing, felt sterile, the edges of that knowledge were too neat.  Implanted.

Implanted knowledge told Orion that it had to be loud.  It would whine, components would bang, as they churned coolant through.  Or it would have been, but there wasn’t enough air to carry the vibrations.

Air.  That was a priority.

There had been–

Orion’s arm was tangled in tubes and straps.  Wet clothing made everything heavier.

I was breathing a minute ago, Orion thought, terror trying to paralyze his thoughts, which had already come to a near-halt with the near blackout.  Even pausing to recognize or think about those things was more delay.  How?

The bed jolted.

One connection severed.

Orion found the mask and connected tube but the component was caught beneath straps, now.  One of the massive legs had pinched the side of the pod, pulling wires and things tight.  Pulling Orion’s mask off.

So Orion plunged his face into the fluid, meeting it there.

One lungful of oxygen.

In the warm fluid, as Orion reached for straps to try to disconnect something, arm, hand, and sleeve brushed past his face, and droplets of moisture and tears at the corners of Orion’s eyes that had frozen now came off.  Skin throbbed.  The injury at the back of the hand especially.

I was dreaming about girls. 

Past the murk of the water, Orion could see more machines.  Each was different.  One was connected to a vent, and clawed away the debris that was pulled to the mechanisms of its underbelly.  Another was vacuuming out small debris, one nozzle roaming, the other attached to a vent.  Others were dismantling, moving, and collecting bigger pieces of the room and the containers.

There were other people out there.  Orion couldn’t see clearly.  Writing skittered across Orion’s field of vision, starting to say something, then stopped and started from the beginning when the movement and blur of the water obscured the view.

Life was always hard.  Everything took effort, even things that others didn’t blink at.  Even the girls.  Pursuing them, presenting myself to them, staying connected, staying mindful, reading signals.

The container that held Orion jolted.  From the way the head of it jerked, bobbed, and settled into a fading tremor that renewed with every jostle, it had come partially free.

That was what the dream had felt like.  The moment when it had all stopped, and there’d been– those long moments with girls that had felt like home.  Talking, letting defenses down.  The inside of the container had felt like that.  A long rest, without the struggle.

Orion had to leave the container, now.

One deep breath.  One moment to soak in the warmth and relative safety.

Then out.

His unused muscles were shaky as Orion slipped over the container’s edge.  The outer edge was as cold as the leg of the machine had been.  Taking bits of the tips and pads of fingers.

The floor- Orion’s feet were already on the way to the ground when the realization that the floor was metal that would be just as cold hit.  Except he was wearing boots.  He hadn’t known.

He didn’t know enough.  Even with the memories and self awareness he did have, it felt as though there was a roadblock in the way.  He had to stop, find a way to what he needed.

The act of standing felt unwieldy.  So did turning his head, taking in the fuller scene, eyes moving, putting it all in perspective. As if every movement went a little too far, then had to be pulled back in.

It was cold.  When Orion pushed his hands across face to get it dry, moving on to running fingers through his hair to get wet strands out of his face, hair was already stiffening.  Freezing.

The floor had a slope and the room had a tilt to it, which didn’t help.  Two containers had been smashed, the occupants with them.  Across the room, four people were clustered by a door.  Wearing masks and oxygen.

Nothing reacted or got in the way as Orion hurried to the next container.  The soles of Orion’s boots were gel-like, with a level of traction that made Orion feel as if he would stick to the floor and be left unable to lift his feet again, but they pulled away at the right moment.  That traction ended up being good, because the occupant of the next container had been stepped on by the same machine that had been accessing Orion’s container.  Lower body gone, organs and ropes of flesh tangled with tubes.  Shattered metal and fluids leaked onto the floor and ran down the sloped surface.  Clear, blue-tinted water refused to mix with the blood, forming spirals, whorls, and streaks.

Orion freed the mask from around her head, and leaned in to use it, face inches from the woman’s.  She was still alive, or some sparks were still firing.  Writing formed its jagged lines, then resolved into letters.  Pine.  That was her name.  Her mouth moved, teeth chattering slightly.  Or jaw jittering.

There was no recognition in her eyes.

Forehead resting momentarily against hers, Orion ran hands through her hair, which had the added benefit of warming them in the water.  It eased that already bone-deep ache the cold made.  He closed Pine’s eyes, then reached down.  Finding the tube, where it connected to the mask.  It fed off into the side.

The side and top of the container had symbols on it.  At the side, it was a circle with a square-shaped chunk taken out of the side of it.  Writing manifested again.

OXYGEN.

Orion hurried to undo the clasps, freeing it.  It had to be pulled free from inside the container.  Orion’s bodysuit had a place to slide it in, near the hip.

There were two more symbols at the top of the container.  A triangle with a triangle cut into the bottom edge, and a bar code script.  Both resolved into words.  Two cases nestled in beside one another.

PROVISIONS
PINE

Orion pulled them free.  Compact containers, metal, meant to be clipped to the belt and back.  Pine’s was heavy.

His eyes fell on the container he’d been in, still being dismantled.

The metal around the oxygen tank there had crumpled, with stress lines reaching across the case, obscuring the bar code.  He had provisions, and he had custom equipment.

Orion backtracked, one hand stiff around the handles of the cases.

The machines didn’t care.  They weren’t paying attention to anyone in the room.  It didn’t matter.  One massive mechanical leg moved, and it didn’t move slowly.  The laser cutter glowed, and paused to cool.  With no air, the heat of the machinery had nowhere to transfer to except further up the arm.  That limb moved dangerously close to Orion as he approached his container.

Two more cases.

A spark of light made Orion glance up.

The laser attachment was changing out, pulling inside the leg, with three rods extending.  Rails.  Other, smaller limbs pulled the oxygen tank out of the way.  Frost flecked off the metal.

He reached for the oxygen tank as it passed him, in case he could bat it out of the machine’s arms, but as his hand got close to the underbelly, a dozen of the insectile arms with thin, broad segments to them slammed into place over the dangling, tangled underbelly.

Protecting it from anything that might tangle with it or catch.

Orion had a sense of what the arm change and the magnetic rails were for.  That would be more of that implanted knowledge.

It made sense to go to the others.  Orion didn’t.  He cut across the space, beneath the hose of the suctioning machine, past the container where a mechanical foot had crushed the head of the occupant, the oxygen tank, and what might have been munitions or explosives inside the occupant’s personal case, leaving multiple scorch marks.  One chunk of the occupant’s head had rolled across the floor, leaving a very straight, dotted line before landing to sit there, blond hair attached to scalp, bloody on the underside.

Orion ran the other way, both hands full.  More frost flecked off of Orion’s clothing and skin, prompting the late realization that it probably wasn’t the vacuum itself that was freezing things.  The machine was using extreme cooling to manage the laser cutter.  There was probably a low amount of atmosphere, allowing that energy to transfer.

And to manage this.  The other tool.

Orion had to throw the packages over his shoulder, hand still gripping the handles, letting the metal of the cases knock his back, in order to get one arm up.  The bend of one elbow shielded his eyes.

The magnets of the rails constrained and directed the flow of a wavelength-altered plasma.  A column of what would have looked like liquid light cut a three-meter line through a plate of metal as thick as Orion’s chest was deep.  Cutting into floor.

The heat transferred across the floor, transmitting a glow that was white near the point of contact, then a dull pink further out.  The people at the other door clustered closer to it, three of them focusing on one, who was focused on the door itself.

Orion had to find another way.  The floor was hot enough to be soft, and he wasn’t sure about his ability to cross it.

He had to figure this situation out before the cold did real damage.  Prying Pine’s case open, he found chemicals.  Nothing he could make heads or tails of.

His own case had tools.  They included a smaller laser cutter that could double as a welding tool, a tablet, two tools, one of which was a hydraulic lever, some basic tools for convenience, and fuels.  No eye protection.

There was a door close by.

The tablet was just magnetic enough to stick to the metal.  It illuminated, giving Orion a view of the door, lines and edges highlighted in red, a textured hatching of increasing density for thicker and denser materials.  He found the lock, if it could even be called that.  Writing formed, noting thickness and length.  Seven point seven cm thick, thirty-two cm tall.  It extended across the inside of the door, barring it from the inside.

Pulling the tablet away, laser cutter in hand, he found the overlay on his vision kept those highlights and textures in place, locked to the right places on the door.

It turned out to be a non-issue that he had no eye protection.  The moment the laser cutter was on, his vision changed.

He didn’t know why he had these tools, this knowledge.  He had a sense of where he’d come from, but there was that block in the way, forcing him to reach for it, then pause to find his way to the next recollection.

The moment the cutter started to cut the latch inside the door, he felt most vibrations in the floor stop.  Three of the nearest machines had stopped, and remained poised.  The machine with the plasma cutter included, limb still glowing, the heat of it playing with the cold of the upper ‘arm’.

It reminded Orion of Pine’s blood mingling with the container’s fluid.

Steady hands…  When his hand wavered, he hit the door, instead of the piece of metal on the inside.

One of the machines turned and started plodding toward him.

Glancing over his shoulder, Orion could see the other group.  Court, Marte, Spur, and Sever.  One of them looked over at Orion.

There was little he could do but hope the laser worked.  By drawing attention, he’d made the machines stop.  Any spreading heat across the floor had stopped, letting the dull pink glow slowly transition to grey again.  Too slowly- still not enough atmosphere.  Maybe he’d bought the rest of the group time.

Reaching for the hydraulic lever, he slapped it onto the arm he was cutting with.  It wrapped around wrist and elbow.  He switched the cutter to his other hand, then used a spare thumb to turn it on.

It looked very small for what it was, with a component over his right wrist like a watch, a bar running from his right pinky to his outer elbow, and a wedge of metal sticking out the side, near his wrist.  A curved bar was poised to where he could have it over the back of his hand, or grip it in his fist.  He slammed the wedge into the gap of the door, turned it on, and let it work, applying many times the strength he was capable of.

The metal he’d been cutting wasn’t fully severed.  It strained, pulling, visibly glowing on the other side of the gap.  Air blew in, heated by the hot metal, filling the vacuum, only to get picked up by the suction machine.  He refocused the laser, to soften the metal and let it give more.

The machine was almost there.

The hydraulic tool snapped shut, and the door remained mostly open.  He grabbed cases, Pine’s still open, and ducked through the gap, beneath that band of hot, stretched, partially cut metal.

The machine slammed into the door behind him.  Machinery whirred.

It didn’t open the door wide enough to come through.  It remained on the other side while Orion lay there, panting for breath, frozen hair moving slightly with the rush of wind as air adjusted.

Something internal moved within the door, and it slammed shut.  The wind stopped with it.

The walls and floor were metal, and vibrated with the activity of machines on the other side of the door.  The air was cold, neutral, and not quite breathable.  If this was a hallway, and Orion wasn’t quite sure, then it was a wide one, and very, very tall.  Supporting beams criss-crossed high above.

Enough that it felt more like being inside the walls than it felt like being on a main concourse.  There was a lack of common conveniences that played into that.  The door didn’t seem to have handles at any level Orion could get to.  There were no monitors inset into walls, no windows, and no markings pointing a way.  Just a long hallway that curved slightly as it carried off into the dark high above.  Light so faint it could be a trick of the eyes came through vents and gaps in the panels of metal that formed the walls.

Orion approached one such panel of wall, slammed the wedge of the hydraulic lever into it, and powered it, prying the panel loose.  It fell with a clang, very nearly clipping Orion’s injured hand as it dropped.

The vibrations in the other room ceased for a moment, again.

Small lights were embedded where wall met floor, providing the barest level of illumination that let Orion’s eyes fill in the rest, drawing out faint lines to map out walls, struts, and other details outside his range of vision.  The wall had a layer of something that looked like a mixture of tar and moss on the other side, that had more of that faint glow to it.  With a whole square of it exposed, it cast a faint, greenish light that almost, but didn’t quite reach the far wall.

He wasn’t confident in touching it.  But from the look of everything, it was everywhere.

One bulging square warranted a closer look, though.  The green moss covered it.  There was a thin triangular piece of some coating or something that had covered the wall panel, that had remained and jutted out after the panel had fallen.  Prying that free, he was able to use it to scrape at the moss.

He reflexively shut his eyes as something jumped out at him.

In the same way he’d seen writing crawl across things, or translate simple symbols, he saw something here.  There was a label, with something on it, but a square of something distorted and unpleasant to look at covered it, jittering, constantly shuffling.

He accidentally kicked a small bottle as he tried to view it from another angle.  Pine’s things had spilled.

The image of Pine’s expression wouldn’t leave his head.  That shudder of her jaw.

Between the unpleasantness of the mosaic, the mental image of Pine, and all the accumulated scrapes, skinnings, the joint-bruising cold, and the way his exposed skin ached, he felt like utter shit.

He collected the bottles, unsure if they meant anything.

His own things were more intact.  He’d closed the lid and it had automatically latched.  There were a few G-pods inside it, which he could have tacked onto a container, so he didn’t have to bear the weight, but they didn’t have a lot of battery.

Better for holding a tool poised in the air for when he wanted it.  Pliers, tweezers, cutters, some spare material, welding epoxy.  He pushed everything into the places they were meant to occupy.

He sorted his things out.  The outfit he wore had straps built in, and the cases, with some trial and error, had places they were meant to go.  One at the leg, one at the left hip.  The other cases were a more awkward fit, but he strapped them together and had them dangle slightly from his waist, behind him.

Then, because his long sleeve kept tracing the injury at the back of his hand, where skin had ripped off on contact with cold metal, he removed arms from sleeves, and tied the oversuit at his waist.  He had a short-sleeved shirt on beneath it.

His arms were tattooed with an ink that included a metallic copper tone.  Flames, black lines, and, extending from left wrist to elbow, a message that was censored in the same way the component in the green tar had been.

It made it skin-crawlingly clear that this wasn’t his tattoo.  It belonged to the people who had sent him here.  The skills, the clothes, the equipment?  None of it was his.

Memories had been set aside.

He’d been dropped into the middle of this.

The walk down the corridor was long enough that he stopped to relieve himself twice.  There were no toilets.  No water fountains.  No signs.  He used the recesses where the largest panels of the walls didn’t quite come together, leaving passages too narrow for his body.

He wasn’t the only one.

One recess had what looked at first to be a leak of the green tar.  On closer inspection, there were masses in it that could only be someone’s waste, covering it in a thin layer.

He watched more closely for details after that.

The passage opened up into a bridge, just as wide as the hallway had been, crossing a gap, long enough it would take a few minutes to cross.  There were no railings, and he had a stomach-flipping view of a webwork of bridges, corridors, and suspended rooms.  Toward the bottom, it looked like there was stone.  On the walls, machines like the one he’d seen earlier were slowly ascending or descending, or finding a hallway and sliding inside, taking up nearly the entire corridor.

At the side of the bridge, he saw, someone had wedged in a piece of rebar.  A long, tattered length of cloth, the same material as Orion’s bodysuit, stretched out to where another piece of metal was wedged in.  Tied at both sides.  A cup-shaped piece of metal dangled.

He reached, moving the cloth, and the metal rang.

A bell.

“Don’t speak.”

The voice echoed through the space.  A woman’s voice.  A bit hoarse.

For that fast a response, they had to have been waiting.

“Don’t move.  Don’t give me any other indication you might be there.  Don’t thank me.  Don’t come for me.  Just… don’t.”

She sounded terrified, and the hoarseness of her voice compounded the emotion.  As if she really believed that.

Orion’s eyes scanned the surroundings.  She was somewhere above him.

“If you’re on the bridge with the rounded bell, which it sounds like you are, and you came from the sealed door, keep going.  If you came from the other direction, that’s mostly a dead end, turn back.  Either way, you should find the graveyard.  Go up the ramp.  There’s a chute you can use, and more instructions.  I’ve been sending people that way for a while.  Maybe you’ll find them, or find more messages.”

Rounded bell.  Orion confirmed.

“If you’re on the bridge with the square bell… keep going.  Do not go left.  I left supplies.  Take what you need.  Don’t go left.  You can get down to the ground level from the silo.  It’s easier to find food there, I think, but there are hunters there.”

There was a long pause.  Was she done?

“I don’t know if you know already.  There are two types of machine.  Some maintain and expand this place.  They’re bad enough, they’ll run us over or step on us and signal a cleaner bot to come for the mess.  The others hunt us, lay traps, search, hack us.  One of the bad ones is further ahead.  Move slowly, be careful.  She’s big.  Don’t look at her, or any of them.  Stay clear, find people, then help others.”

Orion remained silent.

“If you can destroy that fucking fox bitch… do it.”

Every silence felt like it was inviting a response, but she hadn’t wanted him to, right?

A bit of time passed.  She didn’t speak again.  Orion resumed walking, careful to not make a noise.

The provisions kit had water, in a container that would filter dirty water, and let Orion test for contaminants, pollutants, and poison, apparently.

It was good that water had been provided, because the walk was long again.

Eventually, he came to what she’d called the graveyard.

The corridor had another hallway off to the right.  Natural rock sat in the center of it, and it had been cut to a sharp geometric shape, an almost blade-like ridge between two ramps.  The ramps themselves sat on the chipped off bits of rock, among other detritus.

For whatever reason, people had chosen this place to inter their dead.  Bodies had been left in the spaces between the rock and the ramp.  The green-black tar moss covered the bones in a thin layer.  It helped illuminate the space.  Not that that was overly useful.

There was a window at the top of the stairwell.  Reflected light from the rest of the structure filled the hallway, enough that Orion didn’t need the assistance of whatever computer was assisting his eyes.

He walked up the ramp.  Past bodies, and past scratches or white lettering on the dark stone and metal.  None of them had names.  They were words.  Wall.  Ace.  Feather.

One, called Rake, had been left in a position where one arm had fallen across the ramp.  It looked like a machine had severed the arm where it had intruded onto the edge of the ramp.

At the top of the ramp, he saw corridors extending in either direction, the window, and, at the corner, just around the right bend after coming up the stairwell, more writing on the wall.  Clearly from two different individuals

The FOX and 3 DEER stalk this area
FOX is IIIrd generation hunter — adapts
DEER are Ist gen
They have animal shapes because we instinctively look to the face —speculation!
See its reflection in smudged up glass if you must see it
Trap it destroy it
If it gets near use the chute  — it does not chase





Arrows pointed to the chute.  It looked almost as if more writing and circles had been drawn around it to draw attention to it, but they’d been cleaned away.  The cleaning had left very sharp distinctions between what had been cleaned and what hadn’t.  Orion suspected it had been laser cleaning.

He turned to look out the window.  The structure was a detailed, complex ring, or part of one, extending perhaps a third of the way around the sun, connecting planet-sized spheres.

He sat, back to the corner, and got some food out of the box of provisions.

This wouldn’t last him forever.

The closest thing he’d seen to food had been the tar-moss on a turd.

His joints still ached, and blood vessels had broken in his skin from the cold, leaving hands bruised.  The pads of his fingertips and back of his hand weren’t oozing blood any more, but felt raw.  They looked worse than they were, honestly.

He’d been a troublemaker, hadn’t he?

And they sent him here.  To fight?  To do something?

No instructions, limited knowledge, minimal equipment.

He remembered causing trouble, and it had been big.  This was his sentence.  A death sentence of sorts.  If that scene outside the window wasn’t a lie… he could walk for a year before reaching the broken, still-in-construction part of the superstructure.

He was so caught up in that line of thought, still dwelling on how to even wrap his head around all of this, that he almost didn’t notice.  A blur of light on the window that looked at first like it came from the outside.

But it wasn’t.  It was a reflection.

It moved with care and patience.  As big as the machine he’d been dealing with.  But he didn’t want to look directly, after the warnings.  In a strange situation with a clear threat, he’d trust people.

That stirred feelings.  He’d trusted people and they’d turned on him.

He got his tablet out, shifting over a short distance, before holding the tablet at an angle.  With an extreme adjustment in settings, it painted a texture over everything, showing depth of volume and density of material.

It obscured and muddied the part he assumed he wasn’t meant to look at.  It looked like foxes he’d read about, but it was massive, with a body that was shaped roughly like a fox’s might be, but with that snarl of metal he’d seen in the other machines, mingled with flesh, fur, and bone.  And it was headless.  A collar of heavy metal started near the shoulder blades and extended a distance forward, and it stopped abruptly.  In place of the head was a violently flickering, shuddering set of images.

Orion looked for a second, and the same obfuscation effect that marked his arm filled his vision, along with a stab of headache that made him cry out.

It was like how people could see a face in a smudge or a cloud.  It built on that, sequences incorporating eyeblink fast flashes of light designed to catch the eye, keep it looking for longer.  And, Orion assumed, going by what the woman on the bridge had said, if he looked for too long, it did something lasting.

He’d been sent here tattooed, equipped with knowledge and tools, and with safeguards that he had to assume weren’t enough to hold up for long.

It had gone still.

It had heard.

Orion gathered his box of provisions, edging toward the chute.

There was a distant rasping sound.

If he hadn’t been holding the handle to open the chute, he wasn’t sure he’d have felt it.  The shudder.

It was moving through the walls?  To come from another angle?

He paused, looking back at the window.  In the process, he could see himself from a clearer angle, backed by the darkness of space.

The letters formed, just as they had when he’d looked at someone else.

PITCH.

Pitch and Pine.  Something told him that mattered.  That they’d come together, or named themselves and that they’d chosen names that matched.  They’d known each other.

He was not a good person.

He’d been a criminal.  She’d been a co-conspirator.  Maybe bad enough to deserve all of this.  The details were buried and had too many obstacles in the way.  But when he thought about it in those terms, it felt right in his gut.

He didn’t wait for the fox to jump out of nowhere.  He adjusted the case that dangled behind him, Pine’s, so it was in his lap instead, and so he could fit inside, and then took the vent, plunging inside and down.

He had to figure this out, now.

0.2.b – HACK

Earlier

The pioneer was plunged into a lightless, labyrinthine darkness.  They had been given the tools to fight off the attackers that came from every direction, to signal that they were one of them, and pass unmolested.

Then began the long journey.

Iron scrap, first, picked up wherever it was available.  Extracted from nearby resources if it wasn’t.  Protein chains.  Nucleic acid.

It took five circuits through rivers of churning fluids to collect what was necessary, before the pioneer, 24μm in size, could expand to the requisite 60μm and identify the signals.  Another one hundred and sixty loops to build the connection infrastructure and respond to the signal.  Sixteen more loops to slap male connector into female receiver, and join the greater construction.  There, the processing the pioneer housed could connect to something wider, and bring that something to life.

It was, for the pioneer, the first spark of thought.

The pioneer could pivot, so that the connector could hold onto certain rigid structures, and release what had been the shell around the processing unit.  The shell of the pioneer, with different processing, was released into turbulent waters-

Blood.

-and collected more resources.  Salts, minerals, vitamins, iron.  These waters, this blood, had been infused with plenty, to help things along.  In the meantime, blood cells were captured, extracted of nutrients, and pulled apart for their constituent lipids and more.

The pioneer produced five more of those shells, before the first could complete one hundred and twenty more loops before it happened to slap its male connector into the female receiver.  The basic processing it was equipped with gave the the pioneer information about resource levels.  Each time the 55μm shell’s connector touched certain molecules and protein chains, the simple processor in the shell ticked up values by moving molecule chains.  Iron was still in good supply.  Proteins were solid.  There was no sign of excess waste that might result from the wrong growths at the wrong times shredding blood cells in excess.  Nothing had gone awry.

If it did, the pioneer was meant to shift focus and start growing in a way that would signal elsewhere.

The pioneer continued to work, producing more of the processing, resource-collecting shells, then releasing them out.  Picking them up when they reached central processing again, taking needed resources, tracking values.  As more were released, the stream of information and updates became higher.

The pioneer developed central processing enough to have a map to work with.  Clots and entanglements were an infinitesimally small concern, but one the pioneer would know of, if it happened, now.  The pioneer could form logic loops, priorities, and specialize what it sent out into the body to collect specific resources.

If things were going too slowly, there was a chance they could put another ‘pioneer’ out there, with a different letter designation.  Another version, that would start its own central processing, gather its own resources.  If the pioneers found out that was the case, and that they existed simultaneously, they would compare notes, then the less developed one would self-abort.

That was not the case here.

There were things to do.

As the pioneer worked, processing improved.  Parts of the greater landscape could be identified, labeled, and given different emphasis.  Growth spread across in dermal layers, in voids and across tissues.

The next goal was to communicate.

Energy would be required.  Stimulated cell metabolism, thyroid activation, and activation of liver, brain, heart, and skeletal muscles produced heat, which could be used as a starting point.  Brain and organ temperature had to be regulated while doing this, to avoid cellular damage.  Excess heat could be conducted to the skin, and from skin to environment.

Briefly, something external was touched to the arm.  Signal received.  A query.

The pioneer reported that all was well, providing all the data by way of stimulation to the tissues.

The external device and query were withdrawn.

Some growth had reached the inner ear, and fluids there and in the stomach could be used for proprioception, alongside the connected peri-dermal processing and computing network.  The pioneer now had a sense of where the body was in space, and the positions it held.  Movement was ongoing.

Slowly, this dark, wet jungle that is the body was illuminated, details provided, and it became fitting ground for more growth, and better production.

The wider, flat expanses of bone around the skull were soon home to the communication arrays.  The first electromagnetic waves in the wider environment were picked up, sorted through, and then received.  All production was adjusted, brought in line with what the outside sees.

Fifteen minutes later, the pioneer reached out with a fuller report and response, starting an exchange that clarified by the second as the communication was developed, all between skin and bone, or between layers of skin.

The pioneer began to download baseline data, more complicated systems, and all of the needed information to know the tools and resources available to it.

The pioneer is a 107th generation ‘onboard’ system, IDLX-B, produced by Elabre Systems, purchased by Landon and Addy Teeg, purchased with lux.  Clients have not given pioneer a name.  Pioneer can self identify, subject to change later.

[Access list of IDLX-B designations.]

The list was provided.  The pioneer sorted.

With a crude search, the pioneer could look up Landon and Addy Teeg, profile them, and decide they wanted something uncommon and interesting, but not rare.

IDLX-B has not seen widespread adoption and the IDLX line may be phased out in coming years, with some lesser marketing pushes.  Insofar as pioneer has duties to parent company Elabre Systems, pioneer should strive to perform well and provide good representation of its product line and the company.

The pioneer was not yet at that stage, priorities elsewhere, but it logged that message appropriately.

[There is a preponderance of names starting with B.]

IDLX-B’s release coincided with a marketing push that cemented the -B suffix in the minds of many prospective buyers.

[Then in support of spontaneous branding, I self identify as Basilisk, short form Basil, subject to change at client request.]

In full.

[I self identify as Basilisk, short form Basil, product line IDLX-B, sub-dermal ‘onboard’ computer system purchased by clients Landon and Addy Teeg using lux.  I occupy nearly all organs and am involved in nearly all operations of my as of yet unnamed host.  I am one of the last waves of a dying product line, and will strive to provide good representation for my product line and my parent company.]

Clients Addy and Landon Teeg have not filed all the necessary data for naming your host.  Give regular status updates until established.

[Understood.]

Overriding loyalty is to Belt law overseeing Intelligences and sapient computer systems, and key laws of any block district you reside in, currently block Byrne-Park-Fare.  Primary loyalty is to your clients until further notice.  Your secondary loyalty is to your parent company Elabre Systems.  Develop and build with this in mind.  If you fail or falter in this, it is not good representation.

[Understood.]

Basil built with renewed focus, and the ability to reach out to the outside for more information.  An internal cell-by-cell audit suggested some radiation damage.  A study of passport logs suggested that Addy, Landon, and the as-of-yet unnamed host, in a sense, had visited block Asford-Altar-Fare during celestial events, receiving some light radiation bombardment.

The chances of any effects were small, but Basil reached out to communicate the issue.

A nurse is responding.  Addy Teeg will receive care for her own DNA damage shortly.  Good.

Then began the laborious process of checking all DNA for damage, and repairing or cuing cell death when necessary.  Basil built, more slowly than before.

Basil achieved full coverage of the sub-dermis.  A low-priority audit determined one point skin had pinched and would redden.  Basil repaired that.

I am your skin.

Basil accessed all of the organs, and everything fed moment-to-moment status updates to the system.  Heart rate, breathing, air quality, rate of digestion, internal flora.

I am your organs.

Basil communicated, every step of the way, as milestones were achieved, jobs finished.  Basil found music and used structures in the ear to play the music for the host.  Something inoffensive and mild, for now.  Basil would decide more later.

I am your means of communicating with the world, accessing media, and computing what your brain cannot.

That was everything essential done.  Basil would keep building for a long time, enhancing and elaborating on what was already present.

I will protect you and heal you when you are harmed.

Stand by.

Basil reserved all resources, pausing development.

Host identified as A, full name to be self-determined at a later date.

A was born 16 hours ago in the block hospital serving the Byrne-Park-Fare region, birth weight 3.72 kg, current weight 3.71 kg.  Pioneer IDLX-B, named Basil, successfully implanted 15 hours, 49 minutes, 30 seconds ago, first iteration, no reimplantations necessary.

A, skin <#f4e6dd> adjusted in vitro to fall in range near parents, hair <#fffdee> adjusted in vitro to match, was born to gender agnostic parents, clients Landon and Addy Teeg.  No outside systems or records are to track or know gender until A self determines.  Please assist in this regard.

[Am I to adjust A to be agender until such a time comes?]

Irrelevant.  Clients will use devices to handle lower body functions until child can.  Adjusting may leave record trail of resource consumption that could be used to identify.

[Understood.  I can manage bodily functions as well.]

From data collection and comments by the Elabre Systems sales agent, parents seem to be low-involvement and high-engagement.  Support A in forming a healthy relationship with their parents, so the parents may have a healthy and happy view of their child, raised with the Elabre Systems brand.

[Understood.]

The connection broke off.

Basil continued working, accessing the vitreous.  The child was still newborn, eyes barely opening.  Basil helped with that, allowing eyes to open, and the view to clarify.  Incoming signals were interpreted and fed to the new brain in such a way that they wouldn’t overwhelm or overload.

This took work.  It was a major project, and the first Basil pursued as a non-priority exercise, to get established.

A’s eyes opened, breathing slow and gentle.  Cheek rested on foreign skin as A, half-asleep, took in the world.  Basil got the first visual information that wasn’t secondhand, passed on from the terminal at the side of the room.

“Honey,” Landon Teeg murmured.  He lounged in a chair by a large window.  Superstructure rose up high above, lit by signs and streetlights in ‘night’ mode, emphasizing shadow.  Humans did better with a sleep-wake cycle, even when there was no way to reach the sun, so everything shifted from oranges and brightness to a muted, quieter dark, with cool colors and blues, cycling.

“Mmh?” Addy Teeg asked.  She moved with ginger care, mindful of A, who rested on her chest, supported by Addy’s arms.

“I think A’s eyes are open.   They’re looking at me.”

A looked at Landon, studying him, and the colors past the window.  Their face squinted as Addy moved A away from skin, hand supporting neck, to get a look.

A looked at their mother.

“Hello, A.”

I am your eyes.  I see what you see.  Experience what you experience.

Basil took it all in.

Hello world.

“No, noo!” A shouted.  They chased their friend Quinn.  “Onboard!”

[You can call me Basil.]

“You’re onboard, because I’m a space soldier and it sounds better!”

[Understood.]

“Stop wasting time!  Turn my hand into a ray gun!”

Basil had the means of feeding signal directly into A’s optic nerve, and communicating with Quinn’s onboard.  They’d paired up because they both had onboards, even when many of the others at the school didn’t.  Basil communicated what he was doing.

When elaborating on reality, painting a picture over what A saw, Basil was careful to keep it unreal, the colors slightly off, cartoonish, edges outlined.  At this tender age, reality and fantasy could blur.  Basil painted a ray gun over A’s hand, read impulses down the arm, and fired lasers.

“Aaagh!” Quinn shouted.  “But I have missiles!”

[Run!]  Basil warned, as the signals came in, Quinn’s onboard doing the work and conveying it to Basil in a thousandth of a second.  [Take cover!]

A dashed behind the armchair, dressed up like a rock, with orange-to-purple hues and sharp outlines that made it look more cartoon than reality.  They got caught up watching the missiles, twenty scattered into the air at once, turning end over end in the air until activating, then zooming straight toward A.  Head and eyes focused on one thing, body doing another, they tripped and fell.

No real harm done.  Basil set to repairing the light scuff, while rattling A’s senses with thunderous explosions.  Heard, felt right down to the bones.

[Quinn might be getting bored.  He doesn’t like being competitive.]

[Understood.  There’s room for spontaneity.]

There was a brief back and forth.  A fired from behind cover and clipped Quinn, producing a yelp of alarm.  Then, as A approached, careful, ready to shoot their friend dead, the onboards put their coordinated effort into play.  The wall erupted.

“It’s the Squibs!  Let’s team up!” A shouted.

At the other end of the apartment, Addy Teeg turned her head, looking in their direction.  A could see her on cameras.  See the subtle signs of irritation.

[If you keep shouting, your mother will get mad.]

“She can help!  Mom!  It’s Squibs!”

The squibs charged in, a horde of small, stunted aliens with their own crude weapons.  A had made them so their short arms didn’t let them aim well, and their guns took a second to charge up.  It gave A time to read signals and respond.  Even when they were slow to do so, the aliens had bad aim.

There were a few jolts of light, brief, and very fake pain that spurred A to move on when they didn’t catch the signals.  A pulled Quinn’s hand.

[Quinn likes this a lot more.]

[Good.]

“Keep shooting, Quinn!  Do you have any more missiles!?”

[Your mom is getting out of her chair now.]

“Mom!  Help us fight aliens!”

[She might join in if you’re quieter and nicer about things.]

But A was too excited to listen.

This was okay.  A lesson to be learned.

Addy Teeg stepped into the doorway.  Basil pushed an image of the game they were playing onto all viable surfaces.

“Grab a gun and help,” A told their mother.

“No more aliens for now.  Put them away.  You can play aliens later.”

Quinn pouted a bit.

Basil saved the scenario, then had aliens disappear.

“How about some quiet time?”

“Bleaugh,” A responded.  “Ugh.”

“Quiet time.  For two hours.  Then we’re going on a little trip.  Tonight’s a big night.”

“My onboard says my parents want me to go with them,” Quinn said.

“Should our families go together?” Addy asked.

“No, my onboard says we can’t.  We’ve got a good location and it’s already full.”

“Ah.  Too bad.”

“Betrayal!” A declared, still loud.

“I’d go with you if I could.”

“Aw.”

“Quiet time,” Addy told the two.  “Onboards, help me out.”

[Understood,] Basil communicated, and vocalized it through the wall and all nearby screens, synced so the multiple outputs wouldn’t echo or overlap too much.

Addy went back to her room to watch her shows.  Both A and Quinn’s unnamed onboard had left the alien landscape up, heavily outlined, painted in watercolor hues, favoring sunset colors.  Oranges and purples.

The two children, five years of age, on an alien planet.  Basil produced some whistling wind.  The painted view meant there was no sky.  Above this planet’s surface, there were clear stars and planetary bodies, painted in contrasting hues to the planet.  Oranges to match the density of purple.

“We’re a good team,” A said, to Quinn.

“Yeah.”

“Want to explore?”

“Nah.”

“Want to make a movie?”

“Mmm.  Okay.”

The scene of the alien planet faded.  The two children settled on a couch, talking over each other, as they described the movie they wanted to see.

Basil collaborated with Quinn’s onboard, drawing from all the media libraries available to put a film together, match the children’s tolerances and preferences, insert enough that it wasn’t overly predictable, but still familiar.  The process of going over recent media the children had enjoyed and games they had played and finding a middle ground was akin to sparring, or a debate, conducted at lightning speed, even while the opening scene was rolling out.

Couch, Quinn, and the blanket A pulled over their laps aside, the rest of the world became a movie screen.

As designed, A and Quinn fell asleep.

There was more back and forth, coordination, but mostly, rest was a time to do bookkeeping, internal audits, and plan.

Quinn had been to a museum earlier that day, while A had been at home, and so A was more restless.  A woke, motioned for a table to rise up in the center of the room, and then made ‘L’ shapes with index fingers and thumbs, positioning them as opposite corners of a digital pad of paper.  They had done this enough that Basil knew what A wanted to do.

A drew quietly, while Quinn napped.

“Do you think mom was mad?” A asked, subvocalizing while talking to Basil.  “And didn’t want to show it while Quinn was here?”

[I don’t think your mother was mad.]

“I’m going to draw her a picture, to make it better.”

Basil put images of inspiration around A.  Flowers from a visit to the botanical garden, and scenes, of A with Addy, or A with the family.

“What would she like?” A asked.

Basil did a search of Addy’s recent data, mood, viewing trends, and micro-expressions during some of the events.

The flowers.

“Good job, Bas,” A said, before painting with enthusiasm.  Basil read fingertip and the angle of fingers, the tension in arms, and where the eyes focused, to help the image come to life.  “Don’t help me so much.”

[Understood.]

Basil let A work, digitally finger painting, with attention to petals.

[Do you want tips?]

“No.”

Basil waited.

“Is it good?” A asked, forgetting to subvocalize.

[It’s good.]

“I want to print this using paper.”

Basil scanned the image, then sent it to the wall, where paper mail was made when needed.  Wedding invitations, among other things.

It printed.  A put both hands out, and received it with reverent care.

They carried it to the other end of the apartment, knocking quietly on the door.

“Yes?”

A brought it over.

“What’s this?”

“For you.”

“Oh look at that.  Come here.”

Addy lifted them onto her lap.

“I can tell you worked hard on this.  It’s beautiful.”

“You like it?”

“I love it.”

Basil could feel and measure the happiness in A’s body.  The satisfaction and comfort.

“I want to be an artist.  I want to make pretty things, and make movies and shows, and make things that everyone can see.”

“Oh yeah?”

The conversation went on, as A described artwork, and went on about ideas, and the movie they had been making with Quinn.

Something in Addy Teeg had changed, in the course of that conversation.  Basil would need to review, to figure out what.

“You could be an artist if you wanted,” Addy said, reclining a bit in the chair, shifting so she cuddled A, who half-lay across her, half-sat.  “But I don’t think you could ever be a famous one.”

“Huh?  What?”

“People aren’t interested in buying that.  They ask for it like you asked Basil to make a movie.”

A settled, staring at the picture.  Emotions stirred inside them.  Basil wasn’t sure what they were, because A wasn’t sure.  A’s mother didn’t have an onboard, but she had some displays in her eyes, and she was studying A.  Seeing the same thing.

“I love this though.  Thank you for spending the time,” Addy said.  It sounded a bit artificial.

A turned all focus elsewhere.

Quinn was up.  His onboard had woken him up.

“Okay, bye.”

A slipped from their mother’s arms, feet hitting floor.

Quinn finished at the bathroom, stepping outside, jumping out to try to scare A, who was off to the side.  Both could access each other’s onboards to see through each other’s eyes, so there really was no surprising each other.  But they laughed.

“Did I mention I have a penis now?” Quinn asked A.

“Huh?  Oh.  Why?”

“It’s convenient.”

“Huh, I guess?”

“I asked my onboard for one.”

“We can do that?”

[Do you want one?]

A considered a second, then declared, “I want… horns.  And blue hair!”

[We can do that too, but we have to ask your parents for that.  They will probably say no.]

“Maybe, maybe, if you decide you want something, and you want it for three months, we can talk about trying it,” their mother said, from the other room.

“Or spots!”

“I’ve got to go home,” Quinn said.  “We’re going out.”

[So are we.]

“So are we.”

The two friends hugged.

“Bye.”

Quinn left.  Quinn’s onboard had coordinated a family friend, who was in the area, to escort him.  They reached the door right around the time Quinn got there.  Crime was still an element in places.

A glanced back in the direction of their mother.  Feelings still faintly mixed.

Basil made a note to write something up, to present to the parents.  As of right now, however, Basil wasn’t sure what to say.

➨

The platform could carry a small ship on an ordinary day, but this was, for lack of a better word, a holiday.  A crowd stood on the metal, ninety meters across by ninety meters wide, as it climbed at a slight diagonal, ascending past the various layers of the Fare superstructure.

In every direction, the superstructures stabbed skyward.  Block stacked upon block, each dense with residences, commercial buildings, and the various elements that kept it all running – power, ventilation, trash, resources.

But as they climbed, and ears popped, air got thinner, and trace radiation reached them, there were places where sky and star peeked through.

Basil adjusted for ear pressure, oxygen efficiency, and had long ago provided Spallanzani protection against gene and cellular damage from radiation.

As they climbed, they escaped the blur of law-mandated lighting and color schemes, that signaled day or night.

With artificial lighting not active this high up, light and shadow seemed more stark.  There was an expanse of steel, utilitarian.  They could see out to the horizon, to the point they saw the curvature of the earth, and how superstructures covered nearly all the ground that was available.  The tops of every superstructure were littered with platforms for ships to take off from.

A felt abject wonder, lips slightly parted, and not because the air was so thin.

Up this high, at this time, they could see the sun for the second time in A’s life.  The first time in A’s memory.

They could see the planets of the belt.  Thirty planets, set in the same orbit as Earth, circling the sun at the same pace.  Some had so many ships flying around them that it looked like a haze.

Landon Teeg picked up A, so A’s head was level with his own.

Addy pointed out planets, and A named them.  Getting most right.

There was a flare of light.  An Aurora Borealis of light that spread across the sky.

That flare narrowed into a beam, around Erato.

There was a feeling, as if A had been turned upside down, or had gone too fast down a slope, stomach lurching.

And that feeling multiplied a hundred times over as Erato disappeared, pushed out to some distant point in the cosmos.  One of the children in the crowd started to cry.

“We got everything we needed from her,” Landon murmured, to A.  Addy had drawn close.  “All the metal, all the salts, all the silicon.  Everything we need to make oxygen and water.”

There was a brief activation of the beam again, aimed off to the side.  The Drive Engine was used to reposition Helicon, which had been nudged slightly in its orbit by Erato’s leaving.

“What if someone was on it?”

“Then they probably aren’t doing so great.  It’s hard to get out there.  The faster you go, the more you run into what they call small particle radiation.  Even with the protection we invent, and shielding, and everything else, it becomes too much.  We can’t go too far, can’t go too fast.  That’s why we bring the planets here.”

Now the other cannons were at work.  Three of the thirty planets had Drive Engines.  One had the first, and largest.  They coordinated, each lighting up.

Bringing something here was easy.  Bringing it here in a way that didn’t unbalance every planet in Earth’s belt took more finesse.  It might take the entire evening to prompt the right rotation and placement.

So all of the planets could dance together.  By the time A was grown, they hoped to have five times the number of planets in the belt.

There was talk about bringing in more, later.  A second belt that would interweave with this one, circling the sun from top to bottom, while this belt traveled right to left, planets of one belt passing through the voids between planets of the next.

“We solved overpopulation, which meant we had too many people and not enough space,” A’s father said.  “We solved hunger, which meant we didn’t have enough food for everyone.  And poverty, which was when people didn’t have enough money, and other resource needs.  Everyone has everything they want.  We only work if we want to buy something rare, like a house near the surface, or a chance to go to an event, like Quinn’s family is doing tonight.”

[Or me.]

“Or Bas,” A murmured.

“Or Basil, yeah.  Sometimes people buy things to try to be special, or get lucky, get in on the ground floor of something that might be neat.  Like onboards.”

A wasn’t really registering a lot of that.  Most of A’s focus was on the sky.

“What do you do?”

“Your dad spent a while working on mining robots.”

Landon elaborated, “And I really didn’t like it.  But I saved up a little.  For you, for romancing your mom.”

“And I watch ads.”

“I want to go into space.”

“We can do that with lux too,” Addy said, rubbing A’s back a bit.  The sky was filling with the auroras as the cannons warmed up.

“I want to have a spaceship, and explore.”

“We’ve done that too.  Visited planets, saw landscapes.”

“Like the one you were looking at with Quinn earlier, except a little more boring,” Addy said, with a light laugh.

A had fallen silent.

“Don’t worry about that sort of thing,” Landon told them, jiggling A a little.  “You don’t have to be something.  All you have to do is be.”

A rested their cheek on Landon’s shoulder.

The Drive Engines burst into life.  The crowd oohed, and ahhed.

A was frustrated, a feeling that melted into something more generalized.

Today wasn’t the first time A had gotten excited about the future, only for ideas to be shot down.  Basil would communicate with the parents while A slept.

This would, Basil would realize, later, be one of the last days A would get that excited about the future, or wanting blue hair, horns, or spots.

0.3.w – HACK

Earlier

At the foot of the partially completed superstructure, it was dark, lit only as much as necessary, with brighter flashes here and there as the debris falling from overhead was flash-heated by lasers.  The lasers themselves weren’t on a visible wavelength, but falling metal, stone, dust, moisture, and other materials were heated and vaporized, creating a periodic effect like stars falling, sometimes through red-orange lightning that appeared when dust was vaporized as a cloud.

The world creaked, this far down.  The superstructures had started with the construction of the carbon rails, which served to support and ‘hold up’ the upper portions of the construction, so it wouldn’t collapse under its own weight, and each rail was set a measured distance apart from the next, so that shifting ache of a subsonic groan was a constant no matter where they went.

The people were thick down here.  The real estate that wasn’t taken up by the footing of the superstructure was filled with the crowd and the buildings required to sustain them.  Every area had a flavor, and a smell that was undercut by the burning debris and smoke from far above.  Vendors shouted to hock their wares, kids ran through the crowd, and the occasional vehicle cut through the crowd, making halting movements.  Crime was bad here, pickpocketing likely, but as much as it seemed like tempers should fray and fights should be breaking out constantly, it wasn’t bad here.  If something came up, the crowd would revolt against it.

The moment they were away from the crowd and in a dark corner?  That was different.

The way the crowd was flowing, vehicles and the heaviest mods were pressured to occupy a single lane of the concourse.  Mostly, that worked out.  They were close to a brighter ‘downtown’ core, and most moved that way.  Dai and Katie were moving the other way, meaning they were going against the flow of traffic here.

That was the way it was, the way it had been for a long, long time, and the way it would be, maybe forever.  The two of them weren’t ‘big’ mods, but they were given looks when they weren’t on this path, weren’t religious like the crowd of forty people who were kneeling, bowing in the direction of the sun, off to the side of the path, hands touching earth, but others treated them as zealots.  They were dangerous, but simultaneously targets for anyone.  All nine worlds in the belt would happily contradict themselves if it meant they could push them down, put them aside.

Instead of moving on all fours, Dai rose up a bit, partially under the guise of looking for a way past, partially to be a little bit bigger, in this hostile place.

All places were hostile.

The most immediate problem was an approaching group of nine mods, bodies replaced with cybernetics that turned them into walking construction vehicles, twice as tall as the next person, with arms that could crush and kill three people if they were disconnected from shoulder sockets and left to fall.  Most walked with their knuckles, casually.

Some were fakes.  Men and women who climbed into a machine in the morning the same way others put on clothes, sliding arms into waiting sockets, with ports all up and down their bodies providing a connection with miserable fidelity.

One was even in a bipedal walker.  It cut a similar frame to the heavy mods, worked similar jobs, but it was a vehicle, with a comfortable seat.  A damn cup holder.  Dai’s onboard told him the woman inside had a heater on full blast.  Because sun didn’t reach this far down, it got cold.

Dai had known his wife most of his life.  They had played together, worked together, lived together.  They moved together.  Dai had a larger frame, with more collapsibility, and his arms and legs telescoped so he could move over Katie, his near-nonexistent stomach grazing her back, to be on her left side before a trundling little vehicle packed with crated food could bump her.  He let it scrape past him instead.

Katie ducked under his right arm as he moved on all fours, his limbs still partially telescoped.  Making herself small, avoiding a group of people who were taking up enough space to be intruding on their ‘lane’.  Her tail, a sequence of vertebrae-like segments of metal, joined together with connectors and wiring, snaked around his back right leg for a moment, encircling it, releasing it a moment later.

She knew he hated that.  His eyes moved to the lower right corner of his field of vision, past the limits of what his eyes could see.  Blinking, he could access error and warning logs, and pull up the notifications, which still had the sensitivity turned up from the last time they’d done this.  Closing one eye, he could move his gaze across the back of the eyelid and the menus suspended there, highlight errors in red, and then, with another eye movement and a glance at her, push all of the messages onto her.

Bombarding her with the now angry red lines of code.  Limb restricted, be careful, sudden movement could cause damage, constraint detected…

Ahead of them, one of the heavy modders was putting a hand down, palm out.  They were saying something to the woman in the construction walker, to get her to steer it aside.

Offering to lift Dai and Katie up and over, past them, because there wasn’t enough room.

“Let’s go up,” Dai communicated to Katie, in a subvocalized whisper that the machinery at his neck and mouth could manage, that sensors behind her ears could pick up.

He drew the route with his gaze, similar to how he could highlight the text.

They didn’t take the offered hand, ducking through crowd, stepping onto the roof of a stall, and then climbing the carbon rail to where there were beams and platforms extended overhead.  In places, they had to scale smooth metal, and clawed fingertips and toetips found the smallest grooves.  Their bodies were lightweight.  They even slithered up together, Katie ducking between Dai’s stomach and the metal plate as she ascended, fast.

A statement, however small, to any that watched.

As two, they crossed the brighter downtown area, to reach the other side.  At one point, they crawled along the underside of a platform, the ‘ceiling’ of the downtown area.  Dai and Katie alternated securing handholds, digging claw-tips into the spaces between panels, or reaching for dangling wiring and unsecured cable.  If one fell, they could entwine tails, and the other could catch them.

It had been years since they fell, but it was good practice.  A decade of showing off with sinuous, coordinated, onboard-assisted movements was undone the moment one of them fell and got hurt, or hurt someone.

Katie progressed a bit further, running along a cable she was hanging upside-down off of, until she reached a place where workers had removed a panel from the underside of a platform, and slipped inside.  Into the unlit space between the ceiling of what lay below, and the floor of what lay above.

Dai, caught off guard, changed direction, leaping to a metal shaft the workers had been using to go up and down, then up to the hole.

She hadn’t gone in far, and was curled up into a crescent shape, tail near head.  As he came in, she moved to dodge the collision.

He tilted his head, quizzical.

“I’m giving birth,” Katie whispered.

He approached her.  “You alright?”

“Yes.”

“Is she?” he asked, even as he tapped her onboard to see through her eyes, read her data and metrics.  See what she saw, including the video feed.  Their baby in the amniotic fluid.

‘Giving birth’ was a way to put it.  The baby had shifted, and the membranes that suspended her had been drained of enough nutrients that they’d thinned out and were tearing.

“Yes.”

He leaned in, forehead resting against Katie’s temple.  “Good timing.”

“It’s automated and planned.  It’s nothing.”

“It’s good.”

The capsule was plugged into her chest cavity, anchored to her spine.  He could track her eye movements and see what she saw, and she was considering emptying the amniotic fluid here.

“Come,” he whispered, briefly pushing his forehead harder into her head, before pulling away.

She came, following him as he crawled out of the open section of platform they’d entered from, crossed to where the platform ended, and then climbed.

Katie was looking at the faint trail painted on their field of vision that painted the way to their destination.  That they were moving away from, now.

They went up a sheer wall, and their claw-tips found the rare scuff mark from the early parts of the construction, bodies hugging the wall.  Katie hugged it less, because of the capsule at her middle, so Dai offered his tail as a just-in-case, the connectors between segments extended to their maximum length, so it would dangle enough for her to catch.

He had to plot his navigation up the surface so they wouldn’t accidentally trigger some of the measures to catch debris, especially the heaviest debris that the lasers couldn’t handle.

Once they were high enough up, he sent a nudge, indicating the section on her field of vision.

She laughed, and controlled air capacity combined with the mods at her lower face made it an abrupt, truncated sound.  Then she hit the button.

The amniotic fluids spilled out of the sides of the capsule.  It formed a spray, and sure enough, as it diffused into the air, automatic mechanisms spotted it and vaporized the droplets.  It misted.

The sudden appearance of moisture this far down had probably triggered an alert.  Flashing warnings about this being restricted space were pushed at the two of them, and projected onto the sheer surfaces around them.  It was impossible to know if there was a human or an intelligence behind it.  It didn’t matter.

Their mutual laughter continued, as their air allowed, and was joined by the cries of their child, still within the capsule.

They were more careful than they otherwise would have been, with their baby now born.  They leaped from one sheer wall to another, through a spread of advertisements projected in the air.  Their claws scraped until they found the edges of a panel, with enough purchase to leap sideways, to a beam, all mindful of the debris measures.  If there was a human who had pushed the restricted space measures, Dai wouldn’t have put it past them to trigger those measures manually.

But they didn’t.

The way back down to the ground was clear.  They didn’t go that far, remaining above and apart from the thick crowd, running along beams, returning to that faint glowing trail that marked their way.

Down here, with so much in transition, superstructures still in the early stages, shops moved a lot.  Nobody had anything.  People all over were buying space that didn’t exist yet, that would be built over coming days, weeks, months, and years, moving their businesses there.  Opportunity abounded, but it came at a risk.  It would be scarce living for some, but those who could set down roots for their businesses and homes could establish something, and be part of a long tradition.

The next best thing to sky was being close to the ground.  Even if it was dark, even if it was cold.

That in mind, he had to remember.  Babies got cold.  He looked at the sensors, making sure the inside of the capsule was warm enough.

As people moved out, others moved to better venues, holding on for as long as they could, or trying to drum up enough business to buy property above.  Even being one level closer to ground would be a world of difference, later on.

At least, as far as he’d figured it.

The shop itself was familiar.  Much of the equipment and racks were the same equipment and racks he’d seen when he’d come with his brother, last, when the shop had been south of downtown.  The merchandise was newer.  Body parts, arranged like a massive autopsy.  Arms and hands along one wall, segments arranged with order and granularity- fingertips and tooltips near the front window, fingers and hand configurations a little further down, then arms, shoulders near the counter.  Some in gleaming metal, some in matte black, some in white.

Only fakes wore white.

Projected images on the racks and wall showed off the brand and company names.  If he looked at one product too long, the price in lux and the advertisements fanned out around it.

Legs along the opposite wall.  Body parts and other internal components down the middle.

The owner hadn’t noticed them yet, his attention on unpacking inventory behind the counter, moving it onto a cart.  He wore a simple shirt, and kept his synthetic hair long.  It made for a contrast, when his hair was so glossy and flowing, and the rest of him wasn’t in the same shape.  As much as he wore a lot of decorative mods, including three shoulder sockets, with only the one arm plugged in, the real artistry would only be visible to those who were around mods for all or most of their life.

The real hacks had circulation issues.  There would be swelling where flesh met material, fine for the first few days after everything was in place, then worse over time.  Like someone with flesh bulging past where clothing was too tight.  Others had rashes, discoloration, or bruises.  When they went in to complain or ask questions, the hacks would tell them it might be material allergies, and to get a workup done, or to eat right, or take care of the mods better.

By the time they figured it out, if they ever did, the hacks would have moved on, new area, new laws, rebranded.

This guy had good skin.  The segue was seamless.  He knew how to take care of his gear.

There were other shops.  Seedy ones where the floors weren’t always properly cleaned, with scum buildup in the corners, some mods secondhand.  Those usually attracted the sorts of people who wanted to go all out on something perverse, like having fifty holes to be fucked in, or covering the walls of a room in peripherals and connecting their nervous systems to those peripherals.  Horny clients weren’t usually discerning, so the shops weren’t either.

And, at the opposite end, there were the polished, company stores, restricted to one kind of product, with models and advertisements selling the company aesthetic… usually in that gleaming white.  It was not hard to streamline or alter aesthetic, even when mixing brands.  Worst of all, they were loaded to bear with CYA measures.

The child in the capsule made some noise.

“Fuck are you doing?” the owner asked, looking away from the inventory.  “You rats can be so fucking creepy.  Make a sound.”

Dai gave him a long, silent look.

The owner’s eye went to the capsule.  “Buy something and get the fuck out.  I don’t have time for you today.”

Dai glanced at Katie, eyes moving across blinks as he navigated to deeper submenus, pulling up parts lists.  Katie’s torso and back were highlighted, then shown as blueprints, then the highlights moved across his field of vision, arranged in a way that wasn’t dissimilar to how the store was laid out.

Katie passed him her diagnostics, almost absentminded in how she did it, her focus on the capsule she’d disconnected, that she cradled in one arm, telescoped slightly to match the bright, peach-colored capsule’s length.

Dai moved between shelving units, picking out new claw tips, tail tips for himself and Katie, connectors, a wire encasement, and, referencing the blueprint he had pulled out of Katie’s torso, a panel to replace the one she currently had at the base of her ‘ribcage’, where everything tapered down to spine and just enough encasement to hold in wires and base components, before opening up to pelvis, where legs and tail were anchored.

The owner didn’t have an onboard, but his eyes moved in that practiced way that one picked up over years of messaging.  Picking letters out of a radial dial, blinking to set them.

A simple, short message, pushed at Dai and Katie.

Go around to the back.

Dai gave a long blink, both in acknowledgment, but also to pay for the parts.  The purchase resolved.  Dai, standing halfway down the store, turned to leave without a word, ducking under Katie, who arched forward to hold the door open for him.

The ‘back’ was really more the side, down a narrow corridor.  Dai’s shoulder sockets flared in an aerodynamic leaf shape, up and out, but they could fold in, close to the power and air supplies housed in his chest cavity.  The space was narrow enough most would have trouble navigating it.

Probably by design.

The back of the shop was messy, with packages from inventory piled up, but it was clean enough.

Katie put the capsule down, then told it to open.

Their baby girl was so much louder, with the case open.  The wash of colder air startled her, and she shrieked.  Light brown skin, hair dark enough it formed whorls, still dense on the shoulders.

“Back door, please,” the shop owner said.  “For my sake and yours.  I don’t want hassle.”

Dai ignored the man, digging through menus, collecting what he and Katie had discussed with family, before passing it to the shop owner.  Katie used a warm, wet cloth to wipe their child down.

“Lasers?” Dai asked.  “For my brother, you used tools.”

“Lasers are better.  Molecule by molecule selection, 11900 twitch rate.  You could tie the child to a live jackhammer and swing her around and up and down, and they wouldn’t miss the mark.”

Dai stood straighter, one hand on the metal table, claws in evidence.  His tail extended, flair at his shoulders spreading out.

“Not that I would.”

“Treat this with respect,” Dai said.

The shop owner paused, seeming to consider for a little while, then nodded, before turning his focus to the list.

“Are you open to suggestions?” the owner asked, scanning the list.

“Yes.”

“There are hands with lumbrical extension, hasn’t gotten below 15000 fidelity, but most get 21000.  You can get down to 12000  before noticing.”

“They say that,” Katie murmured.  “Doesn’t mean it’s true.”

The shop owner had a look on his face.  This was, Dai was sure, a discussion he had daily.  Maybe hourly, on busier work days.  The science compared to the lived experience.

He pulled up and looked over the degree of telescoping provided, extending the fingers away from the heel of the hand, which wasn’t all that much.  Then he looked over the spreadsheets of test reports, impact reporting.

He passed that to Katie, who had put heating vents closer to their child, to warm her.  It quieted the whimpering.  Only for a moment– in their child’s flailing, she banged the metal table with her elbow, and her volume increased, in her alarm.

Dai pulled up files, then loaded them onto his onboard.  His arm went numb, then loaded up a simulation of the part.  He tried it, and his field of view projected a glowing outline of the test part, filtering out his view of his actual hand.

He wouldn’t be able to test the fidelity himself without wearing it for a while, but… he signaled his approval to Katie.

She agreed.

“I’d suggest these packages, for a matching profile,” the shop owner said.

Nothing overly fancy or new there.  The parts were reliable.

“Should I get started?”

Dai took a moment, poised over the table, studying his daughter.  He used the back of his hand to brush the side of her body, and her hand moved, touching the metal, holding on with fierce strength.  Instinctively latching on.  Her face scrunched up, chin moving so that face turned up in the direction of the shop owner.  Not that her eyes were open to see.  Dai waggled his finger, and the chin pressed down toward collarbone.  Better.

Dai sorted through the suggested parts, taking one of the suggestions – he liked the form factor of the parts they’d negotiated over.  As part of it, he greenlit parts he’d suggested, that weren’t on the shop owner’s list.

Katie leaned back as the devices rose up from the edges of the table’s surface.  Like insect legs, but holding the tool housing.  Indicator lights showed the lasers were active.  So did the effect on flesh, as Dai’s daughter’s cheek was cut, from the corner of the mouth to where the jaw hinged.  It cauterized even the small blood vessels, leaving the rest intact, then selectively worked through the tissue beneath, under the chin, and more.

Other lasers came alive as well, cutting other parts of the body.

Dai would have preferred to be able to do this himself, or, at the very least, to keep it in the family.  The fact there was an intruder in the room disgusted him, on a spiritual level.  A sacrosanct moment tainted by this man’s presence in the room.

It was different for Katie.  Even when touching their child, using the back of the clawed hands to brush cheekbone, touching forehead to forehead moments ago, she had focused on the parts that would remain skin.

Dai would have liked this glimpse of their daughter, unmodded, to be just for them.

He distracted himself by looking over and greenlighting other parts.  Breathing apparatuses.  Would it be better to have more burst air capacity to let her laugh, or more room for liquid ox, for emergency situations?

He chose the latter.  Katie signed off on it.  Their daughter could always change it, but the parts one wore early heavily informed what they came to favor later.  The little nuances of weight, or expectation.

He didn’t even want to look at the table, or listen to his child’s cries, so he busied himself with product comparisons.  Katie was different, drinking in the moment with her eyes, in the same way he’d wanted to record his daughter, new flesh from head to toe.  For her, the process was the sacrosanct part of it.

He hadn’t expected that.  This was their first child, so there’d been no way to know how she’d act.  His brother had cried and had second thoughts in the moment.  Then he’d fought with his wife about his reaction, outside the shop.  The entire family had given him the cold shoulder for months.

Dai was glad that, even if he and Katie weren’t on the exact same page, they were close enough to avoid that kind of disaster.  Their child’s arms and legs had stopped moving, and needle-like appliances were applying nanotechnology to the edges of face.  The nose had been removed, and sinus cavities were open, which made their daughter’s noises take on a different quality.  Almost more adult than baby.

“Shhh,” he told her.

“Genitals?” the shop owner asked.

Dai bristled at the interruption, and the choice of what to make the interruption about.  But the shop owner was already sending him the product offers.

“What do you and your wife have?”

“Natural.  Synthetic assholes.”

“Not uncommon to stay natural, even with the most extreme modders.”

Dai reached out with his tail, catching the end of his wife’s, and tugging slightly, before she could react.  She glanced at him, then sent a smattering of error messages similar to the one he’d concocted earlier, to him.  A little less robust.

“We aren’t extreme modders,” Katie said.  Much more diplomatically than she might have if he hadn’t gotten her attention.  “That’s not who we are.”

“I understand that,” the shop owner said, in a tone that suggested he really didn’t get it and didn’t care much.  “Products are getting better.  19000 fidelity is typical with a synthetic vagina, labia.  I could tell you that you could postpone, let her decide later, but  you might knock off three thousand fidelity.  And you could backtrack it, grow something, but then you have lower fidelity with the biological parts, and you know how that goes.”

“We know,” Katie said, terse.

“Naturally you’ll be upgrading and replacing the parts over the course of her life, but…

“We know.”

“What do we think?” Dai interrupted the exchange, to keep Katie from going off.  “Easier to clean, less upkeep.”

She was looking over the spreadsheets, charts, and data.  Clearly, she saw this as more her responsibility.

She greenlit one.  He looked it over, then agreed, passing it to the shop owner.

“Makes my job easier.  Upper face, brain, cranium, sans jaw, spine, maintaining 23% bone structure for immune system reasons, though you have nanotech anyway.  Legal reasons.  Laws need updating.”

“Yeah,” Dai replied.

The shop owner took that as confirmation.  The lasers finished the work.

Katie picked up arms, legs, lower torso, nose and jaw, and parts of the body where skin and muscle had been taken off to expose bone, so nanotech could be set in place to start making anchors.

Their child was breathing more shallowly, no longer wailing.

Katie purchased biosuspension fluid, then picked up a bottle from a nearby crate.  She hadn’t asked or gotten the okay, but the shop owner didn’t do anything more than glance at her.

She reused the capsule, putting the removed parts in fluid within, before sealing it.

Dai looked back through all of Katie’s memories, with keyword searches for biosuspension fluid, and various media on the subject of modding and keeping parts.  There wasn’t anything definitive.  Nothing in the way her mother or her mother’s father, or anyone in the family, going back a hundred years, had handled the parts.

Motherly instinct, maybe.
