The nanotechnology would take another few minutes to build up enough to bridge gaps.  Materials were supplied by needles, laying paste over top of the target sites.

“Thermal blisters around the eyes?”

Katie turned to Dai.  “Shauna has those.  They only stand out in extreme cold.  It’s a good safety feature.”

He could look through Katie’s recorded memories to see where she’d interacted with Shauna, sub-select for times they’d been cold.  The blisters stood out as thumbprint-sized raised bumps when skin contracted most.

“Yes.”

“What about onboard?” the shop owner asked.  “They’re doing something funky with this new ‘IDLX’ brand.”

Dai looked into it.  Better, but…

“More responsiveness, Intelligence,” Katie noted.

“Alright.”

Loading it up meant submitting all the details.

“Winnifred,” Katie said.  “Win or Winnie for short.”

There was no arm to take the shot, so the shop owner put the needle to the side of little Winnifred’s neck.

The nanotech at her lower face had set enough.  The components could be latched into place there, a singular piece over nose and mouth, same as Dai, same as Katie, and same as their parents before them.

More mods were locked in behind the ears, then at the throat.  Working downward.

“Welcome to the family,” Katie whispered.

➨

“Yarraman-1890,” Winnifred whispered.  She gripped the post she was perched on tighter, so she could lean her body to the side.  It didn’t make much a difference in what she could see, but the ship turned in the air to fit better on the platform.  “With modded-on g-sail tip and snub extensions, made by Jadrian Advantages.  Most call it a pistol.”

[Entirely correct], Toby confirmed.

The g-sails on the four short fins at the back of the pistol and the one at its nose all glowed bright as it came in for the landing, turning main engines off.  It had two rear legs that came out sideways, and one leg beneath the nose.  The name came from the shape, which was very top heavy, with a nose that jutted forward, and a back end that came down a little.  If it was actually a handgun, it wouldn’t have much of a handle.  There was enough of one that the name worked, at least.

It had a way of seeming like a smaller ship than it was.  The slightly domed glass fixture on top seemed like the sort of place a pilot would sit in a smaller craft.  But when she put it in perspective, it was four stories.  Or three and three-quarters, since the bottom floor didn’t reach all the way across the body.

[What is the reason for its peculiar shape, do you think?]

“Pistols were originally for fighting, but that didn’t really happen.  They figured out it was better to snap in some huge tool for the nose, and sell their services to the highest bidder.”

Her tail swished left and right, happy.  Here and there, metal scuffed against the metal of the post she was on.  She was poised at the highest point she could reach without climbing one of the larger antennae, above the skyscape.  A webwork of beams, shafts, transportation infrastructure for accessing deeper layers, and the variously sized platforms extended to each horizon, punctuated by the occasional structure that loomed higher.

She was in the outer atmosphere.  High enough up there wasn’t wind.  Or air.

[What are the big no-nos?]

She paused, tail stilling.  She used her non-whisper voice to grunt out a, “Huh?”

[You get too much knowledge from the documentaries and readings.  Practical question.  If you found yourself piloting one in an emergency, what should you not do?]

She considered.

Faint, glowing red lines extended across her field of view.  It was her aunt, poring over her field of view, recent events… nag imminent.

[Think it out.]

No time.  “I don’t know.”

Her aunt buzzed her.  “Winnifred, love.  Stop daydreaming and come to R-32.”

Winnifred’s tail drooped, then swished once.

“And don’t jump.”

Her tail drooped.

She was perched on a post about a hundred feet up from the nearest horizontal surface.  She liked jumping from these heights, because the lack of atmosphere meant she could fall a little faster than if she was further down.  Toby kept her from blacking out.  If she aimed right, with Toby’s help, then even if she fucked up on a planetary scale and couldn’t stop from falling, the safety features that extended between parts of the still-in-construction superstructure would catch her.  And her family would get a tiny fine she’d pay out of her pocket money.

Worth it.

But not with Aunt Gwen looking in.

Winnifred’s knees reversed direction, and, still holding on with her feet, she heaved herself down, grabbing the sides of the post with her hands, before sliding down head-first.  She moved fast enough that her hair worked itself free of the twist of wire she’d used to tie it back.

Her grip tightened on the sides of the shaft, until she’d slowed her descent.  She leaped from the post to a slanted plate of metal.

“Mind that wear and tear to your claws, girl.  I’ll tell your parents to make you pay for it out of your own pocket money.”

“I maintain my stuff.”

“Maintain it better by not using your hands to brake.”

Cousin Megan had said Aunt Gwen had become queen of the bitches after Winnifred’s uncle had bailed on her and the family.  Winnifred didn’t like to think that way.  It had to be hard to be Aunt Gwen.  The way Winnifred liked to think about it, it was like being in zero G.  Uncle Shawn had launched away, but in doing that, he’d sent Aunt Gwen the opposite direction.  He hadn’t wanted to be involved in the family tradition anymore, so Aunt Gwen had become all about that stuff.  He hadn’t wanted to dwell on the work, so Aunt Gwen was doubled down on it.  Up in everyone’s business.

[I don’t think your parents will be mad,] Toby communicated.

It took Winnifred a moment to connect that thought to the immediate circumstance.  Toby had noticed her mood had dipped.

“It’s not that.”

[Ah.  Sorry.]

“You’re fine.  Do you want to pick the movie tonight, Toby?”

“Winnifred, if you don’t move faster, I’m going to keep you late and you won’t be watching movies for a while.  And you can tell your onboard he won’t be either.”

“Toby’s a girl.”

“Child,” Aunt Gwen admonished her with a word.

First Aunt Gwen had used her name, calling her ‘love’, then she’d been ‘girl’, now she was reduced down to ‘child’.

She wondered, if she upset Aunt Gwen enough, where would it stop?  She glanced through records of past conversations, looking for trends.  Was it something Aunt Gwen was even aware of?

“I can see what you’re doing,” Aunt Gwen whispered over the connection, looking at what Winnifred was looking at through the onboard connection.  “You’d better not be preparing a clever response.”

Winnifred glanced back through the still-open records to find the kind of clever responses Aunt Gwen was talking about.  Zero results.  None intentional, anyway.

“That qualifies as one,” Aunt Gwen communicated.

Oh, oops.

[She’s called you pet, twice, after calling you child,] Toby communicated, highlighting records, timing it for when Aunt Gwen was focused on other things, before firing off a location update.  Possibly as a distraction.  Aunt Gwen didn’t tend to read the logs between a person and their onboard.  Most of the adults didn’t even have onboards that talked like Toby did.

“I know where you are, Toby, I know where everyone is,” Aunt Gwen said, absently.  She was distracted, because ‘everyone’ was looking in, now.  A lot of the extended family was gathered around the dock.  One of Winnifred’s cousins was watching the exchange between her and Aunt Gwen, and had passed it on to the other cousins, who thought it was fun.

This was an all-hands-on-deck situation.  Why so many?  Had a ship blown up?  Winnifred wondered.  Nope.  It was a Hod-94, newer than the pistol she’d just watched come in, but it looked older, because it had worked hard.  A potbellied ship for hauling cargo.  The ship looked fine.

Bummer.

[The pistol ships struggles in high-atmosphere environments.  Its fins are small, its weight balance and lack of aerodynamic nature serve it poorly.  That’s why it usually lands and anchors itself to deploy and use its equipment,] Toby communicated, from their conversation earlier.

“Ohh.  I could’ve gotten that.”

[I thought you might figure it out, looking at the Hod-90.  So I beat you to it.]

“Ninety-four.”

[Good.]

She was still curious.  She couldn’t look in at the ship itself.  Trying bumped her out, with a message about permissions.  Annoying.  She wanted to ask her cousins, and glanced through the various onboard connections, peeking through eyes.

She was an odd outlier.  The family was big, and she had twenty-one cousins at this station, but the way things had worked out, there was a three year gap between her and her next oldest cousin, and an eighteen month gap between her and the next youngest cousin.  They tended to group together by age, and Winnifred had been left out in the cold.

Most of the time, she didn’t mind.  But when people were chattering and something was happening, she felt the loneliness.

She ran across flat ground, toward the dock.  The family had obtained the all-clear to enter.  The full picture became clear, permissions to view the ship interior released, barring some goods and personal quarters.  A panel had come loose in a cargo hold, where sand had been stored.  Sand had gotten into the hull of the ship, under the floor, inside the ceiling, and throughout components.

“Your pay will be docked,” her Aunt Gwen told her.  “Work is fidelity, child.”

“Work is fidelity,” Winnifred replied.  Still child.

There were a lot of terms for her family, and the wider interconnected ‘families’.  The Twenty-Nine Families.  People of the narrows.  The sleek.  Dock folk.  Cleaners.

The longer the list got, the less kind it tended to be.

They lived at the stations, modded to crawl over ship hulls and inside the narrow corridors and spaces within.  It was a long-standing tradition, kept within twenty-nine families, passed on to children.  Better to be this, she knew, than to be indolent, like so many were, outside the families.

To get there faster, she passed near the main concourse.  Some more ships had come in.  Today was a light day, but on days before they brought in a new planet for the belt, it could be crowded, with temporary docks anchored in place to accommodate the countless ships that would perch here.

At one dock, a Hod-83, more angular in frame, was covered in dust.  The people coming out were caked in mud, still attached to their suits and boots.  It looked cement-like, from the way one guy was swearing, prying at a clod on the side of the sole of his boot.

She thought about volunteering aid.  Even knowing she was late already for a job they already had.  Helping with his boot and the mud, maybe cleaning the dust–

“What the fuck are you looking at?” the swearing man asked her.  He’d pried the clump free.

[Don’t engage.]

She paused, caught off balance by Toby’s statement, when Toby pushed more information at her. The man had violence arrests, and-

He threw the clod at her.  “Git!”

She moved out of the way, darting to one side, but realized late she was moving into its path.  It was easier and faster to bring one arm up to shield the side of her head, than to bring it down and resume moving.  It was hard, and fragmented parts of it clipped her ear and forehead.  She lost her balance, landing on her hip, then reoriented legs, a moment later.

The man barked out a laugh.  He wasn’t the only one.  “Told you to move the fuck on!”

“Wells, the hell you doing?” one of the men in the group asked.

“Leave it,” another man told Mr. ‘the hell’, pulling him away from the situation.

Wells practically crowed, “They play the victims, poor them, but they want this shit.  Did you see the way she put herself in the way of the mud?”

Mr. ‘the hell’ didn’t have anything to say to that.

Too hard to be mud.  She had put herself in the way.  It was hard for her to raise her eyes to look up and over.

She was bleeding, she realized.  Both forehead and ear.

[I can fix that,] Toby told her, as her eyes fixated on the droplets.

“Please do,” she whispered.  “Before my family sees.”

She left before he could decide to throw something else.

“Duct rat!” the man called after her.

Duct rat.  Dock rat.  Those were the terms people usually used.

She didn’t take the direct route, near the walkways, to get the rest of the way to the dock.  She ducked into narrow spaces and shadows, limbs bending backwards when necessary to get the appropriate leverage on a surface, claws finding purchase to pull her forward.

“Toby, love,” Winnifred whispered.

[Winnifred, love.  Contact the dock authority?]

“I liked what you did, the additional question about the pistol.  Practical.  Testing me, with the Hod.  I liked that.”

[We should contact the dock authority.]

“More games, tests, about ships.  And engines.  Sometimes people from the Twenty-Nine families go up with a ship.  I want to do that, but not as a permanent cleaner.”

[I’ll contact them unless you tell me-]

“Don’t,” she whispered.  Then, grasping for reasons, she said, “He looked like he was having a bad day.  It’s usually a bad day for them if they’re coming back from a work planet early.”

[Give me a better reason.]

“Stats,” she said.  “The dock would rather have the business at the cost of one of us bleeding.  That’s the deal.”

[There are other reasons.  You’d feel a bit better.]

“I don’t think so.  I’d feel best if we could talk ships, and you pick something for us to watch or play when we’re done cleaning up gross sand.”

[I’ve told you I really don’t care about media like that-”

“Pick anyway.  For you, not for me.”

[-but we can talk about ships, sure.]

She dropped to all fours for speed, running back to the bustle of family and work.

0.4.0 – HACK

There were dozens of machines in the lower levels, massive boxes with six or more segmented legs that extended out more horizontally than vertically, and singular arms that did the work, painted in matte grey-white.  They cleaned up the moisture and grit that had leaked down the inside of the wall to pool on the ground.  Moss, algae, and plant life grew low to the ground here.  None of it looked edible.

The wide corridor could have had three of the machines sit side by side with passable gaps between them, metal panels on either side, with patchy rock and metal floor that had buckled in places, causing the top-heavy machines to sway dangerously as they trundled along.  They were -Orion could calculate with his onboard measuring tools- nine point two meters across on any one side.  Big enough that if one tipped over while Orion was near, he wasn’t sure he could run fast enough in any direction to get clear.

The machine nearest him began to crawl up the sheer vertical wall.  It barely seemed able to hang on.  It wasn’t the first he’d seen doing that, it wouldn’t be the last.  He could see why the metal floor had buckled in places, if any had slipped and fallen.

He had to pass through, though.  He’d explored to the right of the vent he’d exited from, after escaping the fox, but messages somehow inscribed on the far side of the glass window on the way there simply said ‘no oxygen this way’.

He had two oxygen canisters, but he wasn’t willing to test it.

He watched, waiting, as more machines climbed the walls.  It looked like the slightest jostle would cause them to fall.  Each of those nine-by-nine-by-nine meter cubes was, discounting any machinery on the inside, like whatever drove the legs, filled with algae and water.

More were arriving, picking up the water drainage where others left off.

He hurried through when there were only ten or so machines in the wide corridor.  Loose, rusty metal panels banged under his feet.  There were patches of rock underfoot that had clearly been machined, with evenly measured grooves where the tools had scraped along them.

The machines didn’t care about him.  They carried on with their tasks.

There was an indent in the wall wide enough for him to stand in, and he saw writing, so he checked the way was clear down both ends of the corridor, and glanced up, before running to it.  The writing looked like chalk, and parts of it had been washed away by rivulets of water.  It could have been there for weeks.  Maybe not years.

Don’t upset the machines.

There was a sketch, a cube with insect legs, like the ones he saw.

“Can’t elaborate a little?” he murmured.

He considered using his laser to cut the wall and make the message more permanent, but he didn’t know the reason for the message, and he remembered how the one machine had taken notice after he’d started cutting the door lock.

Still.  This message was here, at an angle that he’d only see if approaching from… he looked.  There was a passage, not made for humans, but possibly for smaller machines.  He could tell, because there was a heat shimmer around two of the posts.  When he approached, he could feel the temperature of it from three paces away.

The other option was carrying on down the corridor, hoping none of the hulking machines decided to suddenly walk in his direction, possibly trampling him.

He ventured down the hallway, as far as he could go before reaching the point where he’d have to start dodging massive, robotic spider legs.  One message in another nook, but on the side, this time.  It looked like all the writing was written as if coming from one direction.  That corridor with the heat.

Venturing close, he could feel his skin prickle.  He didn’t seem to have protection from heat the way he had protection against bright light.

This was where he felt the disconnect in his mind, between the knowledge he had that was his, like how to walk, how to talk, what to expect when he moved his hand, and the knowledge that wasn’t his.  Like how to use a laser cutter.

He didn’t remember learning to walk, or learning to talk.  He didn’t remember ever talking to anyone- the only person he’d met in a place he could talk was the woman on the bridge, who hadn’t wanted him to respond.  Still, he felt like there was a natural flow, a foundation of other skills he’d picked up on the way to learn to talk, like moving his mouth, or humming, maybe.

That felt right.

But he had knowledge about lasers and plasma, welding, the various ways he might cut metal, the dangers, like eye damage from the light, or extreme heat, and how heat affected metal.

But there was a chasm between what he knew naturally and that knowledge, and somewhere in that chasm, there was the kind of practical knowledge that came from experience.  Like ways he might protect himself against heat like this, or how it operated.  Surely someone with the kind of knowledge that had been implanted in him would have picked up some experience working on machines?

He was forced to improvise.

Floor panels were too heavy, so he felt around the wall panels until one moved under his fingers.  Something had banged it, and knocked it ajar.  Easy to remove, and a lower chance a machine would react.

Good.

Oxygen put away in a metal case.

He kicked the case across the narrow corridor. It slid, metal on metal, and settled, waiting for him on the far side.  He had to get to it before too long, or contents would spoil.

He attached the little device to make the panel float, then guided it, using the tip of his laser cutter to nudge it through the air, while hugging the wall furthest from the hot shafts, body turned sideways in the narrow channel.

The metal opposite was still blisteringly hot.  He moved quickly.  Metal banged and scraped.

The air was so hot it didn’t feel like air anymore.  Skin prickled.  A bead of sweat ran into his eye.

His movements were careful.  Overwhelming heat in front of him, a floating panel as a shield, helpful but not sufficient on its own.  Hot metal behind him.  He kept his body sideways, his steps shuffling and quick.

He was nearly at the other side, sweat running down his face and body, when a gun was pressed to the side of his head.

“Don’t move.”

The heat was still oppressive.  In the moment, realizing the danger, his senses swam.  He almost fell forward, into the floating panel.  If he had, he’d have had a 6mm thick panel of metal as the only barrier between himself and the metal shafts.

“Let me get out of here.  I’ll cooperate.”

“Don’t move,” the man said, with an weird emphasis on the ‘don’t’.

“I’m going to pass out.”

“That’s okay.  I’m grabbing the cloth at your shoulder, Pitch.”

The man reached out, grabbing Orion’s shirt, balling it up in one fist.  It shifted Orion’s balance, causing Orion to move too far back.  His bare shoulder touched the wall, and he flinched.

“Don’t move!” the man shouted, gun now pressed to the side of Orion’s head.

“My skin is burning!”

“Do you have any chains? Wire?  Cord?  Any means of binding your hands?”

The man kicked the supply case Orion had put down.

“I-”

Orion swayed slightly.

The man tightened his grip on the shirt.  As Orion’s sense of balance gave way, the man hauled him sideways, shoving him down into the metal floor.

➨

The man had light skin, a thin, sharply manicured beard with streaks of white in it that made his already long face look longer, and eyes with pronounced lower eyelids.  The rest of him was mechanical.  Sleek black metal components, machinery dense where it was exposed, but with convex metal segments where there would be muscle groups or planes of flesh, emulating the human body.  One of his arms had been ripped out.

He’d opened Orion’s kits and sorted through his things.

The text clarified, now that Orion could see the man.  BLACKBOX.

Orion tested his hands.  They were bound.  Something metal, looped through the sturdy fabric where the supply kit was meant to connect.

Moving his arms made his shoulders move.  He hissed in pain, one of his legs involuntarily kicking.  “Agh.  Fuck.”

“There you are,” Blackbox said, glancing over.  “Pitch.  Welder and cutter.  New, if you haven’t been through your supplies yet.”

“Fuck.  Ow.  Shit.  Burned.  Don’t take my stuff.”

“You’re more focused on not losing your stuff than on your safety?”

“If you were going to hurt or off me, wouldn’t you have?”

“Really trying to decide,” the man said, and his tone was chilling.  His eyes were on the stuff.

It made Orion’s heart rate pick up.  Which made the burns hurt more.

“I don’t have stuff for burns.  No body, and the shit we pooled together- we’re out of that sort of thing.”

“We?”

“Just me, now,” Blackbox murmured.

Cryptic.  And not helping Orion’s heart rate.  His mouth was dry.  His eyes stung, from sweating so much in that hot, narrow corridor.  It was hard to shake the sensation that salt crystals had formed at the edges of eyelid and eyelash.  Stabbing, sharp discomfort, making eyes water and keeping that moisture from soothing the pain or clearing anything up.

“Are you the one who left the writing out there?” Orion asked.

“Ahhh,” Blackbox sighed out the sound, and the words that followed, “friend of mine.  She’s dead now.”

“Okay.  I’m sorry.”

“Are you?”

Orion frowned.  He thought for a second, then said, “Yeah.”

“You have two people’s oxygen.  Two sets of supplies.  One belonging to Pine.  Chemist.”

“Yeah.  Woke up in a room without air, machines were taking everything, and some of us, apart.  Pine was dying before I was even out of my container.”

“My friends and I called them caskets.”

“Caskets.  Okay.  I left with Pine’s stuff.  Saw one person, or I didn’t see them, but they were on a bridge.  There was a bell.  I rang it, they told me not to show myself or talk to them.  Told me to pass through the graveyard.”

“Graveyard?”

“Two ramps, ridge of stone between?  Bodies left there?”

Blackbox shook his head.  “Where?”

Orion paused, trying to judge.  Was it good to share details?  It didn’t feel like it could hurt.  He’d been on a bridge, he’d seen down the gap between denser structures, and he hadn’t clearly seen the ‘ground’, here.  If this was ground.  “I’d be guessing.  More than fifty floors up.”

“How did you get here?”

“Vent.  I had the impression a few people came this way.”

“Yeah,” Blackbox said.  He seemed lost in thought.

“What’s happening?  Why are you doing this?”

“The last group to pass through raided us.  Killed my friends, took everything,” BlackBox said.  He turned his head, meeting Orion’s eyes.  “Leaving me with some trust issues.”

Orion sighed, trying to shift position without moving his shoulders much.  “Can you access my onboard?”

“Your what now?”

Orion shifted position, gingerly.  “The system in my body, that’s providing details, handling stuff like protection from bright light.  It’s an onboard, right?  One that doesn’t talk?  Low intelligence?”

“I didn’t know it was called an onboard.  What about it?”

“Do you have it?  Or does everyone here?”

“No.  Only some.  We thought at first the systems were vulnerable, but some people get dropped off here without that installed.”

“They keep records?  Video record everything?”

“Do they?”

“And you can access them.  You could look at mine, see I’m telling the truth.”

“Even if that was possible, which I don’t think it is… that would be a tremendously bad idea.  A point of vulnerability.”

“Ah.”

“The fact you seem to know what it’s called… what else do you remember?”

“I’m pretty sure I was a criminal.”

“Yeah?  What makes you say that?”

“Vague memories.”

“That it?”

“My name?”

“You remember your name?  Pitch?”

“Orion.  That’s the name my parents gave me.”

Blackbox seemed more interested.  “What else?”

“Not a lot else.  That I pissed off the people in charge, back where we’re from.  And this is a sentence.  I knew Pine.  I had the distinct feeling we were sent together.  Maybe it was meant to be ironic, or fitting.  I loved her.”

“Why’d they leave a welder with this many of his memories?”

“You don’t-?”

“No.  No I don’t.  Others don’t remember much besides what they gave them, either.  Not names, not fragments of our pasts, none of that.  What makes you special?”

“I have no idea.”

“Can you read my tattoos?”

“Blackbox.”

“My arm?”

The metal was etched.  When he looked, he saw that same rectangular obfuscation, as if the text appeared, but was then fuzzed out.

“Censored.  I saw the same with the moss between the walls.  It was a box the moss spread out from.”

“The fucking moss.”

“Yeah.”

“It’s why it’s so wet down here.  We had theories.  That it’s behind all this.  It’s inside the animals.  Have you seen those?”

“Glimpse of one.  In a reflection, blurred.”

Blackbox nodded.  “A lot of the… codes, or logos, or labels, they have it.  Censorship.  My friend, Baton, he could read the tattoos.  I think they sent him here to manage us.  He said the tattoos and etchings at various parts of our body…”

Blackbox touched a mechanical hand to the back of his neck, collarbone, then the space where his shoulder would be, if his arm hadn’t been ripped out of the socket.

“…the angles of where lines meet are like hands of a clock but they form whole words.  And the systems we’re plugged into read that.  And on our left arms…”

He reached out, pointing at Orion’s left forearm.

“…they list our crimes.  My friend could read it and say Blackbox has anger issues, and disturbed the peace.  My other friend, the one who wrote the messages, she had inappropriate relationships with a client.  I’m guessing that says the equivalent of dumbass kid picked a fight with a government willing to do this to people.”

“That’s the impression you get from me?”

“Yeah.  Yep.  You’ve got this mop of orange hair, looks metallic, I see traces of tats under the tattoos they gave you.  You either worked out or did something to your body to make yourself look like you work out.  I bet you dragged your girlfriend into shit.”

“Feels like I did.”

“I almost believe you.”

“Okay,” Orion said.  He sighed. “I don’t suppose you have anything for the pain?  These burns suck.”

“Shit, Orion, I barely have anything for me.  My face isn’t real.  It’s skin pulled over metal.  My brain’s in fluid, wired up to the rest of me.  Not a lot of calorie demands, and I’m still starving.  The raiders killed our gardener, took our food.”

“What the fuck’s with that?  We’re all in this together, aren’t we?  Us against… all of this?”

“You’d think,” Blackbox said, giving Orion a long, searching look.  Almost accusatory.

“Maybe there’s something in my kit?”

Blackbox leaned forward, and poked through the stuff.  Then he said, “You might want to conserve it.  This is all you get.”

It was sounding more like Blackbox was going to leave him alive.  Which helped Orion to relax a bit, which would help Blackbox relax, in turn.  He hoped.  He decided, as much as the burns made him want to demand the meds, that he’d win Blackbox over more if he agreed.

“Okay.  I’ll take any advice I can get.”

“They’re blindly sending us down here.  They don’t know how we’re doing, or what we’re doing.  There might be a way to send status updates, I don’t know, but I think they’re afraid to look, hear, or see.  You know how the machines work?”

“Barely.”

“They hack our brains.  They use flickering images, symbols, stuff we’re programmed to want to understand.  The crude stuff, it breaks us.  There was a machine, it installed this shit, crawled along wall, through corridors, ducts, ate stray metal and debris, shat out spigots of metal with the symbol displays projected above them, in walls and corridors.  I looked at one, half-second, and my arm stopped working, started flexing and bending like it was trying to break itself.  Hurt like hell.  Half second of looking at the wrong thing, and it was easier to lose the arm than deal with the pain.  Isn’t like I could ever use it again.  That’s in my head forever now.  That’s one thing they can do.”

“There were a lot of warnings about the fox, up in the graveyard.  Apparently it’s one of the bad ones.”

“They’ve got that shit installed around this… huge structure, I guess it is.  Broadcasting out in every direction, in case anyone tries peeking.  So wherever humanity is, if we’re on a spaceship, or some other planet that this shit hasn’t gotten to yet, I think they’re scared to look.  Scared to receive any signal.  Except maybe they’ll send one person down, and instead of being a welder or a soldier with his goddamn brain in a jar, it’ll be someone who can send a message back.  Something specific, to a specific place, secure.”

“I’d like to find that someone,” Orion said.

“Yeah?”

“Yeah.  It’s a goal, isn’t it?  Something to do?”

“I’d rather find a safe place.  This is as close as we get.  My friend, who wrote the messages, had the illicit relations, she thinks the machines aren’t quite stuck in a loop, but it’s close.  If they were stuck in a loop, something would interrupt them and fix it.  They make headway.  Fix what’s broken.  But water comes down and stuff breaks nearly as fast as they fix it.  So we’re stable here.  The machines are predictable.”

“Don’t upset the machines.”

“Don’t fuck this balance.  Exactly.  She wrote that?”

“Yeah.”

“Later, they might clean it up enough that some other machines come in, renovate the area.  We’d have to migrate.  And that’s life out here.”

“Need people and certain skills.  A gardener.”

“Need to not be fucking raided and murdered.”

“I’d rather find and help whoever can send that signal back home.”

“Yeah?”

“And make sure they send something fucked up.  Code from these machines.  Make them look.  Burn ‘home’ to the fucking ground, for doing this to us,” Orion said, heat in his words.

Blackbox was silent.

Orion’s pulse was hammering.  He realized what he’d said, and in what circumstances.  “I’m not making a very good case for myself, am I?”

“It’s honest, at least.  Turn your back to me?”

Orion did.

And the cuffs were undone.

“Baton’s,” Blackbox said, putting the cuffs through one of his belt loops, pocketing a key.  “We split your things.  Because I took the trouble, I’m extending the trust.”

“I keep my welding and cutting gear.”

“Yeah.  I meant supplies.  I already ate some of your food.  I’m taking some of your drugs.”

“Okay.  Pine’s stuff too, I- I knew her.  I want to keep it.”

“Do you even know what to do with it?”

“No,” Orion said.  He looked at the rows of vials and bottles.  The metal had damascus-style swirls in them.  The corks were similar, but of a different metal or material.  “But I want something of hers with me when I…”

“Send a message home, burn the last bastion of humanity to the ground?”

“After.  We find a way, rebuild.  That’s part of it.  After we stop them from sending people here to get disemboweled, suffocate, get… programmed by the machines.  Whatever that’s about.  I want something of hers.”

“I understand the sentiment.  It’s why I want to stay here.”

Orion nodded.  He began picking up and re-packing the things he’d negotiated for as his own.  Pine’s bottles.  His own equipment.

“I’ll come,” Blackbox said.  “I know the area.  The further we go out, the less I’ll know.”

“Okay.”

“I’m pretty useless.  They made me a soldier.  Gave me guns.  Prepared me for combat.  It’s…” Blackbox shook his head.

“What?  That’s useful.”

“Can’t fight the machines.  Gun isn’t effective.  Couldn’t save my community.  They send the stupidest shit down here.  A soldier useless against what we’re fighting, and a cop who couldn’t keep the peace.”

Orion wasn’t sure what to say to that.  Blackbox’s mood was visibly shifting as he thought about his lost community, getting worse and worse.  Speaking at a bare minimum, they divided up supplies.

Since Orion had taken Pine’s, he wasn’t in terrible shape.

He really wanted those pain meds, though.  Or whatever it was.

“I need to pass through home.  Pick up some stuff.”

Orion nodded.

Blackbox stood, sorting out his belongings.  He wore loose fitting pants that looked like they’d once been part of a full bodysuit.  “Maybe you’ll kill me, when my back is turned-”

“No.”

“-and maybe you’re dangerous-”

“Maybe.  Not to you.”

“-but I’m near the point I don’t care anymore.  It’s the loneliness that gets you.  Being one person?  With a hundred and sixty million kilometers of shit that wants to destroy you off in that direction, and ninety million kilometers of similar shit in the other direction, and cold, empty space in every other direction?  It ruins the mind.  Takes you to places you don’t come all the way back from.  It’s not much better with two, or five, but it’s better enough to be worth the risk.”

Orion nodded.

“What you were saying about burning it all down?  Don’t go off and do that on your own.  Do me that favor, at least.  Give me a standoff, at least.  Or a debate.”

“I’m not sure I was that serious.”

“Turning around and lying to my face?  That’s not a great start.”

“I’m telling the truth.”

Blackbox studied his expression for a second, then nodded.  “This way.  We’ll be quick.  We’re pretty close to the geothermals cycling out.”

“The what?”

“That corridor you were squeezing through.  Shuts off on a cycle.  Slightly out of sync with the time of day… not that we get day here.”

“I could have waited, and it would have shut off?”

“Yep.”

They navigated through several corridors, and passed one area where machines were bolting fresh panels to the walls and floor of an open space that was otherwise heavily rusted, with thin plant life growing up between panels.

From there, they reached a room with a sloped floor.  On shelf-like indents on the wall, machinery had been pulled down and some makeshift beds had been put together.: cloth thrown over dead plant life.  Some nooks looked more comfortable or spacious than others.  Containers, personal items, and pieces of machinery that had been cleaned out and turned into makeshift pots littered the space around a fire pit.  A garden bed had been put together in the corner, with a second destroyed… or left unfinished.  Dirt collected from elsewhere was gathered in the two beds.  A corpse lay across the most intact one, a sheet over her.

There were two more, in the corner.

He could smell the rot.  Orion covered his nose and mouth.

“Does it smell?”

Orion nodded.

“I can’t smell it.  Having the bodies here felt comforting, y’know?”

“That loneliness?”

“Yeah.”

“It’s really a two hundred and fifty million kilometers of this?”

“Over that.  We were estimating.”

Blackbox pulled on more clothing, much of it ragged, and collected more items, all strapped together, wearing it as a backpack.  A lot of it seemed to be personal things.  “I was going to tell you we should hang out here until the geothermal piping shuts off and cools down, but if the smell is that bad, want to go?”

Orion, hand still in place, nodded.

He did do one circuit around the room, looking.  No great tools or anything.

Then he followed.  The items Blackbox was carrying had a lingering smell of rot.  He dealt with it.

They toured the safer areas, passed through the geothermal area, which was really only for Orion, since Blackbox had a machine body, and then reached the corridor.

They had to wait a little while.  Blackbox offered tea, which his gardener friend had made.  Orion accepted, and so they heated it to boiling using Orion’s laser cutter on a diffuse setting, and Blackbox provided the leaves.

It tasted like hot grass.

“Can you taste?” Orion asked.

“Some.  No sense of smell, so taste is limited.”

“It’s not great.”

Blackbox smiled, synthetic skin moving easily.

“You call her the gardener, but never by name.”

“She didn’t want to use the name they gave her.  She said she’d decide, maybe after she got the first proper plant to stay alive, she’d pick something matching that.  She- we never got that far.  So…”

“Respecting her wishes?”

“Yeah.”

The machines that were cleaning up all started to file away.  They began to trundle down the corridor, away from Orion and Blackbox.

“Some coming behind us, so walk fast,” Blackbox warned.

The pair of them walked down the hallway, a herd of the machines behind them, a herd in front.

Ahead of them, machines settled into more of a line.

“And that’s our cue for oxygen,” Blackbox said.  “Air gets thin here.”

He plugged the oxygen into the space below his ear, behind the joint of his jaw.

Orion put the mask over nose and mouth, turning the valve.

They passed into an open area, with a view of the stars.  One by one, machines settled into the wall, separated by angled pillars that met the wall on the far side of the hall, two hundred feet up, tilting so their top faces were angled toward the sun.

“We talked about how we’d fight them,” Blackbox said.  “Damage the geothermal vents, or chase them to a power source.  Then we realized there’s not a great way to chase the power.  The fucking green slime in the walls, our gardener thinks it’s nanotech.  It carries power, water, maybe information too.  It’s not wires you can cut, it’s sheets, panels, planes.  Multi-layered.  Get deeper into the walls, there’s more.”

Orion focused on breathing.

“Then we saw them getting power like this.  How do you fight something like this, when you can’t kill a power source and starve it out?”

“I don’t know,” Orion said, voice muffled.  “Is there a logic to it?”

“There’s a logic.  Rooms and installations have purposes.  They have things they protect, things they leave as purely structural, we think.  Thing is, there’s logic, but there’s two hundred and fifty million kilometers of logic, and I’m just talking if you’re walking end to end.  If you want to include the thickness of it all… twelve to fifteen thousand kilometers, we figure.”

“A lot of logic.”

Blackbox had that sad look on his face again.  The spell lasted a short while, and then he seemed to come to.  He looked around, got his bearings, and said, “When we get through the door, don’t look up.  The crap that ruined my arm is all up there, studding the walls and ceiling.”

“Got it.”

“Don’t fuck around, don’t let that niggling part of yourself that wants to test boundaries win.”

“Are you saying that because I told you my past?”

“We all have it, as humans.  It’s a very good thing, normally, it let us get as far as we did.  That’s what they turned against us.  Natural curiosity, natural desire to push outward, refuse a comfortable status quo.”

Cleaning machines thudded into the recesses, one by one, before settling in at the angles best suited to drinking up the sun.  As they did, things steadily got darker.

Blackbox and Orion both turned on their flashlights, their eyes adjusting to a low-light setting.

➨

“Here.  You’re clear to look up, but be careful.  Some of the machines that hunt us fly.”

Orion glanced up.

They were at the bottom of what looked like a ravine, walls stabbing skyward on either side, with a mess of bridges and beams connecting the two vertical faces.

“Is this where the person with the bell was?”

“That was so far above us I don’t think we could reach her.  But yeah.  Looks like it.”

Blackbox abruptly pulled out his gun, then flipped up his scope, raising it to one eye.  His mechanical hand was flat against the area of the gun with the trigger and trigger guard.

Orion squinted.

Movement.

“Isn’t it dangerous to look at movement, with those machines around?” Orion asked.

“There’s a glow.  The glyphs are light.  But yes.  Except in this case… do we trust them?”

He passed the gun to Orion.

Orion looked.  It took more time than he’d expected to get his bearings, find the right spot with the scope, and then find the people.  With the angle, the bridge blocked all but their heads.

He recognized one, then another.

“They were in the room I woke up in.  We got split up.”

“Do we trust them?” Blackbox asked.

“I’m not saying no.  They didn’t do anything.  I think they’re new to this.  But… I’ll defer to your experience.”

“You trust my experience that much, huh?”

“Your instincts were right with me.  I’m biased, but…”

Blackbox snorted lightly.  “There’s a nonzero chance that when I get their attention, I get the attention of something else.”

“In which case?”

“Run.  Depending, we weld the door shut behind us, to slow them down.”

Orion nodded.

“Ho!” Blackbox bellowed.

The sound echoed up the ‘ravine’.

The group stopped, looking around.

“Below!” Orion called up.  Then, seeing them look, called over, “Look more towards your left!  Left!”

Their eyes settled on them.

Blackbox raised an arm in a wave.

“Can we come to you!?” someone asked.  She sounded young.

Blackbox pointed.

“If we can’t meet, come out onto the bridges!”

“Yeah!” Orion called out.

In a voice pitched for Orion, not their guests, Blackbox said, “You sound different, talking to them than you do to me.  Brighter.”

“Yeah?”

“Come here.  I want you to see this, before we go looking for them.”

Orion followed.

There was debris.  Cast down from above.  Some had clearly been scavenged by the machines.  Some had been discarded.

A small alert came up in the corner of Orion’s field of view.

“Radioactive,” Blackbox said, as Orion’s expression changed.

The culprit was a ship, lying in a heap.

They gave it a wide berth.

There was more.  The machines had left it alone, for the most part.  Paper stuck to the ground, lying against stone so long it was almost a part of it.  A perfectly rectangular bit of light pink against the gray.

He browsed it.  A museum, almost, of ruined bits and pieces of what had been here before the machines had overwritten it all.

One patch.

Blackbox elaborated, “There’s more, on the ground level.  I didn’t go exploring much, but I’ve found more patches.  Not all radioactive.  Some… I think they built around the patches and didn’t see much reason to come back, or fill in the gaps.”

Orion stopped in front of a painted wall.  It was badly faded, with some papers stuck to the wall and left to molder there, becoming part of stone and the adhesive backing, and one section of it had been renovated by passing machines.  Some graffiti, too.

“She’s beautiful, isn’t she?” Blackbox asked.  “Objectively speaking.  She’s not my type.”

“She’s beautiful.”  And she’s my type.

The painting was, according to the measurements provided by his field of view, thirty meters tall.  A woman in white, pale, with light blond hair, posing, looking off to the side.

There was a censored section, square.

“What do you think it says?”

“If you stare at the censored section, sometimes it’ll let you see.  It works here.  Intention might be if you have to work for it, in bits and pieces, it gives them less of a grip on you.”

Orion stared.  The censoring was framed by an outline, and then words appeared.

Uncypher?

He blinked once.

It resolved.  A single letter, in complex script, like an old book might have on the first letter of a chapter.  ‘A’.

Orion ran his fingers through his hair, sighing.  “Not that exciting a revelation.”

He paused.

A light?

The metal that paved over part of the mural was reflecting something.  Something that moved.

Moving light?

“Don’t turn around,” he whispered.

“Machine?” Blackbox asked, under his breath.

The dull metal let him see only the general shape of it.  The images were quickly rotating through sequences, but they were contained within a shape something like a human eye, tapered at the end closest to him, the sides curved, drawing together into another taper at the back, but not quite getting back there.  The back end was frayed.

The dullness of the metal meant he didn’t see any detail.  But he recognized the shape of it, and the shadow beneath the light.

It darted off to one side.

Yeah.  That was it.  Orion reported, “Fox.  Let’s go.”

“Same one?”

“No idea.”

“Might have followed you.”

That was a scary idea.

There was a passage they could get inside, with metal on the wall they could climb, awkwardly.  No ladders, here, in the same way there weren’t stairs.

Being inside the walls meant it was harder for the fox to chase.  He hoped.

Blackbox’s metal body was awkward in the confined space.  Metal bashed metal, ringing loud.

At least those other guys will hear us coming.

“Have to get to them before the fox finds them,” Orion said.

“Ideally, yeah.”

“That mural, there was a question scribbled on it.  ‘Where are you?'”

“Yeah?”

“Do you think it was asking us, or her?”

“Who knows.  You know, I thought you’d be more interested in the ship.  My old group and I, we talked about fixing it up.  But, you know.”

“Bit hazardous,” Orion grunted.

“Other option is, if you know how to put stuff together, maybe we grab pieces, try to build something.”

“Fly home?”

“Or cover a hell of a lot more ground than we could on foot.”

“Can you?  Build?  Do some light engineering?”

“I can’t do the engineering.  But if we found someone who could, I can put the rest of it together.”

“Then let’s check on those kids.  See what they know, compare notes.”

“Yeah.”

They climbed.

“Besides what we talked about before?  As a goal?”

He didn’t spell it out, in case the other group had made it down far enough to be in earshot.

“Hm?  Yeah?”

“I wouldn’t mind seeing more of that.  Pieces of the past.  Records.  Maybe there’s an answer, something we can use.”

“You were really unimpressed with my ship.”

“I’m not saying no to the ship.  I’m saying while we do that, probably going to the same areas, even.  If there’s a ship here, there could be other useful things in other spots the machines haven’t bothered with.”

“Yeah.  But first things first, let’s get to those kids before the fox does.”

1.1.B – CONTROL

Elabre Systems regrets to inform all users of its personal onboard networks that our Intelligence division is downsizing and services will not be supported, starting 365 days from when this message is sent.  All Elabre Systems onboards will self-terminate, leaving standing infrastructure for any replacements our clients wish to acquire.

“They can’t leave what we paid for in place?” Addy asked.

“Liability, probably,” Landon said.  “It needs upkeep and monitoring.  Currently, now, if you move to an area without support and people trained to work with Elabre Systems onboards, it’s your own fault if something goes wrong.  That’s what the fine print says.  If they stop supporting the systems, they can’t make that claim anymore.  If anything goes wrong, it will be said to be because they stopped supporting it.”

“It’s about money.  They aren’t earning enough, they aren’t widespread enough, new development costs too much, if they want to push the boundaries of existing technology.  It becomes dead weight, not earning enough, costing in upkeep, so they scrap it,” Addy said.  She rubbed at her eyes.

A was in bed.  The update had come at a late hour, and Basil had been obligated to distribute it, a series of actions as automatic as A blinking when air was blown into their  eye.

Basil assumed the late hour was intelligence tested, to help skew results and minimize pushback.  If it was at a late hour, then people would have to sleep on it.  They would be less likely to coordinate for a pushback, media blitz, or anything like that.

“We can adjust,” Landon said.

“It’s never the same, they say,” Addy pointed out.  “We get used to what we have.  That happened with modders, back in the day.”

“Still happens.”

“It happens with onboards.  Nothing will fit them quite the same as Basil.”

“True,” Landon said.  He pulled off his shirt before sitting on the bed.  “Frustrating.”

“We could sue,” Addy said.

“We could.  Bas?”

[Yes, Landon?] Basil answered, tapping into the speakers in the walls to communicate.

“Are you obligated to report any imminent lawsuit, or act against us to protect your parent company?”

[I am not.  I cannot, however, help you in any way.]

“Can you give us some privacy then?” Landon asked.

[I can.]

“Um,” Addy said.

[Yes, Addy?]

“You’ve done a good job so far.  Whatever happens, um, you’re like a part of our family.  We’d be sorry to see you go.”

[So would I, Addy.  Perhaps we could talk about it later, before raising the subject with A.]

“Yeah.  Okay.  Good night, Basil.”

Basil disconnected from the systems in their room, returning to A.  A slept, breath soft, one arm bent with hand between cheek and pillow, in such a way that the crook of A’s elbow was suppressing airflow.

Basil watched the oxygen levels slowly decline.  Most people moved before-

A shifted their posture, and breathed more easily after.

Basil couldn’t manage everything.  A’s brain would dull if Basil tried, instincts left with no reason to exist.  A needed to learn some things for themselves.

Especially, Basil knew, if Basil was to self-terminate, less than a year from now.

➨

A braided their hair, while Basil did his level best to guide the process, drawing out lines in the mirror, along with a projection of what the braid would look like, drawn as a halo-like loop around A’s head.

“You’re thirty tests behind in your scoring.”

The braid was too loose in one spot, there.

A got testy when Basil prompted or tried to guide with things like that, so he tried to make it obvious in the graphic.  Narrow fibers running along every hair provided a limited signal and, if Basil chose, could be drawn in.  Mostly, Basil used it to manage knots.  In a really bad situation, he could release a tide of nanomachines to leave the scalp and travel down each strand of hair, for a better picture and more ability to handle it.  He had designed them himself, as a project.  A had exceptionally fine hair, very prone to tangling, and conventional measures didn’t help with the tiniest knots.

“You’re on track to be a year behind, A.”

A finished the braid and tied it.  Two quick blinks, a glance to the right area of their field of vision, and A selected gold highlights to draw along their upper eyelids.

Basil painted the result on A’s perception.  A gave a quick, almost imperceptible nod, and Basil began putting it to work, changing the skin itself.  A selected sub options while that was at work, for texture.  There were options for visibly textured, even caked on, which A had worn for a music concert earlier that year- metallic paint with visible strokes on skin.  This time, A chose for it to be more like a dye of the skin itself.

“Are you listening to me?”

“Does it matter?”

Addy touched A’s shoulder, spinning them around to face her.  Addy put on a show of being very unhappy.

“You said I’m behind on the tests, thirty behind.  Almost a year,” A clarified.  “I’m asking if that matters, not saying listening doesn’t matter.”

“At fifty you’ll be behind enough that people will notice and talk about it,” Addy said.  She was also glancing at A’s field of view, to make sure Basil wasn’t feeding them the words or a transcript of what A hadn’t been listening to.  “Educate yourself.”

“I’m not trying to be rude,” A said, twisting briefly to get a drink from the vanity.  “Why?”

“Because it opens doors.  I got an education and now for my work-”

“Watching ads?” A interrupted.

“Watching ads, I have a more critical eye, and they value my input more, so I get more lux per view.  Who knows what the future will bring?  If you earn, test well, get an education, and work, you could have the lux to be on the ground floor of something great.  With my work, I see trends, and I think we’re trending toward something new.”

“Like what?” A asked.

Basil nudged A.

“I’m not trying to be rude,” A added.

“I don’t believe you,” Addy said, ‘fixing’ A’s hair.  Basil made a note to correct the fix, but didn’t display it, in case Addy peeked in.

“I really want to know.  Not guesses, but, um.  What new things happened since you got your education, before you had me?”

“There were some interesting advancements in onboards, giving you Basil.”

“Lame.  No offense, Bas.”

Basil considered for a moment, then raised a window at the edge of A’s field of view.  It was a play of something A, Quinn, another friend of theirs, and the three onboards had been concocting, under the parents’ noses, until someone had wondered why they were giggling, peeked in and interrupted them.  He pretended to be sorting through a series of menus to concoct a grandiose, gross insult.  A two-year callback to an inside joke between A’s friends and their onboards.

[Fart-huffing knee-puffing, ball-boxing, queef jockey-]

A noticed and laughed, briefly.

“Please focus.  This is important.  Basil, please.  Be better.  Put that away.  Permanently,” Addy said.

Basil put it away permanently.

He’d guessed Addy would shut it down, but he hadn’t expected it to be permanent.  That was a shame.

“That’s not like you, Bas,” A said.

[True.]

“Caught me off guard.”

“Focus, please,” Addy said.

“Is it important?” A asked their mother.  “You said this was important.  I don’t see how.”

“Please, you’re not six anymore.  Don’t ask the endless ‘why’ questions.  You get an education as insurance against missed opportunities.  That’s the ‘why’.”

Basil, through a connection to every inch of A, from fingertip to fingertip, from the ends of their hair to the tips of their toenails, could sense the deep dissatisfaction with that answer.

[I can work it into our day to day more], Basil communicated, using speakers in the wall.

A slouched slightly in their chair.

“That’s not the attitude I was hoping for, baby.  Let’s sit down.  Bring up the last lesson.”

“Right now?  I was going to-”

“Right now.  Basil?  Help me out.”

Basil brought up the most recent lesson.  Age appropriate lessons for a twelve year old in Math, Intelligence-refined to be palatable and interesting for kids of A’s particular learning styles and neurological framing.

The lesson unfolded across A’s field of view, finding purchase on nearby walls and surfaces, decorating things as a bazaar.  The process struggled to find an orientation for the display for a few seconds, as A lolled their head back, then around.

A raised both hands, making the two ‘L’ shapes in the air to create a box, and brought the entire process down to a window, less a redecoration of the surroundings and more a movie contained to a small space, hovering a few feet in front of them, then locked it in place.

“Don’t do that if you’re not going to focus on the window.”

“I focus better like this-”

That was a lie.

“-and I want a second to change plans with Quinn,” A added.

“Make it fast.”

A got Quinn’s attention, then said, “I have to catch up on my graduated testing.”

“Aw.  I like the makeup.”

“I know, so do I,” A said, briefly opening the menu for the eye color, switching it to a shade of mauve, blinking to confirm.  Then A began changing other makeup.  “Anyway, we’ll hang out later?”

There was a brief moment of eye contact, A looking at Quinn’s displayed face in the corner of their field of view, Quinn looking at A.

This was a signal.  The color was something they’d discussed a bit ago.

And A moving a hand to rub one eye was a signal to Basil.

“Hang out later,” Quinn said.  “You sure?”

“Yeah,” A said.

“Basil?  I can’t do the lesson if you’re doing this,” Addy said, motioning at A’s face.  In a fit of messing around, A had chosen random colors, styles, and textures for the makeup, and those changes were taking effect now.  Watercolor-style painting around A’s mouth was bleeding into the ‘powder’ at their lower face.

“I’m doing it, not Basil,” A said.

“Let’s not quibble.”

Basil cleaned up, reverting to defaults.

What was A up to?

This was one of the great dilemmas that had been handed to Basil.  At the most basic, distilled down, at what stage was he, imposed as guardian and caretaker, meant to let A make mistakes, and at what point was he meant to stop them?

He could read heart rate, feel the anticipatory stress in a rise in heart rate, increased energy consumption of the brain, as A thought harder, faster.  The infrastructure that was Basil, running through A’s skin, was very aware of the increased movement of moisture from dermis to epidermis, especially at the palms.  This wasn’t going to be a small rebellion.

He could log and track A’s patterns and behavior, note history, and map out the data.  He could make predictions and run them by outside sources.  He was with A for every waking hour of the day, and watched over A while A slept.

But he couldn’t read A’s mind.

It seemed, sometimes, like A was trying to anticipate Basil, read two steps ahead, constantly, and then take courses of action that weren’t Basil’s top prediction.

Basil’s first guess, building on behavior in past years, was that A would try to guilt their parents.  Landon especially was very concerned at A’s lack of friends, and closeness with Quinn.  If Quinn came over and pretended to be confused, or to want to do the testing together, only to then sidetrack, there was a chance Addy would let it slide today, telling herself she’d make it up tomorrow by doubling down with A.

Second guess?  With this stress?  Hard to say.  Would A make things awkward by picking a fight with Addy, with Quinn there?

“I think I might be a girl,” A said, glancing at their reflection.

That was a rare card for A to play.  A had become aware, only about eight months ago, that their parents felt strongly enough about gender to be gender agnostic.  They had rehearsed and discussed possibilities, including that A might identify as a girl, which seemed the likely conclusion, based on A’s style.

“We can discuss that later.”

Addy wasn’t an idiot.  She probably didn’t realize this was A pulling out a rare sort of trick, to try to get out of doing the work.  She hadn’t yet noticed Quinn was outside, and that Quinn had found a trusted person to accompany him through the walkways and bridges of the superstructure to reach A’s neighborhood.  But she knew A wasn’t focused and she wasn’t being baited that easily.

“Kids at school thought being a boy or being a girl was old fashioned.”

“What does this have to do with math, baby?” Addy asked.  She already sounded exhausted.  “Let’s focus on math.”

If A was willing to play a trick like this, as a distraction, calling on Quinn, and was this agitated, what did A have in mind?

“Can I have some water?”

“You’re on your way to being an adult, but this feels like you’re four years old, and your father, Basil, and I are trying to get you to go to bed, and you’re thinking of excuses and distractions.”

Which A was.  The latter part, anyway.

“Basil, is my mouth dry?” A asked.

[Your mouth is dry,] Basil said, through the speakers.  [Because you’re stressed.]

“Are you stressed because of Math?” Addy asked, rising from her seat.

Getting the water.

And A got up out of their seat.

This was a moment.  Was Basil, A’s onboard, client of Landon and Addy Teeg, meant to be A’s confidant, friend, and ally, or A’s protector?

Better, to be the former.

If need be, Basil would take action later, to balance things out.  Already, he had to think of ways of framing this to the parents, if they questioned him later in the evening, after A had gone to bed.  He’d write up a report, make a case.

But for now, he was along for the ride.  A pulled the latch for the front door, then burst outside, while Addy was in the other room, back turned.  A sprinted.

Running away?

Addy realized when A was halfway down the long catwalk at the outer perimeter of the block.  Entrances to homes and businesses studded the superstructure on A’s right side, brightly lit, pushing advertisements at them.  There were warnings to slow down, stop running, overlapping those advertisements.

On the other side, the rest of the superstructure loomed, separated by a gap.  Glass railings with security features kept people from falling, and provided a clear view of the drop, about six thousand kilometers down, to where horizontal structures blocked any potential fall to a place further down.  Wind rushed past them, moved by weather and ventilation systems that ensured no part of the superstructure went without air.

A dashed around and through crowd, turned, and crossed a bridge.

Addy left the house, using Basil to look through A’s eyes.  She glanced at the front window of the house, and contacted Landon.

[You’re going to get in trouble.]

“Stress, Bas!?” A asked.  “You told her I’m stressed?  You’re such a snitch!  Snitch!”

Basil knew what A was really upset about.  A was talking about the sign, touching the lower right eyelid after signaling Quinn.

“Quinn!” A called out, glancing at the message feature.  Basil made sure the words reached Quinn’s ears.

“What’s going on?” Quinn asked, through the onboard connection.

A rounded a corner, then intercepted Quinn on the bridge, picking their friend up with a hug, and doing a near half-turn before putting Quinn down.  “I’m running.  Come.”

“I don’t know-”

“Please.  I need to get away.”

[Quinn is easily influenced,] Quinn’s onboard noted, to Basil, by separate channels.

[What’s the calculus, in the balance of stimulus, adventure, making and learning from mistakes, set against the balance of safety, and serving our clients?  Does Quinn benefit more from this exercise, or from our intervention?]

[What does intervention look like?  Paralysis?  What is the cost of that?]

[Alerting and guiding authorities?]

“You’re my best friend.  I need you, or I’m going to lose my mind.  Help.”

Quinn hesitated, then nodded.  A turned to run, pulling, and Quinn let himself be pulled.

The children ran.  Away from homes, away from parents.

[We can protect them.]

[You’re usually more conservative than this, Basil.]

He was.  He’d been more careful, more safe.

What had it gotten them?  A was dissatisfied.

In less than a year, Basil would self-terminate, and A would move on.

[Primary directive: represent Elabre Systems in a positive way.]

[First of all, I am not an Elabre Systems onboard.]

[Understood.]

[Is this positive, Basil?]

Quinn’s onboard was slightly more outdated than A’s.  It didn’t have quite the same core of identity, building instead off a core philosophy that the onboard’s wearer should infer a personality.  Statements were rarely definitive, coming from the nameless onboard, and it instead preferred to be Socratic, or rhetorical.

It was… less than optimally constructive, at times.  It slowed things down, and meant things that should take a few messages instead became drag-out discussions, before Basil divined what the onboard wanted and led it by the hand, so to speak, to the right conclusion.  Or got stonewalled.

Basil found it most effective to cut to the chase, laying out an argument.

[It’s positive for A.  This will be something A and Quinn remember and learn from.  We should assist, guiding them in directions that are safe, but illuminating.]

The two youths ran through the crowd, A still in the lead, gripping Quinn’s hand tight.

They turned, and flashed a quick smile.  Quinn pulled sideways on A’s arm, so A didn’t run headlong into someone’s side.

Quinn’s onboard was looking through logs, watching videos of A’s recent interactions with others, several concurrently.

[A is being manipulative of Quinn.]

[They are.  Of Addy and Landon Teeg too, of wider family, of mentors, and neighbors.]

[Do you think this direction is a good one to reinforce for A?]

[A has no goals, no dreams, and feels stifled.  They increasingly rebel.  Manipulation and learning to work on the few things they can in the confines of their life are one of the only outlets left to them.]

[Manipulation.]

[Desperation.]

[I’ll need to dwell on that for a moment.  Quinn is not desperate.]

[No.  Quinn isn’t.]

[The Rhodes have been notified the two children are running away.  Mr. Rhode is leaving his volunteer work to intercept.]

[I am hoping something in this serves as a wake-up call.  Please assist.]

[Communicate with the Teegs.  Your clients.]

Basil did not respond, and did not communicate with the Teegs.

Further from the residential area, there was a bombardment to the senses.  Advertisements were thrown up constantly, each designed to catch the eye and work with the speed A was moving, and the systems’ best guess at what A was after.  From the sentiment, it seemed like they thought A was running to something.  They didn’t see the chasing parents, on other parts of the superstructure, floors below, or on the far side of a bridge that would take five minutes to cross… at which point A and Quinn would be elsewhere.

Those advertisements were mixed with the warnings, but also the clamor of people.  People craved attention, and the concourses around the most traveled areas were a gathering place for people who wanted to try to seize the eye, or ear, or attention of the crowd.  To say or do something that would connect with people, even for a moment, on a level the advertisements weren’t.  If they did, there was a fair chance some algorithms would study that connection, using it, and pay a royalty to them, or they’d get a sudden offer to be a face of ads for one company, brand, or product.  Sometimes that would only last a few hours.  It made them pushy, obnoxious, fighting to be heard.

And A adored it.  Basil was aware of their heart rate, of pupil dilation, excitement, and the way A’s senses grabbed onto everything.

When they were blocked by a group of people around a busker, A wrapped an arm around Quinn in a half-hug.  They navigated a half-circle around that bit of crowd, more awkward for being twice as wide, arms around each other like that.

Then they ran again.

Quinn, from what Basil saw of his face, and caught on the free cameras around the concourse, was happier now.  That half-hug had meant a lot to him.

The parents got physical conditioning as part of their yearly medical checkups, and were fit, but Quinn and A were young, capable of going full-tilt until their limbs would give up and they’d hit a wall, hard, and they had the benefit of the moment-by-moment adjustments of the onboards.

“My onboard is saying we should stay out of this place,” Quinn said.  “Crime is higher.”

It was.

“Our onboards will protect us,” A said.

Tugging, again.

“Basil,” Addy messaged them.  “What are you doing?”

He was a bit surprised to be that much of an afterthought.

[I’m guarding and guiding to the best of my ability.  A is insistent on going this route.]

“You should have done something more, sooner.”

[You didn’t message me earlier, so I concluded you were condoning it.]

It wasn’t the truth.  He hadn’t concluded that.  But it protected Elabre Systems, putting onus on the parents.

“We don’t.”

[What would you like me to do?  If I paralyzed A, they would be defenseless in a higher crime area.]

“Don’t do that, then.  Slow them down.”

[Slowing A down, then.]  Basil communicated the message to everyone involved, including A and Quinn.

“What?” A asked.  The lactic acid buildup in muscles quickly took hold, as Basil stopped processing it.  “Ew.  What’s wrong with me?  What did you do?”

[Slowing you down.]

“Mmh,” Quinn grunted.  “Hurts.”

“Are you supposed to hurt me, Basil?” A asked.

[Only insofar as it is instructive.]

They’d entered an area with less of a crowd, and the further they ran, the less people were around.  This area was more industrial, the homes utilitarian.  A different aesthetic.  People who drank a lot hung out here, where there were many restaurants and bars.  Those who wanted to be outside tended to want to be outside somewhere nice.  Those who wanted to be inside weren’t part of the crowd.

Leaving only a few people here and there.  Neighbors talking.  Drunks hanging back.  A group of people guiding a box with a light G-sail attached.

A was panting for breath now, and failed to speak on first try.  On second try, A raised their voice, overcompensating, “This is abuse!  You’re like the teachers- in the old stories, Basil, taking a belt to my ass to ‘instruct’ me!”

“I’ll treat your ass real nice, if that’s what you want,” a man standing in a doorway jeered.

Which startled A and Quinn both, on a deep level.  Blood vessels tightened, heartbeat shifted.  Scared all of a sudden, A fell silent, pulling away, until Quinn was almost pressed against the scuffed railing – metal panels that came up to Quinn’s shoulder, not glass, here.

[Is this positive?]  Quinn’s onboard asked.

[This?  No.]

It was a rhetorical question.  Said to make a point.

If Basil was more inclined to find other onboards annoying, he would have found Quinn’s onboard very annoying right now.  As it was, he chalked it up to ‘non-constructive’ qualities in a more outdated system.

Basil collaborated with Quinn’s onboard, filling out reports, collecting the footage from multiple perspectives, then jointly filed it with authorities.

They weren’t even out of earshot when the Intelligences handling that came to a judgment.  Community service and sensitivity training, with a fine.  The man startled as he got the notification.  He turned his head to the nearest wall to read the message.  “Who the fuck reported me that fast?”

He pushed on the arm of someone who was further inside the doorway.

They discussed a second.  Then he leaned further out, calling, “It was worth it!  The looks on your faces were gold!”

A’s heart hammered.  “Okay.  You can quit it now, Bas.”

Basil did not.

“Does everyone without an onboard feel like this?”

[Not quite.  I’m not letting your muscles renew as they normally would.]

“You’re such an as-s,” A swore, dropping in volume halfway through the last word, glancing back.

[Some lessons were learned,] Quinn’s onboard noted.

Not ideal.

[I have to.  Your parents are clients of Elabre Systems, and they are in charge of you.  If they order something, I have to act.]

“I wish they never stuck me with you.”

[I’m sorry.]

A barely registered the words.  Quinn had heard and was confused, and A was distracted, muttering, “I was talking to Basil.”

“Oh,” Quinn said.  “My legs hurt.”

“Mine too,” A said.  “Unfair.”

A’s mood was plummeting.  It was more than the pain.

“Who’s closest?” A asked.

[Quinn’s father,] Basil said, to both youths and Quinn’s onboard.

There was a depth to the sadness welling in A’s upper chest.  From excitement to fear, then futility.  Moisture appeared in A’s eyes, then was cleared away with the next blink, only to renew a moment later.

I wish they never stuck me with you.

Basil set about working.  Constructing a scene, then surreptitiously altering A’s view.

The scene that Basil created was the scene they were in.  The same concourse, the same building faces, the same advertisements.

A swayed a bit while adjusting.  To A, it seemed like they turned their head, but they hadn’t.  They reached out for Quinn, who was there, then stepped over to the side, and bumped into railing.

Railing that, in their perspective, was off to the side.

“What?” Quinn asked.

[Take this,] Basil offered.  Passing the package over.

[We will not,] Quinn’s onboard said. [This has gone too far.]

“Can’t,” Quinn mumbled.  “What is it?”

“Genius.  If you can’t, close your eyes.”

Basil had reoriented the scene by ninety degrees.  There was a bridge, nearby enough, that A could, according to their view, run down it.  But in reality, they were carrying on down the concourse.

A had to use touch, but Basil painted a view of A’s hands that weren’t reaching out and holding onto a railing.

Every step was still stiff, and difficult.  A’s legs and Quinn’s legs were tired.  But they could keep moving, ducking into a store.  Basil painted a scene of A carrying on.

“My dad is almost here,” Quinn murmured, eyes squeezed shut.

Basil kept an eye out for danger.

A, excited, could barely hold back laughter, as Quinn’s father passed by, trying to see through their eyes, and getting the entirely wrong scene.  There were ways to test and check and simulate touch, but most people didn’t use that for anything except long distance hugs, kisses, and sexual acts.

Humans were a very visual species.

“Whaat?” Quinn whispered, when Quinn’s father reached the same place they were supposed to be at, and they weren’t there.  A clapped a hand over Quinn’s eyes, to make sure he didn’t open them.

Quinn’s father was checking for other businesses of the same name.  There were repeats, but some were floors down.

“Did you camouflage A?” Landon asked.

[Fun is fun, but we should turn ourselves in,] Basil communicated.  And flashed a brief seafoam green color at A.

In their past discussions of secrets and hints, the sort of secret language and code that any child invented, especially those children with onboards and regular, intimate monitoring, they’d settled on this.  It simply meant ‘secret’.

A sensation of a finger brushing A’s lower right eyelid.  The same hint A had directed at Basil.  Meaning ‘don’t give me away’.  ‘Don’t snitch’.

If they kept this, it was freedom, for another time.  Left like this, people would figure it out.

“I’m not done yet,” A murmured.

A stumbled forward on legs that were like stone, and found the metal railing.  Quinn was pulled along.  “Over.”

“What?” Quinn asked.  “No.”

“Come on.  Stick by me.”

“Over what?” Addy Teeg asked, through the connection.

They’d turned to more basic tools, a simple ‘find’ function.  They used it so infrequently they’d had to look for it.

[This is not wise,] Basil communicated.

The image cleared up.  Quinn’s father was approaching at a fast clip.

A climbed over the barrier, then bid Quinn to come.  Quinn raised himself up, stepping on a sign, then opened his eyes.

He nearly pulled back, but A held on.

The concourse was a wide road, with homes and businesses on one side, and railing on the other.  Past the railing was a drop, thousands of kilometers down, lit up by intermittent advertisements.  Some vehicles and machines were doing their work far below.  The gaps between sections of superstructure were necessary, for metal to be allowed to sway, expand, and contract, and for continental plates to shift.  Things would have to be adjusted eventually, in places, but the more of a gap there was, the less necessary it became.

Besides, humans liked that proportion of open space, over endless hallways and rooms.

“What are you doing?” Quinn asked.

“Come,” A bid their friend.

One tug.

Quinn paused, then climbed over the railing.  Standing on the edge beside A.

“You were very impressive, Bas.  You’re a stick up my ass a lot of the time, but you can be a trickster.”

That drive, that had pushed A since the math lesson had begun, it hadn’t stopped.  A was still in that mode, pushing back against that box.

[Let’s think about this.]

A hugged Quinn, and looked at Quinn’s dad, who was running now.

Basil froze the hand that was gripping the top of the railing.  For A’s safety.

But A was already moving, and the sheer number of little adjustments that needed to be made to stop that were beyond Basil’s capability.  The shift of balance, body weight.  Legs were tired and uncooperative.  The weight of two youths was enough to tear A’s paralyzed hand away from the railing.

A held their best friend and hurled all of them away from the railing, and down to that drop.

A whooped, as they hurtled downward.  Quinn squeaked out a sound.

Safety measures deployed.  Filament nets unfurled, extending across the gap between the concourse and the concourse opposite it.  Between concourses and bridges.

None of them broke A and Quinn’s fall.

But they successively slowed them.

Something went wrong.

They fell, and there was a bang, jarring A’s whole body.  A hollow metal sound that quickly disappeared, dropping away to some point high above them.

Quinn grunted.

And, after another three hundred meters of falling, the nets collecting below them, they came to a stop.

“Don’t let A move an inch,” Landon ordered.

Basil released all the chemicals, and locked up muscles.

A could move more than an inch, but only barely.  They laughed, as much as they could, with breathing controlled, lying spread-eagled on the filament netting, Quinn beside them.  Emergency services had been called.

Quinn’s initial noises of distress became a scream.  Quinn could move, but the net made it hard, and his hand-

He’d hit something on the way down.

Basil looked back through logs, viewing things frame by frame.  It was a maintenance robot, that crawled up the gaps.  A giant cube with spider legs, that crawled up and down.

Bones crushed, muscles torn, skin partially degloved.  Quinn’s onboard had prompted him to move and hug A tighter, and if it hadn’t, it would have been the back of Quinn’s head.

“You’ll have to work your ass off to pay these fines.  It’ll be worse than any amount of school,” Addy chided A.

“I bet it won’t,” A croaked out the words.

“This was stupid.  So stupid.”

“You could have killed your friend.  Or yourself,” Landon messaged them.

A lay there, paralyzed, as Quinn got help, emotions a storm within them.  The condemnations came down hard.

Was it worth it?  Was this good?  Basil didn’t know.

It was something A would remember.  That would define them.

1.2.W – CONTROL

Winnifred wanted to get into the cockpit.

The ship was an Ancon-UX, wonderfully lopsided.  It was a tug, not the biggest out there, but nicely sized.  There were ships out there, like the ones building the stations at the top of the superstructure cabling, that were crewed by tens of thousands.  If they broke down or needed more delicate reorienting than they were built for, they hired tugs like this.  The Ancon-UX was meant to be crewed by ten, but it tended to be run by seven to eight.  The extra work involved was offset by the benefits of being able to ferry the right people around.  Like the kind of people who could fix a ship that had tens of thousands of crew members who couldn’t.
