It was so ugly it circled back around to being aesthetically interesting: a flattened rectangular cylinder with a whole lot of engines, clamping on the one side to hold onto whatever was being tugged, and the bare necessities, besides that.  Quarters, dining area, systems, and fuel had been stuck randomly onto the right side as if they’d been magnetized, thrown against the main ship body, and then straightened out to be level, before being welded in place to keep them wherever they’d stuck.  They never went anywhere with an atmosphere, so nobody had paid any attention to it being aerodynamic.

The cockpit was at the front.  Which wasn’t all that usual.  Up front was where crashes happened.  But Winnifred supposed that there wasn’t any good place for a crash to happen, with the Ancon.  Fuel on the one side, essential clamping machinery on the other, main engines on the back.

The last trip for the crew hadn’t been a pleasant one.  A fuel line had ruptured, and automatic systems had filled the main corridor with foam.  They’d had to abort the job, decouple, and fly back, with no easy way to navigate between the side sections of the ship and the back.  The captain-slash-pilot had been in the cockpit, and with one exception, donning a suit to leave the ship and go back to work on fixing the fuel line assembly that had bucked free of the ship exterior, had spent sixty hours in the cramped space, without enough space to lie down.  Others had been sequestered to their quarters.

This was a two-day job.  Because of bad luck, and, Winnifred guessed, corners that had been cut in maintenance, the ship’s systems had reacted with the same severity it would if the ship had been shearing itself in two.  A lot of foam, everywhere, hard and sealed to every surface.

She worked at laser etching a panel she’d just cleaned, trying to work fast when further from the cockpit, and slower when close to it, so she would be in earshot in case the captain agreed to let them through.

Which was really hard when her young cousins were dodging between her and the wall, chasing each other.  They were unclothed, their bodies all black metal and swooping panels that protected more delicate components and wiring from impacts and snags.  No waists- just spines bundled with the bare necessities to carry fuel and waste to the bottom end, connecting upper and lower body, and with long tails.  One of those tails came close to her arm.

Toby beeped out a proximity alarm.  She shut off the laser and pulled back.  Letting go of the laser, she kicked out with one foot, using clawed toes to grabbed the offending tail before it was fully out of reach.  Rhys jerked to a near-halt.  She was pulled a bit after him.  Her foot stomped down, hand reaching up to brace herself against the ceiling, so she wouldn’t keep going.

“Problem?” her mother asked, through a channel.  Her mother was upstairs.

“Rhys nearly bumped me while I was working.”

“Snitch,” Rhys hissed, at the same time Rhys’s onboard was trying to communicate apologies, while dealing with the other signals.  Multiple family members were now jumping into the conversation, criticizing Rhys, telling them about the importance of the work, reminding them that younger kids were meant to be here to learn the trade.

While that happened, Winnifred dragged Rhys down the hallway, to the airlock.

She hit the button to open the door, pushed the kid inside, and then turned.  Ceris was at the end of the hall.

Winnifred pointed.

Ceris was a good kid.  More obedient than Rhys, who was fighting, somewhat ineffectually.  Clawing at Winnifred’s overalls, which was annoying.

Once both kids were in the airlock, Winnifred hit the button, shutting the door, then hit the other button.

Sending them out into the cold void of space.

There were enough family members out there that they were fine.  Their onboards had access to the tools to reel them in, if there was any problem.

She glanced through their eyes to be sure.  Ceris used their tail to catch the edge of the door, then clambered onto the outside of the ship, going straight to the nearest members of their family.  Rhys got harpooned by their mother, caught with a cable line and pulled in.  The woman gripped him by the back of the neck, not even missing a beat in her lecturing, transmitted from her onboard system to her child’s.

“Keep that open,” her uncle Ellis told her, from the other end of the hall.

She hit the button for the door, went through nine different layers of checks and safety measures, alerted people outside, and then pressed her hand down.  It was red at first, but after about five seconds, switched to green.  Her tail secured the laser etching tool she’d dropped.

The door opened.  The air inside the ship vented out.

Winnifred braced herself, gripping a bracket, with her tail looped around a fuel channel.  Her hair was tied back, overdue for a cut, but now it threatened to pull free of the wire tie.  She’d been sprayed with cleaner when Uncle Dylan had been trying to hold up an engine casing and spray it at the same time, and had proven unable.  Toby had been able to manage it, but she was reminded of it when she saw the free locks of wavy hair, bleached a dirty brown-gray.

She wore overalls with a strap over one shoulder to hold them on, and they fluttered in the evacuating wind.  Not for modesty -she didn’t have a body, per se- but because she wanted the pockets.  All sealable or zippable, because they were off planet, in zero-g.  The skin of her face reacted to the change in environment by shrinking tight against the skull, her eyes filming over.

Toby navigated the rest.  Making sure she was comfortable, that her eyes adapted fast.

Her uncle Ellis hauled a chunk of the sealant foam down the hallway, and tossed it out of the airlock.  Another family member harpooned it, pulled themselves to it-and it to themselves, and then used small rockets on their backpack to reorient before kicking off, sending it into the bin they had off to the side.

Others brought the bin closer.

It looked like Uncle Dylan was entertaining Rhys.  So that was it for him being punished.  When she’d been that age, her parents wouldn’t have let up on her after a week, if she’d pulled what Rhys had.  Fuckups around some of the work they did got people killed.

[Lift the panel and get a camera in there?] Toby asked her.

She did.  The panels didn’t reach all the way from floor to ceiling, and were about three by five feet, steel a quarter-inch thick, running along the walls of the hallway, with darker strips above and below.

There was a small, low resolution camera on the end of her tail, and the end of her tail doubled as a wedge between panel and the rest of the wall, so that was nice.

[Scan done.  I’m going to use the factory default as a baseline to work off of, and move some things around.]

“What did they change?” Winnifred whispered to Toby.

He -he was a he, this week- showed her, and elaborated with speech and annotations.  [Ventilation ducting.  Probably to move the ventilation system away from the couple you pointed out fifteen minutes ago.]

“New model of electromagnetic couple, generates more heat.  But the breathing air ran too close to it, got uncomfortable?”

[Seems likely.]

Winnifred put on some music, and rocked shoulders, moving head, in time with the beat, as she resumed lasering.  Which was probably a mistake, because it got attention.

“What are you doing?” Uncle Ellis asked Winnifred.

She tapped a panel with her claw-tip, moving so her uncle had a better view… not that it mattered, when he was already looking out through her eyes.  The panels had come out of the factory etched with imprints of the technology on the other side of them: fuel lines, wiring, struts, and venting.  She’d been replacing it.  Toby was making it so she could keep the same idea, while matching the internals as they actually were.

“You submit that to the work order?”

“Yes.  The owner approved it.”

“Is all this a good use of your time?”

It’s a use of my time that keeps me close to the cockpit.

“It needs a clean anyway, to get the foam film off, takes thirty more seconds a panel.  It’s the kind of attention to detail people notice.”

[Closer to an added two minutes and thirty seconds a panel,] Toby said, just to Winnifred.  It was a flash of a message, but people could see if they went looking.

Shush, she thought.

“It’s attention to detail people should be paying for,” her uncle said.  He stopped using the whisper, meant just for communication between the twenty-nine families, and used plain English, when he wanted to be more of an authority.

Winnifred wasn’t sure what to say about that, except, “I’m ahead on my work.”

“You do good work.  Not like some of your cousins,” he whispered.  His tone had softened, and he’d whispered again, but he’d also prodded a few of her older cousins through their onboards when he said that.  Winnifred internally cringed.

Three voice channels opened, from her cousins to her, but none said anything.  All four of them were watching out of her eyes, glancing over recordings of what she’d been doing for the last hour.

“Are you tired, or can you help me haul?” her uncle asked.

“It’s not heavy, is it?” she whispered.

“Not too bad.”

She went down the hall with him.  They were working down the hallway in stages.  Cutting into the sealant, to reduce it down to manageable chunks, then cutting away the medium-to-small chunks that remained, still clinging to fixtures.  Then they did a final clean, to get foam film off.  A final pass would print and replace any mandatory stickers or anything that needed to be on display, fix any cloudiness on glass, and so on.

She didn’t mind much.  Except lugging chunks of sealant down the hall wasn’t nearly as interesting.  They were in zero-G, so it was as much a question of finesse as strength.  If she got something moving and sent it down the hall, she didn’t want it to collide with a surface they’d already cleaned, marring it, or sending small bits of sealant everywhere.

Her uncle first tried sending the chunks her way, each about as large as she was,  having her catch them, then she’d turn ninety degrees and send them out the airlock.

The bin reached them and attached to the side.  Winnifred was mildly amused at the irony of the tug, being what it was, having something latched onto the side of it like that.

“What could you latch onto a bin?” she wondered.  With glances to the periphery of her vision, she pulled up images of schematics, and lined them up.  The Ancon laid against the side of something big, like a… Hod.  She selected that and brought it up.  Bin attached to the Ancon.  Emergency power attached to the Ancon.  Emergency fuel.

[Rate checker,] Toby suggested.  Small appliances attached to emergency power and fuel to check the rate power and fuel were going through.

[Lifeboats]

She had to pause midway through bringing up the schematic to catch the next chunk and send it flying off.

“Have you thought about going for a stay with another family?” her uncle asked.

Plain normal volume, family-to-outsider voice.  ‘Boss’ voice again.

“Enh?” she grunted.

She dismissed the images she’d been piling up against one another, eyes closed, swiping from left to right against her closed eyelids to clear.

What she was doing wasn’t working that well.  Mainly because she wasn’t a powerhouse.  Her uncle was coming to her, pointing.

She passed him.

“It’s a chance to connect to our wider culture.  Experience different angles of it.  Different environments.  Do you know how it works?”

She had to use the entirety of her body to get the chunks positioned right, before launching them with both feet, hands braced against the nearest surfaces.

“I know how it works.”  There were forty people at their station, which was small, twenty-two of them were twenty or younger, the rest varied between twenty and one hundred and thirty.  Three of her older ‘cousins’ were cousins several times removed, from other families.  They’d be sent here.  Some kids here would be sent elsewhere.  Sometimes the work differed, some of the families spoke different languages or had their own art and dance… and many believed it was important to share that out.  Learning the different work, art, and stories were the given reason for the exchanges.

The subtler reason was that provided a chance to find husbands and wives from within the twenty-nine families, who weren’t overly direct relations.

“It’s a chance to get fuucked!” a cousin messaged her.  He was outside the ship, still looking in after his uncle had prodded him.

Her uncle messaged something to that cousin.  A mild telling-off.  Winnifred didn’t pry.

Winnifred kicked off another chunk.

“In all seriousness, it is a chance to sow your wild oats,” her uncle said.  Winnifred was in the middle of looking up the term -archaic- when he added, “or be sown.”

She could work out what he meant.

“Multiple partners a night, it’s great, you’re on every eligible bachelor’s radar, some families with a hundred men your age, a hundred prospective husbands, and all they care about for your stay is you, they’ll be trying to win you over, Win,” another cousin messaged her.  Keeley was the female cousin closest to Winnifred in age, but a wildly different personality.  “Put some money aside.  Are you synthetic down there?”

“She is,” another male cousin said.  He was looking through a list of Winnifred’s hardware.

“I was going to say if you didn’t have one, you might want to switch to one.  And if you have one, be ready to replace that baby, because it’ll get worn to tatters.”

“That is a myth.  They’re more durable than that,” her uncle said.  He was apparently frustrated with the velocity and aim of her moving the chunks, and had come to her.  It looked like they were each going to be handling their own loads.

“Excuse me, dad, but as an owner of one, they get gross, and they get harder to clean over time, until it’s not worth it.”

“Alright.  Not the mental image I wanted.”

“That’s what you get for not knowing some myths have basis in fact.”

“I will defer to the experts,” Uncle Ellis said, winking at Winnifred.

“You could try having a cock for a bit, while visiting another family.  That’s what Little Gwen did her last time out,” another cousin interjected.

“Okay now,” Uncle Ellis said.

“I don’t think I’m there, yet,” Winnifred admitted.  “For any of it.”

“Booo, so boring,” Keeley messaged her.

“It’s fine,” her uncle said, laying a clawed hand on Winnie’s head.  She minded, mainly because his claws were sharp, with those faint burrs that any edge got if used for work, and it was her hair.  He was careful, but it still prickled.  He let zero-g drift carry his lower body up and head down, until he was on her level, kind of- his legs were way over her head, face upside-down.  “When you’re ready, if you’re feeling the need, or family feels confining, say.”

“Okay.”

She picked up as much as she could carry, using one leg to propel herself, snagging nearby objects with her tail to reorient herself for the next kick.  She passed some control over to Toby, who could calculate and predict orientation and position.

Which made this duller.  When it was routine, repetitive work and she wasn’t even controlling her own body, for most of it.

“This foam has two tones,” she said, to her uncle, moving it to show him.  Dark gray nested inside gray.  “I bet there was someone in the hallway, and so the sealant foam delayed a moment to let them get to their quarters.”

“Yeah?” her uncle asked.

“It’s interesting,” she said.

“I suppose so.  But it doesn’t change the work.”

She wasn’t sure what to say to that, so she resumed lugging stuff up and down the hall.  Or having Toby do it, really, with her having minimal input.

[According to logs, you’re right.  There was a bit of an issue, because the crew member was allowed into someone else’s quarters, and then was stuck there.  There was an accusation of theft.  And property damage.  People who work off world can be territorial.]

“Crew dynamics, huh?” Winnifred mused.  “Tricky.  Thanks, Toby.”

“Hm?” her uncle asked.

“Talking to my onboard.”

It was like that for another two hours.  Up and down the hall with chunks of foam as big as she was.  Some family came in to do other work, and she caught glimpses as she drifted past, but it wasn’t very interesting stuff.  Plugging some things back in.

“You’re slowing down,” her uncle whispered.  “Are you tired?”

“Can I go finish the panels I was doing and rest?” she asked.

“Okay.  If you’re sure you’re not so tired you’ll make mistakes.”

He touched her head as she passed.  Clawed fingers in her hair again.

Toby put her music back on.  She swayed with the music, but she couldn’t get into it before.  Toby wasn’t saying much, she didn’t prompt a conversation, and she felt a little down.

“I must be tired,” she told Toby, trying to place the reason for the feeling.

[Almost done.]

She nodded.

She took a second, looking at the etching work.  She liked it.  The aesthetic.

“I want this when you and I have a ship of our own, Toby.”

[I’ll add it to the list.]

“Have to consider crew dynamics, huh?”

[You do.  Would you buy an Ancon?  Small crew ratio for the size of the ship, interacting with lots of other ships.  You benefit from knowing a lot about various different ships.  Which you do.]

“Never thought about it that way.  Hmmm.  I like Ancons.  They’re like the illegal dogs with smushed faces, but they’re ships.  Ugly cute.”

[They’re not illegal though.]

“I don’t think I want an Ancon, though.”

[Inexpensive, and they pay for themselves eventually.]

“High fuel costs,” she murmured.

[Very.  Partially covered by the work.  You take a contract and then buy the fuel you anticipate you’ll need.]

“Hmmm.  Maybe as a way to get there.”

[A first step.  Ancon first, put in the work, then sell it and upgrade.]

“What do you want, Toby?  Ship or aesthetics?”

[I have told you endless times, I have no opinions about that sort of thing.]

“Toby, love, you must.  I insist.”

[Winnifred, child, I’d be reflecting you, making a choice to make you happy.]

“Not allowed.”

[Pet, I’m not equipped.]

“Oh, I’m ‘pet’, now?  You’re going there?” she asked.  Aunt Gwen’s terms of endearment, that got steadily less and less endearing.  She did it with Toby too, when he was being stubborn, but mostly, he used it with her when it came to this sort of thing.  “Call me a worm, Toby, I won’t change my mind.  You have to choose.”

[The G-Deck.  Ceiling and floor.]

The G-Deck or G-Decking was both illumination and used the same mechanics as a G-sail.  With the right kind and wavelength of power running through the material, gravity from one gravitational body could be favored over another.  G-sails used it as a fuel-less means of helping ships reorient.  G-Decking used similar principles to let people walk around, though it tended to be floaty on all but the largest ships.  It helped avoid muscle atrophy, for those who cared.

She supposed that if she had to have crew, she’d need some.

“What about it?” she asked.

[A color other than green.]

The slightly green lighting was traditional.

“Ooh, do you have a color in mind?”

[I absolutely do not.]

“Slate blue?” she asked.

[Go to sleep, worm.  You’ve got minor cellular damage from vacuum exposure for me to tidy up.]

“Love you, Toby,” she said.

Two of her older cousins were still talking about their escapades.  Another two were drinking, having finished their allotment of work for the day.

She crawled into a vent, using the laser etcher to clean up dust on the way, then settled in where the vent bent at a right angle, legs and tail down one length, spine bent at the turn, and upper body at the other.  She used the telescoping feature of her arms to shorten them as much as possible, folded them at the opening of the vent, and laid her temple against the metal and back of one hand, head sticking out just enough that she could look at that locked cockpit door.

➨

[Look Alert]

Winnifred opened her eyes.  She immediately began moving.

She’d been asleep four hours.  The family had cleared up enough of the hallway that it was possible to move from the nose of the ship where the cockpit was, to the engines.

She was just out of the vent when the G-deck up and down the hallway lit up.  That white light with green at the edges.  She felt that coarse gravity take hold, and dropped to all fours.  After the ceiling panels lit up, things found an equilibrium that felt less like it was pulling her toward the center of each panel of decking.

[Captain on deck]

The captain arrived near the back end of the ship, then stopped in at one of the empty quarters.  Clearing it out, apparently.  One of Winnifred’s aunts offered help carrying, and he refused.

Winnifred checked the long list of work that still needed to be done, and began to work on cleaning the airlock doors.  There was a fine particulate of sealant that got into mechanisms.

The man was middle-aged, with a sagging face, and eyes that drooped at the outer corners, because of that sag.  Unshaven, hair long, he wore a puffy coat, a thick dark blue wool sweater for warmth, orange pants of some thick material, and heavy boots.

“So this is what that work order meant.”

“I hope it’s okay,” Winnifred said, rising up to stand on two feet.  Having gravity again felt weird.

“This you?”

She nodded.

“Reminds me of when she was new.”

“I’m jealous.  I like Ancons.”

“Do you?” he asked.  He sounded like he didn’t believe her.  “I hate ’em.  Fuel lines everywhere.  When something goes wrong, everything does.  It’s like you’re halfway through a game of chess against a better player.  Even the moves that look safe, you realize two moves down the line, you’ve fucked yourself.  If you’re lucky.  Sometimes you don’t even realize.”

“The ventilation moved, because of the heat from the new clamp assembly.”

He snorted.  “Fuck my ass, people complained for six months before we realized what was happening.  Everyone had a dry cough, cost overrun from cooling and couldn’t figure out why.”

“I like those sorts of puzzles.”

He paused, looking at her, then frowned.  “What are you after?”

She had sort of hoped to get to this without having to outright ask.  If the captain showed up, saw the good work, and asked if someone would handle it…  But she had to ask.

“I can clean your cockpit.”

Uncle Ellis was watching this conversation.  A few were.

The man frowned.

“Say, two hundred?  If it’s a concern about, I dunno, waste, mess, I know you were in there sixty hours, I won’t fuss, I admire that.  You stayed with your ship and got her to where she could be fixed and cleaned.  I’ve definitely dealt with worse.”

“In this offer, am I in the cockpit with you?”

“Hm?”

He gave her a long look, silent.

[Are you soliciting him, Winnifred?]

“No!” she quickly added.  “No, that’s- sorry, no.”

“Because I’m not into…”  He looked her up and down.  “That.  And you’re small.  Are you young?”

“She’s young,” Uncle Ellis said.

“Not interested.”

Winnifred stammered, “Yeah.  I wasn’t- I- wasn’t offering.  I like ships.  I’d get a kick from seeing the setup in there.  That’s all.”

The captain stared her down.

Her dad had come in from outside, and was further down the hall, watching and listening, now.

Her face felt hot.

“I’d understand if you felt like you had to clean it yourself, it being your mess.  But we’ve cleaned a broken grey water loop for a ship with two thousand people.  It’s fine.”

“Fine.  I’ll add the cockpit to the work order. I’ll be cleaning out what’s left behind in crew quarters.  If I put things out into the hall, can someone toss them?”

“We can,” Uncle Ellis said.

“I’ll handle the cockpit, then,” Winnifred’s dad said, approaching.

But-

He settled a heavy hand on her shoulder.  “I’m senior in the family, I know our reputation rests on this sort of thing.”

“Yeah,” the captain said.  “Sure.”

He pulled a key from a reel on his belt, unlocked the cockpit, and then passed them, on his way to the crew quarters, barely glancing at Winnifred.

“Someone with access to the cockpit of a ship like this has the ability to steal the ship.  The families aren’t trusted, so most captains won’t say yes,” Winnifred’s father whispered, to her.  “Senior members of the family only.  Give it fifteen to twenty years, we’ll bring you in.”

She remained where she was, unmoving, embarrassed, as he walked past her, entered the cockpit, and closed the door behind him.

➨

“I like ships!  Good recovery!”

Her cousins were replaying the scene over and over again.  Laughing.

The bin had been hooked up, a wall had been moved to compress all the gathered junk together, and the members of the family who had come on the two day job to the Ancon-UX were all crammed into the remaining void, strapped in or grabbing the bars and struts at the edges.  Winnifred held onto a bar with one hand, not moving much, otherwise.

“Food?” her aunt offered.

One cousin clapped two hands together, reaching.  She tossed him a random pack.

Winnifred was hungry.  She looked through her aunt’s eyes.  “Avercade and Yam, please.  And water.”

Her aunt tossed her a pack.

Winnifred caught it out of the air, and caught the water with a foot.

“Thanks.”

“Oh, captain my captain!”  A cousin leaned in closer to her.

Winnifred leaned her head away, raising the pack to the circular indent at the corner of the metal that covered everything from her cheekbones to her chin.  The food pack got emptied, filling her mouth.  Water, pressed to the same indent, flooded her mouth to help rinse out the content, making up for the limited saliva production.

It was thick, and had a good yammy aftertaste.

That pack, about the size of her fist, would be half of what she ate today.  Really, her brain was the only organ that needed the food.  And her skin, and hair.

“Alcohol?” one cousin asked.

“We’re low,” Winnifred’s aunt said.  She passed him a bottle with the same cap as the water, meant to release into the indents.

“Want one, Win?  Drown out the memory?” a cousin asked.

“Can’t delete the recording.”

“She’s too young,” the aunt said.

“You’ve let lots of us have it when we were her age.  We’re done the job, she worked hard.”

“She wanted to work harder!”

More laughter.

Winnifred closed her eyes.

“Might help erase the memory,” Keeley said.

“You lot,” her uncle Ellis said.  “Get lost.  Find another thing to joke about.”

They listened.  From the looks of it, they weren’t finding other things to joke about, though.  As they got close to home, and reconnected to the wider beltway connection, some were messaging more distant cousins of other families.

“You like ships,” Uncle Ellis said, one clawed foot grabbing a strut near the ‘floor’, leg pushing him back to where he could lean into the wall.

“Yeah.”

“Checks out.  Looked through your logs, your history.  You want to own one?”

She nodded.

“Expensive.”

“I know.  I don’t spend much.”

“You’ll have to, soon.  You were struggling with the hauling.  You’re still wearing parts that are meant to be traded out every few years. You’re overdue on that front.”

“Yeah.”

“Two more of those trade-outs, then you’re buying the body you want to wear for the next seven to ten years.”

“I was thinking I could stretch it out.  If I wait another year and a half, I could do it with only one new body between now and when I’m full grown, buying something more long-term.”

“And until then, you’re slower, weaker, you’re breaking down a bit more.”

“I’m okay with the fixing stuff.”

“But you’ll struggle with some of the work.  You won’t be able to hold a panel up like Uncle Dylan was trying to do when he sprayed the side of your head like he did.”

Uncle Dylan was alerted by his onboard that he’d been mentioned in conversation, and threw an empty food pack at Uncle Ellis.  Uncle Ellis didn’t even try to dodge it, and it bounced off the side of his head.

Winnifred caught the pack, and crushed it, her food pack, and her water together in one hand.

“If the wear and tear gets bad enough, you might struggle to hold up panels like the ones you were etching.”

“Yeah.”

“You won’t get as much work.  I won’t want you working with me, if you’re not up to the task, falling apart on me.  The work we do is hard, these bodies are meant to be lithe, light, and efficient, working in tight spaces, lots of environments, with a lot of tools and options.  But the work breaks them down.”

“I’m good at engineering, fixing.  I can do upkeep on myself.”

“I hear you.  But I guess, hmmm.”  He shifted position, and sighed, air hissing from the face-mask.  He looked at her.  “Look at that captain.”

Her cousins were still joking about it.

She’d cringe at the memory of that man and that encounter for years, she guessed.

Uncle Ellis went on, “Look at his ship.  I bet he told himself, he’d stretch things out, he’d do the work himself.  Less crew, more time between official maintenance work and replacements.  And what happened?  Flooded with sealant, pissed off crew.  Broke down, multiple months of lost work.  And that rolls forward, impacts the work he can take.  People don’t want an unreliable tug.”

[That’s a good analogy for Winnifred,] Toby said.

It was.

Winnifred leaned her head into her uncle’s shoulder.

Ellis continued explaining, “They hire crews of rats because we’re thirty percent cheaper than having machines do it.  Machines have a middle man between the factory and the cleaning job, that factors into the price.  We’re our own middle men, and we’re seen as reliable.  So long as we’re not breaking down.”

“Yeah.”

“Have your onboard run simulations.  Look at other family members that stretched it out.  Not just at our dock.  I bet you’ll see the numbers saying the work you lose by being substandard, the cost of repairing things late, you don’t end up saving that much more money.  You’ll be miserable.”

“Maybe.”

[Want me to?] Toby asked.

Winnifred nodded.

[I’ll get back to you.  Can’t pull all the records until we’re planetside.]

“So you want to own a ship.  What about service?”

“Do we need service that often?”

“No, but when we need it, we want it fast.  Say your ox stops working right, or your fidelity for both arms drops to sub-eight-hundred?  Both of those things have happened to me.  Check, right now.  What’s your coverage?  Most techs only have the know-how to work with some companies.  Imagine you’re sixteen days out from the nearest stop with coverage.”

He used his own onboard to bring up a coverage map, based on Winnifred’s parts.

“I could go with parts that have wider coverage.  Or parts that I can do self-maintenance on.”

“You could.  Try.  Make sure you test run those parts, before you pay.”

The way he said that sounded ominous.

“If you like ships, okay.  But… be realistic.  Have a workable plan.  It sounds like you want to take shortcuts.”

“That’s not it.”

“When you have a ship, are you hiring members of the family?”

“Could.”

“We’d run it by the twenty-nine heads of the twenty-nine families, and give you permission to put out a call.  I’m betting there’s enough people out there who are like you, with dreams bigger than the family trade, who’d help you crew a starter ship.  But you’d need to learn to deal with people like your cousins, joking around like they are right now.  Assert yourself.”

She nodded a bit.

“Any crew that aren’t one of us, that’ll be harder in different ways.  The type of people who work off planet are rougher.  Like that captain was.  No-nonsense, no room for ambiguity.”

“Yeah.”

“They hate us.  They look down on us.  Enough of them pay us, we get by, but others won’t hire us even if it makes sense.  They won’t look up to you as a captain, no matter how good you are.  Humanity naturally settles into a monoculture, and anyone outside that, with older ideas about marriage, or raising kids, they don’t like it.”

“Can we not- I’m tired.  Can we put off talking about this?”

“Yeah,” Uncle Ellis said.  “But you know that doesn’t put off the reality, right?”

She nodded.

“Putting it out there… some of the families, you marry the right person, that’s an influx of cash.  Doesn’t have to be a romantic partnership.  You could even come to me or my sister, we’d arrange something.  Some shmuck from one of the nine worlds marries you, you bear him a child, help represent him for the occasional event, standing by his side.  It’s money that could get you on your way.  He’d probably want some controlling interest or say in what you do with the ship, of course.”

“Not that interested in that.  I want it to be mine.”

“Fair, hmm.”

“But thank you for the suggestion,” she said.  Even though she didn’t mean it.

“If you can get to the ninety percent mark, saving up for your ship, come to me.  I’ll cover the last ten percent, if you promise to hire some people from within the family, for crew.”

“Okay,” she said.  “Thank you.”

“Your parents might chip in.”

“I don’t think so.”

“Yeah.  Maybe not.  Well, I’m around if you want advice.  Or a reality check.”

She nodded, a tight movement.

She wasn’t up to talking much.

“It’s not so bad, you know.  What we do.  The work.  There’s a hundred and nine billion people across the nine worlds.  I’d say, a hundred and five billion of them, they stopped caring about work, they stopped caring about where they came from, they stopped caring about the future.  They live in the moment.  Brain dead, only interested in the next big toy, the next piece of media.  Rest of them, they’ve got passion, sometimes for revenge, sometimes something perverse, sometimes, hey, they want to work like we do, and they’re off planet, maybe.”

She was already done with the conversation, and it wasn’t the first time she’d heard sentiments like this, but if she pushed him away or tried to make him stop, she’d lose a lot of goodwill.  She’d pay for it, for a while.

“The families, there’s less than a million of us.  People who don’t work at the docks don’t even know who we are, usually.  We have a culture, Winnie.  Rest of the worlds don’t.  We have fidelity.”

Winnifred nodded.

He thumped the back of his hand against the metal of her chest.

“Keeping that, working to keep that, it has a value I think you’ll come to appreciate when you’re older.”

“Yeah.”

“Keep up the hard work.  You do your parents proud.”

As he said that, he paid her.  Her share of the two days of work.  Four hundred and fifty.  Plus sixty, because she’d negotiated to add the cockpit to the cleaning job, raising two hundred for the family.  Her dad got some of that, because he’d done the work.  Five hundred and eleven lux, total.

“Thank you.”

He left.

In the corner of her vision, Toby was keeping tabs on the conversations where she’d been mentioned or tagged.

“Oh captain, I admire you sitting in your own piss and shit for sixty hours, bed me!” a cousin joked.  Others laughed.

She closed her eyes, wiping the screen, and put on music.

She wasn’t even through the first track when Ceris’ mother came up to her to talk about marriage or visiting other families to meet boys.  She was alone on an island, after all; cousins older than her had already committed or started down certain roads, making plans to go visiting elsewhere.  Younger ones weren’t in consideration yet.

So the busybodies had only one person to focus on.  Her.

Which meant that was most of the conversation before they got home.

➨

Account Balance: 293,426.43 Lux.

That was the value of her body after trade-in, plus everything she’d saved over the last three and a half years.  Everything she’d saved since she was ten.  She’d had to pay for half of her body, that time, from the work and errands she’d done.  She’d gotten to choose parts.  It had been exciting.

Now she had to pay for all of it.  Toby had done the checking.  Her uncle hadn’t been lying.  The math wasn’t encouraging, if she tried to stretch things out.

So she had worked down the list with Toby, sitting at one of her ‘crow’s nests’, a high point with a view of the horizon.  Comparing parts.

She’d chosen a shop and a time that wouldn’t be too busy.

“Full body?”

She nodded.

“Got a list?”

She transmitted it to him.

His eyebrows went up a bit.  “Learning to fight?”

“Huh?”

“Some of these parts, you get them if you’re expecting to get hurt, and have to replace your setup.”

“No.  I’m not a fighter.”

“Slack off on the work?  Your people, you work to save up for this?  Sometimes someone decides it’s better to be a kid than work, but…”

“I’m trying to save money.  I need it to work for two and a half years.”

“Aha.”

“Can I test drive it?”

“Yeah.  SERRATA neck, arms, legs, hand, shoulder, spine…  Let’s see, that’s an 1150 for neck, 1300-W for arms, 1120 for legs.  Not 1300-W, to match?”

“Worse on the stress tests,” she said.

Machine arms pulled the items off the counter.

The display above the counter showed the price.  She was the only one in the shop, so there was no need to hide it or be private.  Maybe he didn’t ever hide it, and it was a point of pride for people to buy expensive.

4827.13 lux
10279.58 lux

15352.52 lux
17301.15 lux
20336.41 lux


“Spine bundle, SERRATA 2200-GT…”

33838.38 lux

“You’re not doing SERRATA for the upper body?  Form factor?”

“Bad in the crush tests.  I do heavy work.  ALTING.”

39978.11 lux.

“Ox is… ALPIN.  Should fit that body.”

51117.40 lux.

“I saw others combining the two.”

“You’ll need connectors to fix the upper body to the rest.  You want a boob plate?  Some girls like the feminine form factor.”

“Spoiler, convex curve.  Um.”

Toby supplied some images.  She chose one.  “Torrid-AAMG.”

52,431.10 lux.

Ostensibly, it was something that would protect her oxygen if her chest cavity was crushed.  But it was mainly aesthetic.  It was a curve of metal that would rise up toward the collarbone from the lower ribs, extending forward.  Almost like it was pushing something modest up, but she didn’t have anything to support.  Literally.  And it was positioned a little higher.  She already had something similar, and it was good to have something in the chest region, or some clothes looked weird.  Or weirder.

“Lower face, ear, RODDING-105.”

She didn’t want to watch the price as it rose.

“No eyes?”

“My onboard’s handling that.”

“Wiring?”

“Onboard.”

[I got you.]

“Brave.  Okay.   Claw tips are more ALTING.  Heart and digestion, small system, STEGGI-05.  You’ve got full body structure, you need strength.  Eight CEPP-2250 configurations…  For your nether regions, KYUSS… TD.  There we go, and an OFF-SI for the back end.”

Final price tag: 92,515.13

Amount remaining: 200,911.3

A little under ten percent of the way to her being able to get a ship.  By the time she was grown… tall order.  But it would be that much more in reach.

“Come on through.”

She passed through to the back.  The lighting in the shop changed, with a message in the window saying there was a job in progress.

She messaged family, to let them know.  Two of her aunts looked in, watching.  Just in case something happened.  Because this was a vulnerable spot to be in.

She climbed onto the table, settling down, head resting on a foam pad shaped to hold her skull.  The metal of the table felt awkward against the metal of her spine.

Every piece of her, disconnected and pulled away.  Blood and oxygen handled by the table.

Reducing her down to being a partial skull, no lower jaw, a brain, a part of a neck, a heart.  She’d lost most of her bones in the last refit.  They were mainly aesthetic.  The law had lapsed and while there was a gap, she’d taken the opportunity to be rid of them.  Or her parents had wanted her to.  She didn’t care strongly either way.  Not about bones she never saw or really felt.  They were a liability if she got hurt.

She was elevated, parts slid into their rough configurations, then connected together.

[Looks a little uncomfortable at the shoulder joint.  I think the bend exceeds what the factory says we should expect.]

She notified the shop employee.

He went and got another.

But that was an omen, wasn’t it?

The job took twenty minutes.  She hated it.  Being helpless.  She wanted a clearer view of what was happening.  Her own engineering.

But it passed.

Immediately, she could tell something was wrong.

The hand with claw tips closed, then opened.  She reached forward, testing limb extension.

When she lowered that hand to the table to sit up better, she felt as though there was a thick piece of fabric between the claw and the table.

The piezoelectric compression, fidelity, it all should be in acceptable ranges.  Fifteen percent worse than what she’d had, but… still well above results that, according to studies and reviews, people were terrifically happy with.

Everything felt that way.

She felt slower.

She swung the legs around to the edge of the table, still feeling that layer between herself and it.

“Is this worse because it’s a test run?”

“No,” the shop worker said.

“Check for me, Toby?” she whispered.

[Checking.  I think this is up to standards.  No tricks.]

“Why is it like this?” she asked.  She lowered the feet to ground.

“The hands are a little worse, the spine bundle that carries the signal to your brain is worse.  That compounds.  That overall feeling carries through every part of you.  Muscles pull a five percent higher latent load, you feel that.  An accumulation of little things.”

It was hard not to feel a visceral dislike of her own body.  She’d touch something, and feel an immediate, kneejerk reaction of grossness, weirdness, or discomfort.  As if she was cleaning up the worst sorts of waste.  Then she’d realize it was her.  Her body.  A mushiness of sensation, or the edges around the sensation were off, and reached her brain as something that felt too artificial, too machine.

“A lot of long time body modders are like this.  It’s hard to downgrade,” the shop owner said.

“Is it adjustable?  Settings?”

“Some.  I won’t lie to you, I’ve had people on this table, same reaction as you.  You can tweak it, get closer to what you’re familiar with.  You can push some systems and setups further, lean on your onboard to filter sensations.  It’s still going to feel like you want to crawl out of your skin.”

“I barely have skin.”

“Figure of speech.”

She tried moving around, shifting weight from one of the feet to the other.  She moved the tail.  That faint mushiness of sensation extended to the ground under her feet.

No camera at the end.  The tip wasn’t strong enough to act as a wedge.

Breathing felt off.

“Do you get used to it?” she asked.

“I could say ‘some’, but this is usually the point in the conversation people get upset, accuse me of fucking around, to upsell, or say I’m lying.”

[People who make similar swaps have a five-year satisfaction rate of 13%.  Obviously, you’re not keeping this for five years.  You’d have this for half that.]

“Which isn’t better,” she whispered at Toby.

[It’s worse.]

She stood there, not even testing the body anymore.  She wanted to wrap her mind around the experience.  With every second that passed, it felt more and more like she was committing this to memory.  Because… she knew she’d come back to this moment.  She’d hate herself, for making this decision.

She climbed back onto the table.

Lying there, she draped one of the arms over her eyes, the crook of the elbow over the bridge of her nose.  She still had a bridge.  Just no actual nose.

“Want to swap out to something more tolerable?”

“Can I have a minute?”

“I have a customer waiting patiently outside.  I’ll serve them, if that’s alright?”

“Yeah.”

The man left the workshop area.  She lay there, hating every moment.

[I’m sorry,] Toby said.

➨

Account Balance: 134 Lux.

Plus one thousand, five hundred owed to her mom after the next three or four jobs.

Her dad had said, “This is why we push you to get every extra bit you can.  Imagine if you’d gotten a few more for the laser etching, on the Ancon job, or for pointing out the engine issue on the Sagar.”

Her mom had told him to shut up.

A cousin had chimed in, “This is why we scam people.”

Now, an aunt was messaging her, asking for her to show up and show off.  Do a few spins, let them see the new body.

She instead climbed to the highest place she could.  A crow’s nest.  A place to sit.  She told Toby to tell everyone to be quiet and leave her alone.

The sky felt so far away, now.  Even if she got there, even if she had her own ship, if she remained like this, she’d be limited to a slice of it.  There was very real danger, if something went wrong with her body and there wasn’t a tech who worked with that specific brand close enough.

“You didn’t lie to me, did you, Toby?”

[No.]

“No trick, where, when you were installed, same day I was born, some hack was slid in there, to get you to help play along with the big scam?”

[Incredibly illegal.  Not worth the extra cash they’d make.  No.  I’m not compromised.]

“You’d say that, wouldn’t you?” she asked, slumping a bit.

[I’m yours, Winnifred.  You’re my client.  Your parents gave you admin privileges from the start.  They think that’s important.  I’m in your corner.  It’s a racket, but I’m not part of it.]

She sat for a bit longer.  “Sorry, to accuse you.”

[It’s okay.  I don’t really have feelings to hurt.]

She turned her head and looked down at the ground.  Machines were fixing up a ship, down there, cleaning it inside and out.

Toby closed the window with the account balance on it.

She brought it back up.

Account Balance: 134 Lux.

A part of her wanted to cry.  But if she did, she suspected family would give her a hard time.  Maybe if she left it up, she’d be able to get past that threshold.  Or she’d cry, but cousins would see why and not bug her.

While she was looking, without saying anything or sending any messages, her mom quietly cleared the 1500 lux debt.

She pulled a water from her overalls pocket and pressed it to the side of the brand new TENSON-3340 facemask.  Her nose and mouth.  Water flowed in.  She could still taste the new material.

She swallowed.  Systems in her throat and upper chest captured the water and put it to use elsewhere.

[I have something, but I worry it’s salt on the wound.]

“I want salt.”

He loaded it up.

It was a pilot training program.  For Ancon-MMs, which were smaller than the Ancon she’d been on yesterday.

She let him load it up, and she let him dress up the simulation.

She settled into the chair, the consoles around her.  Locker just behind her chair and to the right.  Barely any room to lie down.  Or an ordinary human wouldn’t be able to.  She would.  Her type fit well in small spaces.

There were panels… her claw tips ran over the edge of the panels, without quite reaching the buttons, or controls.  The simulation and Toby’s extra effort made it all real.

She was in the pilot’s seat.  Powerful machinery heavy behind her.  The simulation, as she glanced at the documentation, was meant to help her get a sense of the way acceleration felt, how hard it was to stop in space.  There were simulations that would run her through various stops, pulling up beside various ships, hard pivot-and-stops, turning around so the butt end was pointed the opposite way, and using the stronger engines there.  Various emergencies.

“Toby?  Can you do me a favor?  Load me in the highest fidelity simulation?  As if I had a full-flesh body, instead?”

[I feel the need to point out, love, there are members of the family who would be upset at you for even entertaining the idea.]

“I’m not entertaining.  I’m-”

She stopped herself.

Toby set to work.  It took a moment for Toby to find something good, and load it.

“Don’t… don’t make it easier.  I know I’ve messed around, when I was younger.  But don’t…”

[As true as I can make it, then.]

“Please.”

Slowly, inch by inch, Winnifred’s body in the cockpit was replaced by ordinary flesh.  Mouth.  Tongue.  Throat.  Something bobbed at the front of her throat when she swallowed.

Chest.  Body.

It wasn’t mushiness.  It was… a lack of anything ringing true.  The metal fixtures had that piezoelectric response, but also that song, faint, that rang when metal tapped anything hard enough.  Flesh didn’t have that.

The discomfort swelled.  Awareness, of every inch of herself.  The feeling of the water she’d drank settling in her stomach.

It got worse by the second.

This was worse.  Worse than even the downgraded overhaul had been.  It-

[You’re going to throw up.]

“What?”

She was dimly aware of the idea.  She’d seen drunks do it.  But-

The feeling of discomfort in her own skin swelled, and with it, that feeling in her brand new, alien midsection.

Thirteen family members watched through her eyes as she leaned forward and gagged out stomach contents onto her lap.

Uncle Shawn had left the family.  He hadn’t stuck it out.

He hadn’t been able to get used to having an all-flesh body.  His partner hadn’t been keen on him going back.  Or the work he’d have to put in, to get a good enough one.  The resources to get a sufficient body just weren’t there, when he didn’t have the contacts the twenty-nine families had, and they weren’t interested unless he was going to come back with his head bowed, apologizing.  Leaving his partner.

Not long after that, he’d worked an industrial job and he’d made a mistake that, on camera, sure looked intentional.  It was the sort of machinery that hadn’t allowed for any mistakes.  Then he’d been gone.

Winnifred’s parents hadn’t sanitized the story when telling her.

He’d betrayed the family, leaving.  He’d paid the price.

“Toby.”

He reset the simulation.  No vomit on her lap.  No more flesh.  Just her and her new 294,976.55 lux body.  Toby had a good sense of her, and her moods.  That she wanted quiet.  So he gave her that quiet, moving around her body to do routine checks, and continue sanding off the hard edges of her new body, so everything would feel natural and good.

So she sat in the simulated cockpit.  A layer of illusion between herself and the real world.  But she didn’t touch the controls.  She didn’t let herself.  She didn’t run through the simulations, to teach herself.

That was too easy.

She sat there, like that, staring out into space, until the people watching weren’t looking in anymore.

“I need to get on a ship.  Even if it’s not as pilot,” she whispered.  “As an engineer.  I’m good at that stuff.”

[You’re very good at it.]

“I’ve got to find a way to do this.”

[We’ve go to.  I’m in your corner, love.]

She appreciated that, more than Toby could ever know.

It felt very lonely, out here.  There were good things about the family.  But sometimes, in moments like this, when she wished she could explain what she was feeling to someone, they felt as far away as the sky did.

She closed her eyes, gaze swiping against the back of her eyelids, from one side to the other.  Clearing things away.

No more simulation.  If she got into that, she’d love it.  And it would be one iota less drive, one little bit less reason to keep pushing forward.  If she was going to do this, the full reward and experience needed to be waiting for her at the end.

“Test me.  Teach me.  Be hard on me.  Help me get out there.”

[I can.  But do me one favor.]

“I’d do you a million favors.  You’ve got a backlog, Toby.”

[Wait a week.  Or a month.]

“Why?”

[Wait a little while, because if you have a sudden surge of enthusiasm, they might look back through records to find out why.  And I don’t want them to catch me saying what I’m going to say next.]

“Which is?”

[Don’t try out being fully flesh again.]

“Don’t need to tell me twice.”

[Stop talking about going away, or other plans.  Until you say something that convinces me otherwise, we’ll both assume the plan is that you get out there, into space, finding your own path, your own work.  But we won’t communicate anything.  They aren’t your allies in that.]

She let that message sit for a while, sitting on the top of a cable support pillar, so close to the upper edge of the atmosphere, it felt like she could jump off and reach zero-G.

After a little while, she nodded a bit, in answer to Toby.

1.3.B – CONTROL

“Basil,” A complained.

[I know.]

A trudged along the walkway, bombarded from the right side by individual advertisements that jumped out from the signage and postings on any available surface.  On their left side, a giant advertisement loomed, eye-catching colors flickering.  If A walked over to the railing, they would be able to see an attractive model hawking a fashion trend.  The way the image was positioned, the eyes seemed to look over the railing, directly at them, sultry.

It was interesting to glance at the code.  It was open for audit, so Basil could study it.  There were layers of data interpretation so deep that Basil couldn’t hope to dig through it before the data had completely transformed, but he could follow threads through it, and see how the model was generated by an intelligence, tracking each and every one of the 119,000 individuals in a position to view the ad, weighting them by their likelihood to buy new clothes with lux, and interpreting their tastes, before serving something to that target market.

He’d rather be doing what he was doing.  Looking after A.

But it made the ad compelling to Basil, for reasons that went beyond what it was trying to do, appealing to base desire, and a desire to be.  There was one model right now, genderless, hairless, with very full lips and light brown skin, brush-stroke slashes of pink on upper lids, brush-stroke slashes across lips, accentuating shape in the mess of it.

Later, it might switch to two models, to appeal to the two desires in its projected audience.

What part or percentage of that was aimed at A?  It looked like A’s contribution to that image was a bit of feathering around the jacket collar.  A liked that sort of thing, along with a striking color choice.  Not pink, though.

Almost as if reading Basil’s mind, the model turned a corner and the color scheme swapped out.  Pink to light blue.  Red jacket to white.

A glanced over, looking.

What effect did this sort of thing have on a population?  It reacted to that population, but that population’s tastes would be influenced by what it saw.  Would it homogenize taste?

Some of the older teenagers of the group had onboards as well, with a few that didn’t clustering around them.  One of those onboards was more advanced than Basil, but the owner was a degenerate.  Others were more like Quinn’s.

They were spinning off and sharing various reality alterations.  One would repaint one of the coordinator’s pants, so it looked like they had wet or crapped themselves, another would make one kid’s teeth weird, or paint someone up to be cross-eyed.  Most of it was subtle, the sort of thing that the others wouldn’t notice at first.  There was an unspoken game between them, to try not to laugh or startle when they glimpsed any one of the growing pile of alterations.

Basil kept getting alerts when they did something to A.  Wisps of thin hair coming out of A’s ears, matching that on their head.  Clothing adjustments.  He’d reached out to other systems the less advanced systems connected to, for reference, and had a pretty good sense of what was out there.

They’d been here all day, the group had been up to it for a while, and the shock value had worn off.  Basil had shown A what he’d been able to figure out, for a bit, but then A had gotten bored and disgusted with it.  Which was good, because the group was trending more into the shock and disturbing.  Cutting out the butt of pants so ass cheeks were on full display, increasing a girl’s -and other group member’s- chest sizes, or making it so one person who hadn’t turned around for a while had grisly, infected gore on the other side of their body, for a scare when they did turn.

The ringleader of that group was now making clothes increasingly translucent.  A younger member, A’s age, was following suit.  Which included targeting A with the effect.

Basil wasn’t equipped to go head to head with them, and notifying one of the coordinators would put A in a bad position with a group they might be around for a while.

It wasn’t a conversation Basil was invited into, but he felt protective of A.

So he mustered his resources, targeted the weakest link in that group, which was a boy a bit older than A, who had no onboard and was lingering close to any walls or pillars they could use as a screen, blinking and flicking their gaze around to cobble together a little something to contribute.  With no system of their own, they relied on a hub in the wider belt network, and used it for inspiration and to get pre-fabricated programs and media elements.  The trick was, if Basil fabricated enough images of older women, with a specific arrangement of haircut styles, body types, and faces, made games with these images, some scary, some more lighthearted, could he convince the kid that it was the start of a trend?  Or leave them no great options to pull from, with pages clogged with these images?

Could he hit the right ballpark with the average between all them, that when it turned one of the coordinators into a scary older woman…?

It startled the ringleader of the group.  Not a lot.  Not enough to score a win.  But he noticed.

“What are you up to?”

He showed A.  [But you have to keep working.]

A cackled softly.

Which got a startled, horrified reaction, enough that one of the coordinators looked over and started to pay more attention to him.

There was no closing message before they signed out, but from the look the teenager shot A, and Basil’s read of the situation, he felt like he’d played his part well, and they acknowledged that.

A resumed cleaning up, and, after a brief period of good spirits, resumed grumbling.  The grumbling had been an all-day thing too, since before the lunch break, but it had gone away.  Now A was pretty worn out and tired.

For the average citizen, it was one lux to spot trash or something that needed to be fixed.  Another four to pick the trash up.  In the effort to instill some civic responsibility in its rulebreakers, the law here on this block provided two and a half times the usual toward the fines, and two and a half times the usual to A’s pockets.  Every little piece of trash or little mess that was low priority for machines, identified by a citizen in passing.

The idea was that they would gain some appreciation for the little details, the value of contributing to society in a casual way.

A’s fall had forced a number of safety measures to deploy.  Age, past history, and the minutiae of the wear and tear on safety systems, possible risks -like the maintenance robot coming out from beneath a bridge just as they came by- and a variety of other factors had all been broken down in a video that had been delivered the day after.  They’d been assigned a fine, and a ‘volunteer’ detail to pay it back.  The detail would do five different jobs this week, and then A would be allowed to choose any one of the five on a given day, to work it off.

It could have been delivered within seconds of the event, but, Basil assumed, the systems had determined that waiting would mean A was more receptive to the punishment.  A night of rest, first.

Except there hadn’t been much rest.  A had stewed over Quinn being hurt.  When Basil had asked if A wanted help getting to sleep, they’d said no.

Which was good, in a way.  Less good, though, that A was cranky now, thirteen hours later.

[It looks like a group of radicals came running through here.  They tore out all the small postings for a few specific brands.]

Two hundred and sixty pieces of litter or messes to clean up, before they were done for the day.  A bit over an hour of work, at this rate.

As small a thing as it was, it was affecting A a fair amount.  Increased heart rate, shallower breaths, and constriction of blood vessels.

A kept glancing at the interesting mods, and Mechard noticed, flexing.  The mods seemed more for fashion than for purchase, allowing arms and legs to connect at odd angles, while being a little longer than usual.  His hip had a horizontal section from where his leg would start, extending out a foot, before the leg appeared.  One arm was the same at the shoulder, the other at mid-bicep.  His torso was elongated with bands of non-flesh, so his shirt barely met his belly button, and his neck was similarly extended.  He wore loose fitting long shorts, or shorter pants, that hung weirdly on the one leg.  Each of the horizontal shifts involved a chrome-white material that was less than a centimeter thick.  His hair was long, and colored light.

A’s stomach lurched as the elevator slowed.  Basil equalized out the ear pressure, so A could be ready to go while most of the others in the elevator were working their jaws and trying to get their ears to pop.  Superstructures tried to keep air pressure above on a level with what was below, but it wasn’t entirely possible with wind and weather.

They were a few thousand feet down.

A was right out of the elevator, taking in the fresher view.  There was more moisture down here, and lots of the railings had vegetation in planters on their far sides, but the area was different.  Like attracted like, and the people here minded less if there were rust stains on the metal railing, didn’t keep their places pristine, and indulged in various forms of recreation and business that were less likely to work out in the Teegs’ neighborhood.  Advertisements reflected that.

Less of a place to raise families.  More of a place for those who wanted to be left alone, and sometimes made that point aggressively.

Mechard connected to A, and Basil intercepted the message.  The heavily modded teenager had an onboard.

No online presence, no data.

They got to work.  Their work area was something of a park, where people congregated at night to chat with neighbors.  And to drink, sitting on benches and under trees, or at the one large fire pit.  Countless containers for drink and puddles of alcohol and bodily fluids mingled with the smoke that stained the walls.

With that, Basil was able to get enough contextual details to track them down.  Gideon’s clothing choice wasn’t universal, which had thrown Basil.  Different subsets of the group made their own clothing, or rejected what was on offer, buying exclusively from locals.  Different subsets of the group were apparently well meaning, but believed that society was dead-ended, and this was dangerous.  Or not so well-meaning, with the same belief, in a way that made them dangerous.  The girl that was named Gideon apparently belonged to that last group.

The Terracens, the Aquilians, Grey-frocked, the Immolated, Mountain Wanderers, Mountain Terrace Wanderers, Ghosts.  The groups were rarely large, and were scattered across every settlement, every superstructure.  Some seemed to have formed independently of the others, developing their own naming schemes.  Too many different names for Basil to even be able to find and gather them all.  It didn’t help that they didn’t like being connected to the Belt network.

How to communicate that to A?  Basil would have to give A the cliff notes later, after discussing with Addy and Landon.

A shrugged in response to the coordinator, oblivious.

[We will,] Basil communicated.

Vince was quick to recover.  He didn’t have an onboard, but some nanotechnology was injected into his system, did the work, and killed itself, ready to be evacuated with the next bowel movement.

Basil suspected the psychological impact of being attacked that viciously, that suddenly, would last longer.

There wasn’t nanotechnology to help with that.  There would be a regimen of sessions, games, and other activities to help him through it.

A had wanted to visit, so they’d gone to visit Vince.  They chatted, digesting the event.  Some of Vince’s other friends dropped in.  There were some games, sharing of pieces of media they’d put together and spun out, a brief showing of the ad-and-attention program, which the wider friend group wasn’t as keen on.  Then they ate some food Vince’s family network brought.

“I have someone else to check in on,” A said.  “You can come if you want.”

[This might backfire,] Basil noted.

“Good.  If there’s no risk, it doesn’t matter.”

So they left, as a group.  There were enough of them the parents didn’t mind them being out on their own, and they stuck to low-crime areas.  They talked music, food, pointed out good places to go, and navigated their way to A’s neighborhood.

Once there, they had to hunt around.

As it turned out, Quinn was working through education and testing with a family member, slightly older.  The link between A and Quinn was still blocked, but that didn’t stop the physical link.

A approached, nervous.  Then, as Quinn approached too, the pair closed the distance and hugged one another, tight.

“I’m really sorry.  I don’t know if I’m going to get in huge trouble for finding you like this, but I wanted to let you know how sorry I am.  I didn’t realize you were hurt at first, and I thought maybe you got the wrong idea, and asked for the block.”

“I did ask but… not because of that.  You scared me,” Quinn murmured.

“Sorry.”

Quinn nodded.  “I can’t take the block down right now, since it’s really your parents that are doing it.”

“Yeah.  Okay.”

The conversation continued like that.  A introduced Quinn to Vince and Vince’s friends, and then they chattered.

[Are we alright?]

[I worry at how you handled things that night,] Quinn’s onboard responded.

[So do I.]

[That’s good.]

There was no natural dialogue between them.  Basil was, in some ways, alone.  In other ways, he was preoccupied.

There were more people than average, connecting to A and Basil’s onboard system.   Three at first, nothing too unusual, except Basil couldn’t trace them back to Vince or his friends, and there was no reason for it, otherwise.  That number rose unsteadily to sixteen or so.

Then a sudden jump to six hundred sets of eyes, looking through A’s onboard system.

Before Basil could react, respond, or find whatever message or issue had sent the six hundred people to A, the number dropped away.

Basil quietly notified the Teegs and the authorities.

“Basil?” Landon asked, connecting to Basil and Basil alone.

[Yes, Landon?]

“Don’t worry A.  But be on guard.”

[I’m not to warn them?]

“Don’t.  Let the authorities handle it.”

[I’ll notify the Rohdes now, as well.]

“That’s fine.”

Basil told Quinn’s onboard, who told the Rohdes.  The relay of information made Basil worry that the severity of what was going on hadn’t been communicated in full to Quinn’s parents.  Quinn’s onboard, at least, seemed ready to be on watch for anything strange.

[There aren’t any connections like there were.]

[This is good.]

[It’s strange though.  If you assume the girl Gideon got in trouble, and the family was notified, surely someone in the family would check or re-check information?  Revisit the earlier moments, and the people involved?]

[Do you think so?]

[It seems to me that someone told them to keep quiet and avoid being noticed.]

[It’s possible.]

Quinn and A continued their happy reunion, after a painful three weeks apart.  They made plans to go eat with Vince and his friends.  They were unafraid, unguarded.

Leaving Basil and Quinn’s onboard to be afraid and on the alert for them, instead.

1.4.W – CONTROL

Winnifred was in the middle of her engineering lessons, while lounging in her corner of the world.  It really did feel like a corner of the world, a vent that opened into a dead-end of superstructure, where things were meant to connect to the next structure and knit the sky together into a series of docks and platforms of communication arrays meant to carry signals in a loop around the belt.  Her bedroom, such as it was, was a vent large enough she could curl into a half circle, or extend a leg to form a three-quarter circle, sitting with open sky, mostly, sprawling out to one side of her.  She could see the top half of the clouds out to the horizon.

The top half of that vent was decorated with some sketches and schematics, which she’d had to block out while working on her lessons, otherwise it was too much like trying to play chess while the board was superimposed over another one.  She’d started with and zipped through the basic lessons, working with individual components and studying how they worked, most of which she’d already known from working with the family.  She knew about G-sails and calibration, because her uncle had yelled at her for sticking her finger into one that had been opened up, that was being carefully cleaned, years ago.  She knew HTPB-Fluorine engines from cleaning the inside of more than she could easily count.  A game she’d played when she was young had been all about stress points in structures and ships, playing with the parts to see and figure out what broke.  She had that fast.

It had been a strain, though.  There were enough gaps in her breadth of knowledge that the program couldn’t easily fill in the blanks.  Toby had navigated some of it, telling the program to give her a refresher, and the testing had tried to make it more dynamic by throwing scenarios at her that would have been interesting-ish, even if she knew it all.  Still, some of it really did just have to be ‘do you know how this works?’  ‘What about this’?  ‘What about this variation?’  ‘Now this…’

Now she was into the more interesting parts.  Small engines.  Now ‘here are three engines in a sequence.  Something’s wrong with one of them.  Figure it out’.

Her claw-tips moved through the air, touching pieces of the floating image, dragging parts aside, investigating.  She could feel everything, tactile, helped by Toby.

[Did you know flesh hands don’t have the ability to sense wetness by touch?] Toby asked.

“Weird.”

[It’s just touch to them, with slight temperature variation.]

“Is that your way of telling me I have projection oils on my claws?” she asked.  “I can feel them.”

[I was looking at video feeds of engineers and repair techs at work, and I think it’s one of the things that sets apart people who learned from simulations and those who have practical experience.]

“Do I know to wipe my claws off?”

[Exactly.]

Winnifred got a scrap cloth and wiped off her claws, winking one eye.  “You’re so good for this, Toby.  Is there slang for that?  Wet-fingered newbie?”

[I imagine so.  There are enough people out there.  Do you want me to search?]

“Nah.”

[People are coming, by the way.  Try to finish your test.  If they arrive while the test is in progress, it could be canceled because of interference.]

She puzzled over the issue.  where the engine had three possible configurations for how it could fire, different fuel mixes for firing in oxygenated atmospheres and vacuum, and the problem to be solved was a report from a veteran pilot that it was pitching during takeoff– the nose was rising, and they were insistent this was the sort of problem that led to issues down the line.  Winnifred could request diagnostics about any related systems, and the test would give her the data or let her look at the components.

Except it all looked okay, as she ran through troubleshooting and made the engine go through its motions, different fuel lines opening, configurations of the nozzle, and looked over things like the placement of the fuel tank and landing gear.  Would something shift in the process of takeoff?  So what was the most likely related system?

“Can I look at the flight logs?”

[Restricted information, owned by the company,] Toby replied.  [Which isn’t uncommon.  Hurry now, they’re almost here.]

It was hard not to read between the lines, and infer there was an answer that could be given in the next… thirty-five seconds.  Normally the systems handling the tests would catch that sort of thing.

The fact a bunch of her older cousins were coming and it was probably something dumb tied into that thought about the limited time, and drew her to a conclusion.  Someone dumb.

“Test, don’t register this as a correct answer for the testing.  I got this because my onboard gave me an inadvertent hint,” Winnifred said.  “But confirm for me?  There is no problem with the engine.  It’s something wrong with the pilot.”

[Correct,] Toby said, acting as intermediary between her and the test.  [Sometimes the problem an engineer has to handle is the user.  Or the client.]

“I’m proud of myself for that one.”

[How did I give a hint?]

“If it was solvable that fast, it couldn’t be something I could pull up, study, and find, or a test I hadn’t done,” Winnifred said.  She put her things aside, and closed the test.

Her cousins were climbing up the vertical face of the superstructure, toward her vent.  It was a relatively small group.  Most of her older cousins were either partnered up with people or off with other families.

“Win!”

She poked her head out, and at the same time, glanced around.  That glancing included peeping into the eyes of family members, including Aunt Gwen and her parents.  People who typically knew what was going on.

Alcohol, dock meat. and people gathering.

She backed up, moving some of her things from the floor of the vent to side-vents.  Then she sprinted, leaping.  Toby drew out some lines in her field of vision, indicating wind, necessary movements, plotted trajectory.  Images of herself, moving through the air, suggested the marks she needed to hit on the way.  Knees to chest, then feet out, rightward, to meet the wind.

Thirty-five meters out, there was a massive, branching mount for some heavy duty advertising that would go live after the building was finished.  Winnifred sailed across the open air between the vent and the mount, dropping with increasing speed, then, careful with her claws and body, prepared herself to catch it and handle her fall.  She was moving down much quicker than she was moving across, by the time she reached it, and and could touch the surface that was rushing past her, repositioning herself until she could put arms, legs, and tail around the branch of metal without touching it.

There were extensions and spoilers on her updated body, which she had obtained when she’d turned sixteen.  A bar across the chest, as was her preference, to help clothes hang right, and protective segments around joints.  She let those take the brunt of the friction, hugging the metal, with knees drawn up to the hollow, near-nonexistent stomach.

Above her, her cousins were less graceful.  Their metal banged and scraped against the pole.  She could feel the impacts they made.  A couple whooped.

A weird dynamic, where she’d get told off for the wear and tear she caused herself, while her older cousins and even some grown adults would get a pass, because Winnifred cared enough to stop and listen.

She got called a daredevil, pointing to stunts like these, but she was mild mannered, compared to some.

Nobody told her where she was going.  She was expected to find out.  They chased her, being more reckless, nudging her from her comfortable position, the most easily replaced and sacrificed materials of her body scraping against the metal.  Trying to put her off her game.

One of them was Noeh.  A cousin who was eighteen or so, about a year and a half older than her, visiting from the other families.  Winnifred’s family tended to have light brown skin, dark brown or black hair, and they favored black prosthetics.  Some stood out as different, especially those who came from other families.  Aunt Gwen had slashes of red at her shoulders and neck, and picked prosthetics that let her have that stylized accent.

Noeh was wild-natured, prosthetics chestnut, skin pale and faintly sunburned, hair red-brown, clothes grey-green, with a handspan-wide band of flesh from chin, down neck, chest.  From chest down to, well, places his pants covered.  Where he didn’t have the cap that was more common in her family, to keep things contained until they were ready for use.  Just… there, apparently, between machine legs.  It seemed like madness to her.

He had been paying increasing attention to her in recent days.  Probably because he was leaving.  He’d spent time with a lot of her cousins who were closest to him in age.  If there was a checklist or something more, she supposed she was on it.

She didn’t want to dwell on that stuff.

He was due to leave in a couple of days, and some family was going off-planet to work a job tomorrow, so, while he was still around, they had a party.

Winnifred could hear the singing.  Family members whispered it.  A long while back, when mods had been new, and the first members of the family were transitioning from being people who tended to work one job, marrying other workers in the same job, and modding themselves and their children for the work, they’d started communicating using the pitches and volumes that modded ears could hear, that flesh ones couldn’t.  Then, because communicating in those ranges had its own requirements and ways things could be shortened and still intelligible, syllables had been dropped or swapped.

When they whispered to one another, they weren’t speaking English, really.  It could be understood and translated, but really, only by those in the families.

Those sounds and vocal ranges became their own chant-singing, with its own structure, and its own accompaniment.  Metal on metal scratches, the scuff of feet and the rustle of loose fit clothing over prosthetics.

Winnifred’s cousins caught up to her.  Keeley, who had been sticking close to Noeh for a bit now, tugged hard on Winnifred’s overall strap, pulling her off her feet and nearly onto her face.

Noeh, following so close behind Keeley that he could have been her shadow, caught Winnifred by the neck, circling his tail around it.

She backhanded it away, with a touch more force than necessary.  She didn’t like being grabbed like that.  The constriction.  Maybe with that bit of extra force, he’d get the message.

He was gone into the crowd.

She preferred to dance.  She liked the music.  People sang to her onboard, and it was out of sync with the whisper-singing coming from their faces and throats.  The space they occupied was beneath a platform – it felt too exposed to do this above, where others could look over and see, and judge, or appropriate.  There wasn’t enough room to stand entirely straight.

Claw tips scratching metal, glass, or ceramic.  Whisking sounds and rasps, as metal with frayed edges ran against more of the same.  Rustling clothes.  Whispers.  It was a music that required her to strain her entire being, turning up the volume on her ears to hear it.  In the days this music had been made, there was a trust, that someone wouldn’t spoil the effect with a sudden shout, loud noise, or fumbled footstep.  In those days, with older or partial audio mods, it could blow out people’s ears entirely, if people had the volume turned up enough to be fully tuned in.

It wasn’t just sound.  Winnifred matched the pace from the outer fringes, then jumped in.  It was touch, all of them modded, all capable of bending legs in both directions, with prehensile spines that let them touch shoulder blades to the backs of their thighs, if they so chose.  They often slept in vents, personal belongings ready to be packed up and moved somewhere at a moment’s notice, if the vent was needed, and personal space had no meaning, when other family members might come crawling through and past, bodies scraping past a sleeping child’s, who would stir and fall back asleep.
