She became part of the press of bodies, where there was barely more than a hand’s span of space between any part of herself and the floor, ceiling, or the half-dozen people around her.  This was a dance that, if everyone performed it perfectly, would see them meshing together, impossibly close, parts of her body from her face to her tail, claw tip to claw tip, brushing against metal, decorative bits, cloth, and hair.  There were one or two dances in the twenty-nine families that pushed things this close together, but one was a perfectionist’s dance, and the other was more about a constant struggle to be better.

In that struggle dance, and in this one, nobody performed it perfectly.  That was the point.  In this one, it was expected, and part of the dance, to roughhouse, to push, to tug on clothing, bringing others to where they needed to be.  Or push them out if there wasn’t a small adjustment that could bring them back into position.

She could move, rustling past others, who were moving at the same rhythm, vacating spaces that parts of her own body could occupy.  She could look through other onboards and other points of view of dancers, and as she strained concentration, touch, and hearing, focused on movement, and remembering the steps that put them together like the tiled-together pieces of an Escher image, she could almost forget how to find her way back to herself.

Her mother was participating in the dance, and found her way to Winnifred.  For a moment, they made contact, foreheads touching, then pushing against one another, almost as if trying to drive the other out of the dance, or out of position.  In a loving way.  A teenager-and-mom way.

Ceris, new-ish to being a proper participant, at eleven, was struggling, and Winnifred and her mother broke apart to bring Ceris into the dance, at least for the introductory part.  Kids had to learn the steps somehow.

But as the first section ended, the whisper-singing and noises stopped, and they all went statue-still.  Some had chests that heaved, their ox trying to bring in enough that they could both exert themselves and push out the whisper-chanting.  Winnifred was among those who had beads of sweat on their foreheads they wouldn’t have from hard work on a ship.

Ellis, close to the center of the dance, broke that stillness and moment of silence with a sharp rap of clawed fingers to thigh.  It was a hard balance to strike, to punctuate and signal, pushing the line of ‘loud’ without breaking it.  Everyone moved in sync after.  Winnifred pulled on Ceris with a hand at the child’s shoulder, end of her tail at the base of Ceris’s, tugging.

The tempo increased.  Children who weren’t being helped like Ceris was were first to go.  They’d fall from position, get pushed out to the edges, sometimes with surprising force, kids skidding on metal sub-platform floor into the periphery, into waiting arms of family members, who’d cheer for them and laugh, every time.  Hugging them, after.

Ceris was good, for her age.  But she didn’t know all the steps, and ultimately, as she bumped, whole-body, into the arm of an aunt of theirs, she was seized and tossed out.

Another girl, one of Winnifred’s older cousins, got heated as she was pushed and pulled a few too many times, admittedly unnecessarily in some cases, and pushed at someone, and that was okay, that was the point, but she was loud about it, metal clacking hard against metal, and she was pushed out, with less soft cheering and acknowledgement, after.

Winnifred could go with the flow.  She was okay at it.  Great, she thought, considering she hadn’t had same-aged cousins to practice with.  This particular dance was the sort that could be hypnotic, drawing her into a haze where she was short on breath, space, and lost herself, but the jarring interruptions, clashing, and sudden physicality from others meant she couldn’t.

All to a whispered song about past conflicts and attacks on their people.  Strikes, in past generations, before the new economy, which was barely an economy at all.

The tempo steadily increased, the demands of the dance and the exactness required ramped up, and Winnifred’s hand caught on loose clothing from one of her aunt’s.

She saw the writing on the wall and half-scampered out, helped along by some strong pushes.  She ducked low, losing her balance, and dropped to all fours.  Her mother ducked out soon after, putting an arm around Winnifred as they curled up together, watching as things continued.

“Was I in the top half of those removed?” she vocalized, just for Toby.

[Top 40%.]

She was satisfied with that.  “Give me pointers after.  Tell me where I messed up.”

[Absolutely.]

[We eat meat after this dance,] Keeley was telling Noeh, onboard to onboard, so they wouldn’t interrupt the singing.

He faintly gurgled his displeasure.  But the meat and enzyme pack were deposited in the little processor, reduced down to a slurry, and he connected it to the side of his face mask.  The contents were swept in.

[And intoxicants,] one of the guys sent.  [Even for kids.  Special occasion.]

[I’m not a kid,] Noeh fired back.  [But I’m into it.]

Winnifred got her own portion of dock meat and alcohol.  It did not take much alcohol to affect any of them, when Winnifred’s biology was only about twelve pounds of brain, head, and biomatter in her chest cavity.  She took a half-shot.  Enough she could taste it.

The dance was wrapping up.  The entire dance was something of an endurance match, that, as it reached the last few individuals, demanded more improvisation from the dancers who circled one another, heads and bodies winding around one another as both turned, stepping in the same tight circle. One of the women was Seren, a distant aunt, a woman who Winnifred hadn’t associated with much, because Seren and her mother were not on good terms.  Seren was someone who taught dance and points of culture to the twenty-nine families, and often acted as host parent to visitors like Noeh.

The other was Uncle Ellis’ wife, a very exacting woman who demanded a lot from herself and others.  Not a surprising final duo.

The entire crowd joined in, breathing in the same time, making music with their bodies, leaning in, reaching hands and tails forming casual tripping hazards.  It was bad form to actively interfere, though.

Seren won out.  Or Ellis’ wife intentionally lost and bowed out, to let Seren have her status and respect as teacher.

Every one of the twenty-nine families had their own variations and styles of dance.  Noeh and the other visitors were getting a send-off, experiencing theirs, here on Griffey Docks.

Immediately after, with his wife curled up into his lap, her back nestled into the void where his stomach would be, Ellis hummed, a good warning for those with older modded ears to change their volume settings -Toby did that automatically- before he broke into proper song.  An old work shanty, where he worked his ox box overtime, for the extra air and volume.  Winnifred had seen others have to connect a temporary ox box into their chest to get that kind of sustained air and vocalization.

The shanty was accompanied by a mix of whispers and voices that sang along and echoed it.

Winnifred felt warm.  She’d broken into a proper sweat, as much as that was possible, and hair that was normally wavy and dense had relaxed a bit with the moisture.  Her mother combed it, while they sat together and joined in on the singing.

Wood was hard to come by, but they poured chemical into a shallow, contained pool and ignited it, and gathered around it.  Conversations happened around the margins, with some cousins speculating on who would end up married first, and others sharing stories they’d heard from out in the world.  All of the stories Noeh and the other visitors told were new, so they got to be stars for the evening.  If one of the older family members decided to speak, though, usually to tell some point of fact about the way things were for their branch of the family, way back when, conversation kind of had to die.

Winnifred’s father came over from a gathering of his friends, and touched foreheads with her mom, and kept his head in contact with hers even as the rest of him moved around to the far side, where there was a bit of room to sit.  He touched his fist softly to the side of Winnifred’s facemask, a mock punch.

It was a few minutes before the old heads were done arguing over how things had gone, way back when.  Both had gotten onboards late in life, and memory was fallible.  Which felt as weird an idea as not being able to feel wetness.

“Studying ship engineering is good,” her father whispered.  He was glancing over recordings of her past few days.  “Pays well, if you can fix a ship while we’re cleaning it.  We’ve got a few who do that.”

“That’s the plan,” Winnifred lied.

“You’re too distant.”

“I’m the only person around my age.”

“Are we going to send you away to another family, where you have more peers your own age, and see you come back transformed?  A whole new Winnie?”

“Do you want a whole new Winnie?”

“I think you’re lonely.  Sitting in a vent with magnets holding your things to the walls, studying endlessly.  It makes you awkward sometimes.  I don’t want an unhappy daughter.  That’s all.”

She shrugged.  Unhappy was the wrong word for it.

“We have family who pick the furthest place possible on the docks to decide where they make their space,” her father whispered.  “The ones who are too old to work…”

Even the older ones around the fire here did their share with paperwork and forms, or visiting other families to rally support around some issues that came up.  Her dad was talking about the oldest.  The ones who couldn’t, who waited to die.

“…the sick…”

Not physically sick.  That could be handled, usually.  It was those who had had something go terribly wrong with their mods, or with their brains.  Mental illness that eluded nanotech rebalancing and management of brain chemicals, or trauma.

Her father was measuring out his words.  Leading up to something.

“…those with grudges…”

Most of whom went to other families after a split with this one.  Reasons ranged from the petty to the complicated.  When someone had a big enough issue to go live on the outskirts but not enough to leave, it was petty most of the time.

“…and you, Win.”

He tapped his metal hand to her lower face again.

“You’re often the last to arrive for jobs, because you put yourself on the fringes,” her mother whispered.

“But I arrive.  I work hard.”

Her father said, “We give our children a lot of leeway.  You work, so you should have independence.  You eat and sleep as if you’re trying to postpone your needs as long as you can.  Your refit was postponed the same way.  You study at a high level, but you’re still a child.”

When he said ‘our children’, he meant how all or most of the families treated their kids.

“I eat, I sleep, I study, I work.  I got my refit.  I’m nearly adult.”

“You are far from being grown,” he whispered back, and leaned in to touch the side of her head with his forehead.  She leaned away.

“Win, love,” her mother whispered.  “We aren’t condemning you.  Two things.  Spend more time with us.  We’ll make that time enjoyable.  Eat, watch some media, play a game.  Come shopping with me, when we buy necessities, we’ll explore.”

Winnifred nodded, watching her father carefully to make sure he was on board with that idea, and that he didn’t want to keep pressuring her.  Seemed like it.

“Find people,” her father whispered.  “Peers.  Either go to another family to find them, or look outside the family.”

She had to try to avoid looking as shocked as she felt at that suggestion.

“You’re so solitary.  Price told me you-“

Toby brought up the conversation, pulled from her father’s onboard.  Price’s voice overlapped and overrode her father’s.  “-is a child doomed to leap from loneliness to a heart so broken it never heals.  Either because she finds someone and clings too hard, then doesn’t survive when they go, or because she doesn’t, and a heart with nothing to fill it will break under its own weight.”

“What if I fill it with something besides people?  Or a person?”

“You are still so young, and you’re already too comfortable in that solitude,” her mother said.  Clawed fingertips combed Winnifred’s hair.

A friend of her dad passed her dad a cartridge of cannabis.  He pressed it to the side of his face mask, then vented out skunky smoke from the face mask and various vents all up and down his body.  He didn’t normally like the stuff, as he thought it made you useless for work.  It served as a kind of punctuation for what he said next.

“Figure it out.  Broaden your heart,” her father said it like it was an order.  “Find friends?  Don’t be so reluctant to connect to others.”

“I’m not,” she whispered back.  She started to shift position, but he bumped his head into hers, and sighed.

“If you don’t, at minimum, I’ll ask you to make your bed and keep your belongings close to base camp.  We’d parent you the same way we did when we were younger, to set you on a better path.”

The same way Rhys and Ceris were parented.  With a tight leash, parents and other adults in the family not far away.  Ick.

“Make decisions for your social development, as we have to,” he added.

“We’d reach out to another family,” her mother whispered, elaborating.  “Who have a boy that is also struggling to connect.  Arrange something.”

[Say yes,] Toby told her.  [That you’ll find friends.]

“Yes.  I’ll find friends.”

“Good.  And Toby?  My daughter does not need coaching to tell her to listen to her parents.”

[Noted.]

But she had.  She hadn’t been sure what to say to something as simple as that.

➨

She still had her spot, they hadn’t pushed her to leave and move yet.  She could still sleep at the mouth of the circular vent with one arm and her tail dangling over the edge, with a view of the cloud cover below her and starry sky above, and the partial megastructure sprawling out across and over the cloudscape.  The sky was studded with the cables that extended from the anchors in the ground below to the stations in the outer atmosphere.  Dark lines against dark sky, with lights that ran up their length.

Toby was managing the symptoms from the alcohol more than he was processing the alcohol.  She had no liver to do it herself.  She felt a bit like she had a headache.  She’d tried to sleep and failed, but that wasn’t it.  Her mind was a whirr.  The conversation with her parents.  It felt weird, that her dad had taken the angle he had.  Would he really be happy if she reached out to just anyone?  Was it a test, seeing if she’d take the opportunity to find people outside the family?  She’d wondered what had prodded her father to take the approach he had, and then she’d been looking at conversations he’d had with others.  Nothing direct, that she’d found.  Nothing like Uncle Ellis telling him to bring her in line.

Before the party, he’d spent a while looking at the other groups of teenagers, modded and not, in the wider area.

Noeh found his way to her.  With his approach, a few cousins who hadn’t even gotten to bed yet were looking in too.

This sort of advance and meeting weren’t unusual.  People brushed past each other in the vents, and indicated interest.  Oftentimes, the fact they chose that particular vent was an overture unto itself, answered with a hint.  Then they’d find the nearest dark tunnel, together.

It was more unusual and less subtle when she, as her parents had pointed out, tended to sleep further from home base.  Really, her reason was mostly that she liked seeing the sky like this.  The comfortable solitude and avoiding moments like the one that was about to happen with Noeh was secondary.

As he approached, she checked.  Noeh had glanced over all the recordings of her, his onboard picking out moments.  Figuring out her personality, for one thing.  But also looking at moments like her own explorations of her body, and when she’d been considering her body for the retrofit and had simulated a variety of body types and shapes, poking and prodding at herself.  Other moments.  When she’d watched certain videos.

So much of that had been experimental, seeing what the fuss was about.

It was normal, to look at a potential partner.  She’d looked through similar files for her cousins, and in general curiosity about Noeh, seeing what he’d been up to, and who.  Family members had looked at various moments of hers.  Her parents took opportunities to counsel her about being safe, or staying realistic and in bounds about the videos she watched.

Not a big deal.

But he’d looked at her retrofit before this one, back when she’d had the bad fit, that cheap body she hadn’t been able to tolerate in the end, before sinking all of her funds into the body before this one.  When she’d had the component pieces of her body pulled away, and she’d been on the table, reduced down to something small.  He’d glanced at that. He hadn’t even seemed to care that much.

That bothered her more than all of the other private moments put together.  That was a big deal.

It set a certain tone for when he appeared, body stretched across opening of the vent, feet at the bottom, hands gripping the lip where it stuck out at the top.  He flexed a little to show off.

She barely reacted as he drew in closer.  His clawed hand gripped the bars that gave her chest and the clothing she wore on her upper body a more feminine silhouette.

She made the decision then, and shook her head, turning her body away, until his grip was broken by the torque.

“Okay,” he whispered.  “Damn.  Came all this way too.”

“Didn’t ask you to.  No offense meant.  I wish you the best, in travels, with the families, or with ours, if you decide to stay, or marry any of us.”

“Who of you should I marry?” he asked.

“Keeley?” she responded. Keeley and him had spent a lot of time together, and it sure seemed like Keeley had ducked out of going to visit with the family at Howington Station to stay and spend time with him.

“So you’re not a complete idiot with these things,” he whispered back.  “Keeley’s great.”

That phrasing nettled her.  She twisted around to face him.

He’d brought up a video in the background, as if he was checking something, but he’d know she’d look, so maybe it was an intentional thing, to get a reaction from her, or poke at her.  Her spending time with Keeley.  Her watching and participating in videos and games.

He’d closed it before she could look deeper at whatever he was reading into it.

“What if I let you call me captain?” he asked.  Bringing that up.

Bristling, she shifted from a reclining position to crouching in the vent.

He threw up his hands, laughed, and then leaped backwards.  For the same piece of metal they’d slid down earlier that evening, on their way to the party.

She settled back down, but it was hard to relax.  The conversation with her dad had already had her mind whirring.  Now, feeling defensive, agitated, she couldn’t help but add to the pile in wondering what he’d been reading into things.  One embarrassing moment with Keely, where, dared by cousins, they’d ‘kissed’.  Meant nothing.  They’d been young enough that even the older cousins were figuring things out and playing doctor.  Videos where she’d picked out actresses she liked from Generation Light– people picked out to be overmarketed and recur as one age group’s cast of celebrities, to insert into movies.  More for her older cousin’s generation than her own.  She’d liked a couple and put them into every game and show she had Toby spin up for her.

None of it meant anything.

Toby, subtly, changed something in the interface.

[6 people are watching you.]

To…

[Seven people are watching you.]

The subtle adjustment from a single digit to a fully written out number-as-a-word was purely cosmetic, but it made the box in the corner of her vision longer.  She didn’t look at it for more than a moment, but took it as a cue.  She closed out the video and investigation, and watched Noeh for a bit as he continued his descent down to the station platform below.

Then she put on videos of ships taking off and landing on the dock.  Something she’d done many nights.

Trying to be boring.

[Four people are watching you.]

[Three people are watching you.]

It stuck at that.  She peeked.  One was Keely, who was asleep, had stirred half-awake when her name was mentioned, and was on her way back to falling asleep, leaving the view-window open into Winnifred’s own point of view.  Another was Price, one of the family busybodies.

The last was her dad.  He’d watched her poking through things.

“It doesn’t matter who or what you’re interested in,” he messaged her.

“I’m not.”

“It doesn’t matter,” he repeated.  “But marry a man, bear enough children for the family we can keep our culture going.  Do whatever you want on the side.  Ships, girls.”

“I’m tired,” she told him.  “You’re reading too much into things.  It’s annoying.”

“We’ll talk another time, then.”

She was left too agitated to even think about sleeping.

She gathered her belongings, because- she wasn’t sure why.  The feeling of being raw and vulnerable had lingered from the moment Noeh had glanced back at her on the table.  The blueprints of ships and engine schematics were an extension of herself she didn’t want anyone poking over.  She gathered the magnets that held them to the vent, folded them, and put them away.

Marry?  Find someone?  Work out some arrangement?

It wasn’t part of her plan or mental picture.  If she married, her spouse would own a share of things.  Would own her ship.  What other options were there?  A second-in-command on her ship, that she had trysts with?  For romance?  For the purely physical side?  That got messy.  It introduced weird power dynamics.

If she did what her father wanted, she’d marry someone on paper, for inter-family alliance purposes, plug a few wombs into her chest cavity to churn out the requisite three babies, and then leave?  Come and go?  What would having the kids mean, if she had a responsibility and expectation to pay for their prosthetics, until they were old enough to work?  Was she meant to attend official functions with her husband-on-paper, leave raising the kid to the wider family at whatever dock, hangar, or station she called home?  Or bring the kids onto the ship with her?  Would she have an intimate partner on the side?  Or as part of the family unit?  Untraditional, in a way that would get constant attention, but…

That was without getting into the issues of boys and girls, marriage, and breeding.  Which her family was very old fashioned about.  They felt they had to be.  That it was the only way to keep a culture alive.

It felt so hollow.

She hated that her family had made her feel this hollow.  Enough she couldn’t be still.

The indolent average had kids because they were bored, her father had said, once.  It was something to do, challenging and interesting, and even then, they took shortcuts.  That would only get worse, as superstructures were built out and filled up with people.  Some would only do it because they could.

The families did it because they had a legacy to preserve.  So they felt it was necessary and justified to exert a steady, light pressure.

More pressure, maybe, for outliers like Winnifred.

Everything put away, papers folded and packed into a pouch at her belt, magnets on either side to keep them compressed down, she descended.

Toby was quiet.  Which was good.  She felt like she’d lash out at anyone, even Toby, who prodded her right now.

Why couldn’t it be simple?

She reached the dock and tried to calm herself down.  There were four ships in dock.  A X56 Commodious, wide, with sockets at the side that would hold, transport, and drop off the heavy duty sorts of vehicles that tore a planet apart for resources.  The ship interior was crew, facilities and businesses for various construction crews to have a place to rest, retire, shop, live, bathe, seek entertainment.  Right now they were auctioning off space inside and transportation spots for the next long trip.  They’d drop off their ships and settle into a configuration with other similar ships, a kind of indoor city of interconnected ships that people could come and go from.

Less interesting, to Winnifred.

Two Tenures.  Not the sort of ship Winnifred would ever own or want to own, for very different reasons.  They were peacekeeping ships, for breaking up conflicts.  Narrow profiles with complex arrangements of fins and g-sails at the back end.  Fast in-atmosphere, for getting to a scene, with light armaments at the nose, and the rigging for holding drones of various types against the underbelly.  More dangerous than the guns.  The designations barely mattered.  Tenures had been hammered out ages ago and weren’t iterated on much.

A cover lifted off of a sphere on the side of one of the Tenures as she ventured too close, a visible fast-moving red tracking laser darting between her forehead and upper chest.  It was probably more warning than anything truly menacing, since the docks wouldn’t really allow it to operate here if there really was a gun ready to shoot her if she didn’t leave, but she decided to give it a wide berth anyway.

The last was a Tailwind-TX.  The golden goose, in some circles, but they were only called that because ‘golden chicken’ didn’t sound right.  Tailwinds had a reputation for being ships that the wealthy used if they couldn’t stand ‘roughing it’ on an actual ship, flying alongside something else to a destination, or they’d be ships that a captain would have in the hangar of a more colossal ship, for traveling around the planet.  It had enough engine at the ass to get places fast, Prominent G-sails fanned out at the sides for lower-cost maneuvering and flight, often altered from standard green to a gold or a sleek black for the cosmetics, and a body consisting of large, spacious quarters.  With the bulky central body, wings, flared ass, and the ‘head’ that was the cockpit, it really did have a silhouette like the chickens she saw in street markets.

The fact it ‘flew’ best by exiting the atmosphere and re-entering, like a chicken flapping madly to take flight, only to awkwardly land a few moments later, only enhanced into that image.  Too fat a profile to fly fast through atmosphere unless the owner really wanted to spend on the raw fuel.

Tailwinds had seen a rise in use in Winnifred’s lifetime, for reasons that had Winnifred interested now.  The body was meant to have roomy quarters, but with relatively little effort, those quarters could be swapped out for something functional.  It seemed to Winnifred that it was an excuse, for those who wanted the luxury, but couldn’t conscience it.

In this case, there was some clamping from a tug, where one of the four quarters would have been.  What Winnifred was interested in was the wing configuration around that.

It had the engine at the back to be an awkward tug, but it was so awkward.  The g-sails at the side had to fold up and down so they’d be sticking up purely vertically, and would be flush with whatever it was attached to.  That limited applications, and probably meant the application was already in mind.  The wings at the far side came together, sticking out horizontally, to give it that maneuverability.

“Hey!”

She startled.  Toby flashed an indicator arrow, and she turned, meeting the eyes of someone who was close to one of the landing gear legs.  The leg, once extended out from the body, had a whole slew of things, ranging from ladders to cables, out there and available.

The young woman, twenty or so, had clearly picked out her most rugged clothes, which were still nicer than anything Winnifed had owned.  Loose white shirt, to contrast skin, and skintight pants tucked into boots.

“Where can I connect a hose?” the woman asked.

Silent, startled, she pointed a claw-tip at the nearest station.

Then, remembering her dad’s suggestion that she reach out and connect, she decided to meet the woman there.  The station was basically a five foot by five foot panel in the ground with some nozzles sticking out, ringed by a yellow warning square that provided enough warning that people wouldn’t trip over it.  In more trafficked areas, the fixtures would recede into the ground when not in use.  Water, some external power, sewage dump…

The woman didn’t even know which fixture the hose connected to.  Winnifred used her tail to indicate.  “New to this?”

“Yes.  My friend’s dad owns an operation on a few of the planets we’re tearing apart.  We were just on Cecrops.  Watching, touring, flying around looking at scenery.  Some natural, some where the work’s been done, which is interesting in its own way.  Or I thought so.  Another of my friends didn’t.”

“It’s interesting, yeah.”

The woman smiled.  “I got to blow up a mountain.”

“That’s fun,” Winnifred said.  “Careful when you use that.  It kicks.  Turn the connector part…”

She indicated with her tail again.  Still keeping a bit of a distance.

“…that way.  Yeah.  Or it’ll knock you off your feet and you’ll be running over to turn things off, hoping it doesn’t hit you.”

“Thank you.  My friends would never let me live it down.”

“What are you rinsing?”

The woman pointed up at the belly of the ship.  Dust caked it.

“That comes down on your head as mud,” Winnifred warned.  “It’ll ruin your shirt.  And hair.  Possibly your day.”

“I don’t know much about any of this,” the woman said.

“Also,” Winnifred said, pointing.  “That spatter by that one hole in the side there?  It’s not mud.  Whoever was flying this thing decided to dump trash and waste into space, to save a few lux on disposal here.  You don’t want that on you, especially.”

The woman clicked her tongue.  “I wanted to be useful, as thanks.  I didn’t think it’d be this hard.”

“I could loan you coveralls, if you’re making a day of this.  It’s not gross.  There’s no body odor.  I don’t sweat, since I don’t have…”

The woman’s eyes widened.  “I saw you were modded, obviously, but I didn’t figure… wow.  Pretty punk.”

Winnifred, crouching by the station, shrugged.  “Offer stands.”

The woman’s friend was coming outside.  Another woman, skinnier, with dark blonde hair.  The same white shirt, but she wore a jacket, and had nicer boots.

“Do you work here then?  Live here?”

“Both,” the friend answered, before Winnifred could.  “Don’t legitimize them.”

“Legitimize?”

“They’re homeless, ducking around the docks, trying to convince you to hire them instead of robots.  Then once they’re inside, they steal, or scam you.  Sometimes even fuck with you, hold your ship hostage.”

“That’s not all of us.  Or even most of us.  It’s slander from the old days.”

“It’s enough of you.”

“This isn’t like you,” the woman Winnifred had been talking to said.

“They mod babies.”

The first woman gave Winnifred a curious look.

“Don’t you?”

She could answer, say she never had, but she knew what the follow up would be.  Would she?  If she had one?

“I’m going to go.”

“You’re not victims.  You’re not special.  You’re edgy, angsty mod-knobs who got together and thought that if you got enough of your kids into it early, pushed enough boundaries, you could call your style a ‘culture’.”

[You should say something,] Toby told her.

She didn’t want to.  Because if she pushed herself to think of something, all there was, was…

“They’re my family.”

“You’re an embarrassment.  Stay clear of my ship.”

Winnifred tried to think of something else to say, and then decided to go.

➨

The incident bothered her.  Lingered.  She wasn’t sure if it was the last straw among several, or something clearly identifiable to be upset at, that let her redirect other anxieties and feelings.

She’d been working for years at studying engineering when she wasn’t working extra shifts.  Trying to find a way forward.  She wanted a ship, and she’d work her way there as an engineer, and that was a dream she couldn’t even talk to Toby about.  Onboards were open access to anyone who wanted to look in, as a side consequence of Intelligences being mandated by law to be something anyone could audit.  Which the companies wanted, because it drove engagement and helped them further refine the onboards they had elsewhere.  She couldn’t shut people out without specific filings, and getting approved for those filings was a whole other business, that invited more scrutiny than even having family peeking in at her exchanges with Toby, or looking at records of moments throughout her life.  Like her on the table, just a head without a nose or jaw, a partial neck, and a collarbone.

Her thoughts crossing that moment made her practically squirm, anxious and restless.

Could something be a trauma if it hadn’t bothered her as much back when it happened?

It felt like the subject of marriage and kids was the next shoe, poised and waiting to drop.  That if she worked her tail off and saved up, got and worked the engineering job to get on a ship, a curveball would be thrown her way, in the way of fresh expectations.  What she wanted would be snatched away from her again.

Easier to be angry at that woman who owned the golden chicken than at… that.  A situation she couldn’t even fully wrap her head around.

“Candy?” Noeh asked her.

She glanced at him and the history of the candy before accepting.  It wasn’t drugs.  Legitimate candy from a machine at the part of the docks where people called for and got rides.

She took it.  It came in a capsule of metal, and pressing it against the side of her face, the little vent opened, sucked in the contents, and then closed.

“If you were going to fuck with their ship, what would you do, to ground it for a while?”

What would she do?

She could study the Tailwind, the chicken ship, and work backwards from what she’d been doing in her lessons.  What would make the biggest, most complicated puzzle?

User error?  Messing with the ship’s owner, who was also the pilot?

That was complicated, and she preferred questions of engineering.

The ‘wings’, with the g-sails, and how they worked and folded around the clamp.  Replacement parts for a custom setup like that were tough to get, probably custom-ordered and made by agents few enough in number to have a backlog of orders, and it would hamper flight enough that the chicken couldn’t land comfortably and reliably on the sort of rough terrain that a planet like Cecprops would have.  If it could even take off.

Noeh was studying her.

“I wouldn’t,” she said.

“No?”

“Leave it alone.”

She darted off, back toward her sanctuary.  She’d curl up in a vent with puzzles about fixing engines.  Not sabotage.

She’d feel better if she focused on her tests and getting engineering certification.

“Toby, love.”

[You get most affectionate when you’re most upset.  Are you sure you don’t want to talk?]

“Later.  For now I want distraction.  Is the next slate of tests interesting?”

[We are dangerously close to the grindstone testing.]

“What is that?  You’ve made ominous reference to it before.”

[It’s rote and routine testing, for reliability, and making sure you have the composure and love for what you’re doing.  It’s boring and hard for a long time, on purpose.  A lot of employers will look at your grindstone test results, to see if you have what it takes to stick a job through.]

“Can we postpone it?  I’m not in the mood.”

[For a little while.  But part of it is that you have to be able to do the work despite your mood.]

“I know, but…”

[We’ll postpone it.]

➨

On the day Noeh and his group of visitors left, Keeley going with, a new crop of visiting youths from other families were supposed to arrive.  They didn’t.

It wasn’t just at their dock.  People could go home, or stay if they were visiting and had found someone to stay with but they were being asked to stay.  All movement was frozen.  Families were relatively quiet on what was happening, talking among themselves.

Winnifred had to piece it together from what other families were saying, because hers was very quiet.

She soon realized why.

A drone, unmanned, hacked, had crashed into the Tailwind-TX.  Directly into that custom wing job, that maneuvered the wing around the clamp setup.  The wing had nearly come off.  The ship, sure enough, had been grounded.

It sat like that for eight hours.

The entire family seemed to wait in suspense, seeing what the response would be.

James Oden, father of the Tailwind-TX’s owner, a man who ran seven mining and resource collection setups across three planets, filed suit against the Griffey Docks.

The other shoe wasn’t any insistence that Winnifred marry and have kids, paying for the kids mods, at the cost of her own dreams.  It was this.

The amount the suit was filed for was hidden.  It was for Oden and Griffey Docks to work out between one another.  But it sure looked like it was in the range of ten figures.

“I didn’t want this,” Winnifred told her parents.  “I didn’t do this.  It was-”

“Say nothing, claim no fault, assign no blame.  It won’t help anything,” her mother said.

Winnifred fell silent.

“These things happen,” her father said.  “With resentment against us, they’re always looking for an excuse.  Whether accident or intentional, they got one.

Griffey Docks, five minutes after he said that, evicted Winnifred and her extended family from the premises.  They would be trespassing if they were found there.

She could only watch as dominoes fell down.  Predictable, almost, but just enough that she couldn’t know for sure or have any confidence that something would or wouldn’t happen.

The dock owner had friends and allies, with whom he shared information, did business with, and traded employees with.  Two other dock owners decided now was the time to act in solidarity.  Melville Cap and Sherman Station evicted the families living there.

Winnifred and her family, and the families at those stations were meant to leave their homes here today.  Technically, they’d never officially lived here.  They could appeal to the block, but the facts didn’t favor them.

Other docks soon began their own discussions about the ‘dock rats’ living on their premises.  With three notable docks taking action, there were rolling effects.  Winnifred’s family had to go somewhere.  Would that multiply numbers at that destination?  Multiply problems?

Would other people, tied into the politics of all of this, cause problems?  Oden’s hundreds of millions of workers, that would be leaving the planet in a few months, and coming through any convenient dock they could find?

Two more families were banned and evicted.

Howington Station was one of the largest families.  After those two additional bans, and much deliberation, they passed on word.

The same thing Winnifred’s family had put into dance.

They’d fight for their place on the docks.

1.5.B – CONTROL

“Quinn, my girl.  Want to see some actual, real life aliens!?” A called out, arms spread.

Quinn didn’t seem to know how to react to the enthusiasm, or the incoming hug, and rolled her eyes a little, approaching, until A got close enough to fold her into a hug, rocking their bodies side to side.

[Hello,] Quinn’s onboard said.

[Hi,] Basil replied.

[Hi,] V.O. said.

Quinn’s onboard had been a little curt since the last incident, which Quinn hadn’t been there for.  V.O., Vince’s onboard, was easier to get along with.

“Missed you,” A said, hugging Quinn with one arm.  The others in the group were catching up.  Vince, Cowrie, and the musclebound Nos.  “We low-slugged for a while and then raw-dogged some music.”

“I still don’t get what low-slugging is,” Quinn said.

“You know what plugging is?”

“Yeah.  Promotion.”

“Marketing, getting the word out, doing someone’s word of mouth.  Slugging is the opposite.”

“Demotion?”

“Subversion.  Programming people.”

[It’s illegal.]

“Now I’m seeing why I wasn’t allowed to go.”

“It’s a little illegal, but everyone does it.  Gotta find the right moments and people, say the right things, insert it into the public consciousness,” A said.

“Or do it one step removed,” Vince added.  “Get something with a bad image tied to it out there, next to the thing you want to slug.”

“Which was?” Quinn asked.

“Bumping Intelligence-generated music down, so we can get real music out there.  We had a small audience,” A said.

[Quinn is a bit more sensitive than usual and felt left out.  We know it wasn’t your or A’s fault, but…]

[Quinn’s parents made the call.  Got it.  We’ll adjust.]

Quinn had grown out her hair for a bit, and dressed more feminine when dressing up for this occasion – a body-conforming pleated knit.  Unlike A, who had spent a while with no strict identity one way or the other, only really trying on a role in games and interactives, before sliding comfortably into one role, Quinn went back and forth.  In Basil’s observations, Quinn was most often sensitive and withdrawn as a girl, but liked the closeness with A.  Quinn’s onboard seemed sure Quinn would always be going back and forth, as mood struck.

The complexities of a pair of young teenagers finding themselves.  All of the rest of their peer group were doing something similar, though the ones without onboards had to get nanotech injections every time they wanted to make a change.

“You want to sing with us?” Vince asked Quinn.  “I’ve seen you sing, you’re good.”

“My onboard helps.  Throat and vocal control.”

“You’re good,” Vince said.

“But-” Cowrie started.

“But?” A asked.

Cowrie was a colorful kid with hair like a sea urchin, painted in three pastel tones, and a combination of mods and altered biology that put her heart on clear display, skin, muscle, fat layer, surrounding organs, and spine all rendered more transparent than clear glass, if viewed straight-on.  Otherwise, it was more like regular glass.  She wore a top that let her show off the effect, with bands of fabric in sunset hues covering her shoulders, chest and sides of her stomach, and little else.  Her shorts were small, black, and lightly studded in fingertip-wide dots, each a different color.  It was meant to lightly offend the eyes, to grab attention, and then hold it with the heart imagery.

A, who’d stopped in her tracks to face the other girl, was different.  Her hair was long enough it could trail on the ground if she hadn’t tied it up at the back, and the tying meant it was only a handspan short of brushing floor.  Natural waves were strategically placed and set to keep the hair from getting tripped over or getting in the way.  A’s preference was to keep it simple, and hold attention by earning it.  Here, she wore a simple white top and sandpaper textured black pants with simple boots.  For her, body language was a priority, and her body language conveyed a lot in this moment.  Zero tension in her body, but footing and a level gaze that suggested she could go after Cowrie, verbally, or with a slap.  Her eyebrow was arched with the question.

“Image matters,” Cowrie said.

“I like Quinn’s image,” A said.

“You’re biased.”

“And you’re singling out my friend.  What does it matter if Quinn plays a few songs with us?”

“Around people?  Audiences?”

“Yeah,” A replied.

“I don’t mind.  I’d rather be on the sidelines,” Quinn said.

“I mind,” A said, to Cowrie.

“Okay.  This is a lot of hassle for a single ‘but’.”

“Okay,” A said.

Vince motioned in the direction of the building.  “Want to get bonus marks?”

“Yeah.  Let’s go meet some aliens, woo,” Cowrie said, with zero enthusiasm.

[Thank you,] Basil told V.O.

The onboard sent a single confirmation as a response.  It was hard to know if that was the equivalent of a thumbs up, or V.O. being standoffish.  Basil had asked outright a few times, and the onboard had dodged the question.  It seemed to prefer the ambiguity, and Vince, who watched all the interactions, hadn’t said a word one way or the other.

He hadn’t gone through the toddler twos and threes with an onboard, getting it in his early teens, and was much more likely to go with the flow or accept what it said as if it was a rule, not a suggestion from a computer who knew him well.

They walked up the steps of the science center- an elaborate building that took full advantage of the cabling that extended from it to the clouds, allowing it to seem to float, less dependent on there being solid footing and weight-bearing architecture below a given segment.  That configuration meant that new installations could be quite literally flown in and installed.  The floors of superstructure above were successively less and less enclosed, making it seem as if the science center sat at the base of an architectural crater, with an open view of clouds above.

“I really don’t mind,” Quinn said, confidentially, to A.  “I’m not that interested in the music.”

“It’s the principle of the thing, Quinn,” A said, voice quiet, leaning in closer to her friend, making a hand gesture she’d seen in a game.  “Have to draw the line somewhere.”

“I feel more awkward now.”

“They’ll get over it.”

The science building had a public access main floor that served as a museum and a place for showcases.  This particular block, which was a three hour trip from home, out into the atmosphere and down on the other side of the planet, was fairly strict about companies using the showcases to self-promote.  It kept things ‘stately’, which was the word several reviews had used, and it meant thing were untethered enough from various interests and influences that they could claim some uncomplicated educational benefit.

For this group, it meant an afternoon excursion counted as much as two weeks doing tests.  The sheer number of other kids and teenagers around suggested it was similar.

“Oh wow, no ads,” Quinn remarked.

It was something.  The area was protected, with no alerts, ads, and only a dozen or so people tried to get attention for their dancing or modeling.  Music would get people kicked out.  A few people tried and some kids shouted, but they were blips of noise in an otherwise quiet environment.

In A’s body, a tension that had become the norm relaxed, as they absorbed the mood of the place.

In the center of the main hall were several displays that showed the various arrangements of planets in the belt that were in consideration.

The issue was so big picture, with so many implications, that, while war didn’t happen anymore, the intensity with which different groups fought for different belt forms had threatened a schism, with planets threatening to refuse business and even ship landings for specific businesses and groups.  Each of those dynamics circled back to impact the variables for the different arrangements – like mining being less efficient, and might have even been designed to.  Things had stalled out.

In a weird way, Basil had been given an extra lease on life.  With things stalled out, enough customers were waiting to see what was developed during the big stall in business that they wanted to wait… and customers had pressured Elabre Systems to hold off on any big changes.  Now the sword of Damocles hung over Basil’s head.

Not so different than the arrangements of planets, floating above in zero-G.

Things had deadlocked briefly, and much heated discussion was being had over which arrangement was best.  Would they have two belts, then three, or complete this belt by filling it in as much as possible, and then extend the cabling that supported superstructures out between planets?  The latter option required a few advancements and preparations, like the repositioning of the Arcesso engines, and terminating planetary rotation, or have rails that the cable would attach to, that went around the planet. The benefit was that it was a lot easier to fly between celestial bodies and installations in a single, dense belt than to wait for the right alignment if moving from a horizontal belt to a specific body in the vertical one.

The kids walked around the displays, which were physical and floating in the otherwise dark main hall.  In one, massive arrangements of lenses had been erected, and reflected the sun’s light for the planets where rotation had been stalled, with solid installations above and below the floating arrangement that showed how superstructures would move air around to help– not dissimilar to how pressure and atmosphere were moved up and down now.

By another, an example of the rail that would go around the planet was drawn in miniature, an offshoot of the cabling that stabbed up from the science building exerted a similarly miniaturized force on the rail, showcasing how the engineering of it would work.

The interleaving horizontal and vertical belts were a more complicated series of issues.  The planets that passed through gaps between planets would exert a lot of varying pressures on the superstructures, water systems, atmospheres, and more, and while it was a tidier solution on the surface, it introduced scalability concerns and the slowness of getting between one planet and one on the other belt would slow resource harvesting… which was its own scalability concern.

The end of the hall had the third solution, which was to do one, then switch later.  It doubled as a showcase of the Arcesso engines, and a number of children were gathered around, watching the light show, as it showcased how the planets would be moved from one arrangement to the next.

Cowrie raised her hands, touching the aurora-like blurs.  She flashed a smile at a small child who stared, slack-jawed, at Cowrie’s openly visible heart.  She shrieked as Nos picked her up, lifting her over his head.

[The exhibits are to the left.]

“This way,” A called out to the pair.

Nos turned.  Cowrie wriggled, legs kicking enough that a few bystanders ducked to avoid being clipped.

[If we’re not attentive to the exhibits, it won’t count for as much.]

“What have you been up to?” A asked Quinn.

“You could look and see.”

“Or I could ask.”

“Some dance.  Some reading.  There’s a kind of meditation, where you go out into nature and sit for a while.  Mark out a circle, sit inside it, and… get to know yourself.”

“That sounds very you.  Would you simulate it?”

“I was thinking I shouldn’t.”

[It’s hard to find any nature that doesn’t have thousands of people tromping through it.]

“If I worked, though?” Quinn asked.  “And rented out enough space that nobody’s passing within eyesight or earshot?”

“Expensive,” A said.  “What if you went out to one of the mining planets?  Lots more open space.”

“I like trees, though.  Or field.  I’m okay working two years, earning enough to rent some nature.”

[How long?] V.O. asked.

“Three weeks or so.”

“Would you have your onboard on?”

“I’d ask them to go quiet.  All systems still.  No display.  I looked into it, and I can petition the company.  I might be able to skirt Intelligence law and stop all connections, if they’re not doing anything.”

[What do you think about that?]

[Might be interesting.  I’ll come back to a lot to do, if so.]

[It’s a little bit like returning to day one, in a way.]

They passed the exhibits which showed a planet, pulled by the Arcesso engine.  The life before.  The life after.  The damage done.  The image of the planet, covered in shades of blue and teal, each point a population center, and then the scattered dots after.  Torn to shreds by small particle radiation.

Past that, the displays.

“I thought it would be more impressive,” A said.

The exhibit was real alien life.  It grew on rocks like lichen, and spiderweb so thick it was almost crystalline, with geometric and fractal patterns throughout.

“It looks neat,” Quinn said.

“Did we kill everything big, and force it to start over from the simple stuff?”

[It hit an early point and stalled,] Quinn’s onboard said.  [Hexalateral life.  Complex life had too hard a time developing out of the six-faced baseline, and simpler life forms, if they ever arose, got outcompeted.  It reached a self sustaining phase, too hostile to any new upstarts, and stayed there.]

“Wouldn’t it be cool if, by yanking it over here from a galaxy far, far away, we gave some of those upstarts a chance?” A asked.

[We’ll see how things evolve over the next few hundred years.  In the meantime, we’re very careful about interfering,] Basil said.  [Though some say we leave enough waste in space and scatter enough DNA out there, something will get out there.]

“I’m rooting for you, upstarts,” A said.  “What do we call them?  Sub-sixes?”

“That’s a good name,” Quinn said.

“There’s more interesting stuff this way,” Vince said.

They passed displays that showed the effects of small particle radiation, its short half life, and interactive displays of how particles that existed for fractions of a second could stack up as the person changing variables adjusted for distance traveled and faster travel.  Other displays indicated how the hexalateral life forms had inspired new cryptography.

The other wing was brightly lit, and had the aliens from Inuus II.  The lighting was bright enough that many were taking the free eye protection.  Basil took care of that for A.  The surfaces of her eyes went dark as she adjusted to the light level.

As static and sterile as the Hexalateral exhibit of the aliens from Consentes had been, Inuus II was active.  The alien lifeforms were varied, violent, and constantly moving in their enclosures, with metabolisms, reflexes, and a general rate of operation that made humans, dogs, and birds look like slugs.

“I’ve seen these guys in videos and stuff,” Nos said.  He had Cowrie sitting on his shoulders, now.

[The Inui were an accident, and we did a lot of damage bringing them here.  We killed an estimated thousand and ninety-nine out of every two thousand,] Quinn’s onboard explained.  It seemed to enjoy the teaching part, and Basil certainly didn’t mind.  [We might never know the degree to which they were civilized, aware, or intelligent.  We’re still studying them.]

The Inui tended to have hard shells, segmented bodies, and jittery unpredictable movement, but the configurations were unique to each.  One that seemed surprisingly close to human paced along the hard barrier, measuring its steps in time with a passing family.  When they moved out of its range, it fixated its attention on Nos and Cowrie.  It seemed fascinated by how tall they were when put together, head slowly tilting and turning to see them from new angles, before jittering, and trying anew.

All features like eyes and mouths were recessed behind protective carapace, peeking through slits.  It had no expression to betray.

[Inui can be described as one species, or a population of purely unique individuals.  As a general rule, they impregnate by traumatic insemination, wounding prey with natural weapons and then fertilizing the wounds.  Eggs or nascent young develop in the prey, slowing them gradually, while opening wounds wide enough for hunter to get to deeper vitals.  The hunter then finishes off its prey in order of weakest and slowest to strongest, and once it has eaten its fill, protects the corpse or still-living ‘mother’ of its most enduring prey until the eggs hatch.  The offspring are algorithmically iterated on, based on the configurations and genetics of its parents, the hunter and the prey.  Each resulting child is more distinct from each of its siblings than a human is from a mole rat, but it maintains clear inspiration from each parent.]

“Can’t get away from algorithms even if we go halfway across the fucking universe, can we?” Vince asked.

A was silent, quietly observing.

The Inui that was closest to the display was more akin to a scorpion, with a tail that was drawing inspiration from its environment for its shape- the people on the other side of the clear barrier.  The ‘body’ of the scorpion was circular, with short legs that almost tucked in underneath the disc of its body.  That circular body broke apart into pieces with the ceramic-like shell protecting the resulting gaps, stretching enough that the small legs could find purchase on the higher rocks when moving to higher ground.

It was halfway through this process when the tail, with its human-like silhouette, arm-like limbs, neck and ‘head’, slammed into the barrier, plates shifting and head pulling apart, to reveal the stinger and the musculature that drove it- chaotic, hair-like strands covered in what looked like a caking of salt.  The boom as it hit the barrier sounded like a gunshot, on their side of the glass.  Considering it was sound masked, because the Inui were loud, that was something.

“For me?” Nos asked.

It slammed its tail into the barrier again, aiming for him.

“I’m a worthy breeding partner,” Nos said, looking up at Cowrie.

Cowrie leaned in to whisper something in his ear.  Probably something that would get her fined, if she said it out loud.

[I think it’s the fact it’s two of you put together that stands out,] Basil noted.

[To Inui, every other living thing is a potential mate.  Research is being done to see the degrees to which they interact with species from our heliosphere.]

[The Nos-cowrie piggyback beast could volunteer,] Basil suggested.

A snorted.

Both Basil and Quinn’s onboard were using nearby speakers, which let Cowrie and Nos in on the conversation- as well as a few bystanders, which included an older man who shot them weird looks.

Nos groaned, “The onboards are hazing me.”

“Hazing you both.  If it thinks you’re one living thing,” A said.  “I wonder if you could do weird acrobatics or contortions, and seem unique and effective that way.  Get their attention.”

[Many speculate that because this form of natural selection is so fraught, it may be something engineered.  By the Inui themselves, perhaps, or by another species that felt it important, for biological, cultural, or ideological reasons, to set this in motion.]

“Which we might have accidentally genocided,” Vince said.

[They might still be alive.  Exploration into Inuus II is ongoing.]

“And slowing everything else the heck down, right?”

“Wouldn’t it be cool if you could have your ‘finding yourself’ time in alien nature?” A asked.

“With the Inui?” Quinn asked.  “Do you secretly hate me?”

“With the Hexalaterals.”

[From Consentes,] Basil supplied.

“Volcanic rock and crystalline moss?  For weeks?  Even if it was allowed… trees,” Quinn said.

“You want the trees,” A said.

Quinn nodded.

“What about the tree farms at the mining colonies?  They set those up, then leave them alone.  Mostly.  You wouldn’t even have to pay for the privilege.  Or is that too artificial?  Rows and columns?”

Quinn made a so-so gesture.  “I’d still be worried some worker would have to stop in to check tree health and they’d go, ‘what is this maniac doing, sitting naked in a circle in my tree plantation?'”

“You’d be naked?” Nos asked, suddenly interested.

A seemed to get defensive, putting her body between the muscular goon and her best friend.

“I’ll miss you, if you really are gone for weeks,” A said.

Their meandering pace through and between the exhibits was taking them out of this wing and into a complementary one, which was more theoretical.  They weren’t exactly soaking in the science, but they were conversing with it and showing interest, entertaining ideas.  Basil formulated a good pitch for how things had gone so far and submitted it for the education system.  It was received, contributing to their testing status.

The next hall was a break from the glare of the simulated Inuus II atmosphere.  There were refreshments at the intersection, with a line, and a lux cost for an abbreviated wait.

Nobody minded the slightly longer line, so the group settled there.

“Would you do something like what I’m thinking of?” Quinn asked.

“Do you want me to lose my mind?” A asked, back.

“What if you lost it in a good way?”

“Do you want me to lose it in a good way?  Do you want me to change that much?  Do you think there’s something wrong with me?” A asked.

It was a back and forth with rules that they’d engaged in since they were small.  Was Quinn really that insecure, in the moment?

[Basil.]

Basil took notice of V.O.’s message, and then immediately took stock of everything, double checking all processes.

In the noise of constant system updates and data was a mid-level message, that changes past a certain level were restricted and might be audited after the fact.  Which meant Basil had to check to see why… and the why was that they’d lost all contact with the central servers.

[Quinn’s Onboard, do you have access to your company’s servers?]

[No.]

Basil immediately reached for A’s adrenals to produce adrenaline and cortisol.  He increased heart rate.

[Isn’t that overdoing it?]

“Woah,” A murmured.

“What?” Cowrie asked.

“My onboard just jumpscared me, kicking me into overdrive for no reason.”

“V.O.’s taking his cue,” Vince said.  “I wasn’t scared though.”

[Something’s weird,] Basil reported.  It was spur of the moment, but he decided to keep it to silent messages, onboard to onboard.  In A’s field of vision, to be read, not heard.  It left A’s hearing open for all possible sound input.

He compared and shared notes with the other two onboards in their little group, each of them focusing on something different.  Basil checked floor plans, maps, and scanned surroundings, cross-checking faces against his internal databases.

[All of the wall consoles are disconnected from the wider superstructure.]

[Let’s move.]

“Something’s wrong, come,” A murmured, to Cowrie and Nos.

People at the consoles were starting to notice.  A few moved to other sections of wall and support column, where a tap or a connection from someone’s lens to the right point on just about any of the surfaces could bring up the systems.  A few more people than usual were standing off to one side, blinking rapidly, eyes moving, as they tried to make outgoing calls.

Basil navigated them toward the point on the floor plan that gave them the most options.  If they needed to get somewhere secure, in case of a natural event, like some collapse of the cabling.  Or if they needed to evacuate.  Two options there.

V.O. sent directions to a video feed, in-building.  Basil began to watch.  A watched too, in a video feed that existed outside her normal field of vision, but still transmitted to the brain.  She wanted her eyes, to study the surroundings.

A woman had collapsed in the entrance hall, near the model belt arrangements.  She screamed, thrashing.  The primal sound of the screaming was bad enough that Basil didn’t think A should hear it, so he dampened it.

It seemed as if Basil, V.O., and Quinn’s onboard were thirty seconds to a minute ahead of the crowd at large.  A few outliers were already looking for escape routes, trying to warn bystanders, but mostly, the crowd was now at point A, realizing something was wrong.

The woman falling and screaming had been what happened just as the lockdown and loss of connection to the outside hit.

Then the crowd, gathering around, people helpless… Basil saw a reaction, paused the feed, and went back to make sense of it, while keeping another feed running.  The people in the crowd began to drop, fourteen individuals within a second, then more.  What he’d seen was a flinch.  And if he mapped out how they were flinching- they acted as if stung.

He drew out a map, with possible directions that each response could have come from.

V.O., looking at the same scene, pointed out something else.

A man, at one side of the room, holding an umbrella.  Not unusual, given the clouds overhead.

[A single smart bullet, that triggers at a set distance, spraying the crowd with fragments,] Basil observed.

“Someone attacked the crowd?” A asked.

Nos and Cowrie, out of the loop, were only just catching up to the gravity of it all.  Their eyes went wide.

[Multiple someones are attacking the building,] Basil clarified.  There was no other way that made sense.

“Warn everyone,” Quinn said.  “Should we shout?”

[That draws attention to you.  Gets you shot.  Let me.]

Basil pushed the video he’d put together, illustrating the nature of the attack, to the panels and consoles throughout the room.

The science center didn’t want to let him.

[Override.  I don’t have any special privileges, I don’t have any powers.  But this is a matter of public safety.  Run it by the most important person in the building.]

[The first victim.  Loren Long.  Prominent educator.]

Basil could see the feed.

One of the woman’s arms and one of her legs was longer.  Narrow, needle-like spikes stood out from her flesh at the shorter leg’s knee.  She had already screamed hard enough that blood vessels had burst at the side of her neck and in her eyes.

One by one, panels in the dark concession area began to light up, as they showed the feed from the brighter area.

V.O. passed updated information to Basil, who passed it to the feed.

It seemed as if he’d been granted permissions.  There was barely any wait time.

V.O. had studied the crowd.  Every person with a long handled cane, umbrella, or other device was highlighted in yellow, the possible weapons marked out.  A few of the markings were more extreme, because there was something more tactile about the handles.  Umbrellas with chunky grips that might have buttons.  A cane with the same.

As the feed updated, and the crowd reacted, now running for the nearest exits they knew about, some panels turned into what were effectively mirrors.  Reflecting the room, with the offending people highlighted.

[Mark them out as possibles.  Only possible, we don’t want innocents falsely accused and hurt.]

[Go,] Basil urged A.  He highlighted a route.  The crowd was already headed toward the known doors.  Basil marked out one way to the staff catwalk above the displays, with a route to the window.

The crowd surged.  People took action, running over to stop all the marked individuals with potential weapons.  Not all, but enough.  A few were knocked to the ground, disarmed.

Two in the room managed to open fire before people reached them.  One pull of the trigger to shoot.  Another to trigger the radial blast.  Over and over.

Similar things were happening throughout the building.

[Stay low, use the railing for cover.]

A was breathing hard, terrified, now.  They ran, heads ducked low, for the ramp up to the catwalk.  It was dark, disguised, and gated to be staff only, but they could climb over the gate.

Basil quietly passed V.O. and Quinn’s onboard the countermeasures he was already preparing, in case they got hurt.  He sent it out to other onboards in the concession area, but wasn’t sure what their response would be.  Maybe they were already planning something.

The first people who’d been shot here in the concession area were now screaming.

Loren, the first person in the building to be shot, was continuing to physically distort.  The fine needles stuck fast to floor and a nearby display that her elongated arm had brushed against, and, if Basil’s unstated suspicions were right about the nature of the attack, drank them for nutrients, to draw into the body, so it could be changed further.  Fourteen individuals were at the first stage of physical distortion: jaws, necks, arms, legs, and spines stretching out, the first needle-like growths appearing.  Another handful were just about to reach that stage, or just starting it.

A awkwardly pushed her head toward Quinn’s armpit.  Putting herself between Quinn and the railing.  Between Quinn and the most likely source of any gunfire.

She was a character.  She could be impulsive, she pushed at so many of the boundaries that were set, in a way that could infuriate Addy, Landon, Basil, or any authority assigned to her.

She could see what that was.  Basil wouldn’t shut off the feed, and even if he tried, she’d see soon, here.  She knew what the danger was, and her instinct was to shield Quinn.  Fighting her on that would only make things worse, and make their group slower to leave.

[Watch your steps, quiet,] V.O. said.

“All the sneaking out was practice, huh?” Vince asked.

That was another aspect to V.O. that Basil hadn’t given enough credit.  That V.O. was Vince’s, not his parents’.  It shaped the onboard.

“Wish I snuck out more,” Quinn said, with a heaviness of emotion in her voice that drew A’s full attention for a second, with a searching look following.

The crowd was winning the struggle against the suspected gunmen.  The ones who had thrown aside umbrellas and canes were treated more gently.  The ones that weren’t- if they were innocent, maybe they would forgive.

They moved along the catwalk, in shadows where staff members could pass without distracting the people below.

As they approached within an armspan of the window, someone came through it.  Their weapon wasn’t disguised as an umbrella.  The man wore a simple black shirt and textured pants.

And Nos, in the dark and a step behind for so long, seized his moment, lunging.

He didn’t account for the second person that might be coming through.  He was shot in the side, lost his grip, and was thrown against the railing.

The man he’d pushed back aimed for their group, just over their heads, and pulled the trigger twice in quick succession, eyes closed, face turned away.  He’d be caught in the spray.

Six sharp stings marked the entry of nanotech weaponry into A’s back.  One hit the lower spine, and sent a lightning stab of pain to her toetips.

She let out a choked shriek.

[You’re okay, we’re okay.  Quinn’s okay.  Trust!]

A let out a whimper, fingers curling, trying to find some grip or creature comfort in the metal of the catwalk.

Basil’s first priority was to catch the offending particles.  It had to be nanotech, so he’d anticipated the attack, and prepared countermeasures, releasing some into blood for other systems throughout the body to pick up and use, if needed.  He’d held the rest back until he knew where to concentrate them, and now he knew.

Within a minute, he had one of the offending invaders in his grip and was studying it, pulling it apart to figure out what its simple, initial program was for.  Install, expand, same as Basil at the early stages.  Build coils for picking up ambient signal, await further instruction.

Blocking ambient signal would be impossible.  Finding a source was beyond him, and he doubted there was a singular one.

He repurposed an existing coil himself, to see what the instructions that were floating out there, in the noise, might be.

Pretty much as it seemed.

Pain.  Pain, and bypassing all the things a person could do to cope with it.  No passing out, no production of natural painkillers, no going into shock.  The list went on.  Until everything that could hurt was hurting, on and off, unpredictably.

It didn’t, as Basil did, stop where the brain started, or keep that space sacrosanct. What happened there was too complicated for Basil, and not something he was familiar with.

And it set up other parts of the body to harvest and repurpose resources, to grow, extend, and collect resources to grow more.

Loren, in the entrance hall, had a bulging back and right shoulder, flesh stretched translucent in its thinness, looking like detritus and tiny pieces of junk metal had been pushed beneath it.  Except they hadn’t been- they were growing and being built out from under and inside the skin.

“Talk to me,” A subvocalized.  “Don’t keep things from me.  I want to know what’s happening.”

[It’s a mess.  I’m fighting off the nanotech.]

The attackers were immune to their own nanotech weaponry.  The ones who’d been dragged to the ground were fighting their way free of people who were insensate with pain, standing, and holding weapons ready.  Some looked for and aimed for those who’d found hiding places.

[We’re losing.]

“It didn’t work?”

The attackers in the main hall were gathering.  Two of the bystanders were huddled together.  One of them had a tiny hole in his face, that bled a thin trail of blood, similar to the other sites that had caught the radial bullets.

One of the attackers, who didn’t have a cane or umbrella, approached.  He kicked one of the people.

That prompted an exchange of blows.  The two people had no training.  The attackers did.  The people were separated, so different groups could deal with them.  One was thrown against a display, and kicked, while slumped awkwardly against it.  If her neck didn’t break, with that, then it was at least badly damaged.

The man, fists raised in a loose boxing stance, was surrounded, and every time he turned his back to someone, they kicked, or pushed him off balance.  He tried to wheel around, and catch them off guard when they thought he wasn’t paying attention, but one kick caught his knee, and he stopped being able to do that.

Once each of them fell, they were kicked until dead.

Both had onboards.

[I don’t know what to do to help,] Basil messaged.

[We went out with a fight,] the woman’s sent, along with an image, of fingernails in skin, in the moments before she was knocked down.

The onboard was from a company that was an offshoot of Quinn’s brand.

The man’s onboard didn’t talk, but sent a message intended to be relayed to his loved ones.  Not his words, but the onboard’s best guess as to what he would have said.  Basil wasn’t sure what to do with that.  Or if he’d be able to pass it on.

A was looking.  Basil couldn’t hide things.

Nos was screaming, now.  Cowrie was trying not to.

A found her feet, and lunged.

As timing went, it went well.  The two men on the catwalk weren’t paying attention.  She got one of the men from the side, with a surprising strength, and pushed him halfway over the railing.

Basil had made a point, over these last three years, to train A.  A had been invested enough.

Now, as he shifted settings, amped up her nervous system as best as he could without access to the brain, and began to elaborate on her vision with highlights marking out target points, imbalance, and incoming swings.

She turned her focus to the guy she hadn’t pushed over the railing, and tried to go for a throat strike.  He blocked it, and turned in a tight half circle, elbow aimed at the side of her head.

She dropped low.  Then, taking a moment to take in the cues Basil had given her, with one highlighted, drove her fist into his stomach, aimed at an upward angle, to hit the liver.

At that angle, with onboard-enhanced strength, the liver ruptured.  It was the sort of catastrophic injury that would level a grown man and put them down.  Except the man didn’t drop.

A threw her weight sideways, at the man who had head, one shoulder, and one arm over the railing.  To shove him back and away.  He fell back, holding onto the edge.

Really, his best bet was to drop down, land on the display below, and circle back around, but in the heat of the moment, with a primal fear of falling, and darkness obscuring just how far the drop was -about three meters- he held on for dear life.

And, in his grasping for a better hold, gripped her hair.  Yanking her to one side.  A full grown man’s weight hauling on her, hair threatening to tear free from scalp, her cheekbone was smashed into the railing.

Basil blocked the pain.

[Stay calm.]

A let out a shuddering exhalation.

He was doing his best to hand her the most effective information.  He could assess the reach of her limbs, where things stood, predict movements…

She kicked, but not to do damage.  To get her leg where she wanted it.  Both legs opened as the man tried to stand over her, giving her a clear shot he couldn’t close his legs to avoid.

Basil wasn’t sure if it would rupture the dangling organs, but it would be good if it did.

[I’m cutting your hair.]

“Yh.”

Not even a full vocalization.

He managed the scalp, releasing the hair.  A pulled free, half-stood, using practiced motions to aim for every spot Basil chose.

[You’re hurting your hands, hitting as hard as you are.  Don’t be upset if you see it.  I can fix it later.]

A made a small sound.  It would be inaudible to anyone that wasn’t them.  Too many people were screaming out their agony.

[And breathe.]

One of the people on the ground noticed that A was on the brink of winning the fight, and fired one of the bullets.  The resulting spray as the bullet detonated pierced the upper eyelid of the man A was trying to take apart.  Many more fragments peppered A’s back and the back of her legs.

Basil blocked the pain, but kept her aware of the damage.

[I can handle that part.]

A gave a small shudder of a nod, trying to heave in a breath.  She wanted to be crying, or the body, baseline, did, but Basil kept her eyes dry and clear.

She gouged the side of the man’s neck with fingernails, glanced sideways at the man who was gripping the railing, and moved her arm to get him.

The strength went out of her legs.  All physical sensation dropped away, so fast that Basil, who still could sense through the full-body network, couldn’t react or accommodate.

She fell, collapsing.

It was his fault.

He didn’t interfere with A’s brain, or brainstem.  There were other areas he paid little mind to.  Cerebrospinal fluid was far too easy to clog, so he had installations around the spine, but very little floating within the fluid itself.

The fragment that had hit her- something had slipped past the defenses.  It had occupied the fluid.

Glucose, proteins, vitamins, lipids.

He hadn’t noticed or done a full audit, all the receptors taking any signal of a foreign body as damage, blood, a thing to be fixed later.

He could act.  He could filter.

But that would take a minute, and until then, A was paralyzed from the waist down.  In that time window, she was kicked in the side of the head.

Vince took that moment to strike out.  He got hit, then shoved back down.

Loren Long was a drone now, controlled by the attackers.  Others were on their way.  Maybe they expected to go out fighting.  Maybe they believed that with this many hostages, if they could be called that, they could attack any forces arrayed outside the building, and beat a planned retreat, hiding out across the superstructure, finding a way off the planet.

The ones who wouldn’t succumb to nanotech -anyone with an advanced onboard- would be beaten to death.

“What do we do?” A asked, subvocalizing.  She reached for Quinn, but Quinn had her back pressed to the railing, hands near her mouth.

[We play with perception.]

“Tell me what’s going on, keep me in the loop.  Help me,” A’s lips moved with the words.  She was kicked again.

[We need you to scream.  We need your body to change like Loren’s did.]

A shook her head slightly.

[We fake it.  I’ll put you back exactly the same afterward.]

“No.”

If they made it through.

He was already struggling to find a workaround to the restriction against physical changes while disconnected from Intelligence oversight.

There wasn’t one.  Which meant he’d auto-delete when this was all over.

A bit early, but not the problem it could have been.  Perhaps A and the Teegs would get some compensation.

[A.  If we don’t do this, you’ll die.  Is that what you want?]

“No.”

[Then I’m going to have you go to sleep.  For this to work, I need you to-]

Others were looking.  They had accessed the main office, where the man who’d given Basil some override privileges had been, and were now in charge of the building’s systems.  They were using those systems to check the people who hadn’t changed or stated to change next.

Basil cut as many connections to the wider systems as possible, and began letting the invading nanotech win.

“No.  I don’t want that either.”

He went backward.  Back to the beginning.  A core baseline of necessary systems, and a crude mechanism of awareness.  Within her eyes, as she looked at Quinn, he affected changes to signal with light and flashing irises.  Communicating what he was doing to Quinn.
