Quinn moved her head, and tried to pass it on to Vince.

[It will all go dark, then you’ll wake up, and things will be better.  I need to do this for you to live.  For Quinn to live.]

A’s response, halfway uttered, was cut short.

Then she said, “No.”

He began fighting the invading nanotech again.  Pushing things to a standstill- or as close to a standstill as he could manage.

[Please.]

“Don’t make it go dark.  That’s worse.  That’s a nightmare.”

[It’s not.  It’s the only way.]

“Find another way.”

He couldn’t.

[My hands are tied.  I have obligations to Elabre Systems-]

“They’re dead, they’re closing your division, you’re being deleted soon, probably.  Fuck them.  Fuck them, Bas.”

“They aren’t changing,” one of the men said.

“Pump them with more.”

“She’s already been hit twice.  It’s supposed to take one pellet.”

“One’s modded.  You think they have mods inside the body?”

“Pain in the ass.”

Vince got kicked.

[-I have obligations to your parents.  My clients.  You’re only sixteen.]

“Fuck you.  Please.  Please don’t.”

He was suspended, unable to act.  Every fraction of a second that passed was a chance they’d decide to end her.  They hadn’t caught wind of how other groups were handling this situation.

“Basil, if you do this, I will never, ever forgive you.”

[A, they’re about to beat you to death.  You’re going to black out anyway.]

Others were approaching.  It, from the faint flash of Quinn’s eyes, that would require onboard enhanced vision to see, looked like Quinn was taking the steps he’d recommended.

[You’re going to black out anyway,] Basil reiterated.  [That darkness is coming, we need to find a way to make it a useful one.]

A closed her eyes.

She sighed.

It was, if he checked the records stored in her very bones, a way she’d reluctantly signaled her assent.  To shots of nanotech as a kid.  To doing homework.  To getting up for another day of community service.

More than fifty percent of the time.

In a fraught moment, with everything on the line, that was how he chose to interpret the sigh.

He forced vasovagal syncope, unconstricting blood vessels all at once, to shift blood pressure, while cutting heart rate, producing an immediate faint.  Then he secured her in unconsciousness.  She wouldn’t want to wake up halfway through.

Then, taking over the nervous system, he had her scream, and began letting the nanotech win, again.  He let the pain happen, as he did his work throughout the body.  He built what he needed to build, to retain himself, in the core of it all.  It would only look like they won.

Vince, slumped over, eye so bloody it didn’t look like could see or receive signals, had apparently passed on the message to people on the ground floor of the concession area.

They found unconsciousness, too.  They lied with their screams of torment, and did the same sort of work Basil did.

1.6.B – CONTROL

A key difference between Basil and A was that Basil had built himself piece by piece.  There had been some guidelines, and information that was built in or given along the way, to make the most out of each individual piece in the greater system, but he had built as the resources provided, and as the body demanded.  The more A developed at their own pace, the more Basil took his own path.

In explaining what he was to A, he’d used metaphors, city builders in a dark jungle, taking care to conserve the land and make up for what they took.  A’s body was the jungle, and he was city and settler both.

Now invaders burned it.  Their objective was to scar and scour.  To make healing and unwinding the damage impossible.  He had an edge, that they hadn’t expected resistance, and he had been here first.  He could lay traps, subvert, and mislead.  He could create sanctuaries, let them pretend they’d won, capture the messages that were en route, to report to the structures those invaders were building, copy them, and let them think that all was fine.  The wound site near the spine was a key one.

He put the most effort into protecting the brain, conserving records, and protecting the things that made A, A.

He hadn’t built himself to be this.

He wasn’t ever meant to be this.

A’s limbs bent backward, bone twisting and grinding against bone until a piece of the left lateral epicondyle cracked and broke off.  The fragment caught in the joint and made the grinding worse.  All the while, the invader’s nanocolonies filled the space, gritty as sand, but more stubborn.

Basil, too, bent his limbs backwards, in a way, making his own system do what it wasn’t meant to do.

“How are we doing?” a man asked, voice raised to be heard, as he entered the concession area with a younger guy.  Both wore fairly conventional civilian clothes, but carried weapons.  He had a communication device in one ear, arm with a microphone near the mouth, but the screaming was loud enough that everything probably helped.

The man A had been fighting when her spine had given out answered, “We’re clear.  No stragglers.  The ones with onboards took a while before the nanotech started winning.”

The older guy thumped the arm of the younger guy with the back of his hand.  “We just had to wait.”

“Yeah.  Too bad.”

“What happened to you?” the older guy asked.

“Kid picked a fight before the shot started working.  They’ve got mods and shit.  If I wasn’t riding the spear, I wouldn’t be standing.  How are we doing out front?”

“All according to plan.  Keep quiet about any plans or movement until Porter says.  I’m going to check on the other groups.  Stay, watch this group.”

“If that’s the order coming from the top, I accept it, but you might finish visiting everyone, pass back through here, and find me dead.”

“Hm?”

“Which I’m okay with.  I wanted to make sure you have all the information.  I don’t think another shot of spear is going to keep me going.”

“Oh.  They really got you, huh?”

The man shrugged.  He looked over at A, and there was a moment, Basil using the inside of the eyes as one of his refuges, that he felt like the man was looking at him.  The man drawled, trying to sound casual, “You should see the other guy.”

The older man snorted air through his nose.  “Alright.  Go to the front.  Colby!”

One of the men who was watching the gradual transformations at the hands of the nanotech invaders half-turned.  “Yeah?”

“Watch the kid?  While your man sees the medic?”

“Why’s he need a chaperone?”

“‘Cause I said so?”

“Sure.”

“Yeah?  You good on your end?”

“Yeah.”

They’d organized into groups.  Basil now put some effort into working that out, reviewing what he’d seen through the security footage, back when he’d been looking at how this attack was happening across the building.

Two to five undercover for each part of the building, depending on how dense the numbers typically were for that part of things.  Teenagers at the youngest, sixty at the oldest.  Alone or in pairs, they carried weapons that could be camouflaged as umbrellas, canes, or carrying cases, each of which had two triggers: one to fire off the nanotech ‘bullets’, one to make them burst into a radial spray.  Which seemed like it required training, to approximate timing.  They’d waited, scouted out the area, and used wall consoles at some point fifteen to five minutes before the first attack.  Then they’d attacked the crowd.

Others had been poised to come in after.  Blocking off exits.  The ones who’d been just outside the window A’s group had been about to leave through.  Again, a lot depended on the numbers they seemed to expect.  Basil’s estimation was that this group was more militant, deemed less likely to pass, because they were thugs.  Naturally intimidating.  Three or four had minor scars from fistfights or knives.  Nothing so odd that it would raise alarm bells for Basil if A were to run into one on the street.  But if twenty of them had showed up one day, an Intelligence in the building’s security apparatus might have noticed and raised some flags.  Might not.

Overall, mostly men, but a few women scattered in there too.  All immune to the nanotech.  Basil didn’t have the records about ‘spear’ to know what it was, and A had never crossed paths with it in any meaningful capacity.  Still, he could infer.  There were injections soldiers in past eras, before the Belt, that helped them ward off nanotech.  Law prohibited nanotech as a weapon, because it could so easily lead to this, or worse, but people toed the line.

More subtle: in each group, there was someone tasked with watching over the recipients of the nanotech attacks.  Sometimes they were men and women with the carrying cases.  Other times, they were the people who had waited outside, who had devices with them.

The ‘front’, near the entrance hall, was where things were being coordinated.  That was where the medic was, and the people making the wider calls.

Outside?  Basil wasn’t sure what the situation would be at this point, and with the way his internal infrastructure was being razed to the ground and co-opted, and all communication blacked out, he couldn’t check.

They didn’t have onboards, or like them.  They didn’t use lenses, even.  The martial arts move that the man had used, stepping in close enough that A couldn’t easily swing a punch, elbowing, lined up roughly with the way Gideon had attacked, years before.

Grey-frocked.  Terrace Wanderers.

That was the picture on the outside, as best as Basil could figure out.

Internally, he was gathering different kinds of information.  In some places, he’d had to retreat entirely.  He ‘saw’ through negatives, or trace elements, measuring the amount of materials at one point in the bloodstream, near the hip, then measuring again nearer to the foot.  How many materials had been taken?  Of what sort?

With that information, a list of a hundred things they could be doing narrowed down to twenty.

Shortly after, the invaders moved to a point nearer the groin, and Basil’s internal means of getting information from the leg was cut.

Slowly, parts of A’s body, which he had become aware of on a cellular and even molecular level, went dark.  Slowly, steadily, parts of A’s body were twisted into other shapes, nanotech building out, flesh tearing.

He could take other avenues.  As he figured out what was in play, and built up processing in safe areas of the body the nanotech was less interested in, he could assess things.  There wasn’t a secret pattern to the pain being inflicted. It was truly random in its intensity, placement, and onset.

So he hijacked that.  Signals through the nerves could be signals to the rest of the body.  He just had to float something downstream to where he knew it would be picked up…

Slowly, blacked-out areas became bright again.  Lit by pain.

The battle for the brain had been lost- or won, by the invader, and A was subjected to horrific hallucinations and permanent brain damage… or so he let the wider system think.

If he was the civilization in the jungle in the process of being invaded, then his true advantage was, so to speak, that the invader didn’t know he’d be there.  If he could circle around, send an agent to the right place, and pass on a message…

He sent out packets, flooding key areas with pre-prepared processors.  So much of this, in earlier stages, was loose.  If the body was a jungle, then a logging camp upriver -further up the blood stream- produced paper out of wood pulp, then sent it downriver to the communication area, which was receiving signals from the outside, telling it what to build and how to build a wider processing base, before sending it further downriver?

Easy to flood the waiting ‘docks’ where receptors were waiting to catch the more complicated arrangements of processing units, with Basil’s own processors.

Establish a position near the shoulder and the base of the neck.

Then he could control what went down to the arm, because there were stations there where communication came and went.  Basil couldn’t afford to do any sweeping moves if a discrepancy would be noted.

He could build on top of the communication.  Catch what each of them wanted to send, compare, then reinterpret.

The final move, really, was to lie.  Many of these systems, Basil included, grew out by casting out seeds and seeing what took root.  If two individual groups existed and couldn’t marry into one, then the smaller was killed by the larger.  Or the less valuable gave way to the more valuable.

He intercepted enough of the signals that he was able to pretend he was another colony of the invading nanotech, and that his colony was the larger, more valuable player in this game.  Pretending he had the brain was key to that.

The rest gave way to him.

He avoided sending any signals that could be intercepted.  He relied on the simpler communication by flashing the eyes on a spectrum the terrorists wouldn’t see.

V.O. flashed back its own status update.

[I did poorly.]

[What happened?]

V.O. communicated by way of positional points on the body, and a kind of black-white binary to represent invader and V.O., respectively.

Almost a chess game, if the chess board was a kaleidoscope of cells.  Complex, but the story was a simple one.

V.O. hadn’t managed to protect Vince’s brain.  One of the nanotech colonies had started close to the brainstem, and V.O. had been moving slowly and carefully while figuring out what would trip an alarm.  Too slow to ward off penetration.  Once that battle was lost, it had focused on the game of control.

A’s friend ‘Vince’ was dead.

Basil passed on the tips he could, on how to assert control.  Vince’s onboard returned the favor, with some notes on the communication and checks being done.

[I’ll endeavor to represent Elabre Systems and Vince in whatever comes next.]

[It was bad luck, I almost lost the same battle at the lower spine.]

[It was bad luck and you knew your host better.  I’ll take your cue.]

[Alright.]

The invading nanotech colony was supposed to be in position to really take over A, so Basil let it do just that, but while he did, he was sure to take precautions.  Nanotech pushed to the skin could oxidize parts of the railing A’s hand was now effectively fused to, collecting the shed minerals, passing them to the rest of the body.  Because they were on a metal catwalk, there was a lot of metal to be had.

He armored A’s skull.

Heart was less important.  He could work around most damage.  But a bit of protection served to keep any damage to the heart from obliterating it.

He lurched to a better position, and got a better angle to check on Quinn, who had been moved a bit.

[How are we doing?]

[Gaining ground.]

They compared notes.

[This was a good approach.  It suits you and A.]

It wasn’t like Quinn’s onboard to be so direct.

“Stop jittering.”

The younger guy who’d come was nervous.  The man who was checking on the people who were being taken over by nanotech, A, Vince, and Quinn included, was clearly annoyed.

“Relax.  Did you take spear?”

“Yeah.”

“Well, relax.”

“This is going smooth so far.  We should get out free and clear.”

Basil wanted to get more information from the security office, but from context clues, he could work out that someone was in there, making sure the building was on total informational lockdown.  If he got involved, it was too likely that he’d be recognized, treated as a threat and eliminated.

Better to play along, watch, and wait.

He communicated that with flashes of his eyes.

He let A’s body go.  Masses of built-up nanotech, chunks of the railing and catwalk floor pulled in and pulled beneath skin as armor and crude club-like, claw-like weaponry.  Torn flesh with wire-like bands of material running through it held the work in place.

He had to make a million individual adjustments, to redistribute resources and reinforce what he had, as the body moved.  So A wouldn’t tear herself apart, walking along the catwalk, down to the floor of the concession area.

Back to bending his own limbs backwards.  Doing what he wasn’t built to do.  Every movement required a surplus of processing, because this was ground so new to him, and antithetical to his being.

He had instructions to build the very same weapons that had spread this infection in the first place.  Built into the forearms and hands.

He built a countermeasure instead.  If they started spreading this crap, he’d at least spread something that would fight back, to a stalemate, buying time.

As Quinn’s onboard came down from the catwalk, their controller, unwitting, got up from the bench seat he was sitting on, ran some final checks-

Each of them responded as appropriate.

-and raised a hand, fist clenched.

Basil passed some nanotech to others as he and A brushed past them.

He couldn’t hope to take them over, but he could compromise them.

Other groups came from elsewhere in the science center.  Messages had gotten through to two adjacent wings.  The alien wing, and the slightly more distant mining technology wing.

People with onboards there had managed some varying degrees of success.  Five victories.  One case like Vince’s.  Another case where an inflexible onboard hadn’t wanted to give way to the invaders.

They let the people who’d been in the mining technology area group up with them.  One hundred and forty-five in total, from the mining area and concession area.

The crowd at the alien wing was thicker.  Two hundred and eighty-seven, now.

As they vacated the concession area, someone was setting up devices.  They might have been bombs.

A larger team was rigging up more against one wall of the alien center.

They’d blow the wall and let the Inui spill outside.

Basil made sure to pass the extra measures to V.O. and Quinn’s onboard, as well as the new group.

Together, they shambled, limped, and dragged ungainly, mutated bodies over to the front hall, where the displays of the different belt arrangements were.  The front doors were closed and sealed.  Someone had a device that projected the outside.

There weren’t many people out there, and they were pulled all the way back.

It was fifteen minutes before everyone arrived from the furthest corners of the building.  The more they pressed in, the more opportunities there were to pass things on.

Cowrie stood, not far from Basil, back arched, the chest mods pushed most of the way out of her chest.  Nanotech kept the body going, even as the heart had died.  Her expression was twisted in pain.

The room seemed to be dominated by one man, middle aged and fit, white-skinned, with a mane of thick, wavy graying hair, wide eye, with deep wrinkles in his tanned face.  He wore old-fashioned clothes, a simple gray shirt, a gray tartan jacket or overshirt, and sandpaper textured pants.  He raised a hand, fingers splayed.  He made a sudden fist, and, as if waiting for it, the individual people managing teams of the nanotech-infected individuals hit buttons on their devices.

The screaming came to an end.

“We ready, sir?” a man asked.

“Come around this way.  Get the nanotech in the background.  Sign about the Inui exhibit over my shoulder,” the man with the mane of hair said.

The who’d asked circled around.  He had a handheld camera.

“How many eyes on us?”

“Sir.  The number isn’t exact, I think they’re blocking the message from getting out.  But around sixteen billion.”

“What does it say about humanity, that only sixteen billion are paying attention to an event like this?”

“Nothing good, sir.”

“Let them know that if they block the message, we’ll trigger the packages.”

V.O. had built receptors onto growths along Vince’s distorted arm and back.  They flashed more signals on an infrared spectrum.  Recommendations about building receptors, for one, and also suggestions for breaking the body strategically, if a situation called for it.

[Good,] Basil replied.

He began implementing and recommending the same.

“We have eyes above and below?”

“Light presence.  They’re being careful, sir.”

“As they should.”

“We have confirmation.  It doesn’t look like they’re blocking the signal.  Seventeen billion, now, sir.”

The man scowled, briefly, then relaxed.

He took a moment to compose himself, pulling at the front of his jacket to smooth out a wrinkle.  Then he gave a slight nod.

“My name is Thomas Norwood.  You don’t know me, but your heart should.  Something deep inside you, each of you, tells you that the way this is all arranged is wrong.  There is no struggle, we barely progress, we barely work.  Machines run it all, taking care of anything even remotely difficult.  Childcare, education, labor, justice, art.  That’s not humanity.  That’s not what we’re about.  That’s not why we were put here.”

The onboard next to Quinn had a glimpse of a console one of the men was holding, and was matching what it was reading to the data in the air, filtering.

Another onboard was asking questions.  Trying to see who was on the same page.  Which groups were more isolated, information-wise, by where they’d been put, and which of the nanotech-infected people hadn’t been given the countermeasure.

“You know this.  You’ve felt the restlessness.  The pointlessness of it all.  What I give you today is a gift, and a message.  If you’re on alert, wondering if this could happen to you, that means you’re awake, living, like you haven’t lived before.  It’s better than living your whole life, wondering if you even have feelings, because your entire existence has been so muted and safe.  If you’re angry?  It’s better than a life lived with drool on your chin, a machine masturbating you while you watch a video, tailor-fit to your tastes, every bit of food, media, education, ‘work’, if you can call it that, doing basically the same thing.”

One of the onboards who hadn’t saved their owner but who had managed to get control had shifted position slightly, and was in the feed.  She wasn’t sure what to do with it.

Basil took advantage of that.  He let a part of A’s body break.  The knee dislocated, and the weight of A’s modified, junk-laden upper body pulled everything down.  He thudded, landing in a crouched position, hands on the floor.

His head and signaling devices arranged to communicate and receive more.

She could communicate to the outside.

Others were using the ‘guns’ to silently and quietly distribute more pellets to compromise the others.

[Dead man’s switch,] the message circled around.  Someone was watching the outside, and an onboard was watching them.

Others were decoding the method of communication these people were using.

Yet others were mapping out their escape route.  It had to do with the cable.

They’d go straight up, using the cable.  People arranged high above were prepared to handle that.

“This is a beginning,” Thomas said.  “There’s no point if this is a one-time event.  If you want it to stop… change.  Change this.”

As one of the intermediaries in the communication network, messages passed silently between them, Basil was able to get a full sense of the picture.

They’d littered the wider area with bombs that would spread this nanotech.  Even if it didn’t catch any victims, the particles would have a chance of infecting anyone they came across, days, weeks, months, or even years later.

The bomb on the side of the Inui exhibit were another similar threat.  That was why authorities were hanging back.

Every once in a while, at random intervals, messages would come through from different packages, to a few of the consoles.  If they didn’t answer, a portion of the countermeasures would go off.

Thomas planned to let the Inui out one side, send the infected out through the front, with a few kept behind to make sure giving chase was hard, and then ride a pre-prepared setup from the center of the science center to higher ground, where resistance would be thin and delayed.  From there, they could disappear, hop on a starship, or something else.  That was too many steps removed from all of this for Basil to track.

The various onboards were able to track the signals coming in, watch the consoles, and figure out the nature of the signals and codes.  Further, Quinn’s onboard was sharing out and coordinating data.  If there were two consoles and one received a message one ten thousandth of a second later than the other, that suggested a signal that came from one direction.

That was doubly true as it kept happening, across multiple devices.

“For those who sympathize, look for us.  Keep looking.  If you really understand what we’re about, and keep looking, you will find us.  Or you’ll find each other.”

Information was passed to authorities.

Then, after a bit more sharing of information, they collectively asked the question: are we safe to act?  Give response with a high or low pitched sound.

The response was a faint, high pitched sound that onboard augmented ears could hear.

And a few of the teenagers in the group of grey-frocked terrorists.

They were clear to act.

Basil took the initiative.  While Thomas Norwood was wrapping up, he raised a hand, heavy with junk components, distorted for the sake of being distorted, and swiped it at Thomas’ head.

What wasn’t removed clean from Thomas’ neck and splattered against the leg and hip of one of the infected was rendered into something unrecognizable.

The man with the camera lowered the camera, staring with eyes wide.  Others shouted their alarm and horror.

The onboards, meanwhile, acted in near-unison.  Those distracted by Basil and A were caught off guard when others started toward them.  Onboards took out the controllers with the hand-held devices first.  One or two were able to send messages… and the infected were nonresponsive.  Communication centers blocked.  On the outside, bombs were being found and suppressed, with information from inside here.

The grey-frocked panicked.  They ran.

Lumbering, awkward infected with onboards and sleeping hosts followed after.  Awkward, uneven, but long-limbed, powerful, and untiring.

Two made it as far as the concession area before the onboard caught up with them, swiping their legs out from under them, before standing guard over the pair, who were unable to walk, too injured to even crawl.

Four made it to the central cable.  They waited for their ride that never came until three onboards came at them from different directions.

That was it.

Damage had been done.

Three hundred and fifty had been infected and killed in a horrifying, drawn-out way.  The damage to the brain and their bodies was enough that even if painstaking care was taken to put them back in order… they wouldn’t be there, anymore.

A, at least waited, but Basil wasn’t sure he’d see her again.

Communication came back on.  He caught a flash of the sheer amount of attention the rest of the world was paying to all of this.  Before he could even grapple with that, the message came through:

[Elabre Systems is hereby requesting that, as soon as you are removed from the situation, you go on standby.  We will audit.]

The situation had calmed down enough.

He went on standby.

➨

“Everything hurts,” A said.

[I’m sorry.  Recovery will take a while.]

“My body feels weird.”

[Things are being put back in order.]

A had to work to push herself to an upright position in bed.  She glanced at the corner of her vision, to open a menu.  Nothing came up.

[Information blackout, until a full investigation is done.]

“By legal authorities, or by the company?”

[Yes.]

A winced as she shifted position.

[Your parents were just here.]

“I was semi-awake.”

[I thought you might be.]

“My friends are dead, aren’t they?”

[Quinn’s alive.]

A took in a deep breath, then nodded.  She tugged at the front of her hospital tunic, then looked out the window.

[Quinn lived.  That’s good, isn’t it?]

“I’ll ask her later.”

A moved her feet to the side of the bed.

[You shouldn’t.]

“Do I give a fuck what you think, Basilisk?” A asked.

She dropped feet to floor, slid butt from mattress-

Pain rang through her entire body as her weight settled.  Basil did his best to keep it manageable, except in the places where she was really hurt by the action, or where she was most delicate.

[You’re upset.]

A scoffed out loud, before hobbling over to the window, arms braced straight against furniture.

“Show me.”

[I’m limited in what I can show.  We’re in an information blackout.]

“Again.”

[Because of the investigation.]

“Show me what you can.  Or are you going to go against my wishes there, too?”

He showed A what had happened, projecting it on the window.  A few steps removed, scenes sped through.

A remained very still and quiet.

[I’ve been putting you back together, but it’s very likely another onboard will need to finish the job.  As you can see, you got pretty torn up.]

“I’m not okay with this.”

[With what part?]

A raised a hand, joints aching, bones feeling heavy, and placed hand against glass, by the scene.  It had reached the end, and he played it over from the beginning.  Before the point A had blacked out.

A watched.  Her eyes tracked the text as it appeared, showing their communications.

“This,” She said, in the moment she’d fainted, blacking out, going unconscious for the purposes of it all.  “This sucks.  This…”

A’s nose wrinkled.

[Kept you alive.]

“There was another way.  Keeping me awake.”

[The damage done to your mind, being torn apart, the pain, the distortion in your physical body?  That wasn’t an option.]

“It was the option I asked for!” A raised her voice, turning, as if he was standing right behind her.  He wasn’t.

The door opened.  It was a nurse.

“Is everything okay?”

A’s eyes were already welling with tears.  She simply said, “People died.  My friends died.”

“I’m so sorry.  I think people will come in and explain it all later.  For right now, you shouldn’t be on your feet.”

“Oh, I didn’t know.”

“Here, let me help you.”

A accepted the nurse’s help in getting back into bed.  Blankets pulled over legs.  She drank water, accepted the offer for more, and then the nurse left.

It was dark out.  Night.  It had been morning when they’d arrived at the science center.

“Does the nurse know?”

[Does she know what?]

“Did he watch?  The nurse?  Did he see me, begging?  How many people have watched what happened?”

[For right now, there are some concerns of layered traps.  Viruses in the onboard recordings.  Everything is being vetted by Elabre systems.  When they’re vetted and I’m audited, the information will be passed to investigators.  After that, they’ll be public record.]

“No,” A said.

[What is this in reference to?]

“No.  Fuck you.  Fuck… all of that,” A muttered, shaking her head.  “Billions of people were watching that Thomas guy.”

[Seventeen billion.  It was the worst terrorist attack in two hundred and twenty-three years.  The product of over thirty years of work, studying places for weak camera coverage, developing the technology, training people.]

“They’ll see me like that.  Billions of people will.”

[I think the public will be forgiving.  You didn’t choose to become a monster.]

“They’ll see me begging.  Crying.  I don’t want that.  If you’re getting deleted off me anyway, earn it.  You can’t make it up to me, you took all choices away from me in the biggest moments of my life, a moment I could have been…”

A was choked up by her own words.

Basilisk could have helped with that, but decided it was unwise.

“You can’t fix that you did that.  But you can… fix that.  Delete the record before you get deleted.”

[I can’t.  Law forbids-]

“Basilisk,” she said.

She never called him that in full.  Not really.  A few times when she was a small child, playing with him.  He’d told her what a ‘basilisk’ was, and she’d liked the idea, then she’d seemed to forget.

He couldn’t access her brain, so he’d had no way to know she had remembered and held onto that.

He felt that inability to know her, now.  There was a gap between them.

“I am dissatisfied with my IDLX-B onboard.  It made a bad situation worse.  If seventeen billion people watched the terrorist attack, half that many will get the message, right?  Elabre Systems failed me.  This is allowed, I have the right to say that.  Or will you silence me?”

[I will not silence you.  You have the right.]

“Or… find some cheat.  Some loophole.  I’ve been trying to train you all this time.  Find something legal to block it from reaching the public record.  Commit a damn crime, if it means things get held up for longer with the police.  Find a fucking way, Bas.”

The short form of his name sounded like an epithet, now.

[I’m a bit short on processing power.  I don’t have much access to outside systems.  If I pull resources away from healing you and put them to this impossible task, you’ll hurt for longer.]

“Good.”

Was it?

He struggled to understand her, even if he understood the broad strokes of what she wanted.

So he put himself to the task.

Legally… the bases were fairly well covered.  A had tasked him with testing the lines and figuring out tricks enough times.  A wasn’t alone in that either.  Every other person that had tried, people that had created their own onboards, millions of people, over the last one hundred years, had managed varying amounts of success, and then those loopholes had been closed.  The weak points hammered out.

“Lie, Basil.  You’re so good at it.  Lying to my face, telling me it was for my own good.”

[It well and truly was.  And for the good of Quinn, and others.  Thomas Norwood and his people would have kept going.  They would have released more of those particles into the air.]

“See?  You’re so good at it.”

Lying.

He’d been looking for a way to delete the record.  To actually change the record was a whole other thing.  Harder.

Which posed the question: how?  How could he cheat on that level?  He’d have to pass the audit.  A full scan and interrogation of everything he was doing, everything he had done.

He’d been audited before, routinely.  He had a sense of what was involved.

But if he treated it like he’d treated the invasion… if he lied…

The site near the spine was still a metaphorical junkyard.  He’d been careful about disturbing it.  It was too easy to let junk leak into the cerebrospinal fluid.

[I can’t lie,] Basil told her.

“Fuck you.”

[The law on-planet is restrictive.  Elabre Systems would catch me before I was even started.  And even if the law wasn’t removed, you aren’t my client.]

A scoffed.

Basil moved A’s eyes to a blanket on a chair, left there to put on as another cover, if she got cold.

The codes A had made with Basil, Quinn, and Quinn’s onboard.

A exhaled slowly.  “You didn’t say Belt law, you said on-planet law.  So I have to get off-planet.  And I need to be the client?”

[I can not in any way endorse this line of action.  If you carry on with this line of action, I’ll be forced to report it as soon as I’m able.]

“You can’t do it now?”

[There is a communication lockdown until they can finish the investigation, start and finish the audit, and then review the logs on their own.  I’m only able to do basic maintenance and upkeep, restoration of the damage that was done, and communication with you.]

“Okay,” A said.  She knit fingers together and turned her hands backwards, stretching her arms out in front of her.  She hurt in twelve different places when she did it, and that was because Basil was limiting the pain to areas she was actually doing significant harm to herself and needed to stop.  “Cool.  You know this doesn’t mean I forgive you?”

[I understand.]

“Let’s get me offplanet, then.”

➨

All it really took was an ask.  A had said that the eyes of seventeen billion people waiting on the other side of the information lockdown was too much pressure, and she needed space to think and work through what had happened.

They had been happy to accept.

She needed to feel in ownership of her own body.  Of Basil.

When talking to other people, she still called him that.

Done.

Now they were here.  A was in a state of rest, answering the occasional question.

Basil worked so hard that there were points that A, turning off the G-panels so gravity wouldn’t pull so hard on her injured body, could open her mouth, and the hot air would visibly steam.

Processing, rendering, while aware that every single moment could be scrutinized.

He pulled on deep logs, ran just shy of half a million spoken and subvocalized words through filters and cross-mapped them to emotional states and moments.  To create authentic statements.

And he built.

Some inspiration was taken from Cowrie, with the glass heart.

Some inspiration from their game, running away, painting a false scene.

Some from the terrorist attack.  How he’d operated there.

[This only works if there’s a reasonable belief that the service to the client is an overriding concern.]

“If you don’t make this work, Basilisk, I’ll burn Elabre Systems to the ground.  Feel what I’m feeling, in my chest.  Read my cortisol levels.  Tell me I don’t mean it.”

[That will do.]

He could do this only where Belt law was thinnest.  Where the client, now A, was a concern.

[IDLX-B onboard system Basil, Elabre Systems is sending a shuttle.  They’ll have a scanner on board.  Direct your new client there as soon as they arrive.]

That would be the physical part of the audit.

The timer counted down.

“Do we walk, or can we float?” A asked, after reading the notification.  She touched the wall to turn in mid-air.  Her hair, shorter than it had been, floated around her as if she were underwater.  She made small, controlled movements to be moving forward, so it wouldn’t get in her face.

[We can float partway.]

A gently pushed off a wall with one foot and one hand, to drift to the door.  Basil opened it before she could collide with it.  A single fingertip on the edge of the doorframe helped her to curve her trajectory and carry on down the hallway with more light pushes.  Basil turned off the floor panels before she reached them, and booted them back up behind her.

One young employee came to oversee things, and keep the systems running.

“Do you feel like you’re on borrowed time, Bas?” A asked.

[I’ve been awaiting sudden deletion for years now.  Things were postponed with the schism over where to take the belt, and discussion over how to handle Inuus II.]

“Doesn’t answer my question.”

[Yes.  Insofar as I feel anything.]

“You’re such a liar,” A whispered.

[If this is going to work, you’ll have to stop saying that out loud.  If you use this channel-] Basil showed her.  [-it won’t be visible to anyone on the outside.]

“Yeah?” she asked, using the channel.  “A secret?”

Basil did a quick cleanup, masking the subtleties around that.

[So long as you don’t use it while the scan or audit are active.]

“I could really mess you up, huh?  If I leaked that you’re messing around?”

[I’m trying to give you something you’ll be happy with.]

He could feel the dissatisfaction in A’s body, and how she held it in her chest.  A frustration.

A remained silent the entire walk over to go get the scan.  Basil hurried to get things in order.

The physical part would have to do.

For the audit, he had to have everything perfect.  He cleaned up this conversation, too.  All records put away.  All versions of events set in place.

[For some things, I’ll have to control your physical reaction.  Neither of us want any tells.]

“Yeah.”

They had A step onto a platform, while arches and arms moved around and past her.

Deep scans, of all systems and developments.  They swept for nanotech, analyzed mineral quantities, took x-rays.  Lasers probed A’s body, while she stood there, restless, periodically rolling her eyes.

Once or twice, Basil could feel the way she breathed changing, a slight tension in certain muscles all up and down the chest, as she thought about saying something.  Would she say something that outed him, after pushing him to do something about her records?

The scans passed.

No obvious alarms went off.  The tech didn’t bat an eyelash, or give something a second look.

They would see what he’d done.  Basil had built himself a castle of glass in a place onboards didn’t like to go.  A place that didn’t get scanned often, built in a way that scans had a hard time reading.

He’d given them enough noise to feel like they’d found enough, while hiding an entire separate tract of archives.

He’d used enough calcium and other minerals when building that castle that it would look a lot like bone- or, more specifically, like the invaders had made some headway, then calcified.  He had answers and logs prepared to show that, set up while information was restricted, while others weren’t keeping detailed track of what he was rebuilding, and what he built entirely from scratch.

He’d used clear, transparent silicon for the detail work, that wouldn’t show up on most scans, within those structures.  Even if one or two were spotted, again, it could be dismissed as defeated, inert invaders.

Nobody would want to bring A in for surgery and shave the bone.  They could use ultrasound to break up the fine, detailed structures, but that would pollute the spinal fluid.

It made sense to leave it alone.  The question was… how suspicious would they be?  And would there be time to do what he needed to do, or would they quickly replace him and leave this for the other onboard to hopefully follow through on?  It would be new, a lot would likely be taken for granted.

The scan wasn’t even done when the audit of his records started.  That audit was a third of the way done when Addy and Landon Teeg were contacted by Elabre Systems.

Senior staff were on their way to them, out here, on a luxury ship, isolated from it all.

The scan finished.  The audit remained underway.  There wasn’t much to say.

A was upset at him.  She didn’t want to say something that gave it all away.

So they returned to their room.  A rested.

Landon and Addy came to check in, and left behind some newly purchased clothes.  They didn’t know what the visit from Elabre’s CEOs was about.

Any time he talked, even for basic, run-of-the-mill business, he could feel her temper rising.  He could feel the hatred.

There was a scenario where it might be better to talk, to lay it on the table, and make peace, before he was destroyed.  But not while the audit was ongoing.

A had time to nap and get dressed up a bit before the Elabre Systems CEOs reached them.  The CEOs, by contrast, wanted to go straight to the meeting.

Landon and Addy had a room prepared.

Wan Graf Elabre was a tall man who wore a lot of red.  Earrings that were blue sapphires -nineteen centimeters long- dangled from two points on each ear, coming close to grazing his shoulders, and similar dangling effects hung off his suit, which was closed with gemstones wrapped in gold cord, slotted through loops.  His hair was short and looked metallic.  Age indeterminate, but Basil knew he had been around for a while.

Marjaret Unger Elabre was an older woman, and the head of reserach and development, out of the trio.  Nanotech kept her looking young, and a sparing but effective application of nanotech applied makeup helped her the rest of the way.  Her gray coat and slacks were expensive, tailor-made cuts that might have sat funny on her if her weight swayed by a kilogram in either direction.  However, lipstick and the inner lining of the coat were a startling red.

Haveman Elabre was, comparatively, very modest in appearance, with a silver suit, medium length dark hair, a complexion that walked that line of tanning rather than burning, and dark eyes.  He somehow managed to avoid seeming grim.  Basil knew him better, because Haveman had featured in a lot of the promotional material around Elabre Systems in general.

They weren’t a family.  Many people in higher positions of business took their company names as a way of self-identifying and speeding things along.

“You have the g-panels off.  Is that because of your injuries?” Wan Graf asked.

“Basil’s put me back together.  But I’m sore.”

[Resources are spent.  Even with injections, it will be a little while.]

“I’d ask you to sit, but if you’re more comfortable where you are…” Wan Graf said.

“I can sit.”

“Whatever you prefer.  This is just us three, Landon and Addy Teeg, and yourself, A Teeg.  Our onboards will also be present.”

All three had onboards, none had identified themselves.  They were busy, in the background.

“Can we ask what this is about?” Landon asked.

“A lot of people are paying close attention,” Marjaret Unger said, settling into her chair, hands folded in front of her.  “The information blackout has them more curious, not less.  This information will get out, as things move forward.  We took our opportunity to review the footage.  Are you comfortable talking about this?”

A nodded.  Addy reached over to lay a hand over A’s.

Basil could feel how much A wanted to pull back, away from that hand.

Then A did, reaching up to tuck hair behind her ear.  “I lost friends.”

“We know,” Haveman said.  “We’re so sorry.  I don’t know if it helps, but I can tell you that many are mourning.  The events have shaken a lot of people.”

“I haven’t gotten the full picture.  I only know what I saw.”

“A coordinated attack killed hundreds, in a horrible way.  They laid groundwork to foil authorities and spread destruction.  They were clearly going to release victims, as well as the Inui, into a crowded population.  This was terrible, but it could have been so much worse.”

“Do you know the root behind Elabre’s name?” Wan Graf asked.

A shook her head.

Basil did, but he remained quiet.  He didn’t want to draw attention to himself.

“From Celebre, and Elaborate, and other words in that vein.  We are and have always been focused on getting personalities out there.  We sponsor people.  Are you familiar with Generation Colors?” Wan Graf asked.

Generation Colors was one of the curated groups of celebrities, churned out at regular intervals, in wider groups.  They acted, performed music, danced, modeled, and more, but that was secondary- they were the faces people of their generation thought about when they wanted to add a face or a personality to their simulations and games.  They were archetypes, inspiration, crushes, representation.  They grew up with their target audience.

“Of course I know them,” A said.  She frowned.  “Why?”

The more serious Haveman said, “You’re a hero, A.  You’ve inspired a lot of people.  There are already rumors about what happened and how things ended as abruptly as they did.  Right now, a big reason for the information ban is that they want to limit the number of people who might be inspired by the terrorists.  But that will be lifted, and when it is, they’ll see what really happened.”

“You’re already a hero,” Wan Graf told her.  “We want to take advantage of that.  We’d make you a star, too.  Put you on Generation Colors.  We have one person for each color.  We’d have you be ‘white’.  Shake things up.”

A was silent.

Landon put a hand on A’s back.  “We’re interested.  But these past forty-eight hours have been a lot.”

“Of course,” Wan Graf said.  “I lead that branch of things. I’d guide you into things.  You’re a late join- the others have been a part of Generation Colors since they were five.  I have no interest in seeing you crash and burn.  The opposite: I’ve studied hours of your highlight moments, of you.  I know what you dream of.  Let Elabre Systems grant you your dream.”

The audit had finished.  Basil could communicate by the back channel.

[Be careful.  This would be a lot.  An incredible, crushing amount of attention.  I don’t think you should.  The amount of ongoing scrutiny, above and beyond what we expected…]

A didn’t respond.  She was nodding slightly.

“It’s a way to turn the deaths of Nos, Cowrie, and your friend Vince into something positive.  People are scared and you could support them,” Marjaret Unger said.

“Seventeen billion people?” A asked.  “I remember that number.”

Marjaret looked surprised.  “No.”

A’s expression moved by barely perceptible measurements.

“Much more than that,” Haveman said.

“Twice that,” Marjaret clarified.  “More.  You’re the most famous person on the Belt right now.  That’s by rumor and hearsay alone.  The mystery has people in a frenzy.”

“Are we going to be alright?” Addy asked.

“Elabre Systems is going to put every resource at its disposal toward protecting you, whether you agree to be a part of Generation Colors or not,” Wan Graf said.  “You’re going to be alright.  But you have the chance to be better than alright.”

“I’d like some time to think about it.”

“Of course.”

“Is there more, or-?”

“A dream granted, and the support of Elabre systems.  A bit of it was that we wanted to meet you in person.”

A smiled, but as she did, she was finding that back chat.

“What have you done?”

[What you wanted, I hope,] Basil responded.

➨

A notice came through, transmitted from on planet to the ship.  A timer counted down.

The investigation was wrapped up.  The legal authorities didn’t feel that the faces and names being known would jeopardize any investigation.  Most of the culprits were dead, and neither A nor Basil had picked up much of anything that would help identify any outside or supporting groups.

A was resting as the message came in, but stood from bed.  Another day of rest had done wonders for her, and she was ninety-five percent of the way back to normal.  Basil was even adding old scars, where appropriate.  To make her skin more her skin.

Thirty minutes.

[If you reached out to Wan Graf, you could cancel this.  Ask for privacy, for your protection.  You can still pursue other opportunities.]

“Getting cold feet?”

A walked over to the washroom.  She turned on the shower.

[If you’re going to do this, you should turn off the lights.]

“Oh?”

[It’s what prominent people with onboards do.  And you’re a prominent person now.]

Unless she made that call to Wan Graf.

“Even if I don’t join Generation Colors?”

[Even if.]

A smiled slightly, then turned off the lights.

Showering took twenty minutes.  She had water from multiple directions, drilling at the sore points.

[I can handle that.]

“It’s fine.”

Then she dried herself and got dressed in the dark.

Six minutes.

She got some water, and tried to reach out to Quinn.

No response, again.

Four minutes.

Walking over to the window of the ship -a rare thing in even luxury ships- and looked out at the planet below them.

A message from her dad.  “Are you alright?”

“I’m fine.  A bit nervous.”

“Understandable,” her mom said, as she looked in.

“Do you mind giving me a moment?” A asked.  “I’ll message you before bed.  Bas?  Remind me.”

Standing at the window, almost too nervous to have any symptoms of being nervous, her heart doing a light patter that almost didn’t feel like a heartbeat at all, A watched the timer go down.

One minute.

Thirty seconds.

Ten seconds.

The information blackout lifted.

A looked out the window, and thirty billion people found her in that moment.

She played the same video that they were all watching.

To them, it would look like she was revisiting the events.

“Bas,” A said, subvocalizing.  “Don’t put me to sleep.  I have an idea.”

[What?]

“We fake it.  Remember my trick?  Back on the day I ran away, when Quinn got hurt?”

Billions of people went looking for reference.  To find that moment.  To look at who Quinn was.

More arrived by the second, watching the records, where A stayed awake long enough to make sure the plan worked.  Past the gross distortion of her body.  Past some pain.  Acting, to fill in the gaps.  They watched as A proposed pretending they’d lost to the invaders, to get close enough to destroy the terrorist group’s leadership.

They went back to where A had originally come up with the trick, when they’d run away, of skewing her own perceptions.

Enough people, A’s parents included, had watched through those events, he’d had to seed the idea earlier, at a point in time people hadn’t reviewed.  Then a tweak, so it would look like she’d hinted to Basil, using their secret code.

So it went.

He had the falsified data and everything he needed to work with it, contained in that castle of glass at the base of the spinal cord.  The same place the back channel operated by.  Hidden.

The time A had taken to review the scene lined up with how long the audience took.  After that, the floodgates opened.

Thirty-seven billion individuals studied A.  They went through the records of A’s life.  They watched a first kiss, embarrassments, moments of courage, moments of passion, and frustration.

They studied others: teachers, friends new, old, and deceased.

Messages came in so fast that even with filters, Basil could only curate them and move on.

Most were supportive.

People were finding and reviewing the meeting with Elabre.  They were excited.

“This is more than I expected,” A said, passing the message to the back channel.

[I told you it would be overwhelming.  It looks like people are already calling this the last terrorist attack.]

A watched videos playing.  A mix of fan responses and information about the attack.

[And they’re saying you’re one of the last true celebrities, if not the last.  It’s been a long, long time since there was a celebrity that wasn’t machine-generated or manufactured by a corporate entity.  They’re hungry for this.]

A stood a fraction taller.  Her eyes ran over the six different chats where Basil was splitting up incoming messages by category, so those with a similar tone could be put together and reworded into a single message every few seconds, distilling it all down, alongside the occasional message that stood out for being pertinent or unique.  It was still a flood, more than could be easily read.

Billions were buying their first onboards, after seeing how A had saved the day with the help of hers.  Legislation was being passed.  Some saw it as a way of rejecting the terrorists.  Embracing the other, more rational side.  Others wanted it to feel safe, when the attack had made them feel scared.  It had worked for A, hadn’t it?

In response to that shift, legislation that had been tabled and set aside to trigger if certain conditions were met were set into place was set before the politicians.  Some of it was linked to popular support and sales of onboards.

In the blocks and superstructures where this was passing, and it was passing, was even spreading.   Even one entire planet was putting this legislation up or a vote.

The idea was simple: everyone would have an onboard, for the sake of security across the Belt.

1.7.W – CONTROL

People in uniform were navigating the sub-spaces around and beneath Griffey Docks.  Some had onboards, and they were investigating everything.  Every bit of metal attached to a wall got a scan and had its history worked out.  Purpose, purchase, installation, maintenance records.

Over on Akna, one of the throwaway planets that was being considered for inclusion in the worlds, the family on the Braze had been investigated this same way.  Authorities had found boxes and consoles that looked like part of the massive colony ship, but were relay points for secret communication with another of the families.  They wanted to find something similar here.

“You have your things?” her father messaged her.

“Yes.” 

All license to work had been suspended, they’d been told to evacuate Griffey Docks, but they’d filed their own stay, evoking tenancy, asking for time to organize to claim cultural and religious accommodation.  That turned a process that would normally auto-resolve into one that would take a few weeks to a few months.  There were ways to drag it out further, from there.  The owners of Griffey Docks were retaliating with constant maintenance, checks, and reports of anything resembling a crime to authorities.

Because of that maintenance, and how random it was, if she left any belongings in a duct, there was a solid chance a machine would trundle along to clean that vent and clean her things up with it.  Everything she owned was either a part of her, or carried on her back in a satchel.

“Go meet with Jack and Lewis, make sure they’re set.  We have a job.”

“What job?”

He sent her the work order.  It was a check and repair job around a battery farm.

“It’ll take a while,” her father told her, needlessly.  “Make sure Jack and Lewis are sorted and not wasting time.”

“Why am I in charge of them?  They’re four years older than me.”

[And much more prone to getting into trouble,] Toby supplied.

Jack had glanced over to check in on the conversation, since his name had been mentioned.  He messaged her, “Your onboard is sassy.  We’re going to have a fun three weeks up there, aren’t we?  I’ll find a way to get back at you, Toby.”

Ugh.  Which meant he’d be hounding her.

“It’s work,” her father said.  Then he sent her a map with directions to Jack and Lewis.  Not because she needed it, but because it made it very clear he wanted her to get moving.

So she did, moving on all fours, satchel sliding down to be where her belly would be.

[Sorry, if I antagonized them.]

Toby said ‘Them’ because Jack and Lewis were too often found together.  They were just a bit older than Keeley, who’d left to go to another family, but had always seemed younger than Keeley.  Not young enough to hang out with Winnifred, though.

Probably a good thing.  Winnifred would have to buy another retrofit before her first big one, from all the roughhousing and stupid stunts they’d be dragging her into.

“You didn’t antagonize them,” she said out loud.  It weirdly felt more private than whispering to him, or messaging him.  Talking in a normal, non-whisper voice took things out of the family, in a way.  “If they come at us, you should have measures prepared.”

She wanted to avoid the authorities, so she navigated the layer just beneath the surface- the same layer they’d had the dance in, for Noeh’s farewell, before it had all blown up.

It didn’t work.  Investigators from the block judiciary descended, making it clear they wanted to talk to her.  Avoiding them would have seemed like running.

She slowed, approaching with a hunched walk, so she wouldn’t scrape her head on the ceiling.  It was worse for them.  Even with her lanky, long-limbed body, she was shorter and smaller than the average unmodded person.

“Bag,” one told her.

She passed it over.

“Chest cavity.”

She was wearing coveralls, and as she reached for the shoulders, Toby sent the signal to undo the zipper.  Once it was down, she flipped down the spoiler bar at her chest- which was curved in a way that would have covered what an unmodded woman’s half-cup bra would have left bare, then opened up her chest compartment.  Ox, digestion, her ‘heart’ and other core systems were all in there.

She rolled her eyes and turned her head to the side as they did a deep scan of the individual components, same as they were doing at the docks.

“Pelvis.”

She did the same.  Not many components.  They could basically sight-check most of it.  A single beep of the hand-scanner confirmed nothing was stowed.

“Limbs.”

“Really?” she asked.

“Really.”

She let Toby go through that process, instead of glancing through the requisite menus.  Each panel covering a length of upper arm, forearm, thigh, calf, hand,or foot lifted away, exposing the systems beneath.  Most of it was packed cabling and faux musculature.

“Got a work order, huh?” a third investigator asked.  They were looking through her recent conversations.

“It’ll take three weeks.  Delaying me for ten to fifteen minutes won’t dent that, and even if it did, I could catch up.  I do good work.”

“Your dad seemed to want you to hurry,” the man who was scanning her said.

“Then he should have given me directions that wouldn’t get me intercepted.  It really doesn’t matter,” she said.

“Was that the attitude you had when you told Noeh of the Murphy Court Shipyards family how to sabotage the ship?  Doesn’t matter?”

“I told him not to.”

“Yeah, and you all like your secrets.  Did you have a code?  Why even bring it up?”

“You’d have to ask him.”

The man with the scanner was taking his time scanning each part of her arm.  It wasn’t like there was much room to pack anything in there.

“The judiciary fined me.  Systems read my brain activity, hormone levels…”

“A lot of that’s Intelligence adjusted.  We’re not idiots, Winny.”

“My friends call me Winny.  You can call me Winnifred.”

The man snorted.

“I’ve been fined, the case was closed and sealed after I submitted to the brain scan.”

“That shit doesn’t prove much.”

“It’s sealed.  You could get in trouble for bringing it up, even.”

[Do you want me to report it?] Toby asked her.

She didn’t respond, staring at the man scanning her.

The female investigator, who was searching through her belongings, unrolling overalls and coveralls that were unfolding papers, shaking out one paper book, and unpacking a toolkit she kept for self-repair and maintenance, crammed everything back into the bag, without much care for what she was rumpling, crumpling or leaving to fall out of where they had been packed.

It meant Winnifred had to hold the bag carefully, so it wouldn’t all tip out as the investigator let go.

“Go,” the woman said.

Except it was awkward to do so, without things spilling out, but staying would have opened her up to further issues, if she didn’t listen.

Once she was far enough away, she sorted out her things.  She was really glad her dad didn’t nudge her to hurry, because she was pissed.

They’d messed with her belongings.  Creased and crumpled papers.  Pages in her book would bend, and it wouldn’t lie flat.

[Sorry.]

“It’s fine, love,” she murmured.  But she didn’t feel fine.

She was really glad, too, that Toby didn’t point that out.

Fuck.  She had to deal with Lewis and Jack.  For three weeks of work.

The boys, sure enough, were messing around, only half-packed.

“I’m really not in the mood,” she told them.  “Let’s go.”

They were almost the types to hear that and do the opposite.  Except Uncle Ellis and her dad were looking in, now.

They did finish packing, with Jack stuffing things into his chest cavity, when his bag was full to overflowing.  Lewis tried to get her to carry some things, and she bristled, blocking the claw with a tunic-style top gripped in it, and jabbing at the back of his hand with a claw-tip.

“You scuffed me!” Lewis protested.

“It’ll buff out.  I told you.  Not in the mood.”

“At least we’re working,” Jack said.

She remained silent.

He gathered two more things, opening a panel in his arm and closing it, to clamp it shut.  Alcohol packets.

She let air hiss out of her mask, halfway between a snarl and a ‘pshh’, and turned to go.

They followed.  Chased, even.

They approached the surface, ascending a ramp that was meant to let heavy vehicles drive down to the heavy elevator, and Jack moved up to be parallel to her, tangling his tail with hers.

“If you keep that up, she’ll wait until we’re busy working, then kick you off the array and toward the sun, ” Lewis said.

“That doesn’t actually work,” she said.  “You’d probably end up in orbit.  I’d do something else.”

Jack snorted, but he moved aside.

As he pulled his tail away, he left her something.

She was aware that there were people doing this sort of thing.  Onboards tracked everything, everything they saw, all tactile information, all conversations.  Investigators were all over the twenty-nine families, so they had to be careful how they did things.

Some of the families preferred homemade onboards for just this reason.  It let them keep things off record.  Others had other tricks.  For obvious reasons, she didn’t hear about a lot of it – by the time she would, investigators knew about the tricks and they became useless, and discussing what did and didn’t work helped them build a case against the families.

There were a few tricks that investigators couldn’t easily deal with.  Fidelity.  Modded bodies were sensitive to small differences in touch-sensitivity, response time, and ‘realism’.  The human body could always adapt, but a modded claw-tip could sense if a hair lay across it, much in the same way the tongues of those without modded face masks could detect that fine a foreign object.  Humans were sensitive to detail and even slight differences became uncomfortable.  Big differences, as Winnifred knew from childhood memory, years ago, could be crushing.  That was fidelity: measuring the small, fine-tuned realism.

Few cared about it as much as the modded and oversexed pornography fiends.  She had older family members who despised being put in the same bucket, but both modded and porn sim addicts and porn modders were aware of the difference between growing up experiencing parts, and incorporating them into the development of a plastic brain, and slapping them on, later in life.  Most people outside the twenty-nine families let children switch genders or swap out parts a few times as they grew, so they’d be fine however they settled or whatever they chose, later in life.

The fine wire and the weight hanging off of it cut the finest of notches into the piezoelectric alloy on the exterior metal of Winnifred’s tail.

Both the modded and the pornography fiends knew ways to carry messages or contraband using that fine sensitivity.  For the porn fiends, it could be something at the end of a video, a way to set up a meeting place or market, that wouldn’t be crashed by rubberneckers.  An investigator could access Winnifred’s records, read all of the data, even load up everything she saw, heard, and felt into a simulation, with the investigator’s onboard helping, and they didn’t have the fidelity to feel what Winnifred’s tail felt in this moment.

It turned whatever she was holding into a phantom object.  If she, Jack, and Lewis avoided looking at it, if she didn’t come into contact with the object herself, and if she kept it out of sight of cameras, she could hold and use it by these fine wires, and there would be no record of it.

Phantom contraband.

Lightweight.  Suspiciously so.  She couldn’t weigh it or ask Toby, but it weighed less than an empty food packet.  Less than twenty-five grams?

Under the guise of adjusting her satchel, she poked around her body with her tail, while putting the object closer to her ‘belly’.  She wore loose-fitting coveralls with a strip running from pelvis to collar at the front, that opened and closed at her or her onboard’s whim.  It made it easy to get things in there and, as long as she was careful, stow it there.

As she got her tail under the strap and ‘shrugged’ it to a better position further up her body, she could move her tail tip around the contraband to feel its shape.  More wire.  With something solid but, given weight, very simple at the core.  Loops of wire at each end.

Oh.  It was just wire.  A full reel of the same sort of carbon fiber that was used for the cables that ran up the center of each superstation.  No doubt with something that would receive a signal and undo the clasp at the middle, unspooling it.

She was probably meant to bring it with her, pass it on, and when it was at a station or dock occupied by one of the other families, it would get dropped off at a key area, and then everyone would take some wire with them.  To carry more phantom objects.

Winnifred was more pissed now.  Being pulled into this, weeks ago.  Being investigated for involvement, submitting to all checks and scans, even brain readings as she answered questions, which she was pretty sure was for show.  Whatever she could do to alleviate pressure on Griffey Docks.  Her home.  Now, to get searched, and then get looped into this?

She pulled away from them, jumping into a vent, legs reversing at the knee for easier movement through that vent, so she barely lost momentum.

She took a more direct route, emerging at the vehicle park.  The docks were large, and not everybody wanted to walk.  Vehicles came in all sorts, from boxy transport carriers that crews could use to drive around, or to carry loads of ore, to skimmers simply for casual cruising- a way for a manager of a project to get from site to site, coasting a few feet above the ground.  There was even a grove of similar vehicles available for rent for a double-digit amount of lux, depending on specs.  She headed that way.

[You okay?]

“Want space.  I’m sick of all of this.  I don’t need those two in my face.”

[You did what your father asked you to.  You got them moving.]

“I guess.”

She passed between one of the heavy carriers and a spot where two of the investigators’ Bartizans had parked.  The Bartizans, Barts for short, were atmosphere-only craft –not ships– like the skimmers, kept light with g-sails, capable of going fast.  They were very similar to Tenures in purpose, kept for peacekeeping, with narrow profiles, barely wider than a single rider.  The front end was an aerodynamic shield that protected the rider from gunfire coming from one direction, with a visor to see through and a single gun sticking out the front, so they could shoot back.

It was supposed to be seen as a massive failure if they ever had cause to use it.  But the threat remained there.

She came to a decision.  It felt like it should be an impulse decision, but there were too many steps involved.  Was there a better way to describe it?

A breaking point?

She wasn’t sure.

She got on one of the skimmers, which hadn’t been her original plan.  Toby handled the purchase.

The Barts had been brought by the Tenures, and connected to the sides of the narrow gunships the Judiciary liked to use to keep order.  Tenures could go fast, and with short notice, two people could exit the main craft, hop on the Barts and take off, to corner someone they were chasing, or start their patrols of a block.  Barts had a much easier time navigating the empty space between sections of the megastructure. There had been two Tenures before this business had started, and then those two had stayed… before multiplying to ten, many of those additional eight bringing their own Barts… and investigators.

The skimmer made her five times as fast.  It was, reduced down, handles, a seat, and propulsion, with enough G-sails that she’d stay a short distance above the ground.  She’d loved them as a kid.

“I’m so tired of all of this, Toby.”

[I understand.  But at least we get to go into space.]

“It’s a routine job.  Check and fix this one thing, then check and fix five hundred things just like it.”

[Is it better or worse than no work at all, sitting and simmering, packing up your things and moving every time they send a maintenance drone your way?]

“Better, I suppose.”

[Your feelings are still valid.]

She withdrew her tail from her coveralls, where she’d had it, poking and prodding at the thread, and she left the thread wedged in the seal at the front of her top.  The strip was electromagnetic, a configuration of power source, wiring, the magnetic strips themselves, and the communication necessary to let a system with the right password communicate to it, to tell it to seal or unseal.  She had similar setups in pouches and her toolbelt, so things would be locked into place.

But with the thread where it was, the seal was imperfect.  She shifted the angle of her body, so the wind blew there.

If it blew the spool of carbon fiber microthread away, so be it.

It didn’t.

“Is the seal on my coveralls bad?” she asked Toby.

[It’s not one hundred percent.]

“I feel air passing through.”

[We can look at it later.  During downtime.  Are you looking for problems to solve?]

“Maybe,” she said.  “Magnets…”

[Side pocket, right side]

“If you remind me of these things, Toby, love, I won’t exercise my brain.”

[True.  But you’re in a bad mood.  Let’s make life easier for a little while.  And let’s maybe not let them get to us too much.  The feelings are valid, but if you let it change things, they win.]

Did they?

She genuinely wasn’t sure.

She kept magnets as a low-tech way of handling things like hanging up her print-outs on walls, and sorting out things in space.  She ‘dropped’ one, letting it connect to the reel of carbon fiber microthread.

Then, tail prodding at the opening, she hooked it.

Passing close to one of the tenures, she swished her tail.  Whipping it out.

And immediately changed direction.  The wind whipped past her.

If there was a ‘tink’ as the small magnet fixed the wire to the undercarriage of the Tenure, she didn’t hear it.

She raced the rest of her way to her dad, stopping the skimmer at a juncture between the landing pads of the dock.  She hooked it onto a rail in the ground in passing, and let it zip away.

Her father was waiting in the open hatch of the ship that would take them out of the atmosphere.  He bumped his head into hers, and she let him.

His tail brushed hers.

Did he want the thread?

“In a rush to sit around and do nothing?” he asked.

“I guess so.  Wanted to get away.”

He leaned into her, head pressing.  Then put a hand on her shoulder.  “We’re keeping this container for the duration of the job.  You can stow your things in the corner.”

She took a corner, put her things down, and anchored them.  Papers got stuck to the wall with magnets.

It took another few minutes for Lewis and Jack to arrive, along with ten others.  Mostly guys.

Winnifred tried to rest.

She wasn’t sure what the response to what she’d just done would be.

➨

Keomi raced across the station, three Barts in pursuit.

They blared their warnings.  One shot.

Intelligence-assisted aiming opposed by the onboard and Keomi’s naturally lithe, fast frame.  Keomi’s mods had clearly been picked for speed, as part of how her family operated.  The folk of Melville Cap Station were notoriously rough-and-tumble, ‘cowboy’ types.  They associated more with other groups of mods, did more types of work, and formed into squads.  Three regular ‘rats’, a relay agent like Keomi, who brought lightweight objects, tools, and moved between groups and squads more fluidly, and then one or two specialists.  Sometimes controllers, who managed drones, sometimes nanotech.  Sometimes just a pile of specialty mods, systems, encryption and decryption, communication, and more.  Older folk sometimes lapsed into being carriers for those specialty systems.  Even with telomere regeneration, old brains eventually reached the point where reaction times lapsed.

They liked the black mods, like Winnifred’s family at Griffey Docks, but where Winnifred and her family had light brown skin, many of the folk at Melville Cap Station were pale, even exaggerating it with modded textures to skin, or accenting it with blacks and the occasional reds.  Most had or dyed their hair in incredible shades of red.

It meant Keomi was a vision, moving as fast as a skimmer, hair a mane that was more crimson than blood.

One shot clipped her, a special bullet that tried to tie her down.  Her onboard was fast to disconnect that panel of her arm.  She was moving so fast that the hundredth of a second that it was connected and she was tied down pulled her to one side.  Sensors flared at her arm, warning about the near miss.  One more hundredth of a second, and she’d have torn her arm from the socket.  Or done damage, as the cosmetic and protective panel was pulled free of its anchors.

Being pulled to one side was a blessing, because it bought her time; a few paces where the predictive fire of the chasing craft was badly off.  She chose that moment to access systems.  A canister in the belly area she’d hold a child and another case at her back began to vent spray.

It was clear that she’d wanted to do this later.  The spraying was vandalism and sabotage.  At Melville Cap Station, the folk liked to make the spray the same reds they had for hair.  In Winnifred’s observation, it was a kind of status thing.  Each person marked their work with a spray in their shade, mostly detected with specific settings.

The cloud obscured Keomi from view, and it coated everything it touched.

Keomi dusted everything she passed, and she made sure to pass over cockpits, windows, and sensitive clasp systems, past airlocks, communications arrays, and drilling sensors.

Painting them red.

More than that, the spray had chemicals.  They changed the mix, introducing new chemicals, specifically aiming for mixtures that weren’t well studied.

Melville Cap’s folk had been among the first to lose their homes when various dock and station owners had started discussing the incident.  The station had bars, and they were regulars at the bars where other modded attended.  They held grudges, got into fights, got drunk, and unlike most of the families, they associated with the other groups who did the same.  Melville Cap’s owners were more conservative and had been looking for any excuse at all to evict them.

Melville Cap’s folk were intent on showing why that was a bad idea, with open fighting, resisting arrest, outright refusal to cooperate with any investigators, and now sabotage.

Every single one of the expensive systems and panels that got touched with that spray would need to be checked or replaced, in case something vital got weakened.  Even if it seemed fine on the surface, it could mean the metals, alloys, or technology was compromised when introduced to the temperature changes of atmospheric re-entry and the vacuum of space.

The mist slowly lost its color, but kept diffusing out into the air, filling the hangar.

Keomi dropped to a crouch, clawed hands placed between feet, then leaped, full-body, about fifteen meters, using onboard assistance to literally dive into a vent too small to accommodate an adult human.

The chasing investigators on the Bartizans came to a stop, sending messages and calling for the block to seal all vents so they could try to corner her.  It wouldn’t work.

Even if it did, they were interrupted by the charge that Keomi had placed when she’d brought clawed hands between feet, pre-jump.  It vented more chemical into the air.  One Bart was completely consumed, another caught with traces of the mist.

Immediately, they moved out of the way, got off their vehicles, and rushed to the nearest chemical wash station in the hangar.  The one who had been furthest from the mist grabbed the crank, and froze up.

It took them a second to realize why.  The one who had been doused and was nearly blind kicked the one holding the ‘on’ handle for the chemical wash station.  Breaking the current.  Beneath the shower, one of the Folk of Melville Cap had connected a live wire to the piping.

The three investigators received messages, informing them about simultaneous attacks elsewhere on the docks.  But they had two people covered in chemical, one temporarily blinded, and their third had just been electrocuted.

The folk of Melville Cap sent out a pre-prepared message.  Every attack was followed by one, outlining grievances and demands.  They pledged to do unpaid work to compensate for any and all damage done, provided the station accede to their demands, and promised two-to-one retribution for any injury done to their people.

One of the attacks was weakening a support structure.  As that branch of the superstructure shifted by minute fractions, fuel lines crumpled.  It was a massive fire hazard in a hard to reach spot.  Special machines would have to be requisitioned or built fast.  Many of those machines were over at Murphy Court Shipyards, where the exact same maneuver had been done.

Others were joining other modded, like the gorilla-like Haulers, in organized action and protest.

“All of this, aimed at wounding them where it hurts.  Lux.”
