Winnifred roused.  She’d been watching feeds and catching up on what was happening, experiencing some moments by simulation, while curled up in her corner.  It took her a second to pull herself back to reality.  The container was fairly full, some people sitting side by side.  Twenty of them in all, for this container.  There were more at another two containers, around the battery farm.

The statement had come from one of the men from Howington Station, addressing her.  His mods were an intentional tarnished silver, with the flattest planes inscribed with writing, his skin a deep black, head hairless.

[Michal Omorose of Howington.  You know who he is.]

She knew the name.  She stood, but her awareness of the man and the fact they were in zero-G meant it was easiest to grip the textured floor with her claws and push herself into the corner, held there by the backwards pressure and friction.  The only other option would have put her face closer to his, or ‘standing up’ the wrong way would have sent her into a wall, rebounding into him.  The inadvertent impression ended up being that she was avoiding him, or creating as much distance as possible, shoving herself into the corner, shying away.

“Sir,” she said, to try to counter that impression.

“It’s okay.  I’m just a modded worker, I clean up shit, haul debris, and hate sand as much as anyone.  I wanted to talk.”

The official line of the twenty-nine families was that they had no leadership.  But the folk of Howington Station were said to be the first, they were the most organized, the wealthiest, and the largest.  There were three families that owned their stations, docks, or whichever else.  Howington Station owned the superstructure where they resided, which gave them security in these unstable times, and came with an implicit promise, that if things got really bad, there would be refuge there.

“Okay,” she said.

“Toby, we are currently on a work contract through Howington Block and Howington station.  Figtree is sending you a contract, protecting everyone here while we discuss business.”

[Contract,] Figtree sent.

[Received,] Toby replied.

“Read it, as you’re obligated to, then sign it.  You sign it too, Winnifred.”

[It’s sound,] Toby told her.  Toby marked it with the snowflake-like symbol that was her unique signature.

Winnifred glanced over it too, then signed it, moving claw-tip through air.

“Now we can talk,” Michal said.  “The only way this conversation gets out is if they bring down Howington.  If that happens, we’re all doomed, and it doesn’t matter.  Toby is legally obligated to keep what we discuss here private.  So are you.”

“Okay,” Winnifred said.

Her father was close by, watching with a level gaze.

“What did you do with the item Jack and Lewis Griffey gave you?”

“I attached a magnet and attached it to the undercarriage of the Tenure.”

[License TENURE-P107R,] Toby supplied.

“Can I load your simulation and see?”

She nodded.  He really didn’t have to ask.

He started back when she’d been called by her dad, and watched until she boarded the ship.  He had the fidelity to sense what she’d sensed, tail in contact with the carbon fiber microthread.

“Why?” he asked.

He didn’t sound angry, but she could one hundred percent believe he might be angry and very good at hiding it.

“Because I spend all my time doing what I’m told.  Then something I didn’t do and wasn’t a part of ends up mattering more than… everything else put together.  I’m not a mule, I don’t relay.  I don’t want to get in trouble.”

“All of this only works if we work together and play the hands we can.  Melville Cap fights because they can, they have those allies.”

“They don’t have any other choice,” Winnifred pointed out.

“True.  True.”

That seemed to break the stride of what he was saying.  He considered for a second, then leaned into a wall, tail gripping a narrow bit of metal inset into a gap in the floor, meant for chaining things down, and hauled himself down to something resembling a sitting position.  He motioned.  “Sit.  Relax.  You worked hard today.”

Trying to distract herself.

She resumed a similar position to what she’d been doing before he came.  A little more upright.

“Did you want to get caught?  Playing with fire, by attaching contraband to the underside of a Judiciary-issued Tenure?”

She considered for a second.

He tilted his head.  “You wouldn’t be the first.”

“Maybe.”

“You’re tired, you said.”

To Toby, earlier in the day.

“That’s fair,” he said.  “What’s the plan, then?  Do one of our people have to go and grab the contraband, in a very inconvenient spot?”

She’d been acting on instinct, but now, put to the question, she had to turn those instincts into plans.  In a way, it was open ended.

“Sorry, just um, trying to think of how to word it.”

“There’s no rush.  Mind if I eat?”

She shook her head.

“Want something?”

She shook her head again.

She could tell him she intended to get caught.  That that had been the plan.  It could be an action of protest, excused in part by her being angry and frustrated at being searched, her things needlessly damaged and rumpled.

To do that, she’d have to have an excuse that didn’t leave Jack and Lewis as the only potential sources of the carbon fiber spool.  She’d been searched just before, so… that made for a narrow window.  She glanced at a map of the dock and her route.

Toby immediately supplied a heat map of where the investigators were known or likely to have been.

She could mark out a few places.

Or… what?  Say she didn’t want to get caught, but she hadn’t been thinking?  She’d been impulsive in the moment?  That wasn’t the worst idea if she wanted to make herself seem less competent, and get less attention in the long run.  People would be mad, but there were a few hundred people in the twenty-nine families who were being different sorts of upset and stupid.

She was aware Michal was watching her look at the maps.

And the final answer… competence.  Maybe, unless she’d overlooked something vital.  Was this the place to get that attention?

“That was a spool of carbon fiber microthread.”

“It was.”

“With a clasp.  The kind that comes undone with a signal.  That way, if someone’s carrying it, you send a signal when they’re in the right spot, it comes undone, spills out.  They leave it behind.  Others pass by and collect what they need.  So it looks like a spool, but it’s probably a few dozen or a few hundred lengths.”

“Yes.  All organized and coordinated in closed-door meetings like this.  Which only we can coordinate and pass down to visitors, like Ellis.  Or your father.  Who then send people to the right places, or pick it up and place it where they can redirect others to notice it and pick it up,” Michal said.

“You have two options then.  Send the signal.  The only thing they might notice would be the clasp and magnet, which could be explained away as debris.”

“True.  Or?”

“Or trust that the Tenures here will do regular patrols of private docks and stations.  The sort of place where business owners and people that run superstructures keep their ships.  Only using their ships once in a while.  Send the signal while it’s over some of those craft.  Carbon fiber microthreads aren’t detected by conventional sensors or scans, but they will trigger an alert when a communication array or solar array wants to unfold and catches.”

[They go to use their ship to make a meeting or get somewhere in an emergency, get ten different warnings when doing preflight checks.  Grounded for six hours minimum,] Toby concluded.  She hadn’t discussed it with Toby, of course, but Toby knew her.  Good girl.

“Six hours minimum.  Could be a day or two.  They would be left wondering, who did it, when, and how.”

[And it would be frustrating.  Defeats the point of having those craft.]

“Psychological effect,” Winnifred said.  “Hitting them where it hurts.”

“Aren’t you a little spider?  Your father told me you had a head for engineering.  He didn’t mention that you had a mind for traps and sabotage.”

“Can this be my contribution?” Winnifred asked.

“What do you mean?”

“To the effort.  One decent idea.  Then let me back out?  I don’t want to sound ungrateful for everything Griffey Docks have done for me, or like I don’t support this.  But I hate it.  Fighting, war.  People getting hurt.  That… fear, I’m sensing.  That we’re not earning money and if something breaks or if we get hurt, we might not be able to afford a fix or retrofit.”

“It’s all an illusion, you know?” Michal asked her.

“An illusion?”

“Lux.  It’s a false currency, not rooted in anything except pretend market forces.  Lux isn’t an economy, it’s a system of incentives and disincentives, masquerading as an economy.  Incentives to work, produce, conform, incentives to get out there and do more.”

“I’m feeling those incentives and disincentives from the family more than anyone.”

She could track ‘Figtree’ doing a quick browse of her records.  Pulling up abbreviated highlights for Michal.

“You want a ship.”

She shrugged.  “As a long-term goal.”

“Hiring people from Griffey Docks?  Or the twenty-nine families at large?”

“Some.  But I’d rather do more like what Melville is doing.  Finding allies among heavily modded dock workers, hiring independent agents…”

“Gets tricky.”

“I know.”

“I like that.  As a goal.  We need more people who have those big goals.  Like having a dock of their own, or a block.”

She didn’t have a response to that.  She didn’t know if she was supposed to ask for something, or say something, elaborate…

He was still glancing over her records and highlight moments.  She returned the favor.

She could see him growing up, a hard worker, with a strict father that bordered on cruel.  He’d hit a limit, stopped working altogether, and tried to acquire product to resell at the docks, before finding prejudice against the folk got to be too much.  One mugging for his product.  Then, three weeks later, he’d been trashed.  Just short of killed.

That had happened on Inanna.  Second to Earth, where things were supposed to be closest to ideal.

Body damaged, still bankrupted with fines to pay after clawing at someone immediately after the mugging, he’d picked himself up, put his head down, and worked.  Somewhere along the way, he’d started holding his head high, and had started being recognized as a leader and someone to go to for counsel.  From there, he’d become a leader at 59.

He didn’t look very old.  Being bald helped with that.

“You want a ship, and you’re worried that getting involved will burn bridges.  If you get a bad reputation or if employers can check your onboard records and find out you started trouble or sabotaged ships, people won’t want to work with you.”

“Basically,” she answered.  “If I can’t chase my dream I’ll-”

“Wither and die?”

She shrugged.  Not those words, exactly.

“I wouldn’t want to do that to you and Toby.”

She appreciated that he looped Toby into that.

“Give me something else,” he told her.  “Another trick, another strategy.  Even thoughts, about where things are, and what we’re all doing.”

“Is this a test?”

“A little bit.”

She thought for a short bit, then shook her head.  Even if she had ideas, which she didn’t, quite, she wasn’t sure she liked the idea of being the person with great ideas on how to wage war.

“Okay,” he told her.  “If you want this to be your contribution, that’s fine.  You should avoid trouble and investigators.  Come to Howington on Inanna for a year or two.  Best if you aren’t interviewed if they try to connect you to the thread.  That area sees a lot of traffic, no cameras, there’s reasonable doubt.  They’d want to question you and put it on you, but we can keep you out of their grip.  This shouldn’t stick.  The bridge is singed, but not burned.  Work hard, see if you can earn your ship.”

[Or?] Toby asked, echoing her thought.  Winnifred remained silent.

“Or, Toby, Winnifred, we strike a middle ground.  Keep you out of the way.  Bit longer of a stay on Inanna.  Let us borrow your thoughts.  You know ships.  You think about these things in the right way.  Anything you come up with, Howington pays you.  It won’t be a groundbreaking amount, but it’s a few months of work worth.  A few payments like that means you probably don’t have to worry about buying your big retrofit, and can start toward your ship earlier.”

“That’s a middle ground?  It’s not one or the other?  There’s a more extreme option.”

“Join the fight in a serious way.  Let the bridges burn if they’re going to burn.  But trust, at the same time, that the families support you.  Help us, and we help you.  You do your turn, we pay you back.  Howington Station has six decommissioned ships.  Any one you can get flying, you can take.  Crew it with our people, or with our friends.  Do that, and burnt bridges don’t look so bad.”

“I still wouldn’t be able to dock most places.”

“Help us find an outcome where we can.”

“That’s easier to say than to do.”

“So is earning a ship of your own through hard work and determination, when you have other things to pay for.  Which still wouldn’t guarantee you could dock places.  People hate us.  I’ve experienced that.  You’ve seen my records, you know I have.”

More than some.  Being brutalized, his body taken, left in debt.

“What do you think, Toby?” she asked, subvocalizing.

[There are no great options.  His offer of a ship is better than some.]

“I’d hate it,” she said, out loud.

“You think anyone enjoys fighting?  I’d rather have one person who doesn’t want to fight, than ten who enjoy it.  Because that one person is looking for a way to end this.  Look, you’re smart, Winnifred.  You study, I know you don’t fit in.  If you’d been at my station, I’d have pushed for you to be sent elsewhere, where you’d be less lonely.  That’s part of the reason I want you with us.”

It wasn’t the first time she had had family push these ideas at her, asking for a plan from her.  Uncle Ellis.  Her dad before him.  She’d been nagged by Aunt Gwen, talked at by Old Price.

This felt like a distillation of all the other talks together, from someone who had that ability to take things up another level, to crystallize it into a choice.

Betray the her of right now, to make headway to her dream?

Or sacrifice her dream, stay herself, and hope, somehow, that a way became clear.

She shook her head slightly.

[You want to back out.  Take the safe option.]

“When I asked before, if you had more ideas.  You did, didn’t you?” Michal asked.

“If I say I don’t want to be involved, but give you more good ideas, then I’m arguing against myself.  If I want to fight, in exchange for a ship, I’m only giving you what I’d already give.”

“Winnifred,” her father said, his voice low.

She went still, looking over.

“Don’t withhold.”

She hesitated, feeling the pressure from her father, and from Michal, both of whom were silent.

“What if the families broke up?”

Her father seemed to bristle at that.

“What do you mean?” Michal asked.

“The way we are right now, we’re holding onto something that doesn’t exist.  Property, ‘homes’ when we were basically homeless.”

“Some would argue it’s more than that,” Michal said.  “Your father included.”

She glanced over.  He looked stern.

“If you wanted to make them change, show them how the alternative is worse.  If we have no docks… we splinter.  Spread out… everywhere.  Small groups.”

“We’d lose culture.”

“We… we’re connected.  We’d find a way.  We’d have to.  But we’re losing it anyway.  Different families doing different things, we’ll have conservative groups like Griffey Docks pushing back against Melville Cap, both angry about what the other family is doing.  Splinter… make it part of the plan, that each group does something different, and all of us are hard to catch, hard to anticipate and suppress.  There’ll be less anger.”

“You’re not the first to suggest those tactics.  I’ll tell you that.  There are differences of opinion on doing that.  Some think that if we splintered, some people wouldn’t come home.”

She shrugged.

“You included?”

“I don’t know.  Depends on, like… if I’m doing this for a ship, then I’d have reason to come back.”

“Don’t be mercenary,” her father hissed.

Michal raised a clawed hand, to stop her father before he could launch into a tirade.

“You haven’t decided.  That’s fine.  I spoke against the ‘splintering’, as you call it.  You’ve nudged me slightly toward the idea, Winnifred.  I’m far from convinced, but… take that for what it’s worth.”

[You outright said you didn’t feel like you matter.  He’s speaking to that.]

“I am, Toby,” Michal said.

He was more quick to catch someone’s onboard saying or reporting something.

[I wasn’t hiding it.  Simply serving my owner.]

“And I’m not blaming you for doing that.  Take good care of our Winnifred, and Winnifred, think about the options I laid out.  Don’t make a decision right now,” Michal told her.  “I’m sorry to interrupt your leisure.  Rest, catch up on things, we have another day of work tomorrow.  Come to me when you’re ready.  You can message me at any time.”

Winnifred nodded.

Her father was wordless, from the other end of the storage container they were using as shared quarters, his gaze penetrating.

She curled up, her back to him, and selected a few more feeds to request, that would travel their long distance to her to be loaded.

➨

The battery farm was a sort of mini-station, ninety-nine percent automated.  Materials were delivered to the initial setups after being bought, fed into bins, and the machinery processed it all.  Solar panels were manufactured here, in the void, well away from any planet, and connected side by side, and above one another.  Batteries the size of the loading container they were using for quarters were manufactured, connected, charged, and carried away to be sold.  A portion of the money went back into materials to expand the farm.  A massive network of simple solar panels that fanned out through the darkness of space.

All good, as long as it was running.  But things broke, and the power that chained through the panels to the battery sites could be broken off.

They were being asked to check every panel around the ones that had gone wrong, to diagnose, scanning materials to make sure no pollutant or skewed processes had entered the manufacturing process, and re-check settings.  For each set they did, they had to check against the undamaged, unaffected panels further away, as a control.

There were 112,000 hexagonal panels, and change.  Each point of breakage had six panels around it and at least one control.  The work quickly became hypnotic.

She’d watched a lot of the records of fighting.  Lewis had had some on his onboard, and passed her them, so she didn’t have to wait for them to be transmitted from the world out to where she was, a little closer to the sun than Earth, but well away from Earth’s orbit.

Scenes played through her head.

[MOVE]

The signal from Toby was uncharacteristically blunt, sudden, and came with a jolt, borderline painful.

She moved.  Toby provided an abundance of signals, but all were the same.  She had to pick one, and chose, in the spur of the moment, to set foot on the solar panel and use it to kick herself off, while burning fuel in the pack at her back, to add to that movement.

That blunt contact with the panel and the level of force she’d just applied might mean she had to recheck it and each of the six around it.

For how sudden the warning was, the attack came a while after.

But Toby had told her to move and pushed her to keep moving, and she had.

It came fast and had no intention of stopping.  It crashed through panels, and shattered them, while sending ripples through the wider construction.

Those ripples made panels buckle, clasps came undone, and connections that carried power from one to another, in a daisy chain, until they fed into the battery stations?  Broken apart.

The debris expanded out, coming fast, and she had to twist her body.

Glass, even at high velocities, didn’t do much to her, and she’d put range between herself and it with Toby’s warning.

Her body thrummed with the shock of what had just happened, and the dots of pain where glass had scuffed her.

Toby supplied the best shot he’d been able to pull out.  A ship.  Unmanned, moving at high speeds, right for them.

The ship was a small container ship.  A Bainn 105.  Not much different from the bin the were using for quarters and holding their supplies for the long job, but this was meant to travel long distances.  The sort of ship one used if a bunch of miners on a throwaway planet wanted a restock of some basics, plus some alcohol.  Load it onto a ship and send it moving in a straight line.

Usually from another ship or zero-G station platform.

Toby wasn’t supplying the source.

Winnifred dared to uncurl from the ball she’d formed, and turned, wincing a bit as a bit of shattered paneling caught her cheekbone.  No real damage- she had the thumbprint-sized bit of expanding gel there, to absorb heat and protect her face, especailly that sensitive, high-visibility area where skin met mask.

They’d been building something beautiful and intricate, in a painstaking way, and someone had just flown a wrecking ball through it.

“You alright?” her father messaged her.

Spurts of fuel expenditure carried him her way.

She was a bit surprised to be met with a hug.  He touched his forehead to hers.  He messaged her.  “I was worried.”

She glanced over at the damage.  The craft had been square, but the damage unfolded like a circular ripple, with the debris scattering out into the void of space that same way.

“You were closer to that than I was.”

“I worried,” he said.

The damage was too comprehensive.  This wouldn’t be an easy or a fast fix.  Even the arrangement, with a hole now in the center of it, needed to be taken apart and put back together.

“Was that aimed at us?” she asked.

“Or at the people who hired us,” her father said.  “Things are escalating.”

It took nearly an hour before Michal arrived from the second nearest planet, where he’d been looking after other work.  The limitation of onboards and the fact they were distant from the Belt network meant they couldn’t easily communicate or pass on messages.  They didn’t have a communication array.

So Michal didn’t have the best picture of how bad it was until he’d come to see.

“Job’s canceled,” the man told them.  “Retire.  Catch your breath.  We’ll figure this out.”

“Do we know who it was?” Winnifred’s father asked.

“Not yet.  But we will.”

That sounded so certain.

Despite herself, she had Toby search Michal’s records, and requested records of other key members of the family.  Even Uncle Ellis.

It got Michal’s attention, that she was even looking.

This attack could be the sort of thing that motivated more people in the families to act.  If it was faked…

Michal, it seemed, didn’t hold the fact she’d looked against her.

People could be weird, though, caring too much or too little about people searching their history.

They were just entering the container, when Lewis messaged them.  He was further out, collecting spilled materials.

“It was a goodbye sort of ‘fuck you’.”

“Goodbye?” her father asked.

“From who?” Winnifred asked.

Toby was already supplying the answer to her question.  From a friend of a friend of a friend, of the crabby woman who’d owned the Tailwind-TX.  She looked over the records.

“They barely used the docks or went off planet.  Going by purchase records, they’re some angry, rich loon that got invested, happy to have a target to go after.  It wouldn’t be the first time, but that was close to being a murder attempt.”

“Winnifred,” her father said.

She paused, then tuned into what he was looking at.

A ‘goodbye’ fuck you because the judicial authorities were otherwise preoccupied.  There was a Belt-wide order for a temporary cessation to hostilities, on threat of treble penalties.

There were bigger fish to fry.

The second wave of people were coming in.  Angry, noisy about what was going on.  But they caught on, that something had people’s attention.  The third wave of people came silently, their eyes on what their onboards were sharing out to them.

At 10:40am on Earth’s Science Center, the largest across all the twelve worlds, there had been an attack.  Nanotech had been used.

The feed her father had pulled up had warnings she had to push past, to see.

The scenes were still.  Bodies, arched, twisted, torn, and were warped by the nanotech within.  Blood leaked out of the torn parts, pooling below them.  Faces contorted in silent screams.

The nature of the nanotech attack, distilled down to a few informational panels.  DNA damage, strategically located brain damage.  Pain. 

She barely tracked the times, locations, and movements.  The scenes had her full attention.  Authorities with their Tenures and their Barts, and all the variations and similar craft had surrounded the block.  They’d set up at key positions, but there were threats of weapons, so they had to move carefully.

“Our enemies could have done that to us,” Jack messaged them.  He, Lewis, and another few workers were coming in from the fringes.

Nobody made much mention of the fact someone had driven a ship through their work site and scattered the area with shattered solar panel.

It wasn’t her dad’s nature to speak against that, or diminish their enemies.  But Winnifred had the impression that… no.  Their enemies didn’t go this far.  People out there hated the folk, but they wouldn’t torture.

11:50, after a period of transformation and organization, the nanotech-transformed soldiers had been organized, people gathered in the entry hall where the initial exhibits were, celebrating what the Belt was, with its twelve worlds and thirty-two throwaway planets.  They’d started to make an announcement, a statement on why they were doing this.

Stupid reasons.

Interrupted, when one of the nanotech-modified people killed the leader.

Winnifred wasn’t sure what had happened.  The news packet had all the images, collected from feeds, the bits of video, chronology, all the bits of information.  But she had to make a request, accept the lag in how late it was received, then wait for it to be sent back.

With the limited capacity of the communication array on the box ship, sometimes that wait was staggered, because others were asking, and only so much information could be passed through.

But she wasn’t the only one asking for this, interested in how it had happened.

She looked backward from the moment of attack to see who it was, and how they’d managed it.

“Bas,” the girl said, subvocalizing.  “Don’t put me to sleep.  I have an idea.”

A.  Just ‘A’, as a name.

There was some event, planned to start in an hour.  A was sitting in the dark, a guitar in her lap.  Meditating, maybe.

Who was she?

➨

“Control my breathing.”

[Already on it.]

The weight of tens of billions of eyes seemed to make every movement difficult.  A’s stress levels kept spiking.

Her fingers toyed with the strings of her guitar.

[You can still back out.]

She shook her head slightly, then acted as if it was because she’d placed her fingers wrong.

Tens of thousands of messages came at her from all directions.

Asking her why she hadn’t done more.

Telling her she was a hero.

Asking what she’d do.  Would she join Generation Colors?

What planets was she going to?

What opinions did she hold on the great belt debate, that had come up as she’d entered the science center?

Did she miss her friends, Vince and Cowrie?  Why hadn’t she said more about them?

Would she platform another independent band, like the one she’d been in?  She could make that her thing.  Starting, of course, with the person asking.

If she profited or gained notoriety from a bad incident like this, she was a monster.

She deserved it.  She was a hero.

She was a terrible, spoiled person.  How could anyone think she was likable?

He filtered it, caught it.  But she could look at what he was doing, and glance at the messages.

[Focus on other things,] he told her.  Not in the back channel.

Her fingers nervously moved across the strings, without plucking them.

“Five minutes.  Are you ready?” a man asked.

She glanced at the incoming messages, and found Basil had hid then from view.

She looked through his processes, found the folder he’d tucked them away in, and looked.  The first message was blunt:

I don’t know why people are excited.  She’s not good at music.

She looked away, as if stung.

“Yes,” she said, whisper-quiet.  “I think so.”

She wasn’t.

She was on the verge of panic, and only Basil’s intervention blocked it.

You only managed to do what you did because of your onboard.

He messaged her on the back channel.

[Stop reading the messages]

“Don’t tell me what to do.”

“Three minutes.  Do you want lights on, to see what you’re doing, or…?”

“That’s okay, but thank you.  Let my onboard handle it.  Bas, keep it simple?  White spotlight.”

[Okay.]

She adjusted how she sat on the stool, and moved the guitar.  A new one, provided by Elabre Systems.  She worked on her breathing for a little bit, then her cortisol levels spiked.

“Don’t control my breathing.”

[You asked me to a few minutes ago.]

“I’m telling you to stop.  It’s making me feel claustrophobic.”

[I don’t know how I’m supposed to be your onboard like this.  I’m trying to help.  But you work against me.]

“You should have thought about that before you took control over my body, against my wishes.”

She closed her eyes, exhaling.

“One minute thirty.”

Basil was concerned any words of support would have the opposite of the intended effect.

That one minute and thirty seconds felt like a long, long time.

You can back out.  You should.

He couldn’t tell her, because the way she was right now, she’d push back and do the opposite.

“Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five…”

The voice dropped away, finishing the countdown in silence.

Curtains parted.

Basil turned on the light, soft.  They were on a stage, but there was no audience out there.  A sat on a stool, dressed in a simple white shirt and skirt, and knee-length lace-up boots, hunched over her guitar, hair long enough to touch and coil on the ground.

There was an audience out there of fifty-one billion.

Her eyes moved to that number.

Her breathing caught.

Hundreds of thousands of messages directed specifically to her came through every second.

Her breathing hitched, and billions of people saw it.  Two hundred thousand were loading up everything A was feeling as an immersive simulation.  Every clench of a muscle, every slight movement of the finger.

A was paralyzed.  Her inner thigh quivered, and she tried lowering her foot to a lower rung on the stool, found it too far, and retreated, back to the position she’d been in.

Seconds crept on.

[Say you wanted to play a piece of music for Vince, Cowrie, and Nos, but you’re still new to music and you’re too nervous to do it well, so you’ll use words instead.  Mention the other deceased.  They’ll still love you.  The ones who matter will respect it.]

A length of her hair fell across the strings.  She started to move it, and nearly dropped the guitar.

She was actively avoiding looking at the viewer count, but he could tell she was aware of it.

[If you make it about speaking for the deceased, they’ll respect it.  People will follow your music, but it will be manageable numbers, lower pressure.  They’ll follow you for you, A.]

She reasserted her grip on the guitar.

“Play for me.”

He scanned records, trying to find a good rationale, a good response.  He was blindsided.  The only rational answer was:

[You don’t want me to.  You’d hate me if I did.]

“I’m ordering you, as your client.  I won’t be someone who goes out whimpering as I black out.  I won’t fuck up here.  You took control over me before.  Take control now.  Play.”

He did.

Fingers to strings.

“Greatest hits.  Best I ever played, across all the practice sessions.  That way, it’s me.”

[I’m concerned-]

“Fuck your concern and play.”

The first strum of the semi-acoustic produced its rich, sustained sound, with a bit of whine to it.

From there, working purely through the back channel, so nobody on the outside would see his hand in things, he recalled and played her music from her band practice with Vince and the others.

A was not a bad musician.  Her best was excellent.

He put an image of the group with their instruments together on the wall behind her, as the music steadily picked up in speed and intensity.

She glanced back over her shoulder at the image.  Then she nodded, as if to herself.

“We’re putting other photos up, right?” she asked, subvocalizing, her fingers moving under Basil’s control.

It was good she had the presence to ask.

[A bit later.]

She nodded a bit again.

For all that they’d discussed theatrics and presentation, she was a single person sitting on a stool on a stage, not moving much, hunched over, face almost hidden from view by hanging hair, some of which draped over the guitar, and got in the way, forcing him to flick parts of it away, or blow.

The solo had a stretch of long, whiny notes, before the accompaniment came on.  This was a soft introduction to her joining Generation Colors, a homage to those who were dying, and as the other kids in the group started to play their own instruments, Basil put up the images of others who’d died, adding them to the walls around them, while dimming the central spotlight.

A startled as Blue started singing.

It sounded like Vince. Probably intentional.

A bit of a blindside.  If Basil was cynical about things, it was an intentional one.  With the nature of onboards, and the fact anyone could look in, any rehearsal would have been little different from a first performance.  They’d discussed.

A had decided not to.  If the group didn’t mesh… that could be part of the narrative.  If they could, that was fitting.

He let her miss a note on the shock about his voice, then find her stride shortly after.

[A, I’m going to pass control to you.]

“No.”

[Carry on after the final verse.  It needs to be you.  Because I don’t think you’re going to forgive me for this, after ordering me.  I worry you won’t forgive yourself.  Trust me, it’ll be fine.]

They played through the song Vince had written.

As they drew close, she subvocalized, “They stop.”

He communicated to the others.  Some had consoles near them.  Others had onboards.

They finished out the song.  A played on.

He took the first few notes, then ceded control.

She kept going, improvising the solo.  As she went, she stumbled, struggling.

There was that peripheral awareness of the viewer count.

Then the final note dragged out in the silence, tremulous and high.  Tears welled in her eyes.  Frustration. She wiped at one eye, and tried to move her hair out of the way.  It wasn’t cooperating, and she had a moment, hand clenched, like she wanted to fight it.

Green hurried over, leaving the drum set behind.

“That was great,” Green whispered.  “Want to go?”

“We were supposed to play more.”

“That can be it.  That was more than enough.  People will understand.”

I said that to you before, Basil thought.

A was nodding.  She accepted help getting down from the stool, using one arm to pull her hair around it.  Her group was with her in solidarity, stepping off the stage.  No applause.  Just the eyes of billions, following them as they went backstage.  In a way, the performance continued, now unending.

➨

Winnifred felt chills as the solo continued, full of restrained emotion.  The glimpses of A’s face looked intense, angry, upset.  Her hand flew up and down the neck of the guitar.

The rest of the group stopped playing.  A carried on.

Emotions overwhelming her, the notes steadily became more broken, fragmented.  Like it was all overwhelming her, now that the music was stopping, and she couldn’t pour herself into it.  The broken notes a struggle to hang onto that.

She stopped, sound still ringing.

Winnifred had a tear in her eye.  It startled her when A reached up and wiped away one of her own.

The group walked over.  The fact Winnifred could look through A’s onboard and catch the whisper, as Green reassured, and told her it was okay to stop, it felt intimate.

The group walked offstage.  Winnifred backed off, because it felt wrong to keep watching past that point.  Even if billions of other people were.

She’d check in later.

“Holy shit,” she murmured.

[That was something.  The line that’s going around seems to be that she’s an exceptional individual made better by a good relationship with her onboard.]

“Yeah.  For sure.”

[I don’t want to come across like I’m tooting my own horn, but you’re not so different.  You’re exceptional.]

“I love you, Toby.  Toot that horn.”

[Not what I was driving at.]

“She’s doing something big with it all, you know?  I’m not.  I should.”

[You’re doing fine.  Here.  Look.]

She looked.

A had an onboard.  ‘Basil’.  Winnifred had caught that.  But she hadn’t seen the model number.

“Same as us.  IDLX-B,” Winnifred noted.

She went back to what she’d seen in the highlight reel, while waiting for the show to start.

A young ‘A’, gender indeterminate back then, saying, “I want to have a spaceship, and explore.”

The frustration at it all.

Other parallels, the more Winnifred looked.

It felt like it meant something.  She hadn’t felt like this in a long time.  There was meaning, something to drive for.

She didn’t feel so fucking alone in the world, with only Toby by her side.

“I want to fight, and make a difference,” she told Toby.   “Get my ship the hard way.”

1.8.O – CONTROL

The burns on Orion’s shoulders were a constant ache now.  He was sweating, and he wasn’t sure how much of that was from the way getting anywhere took effort.  A part of him kept expecting there to be a flight of stairs, or a doorway, human-proportioned, that would open up into a place where things were placed in convenient reach, easy to access.

The air felt processed, cold, and had a faint organic, composty smell to it, from where the moss had grown out too far, then died.  ‘The fucking moss’ as Blackbox put it.

Owing to the fact he’d started first and Blackbox had only the one arm, he was ahead of Blackbox in climbing the shaft.  He reached the vent opening, and listened, before shifting it.

“Check any hallway before you enter,” Blackbox said.

“Any tips?”

Blackbox managed to squeeze past him, heavy metal body scraping against metal as he reached for the vent.  Orion ended up holding it out while Blackbox reached out.

The material at the back of Blackbox’s hand looked improvised, a plate scavenged from elsewhere that was fixed into place with some kind of adhesive, to cover the more intricate mechanisms of the fingers.  Unlike the matte, nonreflective black of Blackbox’s body, it had more of a reflective surface.

He turned it and angled it slightly.  “The subliminal glyphs they use are usually bright.  So if I look down the hallway and see any points of light, that’s a bad sign.”

Sure enough, there were several blurry spots of light reflected on the metal, scattered at random points along the walls and ceiling.  A dozen, going down the hallway, both ways.

He could hear voices.  Far enough away to be muffled by the intervening corners and corridors, parts of words echoing, but not quite enough to make out.

“What are the chances those things act like alarms and call other things?” Orion whispered.

“Medium.”

“Reactive to sound?  Movement?”

“Low to medium.”

“Quiet!” he called out.  “Don’t move!”

Blackbox pulled his hand back and gripped the cloth at the back of Orion’s waist.  As if preparing to haul Orion down backward.

The voices had stopped.

Nothing had reacted.

“There aren’t any convenient red lights or sounds if it sends out an alarm,” Blackbox whispered.

“Bombs,” Orion said, loud enough the other voices could hear.  “Don’t move, don’t even look.  Wait.”

He said that ‘wait’ with enough urgency in his voice he hoped they’d listen.

There were whispers further down the hall, inaudible.

“Do we go around?”

“I don’t think we have any great alternative routes.  Any other path we take has different dangers.  Or we might get seen by the fox.”

Orion nodded.  He looked at the hand, as Blackbox extended it out into the hallway, moving it, reflecting different parts of the hall.  “Then we do it blind?”

“I’d rather not, with a big group of rookies.  One of them tries to sneak a peek or doubts you, sees a glyph, and reacts, others open their eyes?”

“Right.”

“Since you shouted, and that didn’t seem to draw any attention, you want to try something else?  You climb out.  Eyes closed.  Use that laser cutter.”

Orion thought about it.

“I’ll get in the way of the next set of hazards.  We take turns.  If we reach that other group, they take turns too.”

They were still whispering.  It gave Orion the willies.

Orion nodded.

He slithered out of the vent, getting his torso out, groping blind until he touched moist metal floor, and then eased himself to the ground, cheek and chest touching floor before his legs fully left the vent.  His fingers found handholds to pull him forward.

Bending this way made the burns hurt something fierce.

He drew the laser cutter.

“Turn a bit left.”

“Hold on.”  Orion still had the images and data that appeared in his field of vision.  He had a sense- he searched.

Measuring tools.

He measured, turned to his left, and watched the rulers and the compass with its ninety degree arc -after a slight adjustment on his part- unfold against the back of his eyelids.

He turned a slow circle, finding his position, then locked it.  “Center me.”

“Bit left, like I said.”

He turned.  Then aiming, he fired a short, quarter-second burst.  He could see the orange-red flare, bright enough to penetrate his eyelids.

“Scared me for a second there, Orion.”

“That centered?”

“Close enough.  Let’s start with a close one.  If that’s twelve, your two o’clock.  At the level of your heart, ten feet ahead, there’s a glyph left sticking out of the wall there.  And Orion?”

“Yeah?”

“I’ve got my arm extended.  I shout?  You find my arm, we get you in the vent, fast.”

“Firing now.”

He fired, and made a slight cross motion, then a circle, to cover the most area around the target point.

The light flared.  His eyes adjusted to the glare that penetrated his eyeballs.

“Yeah.  You clipped it.  Must have scarred the projector part.  It’s out.  Next-”

Orion centered himself again, using the coordinates he’d mapped out.

“-yeah.  Eight o’clock, eye level.”

Orion fired.

“Little higher, I think.”

Orion adjusted, and repeated the little cross-then-circle move, to cover more area around the target point, and catch any near-misses.

He heard the metal clatter to the ground, faintly sizzling.

“Next…”

They removed six or seven more in that fashion, with Blackbox giving Orion directions, looking at a reflection of the hallway, blurry and diffuse on black metal, guessing at the needed adjustments based on how the laser appeared reflected on that same material.

“How are you guys holding up?” Orion asked, as he ventured a bit further down the hallway.

There were muttering sounds.

Orion backed away.

“Did they respond?” Blackbox asked.

“No,” Orion murmured.

He was halfway into the vent, accepting prods from Blackbox, when he heard a distant laugh.

Whatever it was that was down the hall and around the corner, it moved in a way that sounded like a cascading crash, a pile of junk in a junkyard that had some load-bearing piece removed, letting a whole pile of it slide down, crashing and banging against other pieces of it.

Too noisy to be the fox.

With it, a brief flare of white against Orion’s closed eyelids.  That glowing hologram projection.  Much bigger than anything the wall-mounted ‘presents’ some other machine had left behind were.  Brighter.

The sound of it faded.  It was going down a corridor, away from him.

“Shit,” Orion swore.  He’d been climbing into the vent, but now he reversed direction.

“What are you doing?”

“They don’t know.”

“Hold on, I’ll come.”

“Don’t have time.”

“Orion.  That laser cutter of yours.  It cuts the panels that generate the hologram, it didn’t do much to the metal.”

Orion turned, opening his eyes, and saw Blackbox was holding one of the fallen glyph generators that had landed near the vent opening.  The laser cutter had an optimal range.  That range was short.  But even sub-optimally, it produced heat, and the panes that projected out the holograms were glass-like.

He accepted that piece of information, and chased.

Blackbox could be heard, running, a dozen paces behind, footfalls heavier.

Orion’s own footfalls were muted by the gel-like padding on the underside of his boots.

He could hear the muttering sound, and he realized why it had felt so eerie.

It was his own voice, and Blackbox’s.  Statements, recorded, and played back, altered in a way that they were wordless.

“Coming to you!  Show your weapons, if you have any!  Arms spread!”

He dared to open his eyes in a squint, since there wasn’t any glow of bright light, and saw the tail end of the machine.  It was built like a weasel, limbs short and body long.  The head was looking around a corner, floating letters and lines of the glyphs radiating around it.  The tail end of its body was two-point two-two meters tall and two point five meters wide.  The entirety of it had to be twenty meters, from tail tip to head.  He couldn’t see the head, and it was a little bit sinuous, so he didn’t know for sure.

They were approaching.  They’d thought, the same way Orion and Blackbox had, that the voices were the people they were looking for.

“Don’t come!” he hollered.  “Trap!”

If the machine had any feelings at all, he’d surprised it.

It turned, its upper body almost folding back on itself as it brought its head closer to Orion.  He flinched away, squinting a bit harder, effectively blinding himself, because a ‘bit harder’ was close to fully closing his eyes.

He aimed the laser for the right general area, and fired.

Doing his best to rake the hologram projectors.

The glare against his now-closed eyelids dimmed by a quarter.  Then a bit more.

The glare diffused, almost disappearing.

A sound knocked Orion off his feet.  It was a noise that was low, bone-deep, and loud enough to make him lose his balance, lose his train of thought, want to throw up, and nearly shit himself, all at once.  Maybe he would’ve, if he’d eaten less recently.

He stopped firing, because he’d lost all sense of where he was relative to the machine.

He failed on his first attempt to get up.

The machine came for him.  Its subtler, slow movements were careful, but when the entire thing came, whatever mechanisms it used, it moved hard, with that crash he could feel.  It didn’t stop making the noise,either, and the sound changed with each movement and reorientation.

Orion managed to gather his thoughts enough to reach out, find a corner, and remind himself of where he was or where he should be.  He’d checked before coming around this corner.  Meaning it took him back the way he wanted to go.

He lurch-crawled around that corner.  It didn’t help him deal with the noise.

The machine came crashing after him, faster than he was.

The noise of Blackbox shooting his gun was barely audible, past the noise the machine made.  Orion focused on Blackbox, using the verticality of the man as a reference to find his own balance, leaned into a wall, and aimed backward, firing blind.  Adding whatever he could.

Blackbox finched, hard, like he’d had a vicious sneeze, straightened, then stepped to one side, bumping Orion’s arm to intentionally alter his arm, while still firing.

As the machine audibly closed the gap, that sound rattling Orion’s bones, Blackbox grabbed him, hauling him backward.  Down the hall, around another corner.

He dared to look that way, the machine behind him, and it took two tries to see straight enough to make out the vent Blackbox was shooting.

He was shoved through the vent, past the vent cover that had been damaged enough it hung from only one upper corner.  He immediately tried to crawl in enough to make room, but even afterward, Blackbox didn’t follow.

He simply lay there, reeling.

Eventually, the sound faded.

He felt bruised all over, he’d scraped himself raw against the vent cover while being shoved through, his ears were ringing, and he was pretty sure, from the way his hearing kept altering by small, measured degrees, that he’d been protected from all of that.

His shoulders still hurt from the burns.

After what felt like an eternity, he crawled out of the vent.

Would it still hint at its location with that whispering and murmuring background noise?  Trying to lure people closer, before it blasted them with sonic weaponry or smashed them with its massive bulk?

His lips stuck together when he parted them, and he realized he’d had a nosebleed.  It had stopped, and was already drying into something tacky to the touch, across upper lip, mouth, and chin.

Moving with ginger care and caution about every new corner or hallway, checking with his tablet and squinted eyes, he found Blackbox, slumped against a wall.

“You alive?” Orion asked.

“Alive,” Blackbox said.  “It got me.”

“Got how?”

“I was aiming for the source of the sound, a panel you’d cut flickered back on.  I caught a glimpse.”

Orion wasn’t sure what to say.

“Haven’t figured out what it did to me yet,” Blackbox said.  “Left a flickering white image stamped on my optic nerve.  Half-blind in one eye.  But that’s usual.  It did something to my brain, too.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Nah.”

Blackbox didn’t say much more, and Orion felt like anything more that he said would undercut the ‘sorry’ or sound unkind.

“…I knew what I was in for, when I agreed to come with.”

“Okay.  I’m still sorry.  Maybe I could’ve handled that better.”

“No.  They were in danger?”

“Yeah.  They were going to walk right into it.”

“Then it’s fine.  You did it right.  It’ll be you, down the line,” Blackbox said.

As if those words were some kind of momentum he could latch onto, Blackbox started to stand.  Orion offered a hand.

Blackbox was heavy, and every inch of Orion had that bruised feeling.

“It’ll be you,” Blackbox repeated, once he was upright.  “And hopefully, it’ll be you, while you’re helping others to get further.  Then it’ll be them, and the people after them.  Hopefully, somehow, some way, one of us gets somewhere we can do something useful.  Okay?”

The okay felt like a challenge.  If Blackbox was using that as a way to keep going… he had to accept it too.

“Okay.”

“Something like sending a message, if that’s the only option.  Or stopping this, slowing it down.  Giving people a way to organize, sustain themselves.”

“Yeah.”

“Yeah.”

They walked in silence, retracing their steps, being careful to check the way each time.

They finally reached the other group.  They were huddled, using the very limited medical supplies they’d been given to start out.

His display showed the names as he looked at them long enough.  Marte, Spur, Court, and Sever.

“Pitch,” Marte said.  “I’m sorry we didn’t get you out.  We thought you’d been crushed.  Then the case popped off the top of the pod you were in, and we couldn’t get to you to fix it.”

“It’s okay.”

“You dealt with it?”

“No,” Blackbox said.  “I took cover where it couldn’t reach me, it lingered for a bit, trying to blast me with sound or catch me with the subliminal glyphs, then moved on.  It’ll be in the area, still.”

“Along with the fox,” Orion said.

“What the fuck?” Court asked.

“It wouldn’t be the worst idea to use what you had in your kit,” Blackbox told Orion.  “I said to conserve it, this might be what you conserved it for.  You look like death.”

Orion considered, then shook his head.  “I think I was protected against the sound.”

“If you say so.  Were you four close?”

All four of the new people shook their heads.  Court added, “Not that close.”

“I was still deafened,” Spur said.

“Same,” Sever said.  “Medical kit helped that, fast.”

“I wasn’t, and I was two steps away from it at one point,” Orion told Blackbox.

“Alright then.  So.  Here’s the big question,” Blackbox said, turning to the four.  “Do any of you remember anything?  From before being sent here?”

All four shook their heads.

“Damn.”

“Are we supposed to?”

“No, I don’t know.  Thought there was a chance.  Sometimes it happens.”

“What do you know?” Sever asked, at the same time Spur said, “We were gonna-”

Everyone wanted to know everything.  It was a jumble, not helped by Court trying to interject to instill peace, but only adding his voice to the chaos.

“Introductions first,” Blackbox said, raising his voice.  “What do you have, what do you know?”

Court was first to speak.  He was a skinny guy, thirty or so, with pale white skin that was even bluish at the temples, though that might’ve been him being paler and more drawn-out after a bad scare and injury.  The way he kept moving his hand up to his head and seemed vaguely surprised at the absence up there made Orion think he’d had hair, but his blond hair was shorn short.  His tattoos were the same coppery tone as Orion’s- the entire group’s were.  He explained that he knew about communication systems.

Spur was a young woman, twenty or so, with dark brown hair that didn’t sit flat, light brown skin, and dark freckles.  She’d wiped her face clear of blood post-nosebleed, but hadn’t managed to get the blood that leaked from one ear.  She had a case with a quadruped drone the size of a dog, and one with a flying drone the size of a bird, and was pretty sure she could remotely connect to them- or to other systems.

“You’ll want to be careful.  Real careful,” Blackbox said.  “You can’t squint a drone’s eyes shut, and if you’re looking through it, you might see one of those glyphs.”

Which prompted a whole discussion about the tools the machines had available to them, the glyphs, and more.

“…I keep hoping like hell I find out there’s a color I can’t see, and that’s it, that’s all I lost,” Blackbox finished.  “I hope that it’s something easy.  Because until then… everything’s scary.  Could be I have an urge to throw myself off any ledge I see.  Could be I have a desire to self immolate, and I haven’t seen any ways to set myself on fire yet.  When it kicks in, there’s nothing I could do.”

“Could it be us?” Court asked.  “Something we say or do?”

“Who the hell knows?”

“Maybe you give up your weapon?”

“Maybe I don’t,” Blackbox said, voice hard.  “Nah.  I’m a soldier.  I give up the gun?  What am I good for?”

“Advice.  Manpower,” Orion said, quiet.

“I could kill you as easily with a punch as I could with a gun,  I’m keeping my weapon.”

There was something in his tone.

Marte was a bit heavyset, with a barrel chest and round face, but a fair amount of that looked to be muscle.  The way skin had stretched to the point of having stretch marks around joints, Orion was willing to bet it was synthetic or forced.  He had a sword that looked dainty, compared to the rest of his frame.

And Sever was a doctor, but of the wrong kind to help them.  A man with long hair, and  bodysuit that incorporated a long coat and toolbelts.

“I could make and fit a replacement arm for you,” he told Blackbox.

“Yeah?  Could you make it stop hurting?”

“Depends on the source of the pain.  Maybe?”

“The brain.  It’s a virus in the meat of my brain.  It’s the only part of me that’s organic.  Even my face is synthetic, I think.”

“I don’t think I could do anything about that.”

Blackbox nodded.

Was he disappointed?

“I’ve got to relieve myself, then let’s get out of here?” Orion said.

“Sure,” Blackbox said.  “So, kids.  I’ll give you the rundown before Orion gets back.”

“Orion?” Court asked.

Orion frowned at Blackbox, then just said, “I don’t want the name they gave me, if they’d send me somewhere like this.”

“Maybe we volunteered?” Spur asked.

“Fine, he can be ‘Orion’, but why are we kids?  He’s been around the same amount of time as us,” Court pointed out.

“Less time,” Sever said.  “He woke up a bit later.”

“Because you don’t know, but I’ve already told him, and fought alongside him.  You shouldn’t trust people,” Blackbox told the newbies.  “There are raiders.”

Blackbox kept explaining the situation while Orion checked a corner, then turned, finding a nook to piss in.

The urine stream came in fairly normal at first, but quickly turned crimson, with a flare of pain, and a lot of spatter.

“Ffuck,” Orion swore, gritting his teeth through the rest of it.  He could feel a stabbing pain in his side.  He leaned into the wall, wincing.

Even after he’d finished and put his equipment away, he leaned into his forearm, which was braced against the wall, forehead resting against arm, breathing hard.

His insides still felt bruised and jelly-like, but were rigid when he pressed a hand against his stomach.

He walked back, pulling out his supply kit, and was just pulling out the injectable as he returned to the group.

“…can’t fight them.  None of the weapons I’ve seen do much more than damage their functionality.  They’re still a lot of power and a lot of metal.  The smallest of them that I’ve seen beat the strongest of us in an arm wrestling competition,” Blackbox was explaining.

“Unless you count the little things that got plugged into the walls.”

“Those aren’t machines.  They’re… installations.”

“Or eggs?” Orion suggested.  “That grow into things like the weasel?”

“Don’t even fucking say that out loud.  You’ll give them ideas.  And I thought it was a lizard.”

Orion shrugged.

He jammed the needle into his leg.

“Change your mind?  You doing alright?” Blackbox asked.

“I’ll be doing better soon, hopefully,” Orion said.  The injectable fluid was a dark gray, and looking at it brought up a menu in his field of vision.  He went through the options, and put ‘internal damage’ at the top, then went down the list.  Bones.  The burns.  Eyes and ears.

It seemed to be a priority system.

He jammed it into his leg, through the clothes he’d been given, and waited as it injected the thick fluid.

Blackbox watched, then as Orion pulled it out, he turned to the others, and said, “Pack up, let’s go.”

People belted on their provisions and put away the cases and gear they’d pulled out during their introductions.  Marte kept his sword out.

They naturally fell into two groups.  Blackbox and Orion in the lead, the kids leading behind.

He glanced back.

Sever and Spur were walking closer together than anyone.

“You know each other?”

“I don’t know anyone,” Spur said.

“But does it feel like you know each other?  Or might’ve known each other, before?  Does it feel natural to be close together?”

“A bit?” Spur asked, like it was a question, turning to Sever.

“Maybe,” was the short-form response.

“Because when I saw Pine, something in me- my first instinct was to be close to her.  Touch my forehead to hers.  I wanted to hug her, save her.  But I was already too late.”

“It was a shit situation,” Court said.

Orion didn’t like dismissing it like that.  “So the reason I ask, is I think I knew her before.  Maybe you knew each other, before?”

“Maybe you all did,” Blackbox said.  “If my old friend Baton was right, and so many of us are here because of crimes we committed, earning ourselves a soft death sentence, it’d make sense for a group to be sent together, if they did the deed together.”

Orion looked at the others, trying to get a feel for what his first instincts might be, with each of them.  Love?  Friendship?  Professional trust?  Something else?

Blackbox gave Orion a long sidelong look, as if silently asking the question, why aren’t you telling them you remember?

Orion wasn’t sure.  He wasn’t sure why he wasn’t sure.  But the feeling persisted.

They crossed into a more open section, which was interesting, if only because it let them use tools like the reflective black material of the tablet -squinting eyes to reduce visibility- to make sure they weren’t being followed.

The space felt like it could be a hangar, with a rise on the one side housing a giant multi-segment window, overlooking… field?  Not flatness, because there were trenches, and some platforms slightly higher than the rest of the ground, with devices that might have been shock absorbers.  A ‘field’ with some natural rises but a mostly flat, obstacle-free expanse felt like the closest parallel to the natural world.

Beneath panels, in the deepest parts of the trenches, and at the footing of some of the shock absorbers beneath heavy platforms, there was more of the green moss.

“Hate it,” Spur murmured.

“You hate it?”

“Have to be careful near some windows.  They look out at other parts of the structure, and those parts have massive gylphs on them,” Blackbox explained.

“Not here,” Court pointed out.

“No.  Not here.  But close by, you get glimpses.  Then your life might be over.”

Blackbox’s words were heavy.

He still hadn’t figured out what had happened, when he’d glimpsed the weasel’s glyph.

“Is it always the same, for every machine?” Orion asked, to fill the silence.

“Varies.  But some specialize.”

“Look,” Spur said.  She pointed.

Shooting stars?  There were a dozen, flying left to right.

No.  They looked wrong.

“More pods,” Blackbox said.

“Do we go meet them?” Spur asked.

“The trajectory they’re on?  Could take years to get to where they’re landing.”

“Could take less time,” Court said.

“Hmm.  Yeah.  Well, we’re heading that general direction anyway,” Orion said.

“Even if we travel for years, there’s no guarantee we cross paths with them.  Even if you slice out a piece that’s ten feet across… you could search a long, long time before you cover all that ground.”

“We found each other again,” Court said.

“I had a sense of where you might’ve been, from Orion’s description.  We lucked out, seeing you on the bridge.”

It took two hours for them to walk across what Orion was thinking of as the hangar.  Then they walked down another narrow corridor with impossible high ceilings, similar to the one Orion had been in, after leaving the room that had had his casket, machines, and Pine in it.

Several of the large maintenance machines passed through.  The group split up, moving to either side of the corridor, and let them by.

Here and there, people could identify odds and ends.  Orion could speak to metal that was structural and things that weren’t, which freed them to discuss why things that weren’t structural were there.  Some might have been for machines to use to climb, or were points that something, made and brought here much later, might be installed and used to fix in place.

Marte was likely to be able to identify weapons.

Sever and Blackbox could identify machine parts.

They crossed a swamp of the green moss,which had leaked out from one wall, covering a floor, before dying, leaving that compost smell.

“I think they repaired something there,” Orion said.  He pointed to a weld where floor met ceiling.  “That’s fresh.”

Spur frowned.  “That cabling looks like…”

They had to stop in their tracks while Spur pulled out the flat box with the quadruped drone in it.  She showed them.

In the wall, three pipes that were a half-meter across each fed into a circular port, which left enough of the port open to the air for, presumably, air intake, or gas release.

The drone had something similar at its side- two cables.

Spur traced her fingers over the body of the inert, dog-like drone.  “Processing is here, in the thickest part of the body.”

“Do we think that’s processing, in the wall there?” Blackbox asked, interested.

“Is the entire structure a drone?” Court asked.

“It’s not out of the question,” Spur said.  “Some level of automation, across the entire thing?”

“We’re bugs on the body of something so big it barely realizes we’re here?” Sever asked, looking at the wall opposite the vent- the closest direction to ‘outside’.

“Not out of the question,” Spur said, again, quiet.

“If there’s processing, I want to kill it,” Blackbox said.  “Ideally, in a way that won’t kill our oxygen, too.”

“I can do readings,” Orion said.

“I could get out my drone, and fly it into the vent,” Spur offered.  “Unless you still think…?”

They’d put off using the drone for much the same reason Blackbox had discouraged the use of Orion’s limited medical supply.  That they might need it more later, and regret not having it.

“This is the sort of situation we’ve been saving it for,” Orion suggested.

“It’s a theory based on what could be visual coincidence,” Court said.

Orion frowned.

“I’m only saying.”

Spur got the thing to take flight.  Orion, meanwhile, measured the density of the wall, using the tools he had.

There was a part of this which wore at him, that was becoming clearer, now that they were in a bigger group.  He didn’t know who he was.  He didn’t have much reference to draw on.

He had tools, he had knowledge that had been dropped into his brain like crates dropped from parachutes to some tribe in the deep woods.  What they could use worked really well.  But the fundamentals weren’t there.

It was lopsided, and left him wondering… what was him?  Who was he?  He was so busy surviving, and busy using the tools he had, he wasn’t even sure what he was after.  Only the thought about getting back at the people who’d sent him there really stuck out.

It made him feel like a machine, in an abstract sense.  Less abstractly, he felt like a tool of tyrants.

Which feelings were him, and which were emergent, from this crazy, dangerous situation?  Was the fact that he’d saved the others a sign of his original self?  Or was it something that came from what Blackbox said, where having more bodies meant he had to risk himself less?

“Woah,” Spur said.

Orion turned away from his study of the wall material and thickness.

Blackbox had a weapon drawn, pointed at Spur.  His eyes were wide and wild, not stopping on any point for even a quarter of a second.  He kept looking at her belt.

“Hold on,” Orion said, quiet.  “What happened?”

Spur didn’t seem to want to speak or move, so Sever was the one to answer, “She opened her pouch, and he turned on her.”

“Blackbox?” Orion asked.

“Don’t move,” Blackbox said, voice tight.  “Anyone else, you try something, you should know my body’s a lot of metal.  I’ll survive, and I’ll shoot while surviving.”

“Yeah,” Sever said.  “What do you want?”

Blackbox, after checking that Spur wasn’t going to move, stepped closer to her, and reached down to her pouch with the gun hand.  Holding the gun with middle finger, trigger finger, and thumb, he caught a food packet between ring and pinky finger.

He proceeded to tear it with his teeth, and pour it into his mouth.

“Jarheads don’t need that much food,” Sever said, quiet.

Blackbox whipped the weapon around to point it at Sever.  Food spilled in the process.

There were more packets, more bits of food.

He kept at it, shoveling food into mouth.  Packets that might have been dehydrated, meant to be mixed into water, poured into mouth.  Trace powder exited his nose as he tried to breathe past it all.

“You’ll damage your systems,” Sever said.

“He doesn’t care,” Orion said.  “It’s not him.  It’s the virus.”

Blackbox ate, took water at gunpoint- even if the fact he had only one arm was limiting, and brought the gun into a place someone might have grabbed it, he was machine, not quite head to toe, but close.  Mid-head to toe.  Strong and combat ready.

Most of his attention was on Spur, who had opened her pouch.

Sever seemed to catch on, and when Blackbox was tilting his head back, trying to get everything out of the packet that he could, Sever reached over and closed Spur’s packet.

Blackbox gagged, hand briefly pressing against his chest, gun still held by three fingers.

“Someone,” he ordered.  “Piece of metal, card, something.  Scrape up the food on the floor, give it to me.”

“On it, Orion said.

He had a hand tool in his kit.  He scraped up the food, then offered it up.

Blackbox didn’t seem to enjoy it in the slightest, and had another gagging, coughing fit.  He breathed hard, his eyes roving, before he backed off, leaning into a wall.

Then he gagged more.

“You have very little biology.  A brain and some synthetic parts to emulate the bare minimum biology to keep that brain running,” Sever said.  “Your ‘stomach’, if you can call it that, needs barely more than a mouthful a day.  You’ve had two full meals for a full human body.”

“Shut up,” Blackbox said.  He closed his eyes, looking at the ground.

“It’s not your fault,” Orion said.

“Shut.  Up.”

Orion knew he wasn’t the only one to see how Blackbox tightened his grip.

Everyone was very still, waiting.

It wasn’t the first time Orion had waited for Blackbox like this.

Today it’s you, tomorrow, it’ll be me going through something like this?  Pain?  Compulsions?  Something else?

He hated that Blackbox had said that.

Because he could see how that tied back into things.  How he, in the future, might do what Blackbox was no doubt doing, thinking of everyone he’d seen suffer, taking in what was in store for him.

“So… we keep food out of sight,” Court said.  “Move it to a more secure pack?”

“Shut up,” Blackbox muttered.

“Can I finish scouting?” Spur asked.

“Sorry,” Blackbox told her.

“I know.  Can I finish scouting?”

The man nodded.  He looked like he was having trouble breathing.

“Let me check your systems?” Sever asked.

Blackbox nodded.  “Just don’t talk while you do it.”

Silently, Spur and Orion compared notes.  She could see from the far end, he could measure from the wall.  He had her fly her drone close to the floor, further on.

“And if you fly that way?”

“Dead end.”

“The other way?”

“Dead.”

“What do we think?” Marte asked.

He’d hung back, quiet while everything happened.

“I don’t know,” Orion said.  “But I’m starting to think that if this is a place where some kind of processor for running this entire place might be…”

“It wouldn’t be standalone,” Spur said.  “It’d be one of thousands.  Maybe hundreds of thousands.  This structure is big on a scale I don’t think any of us can appreciate.”

“Bugs on the body of something colossal,” Sever murmured.

Orion could see Blackbox tense.

“It’s not accessible.  They’re machines.  They have resources.  I think they installed it, then sealed up the way there after themselves.  Or sealed machines in with the system.  If they need access, they cut their way through, maybe.”

“No openings, no hatches, no vents,” Spur said.  “At least, not as far as I saw.  I hit dead ends.”

“Thick walls, every line is welded.”

“Can you cut your way in?” Blackbox asked.

“Do we have months?”

“It’s a way,” Blackbox said.  “We wanted to hurt them.  We wanted vulnerability.  This is a vulnerable point!”

“It might be,” Court said.  “We don’t know for sure what it is.”

Blackbox wheeled on the man.

For a second, Orion thought it might be another violent episode.

“Fuck!”

Blackbox stormed off.

“And fuck this green shit!” Blackbox shouted, as he marched away.

“Let’s pack up,” Orion said, quiet.  “Bring that drone back.  Before he gets too far.”

“Yeah,” Spur said.

Orion knew that would take a couple of minutes.  He took the extra time to organize his bag, and move food to the bottom of his toolbox.

They didn’t have infinite food.  Water had to be boiled, which would need fuel, and containers.  Containers would need cleaning.

“Glad he didn’t see our flesh as something to eat,” Court muttered.

“He had only a glancing exposure,” Orion pointed out.  “Maybe, if he’d looked one second longer.”

Court frowned, taking that in.

“Or maybe it’d be something completely different.”

“We don’t look at glyphs.  Getting it now,” Marte said.

Orion wasn’t sure the guy did get it.  Because he believed Blackbox in this.  As long as they were moving through and exploring these spaces… exposure wasn’t a maybe.  It was a question of when.

The bird drone flew back through the hole, Spur caught it, folded it up, and put it in its case.  They hurried on.

It took them fifteen minutes before they caught up with Blackbox.  He hadn’t waited for them.  Not exactly.  He’d found something, and then backtracked to the last intersection to wait.

Orion could hear it before they reached the site.

Several corpses occupied a campsite in the middle of a wall.  It was hexagonal, ten feet across, and had an aperture they could squeeze through if they turned sideways and made sure bags weren’t in the way.  If Orion’s instincts were right, it was as if they were inside a kind of screw hole, ready for a moon-sized attachment to be screwed in next to it, except it was a hexagonal socket waiting for a massive hexagonal peg.  The slot in the wall would be where the metal or cables extended out to whatever was being fixed in place.

They had died a long time ago.  It looked like a lot of what they’d done had been killing drones and taking them apart.

“I’ll stand guard while you search the bodies,” Blackbox said.  He didn’t say why, but the reasoning was clear.  If he found certain things, it might be that he couldn’t control himself from devouring them.  Wastefully, as a man who couldn’t eat.  “Don’t freak out about the sounds.”

“Sounds?”

Blackbox wasn’t in the mood to elaborate.

They worked through the dessicated bodies, some of which had been overgrown with moss.  Pockets, pouches, containers.

The sound took a couple of minutes.  It came from a bit of machinery like the ones Orion had lasered off the wall, before meeting the weasel.  Cylinders, twenty-eight centimeters long, eighteen centimeters in diameter, with a spike on the end that fixed it to the wall, normally.  The ones the machines planted were stuck into the metal with what had to be explosive force.  This one had been wedged between two panels by humans.

It played music.  Instrumentals, at first, with singing and other accompaniment that followed.

They gathered tools, consolidating them into the largest packs.

Not much food here.

Orion looked up as the music shifted.  Returning to the singular instrumental, which gradually became more broken.

A soft crying sound could be heard coming out of the speaker.

Then it was only silence.

He felt a chill.  Then he decided to bring the canister with him.

➨

The fox watched as the human designated as BLACKBOX left the alcove.  It kept projectors off, to minimize light, and moved in a way that favored silence over speed.

Into a vent system, through the walls.

It found others.  Three moth types, dormant.

It spoke to them in a different manner than it had spoken to the lizard.  The lizard had possessed data, the fox had collected it, to better know its quarry.

Now it transmitted information, so the moths would know how to hunt and respond.

They would coordinate, for the next maneuvers.

2.1.W – SEND

I’ve become a saboteur, Winnifred thought.

She’d arrived on Sherman Station hours ago, had stopped to eat, visit a mod shop for replacement parts and tools, and then she’d decided to explore.

The station was shaped like a top, drawn down to a point where it connected with the cable, while being flat and open at the top.  Different focuses were given to different levels and proximity to the inner rings.  The highest level were where, like so many superstructures, the docks were.  It was also where the highest level of security was.

“Run diagnostics on my new claws?” she asked Toby.

[Running.  How is it feeling?]

“You know as well as I do, Tobes.”

[Sensitive?]

“Feels artificial.”

[It might be the fact you had dull claws for too long and you’re used to it now.]

“Gross.  Could it be shortages?  Because of the issues at all the docks, delays in getting goods out the door?”

[Substandard part passed off as something better than it is?  Very possible.  I think it’s more that you adapted to lower sharpness.]

“Feels weird when I put my feet down on metal.  Heebie-jeebies.  That’s not just adaptation.”

[Yes.  I’m registering heebie-jeebies.]

Winnifred exhaled air hard out of her nose at Toby saying that.  “Find me a shop where I can get piezoelectric coating?”

Toby supplied an indicator and lines showing the quickest routes.  Winnifred took the one that carried her up highest.

It gave her a chance to get the lay of the land, in a way that being on the street couldn’t.

Forty minutes ago, a Graal Percival had been parked on the docks.  Winnifred had seen it when disembarking from the ship that had brought her here.  Once she was far enough away from the docks that security was no longer a hassle, she’d paused to watch ships for a bit.  The Graal in particular.

Winnifred liked ships that did things, that tested and pushed engineering to its limits, earned lux through raw mechanical power, or served a role in the big picture.  She’d never obsessed much over ships that only went fast.  She’d rather pilot a heavy, cargo-hauling Hod over a skimmer.  The Graal series stood out, maybe because of the speeds they could reach, at accelerations that could harm their pilots.  It went back to the limit-testing of engineering.  What was more, it had to land.

When a new planet was pulled in, there was a limit on what was known about it – the people who chose it kept what they were able to work out from the study of the distant solar analogues, and the rest was only known by the long range scans a given person or company paid for.  Companies across the belt and carefully positioned ships would get their snapshots of the planet right after it arrived, estimate the best locations for materials, and then plot their landing points in the seconds after.  Big companies and planets would bid for the best spots, taking whole tracts of land or continents, but there was always some land that wasn’t bid for.

Enter the Graal, which could take off from its position just outside the Arcesso band as the planet was pulled in, enter the new planet’s atmosphere, and land hard.  Staking a claim to a space, first come, first serve.  The rule was, it had to have a human inside.

Hundreds of Graals and other similar makes that would be primed to do just that, taking off from the millisecond that the a-okay was sent, loading the map that barred all territory other companies had bid for, and making the necessary adjustments.  Fractions of a second counted when it came to making the claim.

The entire ship was, when including relevant systems and accompanying equipment or structure, about seventy five percent heat and impact shielding for atmospheric entry and ‘landing’, five percent protection for the pilot, and the last twenty percent was the engine itself.

An opaque gold-colored oblong spheroid with a rocket on the back, and fins to stabilize while providing structure to keep the material of the shielding together.  Every time it landed, pieces needed to be removed and checked.  The landings were hard, things got hot, and a few percentage points could mean the difference between owning what turned out to be a lucrative mining spot, and arriving a tenth of a second behind another Graal or close equivalent, ship banged up, parts needing care, and no plot of territory to harvest to show for it.

She avoided looking straight at it, but she had watched them remove the engine and load it into a vehicle, before covering it.  Other parts went in the back, and then, because it was an irregular shape, they covered it with canvas.  That vehicle had made its way downtown, stopped at a high-end garage, and the work had been done.  Everything tested, parts replaced.

Now it made its way back.  One dock-owned Tenure in front, one behind.
