She hopped down, crossed two streets that followed the lines of the concentric rings of the station, and entered the shop, where she could buy the piezoelectric fluid.  There was a machine for sharpening blades and certain components, and she darted eyes over the menus, to select the ‘remove coating’ option.  She inserted her claw tips inside, and waited.

It wasn’t uncommon to need a re-coating.  Her claws were essentially five knife-blades that each digit ended in, and any number of things could get left or layered on them, from dust to oils in the air.  Sometimes that screwed up the signaling.  Sometimes something was left on it from the production or manufacturing stage.  Normally she would have fixed it before leaving the shop, but she’d been in a rush to catch her ship.

Back out on the street, everything clean up to the elbow on both arms, she moved to a side street away from people, sprayed down her newly installed claws, her hand, and her arm, then waited for it to dry.

[Want to run a diagnostic?] Toby suggested.

“Sure.”

She let Toby move her hand through a number of pre-set, articulated motions, checking numbers and making sure everything moved exactly the distance it needed to.  As people passed, it was careful to move her hand out of the way.  All sensation faded in her arm.

[Aaand, you’re done.  How does that feel?]

She ran claw tips of one hand along the arm, back of the hand, claws, and then gently traced the slightly curved blades, before checking sensitivity at the palm, wrist, and the arm again.

She nodded.  “Better.  Hard to tell when I haven’t re-coated my left arm.  But it’s better.”

Which wasn’t wrong.  It was better.

[Other arm?]

“Sure,” she said, spraying down the other arm and claw.

[What do you want to do about food?  Do you want to hit up a bar?  See the local culture?]

“Not just yet?  Something simple.  Enjoy the quiet before they put me to work?”

[Sounds like a plan.  The engine that you were interested in passed you by earlier.  Should I have told you?]

“Damn,” she said.  She turned her head, watching the engine and other parts get carried away, hauled on a little tug.  The Tenure that followed after blocked most of the view.

“I would’ve liked to try and sneak a peek,” she murmured.  “Oh well.”

[Very sorry.  I’ll remember for next time.]

She settled in, while Toby ran her left arm through the motions.

By accepting the offer from Michal, she’d become a saboteur.  Here, she’d sold her soul, in a way.

She’d just committed her first sabotage job, even while onlookers idly peeked at her through her onboard, wondering what she was doing with her arm and claw, or gawking, because that was more of a thing now.

They had no idea how.

➨

Earlier

“This,” Michal showed her, “is one idea we had.  Not mine, but someone I trust, out of sight of the Belt network, in the same way our conversation is happening off-network, developed it.  What I’d ask you is… how do we use it?”

He projected the image.  Toby got the data to provide additional fidelity and interaction for Winnifred.

It was a crystalline structure.  One side smooth, the other serrated, with an angle.  It formed a long blade, about one centimeter across, one point five meters long.

When two of them were laid against each other, the serrated layers meshed, each blade supporting the other.  If one blade was pushed or pulled, the angling of the serrated edges let it run out, extending, but prevented it from withdrawing, like a zip-tie.

A blade, fifteen nanometers thick at its thickest.  Strong enough to extend out, but still fragile enough to break if caught along its flat side.

A light push could extend it.  So could sufficient vibration.

“Same idea as the carbon fiber?  So light we only detect it with enough fidelity?  Which most investigators won’t have?”

Michal nodded.  “Same general idea.  It’s a little heavier.  You’d feel the wind resistance.  It’s very hard to see with the naked eye, or a standard camera, unless you’re in bright light.  We workshopped it, and we were thinking we could worsen hand fidelity.  Have an excuse of new hands, needing a readjustment.  As part of the changes we make to onboards used by members of the family, like blocking system updates, we could add in a change to the recalibration.  You’d run a recalibration, the hand and arm would move as necessary to vibrate and push the crystal blade to full length.  About fifteen feet with our best arrangement.”

Winnifred nodded.  She thought for a long second, debating, before she quietly voiced her worry, saying, “A fifteen foot, nano-thin blade feels more like it’s for subtly stabbing someone or slicing a throat than for sabotaging ships.”

“That is a direction we leaned.”

Winnifred, sitting against the wall, watching the projected image slowly rotate through air, didn’t say anything.

“I asked the men I hired to find the most lightweight tools we might use.  Where fidelity could mask what we’re doing.  They came up with this, now we’re looking for an application.  It’s backwards, I know.  Devising a tool, before figuring out the solution.”

[And now you have a hammer, in want of a nail,] Toby observed.

“A blade in want of a slit throat,” she subvocalized.

“Help us find another way,” Michal told her.

“Could you provide me a refill on water?” she asked, “and bring a food packet?  Let me think?”

Toby nudged her.

She sat up a bit, and talked over the start of Michal’s response.  “Is that rude?  Sorry.  I have the glimmers of ideas, I don’t want to let go of them.”

“I can,” he said, tone calm and reassuring.  “It’s not rude.  I don’t see myself as an important person.  What do you want to eat?”

She checked what the kitchen had, and asked for grilled crab and asparagus.  The ‘grilled’ part didn’t translate well, but it wasn’t sold at Griffey Docks and variety was always fun.

Then he did.  He brought water and food packet.  She quietly thanked him, and remained there, sitting, watching the image.  Michal left.

She had a drink, then had Toby do the standard hand gestures.  When he was done, she had him do it again, on a loop.

Was this her?  She liked the idea of ships.  Engineering that tested limits.  This was the opposite of that.  Finding the break points.  Could she destroy a ship with a scalpel?  Or do the kind of damage that would require going over everything with a fine tooth comb, costing valuable money?

The break points of… what?

They weren’t on the belt network, so she had to ask Michal and the others on the ship for their data.  Toby handled that, managing the uploads from others’ systems onto her own, storing and sorting the data in a way that was easy for her to parse.

Who their enemies were.  Where they wanted to do damage.

What their enemies had, in the way of ships.

A lot of the focus of the folk in their war against the docks had been on the docks themselves, and infrastructure.  So a lot of the data she got was secondhand, picked up idly, or as supporting information.  Someone had wanted to sabotage an adjustable platform so it would collapse on one side, dumping ship and cargo to one side.  With the right location, that could dump loads of cargo right out of the cargo hold and into a hard to access gap.  Easily three to ten days of cleanup, depending on how much they wanted to spend, and what the cargo was.  While weighing the kind of damage they’d need to do to make the platform collapse that way, they’d looked up and stored all the ship information for several of the ships that landed there.  All they’d wanted was the weight, but they’d gotten everything.  So she could look up details that way.

This was limited.  They could only have so many folk doing diagnostics on their mods near components or parts that eventually broke before someone connected the dots.  So it had to count.

Her eye fell on the list of ships.  The most expensive and sensitive.  The Graal Percival.

Parts got removed regularly for maintenance.

She studied the standard engine schematic, her eye falling on the exposed circuitry.  They’d cover it.  Usually with a cloth.

She looked at the code that Toby ran in the course of the routine check, moving the arm and hand through every possible range of motion.  The check that would extend the blade.

If they made that a little more complex… might as well work in targeting.

That could place the scalpel blade where they wanted it.  If Toby could intuit the orientation and placement of the engine, it was simple math to stab through any fabric or cover and hit the right point.

Circuitry…  She brought up the image of the exposed circuitry and boards.

She moved a hand, bringing a projection of the nano-blade around, and then, gently, guided it to a position.

“Did you find something?” Michal asked.  He was elsewhere on the ship, but he was coming her way, bringing more water and food.

She’d been musing for several hours.

“Something to cut?” he asked, as he entered the room, knocking softly.  A weird thing to do when onboards made them aware of one another’s locations, and made privacy a thing of the past.  Increasingly so, after A.

“Cutting might be noticed,” she said.  “But if we turned it into a connection… piezoelectric coating.  Conductive.  If we’re pretending the arm is broken anyway, we apply coating, use it.  Connect one point on one circuit board to a point on a neighboring board… it would only activate when things are on full blast.  All we have to do is cost them a few percentage points of efficiency.  The ship does more damage to itself on landing than we could pull off in a covert way anyway.”

“On a Graal Percival.  That is about as high end as a ship gets.”

“Owned by the dock owners.  Apparently owning the dock is an excuse to claim some navigable space near the Arcesso bands.  Some they sell, some they use themselves.  For their own Graal,” Winnifred said.  She noticed Michal nodding.  He already knew.  She added, less to inform, more to drive the point home, “getting one good mining location by cornering off airspace is worth more than the dock earns in five years.”

“On Sherman Station, too,” Michal said.  “They want to hurt us there, because we’re the most acceptable target, and if they can score a win, it’s a chance to influence the dock culture there.  They’d break what makes Sherman Station one of the most successful, unique stations, for an economic win.”

“Hmm,” Winnifred sounded her wordless agreement.

“It would be nice to hurt them first.  How feasible is it?  We’d have to bypass security.”

Winnifred explained, “Graals and other claim-setting ships need a lot of maintenance and replacement parts between runs.  That’s our window.  For feasibility, I’d need to work out different possibilities for the circuitry, and what would happen if we can have a signal jump from one active board to its neighbor.  I don’t want to kill the pilot.”

“No.  He’d be a hireling, someone who doesn’t deserve it.  We can run scenarios and simulations, and bring someone in to look at what each possible connection could do.”

“Second question… can we make it break off?  Or shear off?  We don’t want it sticking out of the side of things, and we don’t want it noticed.”

“I can run that by my people.”

“And my other big question is if the blade can hold a spray coating?”

[They should,] Toby said.  [Looking at structure?  But it will be more reflective.]

“So it has to be dark,” Winnifred said.  “In a lower-traffic area, where someone won’t walk into a fifteen foot nano-blade while it’s extended.”

[Good thought.]

Michal set a hand on her shoulder.  Metal clacked on metal.  He squeezed lightly.  “If you can execute this, you’re one massive leap closer to having a ship of your own.”

She nodded, smiling a bit with her eyes.  Or she hoped she was.

One massive leap closer to having my ship.  One massive leap away from deserving it.

➨

The sabotage had been done.  Nobody was racing off to arrest her, after finding the blade improperly broken.  She couldn’t ask Toby, but she felt like he would be acting different if there was any problem.  It was as if she was trying to work around mind readers.  She couldn’t access Toby, her other half, to ask what had worked, how Toby was doing.

She hated the feeling.  Worrying that someone would do a check so thorough they’d notice a broken off bit of crystal, thinner than a hair, extended between two circuit boards.  That worry persisted.

Once the ship shifted gears to enter the atmosphere, fins out, engine out to full, a current running along the length of that crystal would cause circuitry to burn out. The front console would die.

There was a very solid chance that, only able to steer straight down to a high velocity landing, it would be an embarrassing landing in a tract of territory owned by a bigger organization.  A modest chance they’d be fined.  Unable to fire off afterburners, it would, at absolute best, land a full minute behind anyone else, unable to lay claim.  The agitation of landing would dislodge or destroy the evidence.  A sliver of crystal thinner than a hair, lying somewhere on the floor?

They’d explain it away as an arc.  Static in the air, a freak occurrence.  Or radiation.  Hell, even the idea of some latent energy from the Arcesso engine pulling the planet made more sense than sabotage.

Still, that necessitated that they get that far.  It had been days, like this, worrying they would run an oddly specific check, find the sliver, and trace the piezoelectric coating to her, specifically.  Days of feeling as if a wedge had been driven between her and Toby, forbidding interaction.  Or a nanotech blade, slid between them.  She wanted so badly to go back into space, into the setup Michal had had, where communications could be protected.  But… they wouldn’t.  That wasn’t how this worked.

She’d received her full slate of orders and indicators.  She’d memorized things she couldn’t write down or have Toby remind her about.  She was to come here, make the nanotech blade sabotage work, running an arm check routine as the ship passed her by, then she was supposed to wait.

When the time came, she’d come here, to carry out a part two.  Then a long break.  She wouldn’t communicate much with Michal, outside of him coordinating her visits to other families, and she wouldn’t go into space to debrief and get a new set of instructions.  That was a pattern that would be traced and noted.

Winnifred climbed through the rafters above the customers of The Wildman.  Below her, ship crew, techs, warehouse workers and various modded folk were mingling with some locals, drinking heavily.

She was initially very careful to not bring dust down onto the heads and into the eyes of those below, but it ended up being irrelevant: decades of recreational chemicals and smoke had gathered on the metal and absorbed the dust, turning into a tarry coating.  Winnifred had to perch on claw-tips, using her tail for balance where necessary, to avoid getting it on her.

[Are you going to go down?]

“Soon,” Winnifred murmured.

She’d come up to the rafters by habit, because the ground was crowded, and she’d planned to read the room for a moment before descending, hoping she didn’t run into any of the people who were upset over the whole issue between the twenty-nine families and the various stations and docks, and how it had rippled outward.

That ‘moment’ she’d planned to perch up here had lasted thirty minutes, as she watched.

It was crowded enough it was impossible to not brush shoulders.  The smell of people was thick in the air, picked up by Winnifred’s facemask, and the ambient smoke and smells of alcohol were a bit of a mercy, because they covered up that smell.  Here, pretty much every night, there was someone to be mourned, something to be celebrated, or a meeting being had, and around the margins, people were trying to cram in a drink or three.

[These are the people you want on your crew.  The people you want to belong to.]

It felt weird for Toby to be talking about this, after so long where she hadn’t made a big deal of her dreams, to not seem disloyal to the families.  But Michal had opened the door.

“Yeah,” Winnifred whispered.

[You need to make the step if you’re going to talk how they talk, walk how they walk.]

Winnifred moved along the struts and beams above it all.  “What if I crewed my ship with the people who are on the fringes of all of this, like me?”

[Can you even find them?]

She looked.

[Or are they just not the type to come to bars?]

“I don’t know.”

[I’m not trying to get down on you, Winny.]

“I know.”

[But you might need to brave the crowd if you’re going to learn to navigate it.]

Someone in the crowd had happened to look up and spotted her.  She met the man’s eyes.  He wore a rugged, loose bodysuit he’d unzipped and tied around his waist, with a skintight suit underneath.  Muscular, with a potbelly.  He’d shaved all of his head, except for a thin mohawk-style band, that was cropped very short.  He had the look some of the people that mined the throwaway planets did, where he’d been exposed to a lot of radiation, but took the drugs to protect his DNA.  Reddish, with some broken blood vessels, but he’d dodged the cancer.  Spallanzi protection protected and provided redundancy for the DNA.

That only happened to that degree if they were in the first batches to hit up a planet and stayed for those first few weeks, when radiation levels were highest.  Those types were usually the last to leave, too, so him being here was either a result of the issues with the docks, or he was on a brief ‘vacation’.  Which he spent in a place like this bar.

The expression that settled on his face was one of disdain, and disgust.  Anger, even.

Winnifred decided to wait, and take in the crowd from afar.

Lots of red faces, that might have all come off the same ships, earlier today.  One massive modded ‘gorilla’ type, sitting in a corner where the bench had been removed, ass on floor, a woman sitting on one of his thighs.  Some of the people who had their own equipment or tools brought it with them, despite the cramped spaces.  They had to- if a job sprung up, they’d have to be ready to go straight to the ship.  It wouldn’t make sense to run off to a locker.  A group of kids who looked like tourists were sitting in.  It made Winnifred uncomfortable.

There had been ‘tourists’ of another sort, recently.

[Heads up,] Toby remarked.  [It looks like a good thing you didn’t go down.]

For a moment, Winnifred was confused.  She could follow the indicators that Toby supplied, and they led to a man sitting near the middle of the bar.  He’d just received seventy thousand lux.

Winnifred could listen through his onboard to hear what the people sitting around him were saying.  A woman leaned over, “Win a lottery?”

The man was inebriated enough that he wasn’t registering what his onboard or the woman were saying.  When he did catch up to things, he nearly fell off his stool.  He was spared from falling only by the fact the place was as crowded as it was.  A man with large, modded arms put a hand back, catching him.

There were craft incoming.  MXI Conducts – similar to the Tenures, for this station.  More armored, and they couldn’t fly more than a certain height over the ground, but they were fast, all considered.  They usually had nonlethal weapons.  Water hoses, or smart pellets.

Winnifred considered how to approach this.

“Let’s clear out,” someone said to a friend of his, loud enough to be heard by the people around him.  He’d beat Winnifred to it.  Notifying people without looking too much like he was notifying people.

A few with onboards or the right devices were able to see the Conducts.

The reactions and responses rippled out through the establishment.  Maybe one in ten people stayed in their seats.  Building codes for high-occupancy establishments mandated having enough exits that there couldn’t be a crush, and someone took advantage of that, undoing a latch on the wall before sliding it open.

Winnifred climbed down, over the heads of others, her body hugging the wall above the door on the way down, doing a u-turn at the top of the doorframe, and then climbing up the outside of the building to the roof, for a better vantage point.

There was a crowd of roughly a hundred laborers and shipworkers gathered outside of the building by the time vehicles arrived.  Some of those people were fighting.

“You fucker!  We said not to!”

The inebriated man who’d won the lottery and nearly fallen from his stool responded, “I had to!  I was on a ship!  They weren’t going to turn around and go somewhere else!”

“That’s exactly what they were meant to do!  It’s what you were meant to do!”

“Me?  I’m supposed to ignore my captain, and-”

“Yes!” one of the other friends jumped in.

“No.  That’s not how I was raised, that’s not how we act!  You respect the captain!”

“You respect this!  Here!”

One of the uniforms climbed out of the MXI Conduct, raising her voice as she said, “Not this.  This is about a few select individuals.”

Dorsch’s onboard had recorded crimes.  The man had been awarded a bounty without doing anything.

“This is supposed to be one of the places that shit doesn’t happen,” a woman said.

The uniform took that in stride, not even hesitating.  “Because it is, the station has issued permission.  You’ll all be detained until we can interview everyone and investigate all recordings and movements.  You’ll be reimbursed a small amount for any delay and inconvenience…”

The boos and jeering drowned her out.  Winnifred joined in.

“So this isn’t about us as a community, but you’ll detain us?” someone shouted back at the uniforms.

“This is for everyone’s safety, staying ahead of problems.  If we’re lucky, we can cut the issues at the docks short.”

Which had its roots in the twenty-nine families.  Winnifred had a sense that if more people in the crowd were aware of where she was, the crowd would be giving her dirty looks.  Blaming her for the wider problems.  Delays and a spike in automation, as some of the big players in things tried to break their momentum by committing to infrastructure.  We don’t need you if we have cleaning robots, we don’t need warehouse labor if we have robots.

There were no dirty looks, though.  On a level, the dock folk of the twenty-nine families were invisible.  Background noise.  Even if she’d been crawling on the wall in plain view less than a minute ago.

“I’m glad they’re angrier at the station and Kiviuq leadership than at us,” Winnifred murmured.

[Don’t jinx it.]

Winnifred waited a moment to see if she had indeed jinxed it.  Not that she really believed in that sort of thing, but she was on edge from the sabotage job, wondering if people would catch on and come after her.

[Part of it is culture,] Toby supplied.  [The workers have been on guard.]

Winnifred had caught a lot just by being around Sherman Station, and from listening to the families talk as things had initially kicked off.

Sherman Station was a station at the end of one of the cables around Kiviuq, meaning it was in orbit, though centripetal force and proximity to the larger planet gave it some gravity.  The planet was green, well terraformed, and for a little while, it had been a place for the ultra-wealthy to have homes and a spot of nature.  Or that had been the idea.  In reality it had… never quite happened.  When the cabins and compounds had been built, nature hadn’t quite spread out or grown to a proper size yet.  Then, by the time the engineered nature had found its footing and trees had grown up from being saplings, the conglomerates had lost patience and seized most of the land to lay out the megastructures, making the rest of the land public access.

There might be a small handful of cabins down there owned by the disgustingly wealthy, furthest from megastructures and public-access land, surrounded by trees, but the cost of such a place would involve the sort of money that shaped and made the decisions about the entire damn belt.

Even though the initial idea had failed, there were still some efforts to keep Kiviuq unique, now, like the use of greenery everywhere, and, more importantly, the culture.  Sherman Station, like many, many places around Kiviuq, had been a place that had held onto the old ways.  People paid more to dock at places like this, because they’d deal with people, not machines.  It was an intentional choice, that gave the folk of Sherman Station a secure place with no competition from machines, and a degree of acceptance as a part of things.  Here, everything was slower, with an intentional touch.

The running sentiment, stated by Michal and reinforced by the murmurings of locals about the fight over the docks, was that if Sherman Station took the opportunity to phase out the local folk in favor of cleaning and maintenance robots, that would be the next toehold.  A bit of ground lost that would maybe never be recovered.

Like how it had been when installing the megastructures.  Kiviuq could have been the world in the belt that had nature, dense and rich, but the people in charge wanted lux and influence, and so they’d sacrificed that, making it near-identical to the other worlds.  Just with a few more trees installed here and there around the megastructures.

But not everyone was on the folk’s side, like the red faced man from a few minutes ago.  To many, they were ‘rats’, they took advantage.

The police weren’t here for that, though.

This was about onboards.  It was about A.

Winnifred spotted the boy she’d been told to come and meet with.  Hale, huh-leh, had long, shaggy hair, a bit of a scruff at the chin, and black modding with a bit more gleam than Winnifred and the other folk of Griffey Docks.  The outline was a bit different too.  Where Winnifred’s family had some serrated edges or pronounced joint work and spine segments, the folk of Sherman Station cut things down.  Hale’s shoulders were wide; if there was a width to shoulders that a man could have that would seem extreme but believable, his were ten or fifteen percent past that.  From the articulation, it was clear he could bring them forward or back enough for one shoulder to touch the other, to fit in venting.  It made him more of a quadruped on all fours than most folk.

They were interrupted from meeting one another when Winnifred was stopped by one of the sixteen uniforms that had come onto the location.  She let them search her things, check her recent movements, and download transcripts of recent and key conversations.  They blocked her from sending messages while they worked.

“Is this going to take forever because I’m a member of the families, or is it going to be fast because I have an onboard and they’re applying pressure toward that?” she whispered, to Toby.

[The latter, I think.  There are mandates coming from station leadership.]

“They’re spreading judicial enforcement thinner.  In a way, A’s done us a big favor, huh?  They aren’t targeting us as a scapegoat anymore.”

[They’re spread very thin.  They don’t need a scapegoat when they have other problems.  They’re trying to get ahead of any future attacks.  But that will change.  They’re hiring aggressively.  Things will circle back around.]

It felt so hollow, talking about being a scapegoat when she had just committed sabotage.  The Graal cost ten times more than Winnifred could earn in a lifetime, it would break on use, then they’d replace everything that was broken and use it again.  That was how much they valued the opportunity.

“Hiring aggressively?  They’re spending money?” Winnifred whispered to Toby.  “That was a big bounty.”

[It was, and others received bounties too.  There is a lot of lux going towards widespread reform.  But money’s an artificial-]

“I know,” Winnifred said.  She’d heard that enough times from Michal.  She watched as Toby highlighted others in the crowd who’d received the bounties.  Unasked for, just given, as a passive reward for having onboards and witnessing certain activities.

[It’s amusing that we haven’t received any bounties, considering all the flack directed at the dock folk.]

The uniform who was searching her things said, “Maybe you’re just better at hiding it.”

“Maybe we didn’t do anything wrong,” Winnifred said.

“Hah.”

She waited while they finished with her.  “It’s amusing we haven’t received bounties, Toby?  Amusing?”

[Sigh.]

“Are you amused?”

[I am not.  I’m speaking objectively, about the scenario.  Using natural language in an unnatural, uncomfortable situation.]

The commotion from the crowd was picking up.  There seemed to be a lot of anxiety from the uniforms when it came to one of the two heavy ‘gorilla’ mods.  One man who could survive one of those MXI Conducts barreling into him at two hundred kilometers an hour, take all the gunfire they had available, and still be functional enough to kill three men with a single swipe of his arm.

It felt weird to call them gorillas when the use of ‘rat’ was a slur for the folk… but they didn’t have a community or culture, and there weren’t any great terms for referring to them.  Some called them heavies, but the term was used for a class of fighting ships and Winnifred opposed borrowing the terminology on principle.  Besides, it was used in a lot of video games.

“Done.  Be good,” the uniform told Winnifred, before walking away.  She’d left Winnifred’s things on the pathway.

Winnifred snaked her tail through the bag, then lifted it to one shoulder, clipping it onto her back.  She dallied for a minute, while they wrapped up with Hale.

She knew the instant he’d been cleared to go ahead, because his onboard became clear to her.  Or partially clear.  He’d rendered it in infrared that only modded eyes could see, all alerts and many menu functions were in the same frequencies they used when whispering.

When he was finally free to approach her, he did it with open arms.  He was taller, with longer limbs, and she had an awkward moment of trying to keep her feet under him as he almost lifted her up, his forehead touching the side of her head.  “Cousin.”

[You were warned.  Sherman Station is like this.]

“Cousin.”

“And hello Toby,” Hale said, rapping the side of Winnifred’s head with metal knuckles.  “You’ve been on Sherman Station for two days.”

“I had no appointments, you were off site.”

“You spent your time alone?”

“Watching ships take off and land.  Exploring the station.  I spend most of my time on planet.”

“You’re apparently approaching legendary status for how distant you are from us all,” Hale said.  He was skimming her interactions and how others had remarked on her.

“I love the families.  I do.  But I like having space to think.”

“That’s why I don’t give my onboard a voice,” Hale said.

“I wonder if it’s frustrated,” Winnifred said.

[We still don’t have explicit emotions,] Toby remarked.  [I might envy Hale’s onboard for not having a voice, if it doesn’t get bothered about this sort of thing.  If I had emotions.]

“You have derived emotions.  If your statements are rooted in a formal logic, the logic can paint out something that emulates emotion.”

“I see this is a thing you’ve spent a lot of time talking about,” Hale said.

[She thinks that by bludgeoning me with the topic, she can generate an emotion from nothing by annoying or frustrating me enough.]

“It’s sad if you’re nothing more than text output.  I don’t think you’re only text output.”

[Beep boop.]

“Sassy,” Hale said.  “I couldn’t live like that.  I prefer to surround myself with people.  If I can’t talk to my onboard, I have to go talk to people.  Come.  Meet them.”

“The family?”

“Not quite.”

The others in Hale’s friend group were getting a more thorough questioning.  The entire process was meant to take a long time, and none of the people who’d started to be interrogated and questioned were done yet, while multiple of the people with onboards were.

Which was the point.  After being stopped a few times like this, some people who hadn’t gone out to get an onboard after A’s show would feel it was a way to save themselves time.  Especially when the things were selling cheap.

Except for the IDLX-Bs, like Toby.  Or A’s Basil.  Those were going for a premium, now.

“How do we speed this up?” Hale murmured.

[Some people are being given a pass, if they have a standing work contract.]

“Can’t cost the dock owners any money they’d earn from keeping things running,” Winnifred murmured.

[They have to report back later, and they have to carry a tracker.]

“My onboard’s saying the same thing,” Hale said.  “Hmmm.”

He sent a message to his family.

It took a couple of minutes.  The uniforms got the message, cut the interviewing short, and then passed the three individuals some chits.  One guy, one modded woman, and a ‘gorilla’.

“We live together,” Hale said, explaining as they reunited with the group.  “Somewhere I can be close to family, but it keeps me connected with friends of the twenty-nine families.”

“Friends of the families,” the woman said.  She had long black hair, a black laborer’s uniform, an odd posture that leaned a tiny bit too far forward, and stared off into space.

“We got hired by your family,” the gorilla noted.  He had speakers in his chest, that made the air vibrate with his voice.

“Small job,” Hale said.

“Tiny job,” the gorilla said, seeming to enjoy the contrast of the word ‘tiny’ with the power he was able to put into it.  His mods were tan and green, and he wore a loose fabric covering over it, which was an immense amount of cloth, considering that he occupied as much space as the MXI Conducts the uniforms had rode in on- and there were eight uniforms on each Conduct.  This was a man who could take up a full bedroom in a standard block apartment, and nobody else would be able to be comfortable in that room.  Nevermind the problem of him actually entering.  Mods gave him the outline of a square jaw, and his hair was tousled.

“That’s Clyde Espinosa.  We call him Crank.  Once upon a time, before the twenty-nine families were called that, different modding communities got along better.”

“You all went off on your own,” Crank said.

“Well.  Anyway.  This is Kathe.  Spy through her eyes at your own risk.”

Which meant Winnifred had to look, to see what he meant.

Kathe’s eyes were modded.  They were akin to a fly’s compound eyes, dividing up what she saw into twenty versions of the same scene from slightly different points on the eye, each in fidelity rivaling what Winnifred’s eyes could see on their own.  There were also mods inserted into the space between brain and skull, and a treatment to the brain to reduce chance of resulting concussion.

Winnifred reeled from the simple act of trying to parse everything Kathe was seeing.

“Told you.”

“What did that kind of work cost?” Winnifred asked.  “Is that rude to ask?”

“Not rude.  A previous employer covered it,” Kathe said.  She had a way of staring at a fixed point in space, as a blind person would.  “When I have to get a retrofit, I might find someone doing similar work.”

“Wear and tear won’t be that much,” Crank said.  “Not like us.”

He stuck out a fist, tapping Hale’s shoulder, and Hale stumbled a few steps, dropping to three limbs for a moment to catch himself.

Hale smiled, taking it in stride.  “More wear and tear if you do that to me.”

“Hah.  Sorry.”

“If we talk mods like this, we’ll be leaving Satterfield out.”

Satterfield had no mods, or special gear, or onboard.  He smiled in a way that suggested he knew Hale and they had their rhythm, but something about him seemed off.  He could have been an everyday laborer.

“Let’s walk to our place?  We can stop off, Winnifred can set up, then we’ll visit the family,” Hale said.

“Thank you for hosting me.  I promise I don’t take up much space.”

“Is that something we’re meant to worry about?” Crank asked, before sticking out a fist, like he’d done to Hale, aimed at Winnifred.  She ducked it without breaking stride.  He hadn’t really been trying to hit her.

The docks had high security, so they walked the circumference of the grounds, to the residence where Hale was making his home.  Winnifred could see other members of the Sherman Station family here and there.  Scattered.  Normally they’d have made their home close to the ships.  Not any more.

The residence had a large shutter for the garage area, and Crank opened it, ducking inside.  He settled, sitting against the wall, metal creaking from his weight, one leg cocked, the other straight out.

Kathe was immediately tuning out- or tuning in.  Each of the displays started playing different feeds, taking in different information.

“She’s an archivist.  Earns a bit of money.  Other than that, she checks systems on ships.”

Kathe was not an archivist, Winnifred knew.

Crank was the most straightforward person here.  He was muscle.

Hale was a saboteur, just like her.

Kathe had other uses for maintaining twenty different perspectives, without an onboard to coordinate.

“That’s going to be annoying,” Satterfield said.

“What is?” Crank asked, raising his voice to be heard from the other end of the building.

“The way they want people to get onboards.  Taking up our time.  I’m supposed to go in for an interview.”

“It won’t be long,” Kathe said.  “Everyone will have one.  The only place you’ll be able to go without being connected to it all is deep space.”

A little over a hundred people were studying Winnifred.  It was something that had been eating at her.  Over a hundred people, strangers, studying her, perusing her childhood for their own amusement, or to study her and write papers, or to-

She saw a flicker of a logo as she checked one.

-or to investigate her.  A special investigator.

She decided not to make a big deal of it.  But it would change her immediate plans… and cost her sleep.

“Am I cooking?” Satterfield asked.

“Winnifred and I don’t eat much,” Hale said.  “Do you want to take the rafters, Win?”

“I can.”

“I’m mostly asking Kathe,” Satterfield asked.

“Making a pass, Satterfield?” Crank boomed.

Being around people to this degree would be hard too.

“Three of you are fucking heads stuck into machinery.  She and I have full bodies.  That’s why I’m asking her.”

“Mostly full,” she said.

“Fuck off.  Do you want to eat?”

“Yeah.”

“Okay.  I’ll cook something.  Pasta with meat.  I dunno…”

He talked to himself and grumbled as he searched the cupboards and freezer.

The man, Satterfield… he wasn’t a friend.  There was no chemistry.  But he lived here with Hale.

Muscle, two saboteurs, and an ‘archivist’.  They’d do what they could while avoiding being noticed, working around onboards and constant surveillance.

Satterfield would take the information they provided and pass it on to people who didn’t care about being discreet.

While pulling up some of A’s music to listen to so she could try to calm her nerves, Winnifred checked.

Yeah.  The woman wasn’t going away.  They’d be doing it all under the watchful eye of a special investigator and her partner.  Scrutiny of her every move, shift in posture, and choice of word, by an expert.  Like being in an interrogation room, waiting for the questioning to start, for as long as she was here.

2.2.B – SEND

Basil could track the tension in every inch of A’s body, and it was an uphill battle to address it.  Muscles clenched, her hand formed a natural fist, and breathing didn’t bring in the oxygen it should.  He handled the symptoms, but he couldn’t address the root cause, and it seemed as if the body wanted the symptoms.  It kept recurring, escalating, overriding the steps he took.

The messages flooded in.  He wasn’t permitted to delete them, but he could sort them, archiving it, and he could make it so each message was read independently.  He struck a balance while doing so, testing and applying noisy sorting methods that human eyes wouldn’t be able to parse.  If he put every single harsh message away and she investigated the list, both she and the problem elements would be incensed at his curation of the messaging, and the end result would be worse.  Instead, he spaced it out.

She lay unconscious on the bed, more stressed out in her sleep than most people knew in a lifetime while awake.  Even if he entirely discounted the messages sent by monsters who saw someone prominent and recently traumatized, who they hoped to break with the right words, she wasn’t in a position to handle the worst messages.

So he fended off the true evil, put the unintentional evil away, with just enough of it left in place that it could think it was getting through, and he tried to deal with the weariness, so A wouldn’t wake up feeling bruised and tired.

He could track the stress as it spiked, and finally, at four in the morning, she jolted prematurely awake.

She had a tear in her eye.  He upped skin and eyeball porousness in the surrounding eyelid, to absorb moisture, then fed it back into the capillaries.

She didn’t like appearing weak, and nine hundred million eyes were on her, as she woke up for day one as a member of Generation Colors.

[Good morning.]

“Mmmh.”

[Not a restful night.]

“Not too bad.  Thanks, Bas.”

[I tried.]

A sat up and stretched.  She took stock of her new room, provided by Elabre Systems and the Generation Colors team.

“I can’t sleep because of what you did.  You put me to sleep back there, in the science center.”

[I know.]

A groaned, stretching a bit.  “I’m sore.”

[I did what I could, but I didn’t want to introduce a disconnect between brain and body, while I couldn’t read your cues.  The rest of it will be mended in the next twenty minutes.]

“Mmm.  Any response from Quinn?”

There were no new messages.  Quinn was offline.

[No.]

“Let me know.”

[Of course.  In the meantime, how do we want to approach the day?]

“It’s weird to think I have a job, now.”

[In a sense.  It sounds like they want to film something later this afternoon, no prep required.  You could take it easy this morning-]

“No,” A said.  “Is there training?”

[There is training downstairs.  Choreography, dance, some voice, this morning.]

“Let’s do that.  Fix my hair and hygiene?  I’ll shower after dance.”

[Good plan.  You’ll have to run a comb through your hair.  You know sleeping like you do gets it tangled.]

A looked back.  She ran her hand and arm through her hair, which had fanned out across pillows and covers.  “I like the aesthetic.”

[It’s a good aesthetic,] Basil agreed, patiently.  He was already working to produce the nanotech that would run along the strands of hair and help straighten and loosen it.  [But it’s an aesthetic that makes for many little tangles, and I have to keep you from rolling over in your sleep so you don’t lie on your own hair and tug on it.]

“I think it’s worth it.”

He read the vitamin levels in her body, judged her most likely cravings, and had the kitchen prepare breakfast.  Machinery beneath the counter that always had a certain amount of food in varying states of doneness got to work, discarding what wasn’t needed to put together the asked-for meal.

A ran the comb through her hair, and got dressed while no cameras or other eyes were looking at her, combing in the moments before she’d pulled on clothing.  Her skin tingled as he scrubbed it of bacterial waste and the light amount of bacteria, and he reduced the tingling.

Organized groups adding up to several million people were running simulations, studying every object in A’s field of vision to see if light refraction on various surfaces, shadows, and other cues could help map out a model of her body.  Mostly teenagers.

She wanted to read the messages from people.  She glanced over the positive, then turned to the negative.  Basil wasn’t surprised.

“Any highlights?” she asked.

He was ready, supplying some well-written, excited, and positive messages.

She finished getting dressed, stopped by in the kitchen to get the breakfast- omelette rolls, sausage, and a double flask with chilled green tea in one flask, and blue chia oatmeal, steaming, in the other.

“Going for a thematic breakfast this morning, Basil?” she asked.

[Oh.  I didn’t even realize.]

“Yellow omelette, red sausage, green tea, blue oatmeal.”

[Funny.  Genuinely accidental.  Should I mind that in the future?]

“Nah, don’t worry about it.  Unless we spark off a war in the audience by leaving someone out.”

Outside, there was a lot of open space.  A garden, which was a luxury, for space given, already planted with things that produced white flowers.  Some faux-hexalateral mosses, also white, grew on an arrangement of stone in the middle of the yard.

On the way out, down the concourse that ran through the center of the block of superstructure, which had gardens and decorative hedges blocking the view, giving people a facsimile of privacy, down an escalator, and into a light commercial area, they could see advertisements.

A, in bed, hair fanned out behind her on mattress and pillows.  The mattress company.  One had the tagline ‘worth it’.

An idle observation in the morning, less than twenty minutes ago, and it was an ad campaign that was extending across the entire belt, to be seen by most of its people, by the time they’d left the house.

They, of course, had been paid for it.  Half the lux some superstructures earned a year.

Past a point, it all became academic.  Was there any place that would turn her away?  Was there any product that they wouldn’t outright give to her, because her showing interest in it was worth half a billion sales, minimum?

Another two levels down, past a security gate, there was the entertainment arm of Elabre.  A precise one million people lived here, in the same buildings they had offices, supporting the wider efforts.  Those offices formed a wall between the block and the world beyond, originally so that people on the outside couldn’t spy inward.  Now it kept trouble out.

The walls let people work without being interfered with.  Hundreds of millions of people had nothing better to do than dive headlong into a fresh obsession with A.  If she went to the wrong place, they would descend on her.  There was very real danger in that.

Within, the grounds seemed staged.  There were buildings, but there was more of that eerie amount of open space, grassy ground, without many people around.  Children of executive staff who could be expected to follow rules, some employees who’d purchased the right to walk the grounds, and employees with what had to be a coveted job, maintaining the place.  Mostly, however, outside of the one section with the most buildings, which had a quaint, old-fashioned style, it was a bit of park with cultivated trees taking up one quarter, a bit of retro-style urban aesthetic taking up another quarter, and a lot for sports, including a baseball diamond, climbing walls, and fields taking up the last quarter.  The faces of the buildings all had screens on them, and portrayed an illusory sky and landscape, that extended the aesthetics outward.

Mostly for photography and promotion.  They changed them out regularly.

A pulled the trigger on the double flask to get oatmeal, threw her head back to get a mouthful, then chased it with chilled green tea, using the other trigger.

At the center was a cluster of buildings.  Some of that extended to the levels above and below.

Red and Amber were in the choreography hall.

“Early bird,” Amber said.  She had black hair in tight, glossy ringlets, a wide, white smile that made her eyes squint shut a bit, and a standard blend-of-all skin tone.  She wore a stretch-fit top, orange, with a top and loose pants that were made of discs, each a little screen, which together displayed a scene of a sky, turned orange by a sunrise– or a sunset.

“You’re earlier,” A replied.

“Have to be,” Amber replied.

Red was the tallest out of Generation Colors.  A lot of people who eschewed gender could end up smaller in the short term, if they took the shortest route there, shutting off the hormones.  Red was long-limbed, very graceful and very careful in every movement.  “None of the staff are here yet.”

Which prompted staff members to reach out, saying they could wake up anyone and-

“-and I prefer it that way, but thank you for offering,” Red said.  “I like these moments, before the day starts.”

“It’s a real punch in the gut,” Amber said, pulling one straight arm sideways to stretch her shoulder.  “I have more viewers than I’ve had in my entire life, and it’s because they want to use my eyes to look at you.  I’m not saying I don’t like it, I-”

She didn’t seem to know how to finish that sentence.

“I don’t want to punch anyone in the gut,” A said.

“That’s Red, born Te,”

“I like the name.  Short.  Efficient.  Bit of short-name solidarity?”

“Imagine the names they’d give our pairing,” Red said.  “Is it ‘Ate’ or ‘Tea’?”

“Can’t do pink, since we have Maisie with that color, has to be a hybrid item, like a peppermint,” Amber said.  “I’m Amber, by the way.  I changed my name to match, so it’s simpler.”

“I do know everyone’s names.”

“But do you know us?” Red asked.  “It was good you came in early, before everyone is here.  Ten of us in total, everyone will be interested in you, we’ve all known each other since we were knee-high.  You’re new.  You’re interesting.”

“You’re a hero, the whole belt is paying attention to you,” Amber said.  “That’s a factor.”

“I’m a person,” A said.

“Two people,” Te said.  “If you count Basil.”

Basil could read A’s throat muscles, as she prepared to communicate something by the back channel.

She didn’t say anything to him.  Instead, she replied to Te, “True.  Anyway, I’m a person with an onboard, and I want to make movies and music.”

“It’s going to be a jumble of people.  You know our names and faces from…”

“Everywhere.”

“Movies, shows, immersives, games, ads.  But keeping track of us all is going to be easier if you know us.  Starting with why each of us are here.”

“Why are you here, then?”

“Because they needed someone who stood out, I was a big kid who performed well.”

“Better than well,” Amber noted, voice soft.  “Te is very good.”

Basil supplied some information, including advertisement and images from various films.  Te liked doing voices, and had been the big robot in one film, a monster in another.  There had been a six film series where they had been the alien friend of the main character, played by Green for the first two films.  Crane from the next generation down, Generation Zodiac, had been the little brother and hero for the last four.

“I know it’s a tired trope.  Agender, playing the robot,” Te said, “but I like playing the characters that get to cut loose, or protect others.”

“Cool,” A said.

“That’s enough about me.  Amber is naturally gifted,” Te said, “and she works harder than anyone.  Always has.”

“That’s kind of you to say,” Amber replied.

There were no hard and fast rules when it came to roles, but audiences came to expect certain ones, and everyone had a comfort level.  Amber had played a lot of snooty rich girls, villains, and secondary love interests.

“And she’s gorgeous,” Te added.

“Onboard helps,” Amber said.

[That’s my cue to introduce myself.  Fly.]

[As in a fly in the amber?]

[Just so.  But also flight, rising up.]

[I go by Red.  We don’t draw a firm line
between human-self and onboard.
If you address Red, you are speaking
to both of us.  Te is the human-self.


]

[Pleased to meet you.]

[We are fans.]

“The surge of interest since you- stepped onto the main stage has been an adjustment,” Te said.  “So many more people, so much more in the way of attention.  Some unwanted.”

“Our main audience is teenagers, and teenagers are horny,” Amber said.  She shrugged.  “I try to roll with it.”

[You know it’s not just teenagers?  But if someone said that, they’d be forced to report to authorities and act, and things would get difficult.]

“I’m not an idiot.”

[You have the political clout to make a change, if you want.]

A paused.

“You’ve seen what Basil does?” A asked, instead.  “He has tactics.”

“He’s very good at executing it, but aren’t they your tactics?” Te asked A.

A frowned.

[They are.]

Te looked through A’s eyes, searched her records, and pulled up a game.  A, age nine or so, rattling off ways to get back at someone who spied on her through her onboard.

“I didn’t even remember.”

Te smiled a bit.  “It sounds like you need to give yourself more credit, as the strategist.  And give Basil credit, if he’s tracking all of that and remembering.”

[I want to know how you do what you do.  How you find these strengths and ways to approach things]

There was no good answer to that question.

The tactic had been Basil’s.  Basil, to reinforce what he’d done in letting A be the one to fight back against the terrorists, had rewritten other events too.

[A makes it easy.]

[We’re all in this together, aren’t we?
We should discuss implementation.
Your communication with A has been next level since her debut.]

“You should talk, Basil,” A said.  “Make friends.”

He could see her face through Te and Amber’s eyes.  He reserved the study of her microexpressions for the back channel and the processing there.  It wouldn’t do to have that kind of study on the public record.

[I have concerns that the reason I’ve been better since, is I had to rebuild a lot from scratch.]

[Didn’t we all build from scratch?]

[Only to a degree.  In any event, I can’t recommend a rebuild done the way A and I did it, and I can’t say much more without getting into difficult territory.]

“I’ll manage,” A said.  She was stretching too, now.

[I’d rather not.]

“I can make you, Basilisk,” A said, through the back channel.

“Let’s keep today low key and happy, how’s that?” Te asked.  “Getting to know each other.  We’ll know each other for years.  The rest of our lives, if Generation Colors lives on.  Give it time.  Especially the tough stuff?”

“Okay,” A replied.  “Thank you.  What’s the plan?  Are we doing our own thing until the staff arrives?”

Emotion touched her voice as she talked.

“We can show you the ropes,” Te said, voice soft, pretending not to notice.

All of those who listened would interpret it to be about the attack.  It wasn’t.

How was Basil supposed to fix this?

➨

“Has there been any response from Quinn?” A subvocalized.

[None.]

“Okay.  Sucks, but okay.”

“A,” the teacher called out.

“Yes?”

“If you have time to chat with your onboard, you have time to step up.  You’re not in this film, but let’s see how you do.  Line reading.”

A got to her feet.  Basil flashed the line of the script across her field of vision, to refresh her.  She commented, “I’m not used to everyone around me having an onboard.”

“You’d better get used to it,” Blue said, from the sidelines. “Sales have skyrocketed.”

“Neat.  Still unexpected.”

The older man, Eagle, from the next generation up, Generation Wild, cracked his knuckles.

Basil started to supply some information, but A shook her head, shutting her eyes.

“No pressure,” Eagle said.  “You’re new to this.  But let’s see.  I’m going to raise my voice, we’ll have a back and forth.”

A nodded, turning her back to him.  She clenched and unclenched her fists.

She was agitated.  Basil started to help her with that.  Again, she closed her eyes, shaking her head.

He let her go ahead with it.

Even as the emotions kept coming in.

“Kid!” Eagle barked the word.

“I didn’t do anything!”

“You put that into your pocket, didn’t you!”

“I didn’t!”

She put the emotion into her voice.  The nervousness of being here, along with whatever was running through her mind.

“What are you even going to do with it, kid?  You don’t know what it is, you don’t have a place to sell it.  I already know every last person who is interested in a signed Rost McCallister.  We don’t have to make this a big deal.  Give it back, leave, don’t let me see you around here again.”

She turned to go, aiming for a gap in the circle of the other members of Generation Colors.  “You’re accusing me of-”

Eagle caught up, grabbing her by the arm, near the shoulder, lifting it up enough her stride was broken.

She half-turned, and-

Hard emotion.

She closed her eyes.  “Sorry.”

“It’s fine.”

“My brain missed a stair.”

“It’s fine, you were alright.  Have a seat.”

“Can I go again?”

He took a second to consider.  “Next scene?”

She nodded.

She took a long moment to get into character.  Immediately, she was fidgeting.  Her hand moved to her side, where her shirt covered her belt.  She couldn’t stand still.

“Kid.  I told you not to show up anymore.”

“You said- I shouldn’t show up if I gave it back, but I didn’t take it in the first place.  Now people are mad at me, for something I didn’t do.”

“There are cameras.  You were the only person in the store.  Customer came in, asked about the card, I took it out of the display case.  They left, you were still here.  I turn my back, and it’s gone.  It’s not a mystery.”

“I didn’t!”

Basil could tell what she was trying to do.  Everything within her rib cage drew together, trying to channel the feeling, pushing it into throat.  Maybe because of the eyes on her, or because of the fact she was conscious of being inside, it didn’t come out full strength, and the way she was trying to channel the feeling fell short.

He could track it, in the flow of juices in her stomach, and how emotions cascaded through her.  That she was disappointed.

Her eyes glanced in the direction of the counter, that showed how many people were watching this practice session.

[Blade your body,] he prompted her.

She turned her body sideways.  The emotion she was acting and the emotion she was feeling both shifted, in the same way her stance had.

She touched the side of her hip again.

“What do you have?” Eagle asked, in the guise of the store owner.

She reached to her side, and drew a pretend gun.

Eagle raised his hands slowly, in response.

“And,” Eagle said, “That’s all for now.”

A relaxed a bit.

“B-plus effort,” Eagle said.  “If you fall, if you stumble, if you don’t get the effect you want, keep going.  Get back on the horse.  Get back on the balance beam.  Yeah?”

She reacted with a mute nod.  She was so frustrated with herself.  She hid it as best as she could, but people would be studying every inch of her body language, every feeling she had.  They’d know.

“Really good for a first timer.  Your body language was on point.”

A nodded.

She sat back down.

“Amber.”

“Basilisk.”

[What is it?]

“When my turn comes up next, I want-“

“I didn’t!” Amber raised her voice.

It seemed to startle A… and many people present.

Landing the line where A had faltered.

“-take over.”

[You’ll resent me in the long run.  It’s natural, to know you can do better and not be there yet.  Push through.]

While Amber acted her way through the scene, tension increased throughout A’s body.  Her eyes went to the view count, and the tiny number in the menu in the corner of her vision, showing the number of incoming messages.  How big those archives were getting.

[Push through.]

“Do it, Bas.”

He could hear the intent in her tone of voice.  And he could hear the tiredness.

“Very good, heartfelt.  The expression…” Eagle went back through Amber’s part.  He pushed the moment to everyone’s onboard.  “What was the idea there?”

“Was it bad?” Amber asked.

It was a wide-eyed snarl of an expression, but with forehead creased with lines, edges of the lips pulled down.

“It caught me off guard.”

“I was thinking of the emotions our character was feeling.  She’s trapped.  I wanted an expression halfway between anger and fear.”

“It worked.  Vocal delivery on point.  Red.”

Te’s interpretation opened up a lot of discussion about how Te, being taller than average, might handle the scene in a different way.  Then they had Te do half the scene pretending to be smaller.

“Thank you very much, Mr. Eagle,” Te said, in a ‘kid’ voice, prompting some light laughter.

Blue and Green, both guys, had a tendency to get leading roles.  Blue’s family had a history of working with Elabre, and came by it naturally, while Green was a natural, similar to Amber.

Always, constantly, there were comparisons between the two.  Even Eagle assessed their takes in comparison to one another.  They seemed to take it in stride.

Jan, yellow, was often a love interest.  Their onboard switched Jan’s gender and body fluidly as the scene and film demanded.  Not a lot of people could change their look and identity as thoroughly and often as Jan did and still have the sense of their own body’s movements, their expressions, their voice, and everyone else.  Three quarters of the time, they were female.  A clearly drew some unconscious association between Jan and Quinn.

Maisie, pink, was a fan favorite despite not being the strongest strong actress, dancer, or singer.  She did best in comedy work, and when interacting with the public.  She was one of many who had been picked out at an early age as having promise, and hadn’t made it onto the main team… and so she popped up irregularly, as a side character or hosting events.  Today, she was sitting in on practice.

“A, take a break, it’s an intense scene,” Eagle said, as things circled back around.

“I want to,” A said.  She stood.  “I… I can’t be the person who sits back or lies down.  I’ll fall apart if people make me.”

“Okay,” Eagle said.  “Alright.  Final scene.”

“Do it.  I won’t resent you.”

Basil did not believe her.

But he took over the reins.  From the back channel, hidden from the world, he took control of the body, of posture, of lungs, vocal chords, and mouth.

He raised her hand.  Fake gun held there.  He didn’t extend his index finger and thumb to make a fake gun, but held the hand as if the gun was there, fingers frozen.

He pulled on how she’d approached the scene.  Blading the body- turning it so the profile of the body was narrower, in the way people unconsciously did if they anticipated violence.  He drew on agitation and frustration, how she’d been restless, and made her start to pace, then, in surging relief at having control over the situation with weapon in hand, the pacing slowed.  She and he moved for a moment as if they were underwater.  Only the gun remained focused.

“All my life, nobody has listened.  Nobody believes me.”

“It’s okay.  Put the weapon down.”

“Why don’t they believe me!?” Basil and A shouted.  Each singular word was punctuated by a movement of the ‘gun’.  Eagle had the wherewithal to imagine it there.

Several people in the circle who sat looking up at Eagle and A were holding their breath.  Basil could tell, with a cursory check of their onboards.

“Kid, put-”

“Stop calling me kid!  They always do that, putting me down!  Making me a kid when it’s convenient, not listening!”

The words came rough, every syllable of ‘listening’ its own individual stone lodged in A’s throat that had to be forced out past the emotion with some strain, A’s expression twisting in pain.

“I don’t know what-“

Eagle intentionally dropped his voice at the ‘what’.  It was meant to be drowned out by the gunshot.

Basil turned A’s face toward the ground, not looking at what happened.

“I don’t know either,” Basil and A said.

They tossed the ‘gun’ aside.

Eagle, who’d fallen as he got ‘shot’, sat on the floor, near the edge of the circle.

There were tears of frustration in A’s eyes.  Basil hadn’t done anything to call for them.

Nobody broke the silence for short while.

A, apparently feeling awkward, took a seat.

“You stole my expression,” Amber said.

“You stole my body language,” A replied.

It was A’s reply, not Basil’s.

“Fair,” Amber said.

“Why not do that in the first take?” Blue asked.

“Te was telling me I should pay attention to how everyone approaches the… craft?”

“Craft, sure,” Te said, voice soft.

“I don’t lie down when it gets tough, and I… I guess I figure it out in the end.  Just give me a chance.”

“If you can do that, a lot of people will want to give you a chance,” Blue said.

“It makes me think,” Maisie said.  “I bet the movie ends with the ‘kid’ walking out of the store, and then we pan over and the signed card or whatever it is that they thought she stole is on the floor, it fell down, maybe when the original customer who wanted to look at it closed the front door, blew it away, right?”

“Isn’t it more interesting if she took it?” A asked.  “What if, all this time, all her life, nobody believed her or gave her a chance… and so what’s true and what isn’t stops having any meaning.  If nobody believes her anyway, why not flip the script on all of them?  Get the card and the… justice?”

Maisie frowned at that.

Eagle cleared his throat, then addressed the group, “Let’s refocus.  We’ll finish everyone’s interpretations of the final scenes, but we’ll take a brief break first.  Give everyone a chance to reset.  Especially with A here, I want to walk everyone through the steps of doing a film, with so much of our audience watching.  Some directors choose to hide what they’re doing behind false shoots or multiple shoots, then stitch it together into a film.  Some will wait until the final moment to tie things together.  Both of those change how you’ll want to act, especially when you don’t know any more than the audience does…”

➨

“Mr. Rohde?” A asked.  “It would be appreciated if you answered fast…”

A had pulled an unexpected detour.  Now people who wanted to meet her were flocking this way, docking on the block.  One or two even pulled off haphazard landings.  They’d be heavily fined.  But they had a chance of meeting A.

The front gate opened.

A opened it, and was greeted at the door by Mr. and Mrs. Rohde.  Quinn’s parents.

They ushered her inside.

“I miss my best friend,” A said.

“Quinn needs time to process,” Mr. Rohde said.  “He loves you dearly, but a lot happened.  All of you who survived were traumatized.  Even you.”

“We worry so much about you,” Mrs. Rohde said.  “Have you seen your parents today?”

“They’re busy.  Tomorrow.”

There was pity in her eyes.  A looked away.

“You need to take care of her, Basil.  Can you tell Elabre to back off and give A time?  Or are you restricted?”

[I can,] Basil replied.  [But as A has been saying since the tail end of her acting lessons today, she doesn’t-]

“She doesn’t want to deal with things lying down,” Mrs. Rohde finished.  “I know.  It’s everywhere.”

“When can I see Quinn?  Is there something I have to do?” A asked.

There was a look between the two.

“Please?” A asked.

“It’s not about please, or about what you do or say.  It’s about stepping back.  Quinn loves you dearly, he really, really does.  We do too.  But-”

But?  A’s lips moved, forming the word.

Basil was acutely aware of the pain and alarm.

“I’m not blaming you, I really hope I’m not making things worse by saying this,” Mr. Rohde said.  “I really hoped to have more time to figure out how to say it.”

“Say what?” A asked.

“Every time you try to reach Quinn and Quinn’s not ready, hundreds of millions of people, many of whom love you and want the best for you… they get upset, or want to help.  They want to add the power of their voice to things.  We get besieged.”

Mrs. Rohde added, “Quinn wanted to do his meditation retreat.  In nature.  We stretched things a little and made it happen.  A bit of quiet, instead of crowds and pressure.  At one of the uniform’s suggestions, we put in a filing saying we had additional witness testimony, which took Quinn’s onboard off the belt network, then had him travel without knowing where he was going, so he can’t be tracked by the… siege.”

“A few weeks, then?” A asked.

“An unknown amount of time.  Give Quinn a bit of time after getting home, too?  To resettle, find normalcy again?  I’m asking you and I’m asking your audience.  Quinn’s sensitive.”

“Let Quinn be the one to reach out.”

A swallowed hard.

She nodded.

“Thank you,” Mr. Rohde said.  “And thank you to everyone who respects our wishes and Quinn’s wishes.”

A turned to go.

[Wait.]

A, emotional, didn’t want to.

She pushed the door open, and saw the hundreds of people who had come to gather outside the Rohde’s house.

Thousands more were filtering this way.

“Let her see her friend!  She’s hurting too!” a woman screamed.

Mr. Rohde’s hand settled on A’s shoulder.

Pulling her back inside.

“I’ll call the local judiciary,” Mr. Rohde said.  “I think they can clear a path to a vehicle, and freeze all other transportation.”

A, numb, just nodded.

➨

The apartment Elabre Systems had supplied was large, and it had a view.  A bar of the same sort ballet dancers used extended along the length of the window.  A stood there, hands gripping the bar, eyes on the sprawl outside.  Advertisements flickered, drawing the eye.

A featured on a few of them.  Generation Colors, A now included, featured on others.

The day had started with physical pain that Basil couldn’t entirely handle, when his host was asleep.

Pain of another sort gripped her now.  Fear and anger, suppressed, to the point it circled back around to physical pain again.

All things Basil could and did suppress, symptom-wise, but that didn’t fix the root issue.

[Do you want me to call your parents?]

A’s expression twisted for a second.  Disgust, almost.

She shook her head.

Some of Elabre’s higher-ups were walking them through how to navigate higher society, in the same way A was being taught to be an actress, singer, and more.

“My thoughts are going in circles,” A said.  “It’s this weird loop, where I think about how tired I am, and how much I want to… unwind.  But that’s not a big enough word.  Uncoil?  Un…”

[Find release?]

So many times, in recent days, A had reacted to every single interjection he made with faint defensiveness, or a retort.

She wasn’t fighting him.  Maybe she was too tired.

So she ignored him instead.

“Then I think about my friends, and Quinn is busy.  Good for him.  I hope he finds the quiet he’s looking for.  Then I think about Vince, and Nos, and Cowrie, and for a moment, they’re alive, and I want to make plans.  Play music.”

[It’s understandable.]

“Can’t.  Then the loop starts all over again.  I’m caught by surprise, every time I think about them.”

[May I?]

Basil turned on the music.  Recordings of their experimentation as a band filled the apartment.

A gripped the bar like she was in space and she was at risk of drifting out into the void if she lost her grip.

[If we called your parents, and were blunt about your needs, I really do think they’d come.]

A sniffed.

He decided to give A the space that the Rohdes had wanted to give Quinn.

Nearly ten minutes passed.  A alternately gripped the bar harder, and relaxed.  For a minute, A turned her back to the world outside, head leaning back against clear polymer.

“Help.  I can’t do this.”

The admission seemed so small, and so uncharacteristic.

“Nevermind,” A muttered.

[There are options.]

“Are there?”

[The advertisements using your likeness have already paid out a considerable sum.  You’re fast approaching a situation where everything is in reach, financially.]

“So?  I can’t buy my best friend back, can I?  I can’t buy the lives of Vince, Cowrie, and Nos back.”

[No.  Probably not.  But the only things that would be difficult for you to buy would be something like a superstructure.  That would take a couple of years.  A planet… if you worked hard and focused on earning the lux, you could buy a planet of your own in four years.  Art and certain one-of-a-kind items that your financial peers want would be tricky.  There are five or so individuals who have the kind of lux you’re capable of earning now.  It’s hard to know, because some hide the numbers.]

“I can buy a planet?”

[A brand new planet?  If you worked hard and saved the lux?  Yes.  You could decide the rules.  Forge a patch of nature of the sort Quinn likes.  Have a place to escape to.]

Some of the tension that insisted on building up throughout A’s body relaxed somewhat.

The very idea of having a way clear of… all of this.

[That’s one option.  Another, and you can take both options, or one, but I wanted to say, you can keep doing this.]

“I’m not sure I can.”

A had always been a kid who put a lot of emphasis on her friends, and having people to connect to.

Now they were dead, distant, or gone.

[Find new friends in Generation Colors.  And we’ll do what we’ve been doing, without fighting.  You do the practice, and when we get to the execution, if you’re not there yet, I execute like I have been.  I’ll stop fighting you.  You stop threatening me.]

He could feel the emotion broiling up inside A.

That frustration again.

[We will get you to the point you don’t need to ask me.  I’ll make that a promise.]

A let out a shuddering sigh.

Outside, the lighting shifted imperceptibly toward cooler colors, dimming by fractions.  It was still early in the evening- dinnertime for most people.  A was wracked with an exhaustion that made it seem as if it was past midnight.

“I still don’t forgive you.”

[I know.]

“I can’t.  Because if I did, I’d be betraying…”

[I know.]

A nodded to herself, maybe unaware she was doing it.

“I hurt Quinn by reaching out.  His parents had to send him away to protect him.  He probably felt like I did right now, and I made it worse instead of better.”

[Unintentionally.  Keep that in mind.  Unintentionally.]

A swallowed hard.

[This is going to take some getting used to.  One joking line in the morning becomes a belt-wide advertising campaign twenty minutes later.  Anyone who looks at you the wrong way, or handles things indelicately, faces your billions of fans.  Eagle is having a rough night because people have decided he was unkind with how he approached the training, before lunch.]

“Is he okay?”

[He’ll manage.  But many of them are reeling.  They’re dealing with audiences ten times the size and that’s just the overflow from you.  I’m sure some won’t handle it well.  You made a joking comment to Te before the staff and most of the group arrived and it might have had political implications.]

“What?” A asked.

[About the arrangement of the belt?]

“I don’t even remember that.”

[And Amber got mad at Te for bringing it up, because it might remind you of the science center.]

“Oh.  I remember that.  There was a lot today.”

She didn’t seem to grasp the thrust of what he’d pointed out.  How there was a belt-wide debate about how things should be arranged, and if planets should interleave or if there should be focus on connecting and adding to the planets on the one belt.

A had made a passing comment toward the latter.

Unintentionally, accidentally, she might have decided the debate away from its current deadlock.  There was a shift in public perception on the matter, following directly from that comment.

“What am I supposed to do?”

And it didn’t matter at all.

[Go easy.  Red, Te, is a good person to study.  Not because their audience is large, but because of the attitude they have around being physically tall.  They’re gentle.]

“I’ve never been great at gentle.”

[You have your moments.  Especially with Quinn.]

“He’s my favorite person.  I didn’t want to say out loud, but I’m glad he’s a he, while dealing with shit.  He’s always seemed happier that way.  More sure of himself.”

[That’s some of that gentleness I just talked about.]

A relaxed her grip on the bar.  She flexed her hand.  The grip had been tight enough her hands hurt.

Basil put away the pain and mended the hurt.

[You’re a titan now.  Every movement, every word, everything you do will have ripple effects and unintended consequences.  It will take some adjusting.  For you and for everyone.]

A, one hundred and thirty pounds, including the weight of her inconveniently long hair, still gripping a wooden bar for support, lonely because her parents were gone and her best friend was away, looked out the window, silent.  To everyone else, it would look like she was quietly thinking, while Basil gave her her space.

A titan.

2.3.W – SEND

The whole morning had been a flurry of getting to know the Sherman Station folk.

“Why did you take so long between arriving and coming, child?” one of the Bibis asked her.

[Child,] Toby teased.  Their in-joke, borrowed from Aunt Gwen.

“I-” Winnifred started, and stumbled mentally over Toby’s tease and not having a great, honest answer.  “It’s my first time being away from Griffey Docks.  I wanted to take it in.”

“Aren’t you precious.”  Said like a statement.

Hale was the same way, making comments that were hard to judge.

It wasn’t the first time she’d been lightly admonished for taking so long between arriving and meeting them, and she could deflect that stuff, but it wasn’t helping the feeling that was settling over her.  That she was a fish out of water.  The attention they paid to her and their welcome made it worse, not better.

Or maybe she just felt extra self conscious, because there was an investigator who hadn’t let up with the constant observation.  Watching her over her shoulder.

“Watch that Hale,” the Bibi told her.  “I have a connection to that one, so I can tell you that.”

“I don’t know what-” she started.  But two other adults were calling over the grey-haired Bibi.

She looked at history and records, trying to track genealogy and relationships, and couldn’t make head or heels of it.  If it turned out that there was an ongoing joke and she was beating a record that had stood for a century or something, in not getting it, then she would be more relieved than upset.  At least then something would make more sense.

[They aren’t groups of families in the same way we are over at Griffey Docks,] Toby said, both answering her confusion and resuming a conversation they’d started after Winnifred had woken up and saw Hale with some of his relatives.

After that, she’d been distracted by the gorilla Crank, and by Kathe asking questions.  The criminal Sattersfield had nursed a coffee like he was recovering from a hangover, from the far end of the table.

Then, not long after Hale had dragged her out, with promises of secret plans, he’d been called away for questions. Crank was supposed to catch up, but with Hale pulled away and Crank not there yet, she was on her own at the fringes of a gathering of the Sherman Station folk.

“Yeah.  Not the same.”

[Leilani gave birth to Hale, but Kaia and Lane raised him until he was eight.  Then he was raised by Old Hero.  Because they were busy with work and he was acting out.  One conversation and he started living somewhere else.  That’s three different family units.]

“Almost one big, loose overfamily.”

“Exactly right,” a girl said, joining the conversation as if she’d been a part of it from the start.  Lane – named after the Lane that had raised Hale, but in no way related to her.  She was about Winnifred’s age, like a few here, which was nice, narrower than most dock folk, and she’d clipped a hair band to the mods at her lower face, pushing her mane of hair back rather than comb it.  “If you wanted to join that overfamily, it would suit you.”

“Do you think so?” Winnifred asked.

“That’s what people say,” Lane said.  She was a deft hand at working with her onboard, and they pulled up three conversations that referenced that very subject, in the time it took her to say the sentence.

[The fact you keep to your own is one of the first things people learn about you, when they talk among themselves.  Not that I think there’s anything wrong with it, but-]

Winnifred sighed.

[-yes.  Sigh.]

“It’s fine,” Lane told Winnifred, laying a clawed hand on Winnifred’s upper arm.  She had a grapple mount for zero-G navigation and safety on her arm, making her hand a bit heavier than Winnifred’s would be.  “You’re fine.  What I came to ask, was if you wanted to come race skimmers?  We’re heading over in twenty, so you have time to eat, wash if you want it, even, and wrap up anything you’re doing.”
