Losing Toby felt like the bottom had fallen out of her stomach, and her heart and Ox box had dropped away.  Going with Satterfield like this, when he was demanding so much and volunteering so little, all but one of her means of calling for help abandoned, it made it a hundred times worse.

Like Toby had fallen and she was being pulled away from that.

A heavy mechanical sound started to rattle through the entire floor of the station.  It was soft at first, a dull industrial rumble, that built up.

“Faster.”

“Is it the platform?” she asked.

“Shutters.  Move.”

“What’s- why?”

He jabbed something metal into her back, near the spine, behind her vitals.

She moved.  When she moved too fast, too far, he hauled on the back of her clothing.

It was frustrating.  Being treated like an animal.  Every instinct she had wanted to lash out, drop into a sweeping kick, claw at him, use her tail to snare him, or pull that supposed weapon away.  Break his grip.

She realized what he’d meant with the shutters.  Metal shutters were sliding into place over the material of the windows.

“Go, go, go.”

She was going.  She was capable of going twice as fast, but he held her back.  It felt like she was a sled dog, here, hauling him behind.

She wasn’t even that strong.

The street was empty, all doors were shut, many windows shuttered, with similar, overlapping lengths of metal.  Like insect shells.

All the life and character of Sherman Station was gone.  Some of the art remained, here and there, but it felt lonely, isolated.

And then there was nothing.

Lights shut off without a sound.  The light of stars on the far side of the window, paltry as they were, hadn’t even made it past the smoke before.  Now they were shuttered.

All across the station, lights outside buildings were shut off.  Some from within buildings made it through, but it was dimmed, rarely reaching from a house to the far side of the lane that house was on.  Some of those windows were even tinting, letting less and less light through.  People inside moved around, reduced to silhouettes, the outermost outlines of heads of hair colored in dull oranges.

“Slower,” Satterfield told her, pulling on the back of her overalls.

The sound of incoming vehicles filled the air.  The sound was weird.

“Cover!” Satterfield hollered.

“It’s-” Winnifred started, but it was useless to say more.  He was reacting.  She covered her ears and closed her eyes.

There was no explosion, near or far.

“-fake.”

“Fake?”

She started to respond.  In that moment, every sense she had caved in under white and a blare of a horn-like noise.  Every digital display, which included every window and most hard surfaces, turned to its maximum brightness, reversing the near-total darkness with near-total, blinding glare.  The relative silence, which she’d been listening to with care, because of the fly-by attacks, had been replaced with skull-rattling bass.

She stumbled, and crashed hard into ground.  Satterfield was pulled down on top of her.

He was on his feet shortly after, pulling at her clothing.

He shouted something, and it sounded far away and muted.

Her ears were modded, which set a safe maximum for what she could hear, so it wasn’t as damaging as it could be, but the tech in her eyes that was supposed to protect her from flashes and lasers had been burned out by the tool he’d used.

The fact things sounded far away and muted wasn’t from ear damage, but from the fact she’d almost passed out.

She could hear vehicles.

“Fake,” she said.  “I’ll do what you want, get me out of here.”

And more vehicles, coming from another direction.

“Fake.”

Speakers were generating phantom sounds.

They crossed the street and were about to leave it when they were sucker punched by another hit of all-consuming whiteness, and maximum volume noise.

Like a stun cartridge going off in their faces, except it was unavoidable, short of blinding and deafening herself.

Satterfield pushed her toward a narrow alley.

She could hear more vehicles.  She almost second guessed herself, both in the fact it could be another fake-out, and because without Toby, it felt like she was missing an entire dimension to her senses.  As if she had no directional hearing.  Or no verification that she was touching something, besides the fact she could see her hand making contact.

“No,” she said, late.  She pulled free.

He turned, weapon in hand, chasing.

It was two Tenures, each with crews of judiciary officers hanging off the sides.

The second dropped a bombardment.  They exploded outward.

Filaments, that reminded Winnifred of what she’d seen in the alley.

Batteries anchored them to one location, and from each battery was a morass of long hair-like strands, polarized to not touch one another, so they filled the air, waving and suspending there, puffing out to where they could catch on wind.  They connected to other surfaces, though, like walls and ground.

If they’d been in the alley, they would have been trapped there.  At best, between two clusters of filament.

The lights and noise flared again, this time one after the other.  Winnifred ran with hands clasped together, hands behind her head, so the metal of her forearms could cover her ears- the mechanics of her modded hands didn’t let them form a seal around her ears.

She had a throbbing headache, and her vision wasn’t focusing.  She bumped into a wall, got her bearings, and started moving.

He’d wanted them to move faster earlier, because now they were slow.  Making out any of their surroundings was next to impossible, and trying left her open to being blinded again.

It meant she didn’t see and barely heard as they came running.

She could just barely make them out in the flare of the engine from the departing Tenure.  Eight people in uniform, heads obscured by the equipment that doubled as armor and protected them from the sensory bombardment, had been dropped off by the craft.

Four in the lead had heavy guns with what looked like an extension to the barrel, hanging below it, with a very large diameter.  Winnifred was not someone who had gone for a lot of the heavy action movies, or the simulated shooters where onboards painted over everything and kids ran around, shooting each other, looking really dumb to anyone who didn’t have that filter.  She didn’t care about the engineering of guns.  She wasn’t born to one of the families where protest was regular and potentially violent.

She still knew these guns.

Hancocks.  There was probably a fancy prefix or suffix or twist on the name for the nonlethal variant brought to riots like this.  Whenever they popped up in media, it was a given that some real damage would be done.

Everything went white, displays turning on, a flash of light to blind.

No horn, to deafen at the same time.  She could hear the Tenure that had dropped off this group, flying to its next destination, or circling around to support.  She could hear the guns fire.

A spherical charge, like a mine, with small thrusters punctuating the exterior, connected by fiber to a projectile that used its own thrust and the help of the firing gun to maintain a compelling velocity.  A marvel of engineering, with just enough processing power loaded into it that it could track its surroundings and manage its thruster use- a small missile-like bullet and spheroid flailing around it, alternately, simultaneously, or holding off on firing the thrusters to arc in the air.  Picking the target and landing point.

Slow enough that the guns fired, the sound reached her, and in that natural moment afterward that Winnifred thought the bullets hadn’t hit her, everything landed.  Fast enough it couldn’t reasonably be avoided… and it arced in the air to unerringly hit its target anyway.

Satterfield grunted.  In the dark, Winnifred couldn’t see what had happened.  She had little doubt it was minimal, strategic damage to the flesh, or none at all.  The mine charge produced a radial spray of telescoping rods- a starburst of rigid, three or four foot long poles.  Again, strategic placement.  Past limbs, into walls, floor, doors.  Hard to budge, but not ramming directly into flesh.  She knew because one struck her as it extended.  At the very worst, they’d damage the flesh a little, and the judiciary would pay for the first aid.  A quick patch-up.

These weapons weren’t that kind to mods.  One shot crashed through her foot.  It obliterated it.  She wondered if it calculated for the scattered individual blades of her toes.  Another slammed full-on into her leg, above the knee, and then detonated that mine charge, extending the rods from within her, to make sure that there was nothing left from the mid-thigh down.

Winnifred screamed, and the sound was lost in the horn-like blare, that rattled her skull and denied her any sympathy.  There was no pain, she had no readouts because the tech in her eyes had burned out.  No audio signals.  Just a feeling of wrongness.

She could only see -and feel- the cost in Lux, future money, hopes, and dreams thrown down that bottomless pit she’d felt in her middle since she’d found Toby absent.

“I’ll shoot her,” Satterfield said, voice low.  He pushed the gun he carried into Winnifred’s neck, while gripping the back of her neck, pulling her back, so he could keep her in place for the bullet.

The rods from both of the mine charges were narrow, strong, and not nearly as careful about her modded parts as they were about Satterfield’s flesh.  She knew that because he was this capable of talking and acting, while she was prying herself free.

Taking Winnifred as a hostage.

Up and down had been taken from her, with her balance.  She was surrounded by the outcroppings of extended poles in the same way she’d be surrounded by branches if she’d been dropped from a height into the upper portion of a tree.  Some strong branches poked through weak parts of her.  She could push, grab at one, try to pull herself along, but while she was doing that, reeling, blinded, and deafened, she wasn’t even sure what direction to look to see the uniforms.  Some of her efforts got her nowhere, as she realized a rod was in her way.

“I will shoot her!” Satterfield bellowed.

“They can’t hear you,” Winnifred muttered, groping for a handhold, until Satterfield secured his grip on her.  They weren’t reacting in the slightest, but they were wary, still.  “They have ear protection.”

“They also have onboards to pass on the message.”

That would also make for a different sort of reaction.  Reading it in text or hearing it from the onboard, depending on the setup.

They looked like they were preparing to shoot.  The ones on the outer flanks were moving out to either side.

They were here to quell the uprising from the Folk of Sherman Station.  They didn’t care about her.

“Her blood will be on your hands.  Fuckers,” Satterfield addressed the uniforms.  When that didn’t provoke a reaction, he roared, “On your hands!”

A man at full volume a short distance from her ear felt feeble compared to the sounds and flashes they’d been dealing with.

Doubly feeble when nobody seemed to slow down.  He tried to keep Winnifred between himself and them.  He couldn’t, really, because four different mine charges had gone off near them, each deploying an irregular arrangement of telescoping rods.

I wonder if they’ll boot up Toby after all of this, to get a rundown of what happened, and if she’ll be really disappointed.  Stupid girl I invested in and raised from day one was awake and doing her own thing without me for fifteen minutes before getting her idiot feet blown off and dying as the hostage in a game of chicken where nobody flinches.

She grabbed one of the rods, started to pull herself, torso twisting, and in the doing, exposed herself.  Semi-intentionally.  The dull orange light of distant fire highlighted the vague shape of Satterfield’s face, twisted in anger.  She saw him look at her, at her body, and on realizing he was looking at her chest, she gave him a fraction more.

He took advantage.

Ninety percent of her outer shell, such as it was, was paneling and protection, so wires wouldn’t catch on protrusions, to keep dust out, to keep things from getting wedged into finer mechanisms, and so everything stayed bundled.  The chassis of her upper torso was a little shorter than a standard human ribcage, provided a solid base points for head and neck, shoulders, and the spine that extended down to the torso, and half of that, packed up toward neck and shoulders, was vitals.  Heart, ox, food intake and digestion, core processing for the technological side of her.  The modded side.

Satterfield reached up through the bottom of her ribcage and found the wires that extended out the bottom of those vitals.  She could feel how his fingers spread, each hooking around different wires, before gripping them in a fist.

“If you shoot me, my fucking body weight is going to drag some of this shit loose!  How sure are you that you can get to her with this shit in the way!?”

She made like she was going to keep struggling a second, before her predicament dawned.

She was trusting him.  Trusting them.

“Blood on our hands,” one of the judiciary uniforms said.  He was in the central pack, not one of the ones who’d fanned out sideways.  “You kept saying that.  But how much blood does she even have?  She’s a rat.”

“I have enough,” Winnifred said.  “Just enough.”

Throughout the space station, the large g-panels in the subfloor turned off.  The next part of the chaos.  With them, a hum Winnifred barely realized she’d been hearing terminated.

Everywhere but here.  They weren’t stupid.

So, tangled up in a tree-like mess of branches, two people with the Hancock pole-bombs in front of her, one creeping around the edges of the mess of poles to the left of them, another in the more open street to the right… that scene barely changed.  But throughout the station around them, burning debris stretched ceiling-ward, some loose material and paneling floated up, and drifted, rotating around, sometimes catching the light of the fires as it did, and people floated up as well.

One more anti-riot measure.  Taking away up and down as directions.  Taking away footing.  She could see the streaks of other Hancock shots.  Or other weapons- it was hard to say.  Slower than lightning, faster than fireworks.  Taking people out, in mid-air.

She gripped hands together.  With concerted effort, arm trembling from the effort, she broke a finger.  It took all she had, plus good points of leverage, specifically stressing the weakest part with the tip of her thumb, and even then, it was a partial break.  She was supposed to be able to put all of her body weight plus a bit of momentum into this, catching herself on her claw tips.  Jumping across a gap and landing on these claws.  Arresting momentum in zero-g, sometimes by awkward angles.  Some of that was distribution across up to ten different claws, or help from the tail, or a bit of care about angles.

The lights flashed on, blinding, bright enough to take the air out of her chest.  Leaving them totally off guard, if someone wanted to take a shot.

Tail hooking on pole, she used that as a primary point of leverage, and pulled herself closer to Satterfield, so he couldn’t pull something down and out of her.

She twisted off, then threw the claw of the finger she’d broken, at the uniform to the left of her, the one who had to work to move between the poles and the nearest wall, to get to Satterfield’s side for a shot, but who’d gotten a pretty good line on Satterfield’s side, if they wanted to shoot from the side.

She’d envisioned throwing the claw-blade of her finger like a throwing knife.  In a magical world, she’d happen to throw it into the barrel, and detonate what was inside, fucking them up on some equal level to how they’d destroyed her leg and foot, and taken Toby.

More realistically, a cut, or drawing blood, maybe.

The blood spray was massive.  She’d thrown directly at the uniformed person, and the blood spray went off to the left of their leg and stomach, along with chunks of broken armor.

Others fell the same way.  They turned, reacting, but more blood sprays followed.

It took a confusing three seconds for eight people to be demolished.  Legs and gun arms.

One of the small airborne drones turned on a flashlight, illuminating Satterfield and Winnifred.

Satterfield straightened, wincing.  “First aid from my wrist is still running.  Stroke of luck.”

“Are they okay?”

“Okay enough.  Those uniforms have nanotech, nobody looks very dead.”

“But- should we-?”

“We?  There is no we.  There’s me and what I tell you.”  He hauled Winnifred with him, one hand gripping her, one hand holding the gun.  “Cooperate, rat, or I’ll drop you and take one of these.”

She did, some, pulling, or grabbing onto a pole, which bowed, bobbed, or bent with her weight, to lift herself up, while Satterfield also listed.

Kathe made her appearance, offering the final hand.  Airborne drones floated around her.  Ten or so, with more in the wider area.  Gun drones about -Winnifred had to guess- twenty centimeters long, not much wider around or taller than a clenched fist.  They were capable of hovering, and had some attached utility, that varied from drone to drone.

She’d adjusted what she wore.  Now she wore eye and ear protection, her hair was tied up, and she wore a backless halter top, which showed the modded ports in her upper body.  Drones punched into twelve different slots in her back, starting where her shoulderblades were meant to be, extending down to where upper buttocks met lower back.

Reloading, probably.  They’d packed a punch heavier than a shotgun, so they were probably single-shot.

Some of the drones had cabling they could fire out.  They didn’t have a lot of propulsion, so they had to anchor onto a surface, then fire.  They did so, to help Satterfield, and to help Kathe, who pulled, even while the drones navigated the air to orient for the docking procedure.

Kathe handed Satterfield headgear.  He pulled it on, then bent down, pulling off the helmet of one of the injured uniforms.

The moment the helmet was off, three telescoping rods just like the shots the hancocks had fired telescoped inward, filling the inside of the helmet.

“No luck, you’re going to have to suffer, hostage,” he told her.  “Move.  You’re out front.”

“Can’t walk.”

“Crawl, then.”

So she did.  The damaged leg and foot scraped against textured, nonslip floor for traction, and she felt as if pieces of her were flaking away with each attempt.

Kathe grabbed her and hauled her sideways as Tenures flew by.

More interested in delivering paramedic help.

Others were coming.  Kathe directed them through a tunnel that ran beneath an elevated building, through a side door, and then out another building, into a subfloor space.

“They have drones too,” Kathe said.  “But I think they’re mostly deployed on the other side of this floor.  Things got hairy over there.  I was watching while you made your way over there.”

“What else were you doing?”

“Making that headset you’re wearing, Satterfield.”

“We clear?”

“Yeah.  Not much in the way of cameras here, and I’m suppressing them.”

“I was telling Winnifred here that we are very good at what we do.  I’m glad you came when you did, or you would have made me look like one hell of a liar.”

“We are very good at what we do,” Kathe said.  “We haven’t worked this closely together before, but we’ve been-”

“Close enough.”

“-Proximate, in the same situation.  We saw each other work and were willing to work together, after.”

They navigated the sub-floor.  Winnifred wished she had feet.

“I hope you’re not upset with me, Winnifred,” Satterfield said.  “I knew Kathe was close, that she was probably scouting the situation and getting lined up.  I had to buy time.”

“Mm.”

Winnifred wasn’t sure what to say to that.

“We need you,” Satterfield said.  “When we go up there, we’ll have to keep up the ruse of having you as a hostage.  We’ll cut off the system from the Belt network, and have you use the logged data.  Consider it like those tests and study puzzles you had to do, when getting certified as a mechanic and ship’s engineer.”

“I’m still not done.  Certifying.”

“You’re not done but you’ve logged enough extra hours to know things about as well as an old man who’s done it for most of his life.  You care about this stuff,” Satterfield said.

If ‘this stuff’ was engineering, it was so far down the list of things she cared about right now, it barely qualified.

They’d taken Toby.

“As fast as you can, run through those logs and mark out the weak points for as many ship types as you can.  We clear our trail, take the logs with us, leave you.  That’s ninety-five percent of your job done, Win.”

She was ‘Win’ to Toby, her mom, and her dad, and maybe, like, Keeley, back home.  Friends and family, or more accurately, people who were both, to the point it got blurry.

Not to Satterfield, who she’d given a lot of trust to.  Trust that hadn’t been rewarded, repaid, or recognized.

“When nations started using small-scale drones, things got bad fast,” Satterfield said.  “You can consider Kathe one of the few who hold onto that tradition.  Her standing somewhere and breathing while carrying the drone loadout she’s carrying is more illegal than anything you’ve ever done.  If we’re talking Chess and Chaos, she’s our queen, get shit done, on the chessboard.  Our masterstroke.  Our way of cutting past the bullshit of the Chaos.”

“You told her about Chess and Chaos?” Kathe asked.

She sounded almost disappointed.

“Crank brought it up.  Since I explained it, I’m using it to keep explaining.  It’s better than switching up the terminology this late in things.  I’m not that lame a horse, Kathe.”

“Ah.  Okay.”

“As for me, I’ll probably truck on for a bit, scraping by, until they arrest me.  I scrape by, and knowing what you’re doing, being half-reliable, having experience, in a role like this, I guess it counts for enough.”

“He’s being modest.  He’s very good at the ‘Chess’,” Kathe said.  She turned her head, which was effectively blindfolded, toward Satterfield.  “I feel like a juvenile, talking like that.”

Winnifred wasn’t so sure she put all that much stock in Satterfield’s ‘chess’.  The alleyway came to mind.  If they’d gone the way Satterfield had wanted to go, they’d have been snared.

Maybe he had counted on Kathe saving them?  But that felt… shaky.

“Here.  Up.”

In the dimly lit subfloor area, he’d stopped by a shaft that helped support the floor above -insofar as that was needed on a space station- and led up to a hatch.  There were rungs of a ladder, but in areas like docks or anywhere valuable merchandise was loaded and unloaded, things weren’t full access.  After three rungs, there was a lengthy drop.  It meant any thieves would have to bring their own ladder.  Then they’d reach the hatch, which was often locked.

Satterfield used the straps at the back of Winnifred’s overalls and the side of the shell encapsulating her chest to lift her up, then grabbed the calf of her more intact leg, holding it firm so she could leverage herself up.

Kathe followed.  The mods that let her host the drones she did had diminished her physical abilities some.  Not totally- she’d participated in Hale’s game.  But enough she struggled to lift herself up high enough to grab the rungs that led up to the hatch.

Speaking of Hale’s game…

The hatch was unlocked, probably in advance of all of this, and on exiting, the first thing Winnifred could recognize was the football.  Hale’s ugly-beautiful ship, converted into a place for his games.

They had the code to access it.  The door opened, they stepped inside, and the door closed behind them.

Winnifred flinched, full-body, as the lights came on.  It was hard not to anticipate the next big flash like the ones the local government was employing.

“Stay put for a minute,” Satterfield said, training the gun on her.

Her eyes weren’t focusing very well.  She ended up closing her eyes, the metal of her lower face against what remained of her collarbone after her last big retrofit.

Whatever they were doing, it took a minute.

“Okay,” Kathe said.

“We told the Sherman Station Folk to store things for our mutual benefit,” Satterfield said.  “Storage?”

“For?”

“Blankets, general shielded paneling.”

“There’s a storage bay here,” Winnifred said, pointing up.  The area that had been converted into a sports field was a walkway that connected to itself, and rotated on its own around a core of ship.  A mouse wheel that used g-panels and rotation to pull people downward in an approximation of standard planet gravity.  Things weren’t rotating now though.  That core was going to store a lot of the things that might need to be carried throughout the ship.

“It’s not there,” Satterfield said.  He hit a button inset into the wall.  A yellow warning light flashed.

The warning light was some advance notice that a ladder was coming down.  Once it did, a hatch opened.  She could see up into the core area.  Normally it would be a very open room in relative zero-G.

“Hale changed it,” she said.  She grabbed the ladder, and scaled it, happy for a way to move that wasn’t crawling or hobbling on a shattered foot and leg.  She opened a hatch.  “So the ball could fall through the center.  Not storage anymore.  Poor baby.”

“Poor baby?” Satterfield asked.

“She likes ships,” Kathe explained.

“Right.  So?  I don’t want to have to cut every lock.  They said it would be here.”

“Are you stealing from them?”

“I promise I’m not,” he said.  He pointed at a display near her ladder, while walking over to another.

He brought up some images.

Message logs.  Hale discussing things.

She reviewed it.  It seemed genuine.

“The blankets block signals to the Belt Network.  If this is Chess, then they’re going to be cornered, if they aren’t already.  There’ll be mass-arrests of the people protesting.  Kathe will upset that, free them, give them room to start again.  My goal is to transport the blankets and paneling.  A team of Hale and the strongest, most capable people he knows, and if we can cut off the messages-”

“He’ll get in trouble,” Winnifred interrupted.

“They will.  Even accidental evasion of monitoring is a problem and gets you seriously looked at.  This would be intentional.  But it will catch them off guard.  This is how we checkmate.”

“Winnifred,” Kathe said.

Winnifred turned.

“There’s no real reason we’d want the blankets and shielded panels, except to cloak our allies’ movements.”

“Assuming it is that,” she said.  She considered for a moment, then decided it was probably okay.  “Other storage areas, there’s reinforced storage in T-3.  Because sometimes they keep excess fuel there.  Or other delicate goods.  But it’s not going to be here, it’s partitioned, that’s messy.  More secure, but messy.”

“Right.”

“N-2 has a secondary room that can be short term quarters, but is usually used for crew members to store things they don’t want to unpack in their rooms.  It’s convenient.  Blankets and things would store nicely there.  Try N-2-I and N-2-J.”

“Alright.  That cuts it down.”

“T is designation for tail, by the way, and N is nose, and as you get further from-”

“I know my way around a ship,” Satterfield said, a little harshly.  Then, seeming to remember he wasn’t acting anymore, he said a softer, “N-2, I and J.  Good.  Thank you.”

He looked around to get his bearings.  The walls on either side of the rotating band were static, studded with panels and buttons at set intervals, but they were also painted, so anyone could reorient themselves. A fat horizontal band of blue, a thin band of normal paneling, then a thinner band of blue, then normal, and the same, in reverse, but for yellow.  A convenient ‘B’ was left unpainted in the blue.

He hit a button, a door opened, and he stepped through, heading for N-2.

“Winnifred,” Kathe said.  “Here.”

Winnifred descended the ladder.  The moment she let go, there was a yellow flash.  The ladder retracted back into the core of the ship.

Kathe had brought things up on the ship display.  Even when Winnifred didn’t have eye tech, the ship read her eye movements, and moved the cursor.

She kept finding herself instinctively reaching for Toby, or starting to ask Toby a question, or for help.

Losing Toby sucked, period.  But losing Toby’s help made her feel like a small child, fumbling at the world.

“Ships.  The plan was for us to spend time together, and you’d find subtler opportunities to direct us to weak points on ships.  Along the way, we’d secure Sherman Station interests and set up other things.  The problem is, the recent riots are compressing our timeline, and we don’t think I’ll be able to do what I do for much longer.  The noose is tightening, onboards are everywhere, everyone is watching everyone.  My existence is illegal.”

“It might be the same for us ‘rats’ soon.”

“I’m sympathetic,” Kathe said.  “Probably more than you know.”

“Why do you do all of this?  Modding yourself like that?  Hurting people?”

“I problem solve,” Kathe said.  “Sometimes the problems are people being in my or our way.  What did Satterfield tell you about Chess and Chaos?”

“That it’s a reminder.  It’s rarely one or the other.  But they’ll bombard, constantly change things up, turning off the lights, blaring sound, moving parts of the superstructure, changing up the nonlethal weapons and tools they use… or they’ll try to corner their opponents or bait them into doing something stupid.”

“It’s easier to hide you’re trying to get someone in checkmate if they think you’re being random.  And it’s easy to have the threat of a checkmate, legal or tactical, be a component of the bombardment and psychological effect of Chess.  Yes.”

“Did he tell you the history?”

“That people solved it.”

“Yes.  The people who invested in the Intelligence to analyze Chess and Chaos, planned, and anticipated?  It worked, and they’re our Belt government today.  It’s important to keep investing, and keep up with the arms race.  Because they might start pulling so far ahead they stop caring about the rest of us altogether.  And that‘s dangerous.”

“They’re already that far ahead,” Satterfield said, re-entering through the door he’d left through.  He had a carbon fiber cloth sheet  with inlaid protection slung over one shoulder.  Triaxial weave, in black and gold.  He’d found what he was looking for.  “Humans aren’t mentally capable of fathoming hundreds of billions.  Not properly.”

“Disagree, and disagree,” Kathe said.  “I think we have a shot, and I think you’d be surprised what people can fathom.”

She deployed two drones as she said it, and they moved as she did.

“Ha, yeah.  That’s not billions.  Also, Winnifred.  Can we get you to give us your estimates?  Treat it like a lesson plan.”

She turned toward the display.  A crosshair tracked her eye movement, floating this way and that on the screen.  She could squint one eye slightly closed and glance sideways, and it rotated the 3D wireframe model of the ship in question.  An Armstrong.  Classic, not in much use today.

On a level, seeing ships was reassuring.

On another… she didn’t like this.  “Half of what makes a ship a good target is who owns it, who values it.  If it’s in use.”

“Anything you can give us helps.  We’ll prioritize depending.”

That was the issue.  It was taking the choice out of her hands.  But it still left the responsibility with her.  If she told them what ships had the biggest vulnerabilities from attack or sabotage, and someone died because of it?

“I don’t want anyone to die or get hurt.  I’d rather keep doing what we were doing.”

“Not really an option,” Satterfield said.  “And you were reluctant to do what you were doing.  You had opportunities, like when you played the game with Hale, Kathe, and Hale’s friends, and sat on the roof of this very ship, with a view of other ships coming and going, and you gave us nothing.”

“Easy does it,” Kathe said.  She’d barely moved.  A peculiar stillness to go with her slightly slouched posture, making it as easy as possible for the drones to dock, if they needed to.

Satterfield continued, a little less heated, “Now you’ve seen how vicious they get, how little they care about you or any of the Folk.  This is it.  Give us as much as you can, we leave, you remain behind, with the excuse we coerced you.  You can even claim the Judiciary fell for our trap.  They blamed Toby, disabled your onboard, and left you vulnerable.  You sue.”

“They’d settle,” Kathe said.  “Then you go back to Michal, he pays you.”

I get my ship.  Or get a lot closer to having it.

All she had to do was take all she’d learned about ships, loving them, loving how they worked, and pervert that knowledge.

She looked at the Armstrong, and flicked it again with a movement of her eyes.  She knew why the designs that had followed from the Armstrong had made the decisions they’d made.  She knew why the ship didn’t see use today, where the football -the Wrest- still did.  There were flaws, parts that got stressed in repeated atmospheric re-entries, or in extreme weather, if a planet was very cold or very hot.  The cockpit was separated from the main body by a corridor, and that could snap off under strain.  When it did, the ship could fly, but it was a nightmare.  The rear landing gear was frequently modified, because the weight distribution of the ship had originally been designed with it empty of everything except fuel.  With a half-full hold, crew, and other supplies, it leaned back on its ass too much.

She could say that, blink twice and set down a marker, tinted red, write some notes about how the vulnerabilities worked, then move on to the next.

She’d get her ship, and a part of her would always wonder.  Would that knowledge circulate?  Would people start targeting ships more?

Would that knowledge or knowledge like it mean that she could achieve her dream, start to fly, run a simple business, and maintain a crew… only to have it snatched away, because people knew where to stick a bomb, or how to leave the ship dead in the water with the right sabotage?

Even if she skipped over the ships she eventually planned to take, so the knowledge couldn’t come back on her… did she want to live in a world where people did this?

“I’ll keep working with the man who hired us,” she said.  “I’ll help identify targets on a case-by-case basis.”

“Slowly, ineffectually?”

“In a way I can make my peace with.  Where I have some idea of who the targets are.  I can-”  She saw Satterfield and Kathe exchange a look, and paused, before resuming.  “I can pick out some things for… stupidly expensive luxury ships, the biggest ships.  Cases where it will hurt and probably count.  Not… not ships like an Armstrong.  Nobody flies Armstrongs anymore, and the ones who do don’t deserve the sabotage.”

“You don’t know.”

“They’ll have been punished enough by the upkeep and hassle.”  And the pants-shitting terror that you’d have if you were in the cockpit on a rough re-entry and it started headbanging like it was listening to rock music, metal tearing.

“You don’t know,” Satterfield told her.  “It could be the worst person in the Belt.”

“That’s just it.  I don’t know.  It could be the nicest person, and I don’t want to be even partially responsible for that.”

“Fuck.  They sent us a child.”

“Satterfield,” Kathe said.  “It doesn’t matter that much.  We have a limited window tonight.  We have the blankets, we have the panels.  Let’s go help Hale, bring what we can, surgical strike.  Maybe we put a dent in this.”

“Yeah.”

“Yeah?  The ships don’t matter that much.  They’d be nice to know about, but they aren’t as important.  Hale is.”

“Yeah.  Okay.  The blankets were in I, the scooters were in J.  We were wondering about the scooters.”

“Can we have my drones drive the scooters after we’ve loaded them up or-”

“Auto-follow.”

“Perfect.”

Winnifred stepped back and out of the way as the two unloaded.  They didn’t want her help, and she got enough of a bad feeling from them that she was okay keeping her distance.

The ‘scooters’ were small craft, usually one or two person, with bins at the back.  The bins could be adjusted, and with adjustment, a pair of scooters connected together could carry a pile of the paneling.  Others puttered behind, loaded with the black and gold blankets with their Escher-style cubic patterning.

They got them to the door.

“It was nice working with you,” Kathe told Winnifred.  “I’m sorry it wasn’t for longer.  And I’m sorry about Toby.  I hope you don’t run into trouble getting replacement parts.  There’s going to be a spike in prices, with the state of things.”

“Ah.  Yeah,” Winnifred said, looking down at her shattered foot, finger, and leg.  “Shit.”

Kathe smiled.

Then two drones that had anchored themselves to the wall fired the cabling.  It penetrated the shell of Winnifred’s body, latched on, and pulled.

She was pulled backwards, into the wall between the two drones, and hit it hard enough her Ox stuttered.

“What are you-?”

Kathe closed the distance.  Winnifred had one free hand, damaged as it was, while the other tugged at the attached cable that had speared her wrist.  She clawed for Kathe’s face, and Kathe leaned back.

Satterfield, holding a blanket out in front of him, approached her, and took hold of the arm.

She kicked with her good leg, using that too, but he hugged her around the waist, while pinning her arm.

The claws couldn’t penetrate the material.

“Excuse me,” Kathe said, leaning in like she was going for a hug, at Winnifred’s upper body.  She instead put a tool to the back of Winnifred’s neck, where the artificial spine met the architecture that Toby had set up to help join the gap.

From there, they could release her to slump down to the ground.  They pulled her more or less horizontal on the slightly sloped surface, then dismantled her.  They took an arm with a damaged hand, then her other arm. Chassis, spine, tail.  Pelvis, legs.

“This is a kindness,” Kathe told Winnifred.

They left her her heart, her ox, her head, lower face, and the architecture that connected head and part of the neck to the modded body.  Fluids that smelled too -too much- spilled onto the floor.  Blood, fluids.

Everything went into a bin with one of the blankets.  They covered the parts.

“Be angry.  It helps,” Satterfield told her.  “When we’re done with everything, we’ll tell people where you are.  It’ll be a few days at most.  You’ll have a headache from the lack of food and water, nothing more.”

He turned off the lights before opening the door.

All of the scooters filed out.

The door shut.

She was left in darkness.

A long few minutes passed.  Her breathing sounded very loud.

“Computer?” she addressed the ship.  Her artificial heart pounded with her knowledge that if this didn’t work, she was doomed to days of darkness and dread, hoping she’d be found.  “Play Enjustice, by A.  For the motivation.”

The knocking sounds and strums of the song’s opening echoed through the mouse wheel of the ship.

She had to do something.  Toby was counting on her, and she needed Toby.

She had no arms or legs, and no easy way to get some.

“Computer?  G-panels on, for the central band.”

The panels lit up.  She felt herself settle harder against the floor.

No limbs, she was a head and a neck, and her vitals were… just there.  Essential functions unprotected, in a heap below her head.  Artificial heart, ox box, processing, a bag for digestion.  If she pulled the wrong way, or if something compressed the wrong thing too much, or even hit it with enough force… her chances of surviving this dropped by an order of magnitude.

“Computer, antigravity on.”

2.6.W – SEND

Winnifred pushed her head into the floor, to try to give herself a push, as the gravity let up.  Lightly, to give herself time.  Not too lightly, because air resistance was a concern.  She didn’t want to be dead in the air.

Turning the antigravity on meant activating the G-panels in the floor of the ship, getting them to do the opposite of what they were meant to, which was provide some ability to stand.  They were functionally everywhere, even on stations and superstructures, and drew heavily on Belt physics, since the way they worked was to block the influences of gravity of one body, usually a celestial body.  Having closely neighboring planets helped.  Get outside the Belt entirely, and the only switches that could be turned off or on were the Belt and Sun, which would be functionally ‘down’, and properly aligned celestial bodies from the old solar system that were further out, which would be ‘up’, and a weak ‘up’ at that.

Many of those old planets from the solar system had been cast out, so their force on the Belt wouldn’t upset the arrangement, or stress superstructures, anyway.

On stations and superstructures that were connected to the planet with the cabling, g-sails also acted as ways to manage the stresses and forces of the planet’s rotation, and equalize things so those on the uppermost floors of the superstructure wouldn’t have a meaningfully different experience and quality of life from those in the middle floors, and people living near the surface.

G-panels and G-sails, the same thing by different names, barring some aesthetic and framing around the edges, were insanely complex on the subatomic level.  They were also laughably simple, on the abstract, macro level.  Abstracted, gravity was a ‘force’, with quotation marks around ‘force’, where the exchange of particles could be blocked or multiplied by matching or compounding the wavelengths.  It cost more and introduced more problems to keep a ship with a full crew lit enough than it did to block gravity from one direction.  In essence, a ship with G-sails was most often using the sails to make a controlled ‘fall’ toward a target body.

Winnifred had learned the basics as a child.

This child’s play was now a force and a tool at her disposal that could –nay, should— now kill her.

She was a head, neck, shoulders, and dangling vitals.  Ox, heart, necessary elements for digestion, and other base needs.  Central processing kept some of those necessary elements running.  They’d left her her face mask on her lower face, probably because they didn’t want her to die.  Left off for too long and there was a high chance she’d lose moisture from her open sinuses, her jawless, lipless mouth, and if rescue took twelve hours, she could easily dehydrate in that time.  There was a possibility she could struggle to breathe, or have a physical reaction, vomit, and be unable to expel the vomit or turn her head enough to clear her airway.

If they’d wanted her dead, that would have been easier.

She’d read about unmodded babies without onboards or machine help being fragile.  How even a sufficiently deep depression in the mattress could create a pocket of carbon monoxide that they could ‘drown’ in, unable to move away from it.  Any little thing could kill them.

That was her, now.

She had to move, and she had to move the right way.  Move the wrong way, and there was risk.  If she flung herself up by altering gravity, and hit the opposing wall with enough force, she could break the coupling or interrupt the power flow to something vital.  There were things plugged in there that, normally, were meant to be easily swappable, in case of emergency.  If her ox box was damaged during a normal day, normal repairs, and she needed to quickly get something else working, or plug herself into an external supply, it did no good for that connection to be so secure she couldn’t unclasp it and get access to the tubes.  Normally, the fact everything was contained and arranged properly within the chassis of her upper body was enough.

Too harsh a ‘fall’, with her Ox box below her, now, and she could damage it, and impair her breathing.  She would suffocate.

On the other end of things, if she cracked her head against a hard surface, without Toby there to help manage things, that would be another way to go.

She was flipping lightly through the air, head over trailing internals.

She could guess at where she would end up, and at what angle, but Toby wasn’t with her to help project the outcome, or plan the response.  She had never, once in her life, been this close to death, or been this vulnerable.

She didn’t like the angle.

“Wrest,” she spoke to the empty, dimly lit corridor with the glowing floor.  “I’m a returning guest of Hale’s, I’d like to set up for the next game.”

There was a faint response, as consoles built into the walls clicked on.  Like the faintest exhalation.  There was a danger here, latent, and it was one that could paralyze her.  Or even see her killed.  She didn’t own this ship.  There were limits to what it might let her do.  If it thought she was trying to interfere with the ship, or if it put her in the same category as a stowaway who snuck onto a ship, stayed inside, and then tried to subvert the ship’s inner workings to steal it or get access to cargo…

Lockout.  It might stop listening to her altogether.

It was part of why she didn’t want to call for help.  It was too easy for everything to shut down around her, locking her into the room.  With the state of things and the ongoing riot, ‘help’ would be delayed, and-or would be the same people utilizing the flashes, sounds, damaging modded bodies, and trying to corner the protest into some trap.

“Number floor panels, zero directly below me, one-P for the next panel toward port, two-P for the panel past that, closer to port, and so on.  One-S for the next panel toward starboard.”

The ship chimed a confirmation.  She suspected that if Toby were with her, he’d be elaborating on things in the background with some quickly written code, to project those same numbers for easy reference.

If Toby were with her, everything would be okay.  Or more okay.  Mostly okay.

Bitterness choked her.  They’d taken Toby.  They’d taken her body.  Things fundamental to her had been taken away to suit the needs and purposes of others.

She was drifting upward at an angle.  She’d had to, really, because she could only really move her head, and the head was at one end of her body.

As she drifted, she eyeballed the right zone, then said, “Panel one-P, decrease intensity, ten percent.”

She could feel it.  She had prioperceptive receptors in her internals.  She could feel the shift in stomach juices, pulls on her internals.

A faint strain, as the tubes of her insides pulled.  Nothing nearly severe enough to pull them out, but even that faint sensation was a firm reminder that it was a risk.

While her body stuck out into the less altered gravity above one panel, and her head was in the heavier gravity of the other, her rotation shifted.

“Equalize, reduce both fifteen percent.”

Balancing herself out, then letting herself drift higher.

She reached the ceiling, got her head laid against it, and then jerked her head to one side.  “Zero G.”

Stress in her voice could be a factor in any theoretical lockdown, under the logic that a thief trying to steal the ship or gain access to something they shouldn’t would be more stressed than a casual visitor.

It could also be that Hale just didn’t care that much about security and had turned everything off.

She’d gone up and over, reached the ‘ceiling’, which was the circular core in the middle of the mouse wheel, and then pushed herself off in the right direction.  With G-panels along the outer perimeter of the mouse wheel and on the floor of hallways only, she couldn’t control for the side-to-side movement.

Had to bank off of a wall.

Not too hard a hit.

But when she started to move away, she felt a sharp pain in her scalp.

Pulling hair.

Panic fluttered in her chest, as her trajectory shifted.  She was tethered, moving in a tight arc-

The ensuing collision, head jerking reactively, the following swing of her body controlled by the tether of hair, brought the dangling containers, boxes, tubes, and wires of her vitals into the wall with enough force she was briefly stunned.

No help from Toby, to manage sensations, and keep them exactly where they needed to be.  It was a punch in the gut, in the heart, fluids flowing the wrong way, like vomit in the throat, and the stark fear that a tube would come loose, that made coherent thinking next to impossible.

If she hadn’t had the visual components fried out of her eyes by Satterfield, then she’d have a mess of warnings littering her field of vision right now.  She wasn’t sure if her ox box had been damaged or compressed like this – it really did rely on her chassis more than its housing, for protection.  It could’ve just been panic making breathing harder.

Her hair was still tethered.  A strand caught on something, or enough strands that she couldn’t just yank hard enough for the hair to come out of her head.

It didn’t help that Toby had secured everything, strengthening and protecting her hair and scalp against elements and stray sparks from work.

She felt that yank again, and, acting purely on instinct, pulled back against it, again.  Being caught and stuck like this was more dangerous than another full-body impact like that.

Either way, she could pull herself closer, and hit the wall with her skull, instead of her body.  Hard enough she wondered if brain damage was in the cards.  She didn’t know what it took, really.  But she had to get free.

She had a vivid mental image of more hair getting caught, until she couldn’t pull free.  Drifting, suspended in zero-G like this, unable to free herself.  Then someone coming in by another point of the mouse-wheel hallway, and turning off zero-G.  Her body weight could pull her free, she’d drop, and her vitals or brain would be dashed across the floor, fifteen feet below her.

A life punctuated by a beginning, middle, and ending of gory vulnerability on gleaming surfaces, none of it by her own choices, with in-between moments of dreams unrealized.  Dreams compromised.

The realization and emotions that came from that were enough that she barely realized she’d gotten free.

Her head hurt.  Fittings throughout her vitals felt uneasy.  She couldn’t ping-pong her way down this hallway.  Especially when the next head-to-wall point of contact could see hair -or a tube, or a wire- catching on the seam between panels, or some edge of a manual override button or lever.  Or if too much jostling could shake something loose.

She did her best to focus.  It was hard to see, with moisture in her eyes, and with the damage the flashes had done.  She had to gather what she could without throwing herself off course.  Even a sharp turn of her head could make her start rotating in the air.

She felt feverish, and suspected that had to do with the fact her body couldn’t vent the higher temperatures.  Normally, channels and natural heat pumps throughout the body let natural heat be preserved or spent, as needed.  She didn’t have that, now.

Winnifred wasn’t meant to be this active when in this state.

Her goal was the doorway into the hallway that led to the nose.

She rebounded off one wall, more shoulder than head, which was better, but her aim was imprecise.  Then nudged herself off the opposite wall, aiming down, toward the doorway.

She wished she could adjust air pressure, so there was a slight vacuum to pull her into that doorway.  She’d feel it as a strong breeze, but everything counted.  But that got into territory that would ban her from the systems until someone else checked in.

“Open the door nearest me,” she said.

It whisked open.

She wasn’t quite on course.  She decided to trust, hoping that the bumps and shape of her body lucked her into going inside.  Her mind ran through options-

There weren’t great ones.

She hit the frame of the door, and started to move away.

“Panels P-3, P-4, intensity up forty percent.”

Too hard.  But-

She felt herself hit the platform at the base of the door, angle awkward.  If her neck wasn’t reinforced by the onboarding–

She lay there, inside the open doorway, the side of her face on room temperature metal.

She breathed hard for a minute, letting her body cool off, a prickle of sweat on her brow.  Her hair had come undone at the back, and was strewn around her, sticking to the sweat.

The mask of her lower face pushed against ground, she did her best to move by inches.  Her body was a weight, so she could only turn in a circle, with that weight at the center.

Then, laying with her face now pointed the other direction, she could look down the hallway.  This was where the devices had been stored.  The grappling reels, normally safety for anyone working in deep space, to have a good way of reeling themselves in, or moving around without too much hassle.  The small tablets that allowed easy management of the G-panels.  The propulsion kits.

Neither the grappling devices or the propulsion kit were good for her.  The grappling reels were too standardized, meant to pull a body that weighed at least forty-five kilograms to the destination point.  When she weighed this little… it probably wouldn’t even work, for safety reasons, and would pull her with life-threatening force if it did work.  The propulsion devices needed something to latch onto.

There were more things there, that she hadn’t paid a lot of attention to, because she’d been focused on learning the rules of the game and the unmodded players mostly liked the grapple reels, anyway.

It didn’t matter.  She’d struggled to get here, and her second plan had been to get access to tools and resources here.  She could see the container, metal frame with wire walls, trays inset, laid with the various options.  The latch had been flash-welded.  A blob of welding an inch wide that she had zero hope of getting past.

Satterfield would have done that while she was talking to Kathe, or after, when bringing the carbon fiber blankets out.  It was why they hadn’t wanted her in this hallway.

Still breathing hard, from the emotional strain of getting here as much as anything, she worked her way around until she could look straight at a panel.  It recognized that a face was directed at it, and lit up.

Little icon in the corner showed no connection to the wider belt network.  Okay.  She’d assumed.

She navigated to ship cameras.  It was ridiculous to do it here, when she could’ve normally walked down this hallway in ten or twenty seconds, but here she was.

The door to the cockpit was welded too.  That had been her first plan.  The cockpit had a lot of emergency measures and alternative ways to get calls out.  She could’ve called people she knew to be friends.

She wasn’t sure who those people were, right now.  Hale?  He worked closely with Satterfield and Kathe.  Would he be okay with this?

Winnifred felt sick.

She wracked her brain.  She was so used to having Toby to refer to and ask for any detailed memory stuff, or she could go back and review her logs… the only times she couldn’t, normally, was when she was studying.

So… she had to think of this like a lesson in her training as a mechanic and engineer.  A ‘look at these two images, what’s changed?  Why is it important?’, except those were usually engines or the internals of a ship.  There were some work safety ones like that…

Not usually this detailed.

Thinking of it as a lesson helped her get into the right frame of mind.  They hadn’t gone in with a welding tool.  Had they left with one?  They would have wanted to use it late, because it would have set off alarm bells if Winnifred had poked her head in, out of curiosity, and saw this spot weld, or if she’d gone further, trying to help, and saw the one on the cockpit door.

Or any others that she wasn’t aware of, yet.

There was a chance that Kathe’s drones included the equipment to do this, but there was also a chance that they didn’t.  Would he cart out the welding tool, covered by a blanket?  A bit awkward, and then he had to dispose of it…

A final possibility was that it was here.

Her eye movements operated the panel, same as if she had lenses, same pattern of eye flicks, blinks, squints, and staring at a point until the tracking bar that encircled it filled in.

The logs and camera feed had been deleted.  Kathe might have handled that.

Winnifred closed her eyes while she thought, so the idle movements of her eyes didn’t move the cursor around.  Engine, fuel, and hazardous cargo would be stored at the tail of the Wrest, where everything was thicker and reinforced, and there were more safety measures.  Systems were here.  If Kathe had deleted the feed, there were a few ways.  One was hacking the ship.  That could raise its own alarm bells, depending.

Another way was simpler.  If they cut off communications, and wanted to delete minor data storage…

Winnifred turned her head to the other side, opening her eyes.

One panel, much like the one she was just using.  There were essential systems behind it.

“G-panels, floor, give me ten percent normal gravity,” she said.

The floor lit up.

Still no alarm bells, no lockout.

She was able to use her head, smacking the mask at her lower face into the ground, until she was facing down.  She was aware wires and things were twisted, at the base of her.

That would hopefully straighten out while she moved.  With gravity this reduced, she was still pulled to the floor, but could prod the ground with her nose to half-drag, half-float over.

With no hands, and a mouth that didn’t even open, she didn’t have many options.

She pushed a piece of trim close to the underside of her face mask into the gap between panel and wall, then looked at the panel, activating it.  She accessed her systems, cosmetics.

There were little ways that any of these modded pieces could be adjusted.  Some even had a layer of nanotech to be able to change colors, but very few in the twenty-nine families bothered with that.  Some of that was to lock one piece to the next, for seamless fit, arm meeting shoulder meeting torso, in a way that looked natural.  Some was even more mundane.

The lines of a mod, visually, from decorative rims around edges to gaps between pieces.  A quarter-inch gap between panels making up her shoulder and a tenth of an inch gap in the panels of her arm wasn’t immediately noticeable as a discrepancy, but when a mod cost as much as it did, every detail counted.  That meant there were settings to adjust that.

She adjusted the trim of her face mask, separating one line into two.

Creating a gap she could fit another, bigger component into.  Similar effect, but it was harder to get a straight look at the panel and navigate the menus.

The panel came free of the wall.

Her suspicions were correct.

The communications setup had been cut using the welder, data storage raked with a beam, deleting archives, and the hand tool had been left behind the panel.

She used a similar setup with her mouth piece, flipping over to use the panel on the opposite wall, then flipping back to try to grab the tool.  It took two attempts.

A panel at the back of the gun-like device let her look into it to change settings.  She couldn’t operate the trigger directly, but she could access troubleshooting.

Solder mode.

Troubleshooting- test fire, in lieu of using the trigger.

And a careful, thin line, to restore one connection.

Communications were back up.  She nearly dropped the tool as her head jerked in her surprise at how fast it happened, chips lighting up on the board inside the ship’s wall.

That momentary surprise and joy was cut short by the fact communications were blocked, all throughout Sherman Station, while the riot was being suppressed.

Blocked, but sometimes when things were blocked, emergency calls could still go out.  That was risky, and scary, when the word ’emergency’ would sit so close to ‘lock it all down’ in the ship’s internal logic.

She had to figure out an angle to communicate with the people back home.  She trusted them, at least.

She was in the middle of navigating through menus when a sigil popped up.

Judiciary.

She wasn’t sure what that meant, but when she dismissed it, it didn’t close out and go away.  It tucked itself in the corner of the panel’s screen.

She was still working on a way to open an emergency channel to home when she heard a bang.  A door opening.

It didn’t take very long for the person who’d broken in to find her.

Winnifred lay there, face damp with sweat, hair in disarray, organs, for lack of a better word, spilled out on the floor.  Carlen Holder, the woman who had been watching her, was there, a silhouette in the doorway.

She had the lightest body armor on, worn beneath a coat with wide lapels and long  coat.  Her pants legs were narrow, and ended in the same style of white cuffs as the sleeves of the shirt she wore beneath her armor.  Black boots.  The armor, coat, and boots made her look more imposing, physically.  Her hair was black and tied back into a loose braid, with thumb-thick curls winding their way toward the braiding.  Square-ish jaw, superficial wrinkling probably left in by the onboard where it was pleasant and aesthetic, marking her as about forty, dark eyes, eyebrows like horizontal slashes, white skin with minimal makeup.

“Ship?  Standard gravity,” Carlen said.

Winnifred laid her head on the floor before the shift in gravity could make her head knock against it.

Once the gravity was normalized, Carlen walked down the hallway, hands in pockets.

“So this is where you were.  I arrived on the station not that long ago, I tried to track you down when all communications died.”

Winnifred breathed hard.

“Are you in any immediate danger?  I can ask my onboard if you need any repair, battery charge, water…”

“Toby.”

“We can figure out a body for you,” Carlen said, ignoring that.  “Was it the people you were with?  Or looters?”

Winnifred remained silent.

“I’m sorry this happened,” Carlen told her.

Winnifred wanted to cry and she did not want to cry in front of this woman.

“I’m contacting my team, they’ll bring you modded body parts to get you upright, as soon as they can.  Not good ones, but enough you can function.  It might be an hour.  Do let me know if you need anything.  Even a change in position.”

Winnifred remained silent.

“I’m very sorry that this is what your family has done to you.  That this is what they set you up for.”

“You did this more than they did,” Winnifred replied, struggling to keep her voice level.  It made her words feel hollowed out.  Less impactful than normal.

“Can we talk?  While you’re unplugged from it all?”

“Talking to authorities mostly helps those authorities, puts you at a disadvantage,” Winnifred replied.  She turned away.  “You can talk at me.  I’m a captive audience.”

“I’ll talk at you, then.”  Carlen took a moment, walking over, and then found a ledge to sit on.  “I know what I say to you here, tonight, probably won’t change your mind.  But I hope it will sit with you.”

Winnifred stared at the open wall.

“They aren’t healthy, you know?  There’s endemic abuse.  People don’t look or talk about it, but they know that at least ten of the twenty-nine families are… dangerous.  Toxic.  Predatory.  But they’re part of the wider setup.  So while you have groups like Howington Station, gilded, standing tall, noble, even… I think it’s tainted, poisoned even, by the fact they accept other stations among the families.  The Docks at Genoa?  Incest.”

“It’s safe.  Gene editing’s allowed for safety.”

“But the mindset.  The way it becomes tunnel-visioned.  Cultish.  When you’re raised among people, work with those people, sleep with those people, discouraged from the outside world.  We have a whole Belt to explore, and they make their whole world that dock, the ships that land there.  Twist language around, so only a few people on Genoa have the ability to speak to people who aren’t folk.”

Winnifred stared at the open panel.

“Everette Landing?”

“Small family.  Smaller than Griffey Docks, even.”

“But they make their mark.  I know you know what they do to family members who step out of line, or who don’t meet their standards.  They hurt people.  Their own people.  They plug them into systems designed to do nothing except-”

Winnifred was already shaking her head.

“You know this.  I’ve watched the conversations where you were told, years ago.  It’s why I chose them as the ones I brought up.”

Winnifred remained silent.

“Do you condone it?  Or you don’t, but you’re afraid of going against the wider families, to the point you won’t even say, in case it gets out?  There are other families with problems.  But, and this is my point, they get invited to the table.  They get counted as one of the twenty-nine.”

“You’re not my friend.  You’re not helping me.  You took Toby.”

“I do want to help.  Toby is being audited, you’ll get caught when that’s done.  I have zero doubt.”

“That tells me you’re biased, you’ll force it to be true even when it isn’t.”

“But there are options,” Investigator Carlen told Winnifred.  “We believe your colleague or ex-colleague Kathe has injured twenty-four people working for the judiciary, just tonight.  If it’s true, the pattern of activity maps to other sites and other events.  Places where she’s killed.  I had colleagues in my ear on the way over here, saying they think she’s a terrorist they’ve been watching out for, who bounces around on unmonitored ships, to locations with very little oversight.  Mining colonies, where she doesn’t mine, lives the high life while spending her money and finding sympathetic ears, she brings those people to friends, for training or further… let’s call it messaging.  Convincing.”

“No comment.”

“One of my big hopes with onboards becoming as widespread as they are is that she stops being able to hide.  Jhames Satterfield too, though he’s more of an enigma.  He changes his face, we think, and his name.  By the look of things, Jhames has a high propensity for being around protests where people end up dead.  The same way you have a high propensity for being in the proximity of ships and equipment that are provably attacked or sabotaged, Winnifred.”

“So were a lot of other people.  We live on the docks, around ships,” Winnifred replied.

“So you’ve said.  Let’s put that aside.  I and many of my colleagues feel we are so close to a special kind of peace, where over a hundred billion people occupy the Belt, fed, and housed, and healthy.  Where yes, murder will happen, because we’re human, but we can do away with murder from war, from conflict, from jealousy and rivalry.  It will only be crimes of passion and impulse and we can-”

Carlen clenched her fist, clicking her tongue slightly, while searching for how to say what she wanted to say.   “-we can educate, we can make sure people have the tools, to minimize that.  We can rehabilitate when it happens.  We can slay a third horseman of the apocalypse and consider slaying the fourth.”

“Is eliminating the twenty-nine families, ‘educating’ everyone, part of that?” Winnifred asked.

“The answer to that is complicated-”

Winnifred snorted.  The floor felt cold underneath her.  She wondered if they were doing something outside, as a riot measure, if room temperature was weird.

“-and you might get different answers from different people.  I really do think the answer is that no, we need different cultures, in the same way genetic diversity protects populations.  But I also think the twenty-nine families need to think very hard about whether they want Genoa, or Everette, or University coming to the meetings where every family sends their representatives.  Maybe the twenty-nine families should be eighteen families instead.”

“I think…” Winnifred searched for words.  “Weakening ourselves, reducing our numbers, it-”

“I know the arguments.  I’ve heard them, I’ve read them.”

“-it costs.  If we compromise, start attacking ourselves, almost halving our number, that attrition keeps going, we dissolve entirely.  Fixes have to happen slowly, while staying who we are.”

“And I think you’ve heard the arguments and read them too, and they’re something you’re echoing, in case this conversation makes its way back to the ears of people like your uncle Ellis, your father, or Michal,” Carlen told Winnifred, hands still in coat pockets.  She looked sympathetic.

Winnifred hated the sympathy more than anything.

“And I think it’s hypocritical to say what you’re saying, when the judiciary is what it is.”

“That’s a less common argument.  Good,” Carlen said.  She didn’t smile.  Winnifred was glad, because she might’ve snapped and said something stupid, in response to the smile.  Carlen went on, “Winnifred. I really do think you’re troubled and coming out of a bad circumstance.  The peace I talked about is what I really want.  Yesterday, I was willing to press hard, if the pressure and monitoring made you second guess whatever it is they have you doing and not do whatever it is they’re angling to do, putting you in the same room as a terrorist and riot agitator.  Seeing you here, on the floor, I’m reaching out, instead.”

“You know what I want.”

“We can get you a body-”

“Toby!” Winnifred raised her voice.  The emotion in her voice was compounded by the fact she couldn’t emote with her body, banging a wall or throwing something.  Not at Inspector Carlen, but still.  “Toby!  I want my friend back!  My backup!  The one person I can count on!  You crippled me on the night all of this happened and this happened!   I’d rather you take my body, destroy me like this for the rest of my life, and give him back, than the opposite!  This is your fault!”

“I don’t think that’s exactly true,” Carlen said.  “I think you can blame the people who did this, and say this was bad timing.”

“Fuck you!”

It sounded so paltry, coming from Winnifred, when she was this small, barely able to move.  Like a toddler who was small for her age having a tantrum.  Toby deserved better.

Carlen looked back over her shoulder, at the mouse wheel of the main hallway.  Hale’s sports arena.  “Seeing how resourceful you are, and how far you seem to have gotten in the state you’re in, I kind of get it.”

Winnifred wanted to swear at the woman again, but didn’t want to sound as lame as she did.

“You really are a fan of A, huh?  Dragging yourself this far in circumstances this bad?  Getting communication going again?  I bet she’d be impressed, if you managed to get her attention for a minute.”

“Fuck you,” Winnifred said, with less heat in her words.

“Putting that aside for a minute-”

“Why?  Why put it aside?  She deserves-”

“Let me-”

“better!  Toby-”

“Winnifred,” Carlen interjected, with more emphasis, and more volume.

Winnifred fell silent.  She was still heated.

“The Belt Judiciary would be a lot more interested in information on Kathe and Jhames than on what you’ve been up to.  If you shared information, we could expedite things, give you a slap on the wrist and some ongoing monitoring.  Stuff would happen in closed rooms, nobody from the families would know you said what you said, in this conversation, or the ones we’d have, as follow-ups.  We’d impose ongoing monitoring, maybe require you check in once a week, at a specific location, so they can’t send you to the next imminent warzone, for the next sabotage, the next escalation.  It would be annoying, but life for you would go back to normal.”

Winnifred remained where she was, breathing hard from the shouting.  Life going back to normal…

“The audit has to finish, but you’d get Toby back sooner.  If we caught Kathe and Jhames, you could sue them for the cost of the body, get a new one.  Maybe that’s a leg forward on getting to what you want.”

“I’m so tired of being used,” Winnifred said, more to herself.

She shouldn’t have said that.

Saying it provided information, suggested she was being used by Michal.  The families.

“Yeah,” Carlen said.  “I do think talking to me gets you more independence.”

And it cost her so much.  She’d already compromised so much, to make the deal with Michal, moving forward to getting a ship of her own…

Carlen didn’t elaborate, and Winnifred knew the tactic, letting silence sit, so Winnifred might feel the need to fill it.  So, stubbornly, Winnifred didn’t.

The investigator broke first.  “I think it’s an extension of the same thing I brought up before.  Do the twenty-nine families want Genoa, or University, or Everette, as part of things?”

“You don’t get to ask.  Part of the point of it all is you don’t get to ask, or pressure us, or make that change,” Winnifred answered.  “Because you’re the Belt, and we’re the- the little guy.”

“Maybe.  But okay, little guy,” Carlen said.  She shrugged.  “You ask, you decide.  Extension of the same question, entirely in your ballpark or… whatever this game is that Hale had you playing.  Do you, Winnifred, want the twenty-nine families to be a group that uses people like Kathe and Jhames Satterfield?”

Winnifred was silent, unsure if she needed to push the argument and say even that was pressure… or if she should answer, or if answering was-

“And what does it mean, please do think about this for a minute,” Carlen said, “if you can’t?  If you as an individual member of the family can’t push back and say no.  If you’re left like this because of them or people they worked with.”

Winnifred had said no already.  Did Carlen know that?

That this was the cost?  Being left like this?

Winnifred looked over at the panel.

“Tell us what they’re doing, get leniency,” Carlen said.  Distilling down her offer.

“As a symbolic gesture?  Even if I could or would, you- it feels so petty.”

“Symbolic?  I mean, maybe you shape the destiny of the families.  Discourage them from going down this road.  Of using people like Kathe and Jhames.  That’s a symbol.”

“I mean, You already know,” Winnifred replied.  “So I’d be-?”

She stopped.  Carlen looked confused.

“What?” Carlen asked.

Had they not gotten that far with the carbon fiber blankets?

That was-

The blankets blocked the signal to the Belt network.  They’d acquired a large number and were passing them out.  The idea, clearly, was to distribute them to people who could them wrap themselves up in cloaks or clothing of the stuff, as part of tonight’s protest, and then make moves while the local authorities were completely blind.  Something strategic, like confronting the owners of Sherman Station themselves, Winnifred figured.

But it had been a while, all considered.  It had not been overly fast, getting here, or getting access to the panel, re-establishing communication, or Carlen getting here.

Thirty minutes?  Forty?  She didn’t have Toby to tell her the time.  In a situation as fraught as this, where people were being bombarded?  A group of more militant modded folk hadn’t wrapped themselves up and made their play?  There hadn’t been any sightings of Kathe and Satterfield, with their cargo?

“By my head,” Winnifred said.

“Beg pardon?”

“By my head, there’s a welding tool.  Can you cut your way into the cockpit?”

“I could.  Is it sealed?”

“Welded.  Like that lockbox, and a few other things,” Winnifred said.

“As an anti-theft measure, or-?” Carlen asked, but she was doing as Winnifred had asked, and approached.

“No.  Tonight.  They did it tonight, I’m pretty sure.”

She bent down, looming over Winnifred.

Tool in hand, she walked over, examining it.  Winnifred was pretty sure Inspector Carlen Holder’s onboard was walking her through how to use it.

She stopped at the door.  “Is this a trap?”

“The door?  I don’t think so.”

The tool flared bright as it produced the short-range laser that could cut past the melted portion of the door.  It didn’t take very long.

The door opened.

Winnifred could barely see.  Carlen’s body blocked much of the doorway, and it was dark.  Darker than it should have been.

“What’s this?” Carlen asked.

Winnifred got a better view as the woman turned.  The windows of the cockpit, that should have had a view of the station, were all dark.  There were holes punctuating the dashboard.  A security measure meant to protect a pilot from bright flashes and explosions had been forcibly triggered with some strategic holes.

That was a layer beyond what Winnifred had thought all of this was.

The welded toolbox, the welded door?  Winnifred had chalked it up to all of this being premeditated, so she couldn’t escape and report what had happened too quickly.  That the story would be that she’d been robbed and mugged, and that would give her some plausible deniability.  Kathe and Satterfield would go and deliver blankets, empowering the protest, Michal would find another excuse to put Winnifred to work later, maybe after a serious talk about commitment, after she’d refused to help list weak points on the Armstrong and other ships.

Because all of this was training her to do something more.  One step in a longer process.

Was that wrong?

What if she assumed absolutely none of her assumptions were true?  What if she took all of the individual pieces of what had been happening, along with the new context of the cockpit being blacked out, and put it together into a new picture?  One where Hale’s ship was more than a place to keep the signal-blocking blankets and stow Winnifred for people to find later?

“Do you still have a connection to the Belt Network?” Winnifred asked.

“It’s intermittent.  Right now?  No.”

“Or the station?”

“I did, I don’t.  Again, intermittent.  Result of the protests, I’m sure.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re not-?”

“Sure,” Winnifred said, turning her head.  She looked at the panel.

No signal.

“Pick me up,” Winnifred said.  “Bring me into the cockpit.”

“What’s going on?”

“The entire ship is a closed container.  I think this might be a trap.  Meant for you,” Winnifred told Carlen.  “And I don’t want a death on my conscience.  So…”

Carlen stood a little straighter, realizing.

“So pick me up,” Winnifred said, with emphasis.  And the only reason she didn’t shout, was because she wasn’t sure they weren’t close enough to hear and react.

Carlen stepped over, and picked Winnifred up.

It felt uncomfortable, in the same way replaying the scenes in her memories, dating back to when she was just a baby, was uncomfortable.

Winnifred’s mind raced.  What were the options?  Repair, to get a signal out?  Wouldn’t work, if she was right.

What about breaking things more?

“Hold the welder to the side of my face.  Keep it steady.”

“Can I trust you?”

“You have to.”

Carlen didn’t.  She didn’t move the welder.  Didn’t move at all, as she took a second to think.

Took a moment to be terrified, maybe?  Was this a first time she’d been in real danger?

Something else?  A conversation with her onboard, where Winnifred couldn’t hope to hear or see the exchange?

“Don’t-” Winnifred started, hesitating as she wondered if she’d regret saying it.  Or if it would be used in a future case against her.  “-don’t give me reason to wonder if I should be trustworthy.”

Did that even make sense?

“Don’t hesitate while I’m on your side or I might reconsider that stance,” Winnifred added, trying to clarify.  “I’m that mad about Toby.”

Carlen held the welder to the side of Winnifred’s face mask.  Metal against metal, held there by a hand, it was steady, even if the angle for using the alternative trigger with eye movements was awkward.

“Can we cut our way out?” Carlen asked.

Winnifred scoffed.  “No.”

No, they had to do something else.  She cut a panel by the cockpit pilot’s dashboard open, and spotted the switchboard for manual override.

Leaving doors operational…

Leaving G-panels, for safety… just in case…

Everything else off.

That included lights.  Plunging the ship into darkness.
