Winnifred’s eyes had been burned out, but not every change was pure technology.  She’d had Toby living in her body since the day she was born.  Just like with her hair, some of the changes were built in.

It was maybe why her eyes hadn’t been completely burned out of her skull by the white flares.

And, here, it was why she had a range of vision that even most people with onboards didn’t.  There were a lot of the folk in the twenty-nine families moving to channels where they kept the onboards on frequences and channels that the average person couldn’t or wouldn’t access.  Whispers as a means of vocal communication was just one side of that.  Some of it was visual.

Winnifred could see traces of the world.  She just wished her vision wasn’t so blurry from everything earlier.

“What are you-?”

“Shhh.”

If she was wrong, she’d look like a fool.  But she didn’t feel wrong.

She was bait.  They knew the inspector was after her.

They could support the protests from a side angle.  If protests were regularly marked with the death of reasonably high profile people… inspectors, maybe the dock owners, it would change things.

Kathe had said Satterfield was good at the chess game.

That made a lot more sense in the context of maybe removing Inspector Carlen as a piece, instead of bringing blankets to the protestors.

“Boots off.  Don’t shuffle, but don’t stomp either.  We move quiet,” Winnifred murmured.

“You think they’re here?”

“I’d rather assume they are.”

Winnifred wished she could turn on the G-panels, to lift Carlen up.  Floating through the air was a hell of a lot quieter than moving across the floor.  But the panels lit up, and she’d rather keep the lights off and make it hard for Satterfield to get a good shot off.

Kathe… Winnifred wasn’t sure how much the lights would matter.

Once her boots were off, Carlen held Winnifred’s torso against her own, facing forward, vitals nested in her elbow, one hand free.

“I’m going to bump into things.  It’s pitch black.”

“Don’t.  Do you have a weapon?”

“I don’t believe in them.”

Great.

“Welder, then.”

“Yeah.”

They padded down the hall.  Carlen touched the wall at regular intervals.

The door was still open at the end of the hall.  They could see a bit of the mouse wheel.

“Pay close attention to the directions I look.  If I breathe slow, move slow,” Winnifred murmured.  “If I hold my breath, stop.”

Carlen nodded, cheek rubbing against the space above Winnifred’s ear.

Slow, then.

Down the hall to the door.  There was the little platform, then the mouse wheel.

Winnifred blinked hard, trying to focus her very tired eyes.

The drones weren’t actively flying, or pursuing.  Was that because the inspector could have detected them by other means, maybe?  Or a fear that they could be intercepted and hacked?

It was that spot-the-difference scenario from her lessons, again, except one image was brightly lit, and the other was dark.  She could see the mouse wheel, the trace mess from where her body was dismantled.  The clothes thrown aside.

Small canisters, at key locations.

Okay.

Okay, there was a very real chance those were bombs.  Insurance, that the drones could pick back up, later?

What else?  Was there a shadow here or there that could be Satterfield, lurking?

She held her breath as Carlen reached the end of the platform.  It’d be a step down.

So she nudged, head pressing against Carlen’s cheek, breathing very slowly.

Carlen seemed to remember well enough where they were, because she put her foot in the right place.

As she stepped onto the sloped floor, however, her stocking lacked traction on faintly sloped floor.  Her shin hit the side of the platform.

To her credit, she didn’t cry out in pain.  The shin-on-metal sound was not even that loud.

Throughout the mouse wheel, infrared lit up.  Drones, perched in alcoves and nooks, took flight, many of them with flashlight beams in frequencies the eye couldn’t see, strobing violently as they moved.

“Fsst!” Winnifred made a fast, harsh breathing sound, jerking her head.

Carlen touched Winnifred’s face, to figure out which direction Winnifred was looking and jerking her head.  Then she moved.  Sliding, more than anything, on the slope of the floor.

The drones moved like grasshoppers, flying in lazy arcs through the air, to land at the next place, where they could wriggle and hide themselves in the next alcove.  A half-dozen converged on their general location, infrared flashlight beams sweeping, wide.

Winnifred jerked her head again, hoping to keep them out of view of the beams.

But just as five flashlight beams could add up together to illuminate a room, the trace light from all of the drone’s beams came together, and they found Carlen and Winnifred.

At least she’d bought a second or two.

“G-panel, S-1, zero G!” Winnifred shouted.

The floor panel lit up.

Carlen audibly reacted to seeing the drones in the air.  Some had momentum that was still carrying them toward the platform.

“Hatch!  Up ladder!” Winnifred barked.

Up toward the core.  Carlen leaped, catching the ladder.  She took a second to haul the hatch open.

In that one second, one drone was in a position to get a shot off.  A shotgun spray of pellets.

Carlen kept going.

“Right hand turn!  All g-panels on!”  Winnifred barked.  “Fifty percent!”

“I can’t tell if you’re talking to me or-“

“Go!”

Into the core that the mouse wheel spun around.  Which had been modified, so it wasnt as open as Winnifred had been envisioning in the moment.  Right hand turn.

Out one of the many hatches around that core space.

She’d turned on all of the panels because turning one on was a giveaway.  But it would also have the effect of changing drone trajectory.

“Full gravity!” Winnifred shouted, as they emerged.

The drones weren’t dumb, though.  They were intelligence-supported.  Some of that meant they could hold their shots in the split second, instead of wasting them.

So when Carlen leaped down and hit the sloped floor, full gravity instead of maybe the fifty percent she’d been anticipating… that took time, and some drones were positioned to shoot.

Maybe, just maybe, they didn’t aim for Carlen’s head because Winnifred was right there, and made for a blurry picture.  Maybe they were going for the legs.  Because that would be enough.

“Open door to T-1!”

The door opened.  The platform extended at the foot of the door, but it barely mattered.  Carlen pulled herself through, almost dropping Winnifred.  One of the vital boxes dangled, banging against Carlen’s leg.

More canisters.

Yeah.

“Straight through!  Hard left into next door, close it, close it, close-“

The moment they were outside of easy range of the drones, charges throughout the ship were remotely triggered to go off.

➨

Explosions, at the very least, got attention.

They’d made it inside the storage area for hazardous and flammable goods.  It was close to the engine and fuel, which seemed paradoxical, or dangerous, but measures could be taken.  The way a ship buckled when something ignited?  That could be set up, so floor and walls crumpled in a way that absorbed the explosion.

They’d laid the bomb cartridges near fuel, because… of course you would?  It made sense.  To a layman.

But Winnifred wouldn’t have.  Even with the door not fully closed when things went off, the way that explosion rippled out, it pushed specially prepared door panels and wall panels out in a way that folded up against the door, covering the gap.

There was shock absorption and armoring and more, here.  Emergency sealant, of the same sort she’d spent three hundred hours of her life cleaning up.

She’d assumed they couldn’t get out the main door.  Satterfield might even have been waiting out there.  This, as strange as it was, had been the safest place to be.

So the bombs had gone off.  Carlen Holder had slumped against the wall, sitting on the floor, legs shredded but intact.

As she explained it, her onboard had prioritized protecting her from this sort of thing.  Armor beneath skin, to protect against small projectiles, darts, glass, and other minor damage.  She’d opted not to try to stop bullets, leaning on external armor, instead.

Still.  It had kept her running.

So they’d remained here, in the dark.  Winnifred had pointed Carlen to the first aid that was in virtually every room.  Then they’d waited.  Help came.  They were extracted, and when they were, Satterfield and Kathe were long gone.

“A part of me thought it’d be nice to rescue her,” Winnifred observed.

“Who?  Toby?”

Winnifred snorted softly through her mask.

“What?”

“Obviously it would be nice to rescue Toby,” Winnifred said.  “But I was talking about her.  The Wrest.  Turned into a sports arena, then blown up.  It’d have been nice to scrounge up the money-”

-or get the help from Michal-

“-and refurbish her, get her flying.  I like Wrests.”

“Yeah.  Well, I’m more fond of them than I was twelve hours ago,” Carlen said.  “Kept us alive.”

“Yes she did.”

As they were brought outside, she could see how blankets had been connected together.  Drones and some zero-g devices, like tiny panels, had been used to bring that cover over the ship.  That had been what had blocked the signal.  The plan all along.  Not all of the blankets.

It looked a lot like Winnifred had rushed a plan that had been in the works.  Maybe they’d planned to direct the inspector Winnifred’s way in a subtler way, later in the evening.  Potentially, timing could have been different, for outside authorities too.  This could’ve been a bloody distraction that led to the next thing or-

It didn’t matter.

Winnifred’s mind wanted to solve this as a problem, to make sense of it, and maybe through that, to know how much danger she was in.

She took stock, taking advantage of the fact the authorities were questioning her and reviewing released footage from Carlen Holder’s onboard before ‘letting her go’.  It meant Hale wasn’t in her face, asking questions, forcing her to make decisions about how much of the family she could trust.

Had Michal signed off on this?  Was Hale okay with it?  How well did Hale know Satterfield and Kathe?

And where did Winnifred draw the line?  What the hell was she supposed to do?

It was all so fucked.

What she did do was call her parents, and not manage to sob through the entire thing.  A simple update.  Then someone had a question for her, and she stepped away from the console.  Having no onboard communication meant she could walk away from the call and find a moment of quiet.

The next time she was near a console, she reached out to one of the lawyers that worked with the twenty-nine families.

The case was resolved in three minutes.  A long deliberation, probably requiring a double-check from someone somewhere up the chain.  She’d been left vulnerable by the removal of her onboard, which had led to the loss of her body.  Carlen had suggested that Kathe and Satterfield be held responsible and sued for it, if and when they were caught?  No.  Inspector Carlen Holder and the judiciary she worked for would be held too.

As it happened, when Carlen had arrived on Sherman Station, not long before Winnifred had lost her body, Carlen’s idea about locking away onboards for audits and checks had been picked up by intelligences as one more thing to add to the ‘chess and chaos’ pile.

So… there were four others who were suspected of crimes, involved in the protest, who’d had their onboards locked, who were also able to sue.  They hadn’t had the massive damages Winnifred had, though.

They supplied her a temporary body, in the meantime.  Basic modded parts.  No tail.

[Hello.]

And one of the same sort of stock onboards that people who hadn’t grown up with onboards got.  They came with personalities like ‘elegant’, ‘academic’, and ‘mission oriented’.

“Hello, temporary onboard,” Winnifred said.  “Set yourself up to compare notes with and assimilate into Toby later.  Don’t change his personality, override any of the architecture he set up, or change who he fundamentally is, okay?  Just… keep me functioning.”

[I can do that.]

She ran shitty low-fidelity fingers through her tangled hair.  She was a mess.

“I need a body, I can’t stand this one.  So we should go pick that up ASAP.”

The onboard supplied possible places.

“I’ll use some of the funds to charter a ship.  Simple quarters, a place I can wash up, look after my body.  Alone.”

While the onboard mapped out possible routes and plans for that, it was restoring function.  Eyes.  Communication.

There was a tide of messages coming from family.  Her parents, again.  Uncle Ellis.

Was this what A felt like?

“Archive all incoming messages?  If you need an excuse to block any hard-pushed messages, anything but top-level emergencies, lawyer stuff, appointments, make it a part of the legal issues and plans.”

[Easily done.  Sure.]

Her family’s attempts to communicate were shoved off into a corner, tucked away.

They could still watch through her eyes, again.

“I just need a bit of quiet,” Winnifred said, feeling very tired, and a bit… heartbroken?  It was a hard feeling to place.  “Um.  I’ll work.  Keep my skills sharp.  Somewhere out of the way.  Mining planet, maybe?”

[I’ll see what I can find.  Can I apply for work on your behalf?]

“That’s the idea.  I’m not picky.  Earn me enough to pay my way.”

It took longer than it had taken to resolve the case against the judiciary, but not that long overall.  Mining planets were always looking for work, and she had skills many of those workers didn’t.

“The audit will finish in a little while, then we’ll talk, there will probably be charges,” Carlen told her.  “Think about what I said?”

“Fuck you.”

“Yeah, okay.”

Winnifred caught the ship to get to a venue where she could buy a body– she didn’t want to do it on Sherman Station.  On the ship, she had a room that was barely long enough for her to lie down in, or stand up in.  Which was fine.

She used a shared washroom to wash up, then played A’s music while trying to sleep.

A had had a night too, apparently.  Members of her fanbase had broken into a venue.  It made Winnifred feel less alone.  Less scared.

She could even, she hoped, feel a bit proud that she’d made it through, even as she felt… very fucking complicated about every other aspect of it.

But A had performed.

Winnifred closed her eyes.

She woke up to find that A paying more attention to the U.N.I. group -the people who had modded more heavily for their deep space plans- and A’s general awareness and mood levels as she’d glanced over the news about the riots had had an impact.

She hadn’t looked at Sherman Station or Winnifred, exactly, but other protests had been timed for last night as well.

Public sentiment was shifting.  There was awareness.  Discourse.

With one glance from A, it seemed, there was a significant body of the public siding with the protests.  With the families.

As a result, the judiciary was backing down.  Dock owners were reported to be talking.

“Thank you,” Winnifred murmured.

[Can I help you?]

“No.  No you can’t.  Just…”

Winnifred floundered.

This was supposed to be a point she stopped, turned around, communicated with family.  She’d get an explanation, they’d say something… someone would tell her they hadn’t known Kathe and Satterfield would go as far as they did.

She didn’t.

“Let’s work,” she said.  “I took a contract, I’ll finish it.”

[Okay.  Let me know how I can help.]

Then… she had bad feelings about what followed.

She turned up the music.

2.7.O – SEND

Orion

Some people had tried to hew out an existence here, and not all that long ago.  It meant progress was slow, because they were checking every nook, corner, vent, and side alley.

It was almost annoying that they were turning up useful things at the rate they were.  Tools, here and there, a knife that Orion kept, and some fuel.

Their latest stop had found a series of containers, cleaned and sealed, which had clear fluid within.  Six of the ten containers were breached, and the green moss had crept into it, tainting the contents and fusing it to the surrounding area.  The tenth container was on its way.  Orion sniffed it, then winced.  Alcohol.

Blackbox hung back, watching for trouble.  He’d been affected by the mechanical centipede, and on seeing any food or drink, he compulsively ate, fighting anyone between himself and the food.  They didn’t want to risk that he’d try drinking this.  Moss mingled with ethanol and probably ten kinds of mold, if mold grew here.

“Is it a phobia?” Sever was asking Spur.  Orion had missed whatever had been said to start that particular conversation.

Spur shrugged a bit, as much to get the strap for her drone carrying case into the right position as to respond.  She was petite, with brown skin, brown hair, dark freckles, her features almost lost in the dim, or overlooked with her bright coveralls and metallic bronze tattoos where she’d pushed up her sleeves.  “I don’t know.  But there was that spot where someone had clearly taken a shit.”

“Ah, yeah.”

“And the moss grew over it?”

“Saw that too,” Orion commented.

“And ever since, it feels filthy?  It’s everywhere, it feels claustrophobic, almost?  That’s the wrong word.”

“I hate it too,” Blackbox said.  He’d relaxed some in the last bit.  Obviously, being affected by the centipede bothered him, but having a group seemed to help him ease up.  Maybe it was less stress, knowing there were more eyes to watch their backs and watch out for trouble, and he didn’t need to be on point every second time they moved into a new area.  There were six of them, and if they rotated, it was one in six times, now.

Orion appreciated that part of it, too.  It made it easier to stay sharp and focused when it was his turn.

Spur looked up, which made Orion do the same.  There was no ceiling in easy view.  Walls stretched up into darkness, high enough overhead that there was visible atmosphere- moisture or mist that leaked out of vents.  There were gaps between the ground they were walking on and the walls, that were getting more and more frequent as they moved in this direction.  At the bottommost point of the six to ten meter slide down the sloped wall, there was idle machinery.  Not many wires or cables.  Just boxes with some vague industrial use.

Would it be an electrocution hazard, even without wires?  Or would they fall and find every surface around them was too slippery and steeply sloped to get up?  With help, getting back up seemed doable, but for someone alone?  To fall and land in what was essentially a ditch filled with machinery?  That would be it.

That bothered Orion more than a lot of things.  To be frantically and uselessly trying to climb up, falling back down, slowly getting weaker?  To be utterly forgotten and overlooked.

Spur went on, “I keep imagining a panel high up there popping off, and the green shit coming down on top of us.  What if it’s all just… shit and rot, and enough of us have come here, eaten, shit in corners, and died, got converted into that green stuff, and that’s happened enough there’s quintillions of gallons of that, packed in between panels and the rest of the walls?”

“I’m so glad we found this lot,” Blackbox commented, to Orion.

“I don’t mind theorizing and asking questions,” Orion said.

“Hmph,” Blackbox snorted.  He stepped away from the makeshift, moss-compromised distillery, and checked the rest of the nook.

“I don’t think quintillions have died here,” Sever said, taking his turn to inspect the distillery, hands in pockets, bending over at the waist, squinting through his longer hair.  He straightened smoothly, without losing his balance, and looked up at the nearest open panel where the green-black moss was visible.  “There are patches the robots haven’t gotten to.”

“Maybe because their programming is in a rut and they’ve been at this a long, long time?  If they haven’t gotten to a patch in a thousand, or ten thousand years…?”

“More would have faded if it had been that long,” Sever said.

For someone who hated the idea that the moss could be signs that humans had been liquefied for a ridiculously long time and packed away, Spur seemed frustrated at Sever’s interjections, as if she seemed to want to hold onto this idea she hated.

“This is what we’re looking for, though,” Blackbox said.  “Patches.  Ground the machines don’t cover.  Then… we establish a footing, we move very carefully, going outside, find others.  Hopefully, some of us have what we need to cobble together an answer.”

“And weak points,” Orion said.

Any point of infrastructure, something vital to the machines that ran this place.  They’d found one possible one, supplying power, if they judged by the wires that ran through the internals of this place, but it had been too firmly seated and protected.  Buried behind a few dozen meters of metal wall in every direction, no vents or anything that seemed to lead to it.

Maybe there were others, partially in construction, that they could find, or other places they could crack, that would give insights that would help them find more, and so on.

Just… had to keep at it.

“Let’s keep looking, at least,” Marte said.

It was, at the very least, pretty easy to find the nooks and crannies.  The further they went, the more small footpaths branched off, extending into spaces inset into the walls.  Everywhere else, there was a ten meter ditch or waterless moat at the foot of the walls.

“Watch out,” Spur told them, reaching out to grab Court and Sever’s arms.

One of the large cleaning robots slid down the wall, using the inset nook as a rail to stay steady on the way down.

It arrived with a crash, suspension in the machine’s legs catching it, disengaged the rail, and then started marching down the path.

It wasn’t alone.  The second came only a moment later.  Then a third.

“We could march between them,” Blackbox said.

“Could go bad.  Imagine there’s no side path to duck into or road to turn off, and we need a break,” Orion said.  He’d had similar thoughts about the cleaning robots closer to where he’d found Blackbox.  “We’d be stuck either dodging an endless tide of legs, or marching at the pace they set until our legs give out.”

“Yeah,” Blackbox said, by way of agreement.  Orion suspected that if he hadn’t said anything, and everyone had liked the idea, Blackbox would’ve have given a similar warning.

Which meant finding another way around.  It was a shame, because this way had been reasonably open and accessible.  New ways meant new threats.

Marte took point this time.  He was first, and followed Blackbox’s instructions on checking for trouble without risking looking at a glyph.  With things they’d scavenged, they had a few layers of the stuff.

They found another nook, and it looked like a blanket had been sewn together from multiple coveralls.  It had sat there long enough to accumulate a layer of dust and metal shavings over it.

They folded it and took it.

Ten minutes later, navigating from space to space, they found a room.  It wasn’t so different from the room Blackbox had been staying in, with the corpses.  Secluded, hard for machines to access, converted into a home base.  There were two more blankets, suggesting the other had been brought to where someone was acting as lookout or something, and it looked like a lot of things scavenged from elsewhere were gathered here.  Modest strips of metal had been scraped against collected grates and then rough surfaces to sharpen their edges, turning them into shivs.  Lots of containers had been brought too, many of them clearly being cases for other machines.  A water filtration system using stones, pebbles, soil, meshes, and cloth had collected a bathtub-sized amount of water, which unfortunately had a layer of other debris on it.  Ambient dust and air pollution, it seemed like.

Some odds and ends had been collected and gathered on the top surface of a large box, the size of a vehicle, that was too high to reach, so some other things had been brought over, acting like a set of stairs, with the top stair being something people could stand on, using the top of the large box as a wide, long desk.  The things were preserved pieces of paper and artwork.  Traces of history, like what Blackbox had shown Orion.  The blonde woman, the music, the pieces of vehicles.

On one of the more convenient table-like surfaces, and on containers that had been placed adjacent to it, were collected bits of tech.  Just by the fact it was more conveniently located, at a natural height, it seemed like this was more of a focus, and the historical stuff was a side project.

“I’ll look for food and put it away if I see it,” Orion volunteered.

“Yeah,” Blackbox replied.  He stood in the corridor that led to the room, his back to them.

“I can use some of this,” Sever said, as he assessed the table of components.

“Should we set up shop here?” Spur asked.

“We don’t know what happened to the last group that was here, but I doubt it was good,” Blackbox said.  “We can rest, but let’s plan to move, and keep a lookout.”

Orion did a circuit around the room.  One of the blankets had been used as a bedroll, and was situated by a part of the wall where the coating on the metal had been scratched until it was shiny, then rubbed with something dark, staining it.  The image etched on the wall in that manner was of a window with a single curtain, a flower in a vase or jar, and grass apparently indoors.  Past the window was space.  Black, with thumbprint-sized smudges forming stars.

“Orion?” Sever had found a box -an overturned casing for a small machine or component on the wall- that was filled with long, narrow black chips.  Each had prongs on the one end, and claw-like extensions hooking around either side of those prongs, to lock the chip into position after it was plugged in.  He held a chip up as he asked, “You asked if Spur and I remembered each other?”

“Yeah,” Orion replied.  “I think I knew Pine.”

“Do you get flashes?  Do you think if you slept well, or ate well, and had a good day where you could think back, you could get more?”

Orion considered shook his head a little.

“I think pushing it doesn’t usually work,” Court interjected.  The skinny guy with the short-shorn blond hair hadn’t talked much, which was ironic, considering his specialty was communications.

“Amnesia doesn’t usually happen, either,” Sever said.  “Not like…”

He paused, then turned to the group, one bronze-tattooed arm extended, a wry look on his face, eyes sad.

“Not like in pieces of media you can’t remember,” Spur said.  She bumped Sever with her shoulder as she squeezed past him, jostling him out of the exaggerated pose.

“Losing your entire past, yourself, doesn’t tend to happen.  Which got me thinking.  I’m loaded with memories of machine parts and prosthetics.  Patching people up…”

“Yeah,” Orion said.

“And I know enough about that to know there’s more stuff I don’t know.  There are people who are the opposite of him.”  Sever indicated Blackbox.  “He’s a machine body with a brain stuck inside.”

Blackbox turned around at that.  Orion watched carefully, seeing how Blackbox’s eyes and expression changed by the smallest amounts.  It wasn’t a thing Blackbox was proud of.

“The opposite of that, there are people who are all meat, but inside their heads, it’s chips.  And I don’t know the details or engineering of how that works, they didn’t give me that knowledge, but it sits side by side with what I do know.”

“There’s a cliff, to what I know about welding, metal, cutting, forging…” Orion said.  “Suddenly it stops.”

“The stopping point for this stuff is… a little past what I’m telling you.  And it doesn’t feel like a cliff.”

“Is that a clue?” Spur asked Sever.  “Maybe it’s knowledge you had, it was close enough, so they left it in?”

Sever rubbed his chin.

The man liked the flourishes and dramatic movements.  Almost as if he posed, every time he did something.  He did it more when it was his turn to be on point.  When he was most scared.

“Well, that’s something to think about.  What I do know about that whole process is that the person has to be prepped.  Pre-surgery, lots of rest, preparation of the mind.  Then surgery, excising parts of the brain, inserting tech.  Multiple stages- I don’t know specifics.  More rest, preparation, rehabilitation.  Then after that… slide a chip in, the person knows whatever the chip contains.  There are core chips, the entirety of the personality.  Intelligence-emulated, but so close to the original person you couldn’t tell the difference before and after.  And chips with learned skills and encyclopedia-esque knowledge.  In which cases, I think, what you’d get wouldn’t be so different from how we are.  Knowledge that drops off a cliff.”

“You think they took out pieces of our brains and put in chips?” Marte asked, with alarm.

Sever shrugged.  Exaggerated, again.  “What strikes me is Court’s haircut.”

All eyes went to Court.  He brought a hand to his head, which was a slightly uneven cut, hair blond enough and just long enough it stood out as a thin, lighter layer on his head.

“What?” Court asked, bewildered.

“Marte-”

Sever pointed.

Marte had hair that was three or four centimeters long.

“Then I look at Spur…”

Sever reached over and pinched a lock of Spur’s hair.  Finger-length.

Spur didn’t react or slap his hand away, but did give him a pointed, surly glare.

“Then I suppose Orion.”

Orion brushed his hand through his hair, trying to gauge.

“Then me.  There’s a few gaps at this point.  Was Pine’s hair long?”

“Yeah.  It was long,” Orion replied.

“You think they performed surgery?  Did each of us, one at a time?” Spur asked, with alarm in her voice.  “Shaved our heads?  Cut out chunks of our brain?”

“Or augmented, stuck more in there.  Who knows?” Sever asked.

“Ships are coming down fast,” Blackbox said.  “Forty or fifty a day.  But this damn place is so big, and so many of us die, we don’t see a lot of other groups.”

“One of the corpses we saw had silvery tattoos,” Sever noted, long finger sweeping back and forth, indicating Court, himself, Marte, and Spur, as the ‘we’.

“Different for different groups,” Orion said.

“Different, maybe, for different deployments?  I’m imagining a setup, they’re all there, with an arrangement of prisons, or facilities, or one room with an operating theater and a procession of people.  If it’s anything like the chip process…”

He ran his finger through the box of chips.

“…long phases of people in the middle stages, maybe drugged, maybe halfway through a mind wipe.  So maybe Spur and I were in a cell together, or close enough to see each other.  Then we got wiped the rest of the way.  Maybe that’s why we feel vaguely familiar?”

He turned to Spur as he suggested that.

“Maybe,” Spur said.

Orion frowned.  He wasn’t sure he liked that explanation.  Or anything about the subjects raised on the way to that explanation.

“Question,” Marte said.

“I wish to reiterate,” Sever said.  “This isn’t my specialty.  It’s an idea I have ideas about.  I probably don’t have answers.”

“Why the hell wouldn’t they load a single person up with… everything?  Why not give us all all of the information?” Marte asked.

“Couldn’t tell you,” Sever answered.

Orion wanted to put a theory together, but he wasn’t entirely sure he had one, yet.  He held onto it, and chose a different question.  “Do you know what those chips are?  What knowledge goes to what chip?  If that’s-?”

“Not my specialty, no idea.  And no idea.”

“Were they taken from bodies?” Orion asked.

“No idea.  Not my specialty.”

Orion frowned.

The ‘no idea’ came so fast that it felt like Sever hadn’t even tried.  Did that mean Sever was lying?

The man sat on the makeshift chair, leaning over the desk of components, box of chips in front of him, and held a chip up to the a bit of light that was shed from a notification light in the wall, to see it better.

“So you’re telling us we’re chipped?” Spur asked.

“It’s one possibility.  Maybe?” Sever suggested, shrugging one shoulder.  “Maybe it’s a bad idea, because it makes people vulnerable to those machines.  Maybe onboard computers build something more elegant throughout the brain before switching off any outside connection the machines could use against us.”

Orion found the food, a shallow tray of wizened, brown bits of plant sitting in dirt.  He put it away, just in case, then called out, “Blackbox.  I think we’re clear.”

“No corpses,” Blackbox said.

“Good for our noses,” Orion replied.

“Not outside either.”

“Maybe they got turned into that green moss shit,” Spur said.  She was folding blankets.  She tossed some stray clothes into a pile toward the center of the room.  White shirts, stained with sweat over multiple wears, until they were a yellow-gray.  The coverall jumpsuits.  One toolbelt without tools or anything attached to it.  It looked like the clasp didn’t hold well.

“It’s worth keeping in mind.  Cleaning robots might’ve got ’em.  Or whatever killed them also cleaned up the mess,” Blackbox said.

Blackbox worked with Sever to find some parts to repair his machine body.  Spur watched with idle interest and some light input.  She knew how to repair her drones.

Orion glanced over the gathered history, trying to make sense of it, in the way the person who had worked here had.  Was it meant to be chronological?  Was there a common element to papers in one pile?

One piece of paper was torn along one edge, and scribbled with a crude note, in thick black letters.  The same thing rubbed on the wall?  Charcoal?

SNUB HAS IT.

There was an arrow drawn on the paper, and a number.

Orion kept the paper where it was, and glanced over, following the arrow.

Walking over, he found a ‘bunk’, so to speak. A blanket was wedged into a narrow slot in the wall, one end of it caught on a rivet, so it formed a bit of a curtain.  With blanket, a flat surface to lie down on, and some privacy, it served as a private space for the owner.  ‘Snub’.  Orion searched the bunk, and found clippers and a metal tube.

“Parts for homemade bullets,” Blackbox said, when he saw.  “Passing the time.”

Orion bent down, looking up, and found the picture fixed to the surface just above where a sleeping Snub’s head would have been.  He pried it loose, tearing it only slightly, then carried it over to the table.  It fit directly over the piece of paper that served as a placeholder.

The number was a serial number, in the bottom corner of the image, barely visible.  Mixed letters and numbers.

Focusing purely on those serial numbers, he tried to look to that to define the pattern.  The serial numbers incorporated date and location, and going from left to right, there was a timeline.  Inconsistent, imperfect, but… a loose timeline.  Top to bottom, location.

Not every image had one, but by collecting them and mapping them out, it painted a picture of where she’d been and when.

Why was that important? He looked again at the image.  The blonde woman, around his own age, sitting in a circular window, back braced against one side, foot braced against the opposite, to keep her in position, hair drifting around her as if she were underwater.  She wore a dress so light and fine he imagined he could see it settle into individual pores, even though it wasn’t transparent.  A carefully placed arm and the billowing of the lower part of the dress in zero-G kept her modesty.

Definitely the image Orion would have picked to be alone with in his bunk, out of all of them, though.  A random thought reminded him that he’d awoken in the casket with memories of women.  But it didn’t answer the real question.  It seemed like more records had survived of this one person, than of everyone else put together.

He looked at the locations.  Closer to top, almost out of reach, it was planet-bound locations.  Close to top left, ‘science center’.  Horizontally level with that, places like a classroom, a place with gilded walls and crowds in evening clothing, a stage, photographs taken at some monument.

Closest to Orion, bottom of the surface, space.

There was a swathe, diagonally cut across the right hand side of the ‘table’, with just paper notes, or blank surface.  No evidence A existed at all.  Then A returned, appearing on the rightmost side of the table, some scattered images that were less promotional than before.

In lieu of something to write with and a piece of paper, he got out his welding tool.

With settings changed and post-cooling on maximum, he burned out letters into the metal of the surface, in the empty space.

Was this when they asked ‘where are you?’

He had his onboard pull up an image, then copied that over, burning it in.

The mural, of ‘A’.

Then a map.  It was crude, almost abstract, the path a dotted line, landmarks on either side as solid objects.  He noted locations by loose description.  Pillars.  The hangar.  The bridges.

He finished with what he decided was his signature.  An ‘O’ overlapping an N, with a small vertical line through the cross-bar of the N, and a dot over that.

“Does it matter?” Blackbox asked.

Orion turned.  “One of the common elements to spaces where the machines haven’t overwritten stuff?  Her.”

“Could be coincidence,” Blackbox said.

“Could be.”

“What, you think the machines are treating images of her with reverence?  Avoiding scrubbing up a place with-?”

Orion was already shaking his head.

“Okay.”

“But someone thought it was important.  We might never know their thought process, or the logic behind how this is laid out, or why,” Orion said.  “They thought it was important to do.  I like the idea of keeping that effort going a bit longer.  Helping it carry forward.”

“Leaving them a legacy?”

Orion shrugged.

Blackbox clapped a hand on Orion’s shoulder.  He addressed the room.  “I’d like to take a moment.  Remember them.  If you all don’t mind?”

Sever nodded, but kept glancing through chips, holding them up to the nearest light.  Spur slowed, but was midway through folding a blanket that was not a square, and thus, not easy to fold tidily.

“A moment?” Blackbox said, with some emphasis.

Everyone went still.  Spur dropped the blanket.

“People lived here, they were sent here to die, by people who wanted to stay blind and stupid about it all.  Throw enough bodies at a problem, maybe eventually you solve it.  It was stupid and didn’t do any good-”

“Yet,” Court threw in.

“-didn’t do any good,” Blackbox said, anger in his words.  Court avoided eye contact, looking off to the side, toward the corridor.  “Didn’t do any good.  It was awful, stupid, but that doesn’t mean what they did was awful or stupid. They managed a brief, brutal, difficult life here.  Let’s give them a moment.  Give these people and those we saw along the way a moment.  Maybe they were one and the same.  They were trying to do something, they were trying to make sense of it all, they were fighting like hell.  We take what we take from them with respect.”

They took a moment.  Distantly, the machines that were sliding down the wall could be heard, crashing to the floor at a rate of about one a minute, suspension keeping those hard landings from doing any damage.  Between those crashes, there was the faint noise of a thousand systems doing their work within the walls, and the march of machine feet.

Orion thought of Pine.

What Sever had said.

A whole group of them, imprisoned in the same area.  Mixed, Orion imagined.  Some with different crimes, but where people had been arrested together, they’d been held near each other.  Had talked or shouted messages across to each other.  A staggered process, each following behind the others, being stripped gradually of memory, if it had been gradual at all.  Rehabilitation.  Implantation with new capability.

A process that might’ve seen Pine go first, her hair shorn.  Then weeks or months passing, as they gradually got to someone else in turn.  If Orion imagined himself there, someone who knew her, who was in a position to see her be wiped mostly clean… it would have been agony, assuming he’d had any fondness for her at all.

Leading directly into them being sent off in their pods, placed in the same location.  Leading directly into that terror.

Again, he thought of waking up in the casket, his first thoughts and sentiments being about women.  Was Pine a woman he’d loved?

There was nothing except a faint sense of recognition, as he groped for the memories that weren’t overshadowed by what she’d looked like, dying in that casket, bleeding out, terrified.  Whatever had driven him toward a moment of tenderness.  But if he tried placing her in a sequence… one that started with lovemaking, put that sense of familiarity somewhere in the middle, followed by the horror of seeing her striped clean, finalized with her bloody, pointless death?

He felt anger stir.

Anger.  He felt a bit like he was in a room with Pine, aware she was moving somewhere behind him, where he didn’t see her, but knew her well enough to know more or less what she’d be doing.  Pacing.  Except she wasn’t actually behind him in the scene.  That was just a shorthand, a way of describing how the details were entirely out of reach.

It was domestic, but the opposite of calm, despite the fact he was… lounging, her agitated, pacing, in front of him.  They were- not arguing.

But something close to it.  Arguing together, against something faceless.

A back-and-forth, where they amped each other up, reinforced each other.  Building up mutual courage.  Playing off each other.

Until one of them thought it was getting to be too much.  Maybe it was him, pulling her down onto the couch or into a chair with him.  Maybe it was her, going to him.

Something that had played out in variations, many, many times.  Amping each other up, then spending that heat on fierce lovemaking.  Maybe without much ‘love’.  Hate?  It wasn’t hatefucking each other any more than they’d been arguing with each other.  More… angry fucking?  An anger at the world they shared, so an amped-up anger segued straight into physicality between them?  As a vent?

They’d hated someone or something.  Or they’d been angry.  They’d validated that anger in how they touched and fucked each other.  Until, he suspected, one day they’d amped each other up, and instead of spending that energy on each other, they’d done what they’d been amping each other up to.

And the throughline-

He thought of the table.  The continuity.  What the person was trying to map out, with this ‘A’.

Touch.  The angry fucking, them angry at the world but turning that aggression on each other, then, later, the transgression, being separated.  Then separated further as they lost themselves.  Then, in final moments, a reunion.  That moment where he’d rested his forehead against her.

He wished -and he felt like it was a wish that extended back to a point beyond that moment- that he’d been more tender, overall.  That there had been more love.

A melancholy settled over Orion.

The edges around the ideas were blurry.  There were no scenes.  No faces.  No clothes, no moments.  Just… a chronology that felt right enough that things that felt vaguely familiar, sentiments, and instincts all felt like they were in the right place.

“Okay,” Blackbox said.  “Thank you for that.”

“No,” Orion said.  “It was good.”

There were some nods from the others.  Court looked troubled.

It was fucked.  What the hell was happening?  That the people up there had put in the work to prepare them, then send their group and so many others like this, so haphazardly that a lot of people didn’t even survive the arrival?

“Do we need to rest?” Blackbox asked.  “I’ve got a bad feeling.”

“Let’s go.”

“I need to take a dump,” Spur said.  “I don’t want to do it here, right after a nice little moment of silence, but I don’t want to do it on green moss shit either.  I feel like it’d crawl up my shit and into my ass, while I’m squatting.  Then eat me from the inside out or some shit.”

“Thank you for that mental image,” Sever said.  “I think you have a phobia.  These worries aren’t rational.”

“We can disagree on that.”

“Hold it in until we pack up?” Sever asked.

“Sure.  Yeah.”

While others got sorted, figuring out how to carry what they needed to carry, Orion got a piece of metal that was about the size of his hand, and used the laser etcher, etching the image that was on the picture that had been in Snub’s bunk.

While it cooled, he made sure to lean over the table, focusing on each serial number, so his onboard could record it all.  For images and photos without serial numbers, that seemed to be placed with guesses as to where they best fit, he looked at them on their own.

He slid the bit of metal into an outside pocket of his coveralls.  A keepsake.  Then, partially as a homage to the people who had dedicated some time to figuring things out, he left a note.

Orion/Pitch, Blackbox, Sever, Spur, Court, Marte were here
Welder, cyborg soldier, prosthetics, drone controller, sword
The group who lived here were gone, no bodies
They collected tech and studied ‘A’
We took what we needed, held a moment of silence.
We travel clockwise, within a day’s travel of the surface
Sometimes we can see the sun.





Spur tapped the last line, a quizzical look on her face.

“It’s not wrong?” Orion said, unsure.  “Wasn’t sure how to indicate where we were close to the surface.”

“Hmm.”

He etched a similar map to the one he’d done on the surface. with all the papers and images.  Dotted line, landmarks, some script.

It didn’t take long, as he could have his onboard communicate what he wanted the device in his hand to etch.

“I’m ‘sword’?” Marte asked.

“I can’t exactly erase what I wrote.  What should I call you?”

“I don’t even fucking know.  I hate that I’m ‘sword’.

“If I make more notes along the way, I’ll adjust, so come up with something better.”

There was a faint testiness that came with the latent stress.  Spur’s responses, now Marte.

Maybe Orion had been heading that direction, but thinking about Pine and seeing things put together had helped.

They marched, with a brief pit stop on the way, to relieve themselves, and to eat and drink in private, away from Blackbox.

Supplies were dwindling.

Not fast.  It was tightly packed and went a long way, but they were dwindling.  To really survive, they’d need to set up a garden or something, like the group in the nook here had tried to do.

They returned to pathways where there were more of those moat-like gaps between the floor and the wall.  Ditches, if a ditch could be ten meters deep.  When the ditches were interrupted, it was usually a sign that there was a nook, cranny, or some other space that machines needed easier access to.  When it was one that the machines didn’t occupy very often, it was repurposed by those who had come before, to stow things, or with evidence someone had been there.  Sometimes that meant it was an outhouse, now with green moss on the floor.

Other times, minor supplies.

It felt like a lot of people had been in this wider area.  Maybe that meant a nook.

The ditches got deeper, and wider.  It wasn’t long before it seemed like they were on a bridge, or a series of bridges, that criss-crossed in a long, flat grid, each bridge four point nine meters across.  Skyscraper or pillar-like structures stabbed upward in the gaps between bridges, with sloping sides, thin at the top and wide at the bottom.

All dark.  The lights were ambient, dotting the structures that regularly punctured the landscape, or were along the edges of the bridges, just barely illuminating the surroundings.

“Court, you’re on point next.  Then Orion,” Blackbox said.

“How am I supposed to be on point in a place like this?” Court asked.

Fair question.  The area was very open.  There wasn’t a lot to scout.

“Next time we need someone on point, then.”

Court’s expression was strange.

Orion wanted to ask what that was about.  Was he hiding something?  Or was a thought unfinished?  Orion could sympathize with that- he had a lot of those.

He was trying to find the words to ask when Marte screamed.

All eyes went to the man.  Marte looked to be artificially scaled up in body and muscle mass, and he was doubled over, holding his stomach.

“What did you eat?” Spur asked, one hand near her mouth.

“Eyes down!”

“Fuck!” Blackbox swore.  “Machine!?”

Marte managed a nod.  He had one hand at his stomach, other at his sword, but he was in too much pain to draw it.

The hand that gripped the sword moved, thumb extended, jerking up.

Not a ‘thumbs up’ positive.  A direction.

Eyes down, he’d said.

The threat was above them.  Airborne, or clinging to the pillars of structure that were stabbing up from the gaps in the interlocking webwork of bridges.

“Move!” Orion hollered the word.

They were vulnerable here.

“Can you move, Marte!?” Spur shouted.

Marte, having been doubled over, convulsed, going from pushing shoulders toward knees to the opposite, back arching, stomach thrust forward, as he lay on his side.  Spittle and a light volume of throw-up shot out of his mouth at the force of the motion.

Like he was trying to snap his own back.  The backwards arching kept going, his expression a grimace.

A shadow over the bridge.  It was hard to tell, because the lights on the bridge’s edge were brighter than the lights from elsewhere, but it was a shadow.

“Make it-” Marte started, voice strained.

The shadow’s passing came with a trail of cables.  They hit the edge of the bridge, or caught on things, then pulled free, whipping around with surprising force.  None came too close, but they were doing obvious, visible damage to the surroundings.  A chunk was knocked out of the edge of the bridge that probably weighed as much as Orion did, just from wild cables.

It was something that flew, or glided, and its tail was a dozen long metal cables.

Wherever there was damage, all lighting switched to a red emergency mode, and there was a lot of incidental damage being done.

“-stop!” Marte finished, the cry barely understandable as a word.

“You saw a glyph, that’s it,” Blackbox said.  “That’s it.”

Marte’s convulsion reversed.  He, despite being big around the chest and belly, managed to knee himself in the face, flinging head forward and knees up.  Probably doing some internal damage.

Blackbox took hold of Marte’s sword handle, drawing the blade.

One of Marte’s bloodshot eyes looked around.  His lip was streaming blood.

Blackbox used the blade to kill him.  He stabbed Marte in the neck, then, levering the blade, severed spine.  Or the rest of the spine.  The blade cut through flesh like it was easy.

It was a mercy.  Marte would have kept twisting and arching backward and forward until he’d broken his spine and torn himself to pieces.

And they were free to run.

“Go!” Blackbox said.  He took a moment to relieve Marte of some crucial bags and things, cutting straps instead of working out how to get them free.  “I can catch up!”

The blood was still flowing, the now-headless body emptying of its contents.  It pooled on the platform.

“Eyes down!” Spur reiterated.

More shadows passed.

Cables dragged and whipped, in their wake.

“Mmf!” Blackbox grunted.  His mouth was full, teeth clamped onto the straps of the bags, probably bearing nearly a hundred pounds of supplies and things.  He didn’t have a place to put the sword, and he had only one hand, so he handed it to Sever.  He drew his gun.

The welder wouldn’t work at these ranges.

“Multiple!” Sever called out.  Maybe that was what Blackbox had wanted to communicate.

“Do we try down?” Orion asked.

Off the bridge.  Onto one of the pillar-like towers of technology on top of technology, that was between the bridges.  Down.  It would be rough.  Too easy to lose their grip.  To slip or fall.

“No,” Sever said.

Orion didn’t argue.  It was a one word response, barely considered, but… he agreed.

Orion had a sinking feeling in his gut.

From the size of this space, and how this webwork of bridges extended, it seemed like they’d need to run at least a kilometer to get to a place that wasn’t this open to attacks from the air.

He’d put the idea of going down forward because the idea of going across seemed so dire.

That sinking feeling spread to fingertips and toes.

A shadow passed directly overhead.  Close.

“Careful!”

Vision tinted, pulling tablet out, he chanced a look backward through the distorted reflection, knowing that looking anywhere but down posed a chance he’d end up like Marte.

He saw what they were facing.  It looked like a moth, with a fifteen meter wingspan.  The back and underside of each wing had the glyphs.  Because the wings were horizontal, the images of the glyphs themselves were flat.  He couldn’t read the glyphs any more than he could read what was on a piece of paper by looking at it from the side, staring at the near two-dimensional edge.  They glided more than they flapped their wings.

And, more importantly, he saw the cables.  The moth flew low enough that the cables fell to either side of the bridge, running along the edges, rather than along the bridge’s surface.  But one was more slack than the rest, and the dangling loop swept toward them.

He reached forward, grabbing Court, and pulled the man to the right side of the bridge, before he could get bludgeoned or caught by the passing cable.

There was a rapid fire series of bangs, with one very loud crash in the middle of it.  Metal screeched and strained.

“About face!” Blackbox hollered.  “Don’t fucking look!  Eyes on the ground!  Can’t go this way!”

“You know what these are?” Spur asked.

“No!  But I know enough!”

As the area around them illuminated, the white contrasting the red that was now being shed in so many places, Orion realized it was too much, and what the moth was doing.

Cables extended out from the edges of the wings to surrounding structures, and the bridge itself.

Studding those cables were glyph projectors, it seemed.

Like a moth that spun its own spiderweb to get caught in.  Suspending itself in the air, surrounded by the cables that anchored it there.  Then wings lit up, then the glyphs all up and down the cables.

A wall of flickering white symbols.

They backtracked, turned onto another bridge, and another Moth was already setting up there.

Not just glyph projectors.  Or maybe no glyph projectors at all.  Cables had sub-cables, that formed loops, circles, and supporting structures all throughout the ‘web’.

Orion looked away before any of it could switch on.

They were being boxed in.

He didn’t want to ask about going down again, because it was stupid.  The drop was too much.  At best they’d survive the landing with shattered legs, and then, as far as he could see, there was nowhere to go.

“Eyes closed, be careful!  It’s flying beneath!” Blackbox shouted.

A third moth.  From what he’d seen before, they were seemingly scrap technology folded together into delicate, multi-layered wings, cable antennae and multiple cables for the tail.

The moth flew beneath the bridge, in what might have been an S-shape, from the sound of it.  Weaving around the posts that held the bridge up.

When it was beneath them, it used its other weapon.  If it was even a weapon.

The moths used antigravity to fly.  Orion had something antigravity in his equipment, to let tools float at a convenient level.

Here, they used it in a weaponized fashion.  A burst of reversed gravity, with a flip-flop of the stomach to go with it.

Orion’s feet lifted off the bridge.

Others faced something similar.  Floating up.

As the moth continued forward, gravity found them again.

For Orion, it was a three meter drop, where he had to be conscious of the fact the bridge had no railing.  He managed to avoid landing in a way that would see him fall from the bridge.

For the others, it was similar.

Except Sever, who was far enough ahead -originally behind, before they’d reversed course- that he was in just the wrong position, as the moth had banked into the ‘s’, weaving through the supporting posts.  It meant that where others had been sent up by the reversed gravity, Sever had been sent to the side.

He was sent off the bridge at an angle.  He hit the pillar that was off to one side with one shoulder, than haphazardly stabbed at the metal with the sword.

Whatever the sword was made of, it penetrated metal like it was nothing.  The tall prosthetics doctor with the exaggerated movements tried to grab the handle of the sword with both hands, stabbing the vertical surface that was within blade’s reach.

Hoping to impale it, and let drag slow the fall.

The sword was sharp enough -or had some other property that let it cut through panels, metal, and everything else without the slightest hesitation- that there was zero drag.

Sever’s foot caught on a jutting edge, and he flipped.  He banged into the pillar, which was wider at the base than it was tall, and in the third flip head over heels, he cut halfway through his own pelvis, coming in from one side, ending at a point between groin and belly button, before the sword pulled free and came away.  He’d let go in the shock.

Spur screamed, with an intensity that apparently surprised even her.

The sword might as well have cut Orion’s brain, for how distinct the gory image and the sound of Spur’s scream were, as he tried to find his feet, barely trusting gravity or footing.  The only reason it wasn’t worse was the predominance of the red emergency lights, and how they made the blood hard to see.

No.  This wasn’t sustainable.  That one kilometer distance wasn’t even a kilometer anymore.  If it ever had been.  It could have been more.  Wherever they got to could have been insufficient to let them get away, even if they got that far.

“Fox,” Spur said, one word, short.

They’d warned the other group about it.

But here?  This far away?

Blackbox aimed and, firing at least partially blind, shot at one of the moths.

The gunshots drowned out all other sounds.  The red lights and the view of the bridge drowned out most other visuals.

What were they meant to do?

Couldn’t go over, couldn’t go up.  Couldn’t go down.

There were no visible hatches to go inside the bridge.  Nothing visible in the pillar-like structures, even if they could manage the herculean leaps.

Grabbing onto a passing cable seemed like a fast way to die.

Metal screamed.  Pillars creaked.

One of the Moths was flying again.  The one that was keeping them from going the direction they’d been going was still there.  The second moved more dynamically, to block.  The third- he’d lost track of.

He wasn’t sure if Blackbox, Court, or Spur heard him.

No, the third was there, flying high.  It caught at parts of one pillar with the cabling.  There was a sound of something breaking.  Orion’s instinct was that it had caught accidentally on something.

It hadn’t, because the moth used the antigravity again, having positioned itself where falling debris would fall past it.  Now that same debris arced through the air.

A metal box two meters by two meters across hit the bridge well ahead of Orion and the rest of the group.  Something inside it had been managing power, and still seemed to hold a charge, because it sparked.  It produced a fountain of sparks.  It could have been a small rocket, trying to leave orbit.

The light of it was blinding, but it also illuminated the wider area.

No escape routes were shown with that illumination.  A whole convoy of the large repair boxes were on their way, in the distance.

Other pieces of metal, ranging from a long strip of some lightweight metal a few centimeters wide, maybe half a kilometer long, to a hail of fist sized nuggets of something heavier, all rained down.

There was no cover.  Except-

“Around a corner, try to get out of their view!” Orion shouted.  The skyscraper-like pillars in the gaps between bridges could block the view and give them a moment to hide.  Hopefully.

He reached for his belt.

“Fuck, fuck!” Spur swore.  “Fuck this!”

Around a corner, out of view, hopefully.  He had a sense one moth was setting up a block further ahead, the first moth was still blocking their main intended route, and the third was circling around for another strafing attack.

And the fox was apparently out there.

Watching from a distance?

He dared a glance at the tablet, eyes tinted, tablet screen warped.

No telltale glow from the fox’s glyph projection.  It would’ve appeared amid the sea of reflected red lights as a blob of white.

If we get past this, if we keep doing this, I’ll eventually try that, and it won’t be blurry enough.  I’ll make something out, and I’ll go the way Marte did.

Something moved in the image.

His first thought was drone.  Something deployed from one of the moths, that came directly for him.

It wasn’t a drone, but it was close.

Spur had drawn a shiv, and tried to stab Orion in the lower back.  Him turning had meant she lightly slashed him across the back, instead of getting it anywhere vital.

He tried to hit her, swinging his arm as he finished turning on her, but she knew how to move in a scrap.

“Fuck you!  Fuck!” she swore.

“What the hell are you doing!?” Orion bellowed.

“What’s happening?” Court asked.

Court was being too careful to avoid seeing the Moths, and didn’t even know what was happening with Orion and Spur.  Probably sensible, except it left him vulnerable.

“Spur’s attacking-”

Spur screamed, a sound very similar to how she’d reacted with Sever’s death.  It drowned out anything more Orion might have said.

She was small, but strong.  Fit for her frame.  Orion was larger, less small.

She barely seemed to care about the shadow of a moth passing over them, as she kept at him.

“Give me your supplies!  I’m done!”

“You want to split up!”

“I want you-”

She stabbed, he let his arm get cut to have a shot at grabbing at her wrist, and held her.

She pushed him toward the bridge’s edge

The passing moth dragged cable behind it, and did light damage to the bridge.  It startled Spur, who hadn’t been watching her back.

Orion kicked her, hard enough to create some separation between them, then turned, running.

Blackbox and Court were a little further ahead.

“This way!” Orion called out.

He wanted to check his rear, make sure he wasn’t being seen or spotted, but he could hear the dragging cables.  He had to infer.

“Spur lost it!” Orion called out.  “Don’t let her follow!”

“What the fuck, Spur!?” Blackbox hollered.  “Now!?”

Metal tore as a moth flew past a nearby bridge.  Circling around.

Blackbox drew his gun, then opened fire.

Spur’s shriek could be heard.

“Did you hit her?”

“Who the fuck knows?  I can’t look.”

But Blackbox shot again.

Orion ran straight to the bridge’s edge, dropped to belly, and then gripped the edge.  “Pull me up if-”

If there was nothing?

He didn’t have the words, panic gripped him, and taking five or ten or twenty seconds to explain could get them killed.

He lowered himself, hanging from fingertips.

There was a ledge to grip.  It wasn’t wide enough to lay a full finger across without bumping into the platform machines drove on, but he could lower himself further.

“Go,” Blackbox said.

“But-” Court replied.

Blackbox fired.  Not at Court, but it seemed to shortcut them past any argument or debate.

Court began to climb down too.

“I only have one hand,” Blackbox said.

“I know,” Orion said.  “But I can’t think of another direction to go.  Try to follow?”

Blackbox emptied his gun.

Then he followed.  One arm, two feet, a mechanical body.  He stabbed fingertips at surfaces and may have actually forced a bit more purchase by bending metal.

Orion, meanwhile, lowered himself far enough he couldn’t hope to catch a toe on a foothold.

Dangling by arms alone, he could see the underside of the bridge.

He swung, then tried and failed to get a grip on a metal pole that reinforced the bottom of the bridge.  His hand was slick with blood from fending off the shiv.  He wiped it on his pants.

Another Moth approached.

Did they know where Orion and his group were?

It sounded like it might have started off targeting Spur.  She shouted, but if there were words in the shout, Orion couldn’t tell.

The moth swept past them, and Orion felt that gravity alteration that was helping the moth glide so smoothly, seemingly without effort.

Felt the rattle, as cables dragged along the top of the bridge, and, naturally following there and staying there as they dragged, along either side of the bridge.

Orion swung his legs, grabbed the pole with less blood on his hand, and got a grip.  Getting out of the way.

Blackbox hadn’t descended far enough.  The cable hit him.  Maybe four centimeters across, and long, it had a weight to it.  Like being hit by a medium sized vehicle.

Blackbox, however, was made of stern stuff.  A metal body, meant for combat.

He barely seemed hurt as he climbed down further.

Orion did his best to crawl into the underbelly of the bridge, wedging himself where he might hope to be out of sight.  Once anchored all along one side of his body, one hand gripping a bar for extra leverage, he gave Court a hand, gripping the back of Court’s coveralls to lift up, so the process of swinging over wasn’t as hard.

A minute later, wishing he could catch his breath first, a job that was ten times harder even with Court’s help.  Getting Blackbox.  It was a trial, where Orion ended up sticking a leg out, wedging foot between pipe and the surface above them, so Blackbox could stick a leg out and use that as a point of leverage.

Slowly, with just the one arm, but an indefatigable strength, Blackbox found a niche in the underside of the bridge.

Spur, hopefully held at bay by gunfire, then more focused on avoiding the fox and moths than on chasing, didn’t chase, or deploy her hawk drone.

Fox, hopefully, too far behind.

The moths were a danger, but they’d gone too far ahead, most planning to bar the way, one doing strafing runs with wide turns at each end, going very high as much as it went low.

It made another pass, level with the bridge, body turned, and projected gravity.

They’d found spots too anchored in to be dislodged.

By the sound of shifting metal and the strain in the bridge’s infrastructure, Orion could tell that it was doing strafing runs of all the different bridges.

Unless it’s a head game.

If it was a head game, there was nothing they could do.

The position was too awkward and perilous to sleep, but Orion did something similar, trying to rest, breathing slower.

He awkwardly navigated an arm around, to dislodge a container, and got out the storage container he’d clipped to his belt, full of medical supplies.

To staunch the open bleeding, from fist fighting and wrestling Spur while she had a shiv.

The moths moved on.  Presumably, so did the fox.  Spur would have had to.

They remained where they were until the repairs started.  The big box machines came to fix the damage the moths had done.

They extricated themselves, moving slowly, and Blackbox checked the way was clear before they tried climbing over the edge.

Spur had lost it.  Marte had been mercy killed after seeing a glyph and trying to snap his own back.  Sever had disemboweled himself after being flung off the bridge.

Leaving Court, Blackbox, and Orion.

They took a moment where one of the big box machines was standing still, focusing a grinding tool on the torn metal, to duck between its legs.

There wasn’t much conversation.  Blackbox’s mood had darkened, and Court was the least talkative of the group they’d found.  Supplies they’d liberated were gone now.  Some with the people who had died. Others, like the bags Blackbox had been carrying, until he needed all limbs and mouth free to climb beneath the bridge, abandoned and apparently taken by Spur, or cleaned up by a passing machine.

Mostly, they saved their breath for moving quickly along the bridges.  To get out and away from open space.

“Where are we going?” Blackbox asked.  “We were looking for supplies, other encampments, and keeping an eye out for anything that might be infrastructure, keeping this entire damn place running… but any preferences?  No open areas.”

“No preference,” Orion said, even though he sort of had one.  It would have sounded stupid to say aloud.  Space.  ‘A’ had that one image of her floating in space, hair and dress floating around her.  All the images as they’d been arranged, there had been a whole gap in the timeline, before a reapparance.  But then at the tail end, she’d spent a lot of time in space.  “Maybe we stay close to the surface.  Others like us would probably stay closer.  And if they- or we can find any possible ways off this damn place…”

Leaving the other reasons out.  It would have sounded crazy, to say he wanted to chase ghosts.  ‘A’ being one.  Pine was the other, with no particular relevance to surface or depth, left or right.  But she was still a ghost Orion wanted to chase down and understand.

“The surface sounds good,” Court said.

Orion thought about all of Court’s sidelong glances, his reluctance to speak, the shifts in mood after heavy subjects.

Court was keeping a secret of his own.

“Good.  Then we have a direction,” Blackbox said.

3.1.B – MUTE

“People watching over my shoulder are joking half my bodyweight is hair,” A said.  She’d turned on the lights after her morning shower and getting dressed, and faced a wall of displays, which became a mirror as she glanced at it, moved her eyes in one direction, and blinked.  She swept an arm through her hair.

[I’ve had to strengthen your neck to avoid minor damage.]

Basil interacted with the displays, bringing up an arrangement of portraits of A, each with different hairstyles.  Some braided, some loose, some swept to one side, some pushed back.  She turned her body, then her head, to varying angles, and portraits moved to match.

While she decided, Basil did other work.  She’d perspired last night, at the event, when things had looked scary.  She didn’t need to perspire, but people who didn’t could seem uncanny.  Combined with old pollutants from an old building, some blemishes had started forming.  A bit of redness, allergic, and the very beginnings of a pimple.

He sorted that out.

A’s gaze moved between two pictures.  Basil moved them to either side of her actual reflection, then spun out an array of derivative options and combinations of the two.

She didn’t like the combinations, going by the subtle shifts in vasoconstriction, muscle tension, and the hormones produced by the brain, but it was a subtle dislike.

He kept the best and spun out more options, distinct.  One braided, one more messy.

A favored the messy one.  Hair swept to one side.  A bit wind-blown.  Basil adjusted hair follicles and sent nanomachines running down lengths of hair to help ‘comb’ it.  When she moved her arm and hand through her hair, it fell in the right directions.

Further nano-combing helped that along.

“When you suggest something, Basilisk, it makes me want to do it less.”

[I was only providing a list of options.  I had no strong opinion for any of the options.]

“It feels manipulative, whatever you do.”

[I’m sorry that’s the case.  I’m not trying to manipulate you here.]

“So you admit you’re manipulating me in other places?”

[I’m sure every onboard does to some degree.  Every person.  I’m sure you manipulate me.]

A started to change, and Basil turned off the lights.  She nodded slightly, going with that.

Giving the outward appearance that they were in sync.

Basil ruminated on the future.  Would this be the rest of his existence?  He was tethered to A.  Was this a phase?  Would a more adult A look back and realize Basil had been making the least bad of bad decisions?  Would she forgive?  Or would her naturally stubborn nature and the fact everything about this was contained to the backchannel, without release, without outside input, keep her locked on this path, getting worse and worse over time?

Would he, as far as any onboard had a greater sense of purpose, legacy, and dreams, look back and view the work he’d done as a success?  Basil existed to serve, he existed to guide, to provide information, to support.  He believed he was doing that, and that if he were audited at the end of a long lifetime, he could explain it all.

He highlighted clothes in the dark for A to better sort through.

On another level, this was his existence.  He was hated by his host.  There was seemingly no way to make things better.  There was only the illusion, projected to the rest of the world.

On that note, he provided some false images to throw off anyone trying to paint a picture of her undressed body.

“Do you have a plan yet?  If Robert Simes isn’t dealt with, you’ll be caught, my reputation will be ruined.”

[I’ll look for opportunities.  Part of our issue is that we don’t know how he knows what he knows.]

A was dressed.  Her top attached to the upper arms, with criss-crossing straps of material stretched between them.  The design was intelligence generated so the straps would always pull in a way that protected her modesty, without there needing to be a draping mass of cloth in front, even if she raised her hands over her head.  Her dress was similar, made of handspan-wide straps that overlapped, but there was less risk there.

[Chances are slim that you’ll practice dancing later today, but in case there are stunts or other acrobatic activities, that might not be the best choice.  I believe the intelligence tests for usual ranges of motion, but you’ve been known to push those limits.]

“I’ll pack another top, as a just-in-case.”

[Perhaps pants as well?  We’re going offworld.]

“I trust you to control my movements and protect me, Bas.”

Knowing how things were trending, Basil wasn’t sure Elabre Systems wouldn’t just change the schedule today, to spare her the hassle.  She was that much of an asset.

He worried about what that meant in the long term.

“If you can’t find a good way to deal with Robert Simes, they’ll realize everything you did, I’ll be exposed.”

[Give me time.]

And, Basil hoped, maybe A could cool down with that time.  Or new information would come to light.

[Mechard wants to talk.]

“He can message me, I don’t mind.”

Basil could look through Mechard’s onboard -dog- and see that Mechard had noticed, and was working up the courage.

[I advise being gentle.  Your followers were upset with him, it escalated to threats.]

“Good, maybe?”

[Maybe there’s justice in it, after he lost track of you and focused on promoting himself, but if you want to have any friends five years from now, people need to not be afraid that any mistake made with or around you could destroy them.]

[gret] dog sent.

[Hello dog.]

[gret excite.  Mescha grets A?  ok ok?]

dog couldn’t even pronounce or spell Mechard’s name right?

[That’s-]

[okok?]

[-fine.]

“You don’t have to send your onboard to ask permission to message me,” A said.  She checked her appearance, then grabbed a bag and went to the door.  “You’re a friend.  Lots of people message me, already more than I could read in a thousand lifetimes, it’s sad, but I have to have Basil sort and summarize them.  You don’t get sorted, though.”

“Good to know.  I’m sorry,” Mechard sent.

“It’s fine.”

“Not about messaging, or asking about messaging.  I’m sorry I left you alone last night.”

“Yeah,” A said.  She stepped outside.  They were still at the sequestered space for Elabre Systems employees and the generations of tailor-made celebrities.  It was spacious, in a way, and relatively unoccupied.  Basil drew a line across the footpath, in A’s vision, to indicate the route to take.  “Like I said, it’s fine.”

“Okay.  I was worried it wasn’t.  A lot of people seemed to think I screwed up.”

“I hope people don’t get too overzealous with that stuff.  No, I knew you’d self promote, I know you.  I was just glad to have a friendly face from the past to turn to.  If things hadn’t derailed like they had, I’d have looped back around to find you and catch up.”

“Good, good,” Mechard replied.  “That’s a relief.”

“Catch up soon?”

A waited a moment while an elevator that intersected the main footpath passed.

“Yeah,” Mechard replied.

That faint delay.  A lack of full confidence in the statement.

“Yeah.  I want to hear how you’re doing.”

“You want to hang out, spend the day together?” Mechard asked.

Even if Mechard hadn’t been keeping an eye on A’s activities all morning, he had to know she’d be busy.

“Can’t.  Obligations.”

“Right.  Weird mindset.  Obligations.  Normally you don’t have that sort of thing unless you’re running a planet, and even then, you can tell people what you want your schedule to be, right?”

“Sometimes.  Sometimes.”

“I’ll save the update on how things are going with me until we meet face to face.  You do the same?  I’ve got a project I wanted to start this morning.  Design work with someone I met last night.  I’ll have to focus on that.”

“Yeah.  Good luck with that.”

[bbye]

[Bye, dog.]

That effectively ended the exchange.

[It would be good to reach out later.  Close the gap.]

“Basilisk?”

[Yes?]

“Focus on the Robert Simes issue.”

Basil felt less and less sure about what he was supposed to do.

“Or don’t.  Maybe we let it all collapse, everyone finds out what you’ve done, and I blame you.  I’ll say you forced me.”

[If it comes to that, please do that.  It’ll give you the best outcome, and I’ll be doomed anyway.]

A frowned a little, taking in a partial breath before sighing it out.

Basil had called for a ship to pick her up, and she was able to walk out onto a bridge and step onto the waiting vehicle, a personal ship, with thick, armored walls, roof, and undercarriage, each in a swooping style.  The inside was a black velvet, trimmed with wood, the thinnest bands of silver around the wood for accents.

It suggested class, and majesty, and it was a little intimidating.  The sort of thing Robert Simes might have wanted to arrive at a meeting with, if he was facing down a rival.  Or maybe it was a regular ride for someone who wanted a more dangerous image.

It made for a contrast with A.  Basil could look through the car’s internal cameras at her, as she sat a bit sideways in the street, elbow on the ledge of the window, fist set against cheek, as she looked out the window.  The bag with the spare clothes sat by her feet. She wasn’t armored, dark, or dangerous.  Not to the outside observer.

It would be a bit of a trip. The rest of Generation Colors had split up, and the only member of the group who’d come back to Elabre Systems headquarters was Red, and Red had gone out, before the crack of dawn.  A was somewhat unique, alone, in that she had invited her parents, yes, but she hadn’t made plans to stay with them, attend any follow-up events, or stay on Earth for a bit, to see a sight or two.

If A had, it might have been a problem.  There was still that residual problem of the crowd.  They might have tried to crash any follow-up parties or meetings.

So she’d ride out to where some of the others were.  Then they’d convene at a larger ship, which they would ride to Earth to pick those up.  Then they’d go out to a special site, details protected by Elabre Systems NDAs.

Travel around the same superstructure?  There was enough built in the way of moving walkways and elevators that it was fast enough.  Wide superstructures sometimes had small vehicles to help things along.  Movement between superstructures used small ships.  Movement between planets used large ships.  Changing or playing a shell game with vehicles had the side benefit of shaking off some people who might follow.  That crowd, again.

Either way, Basil had time to work.

Robert Simes.  The man who had divined the existence of the back channel.

Basil would need to figure out how to tackle this problem.  This required a wholesale shift of focus.
