He put A second in his focus, and turned his focus to the Belt Network, his own place in it, and Robert Simes.  A man that Basil couldn’t look at too intently without tipping off the man that Basil was paying attention.  That tip-off could, in the scenario that Basil did have to take some extreme or quasi-legal action, get them caught, further down the line.

His own movements had to be covert.  To his advantage, he had the back channel setup, situated in A’s spine, where nanotech was unlikely to go.  He’d swept carefully for any lingering traces of nanotech after Robert had made physical contact, and he was as sure as he could be that A was safe in that regard.

There were multiple routes he could use to study Robert without alerting the man.  The first was records.  This was the flip side of the coin, where it was hard to study Robert directly without alerting the man.  By studying A, Robert had left a trail.  That trail was recorded in A’s bones, and in data stores throughout her body.  Some of it would be moved to an off-body archive later, hosted by Elabre Systems, clearing space for new records, but for now, everything from the last four years or so was recorded in high resolution.

Basil could operate on two levels.  On the first level, he was A’s onboard.  But by acting through the backchannel, he could operate on a subtler level.

He’d treat each piece of free nanotechnology in the body, serving that first, conventional onboard setup like marching soldiers.  Set the patrol routes, the pacing of it, use processing at certain checkpoints to measure and track.

The other side of him sent it’s agents through the gaps in that patrol schedule.  They left no trace, set up their own fixtures in the records that ran amid bone like veins of gold in rock, and collected the data to bring back to the back channel, where more robust processing was in place.

Undetected even by his own self.

In places, he and A had already glanced back to see what Robert had studied and when he’d watched, but neither of them was so stupid that they’d glance back directly at the key moments and biggest clues.  That would have tipped off an audience of billions.  No, they’d just verified that Robert had done any sort of analysis at all.

Now Basil studied Robert.

Yes, Robert had glanced through A’s youth.  It didn’t feel like enough.  Was the man meant to be a genius?  There were developments into better brains, but many had run aground, and the ones Basil knew of were not the sorts that would do well with conjecture on this level.

No, things like chipped brains or genetically optimized brains were snarly from a legal standpoint and illegal nearly everywhere, respectively.  Basil had the impression that either, or any of the various supplemental systems or tools one would use would be more obsessive.  Genetically optimized brains tended to start thinking in a same-y way, and the places that used them also tended to favor rote learning and systems, which also played into that same-y logic.  Chipped brains, powerhouse intelligence systems, and other brain augment tools would have focused on gathering a lot more information.

Was it possible for someone to make that kind of conjecture, seeing isolated scenes?  Yes.  Basil had to admit it was, and it was the sort of thing Basil would be bad at predicting and avoiding.

Was it likely that someone would make that kind of conjecture, and act with the confidence Robert had, to the point he made contact with A and Basil via. the back channel?  No.

Was it likely that the person in question would just so happen to be Robert Simes?  No.  Not very likely.  Great minds were purported to exist -A was thought to be one- and it was possible one such mind could end up in charge of Earth.  To also have the capacity to discover A and Basil’s secret?  Not likely, still.

Which left the ugly lingering possibility that Elabre Systems had completed the full audit of A, discovered the back channel, and decided to keep it a secret.  Robert Simes could have requisitioned the audit, somehow.  Was it possible he had?  Either out of the blue, because A was a person of interest, or because he’d found that first glimmer of suspicion, then got the audit report to answer those suspicions?

Not… likely.

The answer came slow and stilted.  Basil tried to parse why.  He could run a check of facial expressions, body language, assess the framing of the situation, and conclude that no, it didn’t make sense that Robert Simes would see something that got his interest, reach out to Elabre Systems, using his position to get the very private audit report, and then approach A like he had, with the expressions and tone of voice he’d had.

Basil was careful to try excluding the body of records and information he’d been pre-loaded with.  He hadn’t done all of his assessment of human behavior and expressions on his own, he’d drawn on a body of work provided by Elabre Systems, that millions of intelligences had contributed to over the years, in the form of gathering data or analyzing it.  He had to keep in mind that Robert Simes might have his own expensive research done, on how to subtly act in a way that specifically contradicted and evaded that point of analysis.

Basil’s cold, subjective take was that Robert Simes was a bit like a big child, not thinking through what he was doing.  He certainly wasn’t keeping to a NDA.  He’d even provoked the audience to look.  Elabre Systems wasn’t reacting like someone had forced their hand or struck a jaunty, careless match next to their very flammable asset.

[I am coming to a conclusion that Robert Simes is a more dangerous man than I initially thought,] Basil communicated, by back channel.

“You think?  You need to trust me more, Basilisk.  I do have my own instincts about my own life and the people in it.”

[I’m sorry.]

While Basil was dredging up all of the archival data on Robert Simes in the painstaking, patrol-evading, agents sent to the bones to make their circuit around back to the spine manner, A had arrived at the main ship.  It was an Elabre Systems custom, styled after a flagship from one of their media series, and it was very stately, with an old fashioned style inside.  Dark blue carpets with gold trim ran over the gravity panel floors in hallways, while the rooms off to either side of the hall had carpet extending wall to wall, covering up similar, with the trim forming elaborate, interlinked patterns.  Most walls were covered in dark nanofiber curtain, so heavy that A’s hand, reaching out to brush them, barely moved them.

There were staff, maintaining and running the ship, walking crisply back and forth.  Some gave A a nod or slowed slightly as they saw her, as if to give her a chance to ask for something.  At the center of it all, in the chamber where all hallways and major rooms radiated out from, was a lobby area.  Elabre Systems’ logo was set into the wall by the stairs that led to the upper levels and lower belly of the ship, and groupings of statues, often multiple figures carved from a single block, drew the eye.  Past, important generations of Elabre Systems’ Generation series of celebrities.

Planter boxes framed things, with blue thistles making a marked contrast against the white marble of the statues, or white, spiky plants making their own contrast against the dark blue of the walls, as a primary component, though other plants featured.  It evoked an image, like deific figures or living, filled-in constellations against a night sky, where the pods and heads of the plants were meant to evoke stars.

“Miss A?” a staff member asked.  “Would you like a room?  There are some spaces set aside, if you want to catch a bit more sleep.”

“I’ll stay here.  Thank you.”

“Message me by onboard if you need anything at all.  We’re waiting for a few people and then we’ll be off.”

“Thank you.”

Basil kept looking.  The records, looking back at where Robert was and what his responses were as he glanced over A’s history, were only giving Basil a sense of who the man was, and how certain things didn’t line up.For the next approach, he had to be more careful.

Every onboard and most Intelligences across the Belt Network had some demand for information, and pulled in huge sets of data contextual to whatever they were working on, to better predict behavior, draw conclusions, and double check facts.  Basil began doing that for wide portions of the audience, overtly and discreetly, using last night as a reference point.

For anyone looking in, studying Basil, specifically, it would look like he was doing a census on A’s audience, related to the event last night.

Specifically, though, as he took in data, he did his best to draw connections.  Studying Robert Simes too intently ran the risk of raising red flags and drawing attention to Basil, but Basil could study the people around the man, and the people who worked under him.  Many of those people had been there last night, or somehow involved.

Those people had their own patterns.

Just as Elabre Systems had a place where its employees and celebrities could work without the public crowding them, Robert Simes had a place he worked- a small superstructure, surrounded by supporting structures that limited access.  A tower, in essence, stretching from Earth’s surface to the outer atmosphere, surrounded by guards, in the form of other superstructures, and fleets of ships.

Basil, working purely in the back channel, could identify a person, marking that three dimensional image of Simes’ superstructure with a dot, every time that person stayed somewhere for more than three hours.  Each person then became a short series of dots, marking where they slept, socialized, and worked.

He could map the movements and associations of Robert Simes.  Each social interaction became a pulsating star, marked on that three dimensional map.

The question lingered: was the man associating with anyone dangerous, or anyone in Elabre Systems, who might have leaked data?

Was Robert Simes going anywhere, off the grid, with periods of time he was impossible to track?  Yes, he was, but that seemed tied to general privacy, the sorts of deals and discussions that were protected from the public eye until everything was ready to be revealed. All indoors, within his part of his own superstructure, on a planet he effectively controlled.

No indication he had anything deeper than that, in the way of conspiracies.

It was slow going, because Basil had to consolidate the data into a format that he could bring discreetly to the backchannel.

The ship stopped to pick up Bruin.  A background member of Generation Colors.  He was a trim, tall guy who wore a too-large jacket that he’d been given by a member of Generation Wild.

“Don’t hide,” A called out, using both voice and having Basil send it as a message, as Bruin immediately went from the front door to a side room where he could nap.  A was lounging at the foot of one of the statue clusters, going over schedule and possible training.

He ventured into the lobby.

“Unless you really are tired, in which case, don’t let me stop you,” A said.

“I didn’t want to bother you.”

“No bother.  Want to chat?  We haven’t really talked.”

“Sure.”  He made his way inside, pulling off his coat, and set it down, as extra cushioning, sitting at the base of another statue cluster, where he could face A.  A dangling blue nettle hung just over his head, and he tapped it with a finger.

Bruin had achieved some early success in a period piece two years back, but after that, had struggled to break out of that role, with its crisp way of speaking, straight-backed posture, and subtle facial expressions.  Maybe, some -Basil included- suspected, he didn’t want to.  He didn’t seem to enjoy fame, but had confessed to others he worried a lot about letting people down.  Keeping things smaller, in a specific niche, seemed to suit him.

So most of his work had been adjacent to that period piece from two years ago, including sequels and related media, and a game series where he was the model for a young detective of a Sherlockian era helping the player unravel a series of mysteries, that revealed themselves to be increasingly interconnected in a grand scheme.He had a small but intense fanbase, which gave him and A something to talk about, because she had a large and intense fanbase.

“Right now you’re in a good place,” Bruin was telling A, “but what happens when the audience starts clamoring for something and they’re on a different page than you?  Where do you draw the line between what you want and what you’re doing- some of what you want being to make the audience happy, and keep working, right-?”

“Sure.”

“-and then the audience’s wants, and finally, Elabre’s wants.”

“Have you dealt with that?”

“You’ve seen my Tilt games?” he asked, as his onboard Bear provided some images.  Bruin mimed tilting a cap he wasn’t wearing, to match the promotional images of some of the editions.

“I’m familiar, but haven’t played them,” A said, smiling a bit.

“Every game, they try to provide a reward.  It’s all voice acted and modeled by me, for all my parts, hand drawn art, it’s a labor of love.”

“That’s great.”

“A lot of work, even for me.  You can imagine there being six hundred scenarios, lots of nuance between scenarios, depending on choices players have made.”

A nodded.

“But they want to add something on top, keep people interested and excited, make the wait worth it.  There’s a lot of speculation that the final chapter, Tilt: Save the Queen, will be a face to face meeting with me.”

“That’s a lot of work, even if it’s only one percent of players, that’s-”

“A lot, yeah.  Nothing’s confirmed, that’s just speculation.  It would be the players that have lived and breathed the immersive part of the game for a decade, completed a few thousand hours of content and, you know, as the title says-”

“Saved the queen.”

“Yeah.  And after that first wave of players, it might taper off into a raffle.  Give memorabilia to the people who don’t win the face to face meeting.  Or meeting other actors.  Again, nothing confirmed.”

“Sounds like a good sendoff.  But you were saying…?  There’s something else, or something tricky?”

“Right, yeah.  That’s the edition after next.  And it’s… reasonable to expect something that big, for an exclusive set of players.  But that leaves the question, what’s happening in the next release, Tilt:Houndstooth Collar?  Fans came to a conclusion on their own.”

“Yeah?”

He broke eye contact, seeming faintly uncomfortable, now.  “That there’d be scenes, between the player and my character, immersive ones,”  He licked the space between gum and cheek, eyes moving across the room before settling on that dangling blue thistle again.  “Ones I’m old enough to consent to modeling for, at sixteen.”

“And you don’t want to?”

“I want to make a good game.  This is my favorite project overall,” he said.  His fingers knit together awkwardly, wrists resting on knees, and he studied them intently.  “I want it to succeed.”

“Okay, but, please feel free to call me a dum-dum, say I’m new to this, I don’t understand, but-”

“-it’s just, sorry-” he interrupted.

“No, I- you go ahead,” A said.

Given the chance to speak, he didn’t seem to know what to say at first.  Then he said, “A lot of people want it.  A lot a lot.  It starts to feel like they’re deciding how things go.  Can Elabre push back?  How do they make it into this excellent game series if they’re facing down this massive disappointment with hundreds of millions of people hating that…” he trailed off.

“That they don’t get to have sex with you?”

He winced.

[Gentle,] Basil urged.

“Sorry,” A said.

“It’s not… that.  I’d be a model for it.  It wouldn’t be me, specifically.  I do want the game to do well.  I’m not saying they’re considering it, but I’d be surprised if they hadn’t at least talked about it.”

“I think-”

“-and I’m not saying a hard no, if they discuss, and, I’m sorry.  I keep unintentionally interrupting,” he said.

“I think the part where it’s a good game or not?  That’s on Elabre, not you,” A said.  “I don’t think Elabre Systems would do that to you, if you clearly don’t want to.  They’re not awful.”

I don’t think you realize they’ve done similar.  Nothing as blatant, but Generation Wild had its moments, Basil mused.  Perhaps they didn’t have someone like you to speak to, so they never voiced their discomfort aloud, and things moved forward.  You still don’t realize the weight your words hold, and how you stating something can make things happen in a way nobody else in the Belt can manage.

How much did Bruin know?  Had he calculated that a talk like this, with A, would lead to A saying something like that, and force Elabre’s hand?

If so, Basil respected the move.

But the way Bruin was letting words tumble out, interrupting A, finally finding an outlet, maybe, suggested maybe he hadn’t planned this on that level.

“I don’t think your fans would want to do that to you either, if they realized how unhappy that made you.”

“Hm,” Bruin made a noise, quirking an eyebrow.

“It’d sour the experience too.  If, like people are predicting, there’s a chance to meet you later.  If you’re meeting all these dedicated fans, and you have to wonder, for each and every one… what scene did they pick?  It’d taint your own experience, the send-off, and it’d, in a roundabout way, taint theirs.”

Bruin nodded a bit.

“It’s Elabre’s job to make the game a success.  You give your best performance.  That’s how I see it, as someone who has very little experience with any of this.”

And as she said that, a few others who were waiting in the wings sent messages, joining the conversation to add their support.  Amber, Red, Blue…

Basil shifted his focus.  He was aware that A had upset a massive number of Tilt fans who’d truly been fixated on this idea, who were seeing the fallout.  Some were angry enough to trip alarms that he’d put in place, where people might be a threat to A.

A couple were forces unto themselves.  People who’d made it their entire lives to influence this fanbase and achieve a singular goal.

But that was manageable.  They were peripheral, a fanbase two orders of magnitude smaller than A’s.  Basil could notify the judiciary.

Elabre would be scrambling, if they’d really been considering entertaining the idea.

They’d arrived on earth, where two more members of Generation Colors got onto the ship.  Red was one, Krick another.  They were already messaging Bruin and A, so when they arrived, it was a matter of switching to using their voices without the messaging, without a moment of breaking stride.

Krickente was another lesser-seen member of the team.  He had the sort of deep black skin that took on a cool tone, and folds under his eyes that looked perpetually tired or weary, because of the natural folds.  He accented that look, instead of hiding it, with a neon teal makeup on his lower lids- his color, and dark clothes with the same as an occasional statement- today, it was a scarf in the same color, a heathered gray top, and dark pants in sandpaper.

Blue and Green were the big names among the guys, and they competed a lot for roles.  Interestingly, Krickente, or ‘Krick’ for short, frequently beat the pair in popularity polls, partially because the two ate into each other’s vote share.

It struck Basil as a similar situation to Bruin, who didn’t seem to want top level fame.  Many members of Generation Colors had gotten in early, bright eyed and excited, but over the last ten or so years, had gone in their own directions, deciding what they liked about all of this.  Or didn’t.  Krick seemed to like hanging back, doing his own thing, and having people be really excited when he took a leading role.  Even now, he hung to the edges, talking to Red, the graceful giant, and to Bruin, once the conversation had moved away from what A had been talking to Bruin about and onto the events of last night.

Basil kept to his tasks, some processes diverted to taking notes and keeping track of things.  The lobby was slowly filling up, and staff came by to bring food and drinks as requested.  Everyone was studiously avoiding the topic of the murder of Hruby Goldcliff, the woman A had frozen out, by A’s followers.

Amber, Maisie, Genoa, and Green arrived, and with their arrival, the room settled into seemingly comfortable, long-established groups.  Krickente and Maisie went off to one side to chat, with Bruin sort of tagging along, before Red diverted him, following some signal between them and Krickente.

Krick and Maisie wanted to catch up together.  They were close, but almost never appeared in the same media, because Maisie was more of a presenter, or quippy, joking type, for a lighter piece of media, and Krickente trended toward darker, more serious pieces.  Krickente sat with arms stretched across the back of the seat, across the lobby from everyone else, and when Maisie laughed hard enough she had to sit forward for a moment, she leaned back afterward, resting her head on his arm, all of her attention on his face.

Private, intimate, in a way, except for the billions of people who were watching everything here unfold.  Except for the fact that that audience could see everything from pulse rate to breathing, to saliva in the mouth, or flutters in the stomach, rendered as data, interpreted by their own onboards, or by whatever device they were using.

The ship left for the outer atmosphere, with Jan, Blue, and a few stray members taking a smaller ship over to intercept.

Basil kept drawing out the map.  As he did, a pattern was emerging.

Spaces within the superstructure where no movements were tracked or recorded.  Robert’s office was one, but it extended throughout, to whole floors.

Starkly visible when the entire superstructure was mapped out in dots, where people had spent some time working, dots where they slept, places they had long meals, but there were whole rooms that nothing happened.

Basil could then gather more data -which took more time, nanotech evading the patrols, sending the data requests amid the others, compiling the data into the nanotech form, and then making its way back to the back channel.  Some were parking for ships.

Others, blocked by nondisclosure.

Basil began to study the people who worked in those nondisclosed spaces.  Were they paying attention to A?  He tracked them by the elevators they took, the directions they traveled, and the time it took them to get to places where they were visible to the public.  When they disappeared into the void, he created a marker.

In some places, no.  Barely at all.

In some places, those markers piled up.

What were they paying attention to?

Why were they doing it?

Basil could track a single person who operated in that office, who left it and communicated with Robert.  One person of creative gender who left a space where everything was hidden from the public, and met Robert Simes in his office, where things were hidden from the public.

After one of those meetings, the department about A stopped paying attention to A, for the most part.

So that was it.

He began to gather more data, to present everything as a polished package of information to A, when there was a moment.  She hated talking to him, got upset the longer they talked, and so it would be better to be succinct, and to the point.

He was midway through that when he lost access to the Belt network.

This was it, then.

A laughed, unaware.  This was a hard group to break into, but she was finding her stride.

Was that about to be ruined?

[Basil, model IDLX-B, onboard for A Teeg, stand by.

Cease all non-emergency external communication.]

[Standing by.]

[A type E injunction is set into place, pursuant to file 105039.]

[Acknowledged.  My host has experienced traumatic events in recent memory, I would like permission to maintain normal contact and communication, so as not to retraumatize.]

[Only as necessary, IDLX-B Basil.]

They weren’t the only ones to be silenced.  Others were noticing.

“Bear,” Bruin said.  “Why not tell me?”

[Emergency communication only,] his onboard replied.

“What the hell?” Green asked.  Green, always one of the more sensitive and kind members of the group, had been close to Bruin, his focus wholly on his colleague and friend.

Other onboards were giving similar responses.  Depending on model, some weren’t even able to send messages or communicate openly.

[Don’t panic.]

“What is this?”

[We’re under attack,] Basil said.  He could say that here.

Genoa, dressed in gray, jogged up the stairs, to look out the window at the first landing.

He seemed to expect that others would look through his onboard, but open communication had been momentarily scuttled.

The entire ship shook.

Some others ran up the stairs.  Faces crowded in together to look.

A, rather than crowd in, stepped onto a part of railing and, one hand on the post to balance, stepped up enough to look over heads and out the window.

Earth was covered in superstructures, and the structures that weren’t in plain view were cast in their own ‘evening’ lighting, lights illuminated in the relative dark, dimmed lights and cool colors still a marked contrast from the background- the blackness of space, studded with its own lights.

Except all the lights were going out, one superstructure at a time.

The ship they were on shook once again.

“Why are we shaking?” Amber asked.

“What’s happening?  Talk to me, Basilisk.”

[Don’t panic.]

“Give me more than that.”

[When everything kicks off, everyone will want to be the main character.  I think you shouldn’t try.  Find other ways to be useful.]

“This isn’t real,” A spoke her realization aloud, within the back channel.

All lights on the ship went out.  The emergency lights flared to life, dimmer than the ones before.  It was a dark ship, with dark blue flooring, so the effect of the dimmed lights was fairly extreme.  The metallic trim, gold as it led to one wing of the ship, silver as it led to another, seemed to glow, providing just enough awareness of where the stairs were that they could navigate.

The ship was turning, because one of the impacts had caused it to start spinning at a slow rate.

There was a view of the rest of the belt, and the lights going out there.

“This is an attack,” Green said.  “Where’s the staff?”

“Locked off.  They lock off spaces like this and passenger quarters to keep things manageable in a crisis,” Krickente said.

“We need to find a place we can get weapons,” Green said.

Red -now Te, because they weren’t connected to their onboard- reached overhead, to one of the marble statues, and tried pulling down on one arm, to break it off.  It didn’t break.

“Darn,” Te said, letting go and dropping back down onto the stairs.  “I thought it could be a club.”

“Let’s move,” Green said.

“If we’re being boarded, the martial arts we all learned in practices might be useful,” Genoa said.

“The key thing is we shouldn’t be heroes,” Te said.

Green seemed startled by that.

“They might kill the first few who try, to make an example of us.”

Slowly, one by one, people seemed to be getting it.  The fear faded away as new suspicions took their place.

Suspicion without certainty.  Except in A’s case, because Basil had tipped her off by back channel.

The fact people couldn’t be one hundred percent sure meant there was an edge to their reactions and responses that wouldn’t be there, even when they were acting well.

Green led the way down the hall.  They only had access to a subset of the ship, and multiple heavy doors were supposed to separate this part of the ship from other essential areas.

They checked rooms.

“Furniture,” Amber said.  “Te, you and Krick break those chairs down?  You’re strongest.”

“I’m strong,” Green said.

“That’s why I want you in front.  Next room.  Maisie, with Te and Krick, hold stuff so they can keep their hands free.  Genoa?  Hang back, watch Te and Krick’s back, and the hallway behind us.”

“Sure.  I can manage in a fight.”

“I believe you.  So take a chair leg, but hang back, watch them, watch the hallway.”

Amber glanced at A.

“What?” A asked.

“Do you want to take the reins?”

“You’re doing fine.  I’m thinking.”

“Yeah?”

“Basil, can we get any messages out?”

[Only emergency messages.]

“Go with Green?” Amber asked A.

A ducked her head down.

They stepped into a room, and A scanned the surroundings with her eyes.  Basil noted a few things that could potentially be broken down into weaponry.

Metal throughout the ship began to thrum.

That thrumming became vaguely musical.  Haunting.

A ignored it, and opened a wall panel, searching, and found some emergency tools and supplies.  She slid the box of supplies across the floor, to Bruin.

The tools had some better improvised weapons.

The frame of the ship, in the musical straining of it, spoke to them.  “Your ship now falls under the auspice of Father Kabek Gobar.  His sire was the finest of human men, and he embraced a writhing daughter of the Inui, and we were given a Father.  Sing his praises.”

A passed a wedge gun to Green, who jammed it into his belt.  She took a fire suppressor and stowed it at her belt.

“Meet his children,” the metal of the ship told them.

The intensity of the vibrating, straining metal magnified by orders of magnitude.  The curtains lining the hallway, so heavy they might barely give way if a truck ran into them, billowed, briefly.  People in the hallway backed out of the hall and into rooms, so they wouldn’t be struck.

It created a false double vision, where each pillar, now visible with curtains out of the way, seemed to have a duplicate.

And in the gap between them, as they shuddered, something appeared.

It was squat, four-legged, long-tailed, and low to the ground, purple, and vaguely translucent, in a way that revealed its internal organ structure.  It flopped, tail doing much of the work, until it could get all four legs beneath it.

Green fired the wedge gun.  It was pure pressure, meant to force open any door that wouldn’t open or a panel that needed to be removed from the wall, by emitting a massive amount of force in a forward triangle.

It bowled the thing over, forcing it to lash the ground with its tail to get upright again.

Which barely mattered, because an Inui-modified human in robe-like clothing strode out of the hallway, toward them.

Armed with a gun.

“Like before, Bas,” A said.

Like before.

Basil didn’t know what the weak points in an alien anatomy were.

But he could highlight effective areas, work with A’s physiology to augment her strength.

[Work with the others.]

“Stop telling me what to do.  I was going to do that anyway.”

A had punched a man hard enough to rupture his liver.  Now she went after the next closest thing to a proper alien.  A spawn of human and Inui.

Basil directed her to attack lower joints, that bore most of the weight.

Putting the figure off balance enough to shove toward Green.

Green fired the pressure gun again.  At close range, fired into the side of the neck, it was a lot more effective.  The Inui-human hybrid didn’t bleed, and skin didn’t even break, but something internal snapped or dislocated.

Te, meanwhile, had come through this way, and was trying to wrestle the quadruped, and getting chewed up in the process.  Amber stabbed the thing in the underbelly.

“I thought you said we shouldn’t be heroes, Te,” Amber told them.

Te, panting, bleeding, wincing, didn’t have a lot to say to that.

The choir-like singing of the metal continued.  They were calling more.

“Blue and Jan are coming, right?” Green asked.

Amber, after making sure the thing was dead and Te was okay, stepped into the hallway, checking.

The other group met her there.

“I don’t know how far those two will get us.  We have an entire ship of staff, some military trained, some bodyguards,” Amber said.  “And if they’re losing…”

“What do we do?”

“Keep moving,” Amber said.

“Did you guys check the emergency compartment?” A asked the other group.

“Good call,” Krick said.

“On it,” Maisie responded, before ducking back out of sight.

“We might have to get off ship, get somewhere safe,” Amber said.  “It feels like they’ve taken this ship.   It’s- the bones of it are vibrating.”

“Frame,” Green said.  “The frame is vibrating.  And letting those things spill out.  Inui can do that?”

Maisie came back, handing out a fire suppressor, another wedge gun, and a tool that looked like a claw hammer that was all claw, too small to be a crowbar.  There hadn’t been one in the compartment A had opened.

Someone yelped their alarm.  The vibrating metal was spitting out more things, now.

More crab-like, by the looks of it.  And more figures almost identical to the one human-Inui hybrid that had come through, dressed in draping black cloth.

There was a crush of people between A and the hallway.

“Basil,” A said.  “Can we get an emergency message out?”

[We can try.]

“Ask- anyone official enough who is listening, can we break the law?”

[What law would you like to break?]

“Nanotech,” A said, quietly.

With that question and statement, the immersive scenario ended.  Basil felt the connection to the Belt Network re-establish.  The lights came on.  The ship stopped singing.

No more crab in the hallway, dead tadpole-crocodile beast in the doorway, or human-Inui offspring with a broken neck beside the door.

People seemed shaken.

This was the sort of thing that they could not do too often.  It weighed on the sanity of the actors who could start to doubt reality.

But judging by the reactions, audiences who’d watched the entire thing were excited.  A live event, flirting with the bounds of reality and fiction.

“That was a pilot.  To see if people were interested,” Green said.  He’d apparently communicated with someone higher-up already.

“We’re staying in space,” Amber said.  “They’re going to send some people to us to discuss.  We’ll meet, and then have some practice.  Zero-g dance, fighting.  There are going to be a few more pilots this week.  No more surprises like that.”

“Are you okay?” Green asked A.

A seemed a bit startled to be put on the spot.

“I’m surprised you thought about nanotech like that,” Red told her.

“It’s what I know.”

“I couldn’t tell if you’d realized it was an event put together by Elabre Systems or not,” Amber said.  “I worried.”

“I realized.  I’ve been through the real thing.”

Red frowned, then leaned in to whisper to Bruin.

“You are okay?” Green asked A.  “This was a lot, after a night like last night, half of us didn’t get sleep, and we weren’t told-”

“I’m okay,” A said, with enough force that it terminated half the conversations people were having.

“-Hruby-” Red said, quietly, to Bruin.  They’d said one quiet word that stood out because of the way people had gone silent.

“I asked to not be told anything about her, or-” A paused.  She was glancing through menus.  Basil could have hidden the information from her.  He didn’t.  he provided it.

A glanced through the reporting.  She saw Hruby had been killed.

“We weren’t supposed to say anything,” Green told Red, his own voice quiet.

“I don’t want people keeping secrets from me, to spare my feelings,” A said.

“It’s not that,” Green said.

“It’s kind of that.”

“It’s that there’s that checkmate problem again,” Green told her, his voice level.  He ran his hand across his forehead- he’d picked up a sheen of sweat from running around and breaking down a chair.  His onboard kept it to a light beading, but it did have to manage his temperature, and he’d dressed warm.

Perhaps a part of it was that he was that nervous about a misstep.

“Checkmate?” A asked.

“How do you handle that?  If murder becomes a way to get your attention… but ignoring it and giving it no attention suggests you condone it?  There are too many wrong answers,” Green said.  “So Elabre said, just after we woke up, we weren’t supposed to tell you.”

“Which I didn’t agree with,” Red said.  “But I am sorry.”

Red was already getting a message to come in and talk to Elabre higher-ups.

Basil managed A’s emotional load as best as he could.  The tears that were finding their way to her eyes, the breathing, the sweating, and the restlessness that she was suddenly experiencing.

He couldn’t stop it all, but he could dampen it, helping her to maintain her composure.

She was tired- she hadn’t slept after last night.  Now this?  A lot, even on its own.  But it echoed real trauma.  Then Robert, though Elabre couldn’t know anything about that.  A was struggling with Mechard pulling away, no doubt.  Struggling more with Quinn’s absence.

Any of those things could be an excuse for a teenager to get upset, on its own.

What was Elabre thinking?  Maybe they hadn’t expected A to suggest nanotech, twisting the entire situation into a mirror of the science center.  Maybe they’d told themselves the alien nature of it separated this from A’s experience enough.

Maybe they had wanted A upset and off balance.

It was possible Basil would never have definitive answers.

Basil was about to communicate, to everyone involved, that A needed a break, when he saw Amber weaving through the people between her and A.  Red and Green parted.

Amber gave A a hug.

“No practice today,” Amber said.

“I’m new, I don’t want to skip,’ A said.

“No practice.  We’re taking a day.”

A nodded.

“Hang out?  As friends?  Goofing around on this ship?  Or maybe we get dropped off before it stops where it wants to stop?”

A opened her mouth, and Basil had to help support her, because her voice would have quavered.

“Sounds good.”

“And maybe tonight, maybe,” Amber said, to nobody in particular.  To Elabre Systems, “We have a meeting with a general update, with Elabre, catching us up on what everyone else discussed?”

A nodded.

Elabre didn’t send confirmation, but did adjust the schedule on the calendar.

[Yes,] Basil said, as a simple confirmation of that.  He didn’t want to intrude on this.  Amber was reaching out.

“We’ll catch up,” Amber said, to the others.

Staff that had stepped away for the pilot event were back in the central wing, and two directed Amber and A to a room where they could kick back, rest, and unwind.  A jogged off to go get her bag, with the more comfortable change of clothes, then kicked off her boots as she returned.

Happier than she was willing to admit, to have a friend to hang out with.

But before she sat down, she messaged Basil.

“What about Robert Simes?”

[Killing Robert Simes isn’t an option.]

“I somehow doubt that.”

[The problem is bigger than him.  He has enough power to form companies and think tanks on a whim, to tackle anything he finds sufficiently interesting.  That, momentarily, included you.  Six hundred employees pored over your history, becoming experts in you.  Some of them connected the dots about the back channel, from context clues.  They notified Robert Simes.]

A stepped into the bathroom, lights off, and changed out of the somewhat uncomfortable top.

She took moment in the dark, to think.

“Doesn’t change anything,” A told him.

[It means there may be six hundred possible people who know something about you.]

“It might only be Robert Simes.  Basil, it doesn’t change anything.“

She put emphasis on those last four and a half words.

“You have to handle it.  We have no other choice, unless you want me to scapegoat you.  I’d lose these people.  All hope of being a star.  You have to handle it.  Somehow.  Or I do?  I could send people after them, with the right words.”

[That would be disastrous.]

A emerged from the washroom and grabbed a drink from a mini-fridge, flavored water, and tossed another to Amber, who was asking what A wanted to watch.

A didn’t answer Basil, or expand on anything.  She didn’t have to.

[I’m on it, then.]

3.2.W – MUTE

It wasn’t a ship, but it had a lot of the same principles, with a massive engine, structural forces, and environmental forces.  The big distinction was that she was working on a machine that was three hundred and forty meters tall, that wanted to stay put.

The drill was anchored by framing in the form of four curved walls of metal that each covered more than ninety degrees of the perimeter, angled to leave three gaps.  The fourth gap was taken up by outflow and processing, moving the incredible quantities of matter quickly down to where it could be processed.  Once everything valuable had been pulled out, the mud and slough were dumped into other holes and ravines far enough away that they shouldn’t backflow into the hole they were digging here.

For the four walls, the outer walls were smooth, inner walls textured to break up the incoming wind that came through the gaps, and horizontal bridges that were thicker around than the ship that had brought Winnifred here attached them to the engine, letting them act as anchors and stabilizers.

Mud and chipped rock were being shucked off of the drill bit, finding virtually zero traction on the metal as nanotech crawled along its length and did its work.  Because of that, most of the work crew had backed off as much as possible, leaving only the team that was up on the walls, on the bridges, at a few designated safe points on the outside of the machine, and on the small, maneuverability-focused Spadgers that could fly around like hummingbirds, zipping by quickly, stopping on a dime.

Same line as the ones she’d been invited to go engineer and ride on at the Melville Station dock.  Before the riot, and before she’d lost her body.

Winnifred scaled the exterior.  The machinery ran hot, but she’d chosen parts that could operate in extreme heat and cold.  Her mask drew in the hot air, ran it all through her body, using the heat pumps that supported her central systems, which couldn’t do much because the ambient heat around her was so intense, the various backup cooling processes that were doing a lot more, filtered out the water vapor that the hot air naturally collected, and then finally provided it to her Ox box.

Not that she needed a lot.

The exposed flesh of her face was at the biggest risk, but this was where the 1.5cm diameter nodes implanted around her eye sockets came into play.  In extreme cold, her skin sucked back, her onboard withdrawing moisture, and the nodes were visible.  Now, the nodes almost did the opposite, inflating out like an overly swollen black eye, extending compounds throughout the skin, that her onboard then used to turn her skin into a heat resistant polymer.  Nanotech on the surface of her eye let her see without eye damage.

She scampered along the hot metal, finding the notches and grooves a little softer than they usually were.

She found a console and accessed it.  Her onboard helped change the visual settings, so she could operate despite the heat shimmer.  She ran it through its paces, opened a side panel while curving her body into a ‘c’ shape around the hinge side of the panel to avoid the blast of hot air that came out the more open side, then checked the data on the panel against the components.

She tilted her head, and poked a claw inside, while being careful to keep her face away from the worst of the heat, moving some wires.  Deeper in the system, where metal was running hot enough to turn intermittently orange and orange-grey as air currents ran over it, she could get a good sense of the tone and quality of the metal.

“Measurements, please, claw tips as calipers?” she asked.

The numbers appeared in her field of view, fanning out to measure the distance between each claw and the one beside it.  She suppressed a sigh, and reached down, checking.

1.98, 1.98, 1.98, 1.94, 1.95… The numbers she wasn’t using or focusing on faded to near-total transparency.

She couldn’t reach much further.

She closed up the panel and moved on.

“Roughly five minutes before the shroud comes down and you get squashed like a bug, Win,” a message came through.  Her boss.

“Put that in my field of view?”

Her onboard sent that as a reply.  She bit back a comment, and motioned, upper left of her field of view.

“Onboard, put the countdown in my field of view,” she said.  She motioned again.  Something she didn’t want to be doing when she had limited time and when she was about two hundred meters above solid ground, scaling a third generation Kore in maintenance mode, with an external temperature of a hundred and eighty degrees Celsius without a safety rigging.

The number appeared.

“Please pay attention,” she told it.  She was glad it didn’t send the message to her boss.

[I am paying a great deal of attention.  I am incapable of not.  If you would like me to adapt better to your-]

“No,” she interrupted it.

There were six total panels like the last one around the circumference of the machine.  She’d already checked six further up, where it was cooler, and where the gentle slope of the Kore made it easier to perch or hang off a surface.

That left five to do in less than five minutes.

Accessing the panel, then opening the vent, being careful of hot air and steam.  There was less and less water content as the cycle continued, which changed the texture and shape of that release.  It was part of the reason the cycle worked like it did.  Water was an incredible destructive force, and it was a lot easier to account for heat, pressure, physical wear, vibration, than it was to account for water finding its ways to places it shouldn’t be and altering the variables.

When so much of what they were doing was hauling up entire landscapes worth of broken rock with varying quantities of moisture, and when the planet’s environment itself was capricious, water happened.

The way the Kore handled it was to say ‘some of my automated processes to stress test and calibrate generate a lot of heat, so let’s use that’.  Everything inside was rather elegantly designed to manage the heat and steam.  All of it would occur during a natural run-through of various processes.  They’d have readings on the next few kilometers down of rock type and texture, and nanotech on the massive drill bits would be changing angle, texture, and edge to work with that specific rock, because it wasn’t just enough to penetrate the rock or break it up.  They wanted to break it up into the right textures and type of flake.  The optimal results were easiest to push up into the center of the Kore and toward the surface, and easiest to analyze and break apart for the materials they wanted.

That included the sub-drills, that could extend out sideways from the main drill body, targeting rich deposits.

Elsewhere, internal systems would be checking that everything was working right, and that there were no leaks, stresses or other lingering issues.  The drills, once recut on a molecular level and recessed back into the Kore, would spin up to multiple times their usual speed, pushing the internal temperatures up to a multiple of what it was now.

She checked the fourth and fifth panels.  Just one more.  Sixty-two seconds.

“You are aware that you have to actually get off the Kore?” her boss messaged her.  “This isn’t some automated test where you have to do five problems in five minutes.  You need to do your work and get to safety.”

“I’m okay,” she told him.

Panel.

[Emergency lights are up throughout the ship.  A shroud is being dropped.]

“Shut up and let me focus.”

[We should evacuate.]

The ships that had been flitting about like hummingbirds were retreating.  Workers near the top, where things were coolest, were moving at a fast walk or run across the horizontal bridges that attached the four surrounding walls to the drill body.

“Onboard, if you don’t shut up you may actually slow me down enough it’s a problem.  Silence yourself until I’m somewhere safe.”

Vent cover open.  The hard part- verifying the data.  This was the part where having an onboard talking over things would be disastrous.  She was glad the boss wasn’t messaging her.

Then the measurements.  Caliper readings.

She shut the vent, turned the handle to lock it.

Three seconds left.

She dashed upward, scaling the wall with a four-legged sprint, her eyes darting left and right to spot the edges that she could grab onto with claw tips.

When they weren’t finding handholds, she glanced at menus and blinked with swollen eyes to select options.  Calibration, finding touchpoints.  Timing.  Sync with known video of other Kore operations…

The shroud came down like a guillotine.  It was an external cover for the drill, and when the drill was deep in the earth, the shroud could be a cover for the hole, sealing it to manage pressure -only valid near the top layers, sometimes, but a good way to get a fast start- and dropping the rails, produced on site, that would support the sides of the hole.  Through those rails, some supplies were fed through, like power, water, or, in the dire case of drill stoppage, personnel.

In this case, however, it served double duty.  With the drill receded and suspended above the surface, the shroud covered all external layers with a durable outer shell.

Winnifred jumped, calculating the jump so that when that eight foot wall of steel came down, she could graze the outer surface, reach for and tag the same sorts of edges and panels that she’d been using to sprint skyward before, and propel herself a little bit upward.  Running up a falling object.

She drew her entire body together, then pushed off, spread eagled, spine down, belly facing sky.

The bridges running along the topsides were multi-part.  She clipped the bridge with a reaching hand, touching the spot that she’d marked out with the touch-point calculation earlier, slowing her descent by a small fraction, but also changing her angle enough that she could also move through the beam, where there were gaps.  She twisted her upper body around, protrusions of her spine pulled in, so she could skim body against the metal of the bridge.   A lot more drag, that.

This would be the slowest she moved for a good little while.

As she dropped through open sky between the partially shrouded Kore and the wall, she felt her velocity increase.

Nothing to grab onto.  No bridge, no wire.

She tucked one arm and leg to flip over, then extended them again.

A had once jumped off the side of a superstructure.

A had had safety features to catch her.

She’d been trying to escape something, from early on.  It had created a kind of drive in her, Winnifred figured.  One that had given her the strength to deal with the terrorists in the science center when others hadn’t been able to.

To deal with her body being changed when she hadn’t asked for it.

The shroud settled, fitting the outside of the Kore like a glove.  When it did, pressure and various processes forced all of the steam and hot air out.  It billowed around the base of the drill and the opening of the hole, steam meeting mud and the much cooler -relatively- temperature of the outside, here.

It looked a bit like an old fashioned ship burning conventional fuel to take off.

More practically, the explosion of hot air and steam let Winnifred -now with both arms wrapped around her face to shield it- get pushed back and away by the wave of hot air.  Most of what she’d done prior, in running up the shroud, touching the bridge, scraping past the bridge underlayer, and controlling her fall, had been to control the timing and location, here.

It meant she was thrown toward one of the curved walls, where tab-like protrusions studded the inside layer, each about five feet out and five feet across, placed at set, specific angles, sometimes perpendicular, sometimes flowing with one another, that were meant to control the flow of incoming wind and sound, while keeping the wind from making the wall wobble too much.

Lots of engineering went into something that simple.

She grabbed one, swinging as much as was possible, kicked off of another, dropped briefly, and then stepped on another, for a calculated, trajectory-prescribed, onboard-assisted interval of time that controlled for how much stress her leg could take.

Grab another on the way down, swinging more…

Bank off another angled one, whole-body.

And drop about nine meters, to land on her feet, in a standing position, surrounded by the steam and mist.

[I see you’ve just had a near death experience.  Remain calm and don’t worry, I can provide assistance and guidance-]

“You’ve interpreted the situation wrong,” Winnifred told it.  “Abandon your premise.  I’m fine.”

[I’m sorry.  If you do decide you are in fact in distress, I can provide you with some active listening as you articulate the problem, and connect you with trauma assistance resources.]

Winnifred rolled her eyes, and when that threatened to bring up a sub-menu in her field of view, she rolled them the other way and closed them for a second, suppressing a sigh.

“My office, please,” her boss messaged her.

The moisture level in the air was enough that Winnifred was quickly getting drenched from the pure humidity of it.  Water beaded on her arms.  She used claw tips to trace her scalp, moving now-damp hair back, where it could be re-tied into a ponytail.

The internal temperature would be ramping up rapidly, now, with the shroud blocking the usual vents.

“Onboard?  Fix my face?” she asked the onboard.

[Already on it.]

“Cosmetic fixes are prioritized.  I’m about to have a meeting.”

[Understood.  I’ll adjust.]

“Thank you.  I’m sorry I was snippy a minute ago, but you really weren’t being helpful or accurate.”

[I could be more helpful if we re-enabled my adaptive architecture.]

“That would be cruel, I think.  Letting you develop from a series of prompts to being a person, when I know I’ll replace you with Toby?  And you’d either be restricted, trapped, unable to change Toby’s work, or you could change Toby’s work, and that would be unfair to Toby.  You’d be lobotomizing her.”

[I see.]

Winnifred wasn’t sure the onboard did.

[I’ll file that as a ‘not for now’.  To get the full use of my breadth of capabilities and more natural sounding interactions, we should eventually return to the question of enabling this essential adaptive architecture.]

It was a bit of a walk.  She got a view of other facilities.  While the Kore wasn’t the type of drill in use everywhere, the way it operated in cycles meant that there was a certain type of worker that really appreciated working on a site that primarily used this type of drill.  It meant there was a rhythm, usually ten hours on, six hours off, purportedly for sleep.  Then they’d rinse, repeat, with any showering, eating, and other activities eating into the time off.  No vacations, no breaks.

Which was a placid pace compared to some sites, which provided for three hours of sleep.  They usually operated a different sort of drill, targeting high-value patches only, and everyone involved operated on stimulants or brain tweaks meant to minimize the need for sleep, and a ‘rest when we’re done’ philosophy.  They weren’t usually on planet for long.  For the long-termers, who worked those types of site back to back, it was ‘rest when you’re dead’ philosophy.

Machine failure or unexpected shifts in the environment or weather could be an impromptu vacation, or it could have employers calling for people to work so hard that everything before that seemed like leisure, by comparison.

People were said to either be here to earn as much as they could, or because of a personal pride in work, and whichever of the two it was, it tended to mean they wanted to work hard, throwing everything else aside.  Culture around the work sites played into that dynamic.

On the superstructures, there was transportation built into the superstructure in the form of platforms and elevators, or there was space for ships and vehicles.  Out here, it was open, flat ground, with a lot of sky overhead.  Other Kore drills with a similar setup studded the landscape, each a set distance from one another, forming a loose line that disappeared off to opposite horizons.  Much of the work site occupied the band following just behind that line, with facilities and processing set up, ships that took off and landed, acting like mobile facilities, and the encampments of workers that had been dropped off all occupying that four-kilometer wide band.

Behind them was another row of Kore drills, with more anchoring and reinforcement to support them, as they drilled more unstable ground.

And behind that was a landscape of rock shards and mud.  A few ships hovered over it, doing their analysis of the plate.  There were places that rows of drills like this could form intentional cracks in the plate, and open it up like a book with pages falling to either side, allowing access to depths that drills struggled to manage.  The makeup of plate they were currently drilling didn’t allow for it, but from conversation she’d overheard, they’d found one possible, that they’d open up later, before selling the plot to others.  Some of those others would go deeper, if they saw value in it.

Then, when the entire planet had been raked through, everything easily obtainable picked up, the muck sorted through and spit back out, they’d pick up and leave.

She was a grain of sand working on a thimble in a sea of hundreds of thousands of thimbles, and the other odds and ends, arranged on a beach.  It felt a little bit like if she removed her perspective and looked away for long enough, she wouldn’t even be able to find herself, in the midst of it all.

Winnifred wasn’t sure if that was what she was after, or if she wanted the investigator and the other people auditing Toby to lose track.

Wouldn’t that be nice?  If they let Toby go and lost track of her, deciding it wasn’t worth the trouble?  She was a contributing citizen.

Hah.

The ‘boss’ in her case was Emil Shain.  He had bought a ship that he could use as office, transportation between planets, and a place to live.  She could see the man talking to some other people.  He had long black hair, and was gaunt, with virtually no body fat, but no muscle either, in the way some people who spent a lot of time off planet got.  Usually that was a sign they were stretching budgets, eating the bare minimum, not running the g-panels for gravity, and cutting other corners when it came to their own health.  It was odd that he just… looked like that, even when he had a fair amount of money.  Had to.

A part of her wondered if he looked like that on purpose.  She’d spent a lot of time studying him, and trying to figure him out, and interpreting him as someone who liked taking people in and looking after them made him make a lot of sense.  The look, then, would maybe break the ice some, with people who were down and out.

He spotted her and extended a finger, wagging it.

“Hi.”

“My office,” he said, pointing that finger.  “Don’t comment on my ship.  Don’t offer details.”

She obliged, walking toward the office.  Since they were walking alongside, she decided to tell him, “I was in full control the whole time.”

“Office,” he said.

She sighed and walked up the ramp, glancing up at the ship.  A G17 Estrade.  Either he had splurged or, more likely, he had gotten it secondhand.  A lot of attention had been paid to the little details, including real leather on the furnishings and laser-cut black marble for the panels — two of which were cracked and had been filled with what looked like gold, kintsugi style.

For all of that, there was a visible staining from cigarettes being smoked inside the ship, which included brown drippings from the vents.  The ramp led to an open door, probably airing out the ship.  Then a T-junction, with doors to the left and right.

The door to the left was Emil Shain’s office.  The one to the right was a supply room with a hose for rinsing off, because so much of the work on these planets got you muddy.

“I was in control the entire time,” she said.  “I’ve made jumps like that a hundred times.  Maybe two hundred.”

“You’re such a teenager,” he grumbled.  He settled, reclining, and checked his drawers for a cigarette.  It felt a lot like this wasn’t his ship.  Both in aesthetic and in how he occupied the space.

He lit his cigarette.  “This bother you?”

She tapped her face mask with a claw tip.

He nodded a bit.  “Tell me about the checks you did, so I can decide how mad I should be at you.”

“Um.  Checked 82-1 through 82-6,” Winnifred said.

He tapped on his desk.  His eyes glowed faintly, as he looked at a screen with the lenses he was wearing.  Invisible to her, but she could have asked her onboard to guess, based on the light patterns.  She didn’t.

“Then 42-1 through 42-6.  I couldn’t do the bottom row.”

“Because that would be stupid.”

“I’m fine.  I was safe.”

“You think you were safe.”

“I was safe.  I was- my family made me like this.  This body was built for the job.  I had safety measures implanted under my skin when I was a baby.  I’ve grown up in these environments.”

“Your onboard couldn’t even put up a countdown clock and you trusted it to help guide your fall?”

[Permission to speak?]

“No,” Shain said.

Winnifred explained, “The fall guidance was setup before.  It’s my setup, worked on over time with Toby.  Asking this onboard to handle it is different, it’s pulling up a project worked on before.”

Shain sat back in his chair.  It creaked slightly.  He gave Winnifred a level stare.  “Is that how it works?”

“I’m not suicidal.  I’m not even that much of a daredevil, compared to my cousins-”

Mentioning her cousin made her onboard visibly highlight the archive, where the messages from her family were piling up.  A little icon with a growing number telling her how many times they’d tried to reach out.  She avoided looking at it, because she knew they’d look through her eyes, see it, and redouble their efforts.

“-I could have my onboard pull up footage of other jumps,” she offered.

“Onboards annoy me.  Your onboard annoys me even more than most.”

“They’re a placeholder,” Winnifred said.  That annoys me too, honestly.

“Yeah.  That doesn’t make it any better.”

She decided not to say anything more.  He was sitting back, smoking, clearly thinking.

“Does doing the diagnostic in the middle of the reset cycle change the data?”

“No.  I could pull up charts, showing how these panels and systems operate at different heat levels, factory specific and some tests from random system checks-”

He raised a hand, cigarette clamped between two fingers.  “No need to bring anything up.  Say it to me straight.”

“Kore drills are meant to operate at high temperatures, including drilling through magma.  No, the heat doesn’t change anything.”

“So you saved us, let’s say, twelve minutes on the post-reset checkup.  Assuming I’d use the Spadgers to check each panel, while it all cools off.  Limited commodity.”

“Sounds more or less right.”

“What else?  You were measuring.”

“The handoff connectors deep in the panels at 42.  I don’t think you’d notice normally, but while it’s running hot- can I show you?  It really is important.”

He’d been about to protest.  He relented, tapping his desk.

She used it as a panel, black marble texture fading to give her just a black screen.  She brought up her view of the panel, as she’d seen it.  With eye movements, she zoomed in.

“Explain,” he said.

“The side drills don’t have the full complement of features, heatsinks, emergency stops.  So you extend your drill down, and if there’s a valuable side deposit, the main body rotates, side drills extend out-”

“I know how my own fucking drill works.  Holy shit, kid.  You’re one of those smart kids who thinks everyone else is a lot dumber than they are, huh?”

Winnifred wasn’t sure how to respond to that.

“Or maybe everyone else you’ve dealt with up until now really has been dumb as rocks.  I’d understand that too.”

“More like I haven’t dealt with a lot of people that weren’t family, I guess,” she said, quiet.

He sighed, drawing on his cigarette, and motioned for her to continue.

“The handoff connectors link to the main drill and borrow from it.  The way they heat up isn’t even, and looked wrong.  I measured.  It’s an artificial bottleneck, I think the metal stretched, and stretched thinner here.  Which means it’s getting more heat, which means it’s stretching thinner.”

“What happens, down the road?”

“Snap.  You lose the side drill.  Maybe lose a side deposit.  Depending on where the break is or how it melts, it could shut down that entire cooling line, forty-two and up.”

“Visible only because you looked while it was hot?”

“Yeah.”

“We do regular checks.  Bring in outside ships, once every three months.”

Winnifred nodded.  “Some people don’t, which gets bad, and-”

“I look after my ships and my equipment,” he said, interrupting her.

He sounded annoyed.

“I didn’t mean to say you didn’t.  Just that… stuff happens when you don’t.”

“Keep it relevant, keep it short and simple.”

“It’s better to catch it early.  It’s caught.”

“Good,” he said.  “I’ll ask some people who work for me and my friends, who’ve worked on these drills for longer than you’ve been alive, they’ll give me their opinions.  I guess you didn’t save me twelve minutes after all.”

“Hopefully saved you a bigger expense, later on.”

“Yeah.  At the cost of pulling a stunt like you did.”

“I was-” she started.  She stopped when he raised a hand.

“A stunt, still.  One I’d be worried some of my employees might try, with much less success, because some of them are idiots.”

“They wouldn’t have much luck without a modded body.  With the heat and steam alone…”

“I don’t want to encourage that either.”

She was mildly perturbed by that, but kept that look away from her eyes.

“People were getting far enough away to be safe, there was mist, I haven’t heard any buzz about what you did.  Let’s keep it that way.  After tomorrow’s drilling, you can run whatever checks you see fit.  You’re not going to jump off the side of the drill.  I’ll send a Spadger your way when you’re nearly done.  With time to spare, so… plan for that, when you’re timing yourself.”

“Okay.  Yes sir.”

“If you hadn’t pulled the shitty stunt, I’d say some young go-getter spotted an issue, saved us some money, and I was paying it forward, a bit of time off, with pay, while we replace the parts.  It’d make you popular.”

But she had pulled the stunt.

“Can’t do that.  So.”

He sucked on the cigarette for a couple of seconds.

“I have a friend who is operating a drill, he’s shit at it, it’s close to breaking down.  You’d be inside it, so no opportunities for stunts.  He’d appreciate the help of a keen young engineer, whatever she looks like.  But you’d be cut off from the Belt network.  For a while, possibly.”

Winnifred frowned a bit, drawing eyebrows together.

“Maybe that sounds good?  A fixer-upper, decent money, it wouldn’t be me bothering you.  Getting away from it all.”

She had applied for the job across the network, and he’d accepted, but once she arrived, he’d expressed surprise that she was as modded as she was.  She’d chosen that moment to confess that she might be in trouble and that she might not be able to work her full contract, if the judiciary interfered.  She’d really expected him to know already, but in terms of how little he used the Belt Network, he wasn’t very different from the Gray-Frocked that had attacked the science center.  So she’d had to explain.

Now she was in the position of being very unsure if he’d noticed she was being messaged constantly by members of her family, or if he was referring to the trouble she was in.  Was this a way to get more distance, free of that surveillance and nagging, or was it a way to duck the law a bit?

“A friend of mine is being held by the judiciary.  If I was underground and that delayed things in terms of the whole legal process, that’d… suck.  I want her back.”

“Your onboard.”

Winnifred shrugged.

[My predecessor,] her onboard said, unhelpfully.

“I don’t understand that.  I think you’re putting a lot of yourself onto it, filling in the blanks or assuming it’s more than it is.”

“Even if I was… does that change how I should handle it?” she asked.

“Yeah?” he said, more statement than question, but questioning nonetheless.  “Doesn’t it?”

She frowned a bit.

“Alright, look, I do have other things to do today.  I’ll pay you a bonus.  I’m not one to pry, I don’t know how much trouble you’re in, but I will say… think about after.  Where do you want to be, when you’re done earning the money, done getting your friend back?”

“I had a dream, but it feels like every step I take forward, it gets a step further out of reach.”

“Talk to the old hands, alright?” he asked.  “Hear them out, try to listen.  I’m not saying this is a plan, but some of them have been working at this at the expense of everything else.  No families, nowhere to go.  They’re usually happy to take someone eager under their wing.  Learn the good parts, don’t learn the… grit, the sourness, some of them have.  Maybe if you’re lucky, they leave you their earnings so far as an inheritance.  Get you closer to your ship you dream about.”

Winnifred sat up a bit.

“Yeah, I overheard you telling that modded lug.  I’m not saying this is a workable plan, but whether they’re teaching you what you couldn’t learn from studying simulations, getting you to think about the path you’re on, or passing something else onto you, I think you’d benefit.  I sure as shit don’t want you hanging around with the younger crop.  They’d encourage and follow shit like that stunt.”

She nodded.

He stood, so she stood too.

“If the judiciary picks you up, or you end up going back to your family… you can come back.  You’re alright.  If I’m not running a drill, I’ll know someone who does, I’ll tell them you’re alright.  Okay?  There’s a place, after all of this.”

She nodded.

“I feel like I’m fucking this up, and I’m annoyed at you because of that,” he said.  “No more stunts.  No more scaring me by getting close to hot metal, like the last time I brought you in here.  No more falling asleep in ducts, like the time before that.”

She nodded quickly.

“What was the time before that?”

“Staying away from people who blame the twenty-nine families for the trouble at the various docks.”

“That was it.  Yeah.  Get out of here.  Find old people, try not to annoy them too much.”

➨

“Who did it!?” Nikhil shouted.

“It’s fine,” Winnifred said.

Nikhil was a ‘gorilla’, with the kind of gleaming silver-white mods that Winnifred’s family had always disparaged a bit, saying it was the sort of thing rich indolents that weren’t serious about modding went for.

“We don’t fuck with each other,” Nikhil said.  He was big enough that his voice boomed.  “Since when do we bring grudges in here?”

Winnifred felt uncomfortable.

“The rats fucked with us first,” someone said.

“Who said that?” Nikhil asked, turning.

When nobody stepped forward, he slammed a fist into the side of the ship – it was a Bierkist-1081F, one of those bog standard ‘shop in a box’ ships that would land near any place there were people and operate as a store or small restaurant.  There were hundreds of variations, for different setups.

The bang made people cover ears, and some rose out of their seats.

“I’m going to go,” she told Nikhil.  “I’ll find somewhere to eat.  Come with me.”

“They trashed your things.”

“What do you expect to happen here?  Someone admits it?  Or you make an enemy of everyone here?” she asked.  She felt more sad than anything.  Embarrassed.  “The boss doesn’t want any hassle.”

“Tell them that!”

“Come with me.”

Nikhil turned, glaring around the room, as if he could somehow spot the culprit by some telltale sign or expression.

She crawled up the side of him and moved on all fours across his shoulders.  Bending down, she said, quiet, “If you aren’t outside in one minute, I’ll go do my own thing.”

“You should stand up for yourself.”

“Up to you,” she said.

Then she hopped off, onto the wall, and exited through the window that had been left open to let the smoke out- both from the meat in the kitchen and the cigarettes and the various wrapped drugs at the tables.

Her onboard provided a countdown.

“Thank you,” she told it.

[Not a problem.  I’m working within the constraints that I have.  I’m sorry that I don’t currently have the processing or resources to help you with your property, unless you would like help with universal insurance.]

“Nah,” she said.  “Sorry I’ve made your life hard.”

[I have no life, only function, and I have no need for apologies, but I’m glad if the apology helps you to feel better.  My functioning and your life could both be made easier if you re-enabled my adaptive architecture.]

“Not going to happen, buddy.”

[It is step three of the onboard installation.  You need not be afraid, Belt law restricts me from growing beyond my bounds or breaching your boundaries.  In-]

“I’m aware.  I did have an onboard, once.”

[In fact, I’m less likely to breach boundaries or cause problems as I adapt to you.]

Nikhil stepped outside.  He looked frustrated.

He was her age, and he’d been at this a little bit longer than she had.  Despite that, something about him made her feel like he was a kid.  A lack of lived experience, maybe.  The fact he didn’t get this.

He was modded, by his own choice, with his family’s support.  He hailed from a superstructure on Earth that followed certain old cultures, and there were people who got prickly about that, so he should have understood, at least a little.

“There are people getting onboards but not updating them, like you,” he said.  “They might push an update to the laws to force it.”

“They want us to keep eyes on each other.  That’s being accomplished.  Mostly,” Winnifred said.

“Mm.  The people here are saying when they leave the mining planet, they’re expecting to be forced to get onboards when they next land on-planet.  Or Belt law might forbid hiring people who aren’t onboarded.”

“It’s just a placeholder, anyway,” Winnifred said.  “It’d be nice if I got Toby back before they forced anything.  At least like this, my onboard isn’t… realized?  Actualized?”

“No idea,” Nikhil said.  He looked back at the building.  “They ruined everything you had.”

“Except my body.”

“They might do that next time.”

“And I’ll fight like hell, and sue them.  I sued the judiciary, last time around, putting me in that position.”

“Ballsy.  You wanted food?”

“Yeah.  Just a bite.  I’ll eat off your plate.  I don’t eat much.”

“And that’ll make you feel better?” Nikhil asked.

“I don’t-” she started, before stopping, and doing a kind of self-audit on herself.  Physical feelings, emotional feelings.

“What?”

“-I always feel like this, a little.  This isn’t new.”

He looked up at her.

And she chose that moment to jump down, with more force than necessary.  She settled, one foot on his right shoulder, two hands gripping his left, eyes peeking over hand.

“You’re hitching a ride, are you?”

“Onward,” she said.

“Can we stop at a mod shop?  I fucked up my hand punching the wall.”

“What kind of wimpy-ass gorilla are you?” she asked him, climbing up the one shoulder to perch on it, hands and feet together, legs bent.

“One who got decorative flair on the back.”

“Let’s eat, and I’ll buy tools to replace the ones that got ruined when they trashed my living space, and I’ll see what I can fix, first, how’s that?”

“Sure.  Thank you.”

“Thank you for getting mad on my behalf,” she said.

“You should get madder on your own behalf.”

“It’s useless, but thanks anyway,” she said.

They went off in search of food and a mod shop.

➨

“I hold dearly to the philosophy, make it yourself,” the old woman said.  She had skin with deep creases, and long white eyelashes, and she smoked like it was an art form, sometimes forgetting she had one cigarette in her mouth before she lit another.  White smoke from the cigarette and the wispy white hair and eyelashes gave her an ethereal air.  “What are the big expenses in your way?”

“My body.  A ship.”

“Body?  We’re supposed to be past that.  My great-great-great grandfather got us past that.  Food, shelter, health, all covered, for everyone in the Belt.”

“Post-scarcity got us past that,” another one of the old hands commented.

Winnifred shrugged.  “Modded body.  I dunno, sometimes feels like not being past it, having it be scarce, and hard, is the point.”

“Well, for me, figuring it all out is the point, Win.  Your body’s going to pieces?  Build a better body.  Learn to make it yourself.”

“There’s a lot of hurdles for that.  Fidelity.”

“Whassat?” the man asked.

“Response time and quality of sensation.  It’s one thing to have a crappy ship, so long as it gets you to where you need to be, or gets the job done.  But a crappy body-”

“You get used to it,” the woman said.  “Us old folk are used to it.”

“It’s different,” Winnifred said.

“Is it?  Are you sure?”

“My uncle killed himself because he couldn’t tolerate it.”

“You know that for sure, do you?” another man asked.  Not as old as the other two, but it seemed like decades of stimulants or drink had done a number on him.  Features, long-term focus, and speech seemed softened at the edges.

“What are you implying?” the old woman asked the man.

“Have you checked?” the man asked Winnifred, ignoring the question.  “Someone tells me to spend heaps of lux on something?  I check.”

“That’s not exactly what it is,” Winnifred clarified.  “The families, or my family in this case, they don’t get the lux from mods being sold and bought, and they weren’t telling me to spend it, they were just warning about what happens if I don’t.”

“I gotta piss,” the man said.  He had to put hands on table and chair to get to a standing position, and stood awkwardly, once upright, while getting his bearings.  He straightened more, then started off, with shuffling steps.  He paused for a moment.  “I’d check.”

“You can use that computer you’ve got living in your skin, can’t you?” the old woman asked.

“Could,” Winnifred said.

She’d never looked.  She could remember how the story had been told to her, all those years ago.  That it was a sensitive subject that she shouldn’t prod or bring up.  Or, it was implied, look up.

Remembering that, a part of her felt like she knew the answer, even without needing to check.

She wondered if that extended to fidelity.

The problem was, even now, members of her family were watching, listening in.  Making sure she was okay.  They sent messages, in hopes that this time, she’d listen or look.

If she ignored the family’s messages, and took this opportunity to check the story about her uncle, it would cross an invisible line.  Nobody had said anything, she hadn’t ever heard of it happening, but she’d lived with her family all her life, she had seen the way the other families operated.

If she checked the story, or started testing the limits of fidelity, then they’d act like she’d abandoned the family.

They’d come here, to get her.

So long as she didn’t, she could pretend, at least, that she was keeping her distance because the judiciary was paying attention.  The people who watched her could pretend the same.

“You were saying, about making your own things?”

“Make your own body parts, make your own ship.”

“I like the way types of ships have history.”

“Bah, you’re one of those, are you?”

“But I would like to make a ship, just to know the ins and outs, on a level I can’t get through pure simulation.  I wouldn’t know where to set up.”

“You would have to have a place you call home, or somewhere you can keep things,” the woman said.

“Or where to get materials.”

“Honey, baby girl, we mine planets for incredible quantities of raw material, we turn that material into incredible quantities of shit, and then when we have no use for it, we toss it.  It’s out there.  Junk in near-mint condition, discarded to places outside the Belt’s orbit.”

“Huh.”

“It’s how I got started.”

“I like a lot of that.”
