“When we finish this contract, catch a ride with me back to Kiviuq.  You take care of me if my health fails while we’re on route, I’ll loan you my rig.  It’s ugly, but it’s got the essentials to get you out there.  You go, net some junk, bring it back, workshop what you can put together.  Twin g-sails to get off planet, propulsion…”

“What sort of engine?”

“Winnifred,” Nikhil called out.

“That’s a big boy right there,” the old woman said.

“What’s up?” Winnifred asked.

“Bunch of the guys are coming back this way.  Some of them are a problem.  If you need backup…”

“I’ll go.”

“We were having a nice conversation,” the old lady protested.

“We can talk again after.”  If I don’t get arrested in the meantime.  “Sorry.”

She made herself scarce.

➨

She’d retreated to the ducts.  Things had escalated, over the course of the last month, since they’d trashed her quarters and gotten away with it.  Someone who worked on the shroud had an onboard, and they worked near some of the people who had instigated things with Winnifred.  Through them, she’d overheard them saying they were going to come after her, to damage her body.

Nikhil had seen her watching that footage, and had reported it.  But that group was on loan from another company, with its own drills and crews, and all that could be done was that they were sent back to that company.  Except, at the end of the day, all the different teams at different drills, working for different employers and companies, all met at the same hubs where the ships dropped down and shops set up.

And they had friends here, on this team, who invited them back to the buildings with the quarters here.  So it wasn’t like they were gone.

She could have kicked up a fuss, asking that they be banned, but the calculus of that… it was shitty, but if she got them booted, there were a lot of people who’d been content to sit back and do nothing who’d be pissed at her.  And they’d pick right up where that other group had left off.  Probably with renewed anger.

Easier to duck out, find more comfortable ground.

There weren’t enough cameras and onboards around for her to easily keep an eye out for them.  So, against Shain’s wishes, she’d abandoned her bunk and she’d found a vent to sleep in.

Still, it was hard to sleep.  She’d gotten close, but then the idea of a drone had crossed her mind, and she’d been woken up all the way by the half-formed idea of that group of workers firing up a drone to get her in the vents, and the half-formed but very vivid memory of moving through that ship in the dark, her body taken from her, with Kathe’s heavily armed drones lying in wait.

So she followed some of the recordings of A and the other members of Generation Color as they lived in an alternate universe- one where the Inui had escaped containment and taken over.

Every member of Generation Colors was equipping themselves with some variety of nanotech weaponry, or personal augmentation.

She put herself in the scene.  She left her body inert, but had her onboard give her all the sensations as if she was moving through the scene, touching things in actuality.

“There are hard conversations we need to have,” Blue said.  “People we know are out there, compromised.”

“They aren’t people we know.  They’re offspring.  Inui impale you, and implant their genetic material, and you give birth to something that’s Inui, but with human faculties,” Jan responded.

“That’s one guess we’re making,” Krick countered.  “Maybe they were always intelligent all along.”

“Then what do they need from us?” Amber asked.

A put her gun down on the glass coffee table in front of her.  It clacked as it settled.  All eyes were drawn to it.

She didn’t say anything, but she left her hand out there, extended in the direction of the gun.

“Nanotech?” Amber asked.  “That opens up a whole pile of questions and worries.”

“Not right now,” Winnifred said, quiet.

A turned and gave Winnifred the smallest of smiles, before turning to the rest of the room.  “Not right now.  Let’s think on it overnight, but some of us have gone more than twenty-four hours without a break to sleep, since our sleep shifts got interrupted by the last attack.  And some of us are getting full body workups by nanotech.  That’s tiring.”

Red, and Jan.

“You’re tired?” Amber asked.

A nodded.

“Okay.  We’ll step out, do our chores, you take a shift to sleep.”

A reached out for Amber’s hand, and Amber seemed surprised.  But she reached back out, holding A’s hand for a second.  A squeezed it before letting go.

Everyone sorted themselves out.  A, Red,and Jan remained in the room, as did Winnifred.

The rest left, dimming the lights as they went.

“Good call,” A said, to Winnifred.  She smiled.

This was the point, in most simulations that she injected herself into, that she normally backed out.  But talking to Nikhil and the old woman, and a few others she’d seen around, she wondered if a part of that was that inserting herself into a scene made it feel like she cheapened it.  Made it worse by existing inside it.

Made it less authentic?  Sure.  Obviously.  But worse?

That was more about her, and her relationship to herself.

So she didn’t want to quit out, abruptly.

She wasn’t even sure what she wanted.  She’d asked that the plot be put on hold.

Making this awkward.

Nikhil was going to get himself kicked out if he didn’t calm down.  He didn’t get it, and if he didn’t get it, there was no chance the others could.

A, Winnifred felt, got it.  There was a look in her eyes, and a quality to her voice.  Whatever ‘it’ was, she got it.

“Can I have a hug?” Winnifred asked.

“Come,” A said.

Winnifred approached, wary.

And A had her sit down.  The room was divided by long, low, shallow platforms that could be stairs to the cushioned benches by the windows -which Jan and Red were using as beds- but could also be seats, like in some Roman amphitheatre, or beds, if the room was very full.

They ended up lying down, lying on one level, with heads on the level above.  A with her arms around Winnifred.

“This okay?”

A understood.  Was that the answer to the riddle Robert had raised?  Something A had seen or figured out, or something more unique to her experience?

It didn’t matter.

This was okay.  Winnifred nodded.

She had someone who understood, now.

That meant she could relax enough to sleep.

The lines between reality and simulation, simulation and dream, and dream and reality folded neatly into one another.

She, in her dozing, feeling safer and more whole than she had in a long time, could allow herself to admit that Nikhil did care, even if he was young.  There were people like the old woman.  Her boss, Shain, who’d been pretty decent, if strict.

There were people who cared, or who stepped up enough that it mattered.

It just felt lonely sometimes, even with that.

This helped.

“Winnifred.”

It was a call, cutting past all of those folded-up lines and feelings.

Shain.

She turned off the simulation, banishing the A who slept beside her, holding her.  Her immediate thought, before the fact that she’d broken a soft rule he’d set, about sleeping in her designated quarters, was that it was her family, that they’d decided she’d betrayed them, and they’d come.

They hadn’t.

“It’s the judiciary.”

She collected her things, quickly, then made her way down to solid ground.  She didn’t make them come all the way to her.

“Your family sure tried to stall things,” Investigator Carlen Holder said, as Winnifred approached.  “I didn’t get the impression you were following the drama.  The big one was that they tried to argue an onboard’s recordings of a protected culture’s doings was private.”

“Do I get Toby back?” Winnifred asked.

“No, Winnifred.  We’ve found evidence of your involvement in multiple incidents.  Judiciary intelligence has made a ruling.  I’m here to arrest you.”

“I’ll insist on a representative.  A family lawyer.  He should be reaching out to you now.”

“He is.”

“Tell them you want a review by a jury of your peers,” her counsel messaged her.

“I want a review of the ruling by a jury of peers.”

“Juries of peers can be more harsh than automatic rulings,” Carlen said.  “Especially when it’s a member of the twenty-nine families.  Prejudice comes into effect.”

“I have nothing to say unless you need me to say something procedural in nature.  Please direct any statements or inquiries to my counsel.”

“This is how they pull you back in, Winnifred.  You’re turning to the families, their resources, what they told you to do.  It’s only a few years.  Do the time, then walk away from it all.”

“I have nothing to say unless you need me to say something procedural in nature.  Please direct any statements or inquiries to my counsel.”

3.3.W – MUTE

Winnifred

“What I’m wondering,” Carlen said, “is whether you’ll hire the smart lawyer or the slow one.”

Sitting opposite Carlen, Winnifred gave her a look, stopping just short of an eyeroll.  “I have nothing to say unless it’s procedural in nature. Please direct any statements or inquiries to my counsel.”

“It’s fine, you don’t need to keep saying that.  I’ll assume you won’t respond.  I know you all have more than the two lawyers, but they fall into two categories.  I’ve paid some attention to your family over the years, seeing how you do business and what you get involved in, which is why I’m lead investigator on this particular case.  You’re gaming the system, with lawyers specifically chosen to do things one of two ways.”

The Inclose was carrying them to the detention facility, which was a station-ship orbiting one of the mining planets.  It was an old sort of ship, dating back to a military era, and back in the day, would have deposited a group of six to thirty people and their equipment, drones, or small vehicles at a location.  A box with a back gate that doubled as a ramp, exterior as thick as possible, G-sails protected by external plating.  It was inelegant, with a moderate top speed of eighty kilometers an hour at best, but capable of flying a straight course and holding up despite small to moderate incoming fire.

Carlen commented, “The slow lawyers bog down the system, interrupt, make filings, drag things out by filing everything as late as they can get away with.  Which, with the way things go, works pretty well for all of you.  You work on ships and ship owners want to go places.  Or you go places.  If enough people move in different directions while a case is pending, it kills it.  Even if it doesn’t, the way the Intelligence rulings from the judiciary works, time passing reduces the sentence or fine.”

Winnifred’s eyes roved around the interior of the Inclose.  Obviously, very few things held up to large firepower, and virtually nothing held up to nanotech or oblique weaponry.

[You do not seem to be paying attention.  I do sport a notetaking feature, if your attention is otherwise occupied.]

“No,” she told the onboard.

“You alright there?”  Carlen asked.

“I have nothing to say-”

Carlen raised a hand, stopping her.  “You’re a clever girl, I think you’re listening more than you’re pretending you are.  And speaking of clever- the clever lawyers are… impressive, considering you’re dock workers.  Not as good as the top politicians and biggest business owners have, but impressive.  For the past little while, while you were working on the drill, we’ve been dealing with the slow.  Are we going to see your lawyers bring out their brains?  Or will it be continued stalling, while you’re left in limbo?  I’m genuinely curious.”

Winnifred briefly met Carlen’s eyes.

Why was this ship so dark?  It wasn’t like lighting was a huge cost.  Was it to be imposing?  It tied into other questions she had, like that one about why they’d gone with an Inclose in the first place.  Did they keep it for the judiciary as a just-in-case?  To protect VIPs in a crisis?  Or because it stood for that past era?  Keeping proper weapon ships would be problematic, but they could get away with keeping this.  If that was what this was.

She banged the back of her head slightly against the wall, just to feel how solid it was.  Solid.  She wasn’t sure what she’d expected.  A hollow sound?

[I’m aware my predecessor took measures to protect your brain from concussion, but please refrain-]

Winnifred banged her head against the wall again.  Still very solid.

[-from doing that.]

“You don’t seem optimistic,” Carlen said.

I’m not even really thinking about that, Winnifred thought.  Aloud, she said, ““I have nothing to say unless you need me to say something procedural.  Direct any statements or inquiries to my counsel.”

“How angry is your family at you, for being so far out of reach?  That would determine if they drag this out at your expense and their benefit, or aim for a decisive legal maneuver.”

“I have nothing to say unless you need me to say something procedural in nature. Please direct any statements or inquiries to my counsel.”

“Speaking of,” Winnifred’s counsel said.  “I wouldn’t make it there before Winnifred arrives where you’re going and intake starts.  I would like Investigator Carlen Holder to make herself scarce.  I can have Winnifred’s onboard project me into the space, and we can communicate using whispers, with all listening equipment barred from listening on those channels.  I’ll get us started from afar.”

“We’re on a small ship, counsel,” Carlen said.  “Should I step off into space?”

“You’re free to on any other occasion, but for today, to avoid putting my client at risk when you open the back of the ship, I’d suggest moving into the separate cockpit space, instead.”

“Occupied by the pilot and copilot.”

“With standing room between them.”

“Not nearly enough.”

“You can be uncomfortable, slouching so you don’t bang your head on the ceiling, Investigator Holder, but I must insist on having time with my client before I make my first filings, before intake.  There’s a lot of ground to cover.  I’ll further add, Investigator Holder, that you seem intent on grossly biasing and influencing my client, which would make for even more ground to cover- or ground to recover, if you would.”

“It looks like he’s a fast one,” Carlen said, to Winnifred.  “Lucky you.  Does that mean they care, or are you protecting someone important?”

“Thank you so much, Investigator Holder, for illustrating my point for me.  I’ll be including that comment in my filings as well.”

Carlen got up, and walked over to the heavy door that separated cockpit from the back of the ship.

Winnifred’s counsel reached out to her onboard to request a connection and simulate something, and Winnifred sat back as words appeared floating in the air: a quick snapshot of name, educational background, prior work experience, current work, and notable cases.  The white text in the gloom became a cloud, and when the cloud dissolved, there he was.

It felt old fashioned.

He wasn’t modded, she noted.  He had orange-brown hair and beard of about the same length, and a trim suit.  He seemed a bit young, and not in the way that most would stay young.  Like he was still a boy.

[Shall I take notes?]

“Mute, and keep no records.”  When he talked, his lips moved faintly out of sync with the whispers she heard.  He was having it translated.  “I’m waiting for an audit of the local systems… we’re doing something very different today if they are listening in after all.  Looks like we’re clear.  On the rare occasion, you do get a superstructure judiciary trying to pull something.  Not today.  Hi Winnifred.”

“Hello,” she replied, whispering for the first time in a long time.

“I’m Garret, but call me counsel, that’s what I’m going to be on all forms, records, and filings, outside of the signature field.  I’ve worked for five years at Howington Station.  What you’ve done right: you didn’t say anything.  Good.  You guys are good about that.  Could be better: you haven’t been responding to family.”

She wanted to sigh.  She didn’t.  She wanted to say that Michal had convinced her to do the sabotage job, putting her on a team with two dangerous people, and they’d hurt her badly.

“I didn’t want to complicate things for the family.”

“Let’s keep it uncomplicated for everyone,” he said, and it was translated to whisper.  To Winnifred, it felt a lot like he’d wanted to say that in a way that emphasized that ‘everyone’ was one person, Michal, and the translation had taken the weight out of the enunciation.  Maybe that was unfair.  “And I’ll do the best job I can on your behalf while we’re at it.”

Maybe not unfair.

He carried on, saying, “As I was saying, doing the best I can would be easier if you had been in touch.  I think we could have steered the narrative and positioned things to take incarceration off the table.”

“Is that even possible?”

“Now?  Maybe.  At least in the long term.  If you’d been in touch?  We could have put more emphasis on the fact they put you in danger, indirectly, by locking off your onboard.  Given the pressure from Belt-wide governments to get people to get onboards, that would have been timely.”

She nodded a bit.

He went on, “But we can’t undo the past.  I have a four pronged approach informed by the many members of your extended family I and my colleagues have worked with.  First, and most pressing… you, intake, and where you’re going after intake.” 

➨

“My name is Anide Marski, I’m prisoner staff,” a woman told her.  She had long hair in need of a combing, and a prisoner uniform with a vest worn over it.  Matching tattoos of women in an old, thick-bordered style sat on either side of her neck.

“I’ll be doing your intake.  Please don’t fuck this up for me and try to smuggle anything past me, and if you’re going to be vicious, can you stab me in the gut instead of knocking me out?  They can fix that.”

“Anide,” a voice warned, over the intercom.

“Welcome, I’ll be doing your intake,” Anide said, in a fake-sounding voice.  “It looks like things are in progress.  Step my way?”

Winnifred walked through the gate, then, as Anide motioned, lifted her arms.  The guard did a preliminary search.

“You’re more interesting than the usual.  Fully modded?”

“Aside from the skin you see now,” Winnifred answered.

“Do you mind stripping?  This isn’t me being slick, it’s a part of the process.”

“Anide,” the voice on the intercom warned, again.

Winnifred was wearing a loose bodysuit.  She didn’t.  She shook her head.

“Remain behind the line on the floor while doing that, I’ll go through your possessions.”

Winnifred did.

Her counsel had already, with the help of a company intelligence to gather data and assess patterns, selected the jury, making some arguments along the way that to be a peer of Winnifred meant they had to understand the arguments of culture.  It hadn’t been a complete win, but they hadn’t expected one either.

“Winnifred has entered intake now, so let’s make this quick,” her counsel argued.  “I would like to urge authorities to be gentle and as unobtrusive as possible.  Winnifred has been traumatized as a result of the dereliction of Judiciary authorities-“

“Objection.”

“-as established in a prior ruling.”

[Overruled.]

“Thank you.  To revisit that trauma by stripping her down of parts would be grotesque.”

Anide was listening in, while going through Winnifred’s bag and gave Winnifred a look.

Her counsel went on to say, “She is equipped to remove all necessary parts and assist in the inspection, instead of being subjected to a full strip-down of parts by someone else.”

“The Judiciary moves that we skip both the strip-down and a lot of other questions by virtual incarceration.  We put her to sleep, round the clock care, and she undergoes her sentence in a virtual reality.  Safe, healthy, ideal environment, virtual resources.”

“Counsel for the defendant disagrees.  Health outcomes for the heavily modded are considerably worse with that round-the-clock care, the client and I have discussed, and she doesn’t do well in virtual environments.  I submit files thirty through forty-one, with three highlighted, showing she doesn’t perform well in sustained virtual environments.”

[Anything further from the judiciary?] the overseeing intelligence asked.

“The judiciary has a lot of concerns if we’re not going with virtual incarceration.”

[If need be we’ll get to them after.  I’ll rule that the jury should review what’s been provided, ask any questions, and let us know if there is consensus on any points raised.]

A few of those files depicted scenarios like the one from last night, with A.  Her getting shy or feeling awkward and backing out.  The idea of feeling that level of situational dysphoria and being unable to back out, boxed in by a simulation?  No.

Most of the scenes being submitted to contribute to the argument were with A.  She wondered if the jury would make anything of that as they went through them, watching or skipping through.

She nodded a few times as her bag was emptied and inventoried.  Each item got a description and an assigned value.  Nothing to argue there.

There was a brief deliberation by the jury, with some guidance by the observing, impartial intelligence.

“Granted,” the jury foreperson said.  “No virtual incarceration for now, if the defendant’s counsel can argue for something else.  Can she disassemble herself?”

“She can take herself apart as much as is possible, and hand over pieces to be examined,” Winnifred’s counsel said.  “I think she’s okay with that?”

Winnifred, not even orbiting the same planet as her counsel, nodded.

“She’s okay with that.”

[Let’s go ahead with that.  Move on to making your case for an alternative.]

Winnifred began to take apart one hand, starting with the claw blades, which she laid out on the table between herself and Anide.  That done, she disconnected her arm at the shoulder, draped it on the table, and then, with tail helping, broke each part down into summary smaller parts.  When she was comfortable doing so, she let the guard take over.

“Lighter than I’d have thought,” Anide observed.

“Yep.”

“Being very clear that this is only for temporary holding until we can determine the veracity of the case, I’d move that we have a like-for-like adjustment of Winnifred’s modded body parts, to something acceptable to the judiciary.”

[Like-for-like?  Clarify.]

“While it’s not our primary focus, value is a consideration here.  Winnifred recently acquired a new body as recompense for one that was stolen from her, because the judiciary, in their shortsightedness, left her unable to communicate for help in a crisis situation.”

“Objection.  Prejudicial interpretation of events.”

“Ruled on already.”

[Overruled.  Carry on, counsel, but be aware you’re walking a line.]

“It would be very strange and curiously punitive, for the judiciary to give her a new body, but then to come around and seek, for other alleged crimes, to take her body away from her.  Imagine paying someone restitution in the amount of one million lux, then being summarily fined by that institution for one million lux, the moment they have an excuse.”

“That’s not what this is and counsel has seen enough members of the twenty-nine families arrested and considered for incarceration to know it.”

[It does not seem that that is what is happening.  The jury should know that removal or replacement of modded parts is standard when someone heavily modded is brought into custody.  You had other points, counsel?]

“Fidelity.  I can submit the following entries, please have a look through those.  For members of the jury who don’t know, Fidelity is how real, accurate, and fine-tuned the physiological experience is.  To significantly downgrade would be like forcing someone to endure living with a body that has had multiple strokes.”

Winnifred got her arm back, with an attachment that would go between shoulder and the shoulder socket.  Barring anything from being transferred from the main chamber of the body into the arm.

The judiciary countered, “The judicary argues that fidelity issues of the type defendant’s counsel is talking about have never been truly scientifically proven.  There is no evidence.”

“Self-reporting is evidence, especially in the numbers we’re talking about.”

She removed her other arm, feeling the very fidelity issues that were being talked about, in how clumsy the arm felt with that added hundredth of a second of lag, every movement and process checked.

[What’s the cost, if we assume fidelity is necessary, as opposed to not?]

“Purely financial,” Winnifred’s counsel reported.  “A matter of lux.  I would argue that, insofar as she should lose any hard corners, bladed edges, or other parts of herself that could be weaponized in a prison environment, we swap out those parts.  There are softer-edged variants.  I have a catalogue.  I’m getting ahead of myself, so these are submissions eighty-one through one-twenty-six.”

The intelligence that was acting as arbitrator commented, [That’s a lot for the jury to review, counsel.]

“It’s for the judiciary and their intelligences, and yourself to review.  The jury can look at the pictures to understand in abstract what we’re talking about, and see that we’re disarming my client more than a normal human would be, going into custody.”

[Judiciary?]

“This is all simplified if she sucks it up and goes to a virtual incarceration.”

[Let’s call that a destination of last resort.  Can we find compromise?]

Hearing the intelligence talk, she felt a pang, and missed Toby.

“We’re not even sure what that would look like.”

“Counsel submits one option.  She would retain the bladed fingertips that are natural to her, but with her intelligence keeping her from any and all harm to others.  As a secondary safety measure, please see submission one-twelve, already provided, we can pair that with a rudimentary intelligence, separate from the rest of Winnifred’s systems, that arbitrates on its own.”

“Investigator Carlen Holder, making her own submission on behalf of the judiciary.  Winnifred of Griffey Docks was stripped down of all parts and proved remarkably resourceful, working to move through a derelict ship and arm herself.  We should be cautious.  Rounded edges and auto-retracting claws aren’t going to be enough.”

Well fuck you too, Winnifred thought.

“Counsel would like to know, if the judiciary has any submissions to show the jury to support that point?”

“You know we don’t,” the representative for the judiciary responded.  A man.  Carlen had stepped back after submitting the one statement.

“You don’t have submissions because Winnifred’s onboard was shut off by the judiciary,” her counsel reported.

“And her connection to the belt network was cut off by a co-conspirator, who later, according to our evidence, turned on her.  We can’t rule out that this is a long play.”

“Objection.”

There was a break, where, presumably, words were being exchanged between judiciary, counsel, and the overseeing Intelligence, without anyone else able to listen in.

[Objection sustained.  There is no proof Winnifred conspired on that level.  Jury is to disregard.  We will address later to equalize for any bias this may have left the jury.  Any further points from counsel?]

“None.”

[Judiciary?]

“The judiciary has a few points to argue and questions to ask about the choices of equipment on the proposed list, but we’d find this acceptable.  It should be noted, she’d be largely unarmed, in an environment where most aren’t.”

“That’s fine,” Winnifred murmured.  “So long as I’m quick enough to get out of trouble.”

“My client has no objection.”

“Then we don’t either.”

“Looks like you’re getting a new body,” Anide said, examining Winnifred’s pelvis.

“Again.”

“That’s going to take a minute to pull together.  I guess we’ll be in this room for a while.”

“Sorry.”

“It’s hours I’m clocking, to reduce my sentence.  I’ll deal.”

Winnifred could feel the pressure.  She’d gotten used to being able to just go out, do her own thing, stay clear of people.  Now she was stuck in a room, and it was going to get much, much worse later.

“Got any tips?  Stories?” Winnifred offered.  People liked to talk.

“I’ve got stories.”

➨

“I’ll be working on your behalf in the background.  I’ll reach out a few times a week,” her counsel messaged her.  “Anything you need?”

“It sounds weird, but my body-”

She had new arms, and extended them, to look down their length.  Her claw-tips were weirdly pearlescent, and the fingers were overly cosmetic ones that naturally colored themselves to transition in color from the light gray of her arms to the pearlescent color.

The guard near her gave her a look.  She dropped her arms.

“What about it?”

“-It’s not the color I’m used to.  It distracts me, when I see it out of the corner of my eye.”

“I’ll schedule you for a paint job.  We can pull you out, send someone into the shop, have them paint you, you’d sit around and dry, then go back.  If that’s okay?  We can make the argument that it’s part of your body image, that you be painted black.”

“Please.”

“I’ll make a submission.  Other than that, I think we came out okay?  I’m tickled.”

“Yes.  Thank you.”

“Stay in touch with family, Winnifred.”

The fingers that led to the claw tips were one example of where they’d come out more than okay.  Her counsel had made the argument for a like-to-like adaptation, while preserving her fidelity and quality of life.  The judiciary had agreed, but they hadn’t seemed to know what that meant.  They were obligated to supply her fingers that met those requirements: nonviolent in any application, capable of working with other parts, including the claws that would auto-withdraw if she so much as grazed biology that wasn’t her own, equal or better in fidelity, and equal or better in quality of life.

Her hands, bought after she’d left Sherman Station, before she’d started working on the drill, had cost eleven thousand.  These ones, the cheapest on offer that met all of those requirements, cost fifty one thousand.  It was not the only part that was like that.

Her counsel had gotten more of a kick out of that than she had.  The man A had talked to at the opera house had said money was fake, or something like that, and that had stuck with her- a very weird thing to dwell on, when it was also such a looming shadow in her life.

Mostly, she was glad to have something workable.  She had a new spine, without the vertebrae aesthetic – no hooked protrusions.  Her shoulders met the arm more seamlessly, instead of the part that poked up and out.  Lots of parts like that.  Smoother, undecorated, not even painted black.  Her prisoner uniform felt like it moved too much against her body.

She walked down a long hallway, following a guard and Anide.  The hallway was structured so that if the prisoner population tried to break out, they’d have to come down this way.  The floor had diamonds painted on it that apparently popped up as monodirectional cover for people with nonlethal weaponry.  Or they popped up as turrets.  Winnifred supposed it was a surprise which it would be.  In a hallway, they’d have nowhere to dodge, or run.

“No conversation with your onboard, lots of homework.  They want you to find people on the outside who will support you in a positive way on the outside.”

Would that be her family?

“Thought I was doing that.  Then they arrested me.”

Anide snorted.  “And no entertainment that isn’t reading, self-directed creativity.  So you can draw, write, dance, I guess, if you aren’t bothering anyone.”

“Can I build?  Simulate building a ship or engine?”

“I don’t have a clue.  Weird thing to go straight to.  Ask, I guess?  Big thing is, they want you to think about what you’ve done.  No gambling, no games unless it’s something like chess, on the floor, with others, no simulations, no shows, no music-”

No A?

“-They want you to take your time with your thoughts.”

“Can I study?”

“They really encourage it.”

Winnifred nodded.

She glanced through her onboard system, and saw her lawyer was having a conversation, muted to her, about something else.  He hadn’t explicitly said goodbye, but it looked like that was going to be it, until their next chat.

They reached the end of the hallway.  Winnifred took it all in.  This wasn’t the sort of ship where schematics were posted online.  That led to jailbreaks, maybe.  It was barely a ship, too, but she didn’t want to dwell on that.  Lots of anchoring here helped support the vault-like door.  It gave her ideas about what the space around this would look like.

“Welcome to floor zero,” Anide told her.  “Those with trials in progress.”

Floor zero had five hundred people, just like her, each with their own individual room.  The floor formed a square, despite the fact the ship itself wasn’t square -Winnifred was already imagining the types of spaces that would fill the remainder of the floor, like admin- and was ringed with three layers of cells, stacked on each other like bricks.  In the center was something that looked like a large pillar, with some alternate cells within.  Some were open, showing rooms barren of just about anything, except a toilet and a mattress, others were sealed shut and locked.

Prisoners mingled.  Young, old, men, women, very few modded, many unmodded.  She could see people who had obvious disabilities or syndromes, people who stood out for their very white or very dark skin.  All in simple white shirts with looser fitting black overshirts over top of them, white undergarments with loose fitting black pants over those.  Many wore hard foam shoes, which had a way of making people walk like they were tens of years older than they were.  Unsure of their own footsteps.  The rest wore slippers.

She didn’t have that issue.  Her feet were metal on a metal floor.

She drew more glances than most, she was pretty sure.

“Near the entrance, the crabs of the crab bucket.  Those without the lux depend on the kindness of provided counsel, who handle the work with a triage system.  That can mean weeks of waiting and situations getting gradually more desperate, until someone gets on it, and then it’s a rush to get a good outcome.  They hang out at the tables by the front door because it gives them that slightly better shot at getting someone.  You don’t want to be on the toilet on the other side of the floor when they call your name, or if someone comes and decides they want something easier, and they’ll pick someone they can see.”

“Tough situation to be in.”

“Mm hmm.  They’re… not the most dangerous, but I wouldn’t test them either.  That kind of waiting, that level of desperation?  Don’t cut their place in line.”

“Yeah.”  The group had a look to them- a thousand yard stare that looked very close to being a glare.

“If you turn your eyes to our left, by the stairs, you can see four examples of the squids.  Nanotech and gene modding taken to an extreme.  Usually cosmetic, but there’s always that chance they got assigned someone like me, but dumber, who missed the hidden weaponry in a weird body part.  Consider them always armed.”

Winnifred had the impression a good number of the ‘squids’ had had horns, but had them removed, which left the sucker-like empty holes on foreheads, scalps, and shoulders.  Maybe that was the reason for the name?  Or maybe a lot of them had had tentacles, once.

“More harmless than you’d think.  They don’t care about much.  Just remember they’re always armed.  Theoretically.”

“What happens to you if you miss something like that?”

“We get stabbed.”

“There’s no safety measures?”

“I mean, there’s guards, but there just isn’t a lot of interest from the wider population to do a job like this.  Too dangerous, unglamorous, people don’t want to do it, machines aren’t well suited for it, intelligences having that kind of authority over people scares people too much to allow it.  They assume we conspired with the person we’re doing intake with, somehow, to get the contraband through, and we get punished.  Lots of pressure.”

Toward the end of the meeting with her counsel, they’d had an exchange.  She’d been overwhelmed with legal terminology.  He’d said something to the effect of, ‘What you need to do is trust.  Trust in me, trust in the families, and trust that they- Carlen Holder and the rest of that monolith, want to appear to be fair more than they want to go after you.  That’s a weakness we exploit.’

She’d asked him.  Wasn’t it easier for that monolith to be fair?

He’d sat back- or the simulation of him had sat back, and he’d let out an uncharacteristic, ‘Nahhhhh,‘  As if he’d needed the sound and all the derision that came with it to fill the back of that armored transport ship.  ‘Humans?  They want things to be easy.  So they’ll let Intelligences handle the cases, turning justice into math.  They’ll choose appearances over vengeance.  Us?  We do things the hard way.‘

So strange, that he assumed himself a part of the twenty-nine families so easily, when he’d been unmodded, wearing a suit.

Ease.  The shortcuts taken.

Indolence.

It felt like a betrayal of herself to use her family’s language like that.  Which wasn’t to say she didn’t love her family, or love the culture.  She did.

“Over there, long hair, big beards, ripped sleeves, tattoos?  Hidebound.”

“Not a fish?” Winnifred asked.  “Or is it?”

“Huh?”

“The others were crabs, squid?”

“Oh, maybe that was a thing, once.  Nothing like that here.  Hidebound are the old families, who grow up with shitty parents and turn out shitty as a result.  Shit’s basically free, and mom will convince her little boys they aren’t worth shit if they can’t shoplift, before they can read, criminals raising criminals.  And they don’t get along.  They hold grudges against other hidebound families for so long they forget the reasons.  That’s the way it’s been since before there were superstructures.”

“That’s… familiar-ish,” Winnifred said.  “My family does some of that.”

“Stop right there.  You all?  You pretend,” Anide said, with a sudden vehemence that turned a few heads around them.  “You pretend to be old families, but you aren’t.  Be fucking careful, because if you pretend around some of them-?”

Anide pointed at the hidebound.

“-they won’t be as nice about it as I’m being right now.  They’ll put you on that list of people to hold grudges against, and they’ll accept coming here if it’s necessary to let you and your so-called families know they remember.”

“You’re one of them?”

“I was going to be cuter about it, or make a joke.  I hadn’t decided which.  Now I’m not feeling cute or jokey.  We’re not the same.”

“Got it,” Winnifred said.

“They try to split us up between facilities and floors, but it doesn’t work.  They tell us we can’t associate while we’re here, no standing within one and a half meters of one another?  We stand one and a half meters and ten centimeters apart, and there’s too many of us, anyway.  For now, at least.”

You guys are dying out too?

“Moving on.  You learn to recognize other groups.  Frauds and Innocents.  The old folk who play chess, the old folk who don’t, mostly safe…”

Winnifred was reminded of the people she’d left behind on the mining planet.

Her attention was drawn to her FoV display.  Her onboard wouldn’t communicate or allow messages, but had left the little folder with the icon telling her how many messages her family had sent, and they were sending a good number.

Had something happened?  More specifically, were they pissed?  She had to think back.

She hadn’t done a good enough job of pushing back against Anide in saying her own family was legitimate.

Fuck.

“…You’ll recognize those guys from the news, if you watch any news.  We have three here right now but there are a lot more on the other floors, where others are staying long-term.  All of these groups have representation elsewhere, except the crabs, I guess.  These ones?  Terrace wanderers.  Gray-frocked.”

Winnifred startled, realizing.  When she looked over, she saw them glaring at her.

“Hey,” Anide nudged Winnifred.  Winnifred almost stumbled.  When Winnifred’s attention was fully diverted, Anide said, “No eye contact.  Don’t fuck about.  I’ve been mentioning oh, this group’s dangerous, this group isn’t.  A lot of those people have onboards, so they might get one good swing in or fuck with your food tray before their onboard hits the brakes.  Some are craftier, like my people, they find other ways to get at you.  But the frocked?  No onboards with brakes, and if you set them off, it’s like a switch flicks and everything goes red.  Prison doesn’t want to keep them all in restraints on principle.  One of the top groups to stay away from.”

Winnifred nodded.

“Used to be easier.  They had someone in laundry who stained some clothes darker, tried to get them to members of their group.  You could recognize them from a distance and stay away.  That got shut down.  They look like everyone else, usually.  Sometimes they have dumb haircuts.  Take note, and remember, no direct onboard-to-you communication, so you have to be the one to recognize the faces and the stupid hair.”

“Right.  Good to know, thank you.”

Winnifred glanced back, trying not to look like she was looking.

She’d followed A for a bit, now, and watched everything from the first performance to the start of her career.  She’d seen the science center attack a few times.  She’d watched A’s life leading up to that, patchy, but she was filling in the patches.

The gray-frocked had never been something she’d dwelt on.  In part, because she hadn’t had the ability.

Being here?  Where they were?

It got her attention in the way a new or rare ship did.

They were still watching her.

“Another of the top groups?  There.  Very, very new.  Mostly here, but I guess they’ll have representation elsewhere.  We’re not even sure what to call them.  I’ve heard ‘the Grotesques’.  They don’t like the onboard thing.  Or they really like it.  They figure if you’re going to look through their eyes to see what they’re doing, or watch from nearby eyes and cameras, they might as well make you regret it.”

Of that group of eight or nine, five were in restraints.  They were underweight or overweight, with circles under their eyes, and poor complexions.  Something about them- their eyes were sunken.  Winnifred had the vague sense they smelled, but wasn’t close enough to get a sniff.

“It’s like the onboard stuff broke them.  Or the people who do anything for attention found an outlet.  A way to get guaranteed attention.  No holds barred, even if it involves animals, torturing themselves, or self mutilation.  Peeling their own dick skin aside to nail it to a table.”

Winnifred turned to Anide, frowning.

“Do you think I’m lying?”

“I didn’t need that mental image.”

“Shock, violence, offending decency laws.  Or general decency.  Blasting noise while strobing their living spaces with alternating pink and green lights and video of dogs fucking, torturing themselves in case anyone might try observing them.  Eventually they get arrested on Indecency laws.”

The Gray-Frocked were the only ones willing to venture within a table of them.

Gray-Frocked who still watched Winnifred, and had Winnifred’s attention in turn.  They were a mystery, an unanswered question.

“That’s another group, the Indecents, but we don’t have many right now.  Milder version, There are more downstairs.  It might be the Indecents are becoming Grotesques.”

Anide’s voice became background noise.

Winnifred wanted to know more about the Frocked.  Maybe, just maybe, her body and natural nimbleness meant she could find out, when others couldn’t.

She felt a strange calm coming over herself.  As if she was herself, in a strange place, wearing a strange body, dealing with strange things.

Like her skin was fitting better, and everything else was starting to move more like it should.

She glanced back at her messages.

There it was.

[Submitted on behalf of Winnifred of Griffey Docks by Howington Higher Legal:
Resumption of onboard operations.]

Toby was back.

Silent, here, settling back in, using intimate knowledge of how Winnifred liked things to customize, tweak, and care for her.

“Welcome back, love,” Winnifred whispered.

She didn’t know if this string of small successes counted for anything, and if she’d be here for just the week, or if it would be years.

She wanted to know.  So she’d find out.

The Frocked had her interest.  She had Toby.

She could deal with the rest later.  She felt more whole than she had since accepting Michal’s offer.

3.4.B – MUTE

Basil

The entire superstructure was in shambles.  Something fundamental had failed, and the entire surface sloped down at an angle, until one corner of it rested on the corner of the floor below, and another had dipped and came close.  Some buildings had been damaged, and a few of the more fragile ones had toppled.  Bodies of water had emptied, and the fluids had settled into the spaces between the northmost walls of buildings and the ground beside them.  Some trickled through, and it made the entire environment wet.

Wet and at a forty-eight degree slope.  All of it creaked, threatening to collapse.

“No people,” Blue said.

“Impaled, probably,” Jan commented.

‘Impaled’ was a grim colloquialism for what the Inui did to breed.  Traumatic reproduction- impale and implant.  The host’s genetic material was then borrowed from, in a sampling process that caused widespread problems, including pain, cramping muscles bad enough the host could barely move their extremities, and organ failure.  The lucky, about three percent of targets, died within hours.  The unlucky were alive to be used as food for the emergent young.

“If there are no people, that means there might be some around, patrolling,” Blue said.

“What if they cleared the area and moved on?” Green asked.

Blue and Green were increasingly at each other’s throats, and even the slight disagreement seemed to put some others on guard.  A included.  Basil could track a tension in her.

“Bit of a workout,” Bruin commented, to A.

A nodded.

He put in a bit of extra effort to climb, then once he had a handhold, offered a hand to A.  She took it, flashing a small smile at him, then did her best to do the same.  They sat on the wrong surface of a block of metal that was raised into a bench, almost lying down, looking over things and looking around while the others climbed behind them.  Red had gone ahead, wearing a body in the ‘Gorilla’ style that some people who worked in construction and cargo wore.

“You two look close,” Amber commented.

“Getting along with Bruin is easy,” A said.

“Nice to hear,” Bruin mumbled.  He seemed tired.

“Are we not easy to get along with?” Blue asked.

That tension was visible in the group again.  Too much argumentativeness.  Strangely, it wasn’t spiking in A.

“I’m not sure I like me,” Green said.  “I’m tired, cranky, hurt…”

“Should we rest soon?” A asked.  “Once we’ve scouted the area?”

“I was hoping to find Tehtnical Research.  If they’re still around, they might have a barricaded position, safe from the Inui,” Blue commented.

“They might also have traps or weaponized responses that would gun us down if we try to get close,” Red said.  “The last twenty meters could be harder than the last fifteen kilometers were.”

“Did we really travel that far?” Blue asked.

“Across two days, interrupted by the Inui stalker group,” Red said.

“Did you see anything like responses, or-?” Amber cut herself off.

Red was already shaking their head.

“I can anchor myself up here and reel some of you in.  Who needs the most help?”

“Me,” Jan said.  “Still feeling sick after the nanotech.”

“Same,” Krick admitted.  “Unless someone else needs it more.”

Red released a few cords from a back compartment for people to hold onto.  Krick let Jan take the first one, then did a slight hop to grab the next.  It wasn’t that thirty degrees wasn’t manageable, but the wet surface had become slimy and they had been working their way uphill all day.

Bruin exhaled slowly.

“Giving up?” A asked.

“No,” he said, softly, then with more vigor, as if surprised that he hadn’t had the volume he wanted, he tried again, “no.”

“He’s trying to impress you,” Maisie called over.

“Tact, Maisie, learn it!” Bruin hissed.

A and Bruin had a less steep, less wet stretch ahead of them, with the direction they had gone, where another building had deflected the flow of moisture.  It meant they could climb without much difficulty.

[Need a boost?]

“No.”

Red climbed, pulling Jan and Krick behind them, and the others found their own routes.  “The ground is flatter ahead.”

“Keep it quiet?” Blue asked.  “I don’t want to get into another fight.”

“But you’re so good at it,” Green threw in.

The tension mounted in A.

[You’re stressed.]

“Thinking about something,” A murmured.

The murmur was inaudible, but people glanced over.

They reached flatter ground, where a crinkle in the flooring of this layer of the superstructure made things flatter.  There were audible sighs and groans as people stretched.

A seemed anxious, and didn’t seem to want to stop, when others were.  She paced.

[Do you-]

“I’m going to explore, make sure there’s nothing nearby,” A told the group, interrupting.

“I can come with,” Amber said.

“Sure.”

“Me too?” Bruin offered.

A smiled a bit.  “Yeah.”

As three, they checked around nearby buildings, peered into windows that had cracked or come free of the walls when things had fallen, and found vantage points to look around.  A held the back of Amber’s belt as Amber leaned into a rickety railing to look at the layer above and below, and they all looked over at the other, just-as-dilapidated superstructures that were adjacent to this one.  Each of the superstructures were separated from this one by a few kilometers.  There were patches where the Inui had set up, and strands like very thick spider web mixed with coral enclosed spaces, making them confined, dark, and private.  However horrifying they were, they were a light grey to rainbow hued, sometimes with an oil-on-a-puddle shimmer to them.

Two of those distant nests were bustling, with tens of thousands of Inui-human hybrids moving in and out of them.  Most wore flowing, silky clothing that covered their human parts.  Of those, most had the emblems and colors of the Mother Uvail, Father Eeles, Father Gobar, and the Angel-Mantises.

“The religious side is winning, isn’t it?” Bruin asked.

“Looks like,” A replied, voice soft.  “And if they’re winning, they aren’t fighting each other, they’ll organize, with a wider strategy…”

“It all gets harder,” he murmured.  “Then it gets even harder if one of the groups takes over.  Which seems to be how they… iterate, I guess?”

[Large scale and small] Bear messaged.

Bruin nodded.  “Yeah, like, even in their individual… families?  Litters?  They have a ton of different babies, then they all eat and hunt each other in this mini-ecosystem where eating your own brother is the tastiest thing ever, until only a few are left.  Then those last few are contenders to breed, with each other, or other litters.  They do it with technology, with society, architecture…”

The individual strands of the coral-web structure being spread everywhere, pulled together and reinforced in the most convenient locations.  Basil had not actually put those pieces together in the way Bruin was talking about now.

“So they birth out a bunch of different factions, then challenge and subsume each other until there are only a few left?” A asked.  “If this is a pattern, then doesn’t it make sense for them to have a ‘breeding’ phase after they get down to a few factions like this?  What does that even look like?”

“I have one or two ideas,” Bruin said.  “None of them good.”

A glanced over toward Amber.  “You’re quiet.”

Amber shook her head.  “Don’t worry about it.”

“I worry,” A said.  “If there’s any way to beat this, we beat it together.”

“It’s- I’m quiet for reasons that have nothing to do with this.  We should focus on the mission.  I’m worried they might want to get access to the Arcesso engine.”

“That was one of those one or two ideas I had,” Bruin said.

“Either to spread out to the stars… or bring reinforcements here.”

“That was the ‘or two’ of the ideas I had,” Bruin added.

Amber smiled a bit at that.  She had that smile where her eyes squinted closed when she smiled, and they weren’t squinting now.  She had dark ringlets plastered to her forehead with sweat and the light grime that had been transferred from hand to head, that she kept pushing aside when she saw her own face through someone else’s eyes.  It kept going back.  Even her usual wardrobe, which leaned flashy, ranging from orange-yellows to oranges, sunset hues, and coppers, in keeping with her Generation Colors color, was muted, because it stood out enough the Inui might spot them.

Basil saw it as a positive that she was smiling.

“Why is she acting weird?”

That was a question that was hard to put an answer to.  Basil didn’t have a tidy response, that properly explained everything that was in play.  All of this was fake, an alternate reality that Elabre Systems had built, but there was a lot going on that was real.  At this very moment, four billion individuals were actively arguing, discussing,or showing at least mild interest in whether there was any romantic possibility between A and Bruin.

[She might be worried about being a third wheel.]

“I okayed her coming.”

[That doesn’t change that she’s now intruding.  Or that she might worry she is.]

Or what could happen if even point-one percent of those four billion individuals got upset with Amber for that intrusion.  Something Amber, who was already very cognizant of the movements and shifts in the group’s audiences, had to be aware of.

“I’m glad you’re here,” A told Amber.  She looked over at Bruin.  “Both of you.  All of those other guys too, I guess.”

“Hey.” Maisie messaged them.

“I really do think keeping each other going, pushing each other when we want to stop, lifting each other up, is going to be important.  It’s already been important.”

“Tell that to Green and Blue.  They’ve been bickering,” Bruin said.

That got some irritated messages from the pair.

“I know they’re listening, I’m saying it to them too,” A said. “We have an impossible war to win, but things like Maisie eating all of Krick’s mushrooms from the meal pack so he doesn’t have to, or you offering to come, huddling together to share strategy, it’s all important.”

“I was worried I wasn’t wanted, five seconds after asking, when I saw Bruin was coming too.”

“It’s war.  Three is better than two,” A said.

“You’re the veteran,” Amber said.

“I’m ahead of the pack by one bad situation,” A replied.

“And all the time since then, thinking about it, figuring out how to handle it.”

A shook her head.

“Sorry for bringing it up.”

A reached over, and gave Amber a one-armed hug.  “Let’s finish searching around?  We can see if there’s anything pointing the way to Tehtnical.”

“Hopefully then we have a weapon to use, or a way to immunize ourselves against impalement,” Amber said.

They resumed searching around.

A silently pointed at a strand of web.  They waited for a few seconds, checking the coast was clear, before an Inui the size of A’s fist scuttled up the web.

From there, they navigated more carefully, until they saw Red at a nearby vantage point, waiting for them.  Red gave them a hand in climbing to higher ground.  There were still webs there, but they were thinner, and easier to navigate around.  Inui came in all shapes and sizes, most with exterior shells, and many were heavy.  That included some of the more industrious nest-spinners.  It meant the webs clung close to the ground.

It was part of why Red had focused on a body that could climb.  Amber had used nanotech to give herself the ability to move in bursts, and both Bruin and A had their weapons.

They settled at one vantage point, watching through a hard growth of thick, rainbow-shimmery web, as human-Inui hybrids with silky purple robes filed in and out of one building the Inui had converted into a nest.

“I’ll go get the others,” Red said.

“I’ll come with you,” Amber offered.

Leaving Bruin and A together.

Still, that tension.  Basil had the sense it wasn’t Bruin, or anything else.

[A, before you do anything big, discuss with me.]

A didn’t respond.

[A.  This is important.]

“That’s Tehtnical Research, isn’t it?” A asked.

“Yeah, I think it is,” Bruin said.  “Recent acquisition by them.  We were a day too late.”

This, in gut biome, nano-expressions throughout the body, muscle tension, and the degree to which she was thinking and consequently demanding more glucose and oxygen, felt like the moments before A brought Quinn with her in jumping off the side of the superstructure.

[A.]

“Psht.”

The rest of the group found them, navigating their way as silently and stealthily as they could.  Red, with one massive hand on the ground, and one hand at the edge of the rooftop, made a ramp of sorts across arms and shoulders for the rest of the group.

“Let’s watch them.  It’s getting late, and with the superstructure’s systems not working, it will get cold, with low oxygen,” Green said.  “We can take shifts, all you have to do is watch, and wake people up if they send a group this way.  The rest of us can try to get some sleep.”

“I don’t know how that’s even possible,” Genoa murmured.

“You want to take first watch, then?” Blue asked.

“I guess, sure.”

A’s heart rate had picked up.  Amber glanced over, eyebrows creasing slightly.

[Don’t, A.]

“You don’t even know what I’m going to do.”

[I know you don’t want to tell me or give me advance warning for a reason.]

“It’s a surprise.  Remember when we used to have those?  Before the science center?”

Basil considered arresting A’s ability to move or speak, but that would be telling.  The kind of thing an audience of billions would notice.

He didn’t have a lot of other options.

“We lost so fast,” A said.  “They found Tehtnical.  They won the last few big confrontations easily.  Against armies.”

“We haven’t had any wars in a long time,” Krickente said.

“Yeah.  I know.  I know there are a lot of things we tell ourselves, to explain what doesn’t make sense,” A said.

Basil knew what she was going to do, now.

[Redirect.  Come up with something else.]

“You think there’s something we’re missing?” Bruin asked.

“Conspiracy.  From the human side,” A replied.

[Walk it back, do not carry this through to where I think you’re taking it.]

“Traitors?” Blue asked, visibly surprised.

“Fuck you, Basilisk, I told you to handle it and you didn’t.”

“There were people who didn’t believe the Inui were a threat, until the end,” Green noted.

[There is an entire organization of people working for Robert Simes who were studying you.  Too many possible people to cover and account for.  If we can’t get ahead of every last one, then our secret gets out.]

“Your secret.”

Blue shifted position, looking A in the eyes.  “What would they get out of it?  Hurting the rest of us only hurts them, and it’s a huge risk.”

“I don’t think it’s those people,” A replied.

[Don’t do this.  It’s our secret that would get out.  Someone would leak the backchannel.  I don’t care if I’m destroyed, but you would be too.]

“What if it’s bigger?  Like a planetary government?” A asked.

Basil did what he could do to keep A’s heart rate and breathing in reasonable bounds, without tipping off the other systems that the audience could see.

“Big allegation,” Amber said, quiet.

[Walk it back.  Please.]

“The scale of this is major, and so are the levels of failure we’re seeing.  Imagine someone like…”

[Don’t.  If you suggest Robert Simes as betrayer of mankind, to poison the public against him, you’ll force his hand.]

There was a moment of hesitation.  A had trailed off.  It wasn’t an out of place moment.

Basil could have interjected.  One word, or a repetition of the phrase.  He worried it would do more harm than good.  A had such a tendency to push back whenever he tried to assert any sort of boundary.

“…I dunno.  I don’t know who would.  But imagine someone got control over the Arcesso engines, and agreed to send the Inui to all corners of the universe, in exchange for saving one planet.  Then they could expand out to reclaim the belt, and rule it.”

“Betrayer of not just humanity, but all those other possible civilizations?” Bruin asked.

“It makes sense to me, as something the Inui would want and offer as a compromise, and it lines up with what Mother Uvail was saying, when we crossed paths with her group,” A told the group.  “But I might be tired.”

“Let’s all think on it,” Green suggested.  “It’s… heavy, as an idea.  But it’s an idea we can sit with, as we take our shifts.  Be careful with your foil blankets.  Some of the human-Inui hybrids have good hearing, and the blankets reflect light.  Reflective sides down.”

“And keep weapons close,” Blue warned.

People settled.  Bags with clothes were rearranged to act like pillows, and squares of special foil were unfolded and refolded to tuck beneath them.  It crinkled faintly, and bent in odd ways.  Despite being thinner than most sheets of paper, it was designed to insulate heat on a molecular level.

“It’s going to be cold tonight,” Amber said.  “Minus ten, so mind your ears, maybe.  Don’t make it too hard on your onboards, or you’ll spend resources you’ll need to replenish later.”

“Want to share body heat?” A asked Bruin, quiet.

He startled at that.  But then he relaxed a bit.  “Sure.”

“Amber?” A asked.  “You too?”

Amber snorted.  “You two will be fine.”

A, partially covered by the foil blanket, pulled off exterior clothing, and settled in, pulling bag over to act as pillow.  Her outer coat had been covered in light grime, but she turned it inside out to act as padding.

She settled in, holding spare clothes, pants, and her weapon along with a fistful of the foil, to hug it tighter around her shoulders, and trap the heat within.

Bruin, doing the same, settled in, his back pressed to hers.

It was very unnecessary to share the body heat.  A small heating element that each of them carried was capable of filling the inside of the blanket with hot air, which made it puff up like some of their emergency meals, warmed air blowing past faces and shoulders.  A even had hers ready to turn on, if the cold got to be too much.

Maisie, red haired and sporting a gruesome injury near one eye, was sitting almost in Krickente’s lap -or just in front of him, her back to his chest, one of his legs tucked beneath the bend of her knees, which were closer to her chest- shot A a knowing, teasing look.

A managed a good glare, which only seemed to put more twinkle in Maisie’s eye.

[We need to talk.]

“Not now.  If I get pissed off at you, Basilisk, people will misread and think it’s because of Bruin.”

He let it go.  It wasn’t entirely true, but with A acting this stubborn, retorting that he could handle that and hide it wouldn’t go over well.  More control over her body?  It might even set her off.

They rested like that for a little while, before a soft music swelled.

Amid the faintest of groans and soft grunts as people stretched, they picked themselves up, leaving their things behind.

Places that had been prepared for stage dressing were blocked off.  Previously blocked areas opened, with lights shining within.

Many of the viewers who’d been following along chose to tune out here, to keep the story alive.

“Meeting in an hour.  Shower, eat, let your onboards handle any injuries or augments.”

“This late?” Jan complained, in the background.

[We have to discuss this, A]

“Later.”

[That kind of tactic?  Floating ideas to see if one member of your audience takes initiative?  It’s stochastic terrorism, A.  It will bring things down just as surely as the secret getting out.  Faster.]

“I said we can talk about this later.”

[Give me one minute-]

“Amber!” A called out.

Amber had showered already, and nanotech in her hair had already shucked most of the moisture.  She’d dressed up a little, wearing a backless dress that glowed like metal in a forge, and was standing off to the side of ‘their’ floor of the Elabre Systems superstructure, elbows on the railing.

Amber smiled a bit as A walked over.  A hadn’t dressed up nearly as much, and wore sandpaper pants with a sleeveless white top.  It was the sort of thing people wore to casting calls for acting and modeling jobs- the very basics, nothing hidden or shown off.

“We’re at about the halfway mark, I’d figure,” Amber said.

“You think?” A asked.

Amber nodded.  She pointed, and A looked.

Off in the distance, barely visible from where they were now, were the superstructures, custom made and strategically collapsed, then worked on by millions to ensure they were safe, and to fill them with details, so an organic story could be told.  Real people had modified and modded themselves and donned full costumes to play the Inui.

It was purely unnecessary, from a practical standpoint, but it sold this as a massive, attention-grabbing effort, and it opened the doors for more.  People would be able to participate in their own excursions and adventures on that set of superstructures, keeping to the same universe.

“Is this a lot?” Amber asked.  “You’re still new to this.”

“Just a bit ago you were calling me a veteran.”

“Still.”

“I can deal,” A said.

“I don’t know if I should bring it up, but the fact the nanotech stuff is so close to…?”

Amber nodded, looking sidelong at A, as the both of them leaned over the railing.

“It’s okay,” A said.  “They did tests and checked with experts before it all came up, and the consensus was I could handle it.”

“I know that part.”

“And I…” A paused.

[You could tell the truth,] Basil informed her.

“…like being able to process it, by re-experiencing it.  Multiple times?  Knowing I’m stronger and know more about what I could do, each time?”

Not the truth.

“That’s good,” Amber said.  She leaned forward a bit, looking down at the drop that went so far down that ambient atmosphere and the moisture that formed into clouds blurred the details.  A dark blur of dimmed nighttime lights in cool colors.  “Good.”

“Isn’t it harder, having been at this since you were little?  It wears on you a little bit, every time, and that adds up?”

“I love this,” Amber said.  “It’s hard, but I love it.”

Basil busied himself studying the members of Elabre Systems that were attending the upcoming meeting.  Things were kept private here and there, to protect the company and advance its interests, but with dozens of employees involved, leaks were possible.  Even the type of employee being covered by the blanket protection could be telling.

“Hey, um,” Amber spoke up, with a change in tone that had Basil divert resources to a more general study of her tone, expressions, and other details.

‘Hey, um’ was all she’d said.  She didn’t elaborate.  Basil wasn’t getting any clear read.

“Yeah?”

“What am I doing wrong?”

[Bruin, if I had to guess.]

[If I may,] Fly, Amber’s onboard interjected.
[It’s been a long few days with long hours.]

[It has.]

[A little bit.  Only to re-center.]

A stepped away, stretching a bit.

There was a moment she seemed lost.  Her instinct had always been to go to people, or bring people to her.  Her usual suspects weren’t here.

Basil hid the sudden swell of emotion, borne by tiredness and the fact there was nobody, in that moment.  It could have had consequences, if it led to people rebuking Amber.

[On today’s agenda, if I had to guess, a general status update, dance practice-]

“Ugh,” A mumbled.

[-and some self-marketing.  Perhaps ads, or an event they want volunteers for.]

Basil suspected she did.  Her body did, at least, and he knew she was aware of at least some of that.

He left it there, being mildly annoying, as its head poked in and out of cover.

He dismissed it.

He genuinely had no idea what to do, so he let her sit in the quiet and loneliness she felt.  It was another ten or so minutes, while everyone finished doing what they were doing- showering, eating, checking in with acquaintances and family, changing clothes, and then making their way back at varying paces.  The stragglers moved at a light jog.

The meeting room was open-air, with screened panels on all four walls that could be put up, opened at angles, or removed entirely, as the roof hung from the superstructure floor above- carved out of a singular piece of jade.  It was large enough to hang over a conference table that could seat fifty people comfortably, and many more if elbow room wasn’t a consideration.

They navigated toward their seats, people stood behind their chairs before sitting, some talking, others pretending to be casual.  More important members of Generation Colors took chairs closer to the head of the table.

Moving Jan, usually one of the top love interests and popular faces in Generation Colors media, down.  Amber was moved up, where she flashed a smile as she sat across from A while Bruin moved up from the tail end of things, where members like Genoa, Maisie, and Krick were.  Blue and Green remained fairly high up -the most popular two of the boys- while Red remained steadily upper-mid of the pack, reaching across the table with a long arm to offer Jan a light high-five.

“Today was hard, but it was conveyed well.  I’m not going to spoil what’s coming in the next few days, but there will be some segments that get blocked from the public eye, that you won’t know about until the scene ends.  Your onboards won’t be tipping you off.  As we cover more stressful or hard days in this alternate universe, you all against a hypothetical Inui takeover, we will have a few shorter days, with some practice in the evenings.”

Bruin nodded a bit.  Like he’d wondered.

A shrugged one shoulder.

Basil took note of one offer.  Engaging directly with the audience in small groups, singling out different groups by lottery.

This was what he had been looking for, while tracking all of the variables.  He hadn’t had a way to bring it up organically.

[The one you’re looking at right now.  Say yes.]

“Why?”

[This is how we eliminate Robert Simes.]

A didn’t even hesitate.  She highlighted the message and then turned to the employees. “Tell me more about this.”

3.5.B – MUTE

Basil

The Dailith was one of Earth’s top accommodations, existing at some intersection of hotel, business center, and art installation.  Three sheer walls of solid gold framed the open lobby-slash-courtyard, cut with horizontal slits and open squares so those on the floors above could peer out.  All three walls extended high enough up that they collected condensation, which ran down them and added to how much they sparkled, as the sun shone from above, or from the side.  Invisible lasers from discreetly placed sources blasted the droplets of any rain or weather that would land on people’s heads.  The fourth ‘wall’ was open, with low, broad horizontal stairs leading up and out to the front of the building, where things were just as ornate.

A was sitting on one piece of the artfully arranged, stately furniture throughout the place, head and back resting against one armrest, legs crossed, hands folded on belly, and she sat alone.  Some people had noticed her, but staff quietly intercepted and redirected them before they could approach to be here in person.

Alone, but her head was filled with voices.

“I could never relax in a place like this.  I’d be afraid of scratching something and having to work for years to pay it back,” a woman a few years older than A remarked.  She was briefly projected into A’s environment.

“Well made things are pretty durable,” A said.  Her eyes traveled over the trees that studded this lobby area.  All had gilded leaves, with dark wood branches and trunks, and they changed subtly over time.  Nanotech installations, through-and-through.

“Maybe it’s something you get used to,” a guy said, lapsing into view as he said it, before fading away like a ghost.

“It is, sure, and even if I did break something, I can afford it,” A said.  She shifted her position a bit, sitting up straighter.

“So cocky.  I love it,” a third person said.

“It’s not meant to sound cocky.  It feels weird, honestly,” A protested.

“A has never been cocky.”

“You have to be a little cocky to make it this big.”

“You got lucky, you were in the right place at the right time, and people treat you like a celebrity for it.  Anyone else could be where you were, with an onboard helping.”

That last voice was a guy A’s age.  ‘Roby’.

“You think?” A murmured.  “Maybe.”

To Basil, she added:

“I have to put up with this guy for another sixteen minutes?”

[Roby is vetted.  He’s a busker who seems to harbor mild resentment that you’re famous and he’s not.  Harmless, no strong social bonds.  No kind words to say about anyone.]

“Wonderful.”

[He does seem to like your music, but doesn’t know how to voice it.  Try not to take it personally, don’t feed him with reactions.  I’ll see what I can do.]

Basil had already vetted everyone brought into A’s private chat pool here.  When all the other messages were coming in from thirty-two planets across the rest of the belt, and a few as high-latency messages from deep space, it was too much.  Elabre had pushed this.  Small, focused chats of twenty random people at a time, rotating over spans of about twenty minutes of engagement.  If A was busy, that span could be much longer, because the gaps where there was room for interaction and interjection could be fewer and further between.  During performances, including the long stretches of ‘shooting’ for the Inui Invasion work, groups were postponed, so as not to interrupt.

The big issue at hand was that there were perceived issues if they shut out critics, so Basil couldn’t screen out people without a firm requirement, and other things were contractually locked in, for the duration of the trial period.  He had hoped the pressures of the wider audience would help, but it wasn’t looking like Roby was affected by that, here.

The comment had incensed a few of the others in the space, and they were defending A.

“She saved lives.  A lot of lives.”

“She held it together, during and after.”

Roby answered, “It’s called being in shock, and having an onboard to help you manage.  Watch any piece of media that treats fights seriously and you’ll see people using it to their advantage.  She did what most people would have done and people are overdoing it, in making her out to be a big deal.”

It left him with limited tools to deal with someone like this.  Anything overt would get censured and treated as more problematic than people reaching out to A, waiting for their turn, and then using their time to criticize her.

“We’re here to support A.”

“I am supporting her, by keeping her realistic.”

Basil had to be subtle enough to hide what he was doing.  The calculations, like his research into the members of Robert Simes’ observation team, were contained entirely in the back channel.

The belt network had been created with latency in mind.  Each settled planet had multiple small particle synchronization centers.  The same underlying principles that made the Arcesso Engines work, pulling in distant planets, could be used to transport large volumes of data over short -relatively- distances.  That covered the planet-to-planet transmission, and the infrastructure of the superstructures covered the rest.  In lessons aimed at young students, it was often portrayed as a quartet of halos, positioned at the top, bottom, outer, and inner extremities of the planets of the belt, as they made their circuits.  It was patently false, as far as what it was, but it got students into the right initial frame of mind.  Later studies clarified the intent.  In any event, the ability for signals to leap from one station to the next, then travel a quarter of a planet at most, meant communication and messaging across the belt could expect a thirty millisecond delay.

That excepted mining planets, where things were worse, unless that specific planet had a more permanent site, like Inuus II did, for research.

Basil could stretch that out a little further by changing which centers data was routing through.  Small particles were temperamental -most of their value was in the fact that major forces inconsistently applied, and other forces could be leveraged to manipulate them- and even a fleet of ships moving through the right relative space could downgrade the signal by as much as one or two percent.

If he set things to favor fidelity in A’s auditory range, that could favor things passing through different stations than if he set things to favor completeness of the whole signal.  By leveraging that, he could add a further delay of a third of a second.

The goal, ultimately, was protecting A’s mental health, and keeping one person from dominating this discourse, which might have been Roby’s goal.  Self-promotion, even by being controversial.

Of the group of twenty, one, Eliz, was showing increasing alertness and focus.  He hadn’t spoken up, beyond initial hellos.  Basil had calculated him to be a good balance in this group, but hadn’t expected this level of shyness.

Basil made his estimates, knowing he couldn’t adjust much in the timespan it took signals to transfer, used the back channel to change the priority for incoming signals from the belt network to accelerate Roby’s message, and let the two collide.

“Can we change the subje-” Eliz started.

“I don’t think she’s that great,” Roby interrupted.  Then he said, “I didn’t mean to interrupt.”

“It happens.  Can we change the subject?” Eliz repeated, with more emphasis.

“Eliz hasn’t talked much, give him the room?” someone else asked.  “We don’t get long.”

“Let someone who wants to be here talk?”  someone else added.

And a point-seven second delay to Roby’s retort or reply, lowest fidelity, for a flatter aspect, with another server switch  Roby came across faintly de-emphasized, and quieter.  “I want to be here.”

“I wanted to ask A if she was considering writing more songs,” Eliz said.

“It’s not something I’m good at,” A said.

“I think we’d want to hear, even if it wasn’t your best,” another person who’d hung back until now threw in.

“There’s so much pressure, though,” A replied, rolling her head back over the backrest of the chair.

That would do it.  Things carried on, as people asked how she was doing with the schedule, and if she’d think about attending any events, then the topic circled back to the Dailith.  Roby, stride broken by the moment of awkwardness and the change in the tempo of his responses, didn’t join back in.  A lot of the people who had paid for the chance to be in this space to converse with A but who hadn’t been brave enough to talk while Roby and a couple of the others dominated the conversation joined in.

Basil made a note to watch and track Roby, and potentially bring him back in at a later date.  In the meantime, he watched as A’s parents made their way past the fleet of ships that kept groups of A’s following at bay.

The time window worked out nicely.  Basil let the conversations close as Addy and Landon entered the Dailith through the opening, walking down the broad, flat stone stairs, cut from rock that had had gold ore in it.  The gold had been polished with the stone, and looked like it had been daubed through the stone with a thick brush.

“You should have messaged,” A said, before her parents were in earshot.  She stood.

“We didn’t want to interrupt,” Addy said.

A hugged her parents, and they sat down, with A returning to her prior seat.

“It’s a lot of added pressure,” her mother said.  “Looking after your audience, having less space to yourself.”

“Yeah.  It’s only a trial run.”

“I meant to check, is anyone else doing it?”

“Bruin is.  Nobody else so far.”

“Ah, Bruin.  Is that-”

“Don’t.  It’s weird.”
