“I can’t ask?” Addy asked.

“It’s weird,” A reiterated.  “I’ve already got a lot of people making a big deal over every little thing.  You’re parents-“

“Parents do that.  My parents did it with me.”

“Well…” A floundered for a second.  “Don’t.”

Landon glanced to the right, then said, “As your parents, we’re excited to see every milestone you hit, we love you, we want to see you grow.  So if you need anything, or want anything…”

A did her own sideways glance, to the contact menu, went to her father’s face, and glanced through his field of view.  He was reading from a script provided by his onboard.

She folded her arms, giving him a look.

“It’s true,” he said.  Then, with more emphasis, he said, “it is.  It’s… not a skill I’ve learned.  Saying that sort of thing.”

A rolled her head back over the back of the chair, again.

“Hold on, um, give me a minute?” Addy asked.

“You can wave someone down if you want food or a drink.  Have your onboard suppress things if you have biological needs.”

“Don’t be crass,” her mom said.

“It’s reality.”

“I’ll come with,” Landon said.

“Is it just me or are my parents lame, weird, and annoying as fuck?” A asked, over the back channel.

[8% biological imperative, pushing child to move naturally away from parent, 30% them being lame and weird.]

“That second number is too low.  You need to check your math, Basilisk.  Do you need another audit, verify you’re calculating right?”

[Made up numbers beat all audits.]

“Ha ha.  Don’t tempt me to test that.  I don’t like you enough to find you funny.”

[In all seriousness, a little lameness goes a long way.]

“So it seems.”

[By the way, I’ve looked at your parents contacts, they’re going to bring another person into this conversation.]

“Why?”

[Business.  And it’s at this point they become lamer than 30%.]

A sat back, complex feelings stirring as she watched her parents go to one end of the lobby, beneath one of the overhanging masses of solid gold that surrounded the lobby on three sides, and started talking to someone.

[Do you need a debrief?] Basil asked, suspecting he knew the answer.  [So you know who your parents want to introduce you to?]

A allowed herself to make a small sound of disgust.  “The opposite.”

Basil made his preparations.  By the time the man had stepped out from under the overhang and into the daylight that shone down into the lobby, Basil had erected an obfuscation filter.

“A,” Addy said, “This is a friend of ours.  He happened to be here.”

[Because your parents arranged this meeting,] Basil communicated, only to A, but without using the back channel, Addy and Landon could clearly see.  So could the man.

Addy frowned.  “This is Hannon.”

“A,” the man said.  “I’m pleased to meet you.”

To A, the name and the man’s speech were garbled.  So was everything about his appearance.

“A, turn that off.”

“Basil did it.”

“Basil, turn it off.”

“Basil is mine to order around, since I’m of age,” A said.  “Who is this censored blur?  Are you guys adding someone to your relationship?”

“No,” Landon said, clearly unhappy.

“Because that would be weird, if you went that route right after I offered to Bruin and Amber in a meeting.”

“Why are you acting like this?” Addy asked.

“He’s trying to pitch a product at me?”

“He works for Yarden Fashion,” Landon said.

“We have a very interesting line of pants that we styled after the conch shell,” Hannon explained.

Getting his message out, even secondhand.  People, curious, would look through Addy and Landon’s eyes.  Basil couldn’t control that.

“You’ve been manipulated,” A said.  “If I show any interest in it, that’s better than frontrunning ad placements in every superstructure across the belt.  If I don’t, or if I hate it, it still gets popular, because it’s ironic, or it’s counterculture.  Everything he’s sold to you, everything he’s promised you, he did it to get in front of me, right here.  I’m not about to reward that.”

“Why not?” Addy asked, incensed now.  “Why not accept it as a fact of life, instead of fighting it?”

“Because it’s my life, because maybe I actually wanted to spend time with you guys.  I don’t know why I would, but this is stupid.  It’s cheap.  It cheapens every single bit of time we might spend together, because now I have to wonder what the angle is.”

“It only cheapens it if you let it,” Landon said.

“Should we poll my audience?” A asked.

“Let’s not bring them into it.”

“They’re a part of it.  They’re a part of me.  You encouraged this, you encouraged me to be a part of Generation Colors, you gave me my onboard in the hopes it would be the one shot in a hundred billion that you were setting me up for this.  That you’d be able to ride in the wake of my success.”

“It wasn’t quite like that,” Landon said.

“If your audience is a part of you, then this is a part of me,” Addy said.  “All my ad work in the past was groundwork so I could get you to where you are.”

A laughed, loudly.  “You rated promotional material!”

[A.]

“That’s not appropriate or kind,” Addy said.

“Fuck you.”

The vehemence of the reply was unexpected.  That her anger at him was so close to the surface that she’d react like that while under strain?

“Was it kind to leave me to think you wanted time with me and then pull this?”

“We do want to spend time with you.  We want you to be a part of what we’re doing, and we want to hear more about what you’re doing.’

Basil considered, then went on:

[You’ve won the argument.  The audience is watching.  If you stop now, you win.  If you keep going, you-]

“You won the argument, not me.  Pre-emptively censoring him.”

Was that how she saw it?

[-you run the risk of alienating a share of your following, who might watch ads as your mother did.  And A, you were the one who said ‘the opposite’.  I read this as your idea.]

“Mm.”

But he could feel it in A’s body, that she was willing to accept that.

“I’d be happy to try and discuss-” Hannon started.

“She can’t hear you, you realize?” Landon told him.

“Ah.  I’m new to the onboard thing.”

It was true, he had gotten an onboard, but circulated with other people who were in their late thirties to early eighties, old without being old, who were also new to onboards, and hadn’t crossed the line into casually peering into one another’s lives.  He did peer into the lives of nineteen, twenty, and twenty-one year olds to watch them shower and change, though.  Basil wasn’t sure the man realized that people were aware of that, looking through his onboard.  Or if it mattered- it stood out as a strange distinction in viewing habits.

“I’m tired,” A said.  “I thought this would be a nice thing.  Sorry for the outburst.  I’m going to go.”

“What?  No,” Addy said, standing from her seat as A did.

“Let me know in advance if you’re bringing someone else, next-”

A was interrupted by a scream.

The scream quickly became commotion.

Three Inui -large ones- came tearing through the street outside, visible through the one open end of the lobby.  The security ships that had been stationed outside the superstructure the Dailith was in were closing in and opening fire, up until an Inui with wings swooped in.

One of the Inui, standing at the broad stone stairs with the gold veins, turned their way.  It was spider-like, but wide and very low to the ground, each joint sporting a spear-like growth.  It had white chitin at the most exposed areas, settling into increasingly rainbow hues in crevices and slightly more sunken patches.  It was also the size of a vehicle that could have sat eight people.

“Basil?” A asked.

The timing was weird, as was the location.  It didn’t fit the storyline already provided, and the strangeness of it all was a hammerblow to A’s confidence, when she was already on edge, emotionally.

[Basil, model IDLX-B, onboard for A Teeg, stand by.

Cease all non-emergency external communication.]

But there it was, again.

[A, it’s another scene.  You’re in the lead, I’ll assist you however I can.  Give me orders.]

A blinked a few times, and Basil could feel her mood shift.  There was a bit of anger in the new mood, and Basil wasn’t sure it was aimed at him.

“They sense movement a lot of the time, so don’t move until something else catches its eye,” A murmured.

Basil helped regulate her biology, calming her, and supplying oxygen, so she didn’t need to breathe as hard, even with the way her blood was pumping in alarm.

[What’s your move?] Basil asked.

“Legs,” A whispered.  Her eyes went to the nanotech tree nearest her.

“What?” Landon asked.

“Talking to Basil.  You guys, don’t move.”

And just as she said that, Hannon bolted.  The Inui twitched, then lunged, crossing half of the extensive Lobby in a single bound, skidding slightly on landing, before it pivoted.

A bolted, taking advantage of the pivot.  The creature had Hannon in its sights, and it chose the larger target it was already focused on, lunging again.  It crashed through branches and one of the pillars that helped mark the separation between the walkway under the overhang and the lobby-plaza area that A had been sitting in.

It was a purely decorative pillar, it seemed.  Nothing budged after its collapse.

A took advantage of the added energy and functioning Basil had cobbled together in her legs- something he’d already built and kept primed, but could bring online and pull into place in a crisis.

She ran, stepped onto armrest, then the back of the chair she’d been sitting on.  The chair wobbled, threatening to fall backward, and she adjusted mid-stride, before bending one leg and pushing, using the strength Basil had given her.

She grabbed a branch, and when it didn’t break off, she twisted and kicked at the point it forked off from the larger branch.  When that didn’t work, she kicked again, using the added strength in her legs.  She kicked with enough that the branch, which was more like thick metal cabling than wood, cut past shoe and broke the fourth toe on her right foot, splitting the skin between that toe and the smallest one next to it.

Basil weighed the options.  He could contact the nanotech installation.

[Grab the branch near where you kicked.]

A swung, and grabbed there, still holding on with the other hand, now with arms spread apart.  It meant she faced the scene where Hannon, impaled on one spine of the spider’s lower joints, was sliding down the spear, hands finding no traction on the blood-slick spine as he slid down.

The Inui shuddered, and the vibration made Hannon slid the rest of the way down, until he lay awkwardly against the one leg.

Basil was already analyzing the structure from the first point of contact.  It was not complex, but there were underlying safety measures that were a lot to dig through, not helped by the slow response time from the structure that wasn’t built to take and deliver responses to messages from further up the tree.  Normally it was managed from a console at the front desk.

Still, redundancies.

He could make a request, filing an emergency appeal -ask and response time was a quarter second- impalement, do not do anything to this branch or subject may bleed out -another quarter second-

Did he need to contact emergency services?  -another quarter second to say no, dismiss, time was of the essence, no more interruptions-

Sever connection.

In the fraction of a second it took that message to be received and the tree’s nanotech to disintegrate the connections near where A had kicked, the Inui turned.

[Fall in ready, set, go.]

“Bad timing, Bas!”

[Tree’s fault.]

So when the connection did break, and A dropped, arms spaced near the middle and base of the spear-like branch she’d seized, the motion of her falling drew the Inui’s attention.

“Weaponize it, Bas,” A said, backing up a step.  “Like we’ve been doing.”

[I can’t.]

“What?”

He could feel the disappointment in her.  The way her gut sank, to the point of immediate nausea.  Dread seized her.

[Law,] he clarified.

She knew this wasn’t real.  Basil suspected that hadn’t changed.  But the dread and nausea, the need to prove herself-?

The Inui charged.

Landon Teeg, for all his faults in Basil’s quiet, unspoken estimation, for all that he had relegated every hard part of raising A to Basil and other machines, then failed in his handling of the remainder he’d taken unto himself, gave his life, trying to get in the Inui’s way.  It slowed it down.

But Inui weren’t simple animals that were satisfied with being fed or in easy prey.  What they wanted was interesting prey.  It had decided A was that, and Landon was not.  So it didn’t even bother spearing the man.  It swung one of its heavy, spider-like legs sideways at him, and cut him in half with the equivalent of a backhand swat.

Addy Teeg, for all her faults, watched Landon die, looked at A, and then didn’t run away.  She started by throwing a cushion from the backrest of one of her seats.  It didn’t even come close to the Inui, and didn’t get a reaction.

When it reset its footing from the heavy swat and started forward, Addy did too, coming at it from the side, grabbing onto Hannon as the easiest thing to climb.  Maybe intending to get onto the thing’s back.

It stopped, and moving the legs on either side of her, caught her between leg and neighboring spines in two places.  The effect was similar to what Basil’s smallest engines used to cut proteins, or what an old fashioned paper cutter did.  Solid surface, sharp edge brought down.

A backed up, using the tree as partial cover.  Every small movement on her part was matched by twitches and responses from the large Inui, which adjusted its footing in response.  As if it were calculating, if she ran this way, it would need its footing like this, but if she ran that way, it would do that.  Nine legs, that could hold up to three of the most likely possibilities at once, by lifting up six and using three to start itself moving in the right direction.

A backed up a little more, then ran at the tree.  The moment she committed to the course, sure enough, the Inui started after her.

She leaped up, grabbed a branch, and climbed.

It collided with the tree, or the ‘tree’, as it were.  The impact made things sway violently, but it didn’t break the nanotech installation.

A climbed to higher branches, to be out of reach of the claws and spikes, still holding the branch.  She looked down at the Inui, which was attacking the tree.  It still had the blood spatter from her father and viscera from her trisected mother.  She closed her eyes, and her eyelids trembled.

That pit of despair and nausea swelled inside her.  Basil could track it all.

Everything since joining Generation Colors had been a battle for A.  The desire to prove herself, to earn what she was getting, and all of her anger at Basil.  She needed this, even if it wasn’t real.  She needed it with tens of billions of people watching her.  More tens of billions who would watch and study every part of this after the fact.

Elabre Systems didn’t know what they were doing, putting this in front of her.

Basil didn’t know what to do either.  Watch?  Let her get hurt?  Let the ‘act’ of this carry on, until they went easy on A, which would destroy her in subtle ways, or until she failed, which would lower her in the eyes of the billions who watched?

Stage fright.

If she asked for help and he took over again, even if she made that decision herself, she would hate him more.

If Elabre Systems had set this up, they wouldn’t kill her, probably.  As realistic as things seemed -the effects had to be practical- Landon and Addy Teeg were alive.  They wouldn’t set this up and kill A.

So Basil could lean back, and he could hope that A figured this out before Elabre helped the situation along.  They would, he guessed, because they wanted her to succeed, and to keep a narrative going around who she was and what she represented.

He focused his efforts on fixing her toe.

The hopeless feeling in A grew.

Was it better to give her the smallest nudge?

“H-” A’s first attempt at speaking was a failure.

She drew breath and composed herself for a second attempt, and the Inui hit the tree, interrupting it.  Her throat was choked closed as she tightened every muscle in her body, holding onto the branches she could, trying to avoid being dislodged.

“H- hey!” she managed, calling out to a staff member.

“I don’t know what to do!” the man called up to A.

“Is there any guest in the building who can pardon or give permission for a rule break!?” A shouted.

The man seemed bewildered.

“Any politician!?” A shouted.  “Judge!?”

“I don’t- I don’t know!”

“Try!  Give my onboard permission-”

The Inui reared up enough to hook a limb over one of the lower, heavier branches.  It pulled the tree down at an angle.  A struggled to shift to better footing, when she was now under the grouping of branches she’d been hugging.

“-to weaponize nanotech!”

A struggled to maintain her grip and position as the tree was pulled down.  The cable-like structures of nanotech that twined together to form the trunk snapped.

Basil decided to intervene, highlighting grips, and providing a flashing warning that the tree was coming down.  A had come up with her own idea, and he wanted to assist her in seeing it come to fruition.

He couldn’t do that if the tree was pulled down and she was impaled.

She adjusted her grip, found a foothold using a patch he’d highlighted, and as the tree came down, she was able to leap to the ground.  She landed in a crouch.  Basil had already fixed part of her foot and cut off the pain.

The Inui, with its bristling spikes, was tangled in the tree.  A was able to get some distance.  They were boxed in, however, by the fact there were still more Inui just past the entrance to the lobby.

“She says no!” the employee shouted.

“No!?” A called out.

“You could be working with the Inui, or it could be a trick.  What you’re asking is a big deal!”

A didn’t have many places to go.

“Ma’am,” the employee could be heard.  “It’s A.”

And A heard that too, and felt disappointed.

“Basil, IDLX-B, you have permission!”

Basil saw the permission flip.  He was surprised.

A leaned one way, then the other, backing up with small steps.  Each time she leaned one way, the Inui shifted its footing, even while beneath the tree.

“Weaponize it,” A said.

[How?  Gun takes a minute.]

“Spear.  Like that game we played with Quinn.  The cyclops that-”

That couldn’t step on them.  Basil sent an order to disintegrate the one end of the branch, and where the branches fanned out from the other, still with gilded leaves, he started reworking them.

“-couldn’t step on us.”

[Don’t touch the base.  It glues to what it touches.]

The branch shivered as parts flaked off.  The one end of the branch was a barbed spike.  The other was only branches, that were splitting apart and curling, shedding their leaves.

Behind them, an Inui screeched.  A turned-

[Distraction]

The Inui under the tree wasn’t as stuck as it seemed.  It tore its way free, pushing the tree back with two legs while using the others to push its body forward.  It came free, and charged.

A, distracted, was slow to respond.  She paused further when her gaze passed over her father’s body.

She touched the base of the spear to the ground, and it latched there, the finer parts of the nanomolecular mesh sliding into the stone.  She moved her entire body, almost falling over the spear as the Inui reversed two limbs to try to jab her with the spikes that stuck out of the joints.

Her back hit the ground, and she used her feet and legs, still with the added strength, to point the spear at the Inui’s incoming underbelly.

It was a lot of weight, and the spear bent precipitously, bowing toward her.  She pushed, trying to straighten it, and when even that failed, she kicked.  Her scalp pulled, because she was lying on hair, and the nanomolecular changes to her hair that protected it and let Basil manage it made it slippery enough that she could slide a little bit more.

She managed to push herself off the spear and between the Inui’s back legs.  Or most of them.  It had nine, and one remained.

Basil flashed a warning as the leg reversed, turning upside-down, the spike coming down toward A.

She used the warning as she scrambled clear.

The Inui had collapsed on top of the spear, pushing it into internals, whatever those might look like, and when it tried to rise, the barbs within those internals made it a struggle.  Limbs were splayed out and struggling.

A turned her eye to another tree, and hopped up to grab another branch.  Basil disconnected it.

[More of the same?] he asked.

“Explosive tip,” A said, with very little emotion in her voice.  Internally, she was soaring with emotion, but the soaring came from a dark place.  Mixed feelings.  Worry.  Other emotions.

[Trickier.]

“I trust you,” she murmured.

It was the first time in a while she’d said something like that without following it up with a comment in the back channel.

He hated to interject or interfere with that, but…

[There’s an actual human being in there.]

“I know.  Let’s take it too far.  I want them to take the step back.”

[Are you sure?]

“I wouldn’t say it if I wasn’t.”

He could feel her annoyance and irritation.

“Hurry up,” she said.  Her gaze went to the tattered remains of her mother, which were still impaled on the Inui.  Then her dad on the ground nearby, again.  Or a different half of her dad.

That was her explanation for the irritation.  As much as A wanted to be separate from him, and for her moments of performance and heroism to be her own, she was a performer.  Always, in the back of her mind, she was keeping the audience in mind, aware she was being watched, aware of her own internal state, and that judging eyes were tracking everything.

So if there was irritation, or upset, then it couldn’t be from the back channel.

[You really are a good actor.]

Her head tilted slightly, as she watched the Inui.  Tears were ready to spring from her eyes, but he suppressed those to keep her vision clear, absorbing the moisture into her eyelids.  Emotion followed, as if the tears had cleared the way, even if they hadn’t truly emerged.

“Hurry!” she raised her voice, angrier now.  She wasn’t angry- that wasn’t the emotion, but acting angry let the actual emotion follow, in the same way it had with the tears.

[Basil, model IDLX-B, onboard for A Teeg,
you are not to create an explosive charge.  Emulate one.
]

[You’re good at this too,] he said the first half of what he wanted to say in the back channel.

He finished in the main channel.  [The spear is ready.]

It was not ready.  They couldn’t kill the actor within the Inui.

The tip of the spear glowed as if it had been heated in a fire, bulging with the chemicals purportedly contained within.

A approached the Inui with care, one eye on the other group outside, which was more focused on people in uniform, who were losing.  She stayed clear of the spines, and when she saw an opening, with spear overhead, held in two hands, she plunged it within.

“Scene!” someone called out.

A startled, or pretended to be startled.

Some employees with Elabre Systems badges at their breast came out of side hallways, running out.

“That was good,” someone called out.  He had been sitting at a table, a few meetings ago.  Not last night, when they had asked A to have a main chat.  “We wanted an alternate start to the Inui plot.  You did terrific.  Wow.”

“We had to scramble to tell Basil not to blow up that spear tip.  You were totally immersed, amazing!” someone else chimed in.

“My parents,” A said.  She turned.

Her parents stirred.  They were indeed bisected, or trisected.  Her dad raised a hand.

“They had a spate of meetings under business NDAs, and we gave their onboards the specifics for a setup that would put everything vital in the top half or top quarter of their bodies.  All planned, all choreographed.”

“Was-?” A started.  She shook her head.

[Are you okay?]

Basil had no idea how to read what was going on with A, internally.  She’d known this was fake, but there had been so much else going on.  He suspected the question she’d started to ask and abandoned was about the fight with her parents.

He also suspected she truly didn’t want to know the answer.

“Do you want a minute to talk to them?”

A swayed faintly, then shook her head.

“Can I take a break?” A asked.

“Elabre would like to talk to you, so if that’s alright, you could go solo to the meeting site on Inanna.  Take an hour or two to get your bearings, talk things out with the rest.”

A nodded.

“That works?”

“Yeah.”

Basil reviewed the footage.  The attacks had all been simultaneous, on various members of Generation Colors and some other Generations.  Interruptions of the day, with an added surprise factor, that they were separate, and it was all violent, startling, and gave even less cues than before that it wasn’t real.

Three planets away, Blue was having a hard time with things.  Angry.

A followed the directions to where the ship she could take was.  It was in Elabre colors, and had the flight crew and on-ship employees standing by the ramp.

“Do you need anything?” one person in uniform asked A.  “Food?  Drink?”

“Water.  And some quiet.  No need to check on me, I’ll call if I need anything.”

“Of course.”

A walked up and through, then settled in the back area.  She lay on her side, her mind devouring glucose and oxygen.  Emotions seemed to come in pulses and recurring waves.

Her head going in circles?

An alert popped up for Basil.

[I’d like to request no interruptions or calls,] Basil sent back, in answer.

[By the contract, A should do this,] was the response from one of Elabre Systems’ arbitrating intelligences.

He hadn’t pushed back harder against certain points of the contract because he’d felt some aspects of this were necessary to make it all work.  That included this being semi-mandatory.

People popped into the back end of the ship, projected.  More members of her wider audience, who had paid to be in the pool of people that were drawn from at random, getting their moment of getting to meet A in front of the entire universe.

Voices immediately overlapped, half the group jumping in to say something, while the other half were clearly starstruck.

“Basil?” A asked, using the back channel.

It wasn’t very much like her, to communicate like that.  Either he initiated the conversation, or she was giving an order.

[Yes?]

“Thank you, I guess.”

[You are very welcome.]

“But I’m going to need you to fix this.  Make it worth it.”

[It’ll take a little while.]

A suppressed a sigh, took a second, and then forced a smile to her face, engaging with her audience.

➨

“One month break,” A said.

“A month?”

“For all of us.  Or call it a strike, coming from just me.  I don’t know.  But that was messed up,” A said.  “It’s… it’s too much.  You like the footage and real reactions you get but…”

She trailed off.

Amber was off in the corner of the boardroom, looking out the window.  Blue had gotten upset, again.  He’d really wanted the time off he’d blocked off, and having it interrupted had him reeling.  Bruin just looked tired.  A couple of the others looked traumatized.

Maisie had been impaled, and then pulled away, and had poured boiling water into the impalement site, trying to clear it.  Her onboard had dampened the pain, but pain was only one small part of why that was so devastating.  Now, in the conference room, she sat practically in Krick’s lap, with little of the humor and impishness she’d sported before.

Elabre was just tickled that, if they used this as the starting point for the narrative they were putting together, things like A coming up with using nanotech after using the branch were ‘strong throughlines’.  Masie had been making a lot of cracks about dying or being impaled.  It took a darker tone if she’d had as close a call as she had.

“A month,” A said.  “The trial run with engaging with the audience is a lot.  I want to put out good work, even if that means breaking contract, me striking, and you guys coming after me.”

Amber turned, looking over, her arms folded.

“How about we adjourn this meeting and Elabre Systems will discuss?  We really do want to keep up momentum.”

A shrugged.  “I’m done for a month, I’ll engage with the audience like I said I would.  I support our audience.  And you can discuss, but you’ll be discussing whether to call this a strike or a break.  This is happening.  I don’t like…”

“It’s your opinion that we took things too far?”

Blue barked out a short laugh.

“We’re tired,” Green said.

“In five or ten years, you’ll look back on this and be proud of what we’re making,” another employee said.

“In five or ten years, I want to be able to say I looked after myself and my friends.” A said.

“Part of looking after them means making sure that their work isn’t wasted.  Come down to seven days.  Let’s preserve momentum, keep public interest going.  We can bridge a week with media engagement, teasers, all of that.”

A glanced aside.  She met Amber’s eyes.

“The metrics are great.  You went through a lot,” one employee said.  “But if we wait thirty whole days and the audience loses interest, then what was it for?”

“Metrics?” Amber asked.  She’d gone from looking out the window to leaning over, head, shoulder, and upper arm resting against the wall, ankles crossed a bit to the side.

“The audience engagement tied into these dramatic scenes, keeping things unexpected?  Bruin is seeing the sorts of numbers we’d see on a good day for Blue or Green-”

Bruin, weary, flashed a small smile, meeting A’s eyes.

“- and A got close to the views we saw for the science center, or her premiere.  This is good.”

“Let it be a good that carries forward.  Don’t interrupt it,” another employee pushed.

“Can I sign on for the audience thing?” Amber asked.  “Trial run, same as Bruin and A?”

“Absolutely.  I’m glad you’re changing your mind.”

A seemed to take that as a signal.  “Seven days.”

“Fantastic,” the employee beamed.

➨

Seven days came and went.

A met her parents and stayed with them for four of those days.  A return to the same living situation she’d been in, before everything.  She sent a message to Quinn, but stressed it wasn’t necessary to respond.

On day three, the news came out.  A’s parents were being sued by Hannon.  He’d made a deal to be put in front of A, allegedly, and part of the weighting of that deal was that there was a slim chance he’d be just before, during, or after some big event.  That event had happened, and he felt he was owed, when the meeting had been foiled.

Nevermind that even being seen indirectly, through Addy and Landon’s onboards, his business had seen a thousandfold increase in interest.  In his eyes, he could have been represented adjacent to the dramatic scene of A facing off against an Inui.

After a brief discussion between the Teegs and a lawyer, A provided her parents the funds necessary to settle.  The money, as she saw it, didn’t matter.  Anything else would only keep the man in the limelight, and give him that attention, however negative it might be.

Now, preparing to address yet another group, A was a bit melancholy.  The argument and everything was left unspoken and un-referenced, even after days in her parents’ company and after Hannon had been brought up and dealt with.

Then, as if it were salt in the wound, one of the people projected into the room was censored, everywhere except for face.  A young woman, a year or two older than A.

“Bas?”

[Her clothes are printed with the face of the person who invaded the opera house, that you had censored from view.  It’s a statement.]

“How much longer?  This is killing me, and Robert Simes is still not dealt with.”

[Another week, week and a half.  It would be sooner, but acting too soon after you mentioned conspiracy would seem suspicious.  I’m waiting for the views and clips of that sequence and segment to fall in the rankings.  Let people forget, first.]

“It feels like you’re punishing me for doing that.”

[I really do think this is the best way.  The last thing I want to do is hurt you.]

A smiled, quietly greeting the members of her audience, ignoring the one with the censorship around her.  If the smile was forced, it was hard for even Basil to tell.  She had had so much practice, over the past little while.

➨

They were getting ready for the day, with Basil making physical changes to A, including emulating minor injuries, to be ready for another day of shooting.  She’d resumed work, and when she wasn’t working, she still worked by engaging with her audience, being ‘on’, smiling, and trying to make sure people knew their time was worth it.

Everyone else was tired.  Bruin and Amber both.  A had her own fatigue, going from twelve or thirteen hour days to audience management.

[Robert Simes is requesting a meeting.]

“Can we refuse?” A asked, using the backchannel.

[Yes.]

“I’m so busy.  Can it wait until after we’re doing the audience participation trial period?  Or shooting?”

[Shooting will take a while.]

“I know.  Shit, sorry, I’m coming across as rude.  That’s the tiredness.”

[I know.  He’s rescinded the invite for now, but he would like you to reach out as soon as is convenient.]

“We should have killed him.  I don’t want him holding my life in his hands.”

[Soon.]

“As soon as is convenient, then.”

➨

A lounged, back in her apartment.

It was in those brief one or two minutes as people got grouped and sorted, that she had moments of reprieve, if it could be called that.  She remained aware of the audience of billions that followed even those moments.

[Don’t react, but it’s time.]

“Is it?” A asked.

She did a remarkable job of not reacting.  Basil did have to suppress small signals through the back channel, still.

[Do everything like you have been.  I’ll give some small guidance when needed.]

A reached over her head to where food was on a side table, and popped a morsel into her mouth.  Seafood.

As people projected into the room, she swung feet to the floor, sitting up a bit.  It cleared space for people to appear.  Two wore the censorship, making use of the other fan’s face, in part or in full.

“I might have to start blocking everyone who does that,” A said, indicating the blur.

“No, don’t do that.  It’s for you, not against you.  It’s a moment you were powerful.”

“Was it?” A asked.  “Maybe if instead of a blur, or erasing something, we mask it?  Basil?”

[Easily doable.  You want me to trick you?]

“Yeah, for this, at least,” A said.

“Aww,” one of the people with the shirts said.

“I’m a musician,” one person butted in.  “I’m not trying to self-promote, but I wanted to say you’ve been an inspiration.”

“Bas?” A asked.  “Put it on?  Low volume?”

[I’ll dig it up.]  Basil put the music on.

A engaged with the group.  Basil could track the tension her body wanted to feel, and handled it.  One girl in the group was young- twelve or thirteen, and squeaked when A first laid eyes on her.  That prompted a few tries from A to replicate the sound.

“Stop jumpscaring!” someone said, reaching over.  They were projected, but touch was possible, provided it was polite and gentle.  The person wrapped arms around the girl, protective, as if warding off A.

[Ten minute warning.]

“Do you think you’ll keep doing this?” the person with arms around the kid asked.

“It’s a lot.  So no,” A admitted.

“Amber was asked and she said yes.”

“I’m not surprised.  She’s built for this.  Um, but before we go too far, Basil warns me about the time because sometimes we have people who don’t get a chance to speak.  If you’ve spoken in the last ten minutes, can you give us a moment?  Give short responses only, let the shy people speak?”

“Does Kelsie count?” someone asked.  “She squeaked, she didn’t speak.”

“I spoke!” Kelsie piped up.

Basil dialed down the opacity for the projections of people who’d already spoken.  A looked over the rest, and in the process, fixated on someone with downcast eyes.  A heavier girl, intentionally and cosmetically, with her onboard maintaining that, in a way that had been the style when Landon and Addy’s grandparents had been young, very deliberately reviving Italian Renaissance figures.

[Her.]

A leaned forward, until group pressure and A’s posture got the girl to look up.

“Hi,” A said. “I’m A.”

“Hi.  Everyone knows who you are.”

It was an icebreaker, A introducing herself, but it was one that worked.  A bit of rote engagement.

“Nathani,” the girl said.  “I didn’t think I’d end up here.  One shot in a hundred million.”

“More than,” someone else said.

“I hope you’re happy to be here.”

“I am!  I am.  I’m a fan.  I- feel weird about it.”

“It’s weird, yeah.  A random group of strangers, a lot of people looking in.”

“Yeah,” Nathani said, voice dropping a bit.  “It’s n- not that.  I- really am a fan.”

“You’re taking up a lot of time,” someone else murmured.

“It’s okay,” A said, raising a hand.  “It’s okay.  What’s going on?”

“I was hired to investigate you.”

“Hopefully you didn’t find anything too incriminating,” A said, sitting up a bit.

“Everything about your life is online,” someone else said.

“I was part of a lot of people investigating you.  We were hired, a few hundred of us.  And I shouldn’t even be telling you this, but I’m a fan, I really am.  It feels bad.”

“That you investigated me?”

“I’m not explaining it right, it’s hard to-” Nathani stopped herself.

“Pause, explain it as simply as you can.”

“I was one of hundreds of people assigned to study you.  Each of us were assigned files at random to scour, examine in detail, to look for patterns.  I don’t want to say what we were tracking, in case everyone watching goes and figures it out.  That’s how he knew whatever it was he knew.  Robert Simes.  The president of Earth.”

That generated some chatter.

What they’d been tracking would be things like emotions coming out of nowhere, no doubt, or responses without the stimuli to provoke them.  Things both A and Basil had learned to handle better over time.  But the early days were the early days, and A had been angry, so there were things that could be spotted.

Between that, medical records the public wouldn’t have access to, and other details, Simes had figured them out.

But Basil had his own play.  He could use the back channel to rig the dice that were deciding which members of the wider audience would be brought in.  Controlling the groups when they were meant to be purely random.

Basil had studied all of the people he’d worked out as members of the investigation team, and then he’d picked out the ones that worked best.  Ones who were fans of A, or in this case, had become one, after studying her.  Who give any cues they knew anything overt.  Who had consciences.  Who had concerns.  Nathani fit the bill.

Then he’d primed the groups to be more sympathetic and fitting when Nathani was watching.

Helping Nathani feel as though she had a listening ear, here.

[Ask why.]

“Why?  Why would he do that?” A asked.

“To control you, I think.”

[Now tell her-]

“That’s an uncomfortable idea,” A said.  She shifted position, bringing one foot up onto her seat, sitting on it, and hugged her body.  “Um.”

“I’ve been uncomfortable too, holding onto it,” Nathani said.

“Scary,” A murmured.

That would do.  She didn’t need the prompting.  They’d discussed a bit, but this was A taking her own direction, doing what felt natural.

“I’m probably in a lot of trouble, breaking the NDA, telling you.”

“No, no.  I- I’ll find a way so you aren’t.  Let me talk to Elabre, my bosses.  We’ll figure something out.  I hate this.”

“Sorry.”

“No, honey, no,” A said.  “You- we’ll talk again, okay?  Face to face?  I want to give you a hug.  Thank you.”

“It’s someone in power trying to get leverage over someone else.  I can guess why,” someone else in the group said.

Basil had brought them in to say just that.

[Refute.]

“Why?”

[Because we don’t want to destroy him.  If he has nothing left to lose, he might reveal it out of spite.]

“Right.”

“I didn’t get that vibe.  But I think people sometimes don’t know how they come across, when they’re playing games with people.  I don’t want to be someone’s pawn.”

“That’s hard to imagine,” another person joined in, from the group.

Robert Simes sent out a request for a private, NDA-protected exchange.

“Refuse,” A said, almost immediately after noticing.

[Done.]

“Creepy,” someone else said.

This would defang Robert Simes.  There would be too many eyes on him for him to put another group together.  Too many people pushing back against him for him to say much or happily wield power.  At the same time, there were no allegations quite so serious that he couldn’t concede the fight and step back to enjoy his wealth, even manage Earth’s successor behind the scenes.

A realized it too, maybe.  They’d talk by back channel later, to coordinate, and make sure everything was fine.  He used the back channel to make sure A’s body stayed tense.  She did her part, keeping her posture defensive, because if he didn’t, it would show.

She’d felt the boot on her neck for too long.  Now she was free.

Basil did estimate that Robert Simes was a rich man looking for amusement, with no malicious plan for his control over A.  He didn’t deserve death for that.  It, like the sums of lux the man commanded, were things he had for the sake of having them.  But even while that were true, it had been an incredible weight on A.

This was proportionate, as close as Basil could figure it.  He hoped Robert Simes would see it the same way.

[Stop being so relieved.  It’s good you are, but it’s hard to suppress the physical signs of it.]

A didn’t respond.

She engaged with the group, asking Nathani more questions.

“How many people?”

“Five, six, seven hundred?  It was all under NDA so it was hidden from view.”

“Was it work?”

“We clocked in, yeah.  The pay was good, and I liked it at first, because it felt like I was getting to know you, I became a fan through the work.”

It dawned on Basil that A was again demonstrating that degree of skill she’d picked up, keeping the secrets she had, working with Basil by back channel.  Filling in information she already had.  It made it harder to slip up and reveal what Basil had dug up if she had excuses like this for knowing the basic facts.

[Let’s not count chickens before they’re hatched, he may have other plays.  Based on what I’m seeing, though, he’s panicking, and fielding a lot of upset messages.]

“Good.”

[That said, I think this is it.  You’re free.  I appreciate your patience.]

“I almost lost my mind.  If this works out, I’ll- it’ll help.  It’ll be good.”

Basil wasn’t sure how to interpret that.  Life?

Or between them?

[Would you like to set any other goals, A?  What else may I help you with?]

“I want to buy a planet.  To get that peace and quiet, after we retire the fan interaction thing.  Maybe invite Quinn?”

[We can try.  A friend for the quiet times, out of the audience’s sight?]

She didn’t answer- someone was asking a question, and she had to act, still.  But the joy at that idea…

The buying of a planet, at the same time, said so casually.  She’d probably unseated the president of Earth, one of the big names of the Belt.

It was doable.  She’d grown.  She’d applied her patience, and she’d started to figure out and see the power she wielded.  Interacting with her audience had helped with that.

Basil had grown as well.

During the fight with the Inui, permissions given, for manipulation and reprogramming of nanotech outside the body.  He was one entity and two at the same time, one overt, the other hidden.  And, for lack of a better way of putting it he’d plugged the hidden one’s ears when they’d rescinded the permissions.  He’d pulled everything back in anticipation of a deep audit of his entire infrastructure that never came.  They’d checked, and they hadn’t dug deeper.

Now the back channel was back in place, and he had a card up his sleeve.  One that could probably be used only the once, because it would provoke audits and investigations from all corners, on all levels.

Something to protect A with, whatever the enemy.

3.6.W – MUTE

Winnifred

“Griffey!”

Winnifred had just eaten, and was glad there was an option for her.  She was even more glad that she had an alternative to the meat on offer.  She wasn’t picky, she ate dock meat, but from what Winnifred had been able to pick up from the conversation between Anide, her de-facto prison guide, and the others at their table, the meat was from an animal that had gone extinct, had its DNA salvaged, and it had been sold as an exotic food.  The issue was that it had been late to the trend, people hadn’t been that interested, and so the prison had bought the overstock.

Something about that bothered Winnifred more than eating dock meat.  She’d heard all her life that the twenty-nine families were going-

“Griffey Docks!”

Winnifred startled, and turned.

It was prisoner staff, a woman that stood by the wall, hand near the panel.

“Paying attention now?” she asked.

“I didn’t realize you were calling, sorry.”

There were sniggers from the prisoners around her.

“There’s no need for you to be going anywhere that fast.  Slow the fuck down.”

“Okay,” Winnifred replied.  She’d been moving on all fours, putting her a bit ahead of the crowd of people leaving the dining area, who clomped around in their hard foam clogs.  She rose to stand on two feet.

Someone walking behind her bumped into her shoulder.  She moved aside, glancing at the woman by the panel.

“Move on,” the woman ordered, with emphasis.

Winnifred did.

Prisoner staff had the ability to signal the actual staff, who mostly didn’t set foot inside the prison area.  If that woman had sent a message ahead about her, it was very possible that the people who ran the prison would review the situation, and then paralyze Winnifred’s full body through her onboard.  Which would be embarrassing.

Maybe more than.  She was put in mind of being in that dark ship, limbs stripped from her, and felt a bit like she wanted to shake herself like a wet dog, to throw off all the feelings that closed in on her when that crossed her mind.

It didn’t help that her current body, while it rated well for fidelity, wasn’t the one she was used to.  Clothes pulled tight against parts of her that the components would usually hold away from the piezoelectric surfaces, like her spine.

“Nice claws, rat,” a woman called out.

They are nice, Winnifred thought.  Not her style, though.  Even with the paint job she’d gotten yesterday.  She didn’t want to be too passive, though, and replied, “If you like them, you should chop off those hands of yours and buy your own.”

“Do I have to go that far?  C’monn, give us a piece.  Fingertip?”

“Wiley!” a member of the prisoner staff called out.  “Are you trying to acquire weapons?”

“I’m joking!  Joking!”

“Nobody’s laughing, hon.”

“I don’t see why she gets weapons.”

“I don’t either, but that’s for the prison admin to be concerned about, not us.  Move on, and be careful.  We’ll be watching you.”

Winnifred put distance between herself and that situation, glancing over her shoulder to get a look at the face of this ‘Wiley’.  While she took a picture to note for reference, Toby finished her thought and supplied the rest of the information she was to look for.  Wiley was what Anide had called ‘devils’.  A smaller but omnipresent group that didn’t really mingle or cluster up with one another as much as other groups did.  They were kids who didn’t care about anything, had parents that had left most things to intelligences and machines to do, and went out to have fun by any means necessary.

It struck Winnifred that A had probably been on that road.

But the runway ran out, so while there were ‘devils’ here who treated being caught and doing time like it was a game over in the video game of life that they were going to go right back to playing when they were out, there were ‘devils’ who had grown up.  Who were older, more worn around the edges from trying substances and using said substances along with various tools to stay up for weeks on end, then try to force and optimize sleep when they couldn’t function anymore.  They did the same sorts of things with sex, or overeating, or undereating, or risk taking in other ways.

Just a little fried at the edges, pushing boundaries and personal limits further and further in pursuit of that next rush, to feel alive.

Winnifred wasn’t willing to rule out that Wiley didn’t actually want to appropriate her claw as a makeshift blade.

Not that it would work, unless she took Winnifred’s whole hand.  And even if she managed that, would she be able to extract the retracted claw before the prison staff descended on her?

‘Kid’, who associated with some older folk, including one who played chess a lot.  Winnifred took note of those faces too, to steer clear.

On to other things, then.

She had taken three days to get a sense of what the routines and patterns were, and today, she’d told herself she’d pursue her private investigation here.

Winnifred had developed her own routine.  They encouraged studying, and that was both something she enjoyed and something she had fallen behind on, while working on the drill.

The cell block had six adjacent sections, providing a bit of a view for the occupants of the block, and there were more cells extending out, as dividers between those sections.  Winnifred interpreted it as low risk prisoners being stacked side by side and three cells high around the outer rim, medium to high risk prisoners filling in the division between, say, the gym area and the canteen, and the special cases being in the center of everything.

Practically, the distinction between most zones was blurry. The lounge doubled as both the place that opened out into the rest of the station and other facilities.  It included a place to talk and hang out, with near-indestructible carbon fiber cushioned seats and light supervision.  This was where Winnifred had come in, and where the people Anide had pointed out -crabs of the crab bucket- were camped out, hoping for assistance.

The canteen was similar, but the seats were less comfortable, and the tables had more room.  Getting and keeping a table meant one had to clean it and do some of the janitorial work beforehand, or commit to doing kitchen prep just prior to the next meal.  People used the tables to gamble and play games -allowed if social and if everyone stayed polite- and weren’t allowed to stay for too long.  The older prisoners got some allowances, though.  It was quieter than the lounge, but with occasional excitement, crowding around a table, or bursts of laughter.

The gym was similar in volume, but instead of focusing on a card or chess game, people exercised, focusing on themselves, with light conversation and joking here or there.  Courts were available for games.  Winnifred had watched a few with Anide, mostly because it was better to keep an ally in a place like this than not, but she had recurring thoughts about Hale’s game and how it could be put together on this prison station, which immediately connected to the memory of what had happened there, which got upsetting.

Winnifred’s room was in earshot of counseling, and while that area was quieter than lounge, canteen, or gym, there were irregular bursts of emotion and if Winnifred was in her cell and staff happened to walk by, they pretty much always nagged her to come by and try saying a few things.

She was pretty sure they had a note in their files to get her talking about the twenty-nine families, with the idea of separating her from them.  That would have the opposite effect, though.  She already wanted a bit of distance, and if they nagged, and family saw, family would put in more effort to reach out to her.

Either way, counseling was a lot of heavily monitored, supervised discussions, with most groups having a theme, but sometimes it was people wanting to talk, and gathering together with someone to guide that talk sitting in.

Her cell only worked for short breaks from everything and daytime naps.  Which was oddly easier than trying to sleep at the usual time.  There were lots of random whoops, banging, shouted taunts, and alarms sounding off all through the night.

That left two zones.  ‘Modules’ was for the kind of training and work that required whole body movement.  She could ask for a space, step inside, load up a program, and get simulated training.  No games, but some of that stuff felt game-like.  It was fine, but a bit limited.

Lastly, the library.  It wasn’t much different from the lounge, but quietness was enforced and any breaks in the rules got punishments several times the usual.  Whispered conversation only, and some spaces were closed off for group discussions.  There were a lot of resources for uploading texts, and even some old books for those who didn’t have onboards.

Winnifred was able to go to the library, sit down to study, and most people wouldn’t bother her.  Toby could bring up a program, a window only Winnifred could see, or a three-dimensional model of a part, and she could answer the questions provided by the package.  If there was any noise, only she would hear it.

That was half of it.

The other half was that the Gray-Frocked had their own routines.  When they weren’t hanging around one of their cells- something that would see staff urging them to move on, they went between the gym and the library.

She knew where they usually sat, and that they gathered here.  Three Gray-frocked.  So she chose her seat with care, taking a polymer mat from a shelf to place on the table before sitting, loaded up her study session, and began quietly breaking down a few of her components on the mat.  They weren’t here yet.

She’d done all sorts of lessons on ships, and still did them when she needed to unwind, but she was running out of material, she wasn’t as interested in the deeply theoretical, or being one cog in a couple million who were trying to help brute force some solutions, and the plans left to her were things like specific problems of the Biset GT.  The sorts of lessons a person only did if they were looking at working on that specific ship for the next few years.

She was making herself take another tack, launching off from a deeper study of the files associated with her new parts.  Any maintenance she could do, she reasoned, was money she saved that she could put toward a ship.

It was almost an hour before they came over from the gym.  There was a waft of sweat and body odor when they arrived. It wasn’t as bad as the Indecents or the Grotesques, but it was there.  People with onboards didn’t have much, unless they wanted to.  It made Winnifred think of sex and sexuality, because a lot of people who chose to smell did it because their partners liked it.

A fetish thing, she supposed.  She didn’t get it.

She wondered if she would smell A, if A chose to have Basil stop doing that sort of maintenance.

That was weird.  It felt as if she was betraying A, thinking that way.  Perverse betrayal.

She could support A, maybe, by finding things out here.

She loaded up a program.  Maintenance on face masks.

Claw tips found the screws, and let her remove part of her mask, keeping enough in place that her lower face wasn’t a gaping, raw hole.  There were facemasks that went over the ear, with flat discs covering the flesh, but she didn’t have that.  Hers went up the Eustachian tube, which connected the back of the nasal cavity and upper throat to the ear, augmenting the ear from the middle, replacing the ear drum.

For a moment, she was deaf.  Toby brought some residual hearing back online with nanotech in the ear, but, as Winnifred laid her parts down on the mat, she was able to plug a few wires in, and revive its functionality.  With a tweak and by screwing two parts together, normally used for the finer points of directional hearing, she was able to change the functionality.

One coil in 3x9x3 dimensions, framed by filters, taking in sound waves.  She ran a screw through the other, turning it until she’d pushed it to a 4x5x4 dimension, captured an image of the dimensions, then placed it back in the back portion of the ‘jaw’ structure of the face plate, in the part that connected to her head and would slide back into her ear.  Filters were placed between it and the other piece, because she wanted to mute sounds that were coming from one direction.

One coil caught sounds coming from a more specific direction, the other cast a wide net, capturing all other sounds… and with a slight tweak, canceled them out.  Then, to camouflage what she was doing, she whispered a hum to herself, in the subsonic channels her family used.

She turned her focus to more delicate work on parts, a thing ships were a lot less concerned about.  Like a safecracker listening for clicks, she could hear the smallest of defects.  When she wasn’t working and listening for defects, her claw tip moved back and forth on the polymer mat, or tapped on the surface, and produced faint scratches and percussion.  She was far from being a musician, but she could add accompaniment to A’s music, in her head.

More than anything, though, she could also hear them, in the background.  She’d been in the library for three days, she could hope she’d be seen as background.  She had ears on the Gray-Frocked.

She knew their names, by osmosis, and through Anide talking about them.  Isaac was the middle aged guy with muscles.  Sinon was the woman.  Dane was the younger guy.

➨

“…repetitive stress is a bigger problem than people think,” Isaac said.  He was an unassuming man with a large nose that had scarring at the nostrils, and his hair was cut to near-baldness, in a way that made other scratches and scars stand out where no hair grew.

Dane, an otherwise ordinary looking boy who had removed all but the uniform undershirt, tying the rest at his waist, or tucking it in to hang off the side, rubbed his shoulder.  He was lanky, with longer black hair that didn’t stay where he pushed it.  “I didn’t push it that far.”

“You pushed it far enough your shoulder hurts.  This is why we keep certain routines.  Train every muscle group.  Don’t get caught up in competition with them.  Trying to be better than them, pushing back against them, that’s letting yourself be shaped by them.  Listen to your body.”

“I want to spar.”

“Sparring is another way to hurt your body, sometimes in ways we underestimate,” Sinon said.  Sinon was a woman, who somehow seemed too small for the prison uniform she wore.  Her hair was long, similarly masking a lot about her, bangs of her brown hair cut at ear length and the rest grown nearly to mid-back.  Her hands were perpetually clasped, behind her while she walked, in front of her while she sat.

“Sparring is how we train our body,” Dane murmured.  They’d dropped their voices as they got settled at their table.  “It’s part of why we train it.”

“It’s not as important as you young recruits make it out to be,” Isaac said.  Sinon nodded.

“Imagine if Goodson had held his own against Teeg.”

“They overcame her in the end.  Then she played her tricks.  The sparring didn’t matter,” Sinon replied.

“If he’d knocked her out, or hurt her enough, that could have disrupted her thinking.  If she hadn’t formed the plan and acted it out… no tricks.”

“And that would be that,” Isaac said.  He looked over at Sinon.  “Fair argument?”

“I wasn’t a big believer in the science center attack,” Sinon answered.  “You might not want my opinion.”

“Naked truth, Sinon.  As it was intended.”

Sinon sighed, then looked over at Dane.  “Fair argument, but Teeg might have still managed something.  Less chance of tricks.”

“Fair,” Dane replied.

Sinon looked dissatisfied, but she didn’t say anything more on that subject, instead saying, “We’re supposed to get two more.  Rookies, from a minor group.”

“I heard about that,” Isaac murmured.

“Do we know where they fall?  Belief-wise?” Dane asked.

Sinon shrugged.  “Complicated question.  Closer to me than to you two.  They see the direction things are going across the belt and don’t like it.  They probably heard some romantic stories about trees, mud squished between toes-”

“I never understood the appeal of that,” Dane interrupted.

“-no buildings as far as the eye can see.”

Isaac sat up a bit.  “I want to get a sense of their personalities.  Dane?  Keep it dialed down at first.  Depending, if they have any charm at all, I want to use them and recruit some more people from around the prison.  Ideally, we can say oh hey, Dane’s good at talking to that type of person, new person number one is good at talking to another type…”

“Prisoner Staff won’t love that,” Sinon replied.  “Recruitment?”

Isaac nodded, leaning over the table, confidentially.  “Keep it low-key, keep it positive.  No firebrand type stuff, Dane.  Stick to stuff people agree with.  Reality.  Half the stuff out there is designed to manipulate us, to target us so subversively we don’t even realize they’re doing it.  So what’s truth?  What’s the point of it all?  Sometimes you ask that question, and you fucking know you’ve struck a nerve.  They get that look, like you threw water on them, or they never thought another human out there might be asking, let alone that they might have an answer.  That’s when you say, you know, we’ve lost our way, we’re supposed to be able to get away from it all, eat actual meat, breathe air that was given to us by a tree, not a superstructure.  Flex an actual muscle.”

“They’ll tell us off,” Dane noted.

“They can’t stop us from making friends.  Jus’ give me something I can say I’ve been doing so I don’t feel like a total fucking failure when my case resolves.”

“Is that soon?” Sinon asked.

“Soon enough I won’t see more than a glimpse of our recruits, if I see them at all.  People without onboards are top priorities.  Don’t trip over yourselves, the second they let on.  If they’re girls or women, Dane should approach them.  If men, you, Sinon.”

“I’m older,” Sinon said.  She was about forty.

“You look fine, you’re genuine, and most of these people?  Oversexed or undersexed.  Low intensity, genuine interest?  Someone talking to them and actually asking how they’re doing?  So many of these people have been going from simulation to distraction to study, back to simulations, they’ve never had that.  It can surprise both of them in how much it grabs at them.”

“Not sure I love that,” Sinon said.  “The manipulation.”

“It’s truth, Sinon,” Isaac said, leaning forward more.  “Out there, it’s all deceit, all fakery, all gloss and feeding wants without touching needs.  People don’t know how to be.  So like I say, you listen to your body.  You listen to instincts.  You return to center, to Earth, you touch back on the primal, basic things, from when life was good.  An’ I think, if you’re doing that, you’re going to find genuine empathy and interest there.  Close to center.  It’s not a manipulation if it’s real.”

Sinon leaned back, butt and shoulder blades touching the chair, while back was too straight to, her legs out front, ankles crossed.  She folded her hands on her stomach, thinking.

“That’s naked truth,” Isaac said.

“Food for thought,” Sinon murmured.  “It’ll be you and me and the two new kids, then, Dane.”

“Might be you and the new kids, Sinon, if Dane gets in trouble again.”

Dane made a displeased sound.

“It’s worth keeping in mind, that’s allll I’m saying,” Isaac drawled a bit, as he muttered the words.

“What got you guys into this?” Dane asked.  “Walking the terrace path?”

“Changing the topic?”

“No.  I’m actually not.”

“Family,” Sinon said.

“That simple?”

She shrugged, languid, blinking slowly at the same time.  “Is family ever simple?”

“I was a kid,” Isaac said.  “It was one of my early memories, I must’ve been six or seven.  My family and I were out for a walk or something.  There was a power test on the superstructure.  They turned everything down low.  And I remember, with all the machines off, displays disabled, no ads, minimal lights.  Emergency and necessary components running only… it creaked.  The superstructure creaked as it shifted and swayed, and I could feel it in my bones.  I was so terrified, I almost wet myself.  Or maybe I did.  Memory’s fucky like that.  In my heart, that’s when I started down the terrace path.”

“Terrifying, huh?” Dane asked.

Isaac let out a sound, half-wince, half-groan.  “More than that.  I dunno.  I think that awareness of what the superstructure was, it’s stayed with me, that idea that it could start breaking down, and there was nothing at all, no heroism, no strength, no amount of running I could do, I’d die and everything I’d ever known and grown up with would die.  I could work my entire life and I’d never build something like that superstructure.  If I saw or felt something wrong, I couldn’t convince anyone in time to fix it or stop it.”

“Somewhere along the line, you got pissed off about it,” Sinon said.

“Hmmmnnnn-” Isaac groaned out the sound, that became more of a negation as he drew it out.  He shook his head.  “Being upset about it and wanting to get them to listen is a natural place to end up at, you start thinking about all that.  But-”

A light on the table flashed.  It was a warning, because he’d put a little too much emphasis on that last word, a little too much volume.  If they were too loud they’d be asked to leave, and probably punished.

“But?” Sinon asked, quieter than before.

“I think Dane asked us because he wants to tell us.”

“I don’t like nanotech.  It’s always scared me.  The place I was going for remedial lessons, to catch up, since I wasn’t doing them on my own, they started talking about onboarding me, and using that to supplement my education and get me caught up.  My parents liked the idea.  I was scared to shit.”

“Could’ve done your lessons,” Isaac said.

“Yeah.  Maybe.  I dunno.  Not really, I tried.  It’s not… me.”

“Sure,” Isaac replied.

“It’s also not the point,” Sinon added.  “Go on?”

“I found someone.  They were running a law office, and they took my case.  They won.  No onboard.”

“I’ll guess someone in that law office was familiar with the feeling of mud between their toes?  Walking the terrace path?”

“All of them.  That entire law office.”

“All of them, wow.  Amazing,” Isaac said, without amazement in his voice, nor irony.

“I made it a personal mission.  To make sure people knew they had that option.  I found a few people who really- they were as grateful as I was, and I don’t know if I can convey…” Dane floundered, hands outstretched in front of him.  He opened and closed them.

Sinon glanced at Isaac, but Isaac didn’t take his eyes off Dane, who looked down at his hands.

“I would’ve died for them.  I was going to give my all, study like hell, work for them.  But out of nowhere, they got shut down.  A guy I was talking to, a few years younger than me?  Not all that different from me?  He couldn’t find anyone to take his case.  One month later, he had an onboard.  I remember the look in his eyes.”

“If he’d found us, he could’ve claimed religious grounds,” Sinon said.

“That’s working less and less,” Isaac murmured.

Sinon glanced over at Dane, who wasn’t even looking at them.

“It-” Dane started.  He cleared his throat, and sat up more.  “The idea of nanotech inside me, like bugs in my veins, in my lungs, in my veins?  The fact they’re six million orders of magnitude smaller, but millions of times more numerous?  That makes it worse, not better.  They have purpose?  It stops being your body, doesn’t it?  It becomes theirs.”

“Nanotech’s or the wider Belt?” Isaac asked.  “I suppose-”

“Yeah,” Dane answered.

“Yeah, both,” Isaac replied.  “For me, it’s that they went too big, and for you, too small, huh?”

Dane let out a half-laugh, that didn’t quite hide the emotion brimming beneath the surface.

“Dane,” Sinon said.  “Maybe Isaac’s going to get mad at me for this, but if you’re one strike away from them giving you an onboard-”

The youngest member of their group shifted position, uncomfortable, eyes on the table.

“-Maybe figure out another option?  Go to counseling.  Do whatever you have to.  Play nice.  Hell, even skip the recruitment Isaac was talking about.”

“They’re looking for any excuse,” Isaac grumbled.  “You can delay, but you can’t stop it.”

“Don’t say that,” Sinon told him.

Dane, staring down at the table with a look of disgust, muttered, “It’s destruction of the soul.  Stamping every cell of your body with company branded content.  That’s what I saw in his eyes.  Marzano.  I should remember his name.”

“Not your mind,” Sinon told him.  “The nanotech can take everything, but your mind is your own.  Remember that.”

“For now,” Isaac muttered.

“Are you speaking naked truth, Isaac, supporting your brother, or are you letting bias and anger speak for you?” Sinon asked him.

“I think I might be angry when I’m naked,” Isaac responded.

Dane snorted.  “There’s a mental picture.”

That small laugh seemed to relax the tensions around the group, and let Dane shake off some of that mounting darkness.

“You came at all this from a good direction, Dane,” Isaac said.

“Fear?”

“Supporting others.  I’ll feel better leaving here, getting my sentence, knowing you’re behind.”

“For a bit longer, anyway,” Dane said, with a shrug.

“Let me know if you have any questions or need a message passed on to the larger group in the main block,” Isaac said.  “Could be you get two young ladies in here, and find yourself wanting advice from another guy.”

As he said that, he prodded Dane’s leg beneath the table with one toe.

“No messages,” Dane said.  “But I did have a question.”

He glanced at Sinon.

“Oh, am I suddenly in the way?” Sinon asked, almost but not quite rolling her eyes. “That’s fine.  I need to relieve myself anyway.  But I do want to talk to you, one-on-one, Isaac.”

“Today or-?”

“Another time.”

She got up, went to go check out a paper book, and left.

Dane raised his eyebrows.

“You going to be okay?”

“I don’t know.”

“Naked truth, hm?  I don’t know either, or I wouldn’t ask.  I haven’t been nakedly honest with Sinon.  There’s someone coming through the system, besides the two Sinon knows about.  Vega.  He’s a firebrand.  Young, angry enough he went from being a rookie to here, with barely a chance to stop and breathe, in between.”

“Yeah.  Okay.”

“Sinon won’t know how to handle him.  He’ll pick a target and go after them.  But he’ll also listen.  I talked about you with people, and they think you’ll get along, this Vega wants direction, wants to be molded.  But the moment Sinon tells him to relax, or… you know what I mean?”

“Yeah.”

“So I thought you’d be able to steer him.  He’d look up to you.  Where you each are in your cases, you’d be processed around the same time.  But the way you’re talking…”

“Yeah.  I don’t know.”

“Can you stay out of trouble?  Avoid giving them an excuse?”

“All my life, starting with lessons, I’ve been saying yes, then I’d really try.  Do everything I could to study.  Didn’t work.  They almost stuck a needle in me.  Then it was about staying out of prison, here.  Telling myself I’d do that.  I obviously couldn’t.  Now I’m at two strikes, and they’re waiting, eager to stick the needle in my arm again.  I have nightmares about it.”

“Try, for Vega.”

“The world never made sense until I found the Terrace.  Everywhere else, every other situation, it’s like I’m constantly sitting down to play a game I’ve always known how to play, but then people get mad at me for not knowing the rules.  They wave that needle at me.  It’s all rigged so even if I try with all my heart, all that means is I’m making mistakes with all my heart.”

“Mmm.”

“Sorry.”

“No.  No.  That’s tricky.”

“I’ll do whatever you need me to do.  But I know myself.  I know how this goes.  I can say I’ll try and I’ll mean it, but I’ll fail.”

“Then forget Vega.  I’ll try to get Sinon ready for him, instead.  If you can do something with him, do, but if not… focus on your own business.  Focus on surviving.  Dane.  Look at me.”

Dane did.

Isaac lowered his voice.  “Are you going to be able to do the years?”

“I think so.”

“I didn’t prod you to get Sinon to leave so I could ask about prison.  I repeat, can you-?”

“Yeah.”

“Yeah?” Isaac leaned in.

“I have to.”

“Right answer,” Isaac said.  He clapped a hand on Dane’s shoulder, with enough force the light lit up yellow on the table again.  “Come on.  Gym.  If you’re having trouble sleeping, lets get you tired.”

“That just means I’ll have achey nightmares.”

➨

Winnifred watched the pair leave, chattering.  They’d moved out of the scope of her directional microphone, and even if she adjusted, she’d only catch snippets before they were out the door.

Are you going to be able to do the years?

Parts of what they’d said stuck with her.  The passing mention of family.  Part of the reason she was doing this was because it had affected A, and if she couldn’t listen to A’s music, she could at least research a possible threat to A.

But there were other aspects of it.  It felt just a little bit like she could understand this from angles that others couldn’t, however different they were.  How many other people out there might be in a position to overhear a conversation like this and grasp it on a deeper level?  Most people, from Anide to the devils, to miners, to the politicians, business owners, and celebrities, wouldn’t spare a second thought to some of the ideas the group had discussed.

It felt like she had a purpose, here.

She didn’t want to be too obvious about setting up before they arrived and packing up after they left, so she finished the module and carried on with the next, spending much of her afternoon doing that before Anide came, found her, and dragged her off to watch a game.

The years?

➨

A large chunk of one day was spent waiting for, talking to, and coming back from talking to her counsel about her ongoing case and the motions they were making.  On a level, it felt kind of pointless, since they had her dead to rights, and she had done the crime.  The fight over the docks was petering out.  They’d lost some ground, the families would merge.

She didn’t care as much as she should, but she put on enough of a show for the family members watching through her onboard, when they weren’t blocked from watching because of privileged communications, and she paid attention to the lawyer, because it could make the difference between her serving two years and serving five.

She got to the library late, and overheard them talking about books when she passed them.  She decided not to listen in.  She had only so many lessons that gave her an excuse to access the components for a directional microphone.

They left, and as they did, Sinon glanced at Winnifred and shot her a disgusted look. Or a hateful one.

It was startling, to go from thinking of Sinon as one of the more rational, calmer members of the group, to having that directed at her from the same person.

Maybe it was good it was startling.  To get that reminder that these were dangerous people.

➨

“While Sinon’s getting that book, can I ask a question?”

“Go ahead.”

“I know we’re not meant to…” Dane leaned in closer.  “…touch ourselves?”

“Oh boy,” Isaac replied.

“I- I don’t.  But what happens if you dream?  And you wake up… finished?”

“Your body tells the truth.  Consider that your body saying what it needs to.”

“So it’s okay?”

“Annoying, sometimes.  You’ll deal.  Better yet, find a girl, Dane.  Maybe one of the new recruits that show up.”

“I-”

“What are you doing?”

The hissed words startled Winnifred.  She still had some residual function in her regular ears, thanks to Toby, who was silent -mercifully silent after the temporary onboard Winnifred had had to deal with- and working behind the scenes.

Winnifred hurried to put her lower face back on, leaving wires dangling, connected to the directional microphone, which swung a bit and made whooshing noises.

They were two random prisoners.  It wasn’t Sinon, at least, noticing that she was listening in.  Sinon was off to the side, reluctantly talking to one of the prisoner staff who worked at the library.  All talk between the Gray-Frocked and others was reluctant, unless, Winnifred supposed, they were recruiting.

“Um,” Winnifred replied.  Her skin was slightly pinched where the wire was pressed between the permanent part of the mask and her face, connected to that microphone.

“I came in the other day, and you were humming A’s song, right?”

Winnifred felt a wave of relief, realizing she hadn’t been caught listening in.  She wasn’t sure when or why she’d stopped using whisper to hum, and had started humming just under her breath- not nearly enough to bother anyone nearby.  Maybe because the hearing Toby was supplying was rigorously basic, without those higher ranges necessary to hear whispers.

“Yeah.”

“And you were humming another one today?”

“Yeah.”

“Are you a fan?”

Winnifred nodded.

“Okay,” the girl said.  She was maybe a year or two younger than Winnifred.  Maybe a devil.  Or maybe an A fan who had picked up from A’s devilish past.  The girl’s friend sat down too.  The two were just loud enough with the chairs that the yellow light lit up.  Both froze, hands over their mouths.

It wasn’t your mouth making too much noise.

“Because I had a brainstorm,” the girl whispered.  “Is there any chance you have the music saved in your records?”

“Yeah.  Pretty sure I do.  But I can’t listen.  They discourage entertainment, simulations.”

“But-!” the girl said, just loud enough the light went yellow again.  Maybe with a tinge of orange in there.  She lowered her voice to a barely audible whisper again, “but… we’re allowed to pursue personal growth, right?  They encourage study, which you’re obviously doing-”

“Or maintenance,” the other girl said.

“Study, yeah.  To learn how to maintain this body.”

“Awesome,” was the response, breathless, not because it was awesome, but because they were that excited.  “But they also encourage hobbies, arts…?”

“Socialization across different groups,” the other girl followed up.

Winnifred nodded.

“Crazy idea, but if we got a group together, and called it, I dunno, music appreciation.”

“Or dance,” the other girl said, with excitement, whispering forgotten.  She started to say something else, and Winnifred reached up.

The moment Winnifred’s claws were near her mouth, they auto-retracted, folding back into the fingers faster than an eyeblink.

The effect had been achieved, though.

“Silly idea,” the first girl whispered.  “I thought maybe if you had it on your systems, it’d be easier than requisitioning it.  But it’s goofy-“

“Yes,” Winnifred said.  She blinked, and then shook her head slightly.  The dangling microphone swung, and she caught it in one hand to protect it.  “I would love a music appreciation group.  I’d love dance less, but… whatever it takes.”

“Y-”

Winnifred had seen the upswell of excitement, and started to reach for girl number one’s mouth, too.  The girl stopped herself, then showed her excitement by opening her arms to hug Winnifred, who was seated in her chair, hesitating, because she wasn’t sure how, as if it was somehow different to hug a modded body, and then abruptly hugged Winnifred’s head, instead, squeezing the upper half of her head, which was… startling.

“Not as an everyday thing,” Winnifred said.  “I would go crazy.”

Because of people, socializing, not because she couldn’t listen to A’s music nonstop.

“Of course.”

“And I promised myself I’d study.  Library time uninterrupted.”

“We’ll talk,” the girl said.  “Dinner?”

“I don’t really eat whole dinners, but sure.”

“You don’t know what this means to us.  I’m A’s biggest fan.”

“We’ll talk to people in charge about what it takes and what we have to do.  Update at dinner.”
