Winnifred nodded.

As if afraid to scare Winnifred off or change her mind, or overly accommodating the point about the library, they hurried away, leaving her bewildered.

Winnifred pulled herself back together, emotionally, while pulling herself apart, physically.  Face taken apart, inner ear modified into a directional microphone again, set on the table.

“There are at least two unfired guns I know of,” Isaac was saying.

Biggest fan?  I might have you beat.

➨

They were late to the library.  Winnifred worked at her studies, doing an easier module that involved a lot of rote checking, while her mind worked through what she knew.

Two mentions of the ‘years’.  Both cryptic and brief.  Sinon wasn’t looped into that.

Three new recruits coming, one of which Sinon wasn’t informed about.  The group was varied, with some being content to live on ships full time, or stick to work on mining planets, barely making enough from a single small undesirable plot to sustain themselves, setting up a homestead type settlement with the ship for essential necessities, working, picking up, and starting all over again.  Others were more aggressive.

Isaac and Dane were more aggressive.  Not quite to the point they would’ve attacked the science center, but they didn’t vehemently disagree with that attack.  They disagreed with the how of it, not that it had happened.

The ‘unfired guns’ were a series of other planned attacks that had never happened.  The authorities knew of some from people they’d brought in who they’d gotten to talk, but the way things were structured, not everyone in every one of the more militant cells knew.  Isaac knew of two.  Apparently too many of the people who would have managed those attacks had been arrested, though, hadn’t talked or revealed anything, and the ones who’d remained weren’t confident in their ability to see it through.

The idea had been the first attack would be a wake up call and a call to action.  They’d recruit off of their success.  The other attacks would be punishment for those who hadn’t woken up, who hadn’t heeded that call to action.  But the first attack hadn’t succeeded, and in its failure, they’d lost most of their number to arrest.  Increased onboard surveillance, low numbers, and a lack of certain experts after the arrests meant they couldn’t operate the necessary tools, devices, or whatever else.  They hadn’t actually said what the unfired guns were.

The time window passed.  Winnifred finished early, put herself together, got up, and went back to her cell.

She spotted Sinon, and through that, spied Dane on his way to his higher supervision cell, between counseling and the canteen, where guards on either side would have eyes on him.

Isaac was gone, she realized.  He’d been handed his sentence, and moved out of this cell block, which was for people awaiting resolution, and into one of the others.

Winnifred could have sworn out loud, if it wouldn’t have given something away.  If there had been any time that they’d say something vital, or pass on a key message or password, it would be as they parted ways.

She’d been too passive.

Was it time to check in?  Was there a good way to?  She had a package of information and she was ninety percent sure the authorities didn’t know and would value it.

She’d have to run it by her lawyer, next time she saw him.

She tossed and turned on her bed before dinner, then couldn’t get to sleep, because she was annoyed at herself for missing the farewell.  The nightly whoops and hollers, the smells, sights, and presence of so many bodies in prison had never gotten to her this much.

➨

Screams weren’t unusual.  People wanted attention, and they wanted power, and the ability to annoy people by screaming at the top of one’s lungs was still power and attention.

But the texture of the ongoing screams was different.  So was the fact that lights were turned back on.  Not all of them, and not in the cells themselves.  But on the floor, between the door, down the middle of the lounge area, and further on.

Winnifred’s cell was on the ground level, so she had a bit of a better view of what was going on than some.  At every cell, there were bars, and she could see the bodies, arms,  and faces pressing against bars, pushing out or sticking as far through as they could, to try to see.  She wasn’t so different.

Except for the fact it was Dane, and she’d been paying attention to him.

“Get it out of me!” he screamed, at a volume and output that broke his voice into cough-y sort of barks.  It made her think of kids back on Griffey Docks and at Sherman Station, who’d scream and shout at the tops of their lungs, practically hurting themselves.

He’d gouged his arm with fingernails, but the marks were already healing.  His hand reached for his arm again, to try to re-open the wound, but the onboard stopped him.  The way the movement stopped was halting, the way he pulled away jerky.

They weren’t listening or showing any sympathy when it came to his words, so he screamed his horror and fury again and again, raw.

The lights were just enough that the people dragging him could find their way between the pieces of furniture.  As if this commotion wasn’t waking people up.  A man, off to one side, walked over to a panel on the wall, and tapped on it.

Ironic, considering he could have used his onboard.  He had to have one.  Maybe he was new to it.

When he was done, the message was received by Dane’s onboard, and the screams died.  The guy, a bit older than Winnifred, tried to scream, drawing in the breath, and then reflexively made a coughing, huffing sound, expelling it without any volume.

Arms refusing to cooperate in his efforts to pull free, fight, or hurt himself, screams silenced, he was dragged by three people, past Winnifred’s cell.

In the gloom, he met her eyes.  If he hated her for what she was, he was too broken and lost in the moment to show any sign of it.

In that moment of eye contact, seeing that emotion, she was back on a metal table, limbs missing.  On Hale’s Wrest, robbed of her body.

She watched as he was taken to one of the rooms in the center of everything, where he’d be unable to hurt himself.  Staff went in with him, to sit out the night.

Things went quiet, or as quiet as they’d get for a while.  People chattered, and were told to knock it off.

“Toby?” Winnifred whispered.  “Is there a form I can fill out?  Complaint?  Appeal?”

Toby pulled up the form.  In the gloom, the white of the page was bright in Winnifred’s vision.

“Don’t get me wrong.  I don’t like him.  I don’t respect him.  I wouldn’t trust him.  I think he’s hurt people, he’d hurt more people if he got a chance.  But…”

But she penned down her thoughts, knowing Toby would read them.  That she knew this was a phobia, and against his religion.  That she’d been watching him, and had overheard things.  She could expand on her thoughts and give extended notes on request.

“He’s one of the worst people I’ve gotten to know.  Worse than Kathe and Satterfield.  But he’s also a kid who just lost his mentor, who doesn’t fit the world he’s in.”

She lay awake for a while after that, a part of her hoping she’d get a reply to her message, a follow-up to that offer for more information and expanded notes.

Nothing.

The prison, like Isaac’s creaking superstructure, was so big it didn’t hear something as small as her.  Even if she had something to say.

3.7.W – MUTE

Winnifred

Winnifred watched Sinon with the two new Frocked.  They were closer to Winnifred than Sinon in age, maybe a few years older than Winnifred at twenty-two or so, but they felt a lot younger in attitude.  The first thing they had done once they had their cells and access to their commissaries was figure out how much they could get away with decorating, and fill their cells with green.  Plants, both fake and real, images of trees, and more.

On their first day, they had drawn some attention for wearing only the provided undershirts.  The undershirts were thin enough that a man’s chest hair could be seen as a shadow through it, as could nipples, and some wore them to tease, or to broadcast that they were available, so that had gotten them labeled.  Most who wore them like that stayed in their own cells, since the uniform rules were more lax, and this pair hadn’t, so they’d been assigned extra cleaning duties.

They didn’t care that they’d been labeled, and they barely cared about being in trouble.  Blithe, was a word that came to mind.  Anide called them tree fetishists.  Most who were that type were happiest with a property where they had space for a private garden, vacationing to see the trees.

These two wanted more, and leaned just a bit more militant, anti-society, and rejected the onboard technology.  As part of that, they’d found the Frocked.  Now that they’d been arrested, they were a bit of a captive audience, Sinon was teaching them, and Winnifred’s self-imposed task was to keep an eye on that, and see what she could learn.

The problem was that the old group with Isaac in charge and acting as co-mentor to Dane had maintained more of a routine.  Isaac had been moved to a less transitional cell block, and Dane was catatonic, only really shuffling out to the counseling sessions, probably mandated.  The routine had made it easier to listen in, because she’d been able to pretend she had her own routine, hanging out at the library.  These three only regularly gathered at the library, requisitioning a space to read some texts and have philosophical discussions.  They talked on the way there, talked as they left and went to eat, and met up at some mealtimes, but that was the extent of the pattern.  Winnifred had the impression the pair exhausted Sinon a little, and maybe Sinon was shaken or discouraged by what had happened to Dane.

To follow these three, Winnifred was forced to follow them, to gather what information she could, but if she was too obvious about it, there would be problems.  At this stage, she didn’t even know the new recruits’ names.  It was something like Boil, and Riannah.

Winnifred had developed a simple system, that she was still refining.  There was an older woman, white-haired, who spent time at the library and lounge areas.  Winnifred loosely mirrored the woman’s routine, breaking it up slightly by attending the weekly meetings with her group.  She was aware that she stood out more, but if they were going to get paranoid about being listened in on, she hoped they’d notice the old woman who was around them much more than Winnifred was, first.

She hadn’t expected prison to be as loud as it was.  Trays clattered, the foam shoes and slippers people wore were rigid enough they slapped the metal floor, and every person seemed to want to talk louder than the baseline level of conversation.  Laughter, shouts, and patches of things like singing cut through the babble, snagging at her attention.

The energy felt different, and she couldn’t figure out why.  If the tone of conversation had a color, it could have been a light green before, and a yellow now.  Was it more good-humored?  Less?  Or was it more good humored, but in a forced way?  Was it not humor at all?

Now she stood in line for her meal, six or seven people behind Sinon’s group.  It was one of the top things in a thousand Winnifred had to do that felt pointless to her.  She’d rather have the food packet in her cell and skip the line.  The problem was that they thought they were ‘socializing’ her.  Eating routines went in the same category as uniform rules.

She could strain her ears to try to make something out in the general conversation, or she could make use of her limited time and listen to Sinon with one of the two girls.  She chose to listen to the conversation, while watching Sinon with the girl.

“-dog?  Was it a Custom?”

“No.  Old-school,” Sinon answered.

“How did you walk it?”

“We lived close to the surface.  The concourses there are wider.  He was trained to stay close in a crowd, without a leash, and crowds are the reason dogs are so hard to walk.”

“Wouldn’t he run away?”

“He was trained.”

“I didn’t know you could train them to do that.”

“It’s not too hard.  The worst part was the maintenance machines.  Too loud for him.”

“Poor boy.”

“The dogs were nice to have around.  The crowd parted for us.”

“Rienne and me were thinking how-”

The bang of a door interrupted Sinon’s conversation partner.  It was close to the center of the cell block.  Three guards manhandled a grinning prisoner- one of the  into one of the padded cells.  Winnifred guessed the guy was a Hidebound, by his torn sleeves, but he could’ve been one of the Devils.  Shaggy, giddy in his lack of shame.

Sinon turned her head sharply, looking in the other direction, at the wall of cells that overlooked the canteen.  Winnifred looked too, and realized a second too late that her face was in Sinon’s peripheral vision.  She’d been caught reacting.

She didn’t let on that she realized, and tried to pretend it was a coincidence.

“-we were thinking about how maybe one day we could have a planet,” Sinon’s conversation partner said.

“A planet?” Sinon replied, her head not turning.  Her gaze had to be on Winnifred.

“If they built the Belt like they keep talking about, and we had enough space.  What if everyone had their own corner to live in, and we had ours?”

“Who in the fuck is going to give you Gray-robed fucks a planet to yourselves?” someone else in line asked, loud and abrasive.

A guard whistled.

“It’s a hypothetical,” the girl said.

“It’s a fucking stupid hypothetical.”

“Prisoners!  Break it up!” one of the prisoners on guard duty called out.

Sinon’s gaze had left Winnifred.  She’d turned that extra ten degrees, to side-eye the man in line behind her.  Winnifred had switched to watching the angry prisoner and the Gray-frocked idiot.

“It’s a way to stop there being any fights over space.  Everyone gets some nature, we’d want more than most, that’s all.”

“You all killed people.  It was the biggest news in decades.  Nobody’s going to reward you with a planet, are you insane?”

Some guards stepped in.  Sinon finally stopped keeping Winnifred in her field of view, so she could shrug off the first grasping hands.  “Leave it.”

“Step out of line, we’re breaking this up.”

“I wasn’t part of that conversation, and it was harmless anyway.  Leave it be.”

One of the guards grabbed her upper arm with force.  Sinon twisted, one arm making a tight circle, breaking the hold.  She hooked her thumbs into either side of her waistband, and looked at the one guard square-on, seemingly unperturbed.

“Sinon,” the prisoner-guard said.

“Emmons,” Sinon replied, not breaking eye contact with the prisoner on guard duty- presumably Emmons.  “Everyone’s calm.  The situation’s de-escalated.  We’re in line to get food, the kid was dreaming out loud.  Leave it at that, and you’re doing your job.”

There was a tension in the air.  Winnifred wasn’t in the habit of ascribing colors to the tone of a room, but since she’d done it earlier, this would be the opposite of what it had been.  Blue?  Did blue fit ‘tension’?

Sinon was a forty-something year old woman who clearly worked out.  She was faced with three younger, stronger prisoners who were standing in as guards, as part of their prison work.  Winnifred didn’t think those three prisoner-guards could win the three-on-one fight, and for that matter, the prisoner-guards, Sinon, and just about everyone in line had the same feeling.

Not that they could admit it, or call for help.  But they couldn’t look weak either.

“Magh,” Emmons said, to Sinon’s partner.

Not boil or something close to it?  Maybe Magh was a last name.

“She’s fine too,” SInon said.

“I’m issuing you a warning.  Don’t run your mouth.  Read the room,” Emmons said.  To Sinon, he said, “you have a problem with that?”

“Seems unreasonable to me, but I’ll talk about it with the prison staff.”

“You do that,” Emmons said.  “I’ll be keeping my eye on you.”

“Likewise,” Sinon told him.  “A big circle of accountability.”

“You all be good,” Emmons told the people in line.  “Don’t stir up shit, or you delay everyone’s meals.

Things settled.

“I’m not a kid,” Magh muttered, to Sinon.

That was your takeaway? Winnifred wondered.

“The fact that that was your first thought coming out of that conversation says you’re a kid, kid,” Sinon replied.  “I have a lot to teach you.  Hopefully I stay in legal limbo for long enough to get you up to speed.  To start with-”

Her voice had dropped a bit.  Winnifred resisted stepping closer to hear better.

Latent tension and her attention being so tightly focused on Sinon and Magh meant that she startled when someone crashed into her.

“You’ve heard, right?  You’re not that out of touch?”

It was Siss, one of the people from the A fangroup- the same one who had breathlessly asked Winnifred about forming the meeting group.  A personality who was really truly not that different from Magh and Rienne in the Gray Frocked group, in how passionate she was about a subject -A, in Siss’s case, nature and the old fashioned ways in Rienne and Magh’s case- and how…

Winnifred didn’t want ot be mean in how she thought about Siss, or even Rienne or Magh, and she struggled to find a way to frame it in her mind.

…How comfortable she was, not sparing any thoughts to anything else.

Winnifred didn’t want to broadcast how readily her claws would auto-retract if they came close to making contact with someone, because it would let on how vulnerable she actually was.  The problem was that Siss was manhandling her out of line.

“Prisoners!  Rat!“

Winnifred had to put her hands almost completely behind her before raising hand over head, to keep them clear of Siss.  She practically rolled her eyes, as the prisoner guards took notice.

“We’re friends!” Siss called out.

“Yeah!?” the guard asked, voice pitched to be pointed, the loud question aimed at Winnifred.

“Yeah,” Winnifred said.  Maybe not the word she would have jumped to- but in the interest of de-escalation…

“Then you’re fucking cutting in line!” someone barked out.

“Fuck me in the ass,” the guard said.  “What the fuck is in the water today?  Break it up or get out of line, or you’re both going in a watch cell.”

Winnifred gave up and let herself be dragged out of line.  “I want food.”

“Win.  Most of the group gathered for an emergency meeting the moment word started getting around.  Do you know?  Because I’m hoping you don’t, so I can tell you.”

Winnifred tilted her head, frowning at Siss.

“Oh wow, I love you and hate you.  You call yourself a fan?”

Winnifred managed to steer Siss toward the tail end of line.  “I do.”

“A and Bruin?  Last night?”

It took Winnifred a second.  She wasn’t sure how to parse the feelings that washed over her.

Or the aftershock, or echo, or whatever she was meant to call it.  The tsunami after the earthquake?  To talk about events that happened on mining planets?  The realization that this was the reason for the change in tone.  That half of the prison had something novel and interesting to talk about, that people were sneaking contraband and getting dragged off with grins on their faces, and everyone knew what was happening.

“They had sex?”

“She lost her virginity to Bruin.  Unless you count her fiddling around with whatshisname-”

“Vince?” Winnifred asked.  “You call yourself a fan?  You don’t even-”

“That didn’t matter.”

“He was one of her best friends growing up.”

“Nobody cares about that.”

“And people care about virginity?” Winnifred asked, still trying to get thoughts and a storm of feelings in order.  “What are you?  A dark ages fantasist?”

“Virginity mattered a lot of times outside of the dark ages.”

“Okay, but you know-”

“It’s a first.  It’s A’s first.  Firsts matter.  You’ve never been interested in someone, seen they have an onboard, and gone looking?  First crush on a fictional character, first crush on someone real, first love, first kiss?  First chest hair, first… rest of it?  Not to be weird, but to see what happened, in what order, maybe see if there are any odd spots that might plant seeds and pop out a weird kink later on?”

Winnifred hoped the look she was giving Siss conveyed what she was feeling, with the added sauce of… people have done this with A?

“When we finish up her in jail, go our separate ways, I’m so interested to see your firsts, Winnifred… whatever your last name is.”

“Griffey, or ‘of Griffey Docks’.”

“Right.  Weird!”

“Is this a thing people do?” Winnifred asked a woman standing behind her in line.

The woman gave her a one-shoulder shrug and glanced away.

Inconclusive.

“Maybe they forgot to plug something in, in one of your mod things?” Siss suggested.  “Hormone pump box?”

“Maybe,” Winnifred said.  She supposed she’d wondered what her cousins were doing and had glanced at that, but she’d glanced at that, had her curiosity quickly sated, and had glanced away.

“Win, it’s a huge first.  Everyone’s seen it or run the sims, except us assholes in prison, and even here, there are really jank shots going around.  They’re watching out and keeping an eye on every onboard, so you’ll get caught but at this point, what are they going to do?  Put us all in the watch cells?  Can you do shots?”

Winnifred tapped the side of her neck where there was skin.

“They’re all over the prison right now.  Both sides,” Siss said.

‘Shots’ in this case were parceled up bits of media that could be injected in the arm of anyone with an onboard, for instant download and a full-body shift in nanotech to receive the high fidelity experience, hormones, and other changes in biochemistry.  That could include, though it was sketchy and borderline illegal, a tabula rasa state where past memories and experiences could be set aside so things could be experienced new.  In some party circles, doing a rapid series of high octane experiences in the form of shots was a thing.  Sometimes they were made badly, so experiences blended together.  Multiple climaxes strung together into experiencing a childbirth where the mother experienced a fourth degree tear, strung into the experience of that very child being born, strung into rapid-fire daredevil moments, sexual adventures, and ‘shock’ shots with extreme lows.  Often it was all strung together with psychedelics.

Winnifred hadn’t experienced that, she’d barely experienced shots at all, but she’d heard enough from cousins and had looked in through their onboards, to get a sense of it.

In prison, when access to the Belt network was strictly curtailed, shots were also a way to exchange media.

Of A?  This sucked.

“The company that manages A and Bruin-”

“Elabre,” Winnifred cut in.

“Sure.  They were pulling them into private meetings with the audience unable to see, and there was speculation they’d go here, and make it part of the Inui invasion series.”

It wasn’t that she didn’t think Bruin was a good guy, and a good pair with A, from what little she’d seen of them interacting before she’d been brought here.  But the fact everyone was experiencing it made it… cheap?  Weird?  Using sex to sell something was something that attractive buskers and performers who’d found their three minutes of fame did to seize on a good patch and keep their star shining a bit longer, before Intelligences had iterated on it in a million ways, exhausting it of potential, and people lost interest.

Except multiplied by a billion, here.

A wasn’t that, right?

Everything else aside, this wasn’t a sign that A’s star was about to fade?

“So it might not be real?” Winnifred asked.

“Oh, it’s real.”

Winnifred frowned.

“So, you did pretty well for the quizzes and tests we did, to see who was best A fan in our cell block, if-”

“I won.”

“You only really won if you put emphasis on remembering facts.  You study for fun.  That gives you an unfair advantage.”

“You delay my meal by dragging me out of line, bring up this stuff, and now- you get on my case?” Winnifred asked, pivoting midway through that last bit, because she was aware she was upset and she didn’t want to spoil an almost-friendship.

“It’s interesting.  I hear that one group of prisoner guards got caught trying it, and got disbanded, and another was dragging their heels because their friends wanted to.  If you pick a good corner to hole up in and you’re subtle about it, there’s a real shot you can run through five or ten minutes of the shot before they find you and drag you out.  Hm?”

Winnifred shrugged.

“Going to give it a shot?”

“No.  Feels icky.”

“Icky.  Wow.  Well I was seriously thinking about it.  Now I feel judged.”

Winnifred shrugged.

“Is this a rat thing?”

“We actually don’t love being called that.”

“Still.”

“No.  I don’t know.  Doesn’t feel like A, somehow.”

“She’s human, with human needs.  And if you see someone eat a great meal, why shouldn’t you want to try it for yourself?”

Winnifred shrugged.

“It’s funny you say that though.”

“What?”

“I’ll tell you after.  Not here.”

The conversation died there.  Winnifred watched the Gray Frocked from afar.

Rienne, the other Gray Frocked girl, had found their newest member.  They hugged, and it seemed very stiff and performative.  Vega and Rienne then stood separate from the line, chatting.  It looked like a first meeting.

Winnifred could only watch from afar, without hearing.

Two weeks ago, she had overheard Dane and Isaac talking about this one.  Vega was a fairly handsome kid, with wiry black hair, and a build resembling Sinon’s, in how it was muscular, with a serious lack of body fat.  He’d been asked his size, probably, and had given a size or two larger than he was, so his clothes hung very loose on him, leaving collar bone exposed, while arms were harder to see in the sleeves.

He had large eyes with a blue in them, which stood out more because he had one very red birthmark or scar extending from the corner of one eye to the temple.  Or two marks, maybe, that blurred together.  ‘X’ or ‘H’ shaped.  Winnifred would have thought it to be a bullet wound, but Gray Frocked refused a lot of medical treatment and he probably wouldn’t have survived a bullet to the temple like that.

It was a scar, she saw.  He emoted physically as he talked, and had placed himself easily between the two girls, while facing Sinon.  Or mostly between, since he was trying not to look like he was standing in line.  When he was talking to one of them, or when they looked away at some other conversation, he touched their arm to get their attention before speaking.  When he did so, the oversized uniform he wore moved a bit, revealing his arm, where there were other, similar marks.  A birthmark wouldn’t manifest like that.

Within a minute, he went from tapping with the back of his hand to keeping his hand there while he leaned in.  It seemed so transparent from afar.

Sinon said something, and he replied.  It looked like he wasn’t taking her seriously.

All of it immediately made Winnifred feel uneasy.  The way he moved, how calculated it seemed, so very immediately making that physical contact with the two younger women, while disarming Sinon.

The pairs -Sinon and Magh in line, and Vega with Rienne newly arrived- split up, with Vega and Rienne going to the back of the line.

Putting them just a bit behind Winnifred.  Four or five people had joined the line since.

The others mostly ignored her, except for a dirty look here or there.

With Vega, she could feel that laser-focused attention fall on her as she caught his eye.  Not a dirty look.  He studied her in the five or so seconds he was walking up to and past her, his head turning to keep looking as he walked by, and a few people in line looked at her, as if following Vega’s lead.  There was no teasing, no humor, no change in expression.  Not even a dirty look.

It was worse than a dirty look, in how cold it was.

She resisted the urge to glance back at him.

He was staring at her from behind her.  Turning the tables from earlier.

She got her food, and sat with Siss while Siss talked about how an Indecent in a cell near hers had painted every conceivable surface with their own shit.  It had been cleaned, her onboard had filtered the smell, the Indecent had been sequestered away, and she was still grossed out.

“It’s the particles.  Even if the smell is blocked, aren’t the particles there?  Covering everything of mine?”

“Get modded, have an easy, produce less waste, have an easy, disposable package to dispose of waste,” Winnifred suggested.  She pressed her food packet to the corner of her mask, and felt the contents flood her mouth.  The plastic crinkled and sucked in against the cup as it was suctioned empty.

“My problem is other people, not my own!”

Winnifred put the packet down on the table.  “You-”

“You’re seriously done eating?”

Winnifred shrugged.

“How do you not get bored?”

“What?”

“You eat in five seconds, you sleep five hours a night in a vent, you apparently crap in a container you can throw out, like you just did a nasal rinse, you barely wear clothes, you said.”

“Not exactly what I said.  I wear what’s easy.  Overalls or coveralls, normally.  This is a lot more than my usual,” Winnifred said, pinching sleeve between the flat surfaces of two claws.  “It’s not like hot or cold bother me, or that I need to cover up.”

“Exactly.  So that’s not a priority.  You don’t drink, you don’t party, you don’t like people.”

“I like some people.  You’re alright.”

“But don’t you get bored?”

“I don’t know-” Winnifred started, before pausing.  She needed a moment to double check herself, to make sure she wasn’t being offensive to someone who was meat from head to toe.  “-Um.  Should I be more weirded out by the fact you find going to the bathroom entertaining, or-”

“Uh, no.  Not what I’m saying.”

“-do I answer the question and remind you that this is prison, it’s mostly boring?”

“It’s boring on a good day.  On the bad days you’ll wish it was boring.”

“Right.”

Vega and Rienne were getting food.  He really didn’t eat much.

His route to get to where Sinon and Magh were sitting didn’t take him near Winnifred, but he definitely looked her way when he passed, and he took a seat on one side of the table that gave him a steady view of her.

He’d been described as a firebrand, but that wasn’t the sense she was getting.  He’d just arrived, and he was already singling out people to draw closer, people to push away, and… Winnifred wasn’t sure what she was.  A target?

Vega said something to Sinon, glancing at Winnifred.  Sinon looked over her shoulder.  Winnifred tried to look more interested in Siss and other things.

Sinon’s mouth moved.  Winnifred couldn’t even hope to hear, and doubted that if Toby was responsive and if she could make a request, that Toby could even pick the sound out in the midst of open conversations.

She had a guess, but it was a paranoid one.  Sinon, mentioning that she’d seen Winnifred looking their way?

How was she meant to keep an eye on people, if one of those people was watching her?

“Do you miss regular food?”

“I have regular food.”

“You know what I mean.”

“I blend it.”

“But texture, any of that?”

“I’ve felt it in simulations.  I don’t see the hype.”

“Ugh,” Siss said.  Then she looked down at her tray.  “Right now, I don’t either.  Let’s go.  I want to talk to you about A and Bruin more than I want to eat.”

Winnifred wasn’t about to complain.  She couldn’t see much.

Siss put away her tray, Winnifred pitched her food packet into a bin, and they left the lunch hall.  It was only lunch, and Winnifred wouldn’t have even normally come, but she’d wanted to overhear what she could of Sinon’s conversation with the newbies.

She’d gotten to see them meeting, and had overheard bits.

She passed Anide, who was sitting at a table, took note of Siss and Winnifred together, and rolled her eyes a little.  Probably, as she was giving tours to new prisoners as part of her duties at intake, she was talking about the A fanatics using some term she’d made up.  Guppies, maybe, or minnows.

The cell block was round, divided up like the slices of a pie chart into lounge, gymnasium, library, and so on, with the watch cells at the corner and cells dividing each slice and the outside rim from the rest of the station.  Hallways extended out as spokes, and she and Siss walked down one such hallway now, going past the library.  They passed various classrooms and storage spaces for things like paper books, and let themselves into a room.

Here, things were soundproofed, with locked cases against one wall holding various instruments and equipment.  The rest of it was fairly sterile, with text on the walls telling them to clean and respect the space, and some commands for having various types of seating protrude from the wall.  People practiced for choirs and concerts here.  Six people were already in the room.

“Winnifred didn’t know until I told her, just now,” Siss said.

“Man, they gave you a polished new modded body, did they have to cut costs and give you a rock to live under, instead of a jail cell?”

Winnifred rolled her eyes.

“Rock?” Siss asked.

“It’s a saying,” someone else explained.

“Explain what we’re looking at.  The loophole.”

“It’s not a loophole, exactly.”

“It’s kind of a loophole.”

“What’s this about?” Winnifred asked.

“We got permission from the prison to download A’s music, right?”

“Yeah,” Winnifred said.  She hadn’t been part of that process, because there had been some sentiment that it would hurt more than help.  Prejudice against members of the twenty-nine families, and all of that.

“But technically, there are no specifications on format, and we can even say there’s a merit to analyzing different interpretations and scenes that the song is played over.”

“We downloaded the entire scene and all of the sensory data with A’s music playing over it,” Siss cut in.

“Oh,” Winnifred replied.  “Is that what you wanted to show me?”

“Part of it.”

Ugh.

“She’s being all pure, princess of the ivory tower in this one,” Siss explained.

“That’s not it, it’s just-” Winnifred cut herself off.

“What?” Siss pressed.  “Don’t tell me your reason, tell me what you said earlier.”

Winnifred frowned, thinking back.  Toby provided a transcript.  Winnifred’s eyes scanned it.

“Thanks, love,” she whispered to Toby.  The others didn’t hear it, and weren’t listening, and their onboards would have to adapt the subsonic language to Belt English anyway.  It was nice having her friend back inside her, especially in a weird and uncomfortable social situation.  She read, then ventured, “It doesn’t seem like her?”

“So she did watch it?”

“She didn’t,” Siss said.

Winnifred let the others chatter among themselves, trying to pick up on what they were saying, but she felt a bit heartsick, disappointed with everything, and vaguely spooked by Vega back in the canteen, and found the words going in one ear and out the other.  They’d tell her, she was sure.  Or Toby would help clarify.

As much as it was nice having Toby around, it wasn’t entirely the same.  She wished with all her heart that Toby could chime in.  Or that she and Toby had some kind of code that Toby could use, that would give some kind of signal.  Maybe making notifications pop up in one eye instead of the other, to indicate positive or negative, or above the center-line of her field of vision to say one thing, while below said another.

“We’ve been going over it, just audio and tactile, since they did it in the dark.”

There was that, at least.

“Can you pull out your tech and ‘sing’ for us, Winnifred?” someone asked.  Winnifred was pretty sure their name was Squib, which was easy to remember, because they were one of what Anide had described as ‘squids’.  Winnifred hadn’t really interacted with them; they’d only really been around when a lot of people were around.

Squib had that heavy body modification that was in the biological space, instead of the modded space.  From the bottom of their ribcage to the top of their pelvis, there was no permanent connection.  Instead, tendrils as thick around as Winnifred’s wrists reached down from upper body and up from pelvis, periodically ‘docking’ with one another, the tip of one opening up for the other to penetrate, to pass fluids up or down.  Blood, waste, other fluids.

Yet another loophole.  She could use her own equipment and ‘sing’ by having it play music, and the prison didn’t push back any.  But in service of this?

“You have good instincts,” a guy said.  He was a bit of an odd one out, middle aged and heavy, and seemed to be here more because he joined all the clubs and groups he could, than because he was an A superfan.  He seemed interested and happy to be here now, with a front seat for the big news.

“Instincts?”

“Rich thinks it’s fake.”

“We know something is up,” Siss said.  “I didn’t want to broadcast it in the canteen, that we’re piecing together the video, or a bunch of people would crash this meeting, but it’s unusual.”

“People are talking about it outside the prison,” Squib murmured.  “I don’t think anyone’s worked it out.”

Unusual was… good?  Winnifred felt more motivated, pulling apart key components from her head and mask to make a speaker.  She plugged it into a wall panel.

It still felt icky, pulling out the visualization.  A cover of A’s singing played, and with it, there was a feed, of A and Bruin sleeping in their makeshift sleeping rolls, after a day they’d apparently had a bad brush with the Inui.  Winnifred hadn’t been in any position to follow the filming, but the group was smaller.  A few people had been taken out.

As they moved beneath the covers, where there was no light, the visuals shifted to a visual representation of touch, each small point of contact recorded as a value, shown as a number and a hue, that pulled away, lingering, as the sensation of touch did, or shifted, as the sensation did.

“Can we bring up these ones, side by side?” Squib asked.

“The same shot?” Winnifred asked them.

“Different pieces of media, A’s voice playing over the same scene.”

Winnifred frowned.

This felt perverse, but it was going somewhere.

The images synced up.  She saw what they were pointing out.  All of the scenes were subtly different.  Touch sensitivity, firmness of skin and tissues,

While that played, she opened the packet data, to get a sense of what was going on behind the scenes.  There were different ways for simulations to get put together.  Fidelity mattered, and even slight changes in how sensory data was tracked and logged as it shifted from brain to body and back again, was a completely different kind of texture, a different kind of feedback.  Every human being’s brain developed in its own particular way, and the closest they’d come to tampering with that was in some of the ‘smarter human’ business that had fallen out of fashion.

Smarter humans ended up samey, because the processes that amplified the brain also tended to take a strong hand in the development of the brain.  Brain development was the difference between one person having a constant voice running through their head and another not, with neither having any strict impact on actual ‘intelligence’.

Which was a hard thing to define on its own.

As one extension of that, the ways the brain handled sensory data was always different  Some things were the same, or same-y.  The layouts of nerves.  Some weren’t.

People could look at the same picture and see different colors.  It wasn’t as extreme as blue swapped for red, but two people could look at the same hue of green on paper and process it as slightly different, in the brain.  Touch and sound had the same issues.

But to actually create those variations when the data was sent out, instead of in?

Winnifred set things up, then stepped back, pulling a chair out of the wall to sit back at the far end of the room.  Siss bent down, and turned up the volume of A’s singing, and put the scene on loop.

Squib sat beside Winnifred.

“You don’t actually need me to do this, you know,” Winnifred told them.  Her voice was slightly distorted, because she’d removed one of the speakers for the music player.

“Enh,” Squib grunted.  “The way I see it, the reason they go easy on us is that we don’t kick up a fuss.  We listen to music, we put on a show, that we’re trying to grow and learn something.  And we have everything from Dockfolk to Hidebound to Biomods to the old guy.”

Rich turned, huffing.  “I’m not old, jackass.”

“You used the word jackass,” Squib replied.  “You’re old enough.”

“I’m sixty.”

Squib chuckled softly, being intentionally quiet.

This was a good part of the song.  Squib recognized that, and gave it its own space.  Winnifred appreciated that.

“If you weren’t going this extra mile, and we were using the station panels to look for this kind of footage?  Higher chance they crack down,” Squib resumed talking during the instrumental.  “But as long as we’re all being brought together in harmony, literally?”

“Clever,” Winnifred murmured.

“It’s good you’re here.  Thank you,” Squib said.

Winnifred frowned a bit, then nodded.  She pulled her legs up to her chest and hugged them.  “I’m glad.  Glad to have this.”

The music stopped, then the loop resumed.  Siss touched all of the wall panels, so the images displayed, blown up so they extended from floor to ceiling.  It made the comparisons easier.

“Big question number one is… which one is the real A?” Squib murmured.

“I think to answer that,” Winnifred replied, quiet, “you don’t look at A.  You look at-”

She almost said the other systems, as if she was answering a question from an early-year study module.  The sort where there was only, say, a rocket module she was supposed to look at, and the computer was conspicuously included in the picture, when nothing else was.

“Bruin.”

“Bruin had a whole issue, people wanted to get footage of him.  A’s not an asshole.  So… it’s all fake.”

“I’d say half of the people who are talking about this agree with you on that.  Big question number two…”

“Who faked it?” Winnifred asked.  “Do you know?”

“I have a theory but I want to hear yours first.  Untainted by the conversations we’ve been having all morning.”

Winnifred thought about it.

Elabre?

The company producing the Inui film, laying seeds for something plot-relevant?

Or…

“Basil,” Winnifred murmured.

“Huh.”

“A has called him a trickster, before.”

“Rich had the same thought, but the consensus was the old man who’s had an onboard for four months didn’t grasp how tricky that kind of trickster-ing gets.  But I think you get a sense of it.  You know onboards.”

“One’s my best friend.”

“I’d say that’s weird… or sad.  But I’m not one to complain.  Meet mine.”

Squib patted their lap.

Winnifred raised her eyebrows, eye going to Squib’s groin area, covered by prison uniform.

“Lower body.  It’s a separate organism, with its own onboard.”

Her eyes widened.

“I can put a control override in when I need to steer, but that’s only some of the time,” Squib explained, pulling up the bottom of their shirt and demonstrating by putting one of the thicker central tentacles that descended from the ribcage  into another tentacle, that yawned wide to receive the other.  “We still get kids coming in, thinking they had a new idea.  It’s like, trust me, someone’s come up with it before.”

“We don’t vary it up much,” Winnifred said.  “What we use works.”

“The dock folk.”

“Yeah,” Winnifred said.  She was admittedly nervous, because around family, there was a degree of personal and cultural pride around modding.  Around the drill site and in prison, including around Anide toward the end of Winnifred’s intake process, there was so much misinformation and people having issues, it seemed like she couldn’t bring it up at all without getting shouted at.

Squib took it in stride.  “Sell it to me.  The idea, not the onboard, or your body.”

“A-” Winnifred started to respond, then stumbled as the last part of what Squib had said registered.  “A calls Basil a trickster.  We’ve seen him play games with perception.”

“The day she broke her arm.”

“Yeah.  Big one right then.  But I don’t think it suits Elabre.  It doesn’t serve their needs.”

“Publicity.  The fact we’re talking about it right now.”

Winnifred thought about that.  She averted her eyes- Siss had blown up the visualization of two pieces of anatomy meeting, so it took up most of the wall.  A black screen showing body parts, each fold and point of contact shown as a sea of numbers, size and boldness showing pressure, hues varying like a heat map to show the nature of the touch.  Except it was a lot more than heat.

“That’s your guess, then?” she asked Squib.  “That it’s Elabre?”

“Simplest answer.  I’m still waiting to hear the rest of your answer.  How it would even be possible.”

“Basil can’t change things now without it being scrutinized.  People would have found that already.”

“True.”

“But whatever it is, it looks like it was engineered and given to Toby,” she said.  Then she called out, “Rewind to start.”

There were a few noises of protest, but the panel did as instructed.

Hands touched arm, leg, the sides of the body.  The light, thin layers of clothing both had worn to sleep.

She extended her hand.

“Hm,” Squib grunted.  “But that’s…”

“It would have required setup.  Remember the thing with the president of Earth?  At the opera house?”

“I remember.  He implied she had a code.  People have gone crazy since then, trying to figure it out.”

“What if it’s not… language, or looking at a specific object?  What if the code is subtler?”

“This?”  Squib turned in their seat, to face Winnifred more.

“What if… I don’t know.  Nanotech produces waste.  And if you put the right waste in the right spots and shake it up…”

“You’re talking about creating a nanotech primordial soup?  Putting all the right ingredients in the right space with the right conditions, with the idea they’ll chance on a connection, and form certain structures…”

“Yeah.”

“And that’s transmitting a code or special way of-”

“I don’t know.  I’m thinking aloud.  I’m thinking whatever it is, it had to be something Basil could pass on to Bruin with a touch.  Without it being registered.  It had to be set up a long time ago, because… that takes time.”

“The president of Earth touched her back,” Squib said, as if the thought had just dawned.

“Yeah,” Winnifred replied, quiet.

“The crazy thing is, you’d think okay, you know… but A’s onboard would get audited if anyone ever even suspected this, and he’d get in trouble.”

Winnifred nodded.  “It’s only a theory.”

“But,” Squib went on, “Who’s going to audit A’s onboard so soon after Robert Simes was basically destroyed by the public, after digging into A and getting stalkery enough to figure something like this out?”

“I actually didn’t know about that part,” Winnifred murmured.

“I’m not saying you’re right, it makes more sense it’s something Elabre okayed behind closed doors.”

“Maybe.”

“But if you were right… that’s insanity.”

“Insanity.”

“A is the best.  That it’s even something we can entertain as an idea?  Wow.”

The direction and the enthusiasm in that reply startled her.

“Not that I’m seriously entertaining it.  It’s pretty out there.”

She didn’t think it was that out there.

She’d felt something of a connection, maybe a bit of common ground.  And that enthusiastic response that seemed to run away from what Winnifred was feeling…?

She wasn’t sure what she was feeling, except that it was serious.

She sat with the silence that followed for a minute.

“This might be a weird question,” she ventured, turning again to Squib.

“We’re a weird pair.”

“Do you go looking through the old feeds and recordings of people?  To see… firsts?  Or whatever?”

“Sometimes.  If they’re interesting enough.  I did for A.  I’ll do it for you, when I get another shot.  You’re interesting.”

Winnifred hugged her legs tighter to her chest, until the metal plates that covered key internals flexed.

“You don’t?”

“Doesn’t really cross my mind.  I’d rather deal with people as they are.”

“Or not deal with them at all?”

She wasn’t sure what to say to that.  She shrugged one shoulder.

“Siss said you’re a loner.”

She wasn’t sure that she was.  She was surrounded by crowds in prison, bombarded by messages from family.  In demand here.  But she didn’t feel at home in any of those places.

She couldn’t leave, because she didn’t want to take their music away from them, so she closed her eyes, dropping one clawed foot to floor, the other propped up on the edge of her seat, so she could continue to hug her leg.  The tip of her tail traced back and fort on the floor.

A felt like home.  Like she resembled one piece of the family she one day hoped to have.  A ship of her own as a home, a crew as that family.

A’s singing was the soundtrack that played over that.  And she was glad that hadn’t changed, here, today.  A had protected Bruin and herself from the eyes of billions, from people who’d dissect every action and put them up on the wall for further examination, and she’d done it while keeping true to herself, as someone with wants.

A bummer that want was Bruin, but it was good.

➨

She navigated the canteen, again frustrated that she had to wait as long as she did get through the line and claim a food pack smaller than her fist, that she could eat before she’d taken three steps toward her table.

Same with the clothes she had to wear, though she could at least get away with no foam shoes.

Squib motioned.  Offering a seat at the table.  One of Squib’s friends was a squid with some clear skin and musculature -similar to A’s friend from the Science Center- and clear tubes running in and out of the spaces between organs and other vitals.  The tubes, thick and solid, had what looked like gelatinous rodents moving through them.  Largely boneless, furless, and clear themselves, albeit tinted.

Definitely one way to not feel alone in a crowd.  Keep pets inside you.

Winnifred wondered how that would work with members of her family.  They’d be so upset, probably.

Squib had extended one tentacle from their upper body, into one of the chest ports that apparently let the friend reach inside his body to handle his pets.  It wasn’t very appetizing, especially when she wondered, like, was that a tentacle that transported renal fluids?  Or waste?  Was food handled above or below?  Glistening tentacles sucked at one another, or twisted against and through one another to form enough of a grip between upper body and lower body that they didn’t wobble.

It was rare that Winnifred didn’t feel like the outlier in a non-Folk group.

Siss was less than a table away.  It had been a day since the news had dropped about A and Bruin and people had taken to it like they had, and a day since the Siss’s Indecent had smeared his own feces over every nearby surface, and Siss had hung onto her incident with more tenacity than the zeitgeist had held onto A’s business.

Which wasn’t to say that people weren’t still talking about it, in the group, but at least the scene wasn’t being played on every available surface.  People weren’t getting dragged off to a padded private cell and some counseling sessions because they had a curiosity about it that contraband could solve.

“Member of our body modder group back home got the face mask- or something like it.  More cosmetic,” Squib said.

“Yeah?” Winnifred asked.  “It’s handy.”

“He couldn’t stand not being able to eat.  Said he nearly threw up every time he sucked down a meal.  Reverted it fast.”

“Don’t talk about throwing up when we’re eating,” one of their non-modded acquaintances said.

“It’s all I’ve ever known,” Winnifred replied.  “There are a lot of reasons for rejection.”

“Uh, there are, but they’re mostly ones we’ve got over.”

“Your friend didn’t.”

“That’s more… it’s a tough change.”

“Fair,” Winnifred agreed.

“Rates of rejection are rising fast, though,” the guy with tubes in his body said.

“That’s because of Mechard and a whole generation thinking it’s cool, jumping on things, with zero prep and post-op care.  They’re all ‘oh, I’m going to do the wildest thing I can, oh, I’m so unique and nifty, nobody’s ever done a full body piercing before.”

“Conjoined-” the tube guy said.

“The conjoined, nobody’s ever attached themselves to someone else on a permanent basis with their mods.  Trendsetters.  Then it’s all, oh, this is hard to do, this is hard to experience in all the moments nobody’s looking.”

“Except everyone’s looking now, because of onboards.”

“Yeahh.”

Winnifred chuckled a bit, and exaggerated it with her body, because it would be hard to hear and hard to see.

“Bluffing,” Squib said, pointing at her.

“You don’t call someone out on a bluff when you’ve known them for five minutes, brain-gauge.”

“Bluffing?” Winnifred asked.

“Fucking introduce them,” the tube man said.

“Winnifred, this is Turb.  Turb, Winnifred.”

“Of the twenty-nine families, or whatever-?” Turb asked.

“Yeah.”

“Sometimes people see the look and emulate it, without knowing.”

“Huh.  I guess people would do that.”

“Winnifred’s graciously been lending us parts of her body so we can play music.”

“Aw, that’s good,” Turb said.  “I miss music.  Almost joined choir, to hear some.  Wanna hear?”

“I- in the canteen?”

“Ahem,” Turb said.  He sat up straighter, and motioned a few times with his hands.  The fat, gelatinous little rodents in his upper body hurried to different places in his chest, where they could stand up on their toe-less, claw-less back feet.  He sang a short note, “Aaaaa.”

The two gelatinous things mimed him, faint.

“Eh?  What do you think.”

“Terrific,” she said.  It kind of was.

“You’re more low key than I thought you’d be,” Turb said.

Squib elbowed Turb.

“We work on ships and stations, we mostly want to be left alone.  If you see us kicking up a shit storm, it’s usually because we haven’t been.”

“Hm.  I don’t know enough to comment either way.”

“Explain bluffing?” Winnifred asked.

Turb replied, “Bluffing, ma’am, is something we get with drastic modding, or modded senses, or both.  People don’t know how to present themselves, so they fake it.  Or they don’t understand, because they rejiggered how they see, hear, interact with the world, and the learning curve is too steep.  You lose people by the wayside.  It’s important to call it out when you see it, in friends, without alienating them.”

“Yeah,” Squib acknowledged those last few pointed words.  They added, “I knew a guy who modded himself, struggled.  We even called him out a few times.  A year later, he got everything removed, body rebuilt.  Leaves, doesn’t talk to any of us.  Ever since, he was trash talking us to anyone who’d listen.  Loneliest months of his life, he’d say.”

“You get that.  There are some self-centered personalities among body modders,” Turb said.

“Got it,” Winnifred answered.

“Genuine appreciation for art, too.  Living the art.”

She nodded.

“So yeah,” Squib interjected.  “Maybe I’m more aggressive about calling out bluffs, because of him.  You were faking.”

“I was working on a mining planet before I came here.  Kind of had to, because people don’t know how to read body language, I laugh quiet.”

“You laugh and smile with your eyes,” Turb said.  “I saw it when little Heresy and Blasphemy sang.  I see it now, a little bit.”

Winnifred shrugged a little, not sure what to say.

“For the record, I used to look a lot more badass.  I had to downgrade and swap some parts out, coming in here.  I thought it would be a chance to try a different aesthetic, keeping same elements so there’s no hard adjustment period.”

“My lawyer was pretty good on that front,” Winnifred said.  She launched into an explanation of how he’d done it, which they liked, and which she appreciated more, now, as she got to retell it.  At least one of the other ‘squids’ at the table leaned forward to get a better look at her as she explained it.

It made her self conscious, and as she talked, she avoided eye contact, instead glancing around the canteen.

Vega, Rienne, and Magh, looking for a seat.  She couldn’t see Sinon, the ‘mother’ of the group.

Vega had been looking at her before she saw him.  He didn’t flinch away from that moment of eye contact.

He walked her way.

“The claws were how much?” Turb asked.

“Twenty-five thousand, I think?  But I’m increasingly aware… lux doesn’t exist?”

“Aha, see?” Squib asked.

“That’s an A thing, I’m just now realizing,” Turb threw in.

Vega and the two Gray Frocked girls were a few tables away now.

Maybe he only wanted to intimidate.  Maybe he’d only look for a weak mark.

She tried to look confident, instead of hunching over.

Vega stopped near their table.  There was no heat or venom in the word, “Rat.”

She met his eyes without wavering.

“Take it off.  The mask.  Show them what you look like.”

“See,” Vega addressed others at the table, his gaze falling on the unmodded people.  “They don’t like to take off the mask, because it’s all lasered to shit.  Carved out, jaw removed, nose removed.  Because the follow-up question is when, how do you do that to yourself?”

A prisoner guard wouldn’t intervene for what looked like a mild conversation, but it was obvious to Winnifred this guy was here to stir shit.

“We’ve done worse,” Squib answered.

“Have you, though?” Vega asked, almost seeming more fired up at the response, the challenge.  “The answer is that they do that to babies.  Sometimes you have to ask a few times, or push.  But it’s who they are.”

Winnifred wasn’t sure what to say.  But Vega had a script, it seemed like.

“The question I love asking, because it really drills down, gets to the heart of them… is will they do it?  When you have a kid, rat, will you laser it to pieces?” Vega asked.

Winnifred realized his play.  Her heart sank.

Vega didn’t look away from her, but the tilt of his head made it seem like he was talking in Rienne’s ear, and talking to Turb and Squib at the same time.  Conspiratorial, but talking to everyone present.  “It’s amazing.  They deflect, they distract, they’ll say this or that, but they never say no.”

Winnifred sat there, eyes locked to Vega’s.

“No?” Vega asked.  There was no bluff there.  No heat or passion in his words, but a growing enthusiasm, as if he was only just now getting started.  “Say no, and I’ll be super embarrassed.  I’ll fuck off, red in the face, and you win.  Say no and that you agree it’s fucked up, I’ll concede, you’re one of the good ones, and I’ll give you a million lux.”

“I’m not having kids,” Winnifred answered.

“That’s not what I’m asking,” Vega said, smiling as he said it.  The smile was getting wider.

“Are you guys in any position to talk?” Winnifred asked.

“Just because we walk the terrace path doesn’t mean we’re terrorists,” Rienne answered.

“I should really write these answers down before I talk to the rats,” Vega said, to her.  He turned to Magh, “Get them laminated.  Pull out the cards when they give the same old replies, use the same tactics.”

“Who’s deflecting now?” Winnifred asked.

“There are tens of thousands of us,” Vega said.  “A small handful decided to pull a stunt.  How many of you all are there?  About the same number?  Every last one of you exists because a member of your group decided to butcher a baby and fill the bloody mess with mods.”

It wasn’t bloody, but Winnifred wouldn’t help anything by saying that.

“Every last one?  Some do it to themselves.  Because of love, usually.”

“And when they do that, they sign up to butcher their own baby when the time comes.  Love.”

He let the first emotion show in how much disgust he put in that last word.

“Prisoner!  Vega Albaron!” a guard called out.

Vega turned, hands raised to shoulder height.

“Move on.”

They’d seemingly caught that little bit of emotion.  Had he known they would?  Either way, having just dropped the big, messy question, and having fully made his point, Vega didn’t linger.

The conversation at the table didn’t resume.

The indicator in the corner of Winnifred’s field of vision showed the messages she hadn’t been brave enough to start poring through, with fresh messages that no doubt contained thoughts from her family.

They were mad at how she’d handled this.

If she’d said no, if she’d ruled out taking a laser to her child, though, it would be worse.  She’d lose her entire family, and she’d be risking her dream.  How could she have her own ship if she had to worry every time she docked that a member of the twenty-nine families would do a bit of subtle sabotage?

She was aware of the hypocrisy of that worry.

Nobody said anything as she got up from the table, taking her trash with her.

➨

The door didn’t open.

Winnifred, alone in the hallway, formed a fist, and thumped the wall, before resting her forehead against it.

The group that met to discuss A and listen to music wasn’t in this room at this time anymore.  The schedule or location had changed, and she hadn’t been told.

She couldn’t let it get to her.  She’d take a moment in private, get it together, so she could prevent a brave face.

Toby highlighted a message, backed in red.

Winnifred of Griffey Docks, if you have no business in this hallway, please relocate to a common area.

“They changed the schedule and didn’t tell me,” she said, sounding more tired than she intended.

There was a brief pause.  Human, not Intelligence, at the other end.

Understood.  That’s fine.  Please relocate to a common area.

Yeah.

She suppressed a swear, and walked back.

It made her think of her cousins.  Which wasn’t that far off, since her cousins had been about the same age as, say, Squib, and Siss, when she’d seen them.  But she hadn’t expected prison to be so childish, with that kind of cowardly…

Ugh.

No meeting room, then.  No more listening to A’s music, unless she could get the a-ok to keep going, solo.  Except, as Squib had said, the fact they were doing it as a group, with such a mixed representation, everyone getting along, had meant they had gotten a lot of leeway.

She might not get that solo.

A sharp tapping sound made her head turn- and she turned it straight into an incoming elbow.

The full weight of a body crashed into her, and between the stars in her vision and the arm braced against the side of her head, loose fabric partially blinding her, she couldn’t make out any details.  That arm got a grip on her loose ponytail and her head was forcibly turned, metal of her mask scraping against wall.

When she reached up to grab back at the hand or wrist of the person who held her, her hands failed her.  The claws, set to auto-retract if they’d cut or make contact with another person, auto-retracted.  As they weren’t claw tips, but actual blades in the place of the top two thirds of each finger, it meant she had only stubs to work with.

She elbowed backward, but they’d stepped in close, so one of her arms was crushed against a wall, and their body was practically in her armpit, limiting her leverage with the other.

Her tail was her only measure, and she could only try to wrap it around a leg to try to pull them off balance.

It didn’t work, and in the meantime, they reached up inside the casing that formed her ribcage, like they knew exactly what they were reaching for.

It was almost an inverse of what had happened back on Hale’s ship.  She’d had her head and vitals.

Now her head was filled with stars and alarm, and they hauled down on the lower tube connecting to her Ox Box.  Her oxygen.  It was secured, locked in place, and the tube itself was carbon fiber, but there were limits to how durable her equipment could be to direct and sustained abuse while also weighing as little as possible.  Something had to give, and she got a flashing warning in her field of view, bright and red, that there was a tear where tube was attached to the box itself and locked in place.

There were some kinds of damage that mandated she feel at least some pain, so she’d take it seriously, and her body dutifully provided that.

Fingers hooked on a bundle of wires, and pulled them down.  They were as minor as anything, only cordage connecting to a series of lights that she never turned on, because that was more a thing for mod hobbyists that wanted to look flashy.  It did end in a cap, and that was what they were after.

A metal semicircle with a slightly depressed inner portion, some light-management circuitry tucked away inside the depression.  It wasn’t sharp enough to be a blade, but it worked as a wedge, driven in very close to where the biology of her neck segued into the modded portions.

Pain lanced through her, head to toe, and things stopped working.  She fell.

They drove the point -and the damage- home with a kick.  Foam shoe to the part of the half-circle that still stuck out of her neck.

Estimated time for help to arrive, two minutes.

Estimated oxygen, accounting for the leak?  Nearly five minutes before she was in trouble.

They would have just under three minutes to get her stable.  Toby was already bringing up and sending the information that they would need.

The person who had attacked her kicked her, foot to ear.  She hadn’t been quite lying down with face flat against floor, so there was a short distance for her head to travel, bouncing off hard metal floor.

It stung, and the ear-to-floor contact hurt, up until Toby had turned off those unnecessary pain notifications too.  No point in any of it when she couldn’t do anything about it.

Leaving her keenly aware of her situation.  The humiliation of it, lying here in a hallway, helpless.

“If you say they’ll get here in time, I believe you,” she whispered to Toby.

Her attacker was already leaving, moving quickly.  Staying out of view.  They probably knew the directions help would be coming from.

They’d known she’d be passing through.

They’d known how to take her apart.

They’d done this, coldly, calmly, and without revealing themselves.  If they were careful about that, they were probably aware that their onboard would tattle on them.

Vega, or someone close to him, then.

She didn’t have A’s audience.  The only people who watched her with any regularity were family, and she knew they’d see this.  They’d use her as an example.  To get kids to fall in line and be constantly aware that out there, away from the docks and the family, you got hurt.  It would be used against her, when she was finally able to answer the messages family sent her, to pressure her to act like a good daughter of Griffey Docks should.

The opposite of what she’d wanted.

Humiliation was a close relative to anger, and anger was easier to carry.  She wasn’t used to carrying it, but now that she was here?  She’d find an answer.  A way.  Vega, two Frocked, Sinon in the wings, plus anyone they’d recruited in the meantime.

Which led her to the answer to the question she’d been asking herself.  How she’d answer those unread messages from family, prove herself, show it was possible to forge her own way.  Even how to tie it back to A.

She’d have to handle the Frocked.

3.8.WB – MUTE

Winnifred

Winnifred felt around the newly installed tubing for leaks.  Toby, unasked for, supplied the data on airflow, with a small image on the side of Winnifred’s field of view that mapped out airflow.  No leaks.

She tightened it a fraction anyway, then felt for leaks again.  Toby didn’t steady the faint tremor in her hands as she did so.

She would have wondered if she should read into that, but Toby wasn’t allowed to do anything with the intent that she could read into it, so… should she read into it anyway?  Especially so soon after thinking about Basil as a trickster?  Or with the idea that she could read into what Toby was unintentionally signaling?

“Your mother just messaged me to say you should stop fiddling,” her lawyer said.

With sullen reluctance, Winnifred did.

They’d moved to one of the side rooms where meetings were held.  Her family was more expert on anything mod related than anyone on the station, and had wanted the lawyer to take a look.  It was like an interrogation room, probably was one, in specific circumstances, but could turn at right angles.  Right now, the window that would have been a one-way window for station staff to look in through was facing outward.  It offered a slightly tinted view of outer space.  There were doors against each of the walls, but the one that faced outward was blocked from opening out to the void by the coupling that held everything steady.

Metal table, metal chairs that her body scraped and squeaked on contact with.

“There’s a whole war raging right now, over this,” the lawyer said.

The room was dead silent, except for the barely perceptible hum of incoming air and the faintly luminescent g-panels of the floor.  The brightness wasn’t anything compared to the glow of the lights above them, but it gave the room a unique lighting.

“The guards were slow to listen to you, for one thing.”

For an instant, Winnifred was back on that floor, barely able to function while the guards took far too long to start listening to Toby.  When she fumbled, trying to indicate with limbs that had only the barest functionality Toby had managed to put through, they pushed her hand and arm away.

She reached back.

“The prison wants to mark this down as a feud.  And Winnifred?  Your mom says stop.”

She pulled her hand away.  “Let’s make this a one-on-one meeting?  Client and lawyer.”

Her lawyer gave her a long look, then conceded, “Fine.  I have things to say.”

Winnifred brought her feet up onto the chair she was sitting on.  Her hair was a mess.  Her body still felt strange, but she wasn’t sure how much of that was because something was wrong, and how much was because connections were new.

“You shot yourself in the foot,” he said.

Winnifred looked up at him, eyebrows drawn together.

“Talking to the prison authorities?”

“My Ox had just been cut, they took their time getting me fixed.  Try holding your breath for four minutes and then see how clearly you think.”

“Not so hard with onboards.”

“You know what I mean,” Winnifred replied.

“I do,” he said.  He paused, then said, “Be it as it may be, you named Vega Albaron as the culprit.”

“I’m pretty sure I said him or someone he knows.”

“They caught the culprit, a Gen Carrasco?”  He paused, checking if that got any response.  She shook her head.  “Unmodded.  He worked on mining planets, got banned by most major mining companies.  As a side effect, he fails any background check he’s given.  Which means he works in the rough and tumble groups that don’t do background checks.  He was too troublesome even for them, hurt someone.  That brought him here.  Where he’s had no interaction with Vega Albaron.”

“That we know of.”

“That we know of.  They’re saying it’s unlikely, given the places they’ve been in.  They haven’t crossed paths or been out of sight long enough to coordinate this sort of attack.”

“But not impossible?  I can see Vega passing a note to Magh or Rienne.  The other Gray-frocked girls in the group in this cell block.  They could reach out.”

“Nonetheless-”

“And,” she interrupted.  “This guy from a mining planet had very accurate knowledge about what to go for and how to hurt me.”

“Agreed, absolutely.  The issue isn’t the argument, but the venue.  You can bring up those arguments, or better ones, but it’s unlikely according to the prison admin, and if something isn’t on the digital record and there isn’t clear, immediate physical evidence, it might as well not exist.”

“Except when people like Inspector Holder are on the case.”

“Except when people take something on as a personal project, which happens with inspectors, yes.  Gen touched you, leaving trace DNA, fingerprints, and signature biome impressions behind.  They have their culprit.  It’s not the culprit you named, and that creates a problem.”

Winnifred frowned.  It created a problem, and it was a problem Vega wanted.

“They have policies and systems that watch out for any ongoing vendettas.  Usually that’s something that happens with the Hidebound, centuries old family and gang rivalries.  But as it happens, someone somewhere, maybe in another prison, maybe in the judiciary forces, made a note that the twenty-nine families have a history with the Terrace walkers.  You made a false accusation that supports an ongoing multi-generation feud.”

Winnifred hoped the look in her eyes conveyed how unimpressed she was.

“You -and I, as a consequence- have to spend a lot more capital to push for a deeper investigation, changes, or any of that,” her lawyer finished.  “I don’t think it’s worth it.”

“But if we can push it, prove it-”

“Proving it may be difficult.”

“Right,” she said, pausing.  “But if we did, we’d show he’s perpetuating the feud.  That hurts him, right?  It serves the families.”

“It does, and believe me, I want nothing more.  But let me explain.  You asked to stay in this cell block, and for me to slow-roll the opening stages.  It counts as time served, so it’s not a huge issue, it happens a lot.  Safer to stick with the known.”

She’d wanted the time to investigate the Gray-frocked here.

“Yeah,” she replied.

“Things might accelerate, especially if anyone catches on that I’m deliberately slowing this down.  It wouldn’t take much.  Inspector Carlen Holder has been poking her nose in and asking questions, and with this designated as a feud, the prison staff might want to hurry things along, so they can put you in a cell block where the Terrace walkers aren’t.”

She didn’t want that, as much.  She wasn’t sure how to voice that, though.

“Their way of rushing things would be to make concessions.  It means I put something forward, as a delaying tactic, they’d just accept what I want and pass things along, or they’d compromise heavily.  I say we take that and run with it.”

“I’d like to stay a bit longer.  Can we delay a little?”

“For what?” he asked, serious.

“So I can see this through?”

“Revenge?” her lawyer asked.

“No… yes, but not-”

He stared at her.

“Help me out, Toby?” she asked.  She began pulling out the data, and showing her lawyer.

She’d met six, so far.  Dane, Isaac, Sinon, Magh, Rienne, and Vega.  Sinon was a bigot, but relatively passive.  She had a diagram with locations she knew Sinon had traveled to, locations she believed the Terrace walkers were less violent, and locations that Isaac, Dane, and Vega had been to.  Three militant Gray-frocked who’d found each other here.

Transcripts of conversations she’d listened in on mapped out just what it meant to be militant, and what it meant otherwise.  Sinon didn’t agree with the science center attack, but her rhetoric hadn’t ruled out other options.  She was a bigot.  It seemed she wanted to take her time more, laying seeds.

And, on the other end, Isaac, Dane were apparently sympathetic with the science center attack, with their primary issue being that the people carrying it out hadn’t succeeded.  She didn’t have anything on Vega, but… she’d have been very surprised if Vega, based on everything she’d seen and everything she’d overheard in talk about the guy, wasn’t sympathetic as well.

Winnifred didn’t have much to go by with Rienne and Magh and their interactions with Vega.  They were new, and they’d barely stuck their toes in the water when it came to being Gray-Frocked.  It was impossible to gauge if they’d started to be indoctrinated by more militant types but got arrested before things got serious, or if they’d only been around the less aggressive types, but they seemed to be easily influenced, and were now constantly seen in Vega’s company, and that suggested they were on the fast track to being more aggressive as well.

Her eyes darted left and right as she highlighted and pulled out text from the transcripts.

The ‘years’.  Not about prison.

Suggestions of future attacks.

She showed how she’d gathered the information, taking pieces of her body to create a directional microphone.

“I don’t think anyone else knows this stuff,” she said.  “The Gray-frocked are public enemy number one.”

“They were.  People have short attention spans.”

“Is this information we can use?  Trade for a reduced sentence?  While at the same time, hurting a group that hates and targets the families?”

“Did he catch you listening, and this is why you suspect him?” her lawyer asked.

“I think he caught me looking over, but any eye contact would’ve set him off.  He hates us that much.”  She showed her lawyer the scene.

“I saw that when reviewing everything for you.  I didn’t realize the context.  Hm.”

She waited.

“Do you have anything more concrete?”

“That’s why I want to stay.”

“The fact they have this classified as a feud hurts things.  You might be poking around the edges of something.”

“Might be?  Please look.  This isn’t cherry picked.  If you take the time to look and see the context these messages and details are framed in, you’ll see there’s something going on.”

His eyes moved in that telltale way that suggested he was looking through menus and logs.  She waited patiently, feet up on her chair, chin on knees, hands clasped in front of her ankles.  Her tail twined nervously around the chair she was sitting in, exploring chair back and legs.

“Hours and hours of footage,” he said.  He’d skimmed.

“If this is key to stopping another attack like the one on the science center, or more effective than the one on the science center, without an A to intervene, isn’t that huge?”

“And if it isn’t?  You took a shot and missed when you named Vega as your attacker.”

“I was oxygen deprived and panicking.  I thought they might not get my oxygen working in time.”

He raised his hands.  “Be that as it may, you’re labeled as a subversive.  In their minds, you’re alleged to have carried out sabotages against ships and used underhanded means to do so, mindful of the ways onboards, cameras, and the systems you sabotaged work.  Putting everything else aside, if you come to them with information?  Their immediate thought is wow, yeah, that could be serious.  Their second thought is to look at your file, realize you’re good at gaming the system-”

“That’s not it.”

“It’s it, in their minds.  Further reinforced by the false accusation- and before- stop,” he said, raising a hand, as she leaned forward.  “Before you interrupt me, I know you were low on Ox.  It makes sense to accuse Vega.  But in their minds?  Look at how they view the world, the tools they use, the fact very few people are motivated to work and live full time with prisoners like the prison staff do, keep in mind that we’re dealing with Judiciary intelligences for whom snap judgments are de rigueur and overworked human staff.”

“And prisoner staff.  Like Anide.”

Toby supplied the information and connections to Anide, which promptly disappeared as her lawyer dismissed it.  He already knew.  He’d reviewed her logs and familiarized herself with her and everything she’d been doing, at least with a skim viewing.

“Prisoner staff don’t help us in this scenario.  By the time you got enough on board to pass the information to the right people and get them to care enough to look?  You might be at the point they dismiss it anyway, because it’s mass hysteria and hype.  Prisoners telling themselves a story and getting out of hand.”

“It can’t be that hard.”

“It gets harder, because you’re a prisoner marked down as subversive, you’re involved in a feud, which they don’t want to help perpetuate, you supplied false information in keeping with the feud, and you’re a rat that cuts babies to pieces with lasers.”

Winnifred bristled.
