Her lawyer projected an image of a page of documentation, and proceeded to elaborate on it as he continued, “Anything you try to say to anyone that matters is going to have a yellow warning label stamped on it, get a ‘read first’ cover sheet with cautionary context about feuds, have a sheet appended to the end saying the last investigation went nowhere.  And when they look up, the person giving the information is a mod jockey from a baby butchering cult?”

“That’s not fair.  Don’t say it like that.”

“That’s the world we live in.  That’s the prejudice we deal with, Winnifred.  That’s reality.”

She hated that.  She dropped her foot from chair seat to floor, clenching her hands.  She wanted to say something about that but she couldn’t find the words.  The words that ended up coming out were, “You keep saying we.”

“Yeah.  I do.”

“You aren’t modded.  It doesn’t feel right.”

He shook his head slightly.  She’d had a vague sense he was low on patience, and it seemed to boil up here.  Eyes averted, he chewed on his lip for a second, before releasing it and letting out a soft exhalation.

She held firm.  She had a sense of the silent treatment and being pushed to apologize or start acting more ‘appropriately’ from dealing with family, growing up.

“You’re a child,” he said, looking at her.

“Almost adult.”

“No, I’m saying you’re a child.  You have a child’s view of right and wrong, you have a child’s view of the world, and you have a child’s selfishness.  I know the rest of your family have similar thoughts and feelings here.”

She hadn’t expected this, and so soon after being pulled apart and left paralyzed and slowly suffocating, being attacked again had her unable to respond.

“The family has done so much for you.  Given you support, purpose, protection, culture, legal help, and you take it and then turn around and do your own thing.  You have your own dream, but it’s clear you don’t want the family to be part of it.  You drop contact for months at a time-”

“Hold on.”

“Let me finish.”

“No,” Winnifred said.  “I dropped contact to protect family.  I was being investigated.”

“You made things a hundred times harder on yourself by not being in touch.  That’s the thing that’s so infuriating. Every step of the way, you’ll accept help, right up to the point you could really benefit from it, and then you walk away, you end up taking the harder path, and then you act like this wounded child, even acting like it’s our fault.  I’d find it laughable, if it didn’t feel so awful to see you live like this.”

“Laughable?”

“You have no idea, Winnifred.  That your family has given you so much, including the resources that could have helped you here, and you have your head stuck too far up your own ass to see.”

“I don’t have an ass.”

“Yet somehow you manage.  You’re doing it again, right here.  Wounded puppy.  Maybe one day you’ll realize, or be told.  I bet you’ll feel what I feel right this moment.  Or maybe you’ll never realize and you’ll stay at a convenient-for-you distance forever, which would be sad as all hell.”

“I’m trying to live my life, instead of being another… drone, in the families.”

“The fact you say that, calling them drones?  That shows you have zero respect for your wider family.  For cousins who tried to include you, for extended family that helped raise you.”

“It was all conditional!”  Winnifred raised her voice, rising slightly out of her seat as she said it.  “I only had all of that when I was living by their prescribed formula, doing contract work on ships from the time I can hold a tool, visiting all the families until I find a husband, bearing a kid in a canister until it’s time to laser them apart and start the cycle over.”

“Don’t pretend you weren’t given other options,” her lawyer said.  “I talked to Michal Omorose.  He offered you more.  But you did ninety percent of it before backing out.  Then you act wounded because of the situation you got into.  If you’d followed through?  If you’d stuck to the plan?  If you’d kept in touch and let us help?  You’d be clear.  I promise you that.”

“He asked me to do something that’s… it betrays what I really love.  It betrays-  I’d be destroying ships.”

“Did you talk to him?  Did you reach out?  Or did you decide, unilaterally?”

“Even if I did reach out and he gave me a different direction to take, it would be someone else’s plan.  That’s still not me living my own life.”

“Winnifred,” her lawyer said.  “What do you think it is that makes you one of us?  Because it’s not the metal of your body.”

“That’s part of it.  What other people see?”

“It’s what’s in here,” her lawyer said, tapping his heart.  It seemed like he was ignoring her, but then he said, “And yeah, I’m not modded.  People don’t have that prejudice at first glance when they see me.  In some ways, I have it easy.  But I live my life for the family, I lose sleep, I fight like hell, I cry, and I bet at the end of the day, if we asked our onboards to tally it all up, I carry a fuckload more emotional weight for the family than you ever have.”

She shook her head slightly.

“Winnifred?” he asked.  “Look me in the eyes.”

She reluctantly did.

“I’m more free than you are.  Consider that.”

“Are you my lawyer or not?” she asked him.  “Because right now it seems like you’re an agent of the family sent to scold me.”

“That’s up to you,” he said.  “You should decide.  Are you going to use family resources, me included, while being a full member of the family, or are you going to reject both?”

“It’s hard to stay in touch when I can’t communicate on the Belt network.  I already agreed to be in touch with family more after I was arrested.  I had a reason for staying quiet.”

“You had an excuse.  Are you lying to me, or lying to yourself, when you say that?  Because reading between the lines and reading people is a big part of my job, and I don’t buy it.”

She didn’t say anything to that.  He remained where he was, staring her down.

Not exactly someone in her corner.

The way they’d bundled up the cabling and tubes inside her chest cavity was different from the way she usually had it.  She reached back to fidget with it.

He had a look in his eyes that made her drop her hand away and fold her hands in front of her, on the table.

He was the one to break the silence first.  “Decide.  I’m going to do as you’ve requested.  I’ll push for something extreme, to see if they bite, or if they balk.  They’ll probably balk, that buys time.  If they bite, that means they want this situation put behind them so badly they’ll make big concessions.”

She nodded.

“With your permission, if I get a result that we can call a ‘bite’, I’ll accept it.  Sentence reduction, protection, anything else spring to mind?  Conveniences?”

“Toby,” she said.  “This forced silence isn’t fair on him.  Or her.  I’m not sure how she’s identifying right now, he can’t exactly talk to me.”

There was that look again.  Disappointed and frustrated, like when he’d called her a child.

“‘Kay.”

Barely a syllable.

He sighed.  “I’ll do my best for you here.  I’ll try for a delay.  In the meantime, decide.  Do you want my help and the family, or do you want neither?  We’re still working out the difference between a two to four year sentence and a four to ten year sentence.”

She thought about it, then nodded.

“Anything else?” he asked.

She shook her head.

“Okay.”

The projection ended.  She was alone in the interrogation room.

She sat for a moment, considering, then got up, crossing the room to one of the four doors, indicated by a light above it.  She knocked.

The guard let her out, and without a word, led her back to the cell block.

➨

Basil

Basil finished the intensive self-audit.  He took his time in working his way through systems, turning things on, with the faintest of sensations as things came back online, processing and computation humming back to life on a subcellular level.

A played with fire, pulling on clothing at the last minute.  Her hair was damp, and heavy, and there was already a tension in her neck from the weight of it.  He’d done a lot to provide muscle strength and conditioning to manage that weight, but there was only so much he could do.

What would he have done if A hadn’t been dressed when he came back online?  He made notes to have better measures in place.

The connection to the wider Belt network came last.

[Good morning, A.]

“Morning,” she said.

“No offense, Basilisk, but it’s freeing to have you gone and offline.”

‘No offense’ was more polite than she’d been for a long while.  They had finished with the production of the Inui Invasion series, yet to be titled and packaged for audiences that had been avidly watching the filming, and while everyone in Generation Colors had been talking about vacations and catching up with those who’d dropped out of production earlier, A had requested a ‘break from everything’.

So they’d gotten on a ship and set off, with a steep elliptical orbit that put her out of range of the Belt network for sixteen hours.  One full waking day.  Basil had taken that time for a full internal self-audit and behind the scenes shuffling of the system structures.  Rebuilding for the sake of rebuilding.

Off the record: rebuilding to shuffle things up, so people keeping track and trying to figure out what he and A were really doing would have to start from scratch, in some ways.  It was a full cell-by-cell check for anything someone might have tried to sneak onto A’s skin with a brushing contact, a way of laying out secret routes the back channel’s systems could use, and an excuse to turn everything off for those sixteen hours.

They’d had to pitch it to Elabre.  Part of Basil’s rationalization was real: that A was disassociating from her own body.  She hadn’t seen a fair portion of her own skin for over a year, she was guarded against sensations, ranging from the touch of a bystander to the touch of her own hand, she had an onboard, Basil, constantly working behind the scenes to fine tune things, and they’d just finished a movie project where, though A had chosen to avoid any routes or scenes where she had any physical changes, there had been false injuries and exertion that threw things further out of sync.

It was clear that some segments of Elabre’s staff thought she should get over it.  That she was fighting off an inevitability, that her body would become something known to the Belt, sooner or later.  On the other hand, other segments argued that what she was doing was working.  She was popular.  That they should keep it.

From there, endless sub-arguments.  Still, there was enough support from the latter group to support this ‘mission’.

The ship they were on wasn’t large, owing to the fact they’d wanted something safe, easy to fly, and above all else, solo.  A was in the bathroom, G-panels turned to low, illuminating things from below, with just enough gravity that she touched ground, but not enough that her weight pushed her down.  She stood facing a mirror with the toes of one foot propping her upright, her hair floating around her, long enough that the ends touched or nearly touched all four walls.  Underwater, without the water.

[Is there anything you need from me at the present moment, A?]

“Hit me with it.  I know you’re eager to drop a superstructure’s worth of things to do on my head.  Let’s get it over with.”

[Not eager, thank you very much.]

A smiled slightly.

Basil was braced for the biting remark coming off the back channel.  The reprimand.  The rejection.  Nothing.

[The press tour for the Inui project continues.  You have three interviews.  Very casual affairs, no need to prep.  One is with valedictorian students of an old fashioned school on Kiviuq.]

“Okay.”

“But you will help me prep, yes?”

[If you’d like.]

[Elabre is wanting all members of Generation Colors to continue meeting groups of fans, until further notice.  They’d like to trial doing this for a few more months, with everyone participating, in the hopes people find their groove.  Unless you strenuously object, I’m to start projecting everyone when we’re back in range of the Belt network.  20 at a time.]

“Okay.  I might need more breaks like this.”

[We can definitely argue for that.  After flying between planets for the interviews, we’ll have a short break, then we’ll need to get ready for an evening blue carpet event, promoting the upcoming release.  Elabre has lined up some fashion designers to make your outfit, they’ll arrive at your apartment before the event and custom fit whatever you select.]

“For the interviews, can we consolidate?  So I don’t have to travel?”

[I’ll inquire.]

“And no repeat questions?  If I give the same answer to the same question, it makes sense, but people think less of me.  Like I’m an idiot or a robot.”

[I’m sure nobody thinks that.  I’ll rearrange it so the more experienced interviewers are second, and they’ll make some adjustments based on the prior interview.]

“Say I’m sorry, um…”  She stretched a bit, then used one arm to sweep hair out of the way so she could turn to the door without walking face first into it.  “…take some of the travel time we’re saving and give them a few extra minutes, as thanks for being accommodating?  If they want?”

[That’s gracious of you.  Easily done.]

Or perhaps not ‘easily’, as there were a lot of moving pieces.  Basil was already setting it into motion, making requests of the security teams, reaching out to the companies, crafting the messages, and trying to figure out where they should go, that would be suitable territory for both interviewers.  The other company, he anticipated, would want a different venue, because two back to back interviews in the same room or setting would look more like one long interview with different interviewers than anything else.  At least to the casual member of the audience.

On the other hand, a balcony was a problem because A was hounded by audience members.  So there had to be security.  Even now, well outside of transmission range, there was a fleet of ships guarding against any potential interception by an overexcited audience member.

That was its own dance, because A’s ship had its elliptical orbit, going out a distance, turning around, and coming back, using gravity to help, and the supporting fleet of ships had its own mess of trajectories, allowing for different ships in that fleet to break from the formation to give pursuit or take action.  Some, for example, had started stationed out at the halfway point of A’s journey before A had even started, so they would be accelerating less, more able to give chase to someone coming perpendicular to the elliptical orbit.

[After the event is a meeting with Elabre.]

“Really?  We can’t enjoy ourselves?”

[You can, but they want to gather Generation Colors together while you’re all in one place.  I don’t imagine it will be a very complicated meeting.]

A sighed.

She stopped in the single room that served as a lounge area and kitchen, grabbed some packaged food and had a mouthful of nuts, glancing over the schedule as Basil laid it out in her field of vision before turning her eyes to the window.  She looked back at the stars they were now moving away from.

As they got closer to the belt, they got more trace data from the network.

[Bruin’s having a hard time.  He’s on Eingana right now.]

A straightened a bit.  “I thought- didn’t the time window close on that?  People were upset after the one night, but that tapered off.”

[You were gone, and he was in front of the media, as a surprise star of the Inui series.  Things sparked off.]

Basil pulled together the images and clips.  People were taking the worst possible interpretation of Bruin’s statements in interviews.  Implying he thought he was more important than A, among other things.

“How long until we’re back?”

[Four hours.]

A was an older teenager, and she wasn’t above some impulsivity and wild swings in mood, but Basil had always helped manage hormonal balance, among other things.  Once Basil factored in other elements, like the fact she’d kept a massive secret for a year now, A had an emotional profile that was…

Every word he might choose was so loaded.

…Controlled.

Even people running simulations and feeling what it was like to be in her body sometimes had a hard time getting a grasp of it.  It was even more controlled in this moment.

Basil had grown up with her, lived in her body, and had access to some private thoughts -insofar as she vocalized them to him- by the back channel.  Things nobody else had.  Even with that, he had a hard time placing her feelings for Bruin, or her response right now.

Attracted to him?  Very.  Were they physically close friends or was she in love?  Basil had little idea, and the fact A gave so little thought and put so little emotional weight onto the question made it even harder.

If she did angst or feel deeply, or explore those feelings while, say, looking at Bruin sleeping on a couch, the morning after, then those feelings were out there.  Experiences for others to share and take, maybe.

Or maybe it was a respect for Bruin’s circumstance.  That whatever she did could be added pressure on him, when that was something that had nearly destroyed him, before.  A then-B-List actor within Generation Colors being pressured by the public to do certain scenes.

“Trust me,” A had whispered to Bruin, before they’d gone that step too far, and she’d given Basil trust, in that moment.

Which was its own complicated thing.

She turned her eyes from the window that showed the stars they’d been traveling toward, during her period of rest, and looked toward the Belt, and Eingana.

➨

Eingana was a beautiful world with a larger ocean than Earth, and archipelago landmasses that had been created by human intervention.  Those landmasses formed the basis for a lot of the superstructures, while water had been left partially clear.  In a sense, anyway.  It glittered from a distance, and much of that glitter was the dense traffic of waterborne craft and machinery.  The groups that owned and ran Eingana had wanted to make a point of keeping a certain aesthetic profile, even at the cost of profit, and that had become its own value, later on.  Something that would no doubt carry over to any new planets established on the Belt.

“I was born here.”

“How young are you?”

“Fourteen.”

“You must have been one of the first babies here.”

They flew over a superstructure built on a c-shaped archipelago, and within the hollow of that ‘c’, a station was being built, already threaded through with the cabling that extended from sub-aquatic crust to outer space.  Finer work could be done here in gravity and atmosphere than out in space, and it was clearly a passion project, fit together like an onion with each layer of the onion cut to a filigree-fine detail.  When done, it would be lifted away and stationed elsewhere.

“That’s part of a set, right?”

“Is it?” A asked.

“It’s a bigger project.  They’re going to connect it all together when the vertical belt is put into motion.”

“Interesting,” A said.

“You can imagine that station as a puzzle in the Tilt series.  It suits Bruin.”

“It would have to be Tilt in the future, not the past.”

“Tilt: Forward!”

Bruin’s fondness for quaint things had led him to buy a place here, on a superstructure where each layer was shaded by a larger layer above it, with a big emphasis on thin, spindly trees, wind, and housing faces modeled after the old Earth Grecian or Mediterranean style.  It was this fondness for quaint things that had led to him becoming popular as the young detective in games and movies, exploring and getting into trouble in old Earth themed locales.

A’s arrival was preceded by the fleet of security ships, that landed on the concourse, making people get out of their way, then drove a short distance.  Like two hands, pressed together in a praying gesture, touching a table’s surface, then moving apart, to clear a way.

A’s ship was small enough to settle against the balcony, one security ship near the nose, one near the tail.

Members of the crowd leaned dangerously over the railing or even climbed over to try to get a view.  There was cheering, excitement, calls for comment.

A wasn’t alone in leaving the ship.  Nineteen individuals had projected in, taking their turn at being in A’s orbit.  A twentieth had chickened out.

Bruin opened the door before she reached it.

“Can we put this group on pause so I can talk to Bruin alone?” A asked.  “As alone as we ever are?”

[Elabre’s setup doesn’t allow for that,] Basil said.

“I want to include that,” A said.  She glanced at her current crop of audience members.  “It’s not fair to these guys, if they have limited time and I’m asking them to stay quiet for a few minutes.”

[We can make a note to bring it up.  It might be a long shot.  People make their bids to have a chance of being present for a big moment.]

“We’ll be good,” one of the group said.

A flashed a quick smile, before stepping forward and turning to Bruin.

“Hi,” A said.

“I’m your first stop after you get back?  How was it?”

“It was good,” A replied.  “A part of me wanted to keep going, take a few years.  I didn’t have the supplies to do it, though.  And it was only a part of me.”

“I kind of get that,” Bruin replied.

Basil flagged the smallest of vocal shifts at the start of Bruin saying ‘get’.  Imperceptible.  A quick and subtle check verified that Bear had indeed suppressed most of it.  Not the sort of thing one would notice in the first place, or note if one wasn’t looking for it.

“No audience in attendance?” she asked.

“There is a group in the house, Green stopped in to back me up, but we had enough people popping in to yell at me, Elabre decided it was a problem.  He’s outside on the balcony, talking to some of the others.  So I’m clear for the next bit.”

“Good,” A said.

He shrugged a bit.  He looked unsure about what to do.

“Welcome me back with a hug?”

He did.  His hug was tight.

She’d probably realized he really wanted one, but asking for one would be tough.

“Mmm,” he grunted softly, burying his nose and mouth in between her neck and shoulder.  Basil could feel his deep exhalation, flowing through hair and the nanotech there, and between skin and the fabric of A’s top.

“Mm,” A responded.

“Front row seats to the next sex scene,” one member of A’s group whispered, behind them.

Bruin pulled away quickly.

Basil could feel the surge of rage through A.  Cold, suppressed, but very much there.

“Want to hang out?  Watch or play something?” A offered.  “Or we could talk that out.”

Her head turned slightly toward the door and the commotion there.

“Ah.  You noticed the…” he trailed off, searching for a word.

“Angry mob?”

“…Crowd?  I’m hesitant to label them anything like that, might not be wholly deserved or accurate, and it might get me in more trouble.”

“You okay?”

“Not very?” he replied, quiet, eyes on the floor.  He was putting on a brave face though, and smiled a bit as he made eye contact again.  “Thinking about quitting.”

“I’m sorry for my part in it.  Initiating.”

“No.  Not at all.”

“I said to trust me.”

Bruin’s lips parted slightly, but whatever he was going to say, he didn’t.

“So… offer’s open.  Want me to make them fuck off?”

He let out a soft laugh.

“I’m serious.”

“Setting security on them might inflame things-” he started.  But A was already shaking her head.

[Fill me in?] Basil asked, by back channel.  [What are you doing, A?]

“I’ll make them fuck off.  It’s not complicated.”

[How?  I hate to bring it up, but you know that one person died, the last time you rejected the audience?  Be careful.]

A looked toward the door.  She didn’t reply.

“Don’t underestimate that sort of crowd,” Bruin said.  “If you tried to make them stop and failed, it could go south fast.  I don’t want you in front of this stuff.”

“Hey,” A told him.  “I like you.”

Her heartbeat was heavier in her chest than it normally was.  It was hard to tell how much of the rest was cortisol from stress and how much was her feelings for Bruin.  It didn’t help that the two mingled.

“And they hurt you,” A said.  “For what?”

“Tell me not to, I won’t do anything.  You have the lead here.  But I’m mad.”

He seemed surprised by that.

“Mad for you.”

“I know, I got your meaning, but…” he trailed off.

Maybe he was surprised he mattered to that level.  It had to be complicated for someone to be in his position, to be someone who could connect to how A was feeling, as they had in the latter half of their tryst, as A had done to him, and not feel the heated passions or unruly emotion, for much the same reason it was closed to Basil.

“Say no,” she told him.  “Or I’ll go handle it, and then we can talk plans for after.”

“I’m worried you can’t do what you think you can do.  Audiences turn.  I’m worried.”

“That’s not a no.  Okay,” she said.  “Be right back.”

She opened the front door.  The crowd that had rearranged, as much as they could around the walled fences in front of properties and around the two vehicles with armed security that were barring the way.

The wind blew at her hair, and she used an arm to keep it away from her face.

“Give me that list, Basil?”

[Lillian B. Cody.
Alms Almaguer.
Lind Gallagher.
Trick Barcomb.]


“And the person who joined in, making that comment about sex?”

[Jack Bostic.]

A stepped onto the protruding edge at the base of one of the security ships, then onto a higher point, where that lip encircled the landing gear, that could protrude out to the left or right for added stability.  A security officer offered her a hand, and she took it for balance, one hand on the metal that was still warm from atmospheric entry and now being in the hot sun.  She found a foothold, and scaled the rest of the side, until she had a platform to stand on.

Security moved to block people who were trying to climb the anti-climbing grille at the front of the ship.  They were willing to climb on each other to be closer.

“Do I need to say the names?” A asked.  She didn’t raise her voice.  The crowd went quiet.  “You can see through my eyes.  Bruin didn’t deserve this.  They’re listed there.  Lillian B. Cody, Lind Gallagher, Alms Almageur, Trick Barcomb.  Jack Bostic.”

She gave no instructions, this time.

[Hruby Goldcliff died the last time we did this.]

“I trust my audience to be better about things this time,” A said, responding out loud, instead of in the backchannel.

She turned back toward the house, jumping down from the top of the ship.

➨

Bruin seemed shaken.

“You overstepped,” Wan Graf said.  The Elabre CEO had elected to attend, and it was, as far as Basil could tell, a new adjustment.

“I named names.  Names that were stepping up and stepping forward, using their soapboxes to hurt others.  Bruin isn’t who they were portraying him as.  The comment was gross and I can’t- we can’t live like this, with every meaningful moment undercut by some joker who wants to be famous.”

They’d done one interview- A had refused to do the first because the media group associated with Trick Barcomb, one of the people A was freezing out.  Then they’d asked Green and Bruin to hang out.  Bruin had refused, asking to see how the situation resolved.  So she’d focused on her audience, and got ready for the event alone, picking very quickly from the fashion designer’s offerings.  They’d all attended the promotional event, and now they were here, talking to Elabre.

“I didn’t overstep, I stepped,” A said.  “If we’re going to do this thing where we’re catering to audience all day every day, there have to be measures.  Ways to protect ourselves.”

“Open flow of information and a mutually assured trust are key tenets Elabre is helping to promote,” Wan Graf said.  “The games you’re playing are the opposite of that.”

“The sex scene,” Bruin said, quiet.

Wan Graf stopped.  He looked over.  “Meaning?”

Bruin gave Wan Graf a long look.  “It’s the elephant in the room we’re not talking about.  Either you’re hypocrites, and you guys masked data.  Or you’re not, and I have a hundred more questions.”

“Elabre took measures,” Wan Graf lied.  “Keeping your past and your concerns in mind.  A asked for it.”

Bruin’s stare was a searching one.

“And you’ll keep doing it for everyone here?” A asked.

Wan Graf seemed slightly taken aback, but amended, “if they ask for it.”

“Cool.  Good,” A said.  “Because I know some are eager, but are a little intimidated by the eager billions who’d watch.”

“I feel so called out,” Maisie said, from the back.  She laid her head on a suddenly wide-eyed Krick’s shoulder.

“All to be discussed and negotiated in the future,” Wan Graf said.  “But at the end of the day, we do care about the free flow of information, and mutually assured trust.  Our model is tied into that, and it’s why a number of superstructure governments sponsored us in the first place.  If we walk that back or play favorites with celebrities, that gets snarly.”

“Okay, well, figure it out,” A said.  “Generation Colors are my people, I’m going to protect them.”

Every other member of Generation Colors at the table seemed very quiet.  Postures and positions were relaxed.  Maisie and Krick were back by the door, sitting together.  Amber sat on the balcony railing, and the rest of the core team was up front.  Green, Bruin, and A right up front by Wan Graf.

“How far does this go?” Wan Graf asked.  “You being reckless, throwing a grenade and walking away, leaving others to scramble, scatter, deal with the damage?”

“My claim to fame is that I fought monsters and won,” A said.  “I’m going to keep dealing with monsters.  You asked for me, you get what you asked for.”

Wan Graf looked unhappy.

“Or is this you saying you don’t want me working with Elabre?  Are you releasing me from my contact?”

“No,” he said, and there wasn’t any hesitation there, nor rush.  “We’re not.”

“We just released the biggest media installment ever.  You guys seem confident it’s going to be big.”

“We are.”

“Is it that important, that we do this thing?”

“Modeling suggests it keeps Generation Colors afloat, when otherwise it would wane.”

“Financially, in terms of audience numbers.  But mentally?  It’s a lot.”

“We recognize that.  You can opt out.”

“At the cost of not being members of Generation Colors anymore,” Amber said, from the back.  “After it was our entire lives.”

“You’d still be members.”

“Second string,” Amber said.

“Are you unhappy, Amber?  If you’d like to discuss options, or address things, we’d-”

“No,” Amber said.  “Sorry, I’m getting my head around things.  Carry on.”

A turned, giving Amber a long look.

“A.”

Amber’s expression was hard to read, Basil noted.

Almost everyone here was like that.  Maybe more than A.

“A,” Wan Graf said, with more emphasis.

She turned.

“What did you expect to happen?  When you named the names?  Because if you expected retributive justice, that’s a problem.”

“No,” A said.  “No, I knew people would be more on top of things.  I knew it would force people to act, get people to satisfy the audience before the audience felt it necessary to satisfy themselves.”

“The ‘people’ you forced to act includes Elabre.”

A nodded.

Wan Graf looked deeply unhappy.

[Incidentally, the first four people named lost sponsorships.  Superstructures aren’t willing to host them or feature their advertisements.  Their income streams are ruined.]

“The fifth?”

[He was brought into custody.  Protective, technically.  We’ll have to see.  Mostly, they’re taking your cue, where you refused the interview, and are freezing them out, out of fear you’ll refuse to deal with their companies, or visit their superstructures.]

A nodded faintly.

“You say you’re here to stop monsters,” Wan Graf said.

“Yeah, I guess.  I’m not very serious about that,” A said.  “It makes for a good quote.  I want to protect people.  I want to keep people.  I want…”

She looked around the table.

Notably, a few people, like Jan, averted their eyes.

Bruin did.

“I want to recognize that we are people.  Generation Colors are.”

“What happens if you become the monster, A?  Making proclamations, putting people at risk.  A dragon roars from the distant mountains, and a whole kingdom scrambles to prepare for possible fire and destruction,” Wan Graf said.

“I don’t know what you thought you were buying when you signed me on,” A said.  “Do you remember?  The science center was attacked.  My friends were transformed.  They made me into a monster.  But I stayed me.  I kept my values.”

Except that wasn’t what had happened.

Basil thought about saying as much in the back channel, but he didn’t want to disturb the delicate peace he currently had with A.

“I like that,” Green said, quiet.

A smiled a bit.

Wan Graf was silent, staring at her.

“I’m finding myself.  Getting comfortable in my own skin.”

“I’ll talk to my colleagues.  We’ll get back to you,” Wan Graf said, standing from his chair.  “I-”

He paused.

A leaned back.

“-If this is what comes of you taking time off and introspecting, I’m concerned about what comes out of the next little vacation you take.”

“But there will be a vacation,” A said, making it a statement, not a question.  “For me, for all of us.  There will be reasonable limits placed on the audience gatherings.  Breaks, chances to put it on pause.”

“I’ll talk to my colleagues.”

“I’m willing to walk.  And if anyone else in Generation Colors wants to-”

“-break a contract, to be clear.”

“If they want to break contract, I’ll give them however much money they need to fight it.  I was looking at buying a planet, but I can put those funds toward backing them up.”

Wan Graf, standing beside the table, body still turned away from when he’d been leaving, head turned to look at A over one shoulder, didn’t respond or move.

“One way to do this without losing myself is to focus on helping others, backing them up.  Don’t hurt the people I care about.  That’s all I’m asking.”

“I’ll talk to my colleagues and get back to you.  Thank you, everyone, for your hard work.”

“I didn’t work hard,” Maisie chimed in.  “I got murdered early on.  So did Krick.”

Wan Graf forced a smile at Maisie’s light humor.  “There’s still some time before the next project is announced.  Please try to hit at least two out of three of the various training sessions, to keep all your skills fresh in mind.  Dance, music, singing, voice.”

A nodded.  There were murmurs from others present.

Wan Graf left.  Some staff were still bringing through late night snacks, but they filtered out too.

A sighed.

The conference room was very quiet.

[We’ve been lucky nobody died out of the names you listed.  So far.]

“I was sure they wouldn’t.”

That confidence.

He wasn’t sure how to answer it.

“You’re buying a planet?” Blue asked.

“Want to see?” A asked.

Many of the others came, interested, chatting.  Amber and Bruin did not.

➨

Winnifred

There wasn’t much time, then.

A few weeks, maybe, that the lawyer could delay?  Then she’d be out of reach of the Gray-Frocked.

She’d spent some time dwelling on what her lawyer had said.  A lot of it had been less than productive, being angry at herself that she hadn’t been able to form better arguments, or defend her position.

The rest of it?  It was worse, because she’d realized some of what she had been doing wrong.  He’d said she would feel the way he did when she realized, and she worried he was right.

She’d dismantled part of her body to form the directional microphone.  Now she followed after them, keeping her distance.  Her sense of Vega was that he’d want to come after her if he spotted her, so she avoided that.  She could stay around a corner, train the microphone, asking for Toby’s help in finding the right angles, and catch the sound bouncing off a wall.

Vega was charismatic, in his own way.  It was less that he had a charm that drew people to him, and more that he exerted a constant, regular pressure, paid constant attention, and it turned out people were receptive to that.  Magh and Rienne sticking close to him fed into that.  Two young women.

People were lonely, even in this crowded place.

She quickly found out he had recruited three people.  Four, if she counted Gen, the man who had attacked her.  All were unmodded.  One was a woman that was one of the crabs in the crab bucket, waiting for a public defender to take pity on them and help them.  Two were Hidebound, people from families that had crime in their blood, but no family in their cell block.  They needed that community, they’d never gotten around to getting onboards.

Sinon had pulled away when Vega had immediately connected with the two girls, but now a dynamic was forming.  Sinon was taking on a role of teacher, maybe because she wanted to be close, for reasons that ran in parallel to Winnifred’s own anxieties about what the group was becoming.

Were those anxieties founded?  It was still a small group.  There was a hard limit on who they could recruit, if they limited themselves to people without onboards.  Right now, that had to be less than ten percent of the cell block.

She couldn’t retaliate against the attack and the damage to her Ox.  Her onboard complicated that.

She couldn’t just enter the lounge area, though.  It was too wide, too open.

The layout of the prison was like a pie chart, split into its individual slices.  Lounge, library, counseling, exercise… the outer rim and dividers between cells were all walls of cells.  There were prisoners who complained about how this made the cells cold.  For those perched at the dividers between two areas, generally higher risk prisoners, it meant they had bars on both sides of the cells.  Flashlights would shine in on them from either side, if the prisoners who had been elevated to be on guard duty elected to use flashlights.  Ventilation would blow through from one area of the prison to another, chilling the cell’s occupants, smells from the exercise area or canteen would reach the people trying to sleep.

People hated it, as a result.

It did mean a directional microphone could be aimed through an empty cell and at the area where the Gray-Frocked were.  It took some fine tuning, and required help from Toby, but it was doable.

The trouble here was location.  It meant she had to do something she wasn’t good at.

She ascended to the higher level of cells, then crossed the catwalk.  Some prisoners were in their cells, doing their own thing.  She averted her eyes, because a decreasing number of those prisoners didn’t have onboards, and were carrying out activities they didn’t want surveilled.  That was a dream in prison, technically a pre-sentencing area, but Winnifred didn’t know this area of the cell block, she wasn’t streetwise enough to know the cues, and she really, really didn’t want trouble.

Winnifred sniffed.  Toby supplied a PPM for fecal matter, among a medley of other pleasant things.

Winnifred found the cell she was looking for and allowed herself a look.  Single occupancy, occupied by a Siss Shandel, who was sitting at the little desk inside her cell.

“Huh?” Siss grunted.

Winnifred glanced away, because Siss was clearly doing something borderline enough she didn’t want more eyes on her, and fiddled with the directional microphone.

It was a struggle.

“What that guy talked about, in the canteen.”

“It’s no big,” Siss said.  “I mean, obviously it’s a big.”

Was there a chance that Winnifred could say this, then walk it back with an excuse?  If her lawyer was any indication… no.  The excuses and justifications she gave were too thin, and the Twenty-Nine families weren’t buying it. They weren’t giving her the benefit of a doubt.

So this might’ve been burning a bridge.

“It’s not what I believe.  But it’s complicated.”

“Okay,” Siss said.

“I miss our… friendship?  Acquaintanceship?”

“We were friends, you dipshit,” Siss said.  “And what you miss is the excuse to listen to A’s music.”

“Bit of that too.”

“I don’t get why it’s so hard to say no to what that guy was saying.”

“Because family.  Family I’ve been pulling away from.  Find someone with access to the network, they can look it up.  But that family’s my job prospects, my supply for new body parts, it’s everyone I know that sticks around for half a minute.”

“Yeah.”

“Someone near your cell spread shit everywhere.  It still smells, according to you.”

“According to me and others.  We’re trying to avoid mentioning it or reminding anyone.  It makes it easier to put out of mind.”

“Some of us don’t have that sense of smell,” someone said in the next cell over.  “And we’re really fucking tired of people talking about it.”

“I can deal with that smell,” Winnifred said, tapping the jutting mask at her lower face with a claw tip.  “So I thought, in the interest of having an excuse to talk to you again… want to put in for a switch?”

She could see Siss’s eyes light up as she realized that was a possibility.  Then, “You could have offered earlier.”

“I’m an idiot, because I maybe could have thought about it sooner.  But if I’m an idiot, so are you,” Winnifred said.  “You didn’t think of it either.”

“I was hinting,” Siss told Winnifred.

Winnifred closed her eyes, wincing as she recontextualized earlier conversations with Siss.

“Nah,” Siss said.  “I wasn’t, you’re right.  I’m an idiot.  I didn’t think of it either.”

Winnifred chuckled lightly.  Bluffing, as Squib would have put it.  Overly emoting, to convey something, when she couldn’t smile.

Winnifred explained, “I get focused on certain things and it didn’t seem possible until I started thinking about the music group.  How you get leeway if you’re building bonds and making yourselves into better citizens.  We’d be doing that here.”

“Yeah?”

“If it means we’re talking again, mending a burned bridge.  If it means different groups are getting along, becoming the sorts of people who can get on in normal society.”

“Do we want you in normal society, though?” someone asked.

A woman.  Not part of any group Winnifred could discern, but her features were etched with lines as if a deep unhappiness with life had settled in.  She had emerged from her cell.

“Rat?” the woman asked, as if it was a natural extension of her other question, with a question mark and a whole lot of loaded bullshit tied into it.  Siss, sitting at her desk, looked at Winnifred without stepping up to help.  Her eyes fell on the directional microphone Winnifred was holding near her arm.  “That a weapon?”

Siss craned her head.

“I was fixing parts, got to thinking about stuff, couldn’t concentrate, so I came straight here,” Winnifred said.

Siss leaned over in her seat.  Winnifred looked away, but she had the sense that Siss was crushing something up to make powder.  Winnifred was more likely to believe it was a dye for staining some mark onto clothing, as a show of affiliation – something Siss would sell, not use, Winnifred hoped.  Or maybe it was prison makeup.

“That’s ear tech.  Not a weapon,” Siss said.  “She used it to make a radio for our club.”

The other group didn’t seem mollified.  They’d cut off the routes Winnifred would need to take to walk out of here.

Winnifred tried not to look rattled.  “I’m done with my family.  Family’s complicated.  Pulling away from it all takes a while.  I’m there now.”

“So you say.”

“Find someone who has the contraband to dig into my history, or pay prison staff to.  Do anything more than a skim, it will back what I’m saying.  Where I sleep, my emotional responses to some of the regular stuff.”

“To the baby modding?”

“Less that.  But only because… manipulation.  It’s how I was raised.”

No, she could tell she was losing her small audience here.

“I don’t think people want me to switch cells with you,” Siss said.  “The prison might think it causes more problems than answers.”

Winnifred nodded.  “You okay, though?”

“I’m thinking about going full squid.  What do you think?  My heart, at the bottom of an ocean?  On full display?”

“If you were at an event, I think her eyes would stop on you for a second.  I don’t know if that’s good or bad.”

“I was thinking that.”

“And it would be a jank prison mod.  Cardiac?  Don’t die, Siss.”

“That’s less important.”

Winnifred did want to talk more, or dwell on that more.

She also didn’t want trouble.  So, in the interest of avoiding it, she slipped through the railing, her narrow, lithe body making that easy, checked the coast was clear, and dropped to the level below.  The canteen.

“Griffey Docks!  That’s a shot!”

“Toby?” she murmured.  “File an answer, I was avoiding confrontation.”

She’d had the directional microphone aimed, with Toby assisting, and she hoped she’d picked up some things.

➨

Echo-ey voices bouncing off walls, when they walked down hallways, from their religious meeting to the main cell block.

Other conversations, collected from the other side of that wall of cells, aiming the directional microphone between bars and into another area of the prison.

It was all fragmented.  Very little of it was whole or complete.  If she had the time, then she could keep doing this, and it would be reasonably safe.  She didn’t have the time, so she opted to be less safe.

In the corridors past the library, Winnifred walked out to where her meeting room had been, fully aware that the last time she’d been traveling through these corridors, she’d been ambushed by Gen.  Gen, who had joined Vega’s group, which was slowly growing.

The prison wasn’t shutting it down or recognizing it for what it was.

It was one thing Winnifred had managed to collect.  Vega’s strength was his insistence.  That he laser focused onto things he wanted, and didn’t back down.  Listening in, it was clear he was conveying that to some of his group.  He gave people like Magh, Rienne, and Gen that laser focus.

Half of their conversations were them listing off people who were valid members of their group.  So-and-so was unmodded, but they were soft, a danger to themselves more than they’d ever be a danger to someone else.  Someone else would be called a prospective, and then conversation would turn to best methods to approach them.  Customized to each person.

The prison was sleeping on it.  The more Winnifred did this, the smaller her mental picture of the prison staff became.  She had imagined an apparatus before, two hundred members of staff who kept their hands clean by avoiding the cell block in all circumstances that weren’t outright emergencies.  Now what she was envisioning was more in the vein of twenty people, with a few asleep at their desk at any given time.

Prisoners in good standing who were on their way out were converted into prisoner staff, filling the gaps.

But, at the same time, the Intelligences that ran things were omnipresent and unforgiving.  Nobody was sure if things were being decided by human or Intelligence, and the uncertainty made them behave more than one or the other would.

The caveat was that shit like this happened behind the scenes.

So, with the club being an excuse to be in these hallways, she got closer than she should.  One turn of the hallway behind.

If asked by the prison, she’d say she was avoiding trouble.  Or she’d divulge the information she had, and hope it bought her more leeway than actively surveilling other prisoners got her in trouble.

“…they have the combat training on Atira, Akna, and Inanna.  Different environments, different things to learn,” one voice explained.  Names were hard to place, but Winnifred took it to be Vega.  Because it spoke with knowledge and authority.

“What about urban fighting?  Because ninety-nine percent of anything we do is going to happen on the side of a superstructure.”

“Some on Akna.  But other training takes place elsewhere.  I’ll tell you some of that on a later day.”

“I don’t think it’s ninety-nine percent.  What about space?”

“Space is more important.  The most important.  There’s a lot to learn, if you want to fight in zero-G or low-G, that happens elsewhere.  I can’t name the location, but there is a location.”

“It’s hard.  Fighting in zero.”  Sinon’s voice.  “I got my ass kicked every day for a month before I figured it out.  Three more months before I was halfway comfortable doing it.  You have to learn so much of it from scratch.”

The group had slowed.  They were at a four-way intersection, and Winnifred hung back, past two corners, out of sight.

Heavy, clomping footsteps made her head turn.

Gen.  The reason they had stopped at the intersection of hallways was because they were meeting him here.  All of them happening to meet here, in the hallways, where there wasn’t much surveillance, if any.  At most, the Intelligences would yell at them.  On that note…

“Station intelligence, I would progress, but I’m keeping a healthy distance from a gang that has feud-driven reasons to target my demographic,” Winnifred murmured, her mask near a panel.  “Please do not acknowledge audibly.”

The panel next to her head flashed a green dot at her sightline.

She’d said that because a nagging warning from the station Intelligence would be dangerous.  Gen had caught a glimpse of her, and was walking toward that main group.  He wasted no time.

“Ratbitch is hanging around.”

“The one you said hello to, last week?”

“Mm hmm.”

Winnifred backed away, and checked doors as she passed them.

Footsteps tromped her way.  Foam clogs slapped floor.

“Kick vent covers you pass.  Ratbitch can break into a vent but she can’t seal it up behind her.  If she is in the vents, we tell the prison, they lock it down,” Sinon said.

Two door were closed, with activity behind them.

“Maybe they’ll burn the vents, incinerate the obstruction,” Magh said.

That got some soft laughter.  It struck Winnifred how Magh and Rienne got a lot of reinforcement from the others when they were cruel.

All so simple, but it worked.

More doors were closed and locked, nothing audible inside.

Winnifred kept passing rooms that were empty.  Every time, she thought there might be a chance.  Every time, the room would be empty and devoid of cover.

At least she was faster.  She could create a small gap.  She couldn’t go that far out into the rooms and hallways around her cell block, though.  She would get in trouble.

She could try to find a guard station… but that felt like a different brand of trouble.

Quietly, she ducked down, unscrewing a vent cover.  Her claw tip slid into the slot, and her finger could rotate.

She put the screws inside, propped up the cover, and then walked away.

Another empty room.  She checked the coast was clear, let herself in, then climbed.

Her lawyer’s words about remembering what her family had given her stuck in her mind.  A family she’d rejected openly, talking to Siss.

She could position herself above the door, but they might look up.

Instead, she climbed on top of a cabinet.  Two by two feet across.  A bad hiding place.  Parts of her would stick over the edge, or would sit so tall someone on the ground could look up and see most of her body.

Except she could curl up there, then reach down to her spine, and disconnect it.  A person curled into a ball on top of a cabinet would be visible.  A  pair of legs, tail and spine all curled up could lay flat against the surface.

With upper body only, she crossed the room by handholds and small areas of leverage.  Her claws slid between the narrow doorframe and the wall, finding the solid core around the door.  She hand-walked herself forward, across the top edge of a panel that jutted from the wall, and found another cabinet, same dimensions.  With no lower body, she could tuck arms around head, pull spine toward chin, temple against cool metal, and curl up.

Cutting herself in half, in essence, let her hide away like this.

She’d only barely finished doing that when she heard the clatter.  They’d tapped the vent cover with a toe.

She didn’t move a millimeter as they went through the whole process of telling the station that ‘some rat’ had slipped inside.

False allegations being a problem cuts both ways.

She was only ‘some rat’ because there was that pre-existing history.  It would be punished more harshly.  A lot depended on whether the station looked into the history of it.

Two hours.  The station staff arrived, along with prisoner staff, and they called for drones to go through the vents.  Only a couple of the Gray-frocked remained, and they even entered the room, because it was close by, and they wanted to sit.

No real conversation to listen in on.  They got told to vacate, they moved to the hallway.

“Remember how the first time the fish brothers came up, people had concerns?”

“One way of putting it.”

“Then he brings them up again, five minutes ago, nobody peeps.”

“It’s fucked.  But we can use fucked.”

“Mmm.”

“You don’t agree?”

“Did I say I don’t agree?”

“You grumbled.”

The conversation paused as prison staff walked by.

“I figure if we get them fighting each other, they’ll do their work for us.”

“Turns my stomach.”

Which turned the conversation toward food and meals.

Less useful.

Eventually, one was pulled away for some questions, then the other.  Then they were told they didn’t need to hang around.

The prison staff replaced the vent cover- Winnifred could hear the sounds.  Then someone walked into the room.  Station staff.

“Winnifred of Griffey Docks.”

“Here,” she said.  “Trying to avoid trouble.  Sorry about the vent cover.”

“Making trouble while you’re avoiding it, are you?  Get to your cell block.”

She was halfway to hand-walking herself around the perimeter of the room when the prison station employee stepped on a piece of furniture, grabbed the legs, and passed them to Winnifred.

Once she could walk again, she hurried on her way.

➨

The fish brothers, as it turned out, had done something with gene modding or nanotech to their skin, and it had gone wrong.  Flesh, at best, looked like the inside of someone’s mouth.  Red, raw, and glistening.  Most of it didn’t, though, and it dried, then the next time it stretched, it split and tore, bleeding openly.

That had been happening for a long time.  Probably ten-plus years, rather than a single digit.  If they hadn’t gotten it fixed, it meant their genes were fragile or there were other problems.  The process of tearing and healing across different layers of skin had created deep clefts around some major parts of the body, like shoulder and elbow, and finer webworks of scar tissue just about everywhere else.  Their features were flattened out by a mingling of the scarring and swelling, and their eyes were overlarge, bloodshot, bulging, and constantly wet.

Winnifred had seen them around the cell block, but not much.  They traveled in entirely different circles, spending almost their entire days in the exercise area, lifting weights or hanging with that crowd.

But they’d been mentioned, and it was a lot easier to surveil them than to stick close to the other group, which was so fluid, people constantly coming and going, with some very sharp eyes in there.

No, this was better, even if time was running out.

She’d watched, a day ago, as the older brother in his cell was brought his daily medication.  Thirty minutes after taking it, he’d punched a wall, several times.  Winnifred had walked by at one point, and the wall had concentric rings from blood stains, where skin had split and knuckles had been ripped raw.

They didn’t feel pain.

That was it.  They were two big guys who made most people’s eyes water to look at, and they leveraged that.  They’d gone to exercise because they had to do physio to keep their skin from hardening and splitting again, and they’d kept doing it until they were huge.  The modding had damaged their skin, but the rest of them seemed to be tough.  To top it off, they took heavy duty painkillers that meant that if they got hit, they barely flinched.

The fact they’d gone for mods or genetic alteration meant they weren’t possible recruits by the Gray Frocked.  It explained the disgust others had mentioned.

So Winnifred waited, hoping she could follow this trail of connections to a destination before her lawyer sent her a message saying he couldn’t delay any further.

They were doing contract work.  It wasn’t anything fancy.  One prisoner with nice hair and glasses who seemed terrified of everything hired them for the one day before his lawyer got his situation sorted.  Another time, they’d cornered someone.

Now… Vega got up from his table.  They seemed to notice, and got up too.  In the hustle and bustle of the canteen, it was hard for most to notice, but it stood out when Winnifred was focusing on the two groups.

She tried to be more surreptitious when picking up her tray and trash.

A private meeting in the hallways, the Fish brothers and Vega.

She kept her usual distance, reaching inside her chest cavity for the directional microphone that was just about always assembled, now.

“Someone will put money into your commissary.”

“For what?”

“Do you want the long, medium,or short answer?”

“Short to start.”

“Bash a guard.  If you can get his card or password, that’s even better.”

“Who?”

“You want the long answer?”

“Medium.”

“An actual guard.  I know, I know.  But apparently, three of the last four Thursdays, we had proper security on ship.  Investors have been coming through.  Investors change things.”

“Right.  Does this have anything to do with the rumor you have a sympathetic friend upstairs?”

“It doesn’t.”

That was interesting, on two levels.  Winnifred hugged one wall, thinking.  She hadn’t heard a hint of that rumor.  You had to talk to people to hear rumors, so that factored in, but… okay.

And second of all, interestingly, Vega was not a good liar.  That ‘it doesn’t’ hadn’t sold her in the slightest.

“Schaeffer and Bernar Seville,” the announcement system pronounced.  “You’re loitering.  We see you attend art classes.  If that is your reason for being in the hallways, please proceed briskly to your activities.”

Fuck.

“Yeah, okay,” one of the fish brothers said.  “Okay.  We’ll need to know the name, face, and where.”

“I’ll tell you the name and the where.  I-“

“Vega Albaron-“

“I know!”

“-you’re loitering.  We see you attend religious study in the evenings.  If that is not your reason for being in the hallways, please proceed briskly to your activities.”

“-can get you a passable description.  It will be next Thursday.”

The messages were timed, after a certain amount of time spent lingering in the hallways.

She’d entered a little under a minute after Vega had.

The Fish brothers and Vega were already parting, by the sounds of the foam clog footsteps.

Winnifred wracked her brain for something to say to the system.  “System, please understand I-“

She couldn’t speak loud enough to be heard by the panel, but also quiet enough to not be heard by Vega, who wasn’t all that far away.  She switched tacks.

“Toby, please pass on a message asking the station not to announce my loitering, I’m avoiding crossing paths with Vega Albaron, to avoid perpetuating the feud.”

Vega put the request on the screen.  A small red icon appeared in the corner.  The request faded.

Refused?  Was there a restriction, or-?

She hadn’t expected this kind of message system to be online at this hour, since so many attended activities and took classes after eating.  It was all overflow from the library, and activities that risked disrupting the peace of the library, like music.

She tried more doors.

“I’m running, but only to stay out of trouble and avoid someone who I believe will hurt me.  I can explain before tribunal,” she told one panel.

Then she dropped to all fours, knees reversing, where she could run twice as fast as on foot, especially with the claw-tipped toes that weren’t as conducive.

Dropping to all fours and sprinting away would risk her getting a warning.  Worse, she could be paralyzed.

So she moved carefully, checking doors.

She was bound by so many shackles that others weren’t.  She resented it.

She was still pissed about her Ox tube.

She crossed one intersection, and saw that one of the fish brothers was further down that hall.  He saw her.

She ducked out of the way, but the sound of his fierce, long whistle caught her off guard.

She couldn’t run, as much as she wanted to.

Warnings occasionally sounded, from more distant hallways.  Guards had apparently been dispatched.

Were all the doors locked because instruments and other equipment had been delivered to them, and they were worried about theft?

Vega had circled around to the far side of her.  The fish brothers helped hem her in.

Others had come.  Magh and Rienne.  One of the new ones she hadn’t had the opportunity to get the name of.

Maybe, because she was angry, she’d wanted this to happen.  She’d dwelt on what her lawyer had said.  Part of that was that she hadn’t been going all-in on solving problems, only putting in ninety percent of the work before bailing.

That wasn’t especially fair considering everything, but it wasn’t wrong either.

“I didn’t have anything to do with your Ox tube being pulled out,” Vega said.

Telling on himself as he said it.  How could he know or care it was pulled out, if he hadn’t been involved?

“Wish I had,” he added.

“Let’s all walk away” she said.  “You sending someone to hit me from behind says you don’t want to fight, so let’s not fight.”

The only sound was the hum of ventilation.  Guards were on their way, but they weren’t close enough to hear.

He knew the same thing.  He came for her, pulling off his overshirt.

This time, she went for him.

She had wanted to sound like she didn’t want the fight, but that anger lingered, damaging her argument.  She wanted this.

She’d lost everything, really.  Then she’d been kicked while she was down.  Her lawyer had put salt on the wounds.  He was, in the end, supporting the twenty-nine families more than he was backing her.

He hadn’t been entirely wrong, though.  Which was infuriating on its own.

She’d put two and two together, so when she sidled in shockingly close to Vega, it was to dance, her body twisting and arm guarding to limit how hard he could hit her while she moved in close, chest close to his chest.

He hit her, but with her body close, it was hard to get a good swing in.  He used elbow, and elbow hit metal.  He immediately shifted his grip, finding a proper handhold near her armpit, and she twisted back and away.

That tilted her upper body, and her ribcage was the equivalent of a room with a wide open skylight and no floor.  That open floor was his target, as he reached for the internals in her chest cavity.  Ox box, systems, heart…

She turned her upper body first, using a whole body movement and the column of her spine to knock his hand aside, in the same way she might backhand a punch.  Her one leg went sideways, the other bent, and she dropped low enough it wasn’t convenient to reach anymore.

He kneed her in the side, and she had vivid memories of learning to dance.  Rolling with the mistakes others made, in service to the bigger picture.  Her cousins had battered her.  She’d smacked others.

It had been training.  Just like the Gray-frocked trained, the twenty-nine families worked dance into celebrations and trained people in reaction speed, fighting in confined quarters, even in a vent, or fighting in a mob.

He was better.  She could think of natural movements to string together, and react to put herself out of reach when she was essentially toe to toe with him, but while she was doing that, there were moments she’d leave herself open, and he seized on those moments.  When he hit her, the strikes were quick, hard, and efficient.

People he’d seduced and recruited were watching, inching closer, as if waiting for some opportunity or cue.

He jabbed, and she was able to avoid the movement.  Her hand went up, claws retracting in the moment they were close to her.  Didn’t matter.  She put the back of a hand on his upper arm and pushed.  Moving him forward by just enough to let her step behind him.

His elbow came around from the other direction, and crashed into her temple.

She fell into a wall, found zero traction there with a metal body against metal panels, and collapsed onto floor.

Yeah.  He’d been training all his life to fight.  She’d danced.

She wasn’t surprised.

“I’ve seen videos of that.  You get to where your back is to my back, you have that tail, limbs that bend backward.”

Toby was trying to catalogue the damage and sort things out.

Winnifred reversed the direction of her knees, lengthened her feet, and then pounced.  From zero to one hundred in a moment, lying on the ground to coming at him, like something elastic snapping free of tension.

He blocked, guarding his face, stepping back toward the opposite wall in the corridor.

Tearing his face off wasn’t her goal.  Both of her hands went out, and clapped hard against the wall on either side of his head, stopping herself, her face near his.  Her head boomed with pain from the hit to the temple.

“I don’t want to fight,” she said.

She did.  She was still angry.  But this did more damage than something nanotech could heal.

“Obviously,” Vega grunted.  He reached for the vitals again, and again, she lowered herself, dropping to a near-crouch, so they would be out of reach.  His hand moved instead to her face, fingertips catching on the raised edge, where face mask met neck.  He then tried to bring her around to the side, a whole-body movement, smashing her face into the wall.

She twisted, a bit like a corkscrew, one hand reaching past to the wall, to catch on a seam between panels and push.  Sliding herself between him and the wall.

“You’re driven by fear,” he said.  “I don’t have an issue adding fifteen years to my time.”

He probably didn’t.

But he did have things to worry about.  Getting mostly behind him put her in a good position again, where she could remember different dances, different ways to segue into something else.

The tightly woven dances with zero margin for error gave her this.

Two, three seconds where she was right there and he couldn’t touch her.  He got a jab in, made some more space- a tiny bit more because she felt dizzy from the head hit.  As if every number in her head was busy rounding up or rounding down, messing with distances and timing.  He gave himself room to do more…

He kicked, hard, and she managed to avoid it, raising her own leg, shin deflecting.  It made the claws on her foot retract automatically, for safety’s sake.

Someone approached.  One of the other new recruits.  Ex-hidebound.  With him came others.  Rienne and Magh weren’t fighters, but they were already loyal.

The hallway was only about two paces across, and if she could maneuver around, keeping Vega between herself and the mob-

She batted batting aside some kicks from the furthest range he could make.

-she could time things to lunge in.  Vega couldn’t retreat because someone was in the way.  A dance in tight quarters.

She could bend and move in ways they couldn’t in the tighter spaces.  Her body was skinnier, but had power.  She pushed against the wall with one foot to put her body between the new guy and the wall like a wedge.  Twists of her body and careful use and bending of her limbs meant the new guy couldn’t land a good hit.

Making him crowd Vega.

“Fuck off!” Vega shouted.  He pawed at the guy’s face, and pushed hard enough the guy lost his balance.

There.  Good.

She planted her feet down, and one felt like it had a quarter-step too far to travel.  Her sense of balance jarred hard when she corrected for that.

Her ears were made to handle zero-g.  Nevermind that she’d pulled part of that setup up- she didn’t get dizzy.  It was a brain thing, not an ear thing.

The blow to the head had fucked her up.  She couldn’t keep doing this.

There was only a narrow window left.  The guards weren’t fast.  The rest of the group had stopped advancing with that ‘fuck off!’, and she didn’t trust herself not to get even dizzier and collapse.

So she slid her foot into his foam clog, between foot and sole.  She controlled his foot coming down.  She put her tail on the ground.

The metal of the tail had virtually no traction, compared to the foam shoe.  She put hands around his body, one foot near the other, and dropped, her body weight added to his, both of their feet resting on the tail, which slid sharply left.

The both of them dropped into splits.  The metal of her pelvis crashed to floor, legs more or less straight out to either side.

The meat of his pelvis crashed to floor.  Everything on the lower end of that pelvis that the human body didn’t have the good sense to keep tucked away was sandwiched between his descending body weight and metal flooring.

She rose to her feet immediately after.

He couldn’t.

There were still the others.

How much did humiliation count, in something like this?

Enough, it seemed.  Sinon was the most dangerous one there, and she wasn’t volunteering.

Winnifred backed away a few more steps, and that was the standoff until the guards came.

➨

“You got my meaning,” her lawyer said.

“I thought about how I felt so helpless, there wasn’t a lot I could do, when they came at me from behind.  You seemed to think there was a way to handle it.  I thought of family.  The thoughts connected.”

“You did a good job of being mostly conflict avoidant.  You’ll have some classes to take, hoops to jump through, maybe a few more months added to your sentence, for the violence.”

She nodded.

“The Terrace Walkers have been toeing the line too much for too long, the station lost patience.  It might not be today, or this week, but they’re all getting onboards.  So the station can handle them.”

“Why did the station not listen, when I was running?  It announced me, got me into trouble.”

“We don’t know, but we can infer.  My first thought was about the fish brothers’ hint, that possibly someone on staff who is sympathetic to that group.  Didn’t like you.  But it’s more reasonable to think it’s because you’re labeled a troublemaker.  Saboteur, subversive.  I’d need to see prison records.  I’ll file to do that right now, actually… thank you, onboard.  Might take a while.”

Winnifred’s eyes focused on the table.  Brushed steel, with lots of tiny scratch marks from cuffs, trays, and clipboards.

Her lawyer explained, “The prison is going over everything you’ve been looking at, to cover their asses.  The group is getting the onboards, you’ll be moved to your next cell block where there are no Terrace Walkers, concessions I asked for will be put into place.  You get Toby.”

Winnifred sat up.

“Be good, they will be greedy for any chance to take that privilege away.  I’ll also say the Twenty-Nine Families are pleased you scored a win against people that hate us.”

She nodded.

“That’s the good news.  The bad?”

She’d been braced for this.

“The family is disappointed you renounced them, and that you spent any breath at all on the ‘baby butchering’ propaganda.”

What she’d said around Siss.

“Does it matter if it was in service of getting more information on our enemies?”

“Does it matter if I think you’re bullshitting again?”

“I’m not.  Or only a little,” she conceded.

“You can’t walk back that you said that, or that people in earshot heard it.  Some have left this cell block since.  From discussions I’ve had with others, they like the thrust of what you’re doing, but not the manner.  If everyone acted like you are, we wouldn’t have twenty-nine families.  We wouldn’t have one.”

“So… what now?” Winnifred asked.

“I work for the twenty-nine families.  You renounced the family back there.  I won’t be seeing your case through.  I’ve already put in to be moved from the case.  You can hire somebody else or get volunteer defense, when you do, they can request my files and notes.  I was confident I could get you two years, but I don’t think any lawyer you’ll get outside of the families will know the ins and outs of this particular niche.  Get your lawyer to try for six, at least, if it’s not going that direction, get someone better.  Treat four to five years as good.”

“This is punishment from the family, then?” Winnifred asked.  “Because I wasn’t vocally loyal every step of the way.”

“Punishment from you, technically.  It follows from your choices.”

Winnifred frowned at him.

“At the end of it, if you want to reach out…”

“I don’t think I will,” Winnifred said, quiet.

“Okay.  We will always be here with open arms, waiting.  But we don’t exist at your convenience, to be put aside when you want to do your own thing.”

She nodded. “The information I got on the Gray-frocked.  You call them Terrace Walkers.  I don’t know the distinction.”

“It’s what they were called on Akna, where I grew up.”

“Right.  Is that going anywhere?  What happens?”

“People will review it.  We’ll see.  Talk to your new lawyer about that, if it’s a priority.”

“It really feels like I was the only person in a position to hear what they were saying, and what they were saying is important,” Winnifred said.  “I was willing to sacrifice, for that.”

“Mm.”

Winnifred thought about A, and the science center, the music that had come out of it.  The pain in that music.

“I could see myself coming back to the family if it helped get this information out there.  Because it might save lives.”

Her lawyer switched to the subsonic language.  He didn’t have overt mods, but he had enough in his throat to say it, and in his ears to hear it.  “When we created our language, we made a language of whispers.  One for us, that the outside world doesn’t hear.  We’re hated, people don’t trust us. Sabotage both overt and questionable, like the panels not listening to you, are common at all levels.  We don’t have a voice, Winnifred.”

She nodded.

He’d showed up in person to say goodbye and fire her as a client.  The first time she’d seen him, as a matter of fact.  He gathered his equipment and papers into a messenger bag.

He was nearly done when he paused.  “Something bugged me.”

“Hm?” Winnifred made an inquisitive sound.

“While I was waiting, another lawyer reached out to me.  He’s working with the Terrace Walkers.  Gray-frocked.  He’s young, he’s new, and in his mind, there are similarities between the Gray-frocked and us, so he wanted advice.  Which is insulting and inaccurate, but I held my tongue.”

“Makes sense,” Winnifred said, because not saying anything would’ve come across as more insulting and she didn’t trust him to hold his tongue.

“You mentioned before, that Dane, one of the Gray-frocked, reacted badly.”

“Yeah.  He had a phobia.”

“Right.  The lawyer said, and you’re not to repeat this, he said he was rejected as their lawyer, and that was why he wanted advice.  Was there a way to get ‘in’, or win them over?  I replied, I married two, I have one at home, learning his first words.”

Winnifred nodded.

“Ignoring the rest of that awkward conversation… he said they weren’t upset.  That they didn’t care.  Crushed testicles aside.”

He arched an eyebrow at that.  Winnifred shrugged a bit.

He went on, “…Which led to us mutually concluding… maybe they don’t care because they’re breaking out.”

“Yeah.”

“Except they aren’t paying attention to environment, or timing of things.  So is it that?  Or is it an escape that doesn’t care about timing?   It’s a bit like when you get hair in your teeth, but in the brain, instead.  Why?”

He gave her a long look, as if hoping she’d have that answer.

“I don’t know,” Winnifred admitted.

“If you do figure it out, tell me in, I guess, four to seven years, depending on when you get out?  Answer a niggling question and I’ll make it up to you somehow.  Even if you aren’t a client.”

It was a weird exchange, given the tone of their earlier conversation, but he’d offered this freely.

She nodded.  “Okay.  I will.”

“Until then, then.”

“Yeah.”

The door closed after him, then immediately opened again.  A prisoner on staff motioned, and Winnifred got up, to go to her new cell block.

➨

At some indeterminate hour of the morning, in her new cell block, Winnifred curled up on her bed, being careful to not shred the sheets, because she’d pulled off panels to bend them back into shape, then collapsed from fatigue before getting around to putting them back on again.

The thoughts she had been mulling over connected.

Carefully, she raised herself to an upright position.

She knew, now.

3.9.O – MUTE

Orion

Orion bent over the block of metal.  It was one of the squared ‘teeth’ that intermeshed when two doors closed, lasered off, and cut in half lengthwise.  Now he etched the interior with his laser on its finest setting.  He used his left hand, because his arm still had the cut Spur had given him before running off.

“I’m not good at using this,” Blackbox said.  He’d used a metal fingertip to smudge some of the green stuff Orion had burned to draw out what looked like a string of beads lined along two walls.  “I want this, but spiraling along the inside of the casing.”

Orion took a minute to etch Blackbox’s design into metal floor, elaborated on it, then when that was wrong, took a different stab at it.

“The goal is we have the bullet-”  Blackbox traced the outer housing.

“Right,” Orion murmured.

“Core of the bullet is a nitrocellulose thread.  It ignites as part of the gun firing.  Rocket fuel inside the bullet ignites, but only place it can go is past the gallium.  We want to buy time for it to leave the chamber before the ignited fuel is free to blast out the back end of the bullet.”

“Gallium.”

“Or some other metal with a low melting point, the melting point would mean different configuration of beads.  I don’t know what to tell you, Orion.  I’ve got the knowledge in my head.  It’s what they gave me.  Ballistics.  But…”

Orion let out a long, slow breath through his nose.

Blackbox’s voice was low as he explained, “When I asked earlier about how fine you could get things, I thought about a laser-cut microstructure.  It would do the same thing.  Hardened steel cut thin enough to come apart at the time we want.”

“Mmmm.  Takes a while.”

Court was off to the side, taking his shift to sleep.  Orion had just had his, giving Blackbox time to sketch out what he wanted.  Then they’d gotten to work.

They needed weapons that worked against the enemies they were fighting.

This wasn’t it.  This was a higher velocity bullet with a tiny payload.  But if they could make this work, then it meant they could and should keep their eye open for other things, for something that might be more effective.

It still felt like striving for an upgrade from sticks and stones to brass, when their enemy was capable of aerial warfare.

It wasn’t exactly that.  If anything, he was underselling the gap.

Orion’s eye fell on the blackened green slime.

He picked up a tube that had the same diameter as the barrel of Blackbox’s gun.  Standing it upright, he used one hand to scoop up some of the char.  When that wasn’t enough, he burned more.

Using a rod, he tamped it down.

“Carbon plug,” Blackbox said.

“Will it work?  Instead of the gallium?  Delay the rocket jet until the bullet is free of the barrel?”

“Pass it my way.  It needs to be way more dense.  We also need to allow for ignition, so…”

“Metal coin,” Orion murmured.  “Hole in the middle, so the thread can ignite.”

“I was thinking, do we want smoke?  To obscure our own view of these things?”

“It makes it worse,” Court said.  He was lying down at the other end of the room, a bag propped up under his head.

“You’re up.”

“Wasn’t really sleeping.  Who could?”

Orion nodded.  The deaths of the others were vivid in his mind.

“Smoke makes things worse,” Court said.  He sat up, groaning softly.  “When you half-see things, your mind wants to process it, get an answer.  I’d rather disrupt their communications.”

“How?”
