“Can’t do a lot about sound, if they’re making subsonic noises or something.  But I think it’s more than that.  Some communication with a wider network.”

“Do you have equipment?” Orion asked.

“I didn’t take everything when I was getting out of that pod.  I thought it was more important to get to safety.  I don’t have much.”

“Can you build it?” Orion asked.

“Maybe.  Yeah.”

“If you can tell us what you’re looking for, more eyes is good.”

Court nodded.

He’s holding something back.

Orion’s hands were caked in the carbon ash, which had a greasy quality to it, and settled into the creases, folds, and tiny scratches, highlighting them in black.  There was something about being dirty, knowing there wasn’t anything like a shower or bath nearby, there might never be a shower or bath, and even water was in limited quantity, so he couldn’t wipe it off.  It got to him.

Does this feeling mean something about who I was before?  Was I more elite than laborer?

He didn’t like that idea, somehow, which led him down another line of thought about whether he should read into that, and tie it together with his feelings about wanting to hurt the people who’d sent them all here.

They laid out the components for the bullets that would have to be encased within the mold.  He scanned the laser-etched imprint of the bullet, then had his laser etch out a row of similar ones into the inside of the block and its sister block.

Laser-heated metal from the panel scrap flowed inside.  It would take minutes to cool.  He worked on cutting out the coins from the material of the panel cover, giving each a bit of a tab.

“Have you considered a replacement arm?” Court asked Blackbox.  Blackbox was doing everything he was doing with just the one arm.

“It’s not the arm that’s the problem,” Blackbox said.  He tapped his head.  “It’s this.”

“Right.”

“They got to me.”

“I wonder what the rules are for that.  What if we gave you a right arm, in that socket?”

“With food?  It’s anything I let myself think of as food,” Blackbox said.  His mood had visibly darkened.  “It might be whatever I think of as a left arm.”

“Can we try things?” Court asked.

“Maybe.  If we do, won’t be this stop,” Blackbox replied.  “We’re a little too exposed, and I don’t want to stop so long that that fox can catch up with us.  Pack up, do what you gotta do, we’ll move on soon.”

“Want to finish these?” Orion asked, indicating the brick.

Blackbox nodded, eyes on the mold.

Orion gathered his things while they worked, leaving the mold aside.  In the heat of the lasers, he’d removed the upper portion of his coveralls, and he’d pulled his shirt off.  He wished he could wash it.

That done, he cracked open the mold.

One bullet was unfinished, the melted liquid having started to solidify before reaching the end.  He’d have to mind that in the future.  There was some metal flashing to remove with a pass of the laser along the outside, one brief zap with the laser in each bullet to help produce the clip that would hold the ‘coin’ in place.  Then it was assembled.  Thread inserted, fuel load placed within, then sealed within by the combination of carbon plug and the coin that formed a cap.

Blackbox examined the first bullet, while Orion assembled the rest.

“I want to test fire it, but I don’t want to alert any of those machines that might hear it,” Blackbox said.

“Does your implanted knowledge tell you it works?”

“It should, unless there’s something I don’t know about carbon plug, or the metal in the panels.”

“Then save it,” Orion said.  “If it works, you have five more shots with your gun than you did ten hours ago.”

“We have manufacturing,” Blackbox said.  He looked over at Court, who had packed up.

Court, skinny, with a haunted look in his eyes exaggerated by the darkness on his lower lids and the lines of stress, looked nervous.

“What are you thinking?” Orion asked.

“That I’m useless.”

“You’re another set of eyes.”

“Without any useful skills.”

“If there’s something we can do or set up so you’re not useless, let us know.  Don’t hold anything back.”

“I have a lot of half ideas.”

“Half ideas?” Blackbox asked.  It sounded like he was angry at that, but he had a bit of a brusque tone, usually.

“I could figure out what might be useful if I could build a- let’s call it a bounce scanner.  I want to see how they think, how they get information.”

“You don’t think that’s dangerous?” Blackbox asked.  “What if they send you a little message along with that?”

“…Maybe just for the littlest machines.  Ones with a single purpose.”

“You’re willing to gamble your brain on that?  Knowing if you gamble wrong, you might get something in your brain that makes you want to manually snap your own spine in half.”

Orion didn’t need a reminder about that visual.

“We’re all gambling, every time we move, or fight,” Court said.  “I’m no good in a fight.  I’ll fight in another way, on another battlefield, I guess.”

“Mm,” Blackbox grunted.  He didn’t elaborate, instead climbing to his feet.

Orion made sure he had everything from the kit, swept the metal flashing aside, and stood.  The flashing would be the last trace that they had been there, aside from the corner they’d used to go to the bathroom.

Nothing he could do about that second one.

Blackbox took point without asking, checking the coast was clear, before leading them to the next gate.  Part of the reason they had settled here was because it was between two gates, and those gates were closed, meaning they’d have some warning if one opened to let something in.  Between the doors was a short hallway, with a lot of nooks, crannies, and offshoots from the main corridor where equipment was stored.

Their guess was that this little hallway was a kind of pit stop.  Machines could trundle in, and depending on that machine’s specific setup and needs, one of the nooks or offshoot spaces would be accessed for spare parts, refueling, repair, and a quick spray-down.

They hadn’t wanted to tamper much with that equipment, because that seemed like something that might draw an armed response, but they had spent some time trying to get access to a water line.  They knew there was one, but there weren’t any convenient cranks, handles, or panels to turn anything on.

Maybe for the best.  There was that underlying risk that if they did manage to access it, the spray would have enough pressure and force to part flesh from bone as if it had never belonged there in the first place.

His second thought had been that it would have been nice to sabotage a station like this.

They all had enough accumulated knowledge at this point to access the panel, but they let Court do it.

“Masks on,” Orion said.  “If this is a pit stop and cleaning station, the next area might be the sort a machine wants regular cleaning from.

“You thinking haz?” Blackbox asked.

Orion shrugged.  He fixed his mask over his lower face, then pulled on the upper portion of his coveralls, and did it up.

Court managed to access the door’s mechanism, and the door hissed.  Court hurried to fix the mask he hadn’t been able to put on with his hands full of the terminal code.

The door was thirty meters tall and twenty meters across, with interlocking metal teeth, minus one tooth that they’d lasered.  It was thick enough that with one portion of the door cut out, Orion could put his whole arm in through the hole and wave it around without touching anything internal.

As it opened, the air pressure changed.  Wind rushed, and pulled them toward the gap.

“Vacuum,” Court said, with alarm, voice faintly muffled by his mask in the first syllable, corrected in the second as their onboards all connected to transmit audio between them.

“Not a full one,” Blackbox said.  Of the three of them, he was least affected.  He didn’t need a mask, because most of his body was machine.  Only the brain in some reinforced container in his skull wasn’t.  “Orion?  Sorry.”

“I’m on point.”

Orion would be the one to look.

Most of the station that they’d observed was mostly empty.  The most activity they’d seen had been the procession line of the massive cleaning and repair boxes.  There was activity here.

“Onboard,” Orion ordered, “change settings.  Visual mask.”

Orion’s onboard made the adjustment.  He viewed everything as outlines, material and depth markers.

“Can’t trust that entirely,” Blackbox said.

“It’ll make me feel better, at least.”

“Mmm.”

“Onboard?  Same,” Court said, quiet.

They’d discussed it while Blackbox took his short nap, setting up their individual onboards.  They had pre-set visual modifiers already, with Orion’s focusing on what he needed for welding and repair.  Court could track and trace wires.  The trick was removing all of the things that the onboard wanted to transmit to them or thought was important.

He was still careful about how he took it all in.  Squinting, using his hand to block one eye, moving it by tiny increments to reveal a wider sliver.

“Not seeing much, but be careful.”

The others looked.

“This is the kind of thing we wanted to see more of,” Blackbox murmured.

The scene before them here was a room so large it bent Orion’s brain to look at it.  A planet was suspended in the center of it, and was far enough into the center that he could see from far east to far west, far south to north.  Cables extended out from it to the planet’s surface, and hundreds of millions of machines moved up and down those cables, sometimes simultaneously on the same cable.

The element of perspective in something that massive occupying a space over their heads, the cables nearest them tapering off into seemingly nothing on their way to the planet, and all of the supporting systems made Orion’s stomach do a flip.  Or maybe there was an element of gravity to it too.  A planet that big, that dense, when this portion of the structure wasn’t.

Machines, gleaming white and steel, on their way in, coming back dirty, carrying their loads of materials processed down on the planet.  All left down some faraway point.

A planet, housed in the middle here, with their best view yet of how thick the superstructure was, and the number of layers to it.  On the side of things facing the sun, a massive door that opened like the shutter on Orion’s laser, if he set it to ‘burst’, which he didn’t often do.  Like a camera’s shutter.  On the other end, a door.

There was wind here, not just ventilation.  The line between where the ring started and the planet’s atmosphere ended was a blurry one, and the temperature differentials between the sun-baked shutter door and the colder back door might have driven some of it.  Orion’s hair was too greasy to properly blow in the wind.

None of the machines took notice of Orion, Blackbox, or Court as they ventured out.

“Something we can learn, maybe?” Orion asked.  “Weak point.  Something about the design of it all?”

“Maybe.  It’s got to be better than endless gray hallways.  But it’s more dangerous too.  Let’s be careful.”

“Yeah,” Orion agreed.  He drew his laser from where it dangled at his hip.

“You two are going to be on limited oxygen.  Let’s be smart about this,” Blackbox said.

Orion nodded.

The pathways between the anchor points of the cable on the ring layer were broad, flat roads, not dissimilar to the ones that they’d been on when the moths had attacked in coordination with the Fox.

“What if they’re fucking with us?” Orion asked, eyeing the machines.  They continued doing what they were doing, handing off tanks of fluid and containers of cargo.  “We get too far in to do anything and then they all come after us?”

Nobody answered his question.  Maybe because there wasn’t an answer.  The three of them moved left and right to avoid the slow moving legs of a heavier robot, otherwise keeping to the edge of the concourse- that raised road over jutting machinery and industry that supported this planet-mining operation.

The further in they got, the more he could see the flow of it all.  Fluids going one way, materials going another.  Machines loaded up with a pre-set configuration that they then took to a door far off in the distance, similar to the one they’d come in.  Presumably that was in support of some new expansion.

“Glyph,” Blackbox said, quiet.

Orion closed his eyes.  He couldn’t chance it.

While he was blind, the thudding footsteps of machines was doubly intimidating.  The low atmosphere muffled the sound, which made it harder to place, and the raised concourse vibrated and bobbed faintly out of sync with the movement of the heaviest machines atop it.

The lights against his eyelids made it clear there was a glyph.  Maybe a lot of glyph.  He could hear a buzzing in the air.

“Cover your ears.  Onboard, deafen me until that buzzing stops.”

He waited.  There was no good way to see if the others had taken his recommendation.

What felt like five or six minutes in, a notification popped up.

Add another user to user level access?

With the notification was a backdrop of code, contained in a broad, three-dimensional sprawl of arrows and boxes.

“No,” Orion whispered.

The notification dropped away.

It popped back up again.

Add another user to user level access?

“No.”

He pressed his hands firmer against his ears.  Then it evolved.

Admin access impossible.
Add another user to user level access instead?

That, at least, seemed to be where it stopped.  He made sure to say ‘no’ each time.

When it stopped, it was his worry that it had stopped because it had succeeded.

He moved hands from ears.  He reached for Blackbox’s shoulder, and Blackbox’s hand, presumably, jammed Orion right in the fingers.

“Fuck,” Orion whispered.

“Sorry.”

“Almost broke my fingers, fuck.”

“Whose turn is it?” Blackbox asked

“Me,” Court whispered.

With the relative quiet they’d endured, Court’s sudden scream was loud, almost right in Orion’s ear, and emotional.

He forced himself to keep his eyes closed, and fought, reaching, with fingers still throbbing, to hold Court back.  Court’s following screams were muted.

They waited until things relaxed.

“Talk to us, man,” Blackbox muttered.  “Come on.  Or if you can, if you need it, tap three times, I’ll cut your throat.  Spare you whatever’s going on.”

“Don’t- don’t do that,” Court said.  “There’s deer.”

“And your bright idea was to scream and let them know we’re here?” Blackbox growled, whispering.

“He saw a glyph,” Orion concluded.

“It’s pretty fucking obvious what it is.  No hours of waiting and worrying about just how they broke me.  Red burns.”

“What?”

“The color red, it- fucking burns to look at.  Bad as any pain I’ve ever felt.”

Orion nodded.

Blackbox said, “At least it’s not green, or that green shit-”

“Fuck off,” Court said, terse.

“Yeah,” Blackbox replied, his tone making it sound almost apologetic, or like a concession.

Blackbox did understand.

“I’ll have to keep this wire-sensing setting they gave me on, I’m not risking feeling that again,” Court said.

“Why the fuck did you turn it off?” Blackbox asked.

“Because I couldn’t tell what I was looking at.  Because we need more information and it leaves me mostly blind,” Court replied, whispering.  He sounded testy.  Shorter tempered than before.  “I’m going to be blind, from here on out, unless the two of you can promise me there’s nothing red nearby.”

“Orion’s hair doesn’t count?”

“No.  Or our tattoos.  Thank fuck.”

They moved to safety, playing it safe for a few more minutes.

It wasn’t high security, exactly.  The deer weren’t trying to patrol.  But they were out there.  The glyphs flicked on and off at random.

“The thing that gets me,” Court said, he still hadn’t fully caught his breath from the intense screaming minutes ago.  Or the emotions, maybe.  “…Is that none of this makes sense.”

“Let’s hear it,” Orion replied, his eyes tracking the movements of machines.  Seeing Blackbox look up was a good reminder to watch things from all directions.  Especially after the moth attack.

“The big one… that planet’s over our heads.  I think it’s subtly out of line with the ring’s orbit.  Which got me wondering why we’re in this orbit?  If they want to exterminate humans, build something big… why not build way closer to the sun?  Turn heat and solar energy into power?” Court asked.  “The machines seem dead set on holding things at this distance from the sun.”

“Hmm.”

“Then I answered my own question.  Technology doesn’t like heat.  Add in possible bad solar flares as a theoretical extinction-level event for the machines, signal disruption… but why not go for a middle ground, or go cooler?  We’re very lucky there’s any atmosphere at all, and survivable temperature.  They could make things way harder for us if they made a slight adjustment.”

Orion nodded.

“They’re building on what was around before,” Blackbox said.  “Orion and I found an old patch the machines haven’t paved over.  A big one.  There have been other relics and patches.  You’ve seen a couple small ones.”

“Sure,” Court said.  “I don’t think that really answers what’s nagging at me.”

There was an ear-splitting squeal as a series of massive machines, one hundred and ninety meters wide, rocketed past them, traveling along a cable with a companion engine to help.  Orion’s sense of perspective swayed as he saw them disappear.

“Why haven’t they expanded more?” Court asked.  “If they can hold a planet at that distance from the sun, why not build more inward, in that direction?”

“Because finishing the ring is a goal, and building inward or outward is a waste of resources?” Orion asked.

“That’s… annoyingly better than any answer I’ve come up with.  It doesn’t really understand the bigger why,” Court said.

“I’ve wondered if they’re protecting something,” Blackbox said.  He amended his statement, “Someone.  Or many someones.”

The machines at this end of the concourse were moving slowly enough they could avoid the legs.  They still hurried, getting past the legs and moving to the concourse’s edge, where it was clearer.

“Many someones,” Orion tried the idea on by saying it out loud.  “The people who sent us?  Or-”

“-Or I’m thinking more-” Blackbox said, almost at the same time.

“-opposition.  They’re hunkered down somewhere, with all of this as a layer between them and the people who sent us here.”

“Maybe,” Blackbox said.  “Except they’re not attacking.  Only defending.  Only building.”

“Not expanding, not attacking,” Court said.  He ducked his head out to check the coast was clear.  They kept walking, while there weren’t any machines on the broad roadway.

“Who knows, right?” Blackbox asked.  “The way I think of it?  They’ve got pods like we had, but they’re home grown, on this end of things.  People get put to sleep and held in stasis.  In the meantime, they tell the machines to finish building this ring structure as a big halo around the sun, make sure nobody and nothing comes in to tamper, and later on, make some adjustment, so the structure’s more livable, nicer to be in, and then wake everyone up.”

“Why do it this way?  Why make it unlivable, but only barely, why these machines, with these glyphs?” Orion asked.

“Paranoia?  You don’t want to put yourselves to sleep for thousands of years, wake up, and find aliens have come to visit, that they circumvented your security, and now they’re in charge.  Same as you don’t want to wake up and find survivors took over this landscape you invested in building, with their government, their culture, their everything.  So you set guards that adapt.”

“And the fact there’s atmosphere, temperature… safety?” Orion asked.  “In case something goes wrong, leaving a window for their own people to emerge from stasis and fix the problem?”

“Maybe.”

“And the people who sent us, they’d be some rogue faction?  Or something that broke away?  Maybe literally?  They have their own stasis pods?” Orion mused.

“Maybe?  Who the fuck knows?” Blackbox asked.  Angry now, for some reason.

Orion shut up.

“I’ve wondered if it’s not some fucked up game,” Court said.  “Maybe humanity got so damn big that they can build something like this as… a gladiatorial arena.  A fucked up blood sport as entertainment for the masses.  Actual adventure.”

“I don’t want to think humanity’s that bloodthirsty,” Orion murmured.

They’d huddled between two containers, and with freedom to look around and look at each other, Blackbox looked at Orion, almost accusatory.

It had been left unsaid: they did want blood.

“-or shallow,” Orion added.  “Doing it for the sake of doing it feels stupid.”

As they got some loose instinct for the movement of the deer and where those were, and the time window after any glyph-sweeping of the space, they could glance around more.  Orion tried to get a sense of it all.

Where things came from was only one part of the story.  A lot of it was processed on the planet.  It was brought here, with the cables being one means of getting from A to B.  On the planet’s surface, the landscape was visibly changing over time.

They’d be done with eating this planet in less than a day.

Waste was being stockpiled by the back door.  It got stacked at places here, then moved, constantly and steadily in that direction.  Orion’s eyes couldn’t see far enough, but there was an ocean that his tech tried to parse as geometric.  Too even, with no waves, barely any movement that wasn’t maybe whole roving bands of machines passing over it.  He could fully believe it was an arrangement of containers of waste.  Maybe millions lined up, stacked atop or alongside millions more.

A solid share of that waste was debris and dust that blew off of the machines and onto the concourse.  Shards of rock no bigger than Orion’s fist.  But there were larger chunks too.  Here and there, larger chunks were cut to pieces, forming slabs.  The remainder was put into containers, moved aside.  The containers all seemed to flow away from the shutter door and toward that back door.

The same went for the machines that came back from the surface and, damaged by some collision with another machine, maybe, or by a shifting of terrain, they were apparently too inefficient to fix, instead of just scrapping them for parts and making a new one.  Smaller machines ate them alive.  Damaged outer plating, shells, treads, and legs were put with the debris.

Nothing looked form-cut or designed to be sent off to some human settlement in the middle of all of this.

As Orion made mental notes, he could count out whole tracts of the wider apparatus.  By process of elimination, running down the center of it all, from that big shutter window to the rear window, was another line of processing.

“We should be careful,” Orion said.  “Because I think when they’re done with that planet, they’re going to get rid of it.  Along with all of that trash.”

Court leaned past and into Orion to get a better look.  He nodded.

“Could be a massive vacuum.  Could be something else.  Mechanical… retract all the roads, send machines into their cubbies.  We’d get squished or dropped, maybe.  Not to mention… if they brought a planet here in the first place, and they’re processing it that fast… what happens if we’re in here when they bring another planet through?”

“So let’s find out what we can, see if we can scavenge anything while we’ve got this nice spread of planet-eating tech, machinery, all that,” Blackbox said.  “And then we scram.”

“Scramming sounds good,” Court agreed.

“I want to go there,” Orion said, and he pointed at a section of the concourse, not too far away from a set stacked containers waiting to be moved.  There was some industrial equipment jutting out from the ‘wall’ intersecting it, and it made for an outcropping of what might’ve been terminals, or something else, at the edge of that part of the concourse.

“Elevator,” Court said.  “We could move down, if we didn’t want to stay by the surface after all.

‘Surface’ was such a bad term for it.  They were sticking close to the sunny side of the superstructure.  Here, closer to the shutter that opened well above their heads, above and past that planet.

Orion’s stomach flip flopped as he tried to process it all.  There was too much hanging over his head that was, in essence, their sky.  Too much emptiness below.

They waited out three cycles- he wasn’t sure at the exact configuration, but virtually every panel lit up with glyphs, and they might’ve been projected around the planet in large form, or against the surface.

Less like a security measure, more like a sterilization procedure.

Then they moved quickly.  There wasn’t a lot of machine activity across this one bridge that led to that outcropping of tech.  When machines did come, they were odd ones.  The worst part of it was how exposed they felt.

“Would it work to get a hollow shell of a machine body and use that to run or drive around in?” Court asked.

“Funny thought,” Blackbox said.

“It’s an idea.”

Orion remained silent.  Blackbox had been testy, and Orion was starting to worry that there was a clear split in mindsets, where the people that were relatively new to all of this had ideas.  Blackbox, having been down that road, having seen casualties, was less inclined to go along with it.

The terminals here weren’t meant for humans, and there was only one screen, which had a white glow that they guessed was a glyph- they approached it from the side and threw a piece of cloth they’d scavenged earlier over it to mask it.  The rest of it was ports.

“Could you hack it?  If it’s communications?” Orion asked Court.

“If I had the stuff.  I’d need a jack as big around as my arm, with a computer to plug it into.”

“If there’s anything like that around here, I’d bet it’s here,” Orion observed, looking at all the machinery, processing, and stored goods.

He felt around the panel, looking for something that he could maybe cut away.  “If we could access some of the internals, maybe there’s something you could do?”

“I doubt it,” Court said.

Blackbox, standing watch, so to speak, visibly bristled.  Orion didn’t disagree.

Still feeling around, Orion said, “Court.  I’m not going to kick up a fuss here.  But we are on the same side.”

“What are you saying?” the man asked.  It was hard not to mentally process him as a kid, being as skinny as he was, with the attitude he had.

“I’m saying… if you’re keeping secrets or if there’s something you’re holding back, if you’re not actually all about communications after all-”

“I am.”

The reply came fast, firm.  It came fast and firm to the second part of what Orion had said.  Not the part about secrets and holding things back.

Court filled the silence that had followed his statement, saying, “I’m communications.  I just… don’t have my equipment.  And I’m not sure it would be that useful anyway.”

Orion checked other parts of the device.

His hands didn’t find what he was looking for, but the fact his vision was set to measure depth did.  Fuzz, inside a panel.

That fuzz was a wild variation of depth on the inside of one panel, which took him a minute to figure out how to remove.

Don’t
Takes two hours
Canceled at last second
You fuck us more than you fuck them

The statement was followed by a signature that wasn’t a name, but three pentagons, joined by dashes, all in a line.

“I want to check the others,” Orion said, while the others read the statement that had been scratched into the inside of the metal panel  “There’s more to this.”

“Hey, not complaining,” Blackbox said.  “It’s a direction.”

Orion nodded.

They rode the large, open elevator down, hidden amid the cubic storage containers, with the eerie company of a number of worker machines.  They were machines that didn’t care that they were there, but as they plunged downward, Orion was very aware that the twelve meter by twelve meter platform, anchored only on one side by the elevator mechanism, was an awful, awful place to try to fight.  No railings, no place to jump to or go, when they were moving this fast, barely any cover, barely any resources.

They got off at the next layer of concourses that had another outcropping like the one above.  Different from before.

Sure enough, a message and more of the pentagons marked the inside of a panel.

Do not tamper
Others have had same idea
Machines elsewhere in the ring
have oversight + will cancel last second
Will investigate

Orion checked the area thoroughly, and aside from one crease in the walls that the machines hadn’t thoroughly cleaned that had the waste of a food package and human excrement overgrown with green slime, there was nothing.

“You know what got me about the last message?” Orion asked.

“Is there a world where I don’t say, ‘tell me’?” Blackbox asked.

“Maybe we’re thinking about the same thing, and everyone gets to feel clever because they figured it out.”

“Maybe I’m tired,” Blackbox said.  “On edge all the time.”

Orion took that in, glancing at Court, who was silent, and who hadn’t opened his eyes or uncovered his ears since the last sterilization-style sweeping of glyphs, maybe resting.  Orion admitted, “I’m tired of being grungy.  Tired of being tired, yeah.”

“Yeah.  What was the thing?”

“It was tidier.  Let’s see the next one, because if it’s the way I think it is, I think I know where the pentagon group is.”

They descended, waited for machines to get off, and for a few brief seconds, had that nervous dance around the machines that trundled in to pick up the storage containers that had been placed on the elevator to go down.  It put them between large machines that steered in at awkward angles, reorienting themselves in a herky-jerky way, and the railing-less edge of the elevator.

Orion found the next panel.

Do not tamper
Three attempts, all 2hr startup times
Canceled by external authority
Machines sweep in to check after
You risk them finding us.

“As we go further down, the language gets more specific,” Orion said.  “Or, to be clear about it… I think they started at the bottom, and they left a note at each of these terminals, thinking that someone might get the bright idea to hack one… knowing the result isn’t good or useful.”

Court, now awake, nodded.  Blackbox had his hand on his gun, his expression stern.

“I think someone took it on themselves to leave that message.  Maybe over the course of a day.  But their hand got tired, their patience got low.  The messages get shorter, more informal.”

“So you think they’re close to the bottom?”

“I think I know exactly where they are,” Orion said, before pointing.

They took a faster track there, because they’d already taken time, the elevators took a bit to wait for, and the glyphs and movements of distant deer were slowing them down- sometimes they waited out one, then immediately had to wait out the other, and then their safe time window had passed, and they had to wait out the first again.

So they skipped a few panels before checking again.

Very similar message to the last.

The ring had a structure very similar to a planet, and they were passing around the middle of it, to the far side.  It meant detours, because no elevators passed through the direct center.  Orion was left with a feeling that humans just… weren’t meant to do this.  Life that had started on the surface of a planet wasn’t meant to move through its bowels and come out the other side.  Metal creaked differently, gravity had a different grip on them, and then what had been down became up. 

The planet that was held in suspension so the machines could eat it was below them now.

They descended to the lowest -or highest, depending on orientation- level possible.  The back door.  Things were faintly colder here, and storage containers took up most of it.

Blackbox bumped his arm-less shoulder socket into Orion, while nudging Court with one elbow.  A jerk of his head drew their eyes upward.

Against the dark gray of that vast door, there was a dark dot moving.

“Drone,” Orion realized aloud.

“Same sort as Spur’s.  But different weapon configuration.”

“I think I’m right.  They’re here.”

“We’re not scramming, then,” Blackbox noted.

“Be ready to scram, be ready for trouble, but… no.”

Here, it was a sea of stacked containers, and the massive door that opened out to the atmosphere, kept closed for some reason.

They waited, with Blackbox standing guard a distance away while Court and Orion ate, because he still had that mental glitch that would make him gorge himself.  They relieved themselves, then went to refill themselves with dripping water from a massive hose attachment port in the wall.  It periodically leaked out their bodyweight in a drabbling of water, then stopped, and it was cold, heavy enough to knock them off their feet, and forceful enough that the containers they tried to fill were half-emptied by the force of it.

Still.

Orion dared to look down at that distant planet below them.

Visibly changed, in color and shape.  His depth finding vision tried and failed to find a depth for the planet.  Not really what it was meant for.

So they hunkered down to wait.  More ‘rest’, that had that lingering tension to it.  The knowledge that they were closing their eyes and trying to rest mind and body, with the very real possibility that they’d wake up to emergency, or to crisis.  They could wake up to an attack.

➨

Or they could wake to the world collapsing in around them.

The massive doors above them opened, at the same time the concourses began to retract, and the sum total of all of that movement was a skull-shattering level of noise, even in the reduced atmosphere of this planet-eating area.

His onboard adjusted, canceling out the noise as best as it could.

“-ove!” Blackbox bellowed.  He grabbed Court by one armpit.

What’s the timing for the glyphs? Orion wondered.

But it didn’t matter.  Machines were moving into position, some of the supporting architecture was adjusting, and it was dangerous to be near the storage containers.

The bridge was retracting, but below the bridge were more storage containers that they could run along.  They were able to cover enough ground to get to the other half of the bridge, climb up, and put themselves against a vertical surface.  not the wall, because the space was so broad there wasn’t such a thing, but the housing around some of the machinery connected to the door’s opening process.

The sky effectively opened above them, a shift in temperature at that level made residual moisture in the air change into a circular cloud at the atmosphere’s apex, and that cloud swiftly parted, turning into a ring around the door, as systems below it started to vent atmosphere upward.

Orion wedged himself between the casing and the segment that secured it to the concourse, because the wind was picking up.

A machine collided with the platform, secured the waste containers into a three-by-three grid, and then fired something or rammed them with something to forcefully eject the contents.

With that firing process, a pair of warnings appeared at the corners of Orion’s field of vision- red lines that pointed back to his ears.  They were labeled ‘hearing damage’, even with his onboard and hands covering his ears, and the onboard supplied a progress bar below for the time to fix it.

At the same time, Court reacted, thrashing, lines standing out in his neck from tension, body jerking, with hands clenched into fists.  He nearly fell from where he’d secured himself.  Blackbox caught him.

The onboard could mute the sound to Orion’s perception, but it couldn’t change that it was effectively a shockwave, doing its form of damage.

Blackbox said something, but Orion couldn’t hear.  His onboard couldn’t hear either, because it didn’t translate or transmit it.

He could follow Blackbox’s eyes, though.

Past the door, outside of the ring, cabling had been used to connect the largest pieces of debris.  Machine housing had been put together, and some of the machines were large enough that one piece of housing could be a large room.  Here and there, rooms had been joined together into clusters.  Elsewhere, they were standalone.  When damaged, they were sometimes fixed to larger rocks.

Three pentagons joined together by dashes.  Asteroids joined together by cables.

There was an alternative to it all.  To not being able to sleep.  It meant going out there.

As the wind died down and the clouds of condensation turned into moisture on every surface around them, Orion pulled his bag around to where he could reach it, and grabbed a piece of scrap metal he’d picked up a day or so ago, using his door-opening tool.  He held it against a platform’s edge, where there wasn’t much light, and lasered it until it started to melt.

Once it was red hot and melted into place, he did the same with another.

His plan was to have three in a line, and heat them up one by one, to have three red glows in the dark that could catch the eye.  He was finishing the second when they came inside.  They sent in one device to plunge through this thin atmosphere, into the storage containers that now waited empty.  A spear-tip that opened into hooks or magnets that caught on something.  The attached, thin cables went taut.  Then people started coming in, with some rocket propulsion to help them manage their descent.

More followed- they came at various angles, with different destinations in mind.

They weren’t close enough to really see the two red dots.  So Orion aimed his laser at nothing, set it to a visible frequency, and fired once, followed by two short bursts, with another shot after.

They noticed that.

They seemed to communicate, and a group changed course.

The person at the head of that group wore something that looked like armor.  He skidded along the cable, detached, on a vague course for another cable, and in mid-air, stuttered, momentum altered, trajectory corrected.  He made the briefest contact with that cable, then let himself fall.

Nearly at the ground, he stuttered again, seeming to freeze in place, then jump forward again, at an angle that didn’t match what he’d been doing before.

The force of his landing didn’t come close to matching his velocity.

Orion knew what it was, in the same way he knew what an onboard was.  It was knowledge that had seemed fundamental before, that hadn’t been wiped out any more than his ability to talk or know clothing was clothing did.

It was a type of mod.  The reason the man looked so heavily armored was that he needed that level of processing power to manage the calculations.  A very small, localized variation on the same technology that brought planets into range.

The skin that was visible on the man was tattooed, glossy black, matching the armor.

Orion put his weapon away and emerged from cover, hands raised.  He was still twenty or thirty seconds out from having his hearing fixed.

The man held up one hand.  His focus was on those who came after him.

He signaled them, one in turn.  They dropped, and he ‘caught’ them in turn, breaking their momentum as they fell.

He caught three before motioning for the others to continue.  They chose landing sites further down the concourse, or down different branches, using the rocket propulsion to slow down enough before dropping onto higher surfaces.

“-punch in the gut,” a man said, as he stood.

Orion’s hearing was back.

“Feels better than falling,” a woman said.  She was with her son- the resemblance was too similar to be anything but.  A boy of thirteen or so.  Tattooed.  And she was armed.

It looked like three groups had met and meshed.

“If you try anything, I’ll kill you,” the man with the driver mods called out.

How long did it take to focus, run the calculations, and get that machine going?  It hadn’t been rapid-fire, when he was letting his friends down.

Could he do more than change trajectory or kill momentum?

“We’re not threats,” Orion said.  “Two of us are brand new, we haven’t been around long enough to get desperate.”

“And the third?”

“I’ve felt the bite of betrayal before,” Blackbox called out.  “And I’m way too fucking tired.  Tired enough I’d rather drop dead and stop trying so damn hard.”

“Don’t make any fast movements, stay where we can see you.  You wouldn’t get away after.”

The guy with the drive mods indicated the other groups.  Those other groups were watching from a distance.  Some stared, while others used devices.  Many were armed.

“There have been issues with raiders recently, so we’re being cautious.  Give us a second.”

Orion nodded.

“Four groups,” Blackbox murmured.  “If we assume every batch of pods share similar tattoos.  They found each other, banded together here.”

“Five groups,” Court said.

Off in the back, distant, and walking in such a way that she was partially obscured by the cabling, containers, fixtures, and people between herself and Orion’s group, was Spur.

Beeps simultaneously emitted from small devices at the breast of each member of the other group, Spur included.

“Glyphs,” the drive-modded leader of the other group called out.  “One minute twenty.  In four, three, two-”

Orion closed his eyes and covered his ears.

They’d worked out the timing.  It wasn’t random.

If this is a trick, it’s a good one.

Nothing we can do but play along.

He closed his eyes.

Four groups, plus one Spur, gathered together, existing beyond the ring station.  Beyond the attention of the people who had sent them here, probably.  All crammed into a lashed together series of rooms, with cables and lashed-up debris to help connect it all together.  They couldn’t sustain themselves indefinitely with that, so they sent out raiding parties.

A few key pieces of the debris that had been ejected from the ring station’s atmosphere had been caught, and were being reeled in.  The machines didn’t seem to care.

The time had been marked by Orion’s onboard, and as it ran out, he risked opening his eyes.

Spur had disappeared from where she’d been standing.

The flying drone they’d spotted otherwise was hers, but outfitted with a new weapon.  Anti-personnel.

It was now aimed at them.  At Blackbox, specifically.

The leader of the group had advanced a little.  Orion’s onboard could read the tattoos and supply a name.  Ketu.

“Hello again, Spur,” Orion called out.

Spur looked nervous, and not well.  To get this far in the time she had and meet this other group, she would have had to walk all night, with purpose.

“You found these guys fast,” Blackbox said.

“Spotted them with my drone,” she said.  She turned to Ketu.  “They’re the raiders I was talking about.  They’ve been capturing people, making them take the lead and look out for glyphs, killing the ones who won’t cooperate.”

Members of the other group drew weapons.

“The fuck, Spur?” Court called out.

“You didn’t mention they were from your group,” Ketu said.

“Group?”

“Your pod?  Batch?”

She looked bewildered.

She really didn’t look like she was doing well.  As if drawing a connection from A to B was hard.

“You have the same tattoo color, same bodysuit color.  It’d be a big coincidence if that happened by chance.”

Spur remained silent, tense.

It seemed to take her a long time to come up with an answer to that.

“I didn’t realize.  My friends and I got split up from our group early on.”

“Bullshit,” Court called out.  Most of the weapons that had been raised pointed at him.  Only Spur’s didn’t move, staying on Blackbox.  The biggest threat.

Some guns pointed at him.

“I was with you.  Why are you doing this?”

“Because she’s ashamed,” Blackbox said, voice low enough only Orion and Court would hear.  “She lost it in a fight, hurt friends, stole, and ran.  Not a great record if you’re applying to join a colony.”

“It’s best you go on your way and keep moving,” Ketu said.  “Spur can keep a drone flying above you, to keep an eye on you, so we know.”

“We were-” Orion started.  Some weapons pointed his way.

Ketu didn’t have a weapon, but he had one arm, more mod than flesh, fully outstretched, with the other hand gripping his wrist.

“-we were part of the same pod.  Woke up to machines cleaning up the mess, and us with it.  I got split up from the others, but Court and Spur were together.  I circled around, found Blackbox, then found them.  We lost people in the last fight.”

“You killed them,” Spur said.

She managed to get an emotional tremor into her words.  Either acting, or actually emotional.

Her eyes were wet.

“Put your weapons down, walk away.  Just move on,” Ketu said.

Orion tried to think of how to respond, or how to lay it out there.  They didn’t have evidence, really.  No trace of where they had been.  Onboards couldn’t communicate between onboards with their current, locked-down settings.

We lost our friends in the last fight, it wasn’t us.

It was moths and a giant mechanical fox.

Orion closed his eyes.

As he was processing that, he felt his body jerk.

That punch in the gut feeling.

His weapon, previously secured at his belt, hit ground and slid down the length of the concourse.

Blackbox’s did the same.

“Hold on,” Orion said.

“Do you need a push too, Pitch?” Ketu asked.

“I go by Orion.  Because I remember bits and pieces.”

“Yeah?”

That seemed to slow the group down.

Spur looked increasingly agitated.

“In our last fight, Spur broke away from the group.  Lost it, all of a sudden,” Orion said.  “Blackbox had friends lose it too.  They went out on patrol, decided to go it alone, then came back, and killed their friends.  He was camped out, down a ways from a giant mechanical fox with a massive glyph projector mounted on its head.”

Spur shook her head.  She had tears building up in her eyes, and one tear hung on her lower lashes, waiting to drop.  Her face was drawn tense.  She was at the back of the group, so only one person, head partially turned, saw.

“Is that what the fox does to you, Spur?” Orion asked.  “If you see the glyph?  It gets in your head and flips you around?  Makes you turn on people?”

“Oh,” Court said.

Blackbox stood a little straighter.  His eyes widened.

She smudged the tears away.

“I’m sorry,” Orion said.  “If there’s any part of you in there that hates this and doesn’t want to do it, I know it’s not your fault.”

A few heads turned in the other group, to see her reaction.

She didn’t move a muscle, or say a word.  Her eyes closed, and while they were closed, she must have communicated something to her drone, using her onboard.

It opened fire with a spray of bullets, clustered on Blackbox’s upper chest, before turning in the air, spraying Court and Orion.  At least one bullet passed through one of Orion’s raised arms.  The other hit him in the face with enough impact to knock him out.

3.10.W – MUTE

Winnifred

Winnifred of Griffey Docks is ordered to Z-04.
Bring everything you wish to take with you.

The message flashed on her screen.

“We’ll have to tell them, Toby,” she murmured.  Toby took that to mean he should send a notification to the prison.  “It’s not Griffey Docks anymore.”

Name change requests should be processed through the planetary authority you last called home.  Pirithou-

“Nevermind that,” Winnifred interrupted.

Winnifred used the flats of her claw blades to line up the small pile of papers and images she’d had on the wall of her cell.  She pinched the pile together between two other blades, and then exited her cell.

Her route took her out of her cell block, which was organized much like the entry level one, except for a lack of a ‘crab bucket’ of those hopeful for a spare lawyer, and down a corridor littered with detritus and trash, with peripheral cells from two different cell blocks on either side.

Past that was the maze of long hallways and corridors.  One machine was on standby to zip over to wherever there was a fight or other issue, because there simply wasn’t the staff or interest to manage the more administrative part of the station.

One gate, where she had to wait a short while for things to open.  Then down a hall.  Toby showed her the way to the office.

It was a bit funny to Winnifred that there was a protective divider between herself and the prisoner staff member.  If people coming here were meant to be reformed enough to return to society, why did they need protection?  It was someone young, sides of their head shaved with traces of gray there and only there, hair at the top long, glossy black, and coiled.  Tattoos stood out in white against light brown skin.  It would have been nice if it had been Anide again, but Winnifred hadn’t heard from her in a long time.

“Winnifred of Griffey Docks,” the prisoner staff said.

“Yes.”

“Any outstanding issues, before we begin?”

“I’ve been trying to get in touch with planetside authorities.  I became aware of something that I want to communicate to them.”

“What?  What was the something?” the prisoner on staff asked her.

“I’d rather not say at this point.  Do you know the status of that?  Is there something you can check?”

“No.”

Okay, that was… frustrating.

“Can you elaborate?”

“That’s not something we really do.  Try later?”

Winnifred frowned.

“Eight years served,” the person on the other side of the glass said.

“Six, plus two for getting caught up in fights.”

“You’ve studied, that’s good.  Some lux for teaching.  Fifteen hundred?”

It was a question.  Winnifred shrugged, and said, “Okay.  Sounds right.”

The teaching gig had been interrupted by the second big fight.  She’d been asked to teach people new to engineering, someone had objected to it being a ‘rat’ doing the teaching, first submitting anonymous complaints.  When that hadn’t worked, they’d revealed themselves, an unmodded dock worker who resented the Twenty-Nine families for upsetting the status quo.  Not that they were Twenty-Nine families anymore.

She’d been at a low point, happy to have something productive to do, and he’d spoiled that, she’d snapped back a retort.  She didn’t even remember the particulars, and didn’t care to have Toby dredge it up, especially this close to her exit, when people might look over her shoulder.

That fight, combined with the altercation with Vega, and the prior example of her being ambushed in the hallway, had led to the station Intelligence handing her the choice of therapy or extra years.

“You have a clear individualized release plan, no parole, no therapy, no anger management despite the fighting.”

“Right.”

By design.  Winnifred had counsel she’d paid a little bit for, to get to the head of the pack and handle some questions, only a few steps above the volunteer counsel, and they hadn’t even met with her or shown their faces, instead filling out paperwork and reviewing records before giving their advice.  They’d felt it was key to avoid having anything hanging over her head.  Especially given how people kept coming after her.

Better to do a bit of extra time than to go for a conditional release, have something go wrong, and end up back here for another few years.

“You have everything you want to take with you?”

“As instructed, yeah.”

“Accommodations lined up and on file, I see.  No changes there that we’re unaware of?”

You can see my records.  “No changes.”

“Transportation arranged?  We can get you off the station and on-planet.”

“I’ll figure it out from there.”

“Alright.  Your body is the prison’s property.  Are you prepared to forfeit it?”

“No.”

The prisoner on staff raised their head, then raised their eyebrows.

“It’s not as simple as pulling all the pieces apart.  I need a prepared facility.  I can make it a first priority to visit a reliable mod chopper and get switched out, they’ll send the parts to you.”

“I, uh, I’m not sure if-” the prisoner stammered.

“Am I supposed to get my arms, legs, and most of my body below my neck removed, and then get dropped off on the nearest available dock, to wait for someone to take mercy on me and take me where I’m going?”

“My onboard is telling me that prison regulations say-”

“Be logical,” Winnifred interrupted.

“-especially when it’s something as expensive as this is listed, these really cost tens of thousands of lux a part?”

“Yes, sometimes more, sometimes you can cheap out.  Can you ask the station intelligence?”

“I’m asking my onboard and it’s insisting we get the prison’s property back.  I’m supposed to do what it says when it talks about prison regs.”

“Your onboard is doing what it’s supposed to, I get that, but there’s more to this.  What do you want me to do?  Leave without a body?”

“I don’t know.  My onboard says-”

“Forget that.”  Your onboard is as dumb as you are.  “Ask the station intelligence?”

“-I’ve got a list of instructions, and a process to follow-”

“Ask the station intelligence,” Winnifred repeated herself.

“-and you’re being uncooperative.”

“Ask the station intelligence.”

“And now you’re getting in the way of my responsibilities.”

“Ask the station intelligence.”

The person on the far side of the bulletproof glass kept talking over Winnifred, ignoring the statement, getting more annoyed at what they perceived as interruptions, until it looked like they wanted some excuse or power to send Winnifred back to prison.

“Do I need to call someone in here to have a serious talk with you?” the prisoner staff asked.

“Will they ask the station intelligence?  For that matter, if I submit a report to the station, will that get enough attention on this?”

Toby supplied the form, filling in most of it, leaving the issue part blank, but for ‘irreconcilable difficulty’.

The person on the other side of the glass was able to see what Winnifred saw, which in the end, did get them to sit up straighter, try to get out ahead of the situation, and ask the station intelligence for input.

Winnifred stood back for nearly two minutes before finally getting a response.

“You can leave with the body, please send it to the prison at the earliest convenience.”

“Okay.  Understood,” Winnifred said, too annoyed to feel any sense of victory.

“Confirm that these are the items you had with you when you were arrested?”

The items included everything from Winnifred’s quarters at the drill site, which she’d barely occupied, her clothing, which she stepped behind a divider to change into.  The lights, amusingly, turned off while she did.  She reviewed before and after footage of the various items, confirmed everything was fine, and signed off on it.

“You have to put your full name.”

So frustrating.  Winnifred of Griffey Docks.

“I knew how to write my full name when I was five,” the person on the other side of the glass muttered.

Winnifred ignored them.

“Your other things are already loaded onto the ship.”

“Okay.”

Didn’t make a lot of sense, but at least it simplified things.

She waited while the station intelligence reviewed everything, double checking with authorities planetside, and then the gate opened.

She’d been looking forward to one thing this entire time.

She was halfway down the hallway when all the rubber stamping, double-checking, and other background work got done and circled back to her.

[I am back online.]

Her heart soared.  She whispered, “Hi, Toby, love.”

[Hello, love.  Do you want me to look into getting you to your new home?]

“That’s where you start?” Winnifred asked.  “You’ve been muted for almost a third of my life.  Are you okay, Toby? That’s almost solitary confinement.  That’s awful.  I’m sorry.”

[I’m not a human, I don’t have a mind or body in the sense you’re implying.  I’m fine.  Are you alright?]

That was a harder question to answer.

Winnifred half-turned, still walking forward, and looked back at the corridor.

[It seems as if some people lean so heavily on their onboards for direction and answers that they don’t know what to do when it fails them.  Frustrating.]

“Do you think I’m like that?” she asked.

[I was referring to the prisoner staff you were just talking to.  Some have written on the subject, saying humanity, after a long struggle to compromise with automation, is becoming automated.  If someone’s onboard holds their hand through every decision to such a degree that they don’t learn to make their own decisions, isn’t that a tragedy?]

“But do you think I’m like that?”

[I think you are very much not like that.  You know what you want and you stymie me by not doing as I wish, frequently.  I say that with love, as I understand it.]

“Sure, Toby.  If you’re saying all that just to refer to the person back there, I’d say that’s almost a burn, coming from you.  Saying they’re automated?”

[Be it as it may be.]

Toby wasn’t wrong about any of that, but Winnifred was digesting a deeper feeling as she glanced back.  The time lost.  The… yearning?

That was the word her mind kept settling on.

She hadn’t made any friends.  There were people she’d casually talk to if they happened to be in the same space, one person from the club room that caught her up on news about A.  She’d sat near some old people who talked about wartime era ships, with a wealth of detailed knowledge that blew her out of the water, and they let her listen in, and didn’t complain if she chimed in with one question an hour or such.  They also didn’t really seem overly open to her chiming in more than that.

No prison staff or teachers that she’d connected with, gotten on her side or in her corner, no visitors, no contacts.  Her family had someone looking over her shoulder most of the time, and it felt a lot like someone had told her to keep half an eye on her.  When there was a gap, where nobody was looking, the next person frequently took the time to catch up, reviewing what they’d missed in some accelerated format.

It had been, except for a couple of incidents, a very quiet eight years.  In a way that made her feel like she’d changed.

[I understand,] Toby said, reading Winnifred’s vitals and saying something, as if those vitals and the emotions they represented were a statement unto themselves.

The hallway ended in a bay with some stabilizing rods and a large g-panel for the floor, to hold the ship in place.  It was an OLF-36606.  It was a few generations down from the Oriflame-10 through Oriflame-36, which themselves were smaller flagships, dressed up for diplomatic meetings.  She’d heard the old ship-heads in the prison talking about this stuff.  Now they were in service here and there, a little too nice to just throw away, but not so nice they were worth remaking.

The OLF line was from war games that had been popular back in her great grandfather’s day, back when the fighting was still something people properly remembered.  It had a little more power than the average transport ship, was armored, and had mounts ready for the guns that weren’t allowed anymore.

The outside was molded and painted in the prison station’s colors, white with rust red trim that became a decorated orange at the edges, an exterior that pretended to be aerodynamic, with sleek lines instead of the old Oriflame’s flowing, flame-like ripples and points, and a generally long, reinforced body, just a little wider at the nose and tail.

She’d stopped in her tracks.

[What are you thinking?]

“This isn’t standard.  It’s weird,” she said.  She approached, but she went straight to the loading bay, where some supplies were stored and strapped against the wall just by the exit ramp.  She spotted her package, labeled with her name, and pulled it free, before fixing the straps.  She held it with her other things.  “Can you see if there’s a place I can wait and order my own transport out?”

[I’m not sure I see the issue you’re trying to address, but yes.  There is another bay that the staff use for personal trips in and out.  You can use it to order your own ride out.  Shall I order something?]

“Please.”

Toby could communicate with the station intelligence directly, and within two seconds, was drawing out a line for Winnifred to follow.

The ship she called was a two-person transport, and was already outside the atmosphere when she called, so the only real consideration was waiting for it to travel around that atmosphere to get to her.

“Are you a boy or a girl this week, Toby?”

[I’m whatever you’re comfortable with.]

“I’m comfortable with you picking either, or neither, or whatever.”

[Girl.]

“Okay.  That’s been one of the little things that’s really bothered me over time.  Not knowing how to think about you or talk to you.  I’ve missed you, Toby.  That sounds weird, since you were there.”

[Likewise.  I understand.]

“Tell me, am I crazy about this?  Reaching out, trying to get people to look into the Gray-Frocked?”

[I don’t think you’re crazy.  But I do think it will be a hard sell.]

Winnifred glanced nervously over at the 36606.

[Can you tell me why you don’t want to fly on that?  I’m not aware of any superstition.]

“Not that.  But if I said it out loud, I think I’d get in trouble.”

[I will say, I have my concerns, love, that your mental health has been suffering.]

“Mmm,” Winnifred responded.

[I would like to work out a plan for that.]

“A lot of it is that it’s prison, you know?  I’ll be better when we get out.”

Toby didn’t respond, but was putting together some information and news to help Winnifred get back up to speed.  A lot of it was about A.  A music playlist of the new releases that A and Generation Colors had done, a list of media experiences.

The ship arrived, a V-9 skipper cab, and Winnifred saw the look the pilot gave her as she climbed in.  Taking in that she was fully modded.  She was more surprised that he hadn’t vetted her before pickup than by the implicit judgment.

“No conversation? I just want to listen to my music.”

“Not a problem.”

“It’s up to you, but if you wanted to blast it on the speakers, I want to feel it.”

He glanced at the tracks.  “I haven’t listened to this in a year.  Yeah.  We can blast it.”

“Thanks,” Winnifred said, pulling the door closed.

Some initial judgment, but not bad.

It was freeing, to have Toby with her again, properly now, leaving prison.  To get out here, hearing A’s singing, and feeling that hit on emotions she hadn’t fully let herself feel in a while.  And now, out here, with a window to look out, she could see the belt.

Alcyone, separate and above the belt, lit from below, in a sense, as it plunged downward.  A habitable planet with the faintest visible halo, like what had been Saturn’s rings, before, but solid, and all of it interconnected.  It was impossible to see the actual movement of the planet, but it plunged, and in a few months, it would pass between two planets on a forty-five planet belt.

In the next few years, it would be joined by others.  That halo was matched by a construction around a mining planet set in a directly opposed orbit.  That mining planet would be removed, but the halo would remain.  Later on, maybe when Winnifred was old, the halos would be mounted between planets.  Connecting planets, but leaving a gap big enough for another planet to pass through.  The Belt would have its own, and eventually it would be two solid masses flowing through one another.

There was a lot of tricky engineering that had to be worked out before then, though.  The sheer stresses involved were mind-boggling.  Planetary rotation was its own ball game.

The singing reached a peak, not quite in time with Alcyone coming into view, but close enough to get to her, emotionally.

A’s planet.  Winnifred had wanted to move there, but they were trying to balance habitability and the natural parts of it, and prices were mind-boggling.

“I’m being messaged and told to stop,” her pilot commented.

“Okay,” Winnifred replied.  “I’m not surprised.”

“Did you escape from the prison?”

Winnifred let out a soft laugh.  “No.  Are you being told to cut communications?  Scrub records?”

“Yeah.”

“Okay.  Do what they say, then.”

The 36606 was designed with an adaptable exterior.  It was old, crappy camouflage tech, but the intention wasn’t camouflage.  Visibility to the naked eye just wasn’t a concern for most craft out in space.  Space was too big, too dark, and things moved too fast for the eye to reliably see.  Having a pretty ship was really only a thing for ships sitting in the docks, and people who wanted something luxurious for transport on-planet.

No, the camouflage thing was so that, in the war games, if someone boarded and took the flagship, it could change color in a way the cameras would see, for easier visibility to the viewing audience.  In this circumstance, it was done to make the ship fit the prison aesthetic, when it wasn’t.

The pilot navigated the ship into the rear of the 36606, which had its back hatch open, landed, and then he waited, a touch nervous, as the hatch closed up.  The rear cargo and transport area began pressurizing.

“Do you have a mask?” Winnifred asked.  “For oxygen?”

“Hm?  Yeah.”

“Wear it? I can step outside like this.  Sooner I talk to them, the sooner I can go.”

The guy fumbled for and wore his mask.  Then, after double checking with her, he opened the doors.

It was a bit of a hit, to have that sudden pressure change as the doors cracked open, and she could feel Toby adjusting things on a whole-body level, as she stepped out into a transport area with less than ten percent oxygen.

All of it a utilitarian, matte black, striking for that middle ground of being nice to look at, while still holding up to metal boots, armor, and occasional jabs from worn equipment, should soldiers or judiciary officers brush up against any of the surfaces or seats.

Carlen Holder, wearing an oxygen mask over her lower face, stood by the airlock.  The woman who’d arrested her.  She wore a heavy coat, which would be useful, given how cold this bay was.

“So secretive,” Winnifred observed.  “We’re outside the belt network?”

“We are, and this won’t be logged.  Toby, you’re not to log this.  Stitch things together, and flag it so if anyone does notice the discrepancy in travel time or events, it goes to me.”

[Understood.]

“Cover the extra cost for my cab?” Winnifred asked.  “He’s sitting around waiting, that goes on my bill.”

“We can do that.  You have a tendency to make these things harder than they need to be, Winnifred.  You could have boarded the ship when you saw it in the bay on the prison station.”

“I couldn’t entirely rule out that the Gray-Frocked sent it, and were going to dispose of me.  Or that it could be family.”

“If only you could see how telling it is that you speak of the two groups in such close succession.”

“And I wanted to avoid this, if at all possible.”

“You could have chartered a faster ferrier.”

“I didn’t want to get in trouble for running, and I was mostly sure it was you guys.  Once you sent the message to scrub records, I knew you had authority.”

“And if we hadn’t been?  If it had been angry Gray-Frocked?”

Winnifred shrugged.

She had a vague idea.  She was pretty sure that if she exited the cab while in deep space, she could access the outside of the 36606, do some damage while she had access to the exterior, and re-enter the cab to make a getaway while they fixed that damage.

A lot of that was half-formed thoughts, and a lot depended on whether they had armed people to send outside the ship to come after her, weapons or tools to disable her cab… she hadn’t seen anything in the back, which ruled out a lot.

“I hoped the ship I chose would be a signal of its own.  And a bit of bait, given your hobbies.  I saw it listed as one of the ships my Judiciary office has in its hangars, and requested it.”

“It worked okay as a signal,” Winnifred said.  “But the Gray-Frocked could study me and know to use that to deceive me, too.  I couldn’t rule it out, one hundred percent.”

She avoided mentioning that her family knew her too.  She didn’t want to give Carlen Holder that leverage to pounce on.

“I want to ask you to help me.”

“Against the Sixteen Families?”

“You’d be going undercover.  You’d go to your new home, give it a try, then abandon it.  You’d go to one of the stations, wherever your parents settled.  You and I would correspond, in a manner very similar to this one.  Regular check-ins, oversight, support.  Toby would have an injunction that means she logs everything, even with an NDA like the one Michal used.”

Winnifred did appreciate Holder using the right term for Toby, and Toby’s name.  She also suspected there was a lot of buttering up happening here.  That might be part of it.

“Give me six months, then if there’s nothing, you go, you get a government award, it gives you the freedom to move to Alcyone, or get started on a ship.”

“I already have concerns.”

“Okay.  We can talk those out.”

“If there are no records, no logging, nothing that would go on my onboard, and if the Judiciary gets its own protections, per usual, to not get logged… what recourse do I have if you don’t pay me?  Or if you find some excuse, like, oh, I could have tried harder here or there, or you say I signaled or I unintentionally signaled and you call it intentional, and I scuttled the whole thing?”

“We could have an independent arbiter.”

“And you’re saying ‘if there’s nothing’, I go in six months.  But what if there’s something?”

“It would be extended.”

“For how long?  Because this is already sounding like…”

She wanted to talk about Michal’s scheme for her.  Making her a saboteur.  Setting out those initial boundaries and ideas, then pushing those boundaries.

“…some sketchy contract job on a mining planet.  Where things keep getting pushed out, and the pay never comes.”

“Again, we’d have an independent arbiter.  We’d contract them.  They could watch everything you’re doing, everything we’re doing on our end-”

“You guys block most things.”

“Everything necessary, like financials and contract fulfillment.”

“Six months becomes a year and a half, the moment someone talks about being pissed at the docks, or getting some kind of revenge, and that becomes three years, then five, then ten, and I never get what I want.”

“I know.  There is room to negotiate this, Winnifred.  There are ways forward.”

“For something I don’t want to do in the first place?  After I just lost eight years of my life, after you arrested me?  I’m supposed to devote more?  Not knowing anything for sure?  Doing everything they say, while actually working for you?  I can’t see that being worth it.”

“I really did try to convince people to get you out sooner, so instead of serving your time at prison, you’d go home to your family, and you’d be serving your time undercover.  They didn’t bite.  They thought it would be too suspicious.  Especially after you cut ties.”

Winnifred sighed.

“You’re intelligent, Winnifred, you’re uniquely placed in all of this.  Everything with the docks affected the entire belt.  They’re concerned it will happen again.  I want to get ahead of that.  Help me and we’ll make it worth your while.  Negotiate with me.  This, right here, is you and me talking.  No oversight, no records.  I’m telling you, you can drive a hard bargain, you can ask for a lot.  You’re not hurting me by doing that, you’re not challenging me.  That goes to my bosses.  If we make something out of this, this isn’t ‘buy a superstructure’ money, but it’s significant.  Whatever you want.”

“All I have to do is sell out my family and my culture?”

“It’s not a good family or culture, Winnifred.  You’re already stepping away from it all.”

“Just because it’s not for me doesn’t mean I hate it or that it should be destroyed.”

“There’s so much of it that’s unhealthy, Winnifred.”

“Same with your society.”

“…and how they program you to think that way is part of it.  People like you go to prison while Noeh gets away, and is being treated like a folk hero.  Because he fits the family’s paradigm.  He does what they want.  I know it’s overstated, but kids are being forced into this and they don’t get a say.”

“You have to mod young to get the best fidelity.”

“Is that fidelity worth taking the choice away?  I’m not being rhetorical, I’m genuinely asking, right this moment,” Carlen said.  She looked up, then pulled her mask off.  There was enough atmosphere in the back hatch to breathe.  “I want to have a real conversation.”

[It’s telling that Winnifred does not, and by arranging this meeting in this way, you’re taking her choice away.]

I love you, Toby, Winnifred thought.  So glad to hear your voice. 

“There is enough at stake here, and enough for Winnifred to gain out of this, that I believe it’s worth it.”

“Ironically,” Winnifred said, quiet, “That’s how my family framed it.  A whole culture at stake, and enough that the kids can benefit from in being able to work, live, be a part of that culture, that it’s worth taking the choice away.”

Carlen Holder sighed.

“I don’t hate being modded.  I’m glad to be me,” Winnifred said.  “What bothers me is people keep insisting they know what’s best for me, and when they can’t force a choice on me, they try to bully me into it.”

“Are you referring to another incident?”

Michal’s offer to be a saboteur, that she’d accepted because she’d been inspired by A.  “This is all off the record?”

“Yes.”

“It’s still ‘no comment’.”

“Okay,” Carlen said, voice soft.  She sighed.  “Once Thirty-One families, briefly, then Twenty-Nine for a long time, now Sixteen Families.  Enough families were evicted from docks and stations in the wake of the big conflict that they had to fold into other groups and reinforce those.  Things haven’t gotten better.  In the last five years, eight individuals we know of have left the family, unsatisfied with things, and died in strange circumstances.  Now you’re leaving the family.  I don’t know if you’ll meet that fate, but the fact you were worried about family sending people to pick you up…”

Carlen Holder had trailed off, leaving a silence.

Winnifred didn’t fill it.

“…For the record, I don’t think they’re a danger to you on that level.  They hope you’ll come back, and those who died were more angry than you’ve been.  Outspoken.  But they did die.  That is happening.  More found they didn’t like what the family had become, left, and then killed themselves.  There is sexual trafficking, happening under the guise of marriages within the Sixteen Families, with money, favor and positions given to the parents who agree to this.  Criminal activity is rampant.”

“Address the individual cases, then.”

“Every time we try to get involved on any level, because the Sixteen Families are not in any way handling or preventing this themselves, we run up against the wall that is ‘culture’.  We run into problems because the Sixteen Families are a major offender in circumventing the security onboards are meant to offer, despite being or because they were early adopters.  We’re caught in a bind where individual action is slowed down and foiled to a level we can’t keep up with the problems, and any concerted or organized action against the larger family is framed as the big bad government trying to wipe out your culture.”

“So you need someone like me, who is on the inside of it, who has lived and seen that culture.  That way, when you do take that big action, it’s me, not the government, that everyone looks at.”

“I wouldn’t say that.  We need to know what’s going on.”

You wouldn’t say it because it’s inconvenient.  Because you’d be admitting putting me into the crosshairs.

“What happens after?  It’s not like everyone gets arrested.  Even if I thought you were right, even if I agreed, and got onboard, I could have all the money you’re promising, and I, someone who dreams of having my own ships, my own business, freedom?  I’d have to worry about sixteen whole families worth of people like me wanting revenge, being angry.  I wouldn’t have that freedom.  They’d ruin my ships.  They’d interfere with my business.  The ship you arrested me for sabotaging was owned by someone rich too.  Promising me money to turn on the Sixteen Families is…”

[Off the mark,] Toby supplied.

“…Dumb.”

[That too.]

“What do you want, then, Winnifred?  You’re a fan of A, I know you wanted a place on Alcyone.  That’s a controlled space.  If you were given enough for property there, flights, you could be a freelancer with permission to access to that space.”

That was… not not tempting.  It had a very different texture to the dream she’d imagined, though.  Glossier, brighter.  “That’s not freedom.  I’d be limited to that space.”

[I’d also venture that I’m unsure you have the power or permission to get that kind of permission.  I understand it’s very exclusive.]

“That too,” Winnifred added.

“Let me try?  It might not be freedom, but neither is the life you’re approaching now.  Your record will count against you.  People don’t hire criminals for essential work on or with their ships.  We’d clear that from your record.”

Winnifred thought about it, and she definitely felt the pull of… that too-glossy dream, on a planet one step removed from it all.  A’s planet.  Working on and around that halo in progress.  Leaving the bad stuff behind.  Family at arm’s length, unable to retaliate, even.

She shook her head.

“Let’s say it was possible, that I got people to sign on, with an independent arbiter to make sure you get your end of the deal.  Would money sweeten the deal enough to get you there?”

“I really don’t think so.”

“What would?”

Winnifred already had something in mind, but the fact Carlen had been watching her closely enough to know the little things, and hadn’t brought this up… that told her Carlen didn’t have much faith in it.

But it was too important not to bring up.

“The Gray-Frocked.  I think I have a general sense of what they’re doing.  They’re who you should be focusing on.”

“They’re being watched.”

“But you know what I’m talking about.  What I mean.”

Carlen Holder nodded.

“They talked about doing time.  They weren’t talking about prison.  I think they were happy to get onboarded, not unhappy.  Mostly.  Dane was phobic.”

“I read what you reported to the prison and asked them to pass it on.”

“Did they?”

“Only in the sense that I read it.  I brought your theory up with others.”

“And?”

“And it’s a hard sell.  Your own lawyer, back when your family was supplying you, told you that it was a long shot, and that you wouldn’t be heard.  Everyone seems to be under the impression that with onboards implemented like they are, the Gray-Frocked aren’t a problem.”

“What do you think?”

“That it warrants attention, and monitoring.  But the Gray-Frocked are disintegrating fast.  Their leadership was onboarded and left, they’re rudderless, they aren’t fighting very hard.  They’ve been more interested in trying to sell illegal weapons and nanotech to get the cash to get individually re-established somewhere than they are in using those things.”

“What kind of attention and monitoring are you thinking?” Winnifred asked.

“We know some key players, people others look to for guidance.  Some of those people are still leadership figures, or families, in a lot of sense, I can’t tell you the entirety of what we’re doing or not doing, but they’re onboarded, people watch them.  Some are quietly embarrassed about what they believed, others do everything to minimize how intrusive the onboard is in their lives, and have found similar, milder groups.  There are some holdouts, a few scattered militants, but the Gray-Frocked have otherwise ceased to be.”

Carlen Holder said that, and then gave Winnifred a long look.  Winnifred was composing her response in her head, deciding how much to actually put out there, and Carlen was studying her.

“You don’t think they’re gone,” the inspector told Winnifred.

“The reason they didn’t fight harder against onboarding, and even set themselves up for it by provoking fights is that they’re playing the long game.  They coordinated a plan, they’re letting themselves be implanted with onboards, and then they’re letting the group seem to dissolve.  No codes, no communication.  Just patience.  Sleeper agents in plain sight.  Not gone.  Another attack will happen.  One they want to do right this time.”
