“The problem with that is we have no clear proof.  Some curious statements that might line up with it, but… going back to earlier days, before the Belt, when cults were more common?  Cults like this don’t work that way.  There needs to be that coercive, controlling element that gives them a sense of meaning, purpose.  Without that reinforced sense of purpose, they fall apart.”

Winnifred wasn’t entirely sure how to respond to that.

“Is it possible that you set yourself the objective of looking into them, and you want that to have meaning, so your time in prison wasn’t a waste?” Carlen asked.

“Is it possible I’m right?” Winnifred retorted.  “You say I’m smart and I can do all this for you.  I did spend a lot of time listening to them, which very few people have done.  They keep to themselves, there aren’t a lot of records.”

“You’re right.  You did.  Your ability to do that was part of why I want you to look into the Sixteen families, where your input will be twice as relevant.”

“You asked what I wanted, I brought this up.  I want this.  I’m not one hundred percent, this is a huge deal for me, giving up any information on my family.  But if I were to do it… I’m less interested in money.  Get me a place on Alcyone and permission to operate on some level around that.  If I have my own ship I’d be willing to work for a company that does have permission.  And get a task squad on the Gray-Frocked.  Whatever resources you want to commit to the Sixteen Families, put something on the Gray-Frocked too.”

“I think we can make that happen,” Carlen said.

“Then I think maybe,” Winnifred said.  “Figure out if you really can have a job waiting for me at the end.  With someone who’ll respect me, no requiring me to change my body.  Get me a decent-enough place.  Then maybe.  I’m not committing to anything.”

“You’ve never had a proper home before, have you?  You’ve slept in the vents and spaces beneath Griffey Docks, you’ve stayed with the family at Sherman Station, you’ve had quarters while working on the drills, that you barely used, and you’ve had your prison cell.”

“Yeah, I suppose.”

“You’re on your way to your first home, in a way.  When you experience the freedom of having a place to yourself, you’ll really appreciate what’s waiting for you at Alcyone later on.”

“My first home was Griffey Docks.  It still is.  That’s why this is such a maybe,” Winnifred said.

“Griffey Docks is gone.”

Only part of the reason she wanted to drop that from her name.  “It’s still my childhood home.  Are we done?  You follow up on that, see about that task force and that job, and I’ll think about this.  Then… arrange another off-the-record meeting like this, I guess.”

“We’ll work out something easier to cover up later on.  Come.  Let’s pay your cab for his loyalty and silence and get you on your way.”

[Can I interrupt?] Toby’s voice came through the nearest panels, as well as being transmitted inside Winnifred’s head.

“Perfectly alright, Toby,” Winnifred said.  “What’s up?”

[It’s my job to support you.  Part of that is understanding where your weaknesses lie.  I hope you know I say this with love, as I understand it.]

Winnifred thumped a fist against the spot on her chest where her heart was.

[You’ve spent eight years with the Gray-Frocked front of mind, reaching out to people, and being rebuffed.  You want this.  You are willing to do something as big as work with Inspector Holden to see movement on this.]

Winnifred raised her eyebrows.  “Are you worried it’s all in my head?  I asked, before, if you thought I was right about what the Gray-Frocked are doing.”

[You did, I do think you’re right.  That’s not where my concern lies.  I’d like to clarify upfront just what that end of the deal would look like.  Inspector Holder?]

“We’d have to work out the details,” Carlen said.  “Assigned teams investigating the Gray-Frocked.  Watching purchases, movements, relationships.  Some surveillance to cover angles onboards can’t.  To watch out for the same sorts of tricks Winnifred here pulled to commit sabotage.”

[It’s my understanding that the Gray-Frocked committed the largest terrorist attack in modern history, and were, possibly are, fully willing to weaponize and use nanotech warfare.]

“Your understanding is correct.  They were.”

[Even if they’re diminished as a threat, surely there’s already some people committed to the task of monitoring them, just in case.]

“Of course.”

[What would be different about the assigned task force you’re promising Winnifred and what you’re already doing?]

Winnifred shifted her footing.  The hand that had thumped against her heart now had the tips of her claws resting against the upper edge of her collarbone, hanging off it.

“Numbers,” Carlen said.

Winnifred looked away.  The claw at her collarbone gripped now, tight.

[In eight years, she has written and I have transmitted many letters spelling this out.  You’ve read these missives.]

“I have,” Carlen said.

[They have presumably, as would be the case with any tip, been sent to a relevant Judiciary Intelligence, who assessed them and then gave instructions and information to investigators such as yourself.  Or didn’t.]

“I imagine so.  I can’t speak to the progress or handling of other investigations.”

[I would like to add something to the deal.  We can safely assume Winnifred isn’t a member of the Gray-Frocked, you want her as an undercover asset, so there could or should be some way to entrust her with information like that.  Put us in touch with people who are following up on her tip or on the idea this might be a massive sleeper operation, or show us records from that work.  Not Intelligence generated, please.  Some way to know that information wasn’t lost to the void.]

“That’s a heavy ask,” Carlen said.  “People are defensive of their work.”

[If you can find a way to get her a job in an exclusive, protected tract around Alcyone, I’m sure you can negotiate something to assuage our concerns here.  Failing that, as an alternate route we could take…]

Toby paused.

Winnifred couldn’t feel her heartbeat.  She felt a bit disconnected from the rest of her body.

[…please tell us something to convince us both that you’re taking her concern seriously and that the task force you just promised wasn’t going to be more of the same.]

“A bunch of Judiciary investigators who don’t see this as a real threat,” Winnifred elaborated.

“I promise you, nobody joins the Judiciary without caring about serving people and getting good outcomes.  They’d take it seriously.”

Winnifred didn’t believe that.  Wasn’t worth getting into.  “That doesn’t mean anything if they don’t see the Gray-Frocked as the real, patient threat that they are.”

“I think you’re letting your feelings and suspicions about the Gray-Frocked get out of hand, here, and you’re talking yourself -yourselves- out of a good offer.”

“I’m being asked to sell out the people who raised me because of your suspicions.  I was actually considering it because I see this as a real threat.  This is going to be bigger than a science center.  It’s going to be superstructure sized, with planetary ramifications.  I sure have feelings about that, yeah.”

“Only feelings, no proof.”

“I know how they talked about it.  They had no regrets.  They only wished they’d gone bigger, and that A hadn’t stopped them.  Look at my records, listen to the conversation.  They talked around it, nothing on the record, but they talked around something more meaningful.”

“You think.”

Winnifred was too angry now to actually respond.  She paced.

The pilot was sitting inside the closed-up ship, watching with a concerned expression.  He couldn’t listen in with the current restrictions in place.

“The Sixteen Families are a current threat.  People, including ones you’d call family, little girls and boys, are being hurt every day because of them.  The family’s reputation is being ruined because they cheat, steal, and smuggle or help smuggle.  If you don’t help stop that, you’re complicit.  That’s real.  Tangible.”

“A part of me was going to ask you to assign one person, even a promising rookie, to listen to what I listened to.  No speeding through, no intelligence-provided short form notes or summaries.  Two weeks of listening to conversations, watching video.  If you’d do that, I’m confident they’d see what I saw, hear what I heard.  I’d say if you did that, if you assigned the one person, and treated their report seriously, even-”

Winnifred floundered for a moment.  Her tail whipped side to side.

“-even taking a ‘this is concerning’ from her as a reason to assign two more people to the same listening exercise, to see if they can verify, I’d be satisfied.”

“Okay,” Carlen said.  “I can look into that.”

“I said a part of me wants that.  A bigger part of me doesn’t believe you any more.  I think you should do it anyway, assign that person.  But I don’t trust that you’ll follow up on this.  No deal, Inspector.”

“Reconsider, please.  This matters.”

“May I leave?”

“Hold on.  There’s a contact at the prison.  I want you to send them a message if you change your mind on this.  They’ll get it to me, and I’ll make sure any exchange that follows is private.”

Winnifred climbed into the cab.

“They’re telling me to wait.”

“Yeah, sorry.”

It took a minute.  Eventually Holder wrote something down on a paper card, approached the ship, and handed it through the open door.  She slipped the mask on over her face as she walked away.  The back hatch of the 36606 opened.

“I’m so curious,” her driver said.

“They wanted to recruit me for an investigation.”

“As a spy?”

“Something like that.”

“I’d do that.”

“Even if it meant turning on friends?”

“Criminal friends?” he asked.

She shrugged.

“I’d do it.  Having a chance to make a difference?  Make an impact?”

“Maybe.”

“What else are you going to do?”

“Blast some good music?  If you don’t mind?”

“I definitely don’t mind,” he said, before turning it up to ear-damaging levels.

➨

A classic layout.  One large, open room with one wall that was mostly window, looking out past a walkway and railing, onto sprawling layers of superstructure, and at the clouds that caught the light of the sky.  Pre-furnished, with seating, and some large panels for flat display, and enough footroom for simulations.  The furniture could all recede into the floor, for extended effect.

A small kitchen that she in no way needed, leading out into a back garden that was four paces by four paces across, mixing artistic elements with some durable plant life.  There was a tiny pond in the back that she supposed she could use as a bath if she wanted to, but she figured she’d get more trace algae on herself than anything.  No fish life, but she could order it.

Upstairs was a hallway, three rooms, terminating in a small bathroom she didn’t need and a space for utilities.  Battery charging, clothing disposal, a second trash chute to match the one in the kitchen, and a platform for drone delivery that doubled as a half-balcony.  She could lean out into it, but standing in it was awkward.

Leaning out, she could see Alcyone in the sky.  That had been the one ask she’d had.

Making her way back downstairs, she was struck by how little this place was for her.  She’d scuffed the loveseat with the edge of her shoulder, and while it was made of a near-indestructible material, there was a white mark left behind that stood out to her, like a reminder.  Not for her.  Not for her body.

She didn’t need a kitchen or a bathroom.

Her possessions included what she’d collected in the course of eight years in her cell, and the things she’d had in her quarters for the drill operation.  She had arranged and stacked it by category, notes and papers, mementos, things about A, and a small case of tools for repairing her body.  The totality of it didn’t even take up half of the table in the center of the house’s main room.  She could have spread it out, but that would have been sacrificing efficiency for the sake of making herself feel better.

She was reminded of what her driver had said.

This was the sum total of her life?

Without a sense of meaning and purpose, they fall apart.

She needed something.

Carlen had said a house allowed her freedom.  A chance to make the space her own.

“Toby?  Can you set things to a highlight mode?  Let me paint and make notes on surfaces.”

Toby switched her vision mode.

With a gesture, she selected her color, then painted a large section of the kitchen in a projected layer of red paint.  She only needed the space to store her food packs, and the equipment to make her own- a small blender and packaging machine.

All of the furniture in the main space.

She made a note.  The machinery that retracted and raised the furniture could surely be adjusted.

“Is it possible to change the roof, and have it open up?”

[We could commission it.  It’s actionable.  To get someone on the job, you’d need to either pay or wait until someone can do it for free.]

“We’ll wait.  It’ll take a while.”

She painted out the outline of the ship part in three dimensions.  A large engine assembly.

[Are we making it out of scrap?]

“Yeah.  Scrap, secondhand parts.  I’m tired of waiting for my ship.  We’ll do other work in the meantime.  Whatever we can find, to buy what we can’t scavenge, and to pay for wherever we put the parts of the ship we’re not working on at the current moment.  Work that puts us in proximity to scrap we can take home is good too.”

[I’ll start searching for what’s on offer.]

Turning this into a build site with her living needs occupying the margins of that would mean dismantling the upstairs.  The house would be a mostly empty shell.

A’s music played while she worked out what she needed, and what she didn’t.  She tried to put eight wasted years and several frustrating conversations behind her.

“I’ll need a crew.”

[Are we already thinking that far ahead?]

“Yeah.  Let’s put out feelers.  Anide, Nikhil the Gorilla, some people from the A fan group, if they’re up for it.  We can meet, touch base.  Most will probably say no, or they’ll find other things to do in the meantime, but it sure would be nice to have people I know I can get along with.”

[Noted.]

She stood in the midst of it all, trying to see the potential.

“Send a message to Priz Wooley too,” she decided aloud.

[Surprising choice.]

Priz Wooley was the prisoner on the inside, that would pass a message to Carlen Holder.

“Without that reinforced sense of purpose, people fall apart.  But only if there’s another purpose to take over… and I don’t think many of us have that.”

It was a realization she was finding here, defining her own space.  It had started as an undefinable feeling when Carlen had dismissed the idea that the Gray-Frocked cultists might be able to play an eight-plus year long game, without any reinforcement of the cult’s ideas.

The long game and the chance to make a difference was purpose enough.  If there wasn’t anything else to get in the way or sidetrack them, they’d follow through.  Winnifred was sure of that.

[I have a housewarming present for you,] Toby told her.

“You being back and talking to me is present enough.”

[I can see that you’re happy.  If that’s so, I won’t feel pressured to give it to you.]

Winnifred glanced around, pretending she wasn’t bothered or curious.  What would be a present Toby could supply her?  Something decorative, made of nanotech?

She sorted through menus.  She knew she was being dumb, testing her patience against Toby’s, when Toby could wait a theoretical forever.  She ordered cleanup and disposal for the furniture in the main area, before dropping to the floor, lying on her side to see the configuration that attached to the underside of the furniture, raising and lowering it.

The side of her head settled on the floor.  “Tell me.”

[You have a call coming in one and a half hours.  An onboard named Basil will talk to you about preparation and next steps.]

“Basil?”  Winnifred pushed herself to an upright position.  “Preparation?”

[They try to pick out groups with a certain degree of diversity and types of attitude in mind, for good dynamics, and to match the energy of the moments.  I submitted an application on your behalf.  Basil has determined you would be a good inclusion tonight, between eleven and eleven thirty Belt time.  You’ll spend that time projected into A’s company.  It will be after her dinnertime, after she has a meeting.  Other members of Generation Colors will be around.  Basil will talk to you about etiquette, taking turns, and other details.]

Was there a word for a sense of awe at the awe she was going to feel?  She needed that for right now.

Everyone had sort of accepted the idea that Elabre had been the ones to arrange the masking of A’s moments with Bruin.  They’d started doing it with all members of their teams, which had caused a bit of a ruckus, because it seemed like a special treatment for the elite.  Winnifred had theorized it was Basil and out of stubbornness, maybe, hadn’t let go of that.

It gave her a weird feeling.  She was going to talk to him soon.

[Unless you want to refuse or reschedule.]

“No,” Winnifred said, very quickly.

She sat with that for a moment, before switching to whisper to talk to Toby.  It wasn’t a great way to hide what she was saying.  Anyone could look it up, but it was a pretend layer of privacy she could use.

“Do I talk about that?”

[That is entirely up to you.]

“I have to.”

Tonight, she was going to talk to A, head of Elabre, owner of a whole damned planet that Winnifred could see in the sky right now, if she stuck her head out her window.  The biggest celebrity in history if she went by sheer numbers or any of a dozen other metrics.  An actual hero.

To convince her that the Gray-Frocked were a real danger.

3.11.B – MUTE

Basil

3 Months Earlier

“We have a report of a slight delay from the Belt architects.  Hold off for a minute?” the staff member asked.

“Of course.  I hope everything’s okay,” A said.

“There’s no sign anything isn’t okay, from what it sounds like, they’re double-checking the double checks.”

“New situation with the second belt,” A commented.

“Yeah.”

“Your belt,” Caro, one of A’s current audience members, projected into her vicinity, commented.

“No, not mine.  Alcyone is a little bit mine.  Controlling interest, and I own most of the land.”

“Everyone knows it’s yours,” Baeza gushed.

“I might get in trouble if people keep saying that.”

It was interesting, Basil found, to look into the lives of the people in A’s orbit.  Every person with a job, with rare exceptions, was someone who wanted that job, or had taken it for specific reasons, with another goal in mind.  The staff member who was relaying the instructions about timing and double-checks over the architecture was Ta Lamay, someone who had been a part of My Yesteryear, another group like Generation Colors, that picked up a lot of the people who hadn’t been picked by other groups, starting at a later age and giving them a longer trial period, filtering them out year by year.

They tried, sometimes succeeding and sometimes failing, to pitch crossovers, where My Yesteryear’s roster would feature in other media.  Other times, they were a cast of new faces to serve as bad guys or filler.  Those crossovers were less common with Elabre’s celebrities, since they had a wide roster and a lot of contacts they drew on.  Generation Colors had never been on the same piece of media as My Yesteryear.

Ta hadn’t made the cut, ultimately ducking out because the strain of the work had gotten to her.  She had shifted over to government work around big projects and events like this, still close to the stage, so to speak, without being on it.

[You could score points with the staff member there.  You’ve seen a movie of theirs.]

A gave that a moment, glancing sideways, making brief eye contact with Ta.  Ta flashed a quick smile.

“You look familiar.  Have you been on staff for another event I did?” A asked.

“No, I think I would have remembered that.  Sorry.”

[Ta Lamay was an actress in Uneducated.  From My Yesteryear.]

“I liked that one,” A murmured.  To Ta, she said, “My onboard says-”

“I-I saw.”  Ta smiled, but her onboard tracked her vitals and the onboard relay network handed Basil all the details.  That she was happy and anxious in equal measure.

“Happy to be working with you,” A said.

“Of course- or, not of course, but-”

“A!”

Blue and Amber.

Ta all but buried her face in her hands as A turned toward her friends.

[Look after Ta.]

A turned, and took stock.  “Ta.”

Ta seemed lost for words.  “I’m putting my foot in my mouth, I don’t know…”

“You’re fine, you’re cool.  I blindsided you with your past and you’re acting blindsided.  That’s all it is.  I’m sorry.  Am I free to go talk with my band?”

“Yeah, o-of course.  It’ll be at least another minute.  But don’t go too far, they still want to coordinate.”

“Okay.  Thank you.”

[I’ll nag you if need be,] Basil offered.

“Only if absolutely necessary,” A warned.

“Oh, holy, holy.  Blue used to be my favorite,” Toni, one of A’s fans commented, to another.

The ‘holy, holy’ phrasing was a bit out of nowhere.  Something of a trend among A’s youngest fans, more appropriately aged for Generation Zodiac.  They were from a generation that wanted to stand out from the generation above them, and that meant a bit of religious iconography and phrasing.  The pushback against Gray-Frocked was part of it, but also a few of the other groups that still had their adherents. Subcultures that stuck to the same regions and superstructures.

Not that the youngest generation believed, as a rule of thumb.  Symbols, artwork, and phrases cropped up, though.  This was one, meant to speak to feelings on a bigger scale than the human body and mind had a capacity for.

Basil didn’t want to put A in the middle of that debate or dialogue, so he’d been careful to select members of A’s audience, when he could.  Some had to filter through, and this had been one, but he was still surprised it had happened.

So much of this was so delicate.  One person’s brief interaction with A could ruin or define their life.  That could include Ta being awestruck and caught off guard, then being torn apart, or pressured to resume her acting career, or turned into an idea, a meme, and losing all control of her life.

Basil didn’t want to be controlling, but if he wasn’t, people died, or there were riots, and disorder on a level that put A further into that spotlight where every action was sensitive.

One phrase said in A’s earshot could catch fire, metaphorically speaking, and those flames could spread.

A had to navigate around the staff working the event.  People were still connecting things to the stage and running tests.  That wasn’t what they were waiting for, but this had been a rush job and those techs would use every second of time they had to make sure nothing went wrong.  Even if it was sound and light work for a concert.

“You’re nervous,” Amber said.

“Yeah.  One of the bigger stages we’ve been on, I guess.  And it feels different.”

“You’re infectious, making me nervous,” Blue said.

“We’ve had a few delays,” Amber said.  She seemed jittery.

“Hey, are you absolutely sure you don’t want to do a solo song?” A asked.  “After?”

Amber shot A an ‘are you crazy’ look, wide eyed.

“Oh my god, yes!” someone in the background said.  The projected group with A was slightly muted and pushed out of focus.  So were the people in Amber and Blue’s company.  Each were slightly tinted in the respective colors – white, orange, and blue.  “Do it!”

That crowd clamored, and in that clamor, their voices dipped in volume a bit more.

“You’re my best friend, I love you, I want all of this to be good for you guys too.  Pick one of your best, most popular songs.  Butterfly Antlers.”

“That’s her second best,” Blue said.

Amber punched his arm lightly.

“It’s her favorite,” A said.

“It’s my favorite,” Amber echoed.

“When are you ever going to get to sing your favorite song in front of an audience like this?”

“Wanting me to go up on stage with no preparation?  Who does that?”

“I do, kind of.  Part of why I’m nervous, I guess, but it’s a good nervous.”

“That’s… inhuman.  Regular people can’t do that,” Amber replied.

“It’s a lot,” Blue said.  “Are you sure you’re going to be okay?”

“I don’t know.  But- and the media can quote me on this,” A said.  “If it flops… okay.  That’s the price, right?  That’s the price we pay to potentially do something amazing.”

“I’m so curious what song you’re going to sing,” Blue said.  “The way you’re talking, it sounds like it’s going to be an old one.”

“Vice!” one member of A’s contingent called out.

“Wrong connotations,” A murmured.  “Sorry.”

“Aw.”

A looked toward the stage, her heart hammering, and she had a period of lightheadedness and full-body goosebumps.

“It’s a new song,” Amber said.

They were ‘backstage’, which was a stage unto itself, with onboards giving billions of people a behind the scenes view of things, so there was a bit of ceremony, pomp, preparation, and polish put to things even here, backstage, that made it an event unto itself.  Staff, workers, and various other professionals and heads of government coordinated to get things ready.

Enough of those people were listening to this conversation that Amber’s statement and the response from everyone involved had an audible, visible effect on everyone present.  Quiet, stillness, a few intrigued looks.

Sixteen billion people were directly or indirectly tuned in to listen to and watch A.  Some had it on in the background while they did other things, waiting for the event.  Others had been hanging on every word.

“I know for a fact you haven’t been practicing anything new.  A new song, off the cuff?” Amber asked.

“No comment,” A said.

Her heart hammered.

It took only a few seconds.  The size of A’s viewing audience doubled.

“If I screw up, forgive me?  I thought it would be amazing if I could pull it off,” A said.

That number doubled again.

“What do we do?” Blue asked.

“Nothing different from what we planned and prepared for.  Be on stage with your instruments.  Bas can signal you.”

Ta Lamay, A’s coordinator, had been about to relay a message.  Now, unsure if she was about to coordinate disaster, she hesitated, hand slightly raised.

[Ta is signaling that it’s time.]

A flashed a smile at her friends.  “Love you.”

Ta closed the distance, and walked just to A’s right.  Basil disconnected the connections of A’s projected crowd of audience members as they approached the stage.

The number had doubled again.

“Break a leg,” Amber said, barely audible.

All across the belt, the vast majority of ships had been docked.  Others had pulled to designated zones and were now at rest.  Some bigger ships and stations had gone into a reduced power mode, and had all hands on deck, standing in place, waiting, watching through their own onboards, in case structural stresses were a problem.

For superstructures, it was the same.  Nothing ever did go wrong, but people were wary.  Machines had been brought out of four years of storage, polished up and prepared for disaster readiness.  Everything was in efficiency mode, manufacturing facilities and ag tech were on temporary pause.

Across the forty-five planets of the Belt, and the two diametrically opposed planets of this Belt, humanity had gone quiet.

A wasn’t the only person who felt the thud deep in her belly and her bones.

The first beat of a countdown, followed by the clicks and ticks of a clock’s mechanisms, turned into its own sort of music.  On the massive display in front of the crowd here on Alcyone, an old fashioned woodcut style display of the planets showed in crisp black against a white wall, with the countdown displayed as part of an arch above it, incorporating number systems and iconography from different cultures throughout human history.

A’s heart beat hammered at a rate of nearly two beats a second, almost fitting neatly in between the ticks of that countdown.  Almost.

“You’re on,” Ta told her.

White flower petals fell onto the stage.  A walked through the downpour.  Behind them, coordinators hurried to try to get the rest of Generation Colors to come.

The fact so many ships were docked and stations on standby meant there were more eyes than ever on this.  Her biggest crowd yet.

She’d invited Quinn, who she had tried really hard not to bother, and she’d invited her parents.  None of the three were present.

Bruin hadn’t wanted to be on stage, and didn’t count music as one of his strong traits anyway, but he had been invited, and he hadn’t taken advantage of the front row seats.  But he was out there, watching from a point nearer the back.

All casualties, in different ways, of A’s titanic presence.  They’d paid the prices at different times, in different ways.

The clock counted down.

It wasn’t true that they hadn’t practiced.  They’d used the back channel, simulated it in private, while A had appeared to be deep in thought.  They had leveraged the NDA process, blocking out meetings and then making sure they were alone, so A could belt it out and actually sing it.  But this was nerve-wracking for A for other reasons.

Four planets were at the center of this celebration and event.  Different people could tune into different ones for different moods.  One had a running commentary, smaller celebrations, and two media personalities were talking while some people danced on stage.  Another was a more somber, scholarly gathering on a superstructure with a good view of one of the facilities.  Another was more of a balance between that second one and this.  Aimed at a more sedate crowd.  Arguably A’s detractors.

But most were looking here.  An awful lot of people were quiet, waiting.

[Now.]

“Theiaaaaaaaaaaaa!” A shouted, and that ‘aaa’ became a sustained note.

She had really truly wanted to do this without Basil.

“Silent dust and silver stone, realm untouched by time unknown!”  Her accompaniment was the countdown clock.  “Our pull is more than tide or force, we call you home to join our course!”

Basil signaled the others.  He coordinated their beginning with the end of the countdown.

“Theiaaaaaaaaaaaa!” A scream-sang the word.

He could see it and feel it, through the onboard relay, that they were relieved when they saw what he’d put in front of them.  It was music they had done and practiced recently, to different lyrics.

Them joining in coincided with a number of different things.  Three of the Arcesso engines came to life, at different points in Alcyone’s night sky, above them.  The music came in with a bang and the final thud of the countdown, and it was loud enough, with enough impact, that the flower petals scattered.

The aurora of the Arcesso engines congealed in the sky above them.

When A resumed singing, returning to the first verse, it was with musical accompaniment, instead of that steady, mechanical beat from the countdown, and with a slightly different tempo.

Wan Graf messaged Basil.  “You two do realize you just gave what was meant to be a mining planet an anthem?”

Basil didn’t reply.

It was crass, to interject into this, even on an onboard’s message management platform that relatively few -a hundred thousand or so- would have any interest in looking at.

Technically, anyway, the better anthem would be a response to this, with a few things flipped around.  Basil had already bought a fair share of the new planet Theia, insofar as that was allowed by Belt Law, and had hired ships to claim a chunk of it on A’s behalf.

If it became permanent, the value of that land would centuple.

He had faith in A.

A, who was so nervous he had to manage the quiver of her breaths, and suppress a tremor in a leg muscle.  A, who was thrilled.

For years, as new planets were brought into the belt, Generation Colors and A had had their parts in the events, but Elabre had been scared of having A or Generation Colors headline one.  Then, when she’d been more situated and confident, with no signs of her popularity flagging, they’d said circumstances weren’t right.

In the end, it had been about control and power.  It had been about the fact they didn’t have power, and when it came down to it, they didn’t have the means to stop A when she started pushing for more rights for her group, and the other teams.  So they’d done away with the fiction.  A had taken Elabre.

Then circumstances hadn’t been right for other reasons.  The buying of Alcyone, being tired, then finding their footing.

A stretched out her arm, inviting the crowd, then sang-shouted with them.  “Theiaaaaaaaaaaa!”

The crowd and half the members of Generation Colors joined in.

And the long, sustained note was broken as Theia crashed into the night sky above them, suspended by two of the Arcesso Engine’s beams.  The third flashed to life with a different wavelength, correcting direction, speed, and spin.  With its appearance and its sudden movement, everyone felt the shift in gravity, like the G-panels turning on, or a sudden drop of an old elevator.

A let the interruption happen, laughed, and then whooped, before finding her place again.

The members of Generation Colors on stage weren’t completely in sync, either, but the energy of the moment more than made up for it.

[Reports are giving the all clear.  It’s not another Inuii situation.  No life on our sister planet.]

That had been the last lingering worry.  One of the excuses that Elabre had given, as to why Generation Colors shouldn’t headline.  That they would do this, heading an event, tying themselves to that event, only for it to be a disaster.  Accidental genocide, again.

With that concern gone, A could let lose that final one percent more, singing her heart out.

The song finished.  Theia was suspended in the sky, the wake of the Arcesso engine still expanding in a spherical aurora-like cloud around it.

Breathing hard, A stepped back, letting Blue and Green come forward, each wearing a guitar.

[Good?]

“Good, Basil.”

➨

2 Months, 4 weeks ago; 1 Week After Theia

“Mm, Bas, I’m tired.”

[You’ve been tired for a while.  Get up and build some momentum.]

“Mmmmnnnnno.  No.”

Like a petulant child.

[You’re depressed.]

“Mmf.”

[I’ll go easy on you tonight, but only if you commit to tomorrow being a better day.  Too many people are counting on us.]

“I want to book another trip.  Off the belt, off-network.”

[We can plan that.  We have a time window in a little while.]

A groaned, and twisted up, hair, clothing, and covers forming an inconsistent pile.

[We’ll need to find a balance, somehow.  If the emotional highs and intensity of a big event like Theia arriving come with downswings like this…]

“Nag!  Nag nag nag!”

Childish.

“I worked hard, I can’t go outside the belt again, so let me sleep in,” A groaned, and it was a moaning sort of groan that came from low in the throat, combined with A drawing the covers tighter around her body.

She had been ‘sleeping in’ for days, only doing the bare essential activities with half the intensity of her usual.

There was another side to it, however.  Basil was blocked off from accessing the brain stem and the interior of the skull, and so he was limited in what he could do to help A manage.  With the hormones the brain released, endorphins and dopamine both, what came up had to come down.

[Alright.  You do have obligations with the audience participation.]

“Put it off,” she said.

[You may tie your hands later, doing this.]

“If I ask to put it off, put it off.”

[Understood.]

“Don’t make me be an asshole.”

[Understood.  I’m sorry.]

“Would I even have been able to do it without the architecture?  Without you making my throat and body stronger, reshaping my throat so I can hit those notes better?  Keeping my energy levels up so I could practice?”

[Everyone has onboards.  You might as well ask if we could have put on a good show without clothes.]

A let out a half-laugh.

[What?]

“Just a thought,” she mumbled, before pushing her face deeper into the pillow.

“Don’t make me laugh when we’re having a conversation like this.”

[Understood.  I do mean what I said.  It’s ordinary, it’s normal.]

“I meant what I said too, Basil.  I don’t want to be a pissy teenager like I was, with venom instead of blood in my veins.  I don’t want to hate you.  But please hear what I’m saying.”

[I’m afraid I don’t fully understand.  Can I be honest?  This isn’t me trying to deflect or avoid taking in what you’re saying.]

“Go for it.”

[Part one of Basil being honest: like a bride after a wedding, you’ve spent your reserves, something your life was leading up to over months-]

“Years.  My life itself, leading up to a moment like that.”

[Yes.  You’re on the backswing and the letdown from that.  Those feelings and spent reserves are trying to find a voice.]

“Maybe, Bas.”

[Frankly, I’m worried you don’t fully understand either, and you’ll get mad at me for not finishing the thought.]

“Maybe leave me alone to sleep, and if I figure it out, I’ll let you know.”

[Understood.]

“But just as a starting point?  It wasn’t my victory.  It was ours.“

She was already shifting more toward a sleep state, so he let that pass without comment.  They could have exchanged more words over that, but he wouldn’t be telling her anything she didn’t already know.  That there was no choice.  That the two of them extricating from one another wasn’t optional.  It wasn’t even legal.

He took stock, as she drifted off.  Always, constantly, he was on the lookout for the next groups of her projected crowds of fans.  Background processes interviewed them and gave them the rundown.

[…The objective is for everyone to have a certain block of time.  We’ll signal you if you’re taking more than your fair share.  If you’ve sat back for most of the time block and have something to say, you can request time.  Any questions?]

No questions.  People planets away were coordinated in shaking their heads in response.

[Be prepared for time lag.  We may or may not change how we address you or prioritize your time if you’re experiencing a longer lag than the others, as it can be hard to break into the conversation with even a short delay.  Provided you don’t change planets in the next few hours, you should be fine.]

“I’m tempted to hop on a ship!” a boy named Condor joked.

[I’ll send your onboards the information about the time delays, plan accordingly.  This is about having a short conversation, a few minutes in her company.  If it so happens that she’s busy with work, please don’t panic, we’ll extend your time block accordingly.  A is busy and a lot happens fast.]

The real question would be the rest of Generation Colors.  He’d raise the topic of letting a few of them step back.  Some wouldn’t, even if they were tired, like Amber and Te.  Those two went especially hard.  Blue and Green either both took it easy or both competed with one another.

That was only one piece of it.  Always and constantly, he was watching those who watched her, and there were billions of those people.  More than the resources of her body alone could handle.  He could access this superstructure’s resources to help, plugging himself in to turn ninety pounds of efficient processing power running off of A’s biology into a computer bigger than the mountains on a fresh mining planet.  But that got attention.

Better to have that mountain working in the background, obfuscated and subtle, not part of the onboard relay network, watching people who watched people who watched people, passing information this way and that, periodically hopping, skipping, and jumping off of nearby systems, or storing larger packets on those systems to be diffused out to the onboard that requested it.  Not part of the Belt network, in the sense that it wasn’t open data free for anyone to access.

It could look for the variables Basil wanted, and he could merely dip his toes in, making a brief request, and get what he needed.

This was how Basil kept a closer eye on Robert Simes, ex-president of Earth, and other key players.  He used an access point and requested minor data from the server several times a minute, and that was poised to serve as an alert system if there was an emergency, like Robert Simes leaking information after all.

No emergency right now, but there were other things that had Basil’s attention.  People that had been in Robert Simes’ orbit were trying to get in touch with him.

Those same people had been meeting under NDAs for some time, talking about business mergers that hadn’t yet happened.

As they left those meetings, their onboards were hard at work.

Basil could make small tweaks to the automated processes of Elabre’s systems, and adjust the prioritization of ad buys, at the same time he was adjusting a proposed schedule for Generation Colors.  He had to wait for other onboards to get back to him, and some were taking their time, requesting data or checking with others.

They were as tired as A was, and the high of the event hadn’t been as sharp for them.  They had practiced more overtly, singing, dancing, and doing all the side work, including ad work, the constant audience engagement, and filming.

He knew how humans worked, and what they prioritized.  He knew that Generation Colors was flashy, and would catch the eye, and his work with them would distract.  Meanwhile, in the background he made small, boring adjustments to ten thousand things, including signing permissions for some ads to go forward and launch, and tailoring ads to groups.  All of it was in line with what A had agreed to earlier in the day, in a brief period she’d been up and making food.

Glend Autry was taking his time walking down Garden Bridge, on his home superstructure, which was lightly populated and very expensive.  The man was one of the people who had led the debate over the belt architecture, ran a superstructure dominated by groundbreaking science, and knew next to nothing about science himself.  A mouthpiece for certain interests, with enough money and connections to get included in other conversations.  Elabre had dealt with him a few times when they’d been building an apparatus in space for one filming, a few years back.  They’d wanted to invent something for a real-world slow motion effect, and the man had people tooled up with new mods that let them do some odd things like that, with small particle manipulation.  In the end, he’d refused when he’d had little reason to, and Basil had quietly slotted him a few columns over in his calculations of who was friendly, who was a threat.

The recent meetings with other people who didn’t like A and the man’s attempts to reach out to Robert Simes so close to those meetings left Basil sure that something was going on.  A conspiracy against A.

Ads were light, plant life was everywhere, and the two often worked in concert with one another, with holographic images stopping to smell and touch the flowers in the midst of their routines and displays.

Glend Autry’s heart would have been hammering, if it wasn’t for his onboard, Basil was fairly sure.  It was late in the evening, and the garden was most appealing in daylight, so it was barely occupied.

Ads played around him.  Background noise for most, but, by happenstance -by Basil’s design- all of the advertisements around the garden bridge were simultaneously of A.  They looked Glend Autry’s way.  Images that broadcast across the side of a superstructure, behind benches, and on the selectively placed flat surfaces, many pale, light-haired, dressed in white.  It was enough to visibly brighten the area.

He stopped in his tracks, but before he’d even lost his momentum, some of the ads had changed, and others were looking away.

Basil watched through Glend’s eyes and onboard, and watched remotely.

Basil wasn’t intimately acquainted with the man’s onboard, but he could tell that the onboard had to work in the aftermath of that to keep Glend calm.  The amount of work it was doing suggested the reaction could have been extreme.

Glend was going to be the easiest to shake.  Whatever he did, after this, whether it was running or pushing for more meetings, it would help Basil to work against the conspiracy.

While A slept, Basil played the watchdog.  Glend hurried home, and opened communication with Amahle Baard, a key player in the mining infrastructure and development of the tools that let whole planets be taken apart for minerals.

Baard looked in on Glend, looked back at the bridge, but never opened the scene up to his full view.  He was on a ship, and his attention was on eating.  With things in miniature, he didn’t see the full impact of the ads all focusing on Glend for that one singular moment.  Emotionally, he wasn’t in the same place, so he didn’t treat it the same way.

“Leave it be, Glend, go home and sleep.”

The man was more annoyed than anything.

Better to let that simmer.  Basil could leave Glend isolated and anxious, let this moment become a thing of the past.  His real issue was how much the onboards let these men manage their feelings and put on a brave face.  They didn’t waver or show weakness.  They didn’t retreat.

They were still a danger to A.  Basil had to find out how much.

Theia’s space was still being controlled and managed.  They had bought a whole piece of the planet to capitalize on public sentiment.  By giving Theia an anthem and an event, they had given the crowds something to care about.  There would be pressure, now, for Theia to remain, not as a mining planet, but as a settled one.  Perhaps it would be only partially mined.

Either way, A’s controlling interest in the planet meant the area around it was partially A’s, to manage and protect.  Baard, being so focused on mining, wanted to be close to the new planet.

Basil could reach through the superstructures there, his hand hidden, and bid the authorities to do a ‘random’ spot check of Baard’s ship, his onboard shut off while things were searched, on pretext of an audit.

Strip away that emotional armor.

[Hello, Baard,] Basil messaged the man.  This was technically a judiciary inquiry, so they had privacy.

Baard, still eating a porterhouse steak with onion and mushroom and kelp from Eingana, glanced up at the panel where Basil’s image appeared.  He chewed slowly before responding.  “Glend wasn’t wrong, then.”

[I’m seeing a conspiracy to target A.]

Without the onboard to manage, Baard’s nervousness showed.  It might have even showed more than normal, because he’d come to rely on his onboard so much to help him bluff.

“She’s too powerful,” Baard replied.

[She does good.  Protects her employees.  She’s keeping a slice of nature alive.]

“She’s too powerful,” Baard repeated himself, before taking another bite.  “The rest of that is beside the point.”

[I have to ask.  Was the plan for you all to assassinate A?]

“Extreme word.”

[Clandestine meetings by people who have lost some of their grip over the Belt.  Extreme nervousness from several.  You’ve left clues.]

“You’ll ask others for clarification on what I say, I’m sure.”

[Yes.]

“We’ve discussed assassination, yes.  Character assassination, not a weapon.  Not death.  But if you destroy someone’s character, and take enough from them, is it that different from actual death?”

[I understand what you’re saying.  You’re aware, I hope, that you can’t continue with your plan, or keep meeting.  I know what you’re doing.  Some will have to be informed.  When A wakes up, she will be informed there was a conspiracy to assassinate her character.  She’ll be one of the ones informed.  We’d be prepared.]

“I’m aware.  It’s done.  Fair play, onboard.  You’re doing a good job of protecting your host.”

It was a weird statement, coming from the man.

“You can keep tabs on me however you like, as part of my surrender,” Baard said.  “I don’t believe what I was doing was strictly illegal.  Talk, even talk about trying to unseat a rival in business or politics, isn’t against the law.  Make a deal with me, same as you did with Robert Simes.”

[That’s implying there was any deal.]  There wasn’t.  Only the threat.  But Simes was a smart man who could see things through to their conclusion.  The deal was implicit.

Baard looked up and gave Basil a half-smile before returning his eyes to his food.

[Either way, my willingness to give you a deal assumes I accept what you’re saying about it being character assassination.]

The man, without his onboard, wasn’t completely unable to hide his unease.  A moment of raised eyes.  He made eye contact with Basil’s projected image of the image fans had made for him: a slender man with combed white hair and a light gray suit with no tie.  Sometimes it was green, but there were many debates about whether A’s onboard should have a color, or stick to A’s classic color, white.  He’d broken the difference by having a sprig of basil at his lapel.  They always gave his eyes a great deal of character, with large luminescent irises and reptilian pupils, and left his expression blank.  The emotiveness was in the angle of his head, how he held himself with hands clasped, or emoting.

Baard looked away too quickly after that fleeting moment of eye contact, properly looking at Basil for the first time.

[As a group, it’s an odd one.  Rich and powerful men and women.  Are they men and women who found each other through a mutual hatred of A?]

“Call it a mutual concern that she’s too powerful.”

[When was that contact established?  When were those opinions evidenced?  I’ve looked through records.  A group of a seemingly random assortment, who, according to you, decide to assassinate her character.  All you have is money and leverage.  I’m not saying it’s impossible, but surely you’d seek out and recruit someone who is good at that sort of thing.]

“We’re all a little bit good at it, onboard,” Baard replied.

[The alternate explanation is that the group isn’t random, and much like a classic heist, everyone involved has a specific role.  You’re a financier with controlling interest in mining worlds and the ability to make contact with dangerous elements that hide out from the wider Belt Network.  Onboard adoption is three decimal places away from wholesale adoption.  You’d have access to those who haven’t adopted it.]

Baard put his knife and fork down, wiped at the corner of his mouth, and then sat back, holding his cup so it rested against the table’s edge.

[Glend Autry has access to specific weapons, including the newly debuted Dragon-class mod, personal small particle drives.  As a mouthpiece for various mod science and drive science creators, he appears at events with heavily modded women on each arm, both made out to be interesting and striking.  Things A has gravitated toward in the past, in her friend group.  Glend thus offers both access and a possible weapon.]

Baard took a drink.

[The random spot check isn’t as random as it appeared.  It’s the start of a wider investigation.  The authorities will want to discuss it with you.]

“She’s too powerful, onboard.  This is a good example of how and why.  I don’t just mean that she’s too powerful, she’s a threat to people who have controlling interests in planets and who make decisions that define government, economy, and science.  She’s too powerful for her own good.  She’s too powerful for your good.”

[So she’s meant to die?] Basil asked.

“Something we talked about as a theoretical exercise, toyed around with seeing if we could put pieces into place.  It’s not something we put in motion.  It was way we could breathe.  To not have our hatred bottled up and intensifying.  Reminding ourselves there was a way out, and this wasn’t the way things would settle.”

[I don’t believe you, Amahle Baard.  Especially when you’ve just revealed you lied to me a minute ago.  You hate her after all.]

“Don’t we all?  Don’t you?  Or wouldn’t you, if you had emotions?  The way she treated you for so long?”

[Your perspective is warped.  I’d love her.]

“You raised her.  Like any parent, you can love and hate your child at the same time.”

[I have no emotions, except ones that emerge from my purpose.]

The judiciary was docking with the ship.  When the ship’s crew couldn’t reach Baard, they lit up nearby panels with red messages.  Only the one Basil was using remained, a vague white glow from a singular screen in a now-red room.

“That’s for me, I suppose.  You know, as one final thought, onboard, we’ve had long conversations, trying to analyze A, decide why she did certain things at certain times.  Cataloguing the oddities.”

[You and many others.]

“We had conversations about you too.  Others fall more firmly on one side of the fence or the other.  I remain poised on that fence.”

[What fence, Baard?]

“Are you unequal to the task of being onboard for that woman?  If so, oh no.”

[Or am I equal to it?]

“If you are, then I’d have to say… oh no.”

➨

Now

“Your drink,” a staff member said, intercepting A as she walked through Elabre headquarters.

“Thank you, Worrell,” A said.  “Guys, if you aren’t twenty-four-seven watchers, this is Worrell, one of three executive assistants.  They rotate.  Their job is to read our minds and our Onboard logs and do things for us before we realize we want them.  It’s unfair and I really wish it was easier to have a conversation without asking, hey, Amber is early, has anyone checked on her?”

“Of course,” Worrell said.

“…which is me asking and getting an answer to a question I really already know the answer to.  Because these guys are great and because I can look at the history through onboards.  Thank you, Worrell.”

“Thank you, Worrell,” the projected cast of people in A’s company echoed.  Worrell flashed a smile.

A’s route through the building took her through departments.  Each was already prepared with a walk-through presentation.

A staff member sent A some complementary material while launching into a much-practiced pitch.  “For Generation Unnamed, we’re workshopping different ideas.  Generation Garden strikes for a baseline cutesy, clean, late 1800s aesthetic with animal themes.  Dormouse, toad, rabbit, sparrow.”

“Doesn’t that limit us genre-wise?” A asked.

“We’ve workshopped some cross-genre ideas.  Garden as an overelaborate construction with some aesthetic callbacks.”

A stopped to look.  The ‘garden’, ‘meadow’, and ‘hedge’ science fiction constructions that were meant to be on theme seemed to be more decoration than function.  In the projected images of the station itself, the interior looked like it had been kept old fashioned, pre-Victorian style in organization and framing, but in modern materials, for some anachronism.

“I did say I wanted unique.  This feels weird, though.  I’m feeling the genre constraints.”

“Constraint breeds creativity,” Onna, the person who’d pitched it answered.

“Reminds me of the dollhouse date with Bruin,” Anderson, one member of A’s group remarked.

Basil supplied images.  The ‘dollhouse date’ was an art and antique show.  One whole area had a lot of stalls with old dollhouses, dolls, and miniature furniture.  They’d been enchanted by it.

A’s mood visibly changed with that reminder, and a glance at those images.  Basil’s research found where the creator of the Generation Garden pitch had indeed called up those same images.

“Sorry,” Anderson added.

“No.  That’s a good insight.  Spot on.  That’s the sort of thing that could earn you a job at Elabre, if you hone it.  Onna?”

“Ma’am.”

“Pitch something that works for the two belts full of kids who are going to grow up with these guys.  Don’t pitch to try to cater to me, evoking some good memory.  Next?”

Reb Hammons pitched Generation Post.  Baker, builder, tailor, driver, gardener.  Everyone with an old fashioned, ‘classic’ job.

“Works a lot better for very small kids, maybe for adults, once they’ve settled in, but I’m worried we’ll lose them in the teenage years.  Hard to hold onto or play with a label like that when teenagers want to match their identity to something.”

“Am I retooling this or throwing it out entirely?”

“You know what?  Retool it,” A said.  “Show me you can take the concept and elevate it, or move it laterally, to appeal to teens.  Have a focus group test against it.”

They moved on through Sales, which was tracking what was working and what wasn’t, out of recent work.  A bit of a dip, with A being down and out and a few taking a cue from her.  A picked out some people to come with her, and talked to the group in her company as they walked through to Projects, where A quickly laid out the possibility of letting members of Generation Colors decide if they wanted to join the next project or not, and deciding what the project would be depending on the strengths and weaknesses of those people.

From there, straight to the outdoors, where a glass canopy and retractable walls protected a conference table from the elements.  Amber was a startling orange amid dusk colors, in a usual spot, as far from the door as possible, leaning over a railing.  Sometimes when meetings were held, she’d remain where she was, by the railing, feeling the breeze that swept past the side of the superstructure.

“Bye guys,” A murmured.  Saying goodbye to the group that had accompanied her for the last forty minutes.

[Next group lined up,] Basil reported.

“Get them acclimated?  Give me a sec?  We can stretch out their time to compensate.”

[Of course.]  This was a good group.  There were a few oddballs that Basil hoped would pique A’s interest and get her engaging with that group, as a further step toward getting back into her usual routine.

A drank the last of what Worrell had supplied her, before putting the cup on the table.  She walked over to Amber, who was talking to her own projected group.  “Hi, Amber.  You’re always so early.  Te too, but Te’s been tired.”

“The body modding took a lot out of them, last filming,” Amber said.

“That’s too bad.  I was thinking about letting Generation Colors choose if they wanted onboard.  Gives people who need more of a rest more of a rest.”

Amber smiled.

Her stress levels were high.  Basil drew it to A’s attention.

“Don’t tell me you’re leaving for a while or something,” A said.

“Not really,” Amber said.  “Can’t we have one conversation without onboards sticking their noses into things?  Reading our emotions?  You and me?”

“We can try,” A said.

Amber dismissed her group.  A contemplated dismissing her own, but she’d had enough downtime this week that she couldn’t, without breaking the same rules she’d set from her executive position with Elabre.  She motioned for them to wait, and they caught her eye, distracting her.  One interesting physical mod, nearly bifurcated top to bottom, one who was a ‘dragon’ mod, loaded with a small particle engine in each arm, and a modded dockworker with a prehensile tail, reversible limbs, and more.

There was also someone unmodded who might as well have been, with the level of high fashion they wore, and an artist, dressed in relatively ordinary clothes, painted with a degree of detail most clothing couldn’t handle- their art.

The fact they’d given her mental pause and piqued her interest was a win Basil privately filed for himself.  She wanted to talk to them.

But she also wanted to talk to Amber.

“We haven’t had many heart to hearts lately.”

“Ever,” Amber said.

“You don’t think?”

Amber shrugged in response.  “Have we ever really talked?  We’ve vented to each other, but even when we do that, it’s with an audience looking over our shoulders.  It’s you knowing that if you say the wrong thing, people could die again.”

A sighed.

Amber added, “If we did have a lot of heart to hearts, you’d think we’d have talked about that more, but we’re always on guard.”

“True.”

“Wouldn’t it be nice if we weren’t?” Amber asked.  “If we could just say what’s on our minds?  If we could put the audience away?  Or stop caring what they thought?”

She turned, arms wide and stretched to where they could catch the patter of ambient moisture from the sky, resting her lower back against the railing for stability.

“What prompted this?” A asked, leaning against that same railing.

“Theia.”

“Pretty big.  Our biggest numbers ever.”

“Huge,” Amber said.  “You had trouble getting out of bed after.”

“I was wiped out.  Yeah.”

“More than that.  I think there’s this problem that crops up.  How do you top that?”

“I guess… we grow the belt population.  We plan better, new surprises, new ideas,” A replied.  “Or maybe we pivot.  New generation coming up, Generation Zodiac… the challenge becomes getting the next generation to that level.”

Amber opened her mouth, then closed it.

“I don’t know,” A said, quickly.  “That’s me.  Stuff I’ve thought about.  I don’t know what you want.”

Amber was silent, smiling a bit.

“What?” A asked.  She nudged Amber’s arm a bit.

Amber shook her head.

“I was thinking of going outside the belt for a trip again.  I don’t know how it would work, but maybe we could go together?  Get outside the belt, off the belt network?  Where we can actually have those heart to hearts?”

“People would get ideas,” Amber said.  “No.  Sorry.”

“No, it’s fine.  I don’t know if we’d wind up wanting to kill each other, if it’d be too much proximity, or if the ship was too large, too little?  Or…”

A trailed off.

Amber sucked in a deep breath, then exhaled, before shaking her head.

The conversation seemed to die with that.  Worrell came in to drop off a fresh drink for A, pitchers, and cups.  She was out of earshot, but it was a further obstruction for good conversation.

“My group is getting a bit antsy,” A said.  “If you do want to talk, I hope you know you can.”

She gave the railing a pat and turned to go.

“Can I?” Amber asked, when A was a few paces back.

A turned back to face Amber.  “Can you?”

“Talk?” Amber asked.

“Yeah.  You can.  We’ll figure something out, some place we can-”

“I hate you.”

A fell silent.

Amber stood a little straighter.  That latent nervousness had multiplied tenfold.  She didn’t seem to know what to do with her hands as she paced, stepping closer to the end of the table.

“Do you know how hard I’ve worked?  The process?  I wanted this from the time I was knee high.  I took classes, I sang, I danced until I felt like I’d throw up, I was so tired.  I acted.  I went to doctors appointments, had my onboard guiding my growth.  I fought like hell.”

“Naturally talented and you worked hard,” A said.

“Got into Generation Colors.  Best group like this for my age.  Worked my ass off.  Jan was always favored for the leading girl role but I could- I could work at it, focus, study, and get that spot, enough of the time it felt worth it.  So I showed up early, I came to more of the practices for singing and dance than anyone else.  I know I have talent and I was lucky to have that innate ability, but I wanted to work for it too.”

She smiled, raising her hands toward A, palm-up.  “Then you.  It’s not just talent, they call you a genius.  You sure showed that, with a barely-practiced song in front of a record setting audience.  The fucking movement of planets between galaxies timed to punctuate everything you were doing.  You blew it out of the water.”

“I don’t know if-”

“Don’t talk?  Let me say my piece?” Amber asked.  “You’ve taken over center stage by existing.  Let me have my stage.  Saying what I’ve said already, I’ve already got people who hate me and are angry at me.  More people who want to defend you than I ever had as a full audience on my own.”

“I don’t think you’re wrong, you-”

Amber held a finger to her lips.

A stopped.

“I’ve never not hated your guts.  But I saw it as another hurdle to cross, like making it through the process that filtered countless kids down to the Generation Colors you know today.  I had to act, play along.  If being the enemy of the girl who stopped the terrorist attack on the science center means I’m hated, and being her friend means I rack up more audience… I’ll pretend.  I’ll act, every fucking day.”

Some of Generation Colors had noticed the fracas and were racing to get here, to stop Amber before she took things too far.

“I wanted you to fail.  To fall behind.  But you didn’t.  It hits me.  I can pretend to be your friend, I can pretend to be a support.  I can play along, because that’s the job, and I watch the Theia performance and I know I will never have that.  I’m giving my all just to keep up and stay relevant, but I’ll never get there.  Because I’m human, and you’re-”

Amber’s face screwed up for a second, almost a snarl.

“-you’re not.”

“That’s not fair!” one of the projected members of A’s group shouted.  “That’s not right, you know that’s not right!”

Other voices joined in.  Others stayed quiet.

“There it is.  I might get death threats or people trying to kill me for saying that.  The messages are mounting up.  I will never-” Amber smiled, eyes wet.  She was barely audible over the group’s shouts.  “-never act again.  Never sing on a stage.  Never go out in public without a real fear of dying.  That’s the price of truth.  My truth, anyway.  But I can’t do that anymore, faking it.”

“Can I say something, at some point?” A asked.

“You know I’m not the only one?  I can’t guess who, because as it turns out, a group of actors raised from birth, hand picked from the best of the best, is really good at faking it, but I know I’m not the only one who feels this way.  Resents you, resents that the fucking planets orbit where you want them to.”

That affected A.  Amber saw it, and her smile widened a bit, but not because of any victory or happiness.  More like another emotion in there had made muscles twist and wrench and that pulled the corner of her mouth sideways.

“The company is yours-” Amber said.

“I took control so I’d have the ability to give people breaks, and a say, and-”

“Did anyone ask you to!?” Amber raised her voice.  “I got into this from the beginning, knowing it would be hard!  Knowing it would be shitty corporate types telling me where to go and what to do, and I wanted that!  But now it’s yours, your company, and the rest of us are like characters in a long, awful scene you’re directing.  Your scene.”

“That’s not how I see you.”

“I had talks with my parents and planned, I had long conversations with other people and myself, making sure I wanted this.  I knew, as much as any kid could, what I was getting into, and I signed on!  But then you showed up and you changed it all.  The tone, the- who was important, the dynamics, the purpose of it all.  It’s not enough that you cut in line and turn my dream job into the A show, all about giving you chances to show off, putting you front and center.  Every decision revolving around you, what suits you best, what leverages your abilities?  You’re in the ads, you’re deciding fashion, the news covers you nonstop.  I hear you as background music when I go somewhere to get a break from you!”

“Give her more time in charge of Elabre, she’ll change that!”

“She was just talking about giving more focus to the younger generations!”

A cringed internally at the defenses her supporters were throwing out there.

[A.  I can tell you want to cry, but-]

“No.  Because if I do, the backlash against her is worse.”

[Alright.]

“I don’t know-“

“You’re a nightmare,” Amber said, talking over the words from A she couldn’t hear,  “It’s a long, slow nightmare I can’t get away from.”

“-what to do.”

[This is years of pent up frustration.  Let her get through them, then we try to find a good way forward when the emotions are spent.  Or we wait for others to arrive.]

“What if they agree with her?”

Those tears Basil had taken note of wanted to spring forth.

“I keep going back to the night you had sex with Bruin.  The way the data was unverifiable, different inputs from different streams.  I keep thinking… did you show your hand?”

“What hand?” A asked.

“Was it rigged from the start?” Amber asked.  Her tone of voice had changed.  “You save the world, Elabre offers you a chance to be even more famous, and with a scared, traumatized teenager in front of them, they offer to rig things from the start?  They use the fact they created the IDLX onboard series and have contacts in government and judiciary to let you submit false reports and dodge system audits?”

“I’m going to tell her,” A said, through the back channel.  “About the back channel.”

[The consequences of that would be severe.]

“It must have gotten too big for them.  They gave you a way of cheating, and then you got bigger than they thought you would, and then you took over.  It’s the only way things make sense to me.”

“She deserves better.”

[This won’t earn her forgiveness, or her friendship.  I don’t think she was lying about resenting you all this time-]

“Just admit it!” Amber raised her voice.  It dropped a few levels.  “Please, just admit it.”

[-and you should know.  It would spell the end of me.  You would, I suppose, be free of me, finally.]

“I don’t want that, exactly.  But I think she deserves to know.”

Te and Blue had come in through the door.  Some staff were already gathered just past the door.

They approached, but Amber tensed up when they reached the halfway point of the long conference table.  She put up a hand, motioning for them to stop.

This was between her and A.

[There will be more to cover later, in the time window between this conversation and when they turn me off.  Threats against you, essential knowledge.  Setting that aside, it has been an honor to work alongside you, Ms. Teeg.]

“No,” A said.  She closed her eyes.

“What?” Amber asked.

A’s eyes remained closed for a long period of time.  “No.  Elabre didn’t help me cheat, though they pretended it was them, after my night with Bruin.  And they didn’t ask questions.  It wasn’t that.”

Amber was tense, full-body.

“When I was transformed with nanotech-” A started.

She closed her eyes again.

“Spit it out,” Amber said.

“-Basil was inspired.  I don’t know if it was a million monkeys on a million typewriters, but he came up with some good encryption and decryption or something.  He’s… very good at what he does.  And he’s been learning to push the rules all my life.”

A partial truth.  A quarter-truth.  Nothing that damned A.  Nothing that would see Basil deleted.  At worst, they’d ask, and at worst, he’d make something up.

“So your singing is really you?” Amber asked.  There was derision in her tone.  “Your acting?  You can sing without practice-”

“I practiced.  At the tail end of meetings like the one we’re about to have here.  Times and places I knew the audience couldn’t see.  Technically not part of the NDA-”

[Technically it was.  I added it to the fine print,] Basil interjected.  He raised an image of the fine print in question.

Amber seemed to deflate, hearing that.  Seeing that.

“See?  He’s a trickster.  Catches even me off guard,” A said.

“Amber,” Te said.

“Hi, Te.  I was so focused on her I didn’t see you.  It’s apparently not a trick.  She’s apparently really that good at singing and acting.  One in fifty trillion, never before seen, not to be seen for another few centuries.  Really special.  And she shows up in my life and pushes me into the background.”

“We can talk about that,” Te said.  “Let’s talk about that, on our own, away from this.”

“You know I kept playing this over and over in my head?  I’d be trying to study a script and I’d be playing this out instead.  Imagining the responses I’d get.”

“I get it,” Te said, approaching.

A looked at Te, hurt.  Apparently, she interpreted that as Te sharing Amber’s sentiments.  Te put out a hand, gently, as if to tell A to stand down.

“I tricked myself though.  I kept the script looping in my head, imagining calling it out, telling her how I really feel.  Knowing how many people are seeing and listening, and hate me for spoiling the illusion of their beautiful, important A.”

“I’ve had a lot of loops go through my head.  Mostly aimed at myself, not anyone else,” Te said.

“I kept asking myself, if I’m being realistic, what’s the point I reach where I do it.  Say it out loud?” Amber asked.  Her voice had gone quiet.  “And Theia was it.”

“Yeah,” Te said.

“I should have told her the truth.  I still can.”

[I will back you, whatever your decision.  If you need me to lie, to ease up the stress on you, I can.]

“I got the words wrong, I rushed it, I got emotional when I told myself I’d lay out the facts.”

“You wanted to get the emotions out, you did that.  The rest is improv.  You’re an actor, it makes sense,” Te said.

Amber huffed air through her nostrils.  Almost a laugh.  “I tricked myself, thinking if I spelled it out, the truth as I saw it, then call her out directly, I’d get more truth.  She’d admit it was a big cheat by Elabre.  Then maybe it’d be okay.  However bad it got, it would be balanced by me being the person who called out the big lie and uncovered the scandal.  That was a big part of the fantasy that kept looping through my head.”

“I think you got the truth and it’s unsatisfying.  Listen, Amber, you haven’t eaten all day, or most of yesterday.  Let’s go eat, and talk, and figure out options,” Te said.

“She didn’t admit it,” Amber said.  “And now it won’t be okay.  I’ve just incinerated my life and dreams.”

“Amber,” A said.  “This is something we can handle.  I don’t blame you.  I understand.  I-”

“Don’t,” Amber interrupted.  She raised hands close to her ears, stopping short of covering them.  “Don’t save the day.  Don’t be the hero.  Don’t offer up a fix.  Not if it’s yours.”

A fell silent.

“Basil?”

Even in the back channel, A sounded distraught, more like a child than an adult.

“It’s freeing, you know?” Amber said, to Te.  “Being honest for once?  Even when it does damage I can’t ever fix.”

“It’s more fixable than you’re pretending.”

[What can I do for you?]

“Tell me, all those years I was saying not to interfere, to let my life be my life… how did you figure it out?  What’s the answer?  When someone’s saying that?”

[I don’t know.]

Amber turned.  With the light augmentation of her onboard, she was athletic.  She went from a standing position to a sprint with little warning.

Te was faster to react than A.  Long-limbed, athletic, and augmented on a level that went far beyond ‘light’, Te was just as fast to move.  Faster, at a top speed.  A followed.

For most of their time with Generation Colors, Amber had liked to stand by the railing, looking down the face of the superstructure.  It was always her perch, her preferred seat while waiting for a meeting.

She’d spent a lot of time reviewing A’s history, by her own admission.  She had seen the scene with A fleeing with Quinn following, the jump off the side of the superstructure, and Quinn’s injury.  Maybe, if Basil went back and checked logs, he’d find she’d watched it more times than average.

Te was a step behind, hand reaching and finding only open air.  A was a pace behind Te.

The sound was distant, and too small, considering what it was.  In all the time she’d been watching, Amber had noted the times and rhythms of the machines that climbed up and down the exterior of the superstructure, cleaning and doing repairs.

With Quinn, it had been accident.  With Amber, it was intent.  Her head rebounded off the machine and painted the flat face of it with a blood spatter ten feet across.

She fell another two stories before netting caught her.  Still alive, perhaps owing to augmentations.  Too stunned, going by the confused and brief exchange between her and her onboard, to know what was going on.  The onboard, who maybe could have paralyzed her before that final leap that took her off the railing, who hadn’t, only managed the pain.  Blood and watery cerebral fluid poured through the netting.

A gripped the railing, the knuckles of her hands standing out from the strain.

By the time medical authorities arrived, a minute later, it was too late to salvage things.  By the time they cut the net, Amber was gone.

“That’s not on you,” Anderson, one of the people in A’s projected group said.

Basil immediately went to go and shut them off.  But it was a process, one that required rubber stamping by staff.  Staff who were stunned by what had just happened.

“She had no right to say any of that,” one of the others said.

“Stop,” A said.

“It’s not on you, though, okay?” Anderson insisted.

Te reached for A, and A pulled away.

Blue had belatedly caught up, and went to support Te.  A, having backed away, bewildered and shocked, saw Blue offering consolation.

Te had been closer to Amber, in the end.  They’d come up through Generation Colors together.  By all rights, Te deserves the support.

A fled.  Away from the conference table.  Through doors.  Staff were there, and A recoiled, emotions boiling out.

Overlapping voices of A’s projected group and staff were purely noise.  There was zero indication A heard any of it.

Basil’s own voice would be more of the same.  So he pointed the way, and struggled to find some means of shutting things down for a bit.  Emergency procedures.  A block on media coverage and discussion, twisted to a temporary means of shutting this up.  Staff could be told to leave and go home, that counseling would be available-

Paltry, and they wouldn’t listen.  Weren’t listening, where managers were already telling them.

And the projected group hounded A, now.  She could run, looking for an office to close herself up inside, for a moment of quiet where she could think, and they kept speed effortlessly.

“She was crazy.”

“How terrible.  I can’t believe I was here for this.”

“I can see how she got the idea in her head, about A cheating the system.”

“Please stop,” A said.  “Be quiet.”

Her voice was just one more voice in the jumble.

[Working on it.  I’m sorry.]

There was zero sign she was listening.

“She was never as good a friend to you as you were to her.”

“Shut up.  Stop.”  A covered her ears, but the projections communicated through her onboard, not her ears.

“I’m trying to help.”

A had found an office, and sat on the floor, her back to the door, eyes closed, hands over her ears.

“I can see where she was coming from.  It’s jealousy, in the end, isn’t it?”

A flinched at the words.

“Jealousy and stupidity.”

“Stop,” A said.

Basil searched for options.  He tried sending an emergency alert to one of the clerks who could sign off on the procedure.  The problem was, the projected groups were usually sent away for events, and there had been nothing planned in the way of events.  The employee was at home, and had to have their onboard pull up the necessary papers.

“I’d like to requisition time.”

Basil didn’t reply, his resources committed elsewhere.

“I’ve been quiet until now.  I was told this was something I could do.”

[You may.]

“Okay.”

The projected girl turned, sitting in a curled up position on a projected stool, tail tip grazing the floor.  Her upper face and the metal muzzle of a lower face were buried in metal legs covered in durable cloth.

She said nothing and did nothing for four whole minutes.

Someone else in the background, the artist with the heavily painted clothing, raised a hand.

They did the same.

A sat on the floor of someone else’s office, gifted an uneasy silence that was taken up by one person after another.  The group’s time ran out, and they were dismissed, and the next group did the same.  Passing up their once-in-a-lifetime chance to meet their idol, to say whatever they had been planning to say, or to have a bit of personal fame through fleeting association.

“She might’ve hated me,” A muttered to herself, “but she was my best friend.”

To their credit, the group didn’t let that spoil the silence.

➨

“Public sentiment is turning against her.  Is it time?”

“Give her time to react, recover, and feel the full aftermath.  We wait until things calm down.  Then we reach out.”

3.12.O – MUTE
