Blackbox’s readouts told him about the damage to his body.  Six anti-personnel rounds to the chest.  The impact had been enough to drive him to the ground, and push part of the plate inward, where it pressed on other components.  Enough shots had landed within a couple centimeters of one another that there was some tear-through.  He didn’t see any warnings about internal damage, so he put it out of mind.

There were nine people present, and more people a distance away.  The airborne drone had turned to open fire on other people that had dropped down onto higher or more distant ground.  There weren’t many- a few had already left to go scavenge or do whatever it was they left their settlement to do.

He flipped onto his belly, got knees under him, and used the side of the hand that wielded the gun to lurch to his feet.

Others were rushing to get to clear cover, and in the chaos, he didn’t trust himself to land a clear shot on Spur.  It was frustrating to see the people closest to Spur running away from her.

“Stop her!” Blackbox bellowed.

One person listened.  The thirteen year old boy who’d come in with his mother.  Spur was average height for a woman, slight of build.  The thirteen year old was the one person in shouting distance who might not be able to physically outclass her.  The boy wrapped his arms around her upper body in a bear hug, and with momentum, threw the two of them to the ground.  Spur’s head cracked against the platform.

Good.  She was effectively someone who had pulled out a gun and opened fire.  The distinction was that the gun wasn’t in her hands.

Blackbox turned his weapon toward the ‘gun’, here, since he couldn’t shoot Spur with the kid on top of her.  The flying drone soared above them, taking constant evasive action.  It was a speck, but the bullets it fired weren’t, coming in sprays of five to ten shots, all exceedingly accurate.

The irregular bullets he had made with Orion didn’t lend themselves well to distance.

Orion.

Orion lay on the platform, with an open head wound, blood cut with cerebrospinal fluid leaking into and through the grating.

Nine people here, four with gunshot wounds, two of which were down.  Another six or seven were on the fringes.  He hadn’t kept track of who was going after all attention had gone to Spur.  He could have checked with his onboard, but that took focus he couldn’t spare.

The mom was helping the boy, now.  A sideways swing of the woman’s arm brought the side of her wrist into the bridge of Spur’s nose.  Good.  That kind of pain and distraction was the sort of thing that would disturb her ability to control her drones.

“Giving medical care to my friend!” Blackbox hollered.  “Watch for the other drone!  Dog-type, fast!”

“More than one drone!” Ketu relayed, to people further away.  Gunshot noises partially drowned him out as he kept shouting.

Orion couldn’t wait any longer.  Blackbox raised his gun to his mouth, and he bit the barrel, freeing his one hand.

On the ground, Orion was convulsing, spit flecking his lips, his breathing irregular.  Crimson blood mixed with coppery orange hair, and he wouldn’t last long.  Blackbox dragged Orion a short distance, until they were beside one of the large, blocky anchors that held the walkway bridge up.  They could at least have cover from one angle.

Blackbox had been given some knowledge about battlefield medicine.  Onboards could do a lot, but they had limited resources.  New flesh had to come from somewhere, and without that, there had to be sacrifices.  Blackbox didn’t have any good, immediate ways to supply those resources, but he could help staunch the loss of others.

He tried to keep aware of everything happening around him.  The drone in the air, the two people struggling to pin Spur down.  Hitting her or hitting her head against something.

And Orion.  The convulsions had a purpose.  The onboard was struggling to manage Orion’s posture, so he’d stay put.  Face down, face turned to the right, the hole in his head would point straight down and he’d lose many times the fluids.  Face up, head turned, it wouldn’t be as bad.

Blackbox helped by forcing Orion’s head to one side, then kneeling on the man, shin across Orion’s shoulder, knee butting up against the side of Orion’s jaw.

Inside his kit, he had some materials he’d saved.  Others were partially refined, though he hadn’t sat down to really do the work, as much as he kept meaning to.  There were ways to make this better, to fit tech into the components.  There were always other priorities, even though he had a few of the bits and pieces.

The goal wasn’t to be pretty.  The goal was to patch a hole, and this was a bad one.  He had a series of plates for replacing armor and body components in one pouch.  The metal plate that was bent into a ‘big dipper’ one-hundred-and-thirty-five degree curve was a shallower, broader angle than the ‘little dipper’ curve.  There were nicknames that people who worked with these sort of components had for them that had been included in Blackbox’s provided knowledge, many of which he lacked any context for.  Maybe the people the information had been distilled from hadn’t known either.

Either way.  He placed the plate against Orion’s scalp and forehead with enough force it would stay in place, and then hurried to glue the edges to skin.

Blackbox wondered if they –he thought the word like he was swearing- had done any damage when taking his brain from his body and placing it in a container.  Had a hand or machine part pressed too hard on a lobe?

The reason he wondered was that he had such strange, out-of-place feelings, sometimes.  Orion in this moment looked so much like the others he’d known.  His group.  Orion had drawn the connection to the fox.  Blackbox hadn’t been betrayed after all.  It was better, because they hadn’t meant or wanted to.  Worse, because they hadn’t meant or wanted to.

Gun sounds reminded him to stay aware of the situation.  Mom and son had Spur pinned.  The drone took evasive action, so far away Blackbox might have been able to hold up a finger and block it from view… if it wasn’t moving so fast.

Help them, he thought.

The rest of the group, or most of them, anyway, were focused on the drone in the air.  They had weapons and tools out.  Three had guns, and a fourth and fifth had devices Blackbox couldn’t name.  One looked like it might be a grappling hook, but it had no rope.  It latched onto a surface, the person would run to a new spot for cover, hold out the two-handed, overly heavy launcher, and the grappling device would fly back into the launcher.

The other might have been a laser pistol firing lasers on a wavelength outside the ability for humans to see, but Blackbox could see in those light ranges for laser weaponry, when his settings were right, and he couldn’t see anything there.

Off in the distance, the flying drone avoided the gunfire with evasive action, and as that action took it too close to some of the supporting mechanisms for the giant door that the machines tossed everything out of, and that this group was using to enter the facility, Ketu acted.

Maybe Blackbox shouldn’t have been surprised, knowing this was similar technology to the drive engines, but Ketu used his drive mods to target the flying drone when it was a speck, shoving it with considerable force into the wall.

The wall was made of interconnected panels, each an armspan across at most.  The impact knocked a few free, and they fell.  In their wake, the black-green slime poured out with enough force that more panels broke.  The slime flowed down until it hit raised bridges and catwalks, filtered through grates, and as the panels above broke and more of the fluid poured out, it came down with enough force to do structural damage to railings and push crates out of place.

Red lights flared to life around those areas, many of them flashing in rapid patterns that he averted his eyes to.  The effect, even peripheral, was a slash of red in the otherwise well-lit interior.  There was an audible shift in the noise of the wider complex as a number of the machines altered their courses.

The thing was durable, though.  It went from standstill to a solid seventy kilometers an hour, hit uneven surface, and spun in the air before correcting its position and taking aim again, moving far enough away that Ketu’s next push couldn’t drive it into the wall again.

“Orion here needs medical care!” Blackbox shouted.  His mouth was free again, now that his one hand wasn’t occupied patching Orion’s head.

“We don’t have much!” Ketu shouted.  Ketu was tracking the drone, his engines revved up.  Steam and visible heat shimmers moved through the air above Ketu’s body, and sweat ran down it.  Maybe more than sweat.  Coolant, possibly, to try to keep him from cooking as his engines ran hot.  He glanced over one shoulder.  “We use our medicine for our people first, strangers second!”

Blackbox was aware of the gun in his hand.  That he could point it at Ketu, and maybe force the issue.  Not a good idea, but Orion was in bad shape.

“We have eyes on the second drone!?” Blackbox shouted, instead.

He asked, and a few people glanced up.

Someone more distant shouted, “No sightings!”

Blackbox glanced over, and saw they were looking high, and aiming high.

“The drone is a quadruped!  Ground-based!” he hollered.  Had they not properly heard or relayed the information, when he’d told them before?  “Fast and armed!”

“Quadruped drone somewhere!” the word went out.

People moved, taking new positions, while the effort to take out the airborne drone continued.

Blackbox thought about shouting more orders, but people seemed distracted as the airborne drone took an opportunity to lay down more fire- innaccurate spray that sent Ketu running for cover, and scattered another group.

Better to do it himself.  Blackbox hurdled one railing and went to where the mom and kid were, his eyes on every side path and angle.  She had to be frustrated, two people on top of her, her drone unable to get close.

He almost missed it, because its body had similar structure to some of the containers.  The drone jerked and then sprinted off.

Blackbox took aim and shot, before it could disappear behind piled up storage containers and some stacked, corded-together thirty-foot steel rods as thick around as Blackbox’s chest.

One of the quadruped legs gone, or mostly gone.  The machine tumbled, belly over back, flipping.  Forward momentum helped carry it past those storage containers and out of sight.

Blackbox sprinted, feeling the absence of his arm.  Even running, the lack put him faintly off balance, and he couldn’t grab onto a railing or put a hand out against a storage container to slow himself down.

He could almost hear it.  The leg’s housing was too damaged to support weight, but wires threaded through it meant it was dragging the remains behind it, scraping catwalk and grating, making faint ‘tk’ sounds as it caught on faintly raised lips where one section of bridge connected to another.

In pure silence, he could have tracked it.  In this noise?  No.  With the atmosphere being what it was?

That, in retrospect, might’ve been part of why he hadn’t been fully heard when he’d tried to alert them before.  His onboard was tracking and amplifying noise as part of general atmospheric adaptation.  Theirs might not be, if they had some form of wireless communication.

The area he was venturing into now and the area that Spur, the mom, and teenager were at was where sorting was managed.  Machine arms stood still, no work to be done, near neatly stacked containers, and the floor and bridge above both had large, uncovered holes where containers could be passed up or down to other levels.

The machine hadn’t stopped when it had fallen.  It had picked itself up and disappeared while it was out of Blackbox’s sight.

“Kid, lady!  Good job getting Spur, but watch yourselves!” Blackbox shouted.

Not a lot of railings, and the ones that did exist were for machines.  There were a lot of individual stacks.  There was a lot of cover for the machine.

He didn’t get the sense that they were responding fast enough.

There was movement out of the corner of his eye, and he turned, gun raised.  The quadruped.  Triped, now.  It dragged its ruined leg behind it, but even like that, it had moved fast enough that he hadn’t been able to get his gun on it before it was out of sight.

He jogged ahead a few steps.

It backtracked, taking evasive action.

“Drone on the ground, coming at you!”  He knew, though, that they couldn’t back off without giving Spur a chance to get away.

He turned at a right angle, to travel from one four-way intersection of bridges to the next.  If he could line up a shot-

It was already moving in response.  Sparks and fragments of dark metal from the disintegration of the damaged leg were his only cue.

A bullet hit him in the back, between shoulder blade and spine.  He stumbled, but did not fall, staggering until he was behind cover, before he even tried to fully regain his balance.

A second bullet pinged off of his newly acquired cover.

He glanced over his shoulder, careful.

That airborne drone was in the air, distant.

She had a bird’s eye view of the layout here.  Of this grid of bridges, stacked with its shipping containers.  Of him.  She could move the drone on the ground accordingly.

The scraping of the drone’s movement told him it was one lane over, on the grid, hidden by stacks, roaring by.

He went from crouch to all-out run, fully aware he was moving in a straight line.  His goal wasn’t to reach the drone.  It was to get to the destination first.

Spur, the boy, the mother.

He hurdled one pile of containers, and put himself on top of another pile of larger ones.  High ground.

A bullet from the airborne drone hit metal near his foot.

He saw motion, saw the crash as they slammed Spur’s head into metal.

Neither of the two drones under Spur’s control reacted or changed what they were doing this time.  She could pilot them autonomously, as if they were her arms or her legs, and she could give them orders and trust they would follow those orders.

They had their orders.  The airborne drone was told to gun down every human except Spur.  Maybe Blackbox and Ketu in particular.

“Ketu!” Blackbox shouted.  “Put me in the air!”

Ketu didn’t.  The man’s mods were discolored from how much he’d been using systems that were meant to cool down over a long period of time.

Blackbox put himself in the right place, standing on storage container above the mom and the boy, who were holding a bloodied Spur.  But the drone was small, it was fast, and it could move through gaps.

A single gunshot.  Far more powerful than the airborne drone’s.  A tight shotgun spray.

If Ketu had thrown him into the air, then maybe Blackbox would have been able to get eyes on the drone while it was getting to where it was getting.  Instead, it had moved through the gaps between stacked containers full of natural resources, found its line, and fired, putting a spray of bullets into the mom and the son.

Blackbox leaped across the bridge to the storage containers parked on the other side, his hurdle clearing the gap that medium-sized machines would travel down.  He landed, ran atop the stack, and got to the stack that the quadruped drone had used as cover to fire from.

It had two ways to go, really.  Left, toward Spur and the two shot people from Ketu’s group, or right, away from it.  Blackbox was ready for either.

It chose the latter, but it was a feint.  Out of the stack, into open space, only to reverse course, and throw itself off the side of the bridge.

Blackbox, already moving to shoot it, turned his wrist and shot it out of the air.

The bullets they’d forged weren’t fine tuned to hold a trajectory over long distances.  Weight was subtly off, surfaces weren’t refined, and the rocket fuel that turned a bullet into a small missile while also intensifying its effects wasn’t perfectly even in how it kicked off- that was more inexact details at play, from the molding process.

Terrible for shooting an airborne drone that was two thousand meters out.  The variance was too much.

For this, though?  A quadruped drone falling through air?

One shot, one thoroughly destroyed drone.

Spur had extricated herself and was running.  Her air drone laid down cover fire, focusing on Ketu.

Ketu, steaming hot, used his engine to stop that drone’s bullets dead in the air, then used another activation to fling them at the drone.

Clipping it, from the way it flew.

But again, they were focusing on the gun, not the gunman.

“Two of yours are injured here!” he shouted.

He reloaded, then fired one shot at Spur.

It stopped her from simply sprinting off, creating distance.  It gave him a chance to duck down.

He could see them clearly enough to read their tattoos.

CIRCLE.

The boy.  Short-haired, with skin nearly translucent where an old injury had been healed.  That was what you got with onboard assisted healing without any extra resources to help it along.  It made for a stark contrast with the crimson of the blood and the open wounds from the shotgun spray.  Part of his arm was in tatters and wept blood like the distant ceiling shed slime.  Not pouring as if from a spout or a singular wound, but such a mess that it fell out intermittently from every available point.  Circle used a gloved hand to try to cover it, but the hand didn’t cover the entirety of the wound.

WEST

The mom.  Her hair was in a single brown braid, and twisty strands stuck to her face, where it was bloody and sweaty.  Like her son, she wore a bodysuit that was a dusty green color with gray trim, and had silvery tattoos that turned black where the brightest light reflected off them.  Mom lay on the floor, hand at the side of her neck.

“I’ve got a plate,” Blackbox said, pulling out his bag.  He kept an eye out for Spur.  She hadn’t stood up or moved away from the cover she’d taken.  “West.  Are you his mom?”

“Yeah.”

“How are you doing, West?  Bleeding?”

“Not great, but focus on Circle.”

It looked like Circle had caught most of the flack.  The spray had caught the back of West’s head, some of her neck, and her shoulder.  Blackbox examined it.  Bleeding badly, but it looked like her onboard already had a handle on the clotting.

“Are you not getting up because you can’t move?”

“Couldn’t breathe at first.  Onboard’s on it.  Focus on circle.”

“Moment you can move a hand, you gotta tell me,” Blackbox said.  Spur was a problem.

He patched the arm, gluing it at four points before drawing out the long line of glue to seal it to skin.  The arm wasn’t the only injury.  The spray had hit arm, the side of his body, and leg.  Widening bloodstains and perforations in the fabric made it very clear where.  He needed to get a better idea of how bad.

He pulled out the panels he’d likely need, set them on the ground by his gun, then bent down and used a combination of his teeth and one hand to tear clothing to get better access to the wounds.

“Wait,” West told him.  “Stop.”

He sat up.

“He might die if I don’t do anything,” Blackbox said.

“He-” she started, before stopping.

Frustration welled in Blackbox, but he took the moment to look over, and make sure nothing had changed.  Spur was still there, he was pretty sure.

The airborne drone had moved a lot closer.  She wanted help covering her retreat.  The shotgun shot and the fact she’d slipped away had drawn attention to her, and she probably knew that people were converging on her.

He glanced down at Circle, and the widening puddle of blood.

“Let me help him,” Blackbox told her.

“Don’t tell anyone,” she said, quiet.

Whatever he’s got going on, I’m dealing with worse.

And it was.  Of fucking course Blackbox’s situation was worse, right?  Metal body, missing arm.  But what he glimpsed when he cut fabric at the hip was a jury rigged catheter setup.  And a mom willing to delay medical care…

He put it out of mind.  He didn’t investigate the why of that, he didn’t need to.  He made sure there were no leaks, then moved on to the bleeding wound.

The arm had taken it worst, with the angle the shotgun spray had come in, and how Circle had been positioned.  The hip wasn’t great, though.  Blackbox started gluing another panel.

West reached out, putting a hand over it.

“Can you move?”

“Almost.”

“Hold this in place, when you can move-”

“Glyphs!” Ketu shouted.  “Five, four-”

“Glue it.  Shit.”

Ketu rapidly opened two storage containers.  Blackbox wasn’t in a position to see what was in the first, and sand poured out of the second.

The third was apparently empty enough.  Ketu ducked inside and shut the doors, shouting, “-Two minutes!”

Blackbox wasn’t in a position to take cover.  He considered a moment, and then crouched, knees apart, so the legs would even provide some protection.

His one arm on the floor by Circle’s head.  His body a shield for Circle and West.

Two minutes.  Two minutes of deafening himself to everything, being blind to everything.

He hoped Orion was alright.  He hoped, even, that Orion was alright, but still hurt enough to not be a target, if Spur dared to try operating on any level with the glyphs active.

Or was she immune?  Did the Fox want to preserve her as an asset?

Two minutes.

Having seen Circle hurt, and Orion lying there with a hole in his head, with the memories of Marte and Sever dying fresh in his mind, he thought about his original group.

They’d built something.  They’d carved out corner of this blasted metal hellscape and made it a small home.  They’d made dirt, collecting organic matter, grown something green that wasn’t that fucking black-green slop.  Dirt that could be touched and squeezed between fingers.  They’d gathered cloth and made blankets and bedrolls, and they’d huddled together.

They.  The others.  Blackbox couldn’t touch dirt, or enjoy the difference a blanket made.  He wasn’t cuddly, or worth being close to.

To touch his flesh to something organic, soft, or warm, he’d have to crack his brain out of the container it was kept in and make it a dying action.

He-

His thoughts were interrupted when he was shot.  He couldn’t feel the rattling impacts of other bullets nearby.  Two bullets, upper shoulder, where he had armor, and lower back, where there shouldn’t be anything vital.

He had armor there, but he still ran a quick diagnostic.

She was being more conservative with her drone’s ammunition.  She’d spent a lot of it earlier, now it was more sparing.  Whatever the fox had done, it didn’t turn her into a precise weapon against others.  She was reckless, tired, impulsive, even manic.  She’d traveled without sleep until she’d found this group.

Diagnostic done.  Some damage.  Upper shoulder was fine, while the lower back was mechanical.  That would be a misery to fix.

“Fuck,” he swore, between grit teeth.

He’d been on his way to a warmer thought when the bullet had hit.  Which was the way this all worked, wasn’t it?  They’d struggle to find meaning and then whatever they found, it would be interrupted by hot lead or cold metal.

He watched the timer tick down, waiting.  He’d hoped this could be a pause button in the midst of anything, he’d wanted to focus, calm, to be able to act and end this quickly.

He came out of it angry, instead, and for a moment, he thought the glyphs were still active.  The flashing red warning lights that had been around the hole in the wall were everywhere, filling a solid section of the chamber, disorienting.

What the fuck was the point of it all?  What was he fighting for?

If that was glyph-like, drilling in some repeating pattern into his brain, he was done for.

It hadn’t been a pause button, either.  Spur had opened her eyes and she’d run.  Blackbox couldn’t see her drone, and she wasn’t behind the cover she’d taken, having run off.

He tried to stand, and he couldn’t.

“Push me to a standing position,” he said.

A groaning Circle wasn’t able to, but West flipped onto her back and put her feet on his chest, finding purchase where the armor of his upper chest formed a lip.  Most of his vitals were there.  She pushed up, and got him upright enough he could lock some things down.  He wouldn’t be able to bend at the midsection, but he wouldn’t bend down and find himself unable to stand again, either.

“Thank you,” West said.

“Take care of him,” he replied.  “Brave-ass kid.”

“I hate it,” she said.  “I wish he was a coward, instead.”

“Yeah,” he told her.  “But this all could’ve been ten times worse if he was.”

She didn’t respond to that.

“If I don’t make it through this, take care of my copper-haired friend over there?  Orion?”

“I’ll try.”

That arranged, he lurched into a run, gun in hand, and found himself in roughly equal stride with Ketu.  The man still visibly steamed, with faint heat shimmers visible around the armor.

Was there a thank-you?  An explanation for the lack of help earlier?

Nothing.

“Did you see where she went?” Blackbox asked.

“Three consoles.  Two here and here.  One below us.  You take the left one,” Ketu said, and he pointed.

Alright.

Grating, but efficient.

“How many damn bullets did you give her?”

“She stole them.”

Right.

They parted ways, each going down a separate bridge in the grid.

He heard her before he saw her.  She was at a console, a pedestal slightly taller than she was, necessitating she stand on a large, spare hook from one of the crane assemblies to interface with it.  She typed with one hand and operated a device with the other, wires strung from device to console.  She was actively vomiting, continuously and reflexively, making gasping, wheezing, coughing sounds when she wasn’t actively, whole-body straining to empty her stomach further.  She’d probably inhaled some of it, by the sounds of it.  One arm had a line of bile and vomit on it from wrist to elbow, from wiping it against the screen she’d covered in bodily fluid.  The other arm twitched and convulsed in ways that caused her obvious pain and inconvenience.

They got me with that one.

She saw him in the same moment he raised his gun, and let out a gargling squawk of a scream, as she dropped out of sight, coughing a spatter of bile.

Maybe, if he hadn’t been so startled by that, or caught by the dark look in her eyes, which were streaming tears, he might’ve shot her before she ducked behind the console.

He was close enough.

“Here!” he bellowed.

She was first to make her attack, so to speak.

He recognized what it was, too late.

She’d saved some of whatever meal-

-she’d eaten.

He was already throwing himself off the bridge by the time the thought finished. She’d tossed it over the edge and he’d followed it.

It was a long, long way down.  There was a set of bridges below the ones they were on, with their own machines, stacked storage containers, consoles, and architecture.  He didn’t land there.

He snatched the food, wrapped in wax paper, out of the air, and shoved it into his mouth, slamming it in deeper with the back of his hand.  He’d let go of his gun, and crushed it between his chest and his arm, almost losing it again as he forced food deeper into his mouth.

He hadn’t given himself a lot of spin with the way he’d jumped, but he had time to turn in the air, from belly down to belly up, to belly down again, before he hit solid ground.  Metal body crashed against metal.  His field of vision filled with warnings.

He was dimly aware that the gun he’d let go of had fallen, and settled a good distance away from where he’d landed.

Blackbox had, if nothing else, been made sturdy, but that sturdiness was tested.  His entire midsection felt like it could break apart from his lower body at the waist as he grabbed a railing and hauled himself to his feet.

He went looking for his gun, and had to wait for machines to pass before collecting it where it had landed, resting at the base of a pile of tanks filled with fluid.  Some of that fluid had leaked out.

While that happened, the intermittently flashing red lights all went off, and the white lights they’d replaced didn’t come on.  Only some general lighting around platforms or that came with certain tasks, like welding, remained.

His onboard gave him something resembling night vision, turning up light sensitivity and highlighting contrasts.  The positions of known people were marked with circles and blob-shaped arrangements, loose, as voices were recognized but positions weren’t.  If it was a place they could have walked to, a place they could be, based on the shouting, it was included in the blob.

A singular sighting of Ketu, glowing orange-white at the extremities of his mods, was highlighted, then fixed.  Even when Blackbox’s eyes weren’t on Ketu, he had a sense of where he was.

The whole process drew his attention to who was shouting, and how much.  What took another two steps was figuring out why.  At first, when he spotted Court looking over the railing, he thought it might be him.

It was something below him.

He could look down at the planet that was suspended here in the center of this massive space, and he could see the source of that warning.

Machines were leaving the planet in droves.  Some, too distant to see, he was thankful, had glyphs.

He turned his back to that, resolving to keep looking up as he climbed.

An elevator would have been nice, but there wasn’t one.  There were storage containers that stacked up so high that he could climb them and reach the level of the floor of bridges and platforms above him, though, so he set his eyes on that.

It was a bitch to climb with one hand, though.  Especially if-

Lighting changed again.

He saw glyphs that weren’t so distant.  Ones he could make the shape out of.

He closed his eyes.

Another two minutes?

No.

He kept moving, eyes closed and sound muted.

He knew where he needed to be.  Climbing storage containers, stacked right beside a massive drop.  If he fell, he might not land on the next bridge down, or the bridge below that.

It was even possible he could slip here, the metal along his arms, legs, and body lacking traction, or some of his tattered bodysuit could catch on something, causing him to lose his orientation, and he could fall, essentially, from what was effectively outer atmosphere of that planet that was now below them to the surface of that planet.

When he couldn’t find purchase with his hand, reaching over an upper edge, he kicked, driving the toes of his foot into the metal of the side until he punched through.  With that, he could push himself up a bit more, and reach far enough to secure a grip on the raised edge that kept containers stacked atop one another from slipping or sliding off.

He reached the top, and couldn’t find a good way to climb, so he waited those last thirty seconds before opening his eyes.

Green slime cascaded down from the ceiling.  Above them, the mechanism that controlled the door that planets could be sent in and out through was rotating.

As it did, cables that had been tied to the outside of the mechanism snapped.  He could see more of the makeshift space station, interconnected rooms and cabling tied to one another, lashed to the outside of the machine’s ringworld-in-progress.

That was Spur’s intent.  To cut that off.  Cut the ties, and let that entire settlement float off into the oblivion of space.

Blackbox lunged, jumping, until he got a grip on the railing, then swung his lower body, again feeling the precarious weakness at his waist.  He kicked up and over, and got a heel onto the base of the bridge, and then managed to climb onto it.

One more level to go, and the way was clearer.  There were machine arms that moved containers up and down.

He could run up one.

Three people were focused on Spur.  Spur, in turn, had brought her drone around.  It was damaged, and kept listing to one side and downward, then jerked and made a concerted effort to climb, before repeating the process.  The drone’s gunfire drove them back and gave her a chance to run for an escape route.

Blackbox shot it out of the air before it or Spur saw him.

He hoped she didn’t have more food.

There was blood in the thin vomit she was still reflexively, second-by-second, trying to regurgitate.  She’d been shot, and she was hurt, and as she saw Blackbox climbing up behind her, she knew her escape route wasn’t as clear as she’d hoped.

She ran.

He was too damaged to catch her alone.  Two of the others weren’t in position.

But by chasing her one way, he could force her out of cover.  Which gave them an opportunity.

“Throw her!” Blackbox shouted, as he broke into a limping run.  “Don’t shoot!”

Someone shouted something in response to that.  He knew what it might be- that she needed to die.  He didn’t care.

He’d glimpsed Ketu’s condition.  The way he’d overheated.  The fact he was moving slower and not giving chase.

“Even if it’s the last thing you do here!  I can’t catch her, and we can’t let her-”

Ketu crashed to the ground, onto his belly.

Fuck.

He’d been about to say they couldn’t let her get to a console to continue what she was doing.

Blackbox pushed himself a fraction harder, aware of the damage to his body.  That they’d need time.

Then he saw dust, debris, and flecks of slime kick up, with that very faint trace of glow in the air, as Ketu used his engine.  It didn’t accelerate things, or boost them.  It took something at a standstill and set it into a new position, or put it into motion, sometimes at dramatic speeds.  Or it did the opposite, putting something at that standstill.

He’d gone to the ground to get a different angle.  Instead of pushing Spur forward, Spur was thrown forward at a slight upward angle that meant feet weren’t touching ground.  She wasn’t expecting it, she didn’t control it, and when she came back down, it was with a stumble and a fall, followed by a sharp cough, blood and bile only spattering the ground.

Blackbox got her, throwing his gun aside because there was no place to holster it that didn’t risk her taking it from him.  He picked her up one-handed and drove her to the ground.

Through slatted grating, he could see the lights of glyphs on machines, without seeing the glyphs themselves, with the shadows of the machines behind and around them.  They came off the planet below and into this space, and the visual effect was eerie.  A serpentine construction loaded with storage containers traveled up from the planet with antigravity sails and thrusters blasting, and the fact Blackbox couldn’t get his head around the scale of the planet made it seem as if it was emerging from a point, expanding as it approached.

Spur whimpered, coughing up more bile.  He imagined she’d torn her throat with the constant vomiting.  Her eyes were wet with moisture, one was bloodshot, possibly for the same reasons the skin around the eye was bruising and cut, and the corner of her mouth had split, as if she’d opened her mouth so wide the skin had torn.

He didn’t know what to feel, or what to do.  He hated her.  He feared her.  He felt bad for her.  He knew, objectively, she wasn’t to blame.

“You’re alright,” he told her.  “We’ll figure something out.”

She continued to struggle.  Her response was a wordless sound halfway between scream and squeal, antagonism, resistance.

He broke one of her arms, because he couldn’t manage her if she had two, and she didn’t even notice.

The machines were flooding in, and they had to go.  There was really only one escape route.

➨

Orion

The room was just a bit too small to be comfortable.  Thirty-nine meters squared, cube-shaped, and that was without furniture.  A single g-panel provided both the light and the gravity, but it ran at low intensity, a second late to adjust, and there was a resulting feeling of being adrift in an ocean where the room moved this way or that.  On a boat in a rocky sea.

Enhanced tenfold when someone used the room he was in as footing or a thing to bound off of.  He didn’t have a clear view of the outside, with only the door having a slot-shaped pane in it, but what he had seen was that the rooms were connected with a webwork of cable and the people outside were wearing suits, going back and forth, repairing damaged cablework and attaching them to the outside of the machine’s ringworld.

He could see the outside of the ring better this way.  The way bits stuck off and out from it, the long, smooth sections, with windows, piping, components, and structural elements arranged in a way that felt like a foreign language.  Like a foreign language, there was a logic, a flow, but he couldn’t make heads or tails of it.

Here and there, when the room he was in whipped one way or the other, as others moved, people climbed on it, and things drifted, the window he could see out of would snap shut.  Protecting him, he presumed, from a glyph or more than one glyph on the outside of the station.

His head pounded.  A metal plate covered part of his scalp and forehead.  Blood stained the collar and shoulder of his bodysuit and shirt, and he dimly recalled what had happened.

This was safety, quiet.

It was also a claustrophobic box with only cables as thick as his finger connecting it to the ring.  If those cables snapped or something happened, he’d float into cold, black oblivion until he starved or took it on himself to end things.  Maybe, maybe, he could try venting oxygen to reverse course, but that was it.  Easier said than done when they had confiscated his things.

So he slept, diagonally across the floor, because the other option meant an arm meant to stretch over his head would easily butt up against wall.  He let his onboard manage some of the healing.

It took a while, but Court came with Blackbox.

They let themselves in, attaching an airlock, because giving every one of these rooms an airlock of its own was too difficult, apparently, and let themselves in.

It was a room that felt small for just Orion.  The three of them were bumping knees.

“You alright?” Orion asked.

“Still doing self-repairs,” Blackbox said.  “I’m more curious about you.  Whole?  Any brain damage?”

Orion shook his head, and touched the metal plate.  “I think I’m okay.  Thank you for not leaving me for dead.  I assume this was you.”

Blackbox nodded.

“What happened with Spur?”

“Imprisoned, but she stirred a lot of shit and interrupted their resupply plans.  She was using consoles, I made the call to keep her alive,” Blackbox said.  “If she had information put into her head by the fox, some form of access, to increase the damage she can do…”

“That reminds me of what happened to us,” Orion murmured.  “The skills.”

That broke Blackbox’s stride.  Court leaned back a bit.

“Something we weren’t thinking enough about.  Yeah, maybe,” Court said.

“Maybe,” Blackbox said, before finishing his thought.  “I was dwelling more on the fact we could use that access.  Not everyone agrees.  Spur included.”

Orion nodded.  He thought about that for a second.  “Fuck.”

“Oh, yeah.  Fuck,” Blackbox replied.  “They’re interested in taking you on, Orion.  For the welding.  They can use that.  I told them you might not be that interested in staying.”

“No,” Orion agreed.

“They’re pretty set on this way of doing things,” Court said.  “Making this outpost.  Expanding it.  I might’ve made enemies, I raised the idea, the machines might be adapting to us.  The fox is a new thing, apparently.  The machines are already figuring out angles to reach them out here.  What’s the next step?”

“It might’ve come across a little different from someone who’d helped more,” Blackbox remarked.  “You could’ve told me and I could’ve relayed the idea.”

“Yeah.  I guess.”

“I didn’t help much at all,” Orion said, touching the metal plate.

“I used Spur’s medical supplies to help you along,” Blackbox said.  “They said they kept theirs for their own people, so I argued for using Spur’s for us.  Arguing to keep Spur alive, eating supplies, arguing over the medkit, telling them their plan is flawed.  We aren’t making great friends, here.  But we did help out by alerting them to Spur and stopping her, so they’re tolerating us.”

“What are they like?”

“Efficient, single-minded.  I like a few of them, I want them to come with us,” Blackbox said.  He glanced at Court.  “But before I finish that thought, you should tell him.”

“You might wonder how we convince people here to leave a cushy situation and come out into the dangers of the structure,” Court said.

“Which really wouldn’t earn us friends,” Blackbox said.  “Poaching people?”

“Yeah,” Orion said, voice soft.  His eyes roved around the room.

“No bugs,” Court murmured.  “I’m okay at checking that sort of thing.”

Orion nodded.

“I’ve been holding something back,” Court said.

I thought you might have been, Orion thought.

“Do you remember my specialty?” Court asked.  “You’re welding, Blackbox is a Jarhead.”

“Communciations,” Orion replied.

“They filled my head with ways to get a communication network going.  Communication between settlements, messaging.  Not a lot of it is useful, with this being the way things are.”

“Too much risk of machines cracking whatever he sets up,” Blackbox said.

“But they also gave me something else.  It’s in my head.  I can only build it in a few different locations.  They want a message.”

“They?” Orion asked.

“They,” Blackbox replied, with enough anger in his voice to make it clear.  The ones who sent them here.

“They want consensus, and our tattoos provide the signatures for that consensus.  If everyone gives the okay, the machine would send a single message.  Safe or unsafe.  They should thank us for letting them know by sending supplies.”

“I’d guess if they get enough ‘safe’ votes, they’ll consider it clear,” Blackbox threw in.

“But if two hundred people give consensus and agree it’s safe, it gives coordinates,” Court said.

Orion took that in.  “Why hold that back?”

“Because I was pissed, and I thought if I told you, you’d twist my arm to get this built and send them a ‘not safe’ vote or something.  To get the supplies, but do the right thing,” Court said.  He paused.  “I don’t want to do the right thing.  I want to hurt them.”

“I let on how much I hate the fuckers who sent us here, how much you and I hate the fuckers, and that’s when Court let on what he knew.”

Court elaborated.  “A way to hurt them.  If we could somehow send a ‘safe’ vote with two hundred people… we can assume they’d think we have a good settlement going, and they’d come for a visit, or send a whole lot more people down, to build on whatever we’ve done to get up to two hundred people alive and thriving enough to build this machine.  We can also assume they’ll look before they leap, at least in our localized area.  What if we made them look at the Fox?”

“That might backfire, if they come after us down here,” Orion murmured, taking that in.  “But it’s in the right direction.  How many people at this leashed asteroid colony?”

“Just under eighty,” Blackbox said.  “But they know where there are others.”

“Enough to send a message,” Court said.

4.1.B – ESC

Basil

[I don’t think this is a good idea.]

“I don’t care what you want, Basil, I care about what I need.”

A’s home on Alcyone was a four-story tower perched on the top of its superstructure, with a g-panel driven water pump pulling natural water up and out, so it could have waterfalls on three sides.  Different aspects of the superstructure played with the water.

Greenery played with the rest, with strategically placed plots of trees, gardens overflowing over the edges of railings.  At the base of the superstructure, where there wasn’t water flowing into that water system, there was a narrow island chain, covered in woodland.  It had been seeded and was still young, still struggling for reasons not yet fully understood, but it was finding its feet.

A walked down the walkway, from an area of her home that fed out into garden, which was made for hosting.  The walkway extended out over increasing amounts of water with floating vegetation in it, to a round landing pad.  In her company were the guests on the list, her audience, tinted an ethereal white.  Many, but not all, maintained that ritual of trying to support A, hands clasped in front of them, heads bowed with eyes shut, silent.

A’s ship was protected by waterfalls on two sides.  She had added a few decorations over the years, matching it to her personal colors, but it remained fundamentally the same.  It was small to the point it would make some people feel restless for longer journeys, with floors and ceilings so close together A could touch a toe to one and finger to another, the kitchen and dining room were the same room, and the lounge area had some necessary systems, supplies, and tools for ship maintenance packed in beneath the seating, beneath the coffee table, and in the corner.  The cockpit, which wasn’t necessary except in rare circumstances, was a sphere set disproportionately above and in front of the ship, for maximum field of view in case of a manual landing or other event, like needing eyes on the ship’s exterior.  The floor of the ship had a band of carbon lattice running from the cockpit to the rear chambers, so even from within the sphere, it was possible to look down, past the short ladder, and through the floor of the ship to the ground.  Without the decorative elements raised up and fanning out around it, that cockpit looked ready to fall off.  A very small apartment with the means of flying, more or less.

As much as Basil disagreed with this decision, he had reached out to A’s security teams, and those people were boarding their ships.  Three people to each ship, each ship armed and ready to flank.  Others were already deployed, waiting at predetermined points.  That was their job, to be ready in case A decided to go at the spur of the moment.  They spent days out there, then moved on when their relief arrived, relaying out, and making sure that area of space was clear.

[If you walk away from things while they are this tumultuous, we can’t know the situation we’re going to come back to.]

“If I don’t walk away from things now, I’m going to do something you and I will both regret, Basil.”

“I’ll tell them about the back channel.”

[Give me ten minutes.]

“It’ll take a while to get out of the belt anyway.  Use that time.”

[Ten minutes over and above that time.  Please.]

“No.”

Basil hurried to line everything up.  Contingency plans, tracking for major players, security measures…

He still had the illegal nanotech access in A, that the back channel managed.

If he did something to prepare her, even giving himself an emergency wakeup for a moment of crisis, that was something that could be found if something happened and she was subject to a full-body audit, or if he was woken up at the wrong time.

“You killed Amber,” a woman said.  “Selfish bitch.”

Basil was already taking the steps to cut that connection.  It came from the wider belt network, so it was slightly delayed.

By the time A turned, to look at the projected woman in her fan-group, the connection had been cut.

She closed her eyes, standing halfway down the ten-meter walkaway.

Stock still, emotionally reeling.

[I’m sorry.]

“Are you?  You curate those groups.  Trying to delay me, Basil?”

[That’s not who I am or what I am.]

A let out the smallest of huffs.  Not an almost-laugh.  An almost almost-laugh.

Dangerous.  She didn’t normally do that.

[Not with you, at least.]

She remained where she was.

There wasn’t anything Basil could do except scramble to try to build something that wouldn’t collapse when the inevitable came.  Countermeasures, flight plan, tracking groups, notifying authorities, planning around Elabre and the things that would happen there.

“A, if I can speak,” a man in the projected group said.  “Don’t listen to that woman.  You didn’t.  You were a good friend.  And Basil?  Maybe do what the rest of us are doing?  Let A do what she needs to do.  It’s really disrespectful that you’re talking to A or telling her what to do.”

It wasn’t that simple.

“Yes.  Please.  Silence from everyone.  You included, Basil,” A murmured.  “I need time and space to think.  A few days, or a week.”

She resumed striding toward the ship.

The man looked proud of himself, even as people turned on him for breaking the silence.  The man had no conception.

“What you’re doing, promoting Amber’s message?  It’s morally wrong.  Suicidal impulses is understandable as a human impulse-“

“You’re an idiot.”

“Please stop talking,” another person in A’s orbit said.

“-it’s an impulse, it happens, but-“

“It wasn’t an impulse.  That was premeditated.”

“Okay, but exactly, it’s morally wrong to let that be a way of communicating a message.”

Basil dismissed that group.  He cheated the system to ‘randomly’ select people who would be more inclined to stay quiet.

A climbed into her ship, her stomach hurting from internal turmoil, very close to being sick to her stomach.  She hadn’t slept, and even with that put aside, her neurotransmitters were flooded on the one side and completely depleted on another.  Her body processed that as a crushing fatigue.  Joints ached.

He did what he could.  If she was committed to this path, he wanted to help, reducing the pain, making it a bit easier.  Maybe helping would even speed up this process.

Already, there was infighting in A’s fandom, intensified over the last nine hours.  Night had ended, the day had begun, for what little that mattered or made sense when they’d had to travel between worlds.  As the infighting continued, cracks had formed.  Some of A’s supporters were drawing on some old social norms, trying to shut down discussion by saying it was bad to let suicide be a statement or an effective tool.

The idea wasn’t wrong, and survived in some media, but had disappeared into the background when the dialogue and laws around the subject had changed.  The ennui of life in the superstructures combined with ongoing studies into psychological contagions and psychocultural bezoars had necessitated some reframing and adjustments to policy.  The discussion around those reframings and adjustments and the swiftly diminishing number of non-legal options meant people weren’t talking about it in terms of social norms and de-legitimizing it as a tool anyway.

So this was a throwback, in much the same way the science center attack had been.  With terrorist attacks, there was a bubble of artificiality, where families of those who died in a terrorist attack collectively and quietly agreed to call deaths an accident so terrorists wouldn’t get a statement, achievement, or find a point.  If they agreed to that, they got more cooperation, justice, and media focus on their families.  That bubble had popped with the science center attack, intentionally, with the Terrace Walkers putting in extra effort to spread their message.  Amber, in the same way, had penetrated the layers of defense here, with her popularity and the fact she was adjacent to A.

So that throwback point of discussion came back up, but it did so in a lopsided, self-serving way, from those who supported A and wanted to shut down the discussion, more than anything.  Basil was certain that would crack.  It was the most obvious, people were already subtly losing patience with it, and the norm of disarming suicide as a tool had never worked in such an insistently prescriptive way anyway.

None of which he could discuss with A.  He wanted to monitor it, and monitor fifteen thousand, four hundred and twenty six things like it.

A had chosen her ship to be easy to fly.  Platforms extended out to part the waterfall and give A clear air to fly out, and she wasted little time in getting into the air.  Some ships had mechanical arms or robots working within, to handle necessary tasks, like the bag A had tossed onto the table in the kitchen-dining room area when she had passed through.

He made a visible note, unobtrusive, notifying her, while doing the pre-flight check-ups.  She didn’t care, she was singularly focused on getting away from it all.

He did sympathize.  He cooperated as best as he could.

He was also aware that if she was gone for a few days or a week, even if she did find her center, she would also come back to find disaster, that would do so much more harm in the long run.

The downside of g-sails and g-panels was that they based their directionality around major gravitational bodies, selectively deciding which bodies of gravity applied.  For takeoffs, landing, general maneuvering, that was fine.  Skimmers and other fast-moving craft meant for use around superstructures or covering distance on mining planets tended to pick a single direction and travel that way as far as they could, without much turning or orientation.  There weren’t many barrel rolls or ninety-degree turns, unless a ship had an excess of secondary panels that it used and switched between.

A flew her ship as if it was one of those ships.  The contents of her bag spilled.

They left Alcyone’s atmosphere within moments.

He had until they left the belt.  He had to patch things and piece together a few interests to hold things together for a few days, to a week.  It couldn’t be overt, or that would be a scandal of its own.  Companies were spun up and given direction.  Mountain-sized engines provided the material.

The entire direction of Elabre would need to shift.  That was ultimately up to A, but she left the background of it to him, and that meant staff changes, it meant contacting different agents and organizers.  Things were being built that would have to be stopped and canceled.

The public opinion around A was souring.  That was outright dangerous.

But more than anything else, as he did what he could, managing everything in the orbit of the most popular and powerful person in the belt, there was something he needed to check off.

[I’m sorry, A.  For everything.  For not noticing.  I’m so very sorry about your friend.]

“She wasn’t my friend, apparently.  I don’t get to have those.”

Basil wished he counted.  He wished she wasn’t feeling such hurt and fear that her body physically hurt.

He let that be the last thing he said to A.

“When we’re outside the belt, please self-audit until we’re back in range, Bas.”

Basil worked until the last moment, on details as minute as molecules inside A’s body, as he prepared to park himself outside of range of the audit’s view, and as vast as Alcyone was, he wanted to ensure nobody would move it without the right permissions.

They passed out of range, and he shut everything down.

➨

Three and a half months.

As he concluded the audit process that cut him off from A, the information came back in fragments.  Stress and alarm were immediate, but so was his access to the file structure that told him she’d been pursuing art.

They didn’t have access to the belt network.  That system was damaged.

So was the ship.  Decorative rays and fins that stuck out from the globe-like cockpit, outfitted with quarter-size, narrow g-sails for more nuanced maneuvering, broken off.  Floating through space, quite a distance away.

Notices from A’s security company.  That was a swell of information.  Asking how long it would be before A returned, questioning if she needed supplies.  She wasn’t outfitted, they believed, with enough for three and a half months.

She hadn’t been.  There was evidence she’d used recirculated material.  Biowaste and recycled water could be fed through systems and mixed with a high-yield formula to produce an unappetizing slop that could keep her body going, for up to two weeks.

Other messages from security notified A that there had been a security breach, they regretted-

The rest of the information came in.

Basil had the full story.

[I’m here.  What do you need?]

“Someone’s attacking me.”

[I know.  Can I fly?]

“Please.”

A’s hands shook as she stood.  She wasn’t in the cockpit- the sphere was ajar, and foam surrounded the gap, partially filling the narrow aperture that she had to climb into to get into that sphere.  There was no point besides the cosmetic.

He could see the logs of the ship’s prior movements, post-damage, calculate the trajectories and possibilities with the help of the ship’s computer, and plot the best ways to get where he needed them to be.

“Sweat and bits of foam dust in my eyes,” A said, as she upended a container of water over her face, before tossing it into a corner and pulling out a toolbox.  It looked like she’d already raided it before.  “Two other ships.  I don’t know where the third security ship is.”

Basil had a sense of it.

A had stayed out for a long time.  Three months.  She’d rationed out food, and then had run out.  Not because she was stuck, but because she didn’t want to go back. Three months with barely any human contact, outside of a few check-ins with security services.  She’d read, painted, paced.  From what he could see on the cameras within the ships, she’d tried to write something for Amber, or about Amber, and had then spent more time trying to write to Quinn.  To Basil.

He blocked himself from reading that before he got any further.

She’d read the emergency manuals and found out about the recirculated food.  She’d tried it for a short while and decided to go home.

The messages from security painted a picture.  A’s long stint and lack of communication had led to the security office moving people around, committing to sending help out if anyone moved to intersect with A’s route, otherwise contenting themselves with a loose ‘fence’ of ships ready to move to intercept.  They had thought that it was unnecessary to have a full complement of ships way out past the belt covering A from twelve different directions when nobody was within even a day’s travel by ship.

Which brought them here.  One of the teams on one of A’s few remaining security ships had gone rogue, and had let another ship, possibly armed, past.  The other security ship that was meant to be nearby was absent.  Many of the others had been withdrawn, and had to travel for a little under an hour to get out this far.

Leaving A here, dealing with one ship in the black, only really visible and trackable if it was within fifty thousand kilometers, and the security ship poised to intercept her, blocking her from getting within range of the Belt network.

“They’ve been trying to board.  They used cable guns on their first flyby.”

Which had torn off the more decorative g-sails, which hampered mobility and cut maybe 8% off their TL̅KMH acceleration numbers.

The attacking ship, which Basil labeled the black ship, was faster and at least as nimble as A’s ship if it were undamaged.  The security ship was more maneuverable.  Both were armed.  Cable guns for the black ship, short-range weaponry and some ship-stopping weaponry for the security ship.

A was hungry, her defenses down.  Maybe there was a component of self abuse to the hunger and isolation.  Maybe she’d just wanted to stay away that badly.  Either way, it left her in poor shape.

As much as anything, he had to support and fix that.  His own survival didn’t matter, but they were precipitously close to a downward spiral where her own energy and system wouldn’t keep him going, feeding his energy needs, and he wouldn’t be able to help her.

[You did a good job getting away after that first attack.]

“They wanted to board.  I got up into the cockpit, the foam was still sticky, and saw how the cables were hooked, loops with a bit of slack, I could break away.  Not that it did much good.  I think there’s two of them in the one ship, they both came and I didn’t get the impression there was someone else back there, figuring out what to do when I started to pull back.”

[You managed to get access to the belt network?]

“I thought about trying to send out a call for help.  Then I realized partway through they probably have a way to block it.”

[Probably.  Though they might think they can handle this before help gets here.]

“I turned it the other way around.  I tried to make noise, to make you think there might be a connection and wake up.”

[It worked.  Good work.  At the very least, there are two of us now.]

“Do you know what they want?”

He didn’t and he couldn’t.  They didn’t have access to the belt network.  There had been no communications or warnings.

[I don’t know, but I have my suspicions.  It doesn’t matter for now.  For now we need you to survive.]

She changed her shirt, which was soaked through with sweat and the water she’d poured over her face.  She closed her eyes, but it was still a startling lack of modesty, considering Basil was active and all of this was recorded.

They had other priorities, really.

He could feel the weakness of her arms as she pulled it on.  She hadn’t been heavy at all to start with, unless he counted her hair as part of it, and she’d been on a rationed diet for several weeks now.  Add in the lack of onboard maintenance…

“I don’t know what that other ship is doing.  Did I damage it?  It’s made four runs past me.”

[It’s at least as fast as us, more maneuverable, armed, and I strongly suspect it has better sensors.  It’s flying in a calculated pattern so that even the fact its mass blocks out our view of a few stars at a time, we’re not in a position to get a good read.]

“This was planned, then,” A said.

[It was.]

Basil piloted the ship through empty space, trying to assess if there was any possible way through.  There were no planetary bodies out this far- the Arcesso drive had been used to remove the ones closest to the belt, and A hadn’t been traveling nearly long enough or with enough intensity to approach Venus, if it were still around.

Had it been, Basil could have anticipated an approach that used G-sails to better effect than the security ship could, pulling ahead or slingshotting around the planet in question, and then escaping to reach the belt network.

Which might not have worked, anyway.  The security ship could have shot them, potentially.  He didn’t know quite enough about who they all were, to know if they would.  Not having access to the belt network limited him.  He couldn’t guess how they’d act, or what sort of strategy they would use.

They were at least moving in anticipation of even small adjustments from the ship, they didn’t know Basil was at the helm, so his slight movement of the nose provoked the black ship to move, and the security ship to drift slightly, its angle changing, so it could take effective aim if it had to.

Which gave him the opportunity to activate selected g-sails, bark a single momentary emission of the rear engine, and reorient them, so he could fire everything he had available and fly away.

Both the black ship and security ship would have to chase, now.  The security ship would fly in parallel.

That bought him and A time, while also making the black ship a little less stealthy in its navigation.

[The cameras don’t show much about the black ship.  Did they communicate anything?]

“No.  I don’t think I would have picked up before, anyway.”

[Any logos, affiliations, anything about appearance?]

“The ship exterior is black, no lights.  They were wearing masks but were adapted to space, I think.  Or the bodysuits made it look that way.  I saw definition in one of their arms.”

[Flesh exposed to vacuum?]

“Yes.  Why does this matter?”

[I’m trying to figure out who they might have been.  Who they are.  One possibility is that you have political enemies who paid to have professionals deal with you.]

“I have political enemies?”

[You have a planet, power, and influence.  Yes.]  Basil restrained himself from naming names, or reminding her of conversations via back channel.  If he named anyone, like Robert Simes, and it wasn’t Simes, that would make Simes more of a problem later on.

“I don’t want to have political enemies.  I wanted to make music and look after the guys at Elabre.”

[I hate to touch on a sensitive topic, but it’s a possibility it’s an ex-fan, or someone who was never a fan to begin with, who resents you and wants to destroy you.  They either got organized very quickly, or they’re opportunists, hobbyists of some sort that already had the ship and costume, who realized they were positioned to lash out at you.]

“And quickly pulled together a plan.”

[I’d like to show you some images,] Basil told her.  [See if you can identify them.]

“I thought I’d get ready in case they try to board.”

[Depending on what your answer is about the images, they might not try to board.  They might disable systems and the ship from the outside, until it can no longer sustain you, and make it look like an accident.]

A seemed startled at that idea.  Her eyes flitted to the foam near the ladder to the cockpit.

[I can help, but that’s a lot easier if we know.]

“Show me.”

He had to go by stored reference from her personal experience and his own logs, sometimes put together with images from the ship’s database.

“No pouches,” she muttered.  She kept getting clothes on as she glanced over the images.  “Sleeker.  Narrower bands at the shoulder.”

[Flaunting the fact they can show skin in space?]

“Yeah.”

He pulled up some images.  A range of products promoted by the Neptunians, the gene-modified deep space travelers.

“Spot on,” A said.  “That’s it.”

[Hobbyists and opportunists, then.  This isn’t a professional hit.  A lot of the people who wear that style are into risk-taking stunts.]

Basil pulled up images of the group.  A guy leaping from the outside of a ship toward atmosphere, while his friends freaked out.  He had no cable, no equipment to get himself back.  They managed to get someone to come out of the ship to rescue him before he got close enough to start plummeting through atmosphere.

Another case Basil put at triple-time, where sixteen and seventeen year old kids on the outside of a space station leaped from one arm of the station to the other, trusting they’d catch themselves on arrival, and that their leaps wouldn’t send them on the wrong trajectory.

He mixed in some videos of the same kids doing other activities.  A trio of girls pretending to act clueless as a mudslide from a mining drill barreled toward them.  They got fully caught in it.  Another group surfing the wake of water created when a piece of a superstructure in progress on Alcyone was dropped into water.

“How does this tie into them suffocating me to death?” A asked.  She sealed the bodysuit she’d pulled on.  It meant her hands and head were the only body parts exposed, and she had gloves.  That made Basil’s job a little easier.

[It doesn’t.  Humans like to matter.  The Belt is bad at making room for that to happen.]

“Reminds me of what Amber said,” A said.

Basil hadn’t been planning to mention that directly, but since she’d brought it up… [They feel Amber represents them.  They’re twisting what she said into rationale to showboat.]

“That’s not who she was.  I know I get a failing grade in knowing Amber-”

[She hid her feelings well, A.]

A paused, as if she’d lost her stride, mid-sentence.  She repeated herself, instead of saying what she’d been planning to say, “-it’s not who she was.”

[They want to matter, they want a fast road to fame.  They want to go up against you, and here you are, isolated and weakened by rationed meals, and if they kill you, they’ll spend their life in prison, but their names will be tied to yours when people in the future write of this era.  That’s my assumption.]

A’s eyes went to the window.

[I’m sorry.  Let’s deal with them.]

A nodded.

She stared out at the stars, emotion heavy in her chest.

He gave her a moment.  He was keenly aware that this was yet another situation like the science center.  That A had harbored a years-long grudge over the fact that he had taken her opportunity to act.

He couldn’t do that here.

“I remember reading about a person on a mining planet, so far underground he was being crushed by the pressure.  Even with his equipment.”

[Yes.]

“And at one point he became aware of the amount of rock directly over his head.  A thousand mountains worth.  If he didn’t find his way back to the tunnel network he’d come down, there was no way to dig his way back to the surface.  Not with that kind of material.”

[He wet himself.  Oxygen deprivation and delirium probably factored into that response.]

“No.  It was a real response.  That’s not my point.  Space is worse.  It’s not solid rock, it’s emptiness.  It’s not thousands of mountains, it’s more.  It’s terrifying.”

[Has your mind changed, A?  About coming out here like this?]

“No.  You’d like that, wouldn’t you?”

[No, I wouldn’t.]  Basil was a little alarmed that she was that wrong.  He did want her to have outlets, and escapes.  He didn’t want them to be three months long in the middle of a crisis.

It wouldn’t be worth litigating that.

“It’s scary like this, out here.  Especially with part of the ship ripped up, cockpit nearly torn off.  Foam doesn’t feel like it’s enough to keep me safe.  Thing is, Bas?”

The use of ‘Bas’ didn’t seem like it suited her in this moment.  She used it more when she was getting along with him better.

[What is the thing?]

“They’re scarier.  The fans.  They were scarier before some of them decided to kill me for the fame.  It’s scary not having choices, and having an audience like that denies me choice.  It was scary before and now they want to kill me?”

[You still have far more supporters than enemies.  The problem we now face comes out of a minority opinion held by a minority share of a minority share of your potential audience.  But the world is vast, well over one hundred billion people occupy the Belt.  Even a tiny percentage of one hundred billion is enough.  Enough that someone will look for and find an angle and an opportunity like this.  It’s a risk we can minimize and when we come to a situation like this, we can handle it.]

“For all we know, something’s happened, and it’s a lot more than a tiny percentage of people who want me to die.”

[Perhaps.  Then we’ll figure it out.]

“If they want their name attached to this, they’ll want it to be face to face?”

[That’s my prediction.]

A nodded.  Her eyes roamed the cabin, looking over her art.

“You’re confident we can handle this.  Does that mean you have a plan?”

[It means I trust you.]

[It also means I have some unlicensed nanotech available through the backchannel.]

A tensed a little at that.

[I think we should let ourselves be caught with the cables.  Let them board.  Then we trap them.]

With the tools they had available…

[Foam,] he added.  [If we damage the walls, as they pass by the kitchen area, we can bury them.]

[The question is how far we want to go with the nanotech.]

“The other question,” A said, “is what does the security ship do, then?”

Not addressing the nanotech.

[There is a very real chance that they leave.  They may not want to get caught up in all the drama that will follow the death of a major celebrity.]

“What if they decide to finish the job and shoot us out of the black of space?  Covers their asses, and… I dunno.  I don’t know what their motive is.”

[They could.]

“How long do we have?”

[Ten minutes before they close the distance, give or take.]

“That long?”

[That long.]  Space involved vast distances and any movement that wasn’t handled with the arcesso drive was limited.

“I have an idea,” A said.  “I need your help.”

[Whatever you need.]

She picked up art supplies.  Her eyes moved, selecting a drawing program.  Using it, she drew lines onto her field of view.

He didn’t immediately understand her meaning, but she blinked, took two steps to the side, for a side view of the same area of the cabin, near the ladder, and then painted again.

[I see your intent.  Yes.]

An illusion.

She grabbed art supplies, nanotech paint, and swept more to the floor, kicking a few brushes and containers.  “Tell me who we’ll be fighting.  You’ll need my body to do this, so prepare me.”

[First, give me permission.  It’s your body.]

“You have my arm.”

She put her arm out.  Basil needed twenty seconds to get the necessary components into place for more nuanced manipulation of the nerves.

He moved her arm, picking up a red nanopaint pencil, and began to sketch out a blood pool.

[They’re called cowboys or void cowboys, but there are a hundred activities and twenty different names for the different subgroups.  Most of their focus is the vacuum of space, and flinging themselves into or across it.  Common to most is that they play stupid games and take risks for attention and thrills, and heavily mod themselves.  Those mods are biological alterations and mechanical replacements, more discreet than most, but you can see signs in the shape of their bodies, especially their necks and chests.]

“Bio and mechanical mods, right.”

[Thick necks, broad shoulders, thick upper chests, where they have the most mods.  High oxygen capacity, usually a liquid air supply reserved in tertiary lungs, or they’ll have ox boxes- that’s an older thing.  The longer they can go without air, the better their odds with small stunts, and the further they can push themselves for big ones.  You cannot choke them out or suffocate them.  They have endless stamina, you have less than average right now.]

A nodded, lips pressed together.  Basil rapidly moved her arm back and forth, lines straight and pressure perfect for the application of the nanopaint.  It applied nicely to the glass of the g-paneled floor.

[Their skin is altered, it’s insulating and resistant to extreme heat and cold, as well as abrasions, some cutting, and stab wounds.  Their outfits are more insulation and style, not something for a disaster or fight.]

“There’ll be two of them.”

[Yes.]

“They might be armed.”

[They have tools and equipment they like to use,] Basil replied, before pulling up the first.  It was akin to a grappling hook, but with different possible heads.  Some penetrated metal and could penetrate flesh.  Others were magnets.

➨

It wasn’t any of those weapons.

The cable guns didn’t fire to penetrate the ship with grappling hooks or magnetize, but shot past, with the projectiles that fed out the cable operating by some guidance technology and light thrusters.  It was two loops that went around jutting edges of A’s ship, before pulling taut.

Fully taut, this time.  They’d learned after the first time.  The bottom side of the black ship was armored, but they’d wanted to avoid a heavy collision, presumably, to have less evidence.  This time they went for it.

More ship damage.

As a pair, they floated around the outside of A’s ship, moving expertly across its exterior.  They were built like exaggerations of competitive swimmers, but moved like ballet dancers.  One didn’t even look at his foot placement as he put a foot out, touched the cable, and slow-walked along it, before pushing off.

He met the outside of A’s ship with both hands out, hands forming the gentlest of resistance to arrest his momentum, but not so much that he’d push himself away from the ship.  His hands, both out in a ‘stop’ position, moved sideways, and he caught the edge of the frame.

He went straight to a window, to peer inside.  The inside of the window was marred with blood spatter.  Basil watched through cameras.  The man’s lips moved constantly, a low chatter, communicating what he saw to his partner.

Then, using toe tip and one hand, pushed himself sideways, body skimming the outside of the ship.  To him, a seam between two panels was as good as a handhold.

The other one was harder to track, and investigated the cockpit, before moving along the length of the ship.

They reached the back hatch, that worked as both airlock and a loading ramp, though the ship wasn’t big enough to load or haul much, and manually broke their way in.

The moment the inner door of the airlock opened, they blasted the interior, filling it with coolant and water vapor.

Ice crystals formed along every surface.  Wall panels were sealed to one another, any mechanical traps would be foiled, many guns wouldn’t work, and the coolant was one that interfered with many explosives and incendiaries.

Basil kept A in a hibernating state.  He’d done some work on her skin, and now put nearly all resources toward adapting and minimizing damage from this chemical cold.

“Wait for the mist to clear,” one of them said.  A woman’s voice.  “A, we’d like to introduce ourselves!”

A couldn’t have responded if she wanted to.

“We’re investigative reporters, we’ve come a long way to have a chat with you, away from the hustle and bustle of the Belt,” the woman called out.

The man guffawed.

The guffaws faded.  There was a moment of silence.

The man’s voice was quiet.  “Was she injured when we cabled it?  Who’s been flying?”

“The onboard is supposed to be off.  Be careful.  Start by dousing her.”

The man came through, and sprayed straight at A- or what appeared to be A.  The room filled with the freezing mist.  Both the man and the woman were bare-armed, and didn’t flinch as the trace amounts of spray and freezing mist that came back at them crusted on flesh.

“Don’t kill her.  We were going to ask.”

Even Basil’s ability to hear through various microphones and sensors was being obscured.

They paused until the mist began to clear again, then advanced, checking every corner and behind every fixture.

The man inched forward, and looked momentarily confused.  From the doorway, it was clearly A, lying on the floor of the ship, blood pooling beneath her.  As he advanced, however, that image distorted.  A forced perspective image, like the sort children sometimes did on walkways.

A, meanwhile, had used Basil’s help to paint herself to match the seating, cushioning, and wall of the lounge area.

She moved away from the wall and, with only the noise of fabric faintly cracking, a sound that was lost in the din of cracking sounds, creaking metal, and ice crystals settling, she slid a cutting tool into the lower back of the woman.

Basil marked out the targets.  Kidney, then between ribs.  The knife was barely long enough to reach past the ribs, but it was the sharpest thing they had.

The woman supposedly had a reservoir of liquid air in chambers in her back.  Perforated at an angle, they emptied into the pleural spaces around the lungs.

Liquid air wasn’t liquid oxygen, but was an oxygen rich stabilizer fluid that could empty into the lungs and communicate oxygen through the lung tissue.  They kept it on reserve, like a backup parachute, giving them roughly six hours of air, at the cost of no longer being able to speak without devices.

It was darkly ironic that the fluid taking up space around the lungs made it next to impossible to breathe or speak.

The woman twisted, trying to elbow A, but A’s hand was more or less fused with the knife, and A was already leaning forward, applying her own body weight to the butt end of the knife to get it through cloth and skin.  Not so necessary an effort when the blade was this sharp, but it meant that when A fell sideways, she dragged the blade out toward the side of the waist.

A fell sideways, alongside the woman.  The man had already turned, and now bellowed, “Alysse!” before raising his sprayer.

“No!” A started to say, but her mouth froze.

[If you use that, she dies.  You’ll freeze the liquid oxygen and her lungs with it,] Basil informed them, using the ship’s speakers.  His voice cracked and broke.

A put the blade to the woman’s throat.

“Don’t be stupid.  That won’t-”

“Give me a location,” A said, talking over the man.  “Where the knife won’t kill her if it’s put inside, but will kill her if removed, after.”

Basil did, using the back channel.

And A pushed the knife into the woman’s neck.

“Shhe-” A wheezed.

[She’s already bleeding out,] Basil said.  [She’s suffocating.  You know her by name.  Surrender quickly, supply answers, and she’ll get care.]
