“If-” A started.  She still couldn’t form words.

[If she removes that knife, intentionally or because you’ve killed her and she falls, Alysse bleeds out within fifteen seconds.  Her onboard won’t be able to repair it in that span of time.]

A nodded.

The man’s expression changed.  A scowl of disgust.

[Put the coolant aside.]

The man disconnected the straps, then tossed it into the corner of the lounge where A had removed a cushion so she could lie across the gap.  It was a heavy tank, with an awkward apparatus, and he showed his strength by how easily he tossed it.

[Two paces to your left, beneath the part of the bench seat closest to you.  Pull out a box.  There are-]

The woman in front of A jerked, convulsing.  Her breath was strained, and she coughed silently.  A had to move carefully to avoid having the narrow knife go through another vital part of the throat.

[-there are clamps in there you can use to restrain your ankles.  Through the base of the ladder.]

The man got the box, pulled out clamps, and did just that.

[Second set, wrists.  A will come in a moment.]

A extricated herself, following Basil’s instructions on the use of smart bandage and a nanotech injection to handle the wound, before sliding the blade slowly out.  The bandage adapted.

They left the stomach wound open.  A walked over, and kicked the part of the clamp that locked, securing the man’s wrists.

He settled into his awkward sitting position, arms and feet out in front of him, back to the wall.  He had tousled blond hair with a lot of volume, was athletic and chisel-jawed, and had that neck that was almost as wide as his head- wider at the base.  His body was broad shouldered, with a sizeable upper chest, narrow waist, and long limbs, dressed in a black bodysuit that left arms, shoulders, and neck bare.  Skin had cracked and bled in a couple of places, but the cold didn’t seem to be affecting him nearly as much as it was A.

[The moment you stop giving information, medical care stops.  If we get in reach of the belt network and I find out anything you’ve told me is wrong, we’re going to assume maximum danger and change our priorities, flying to safety first, medical care second.]

“You ask, I answer,” the man said.

[Why do this?]

“Her days in the spotlight are numbered, people want to know the big secrets before you’re gone.  That’s valuable.  We’re investigating.”

[Leading with catastrophic ship damage.]

“That was you.  You pulled away, dragged against the cables.”

[And lethal weapons.]

“Not that lethal, you have an onboard.  Pain isn’t real.”

“Pain-” A started, before coughing.  She breathed hard, trying to get the words out, past damaged throat.  “Money, power, trends…”

[What are you saying?]

“…friends,” A mumbled, before coughing.

“Pain isn’t real, onboards can switch that off.  She’s doing it right now.  It’s about will and wills.  So we told ourselves, we want to know, let’s test our wills against yours.  We thought we’d investigate.”

[Interrogate.  Torture?]

“Nah,” the man said.  “Not really.”

Basil considered pressing him on this.  He didn’t.

[The security ship is cooperating?]

“In the Tenure?  Cousin.  Once we realized how thin security was, we got to talking.  He was coming out this way.  We followed, kept communications open, after a while, he said yes.  Even if we go to jail and get out, and split proceeds three ways, the information we’d get is worth more than he could make in a lifetime piloting a Tenure through deep space because she likes her alone time.”

[A, may I make a suggestion?]

A nodded, silent.

[Secure her.   Then we raid their ship.  Let’s get you the nutrients you need to rebuild and repair your body, and we’ll figure out what to do with the security ship.]

“His name is Callison.  He’s jealous of us, he agreed to be included, not for the money.  Give me the chance to talk to him, I’ll get him to listen.”

A shook her head slightly.

[No?  That’s what your gut is telling you?] Basil asked her.

She nodded a bit, before rubbing her neck.  Frozen flesh stuck to her finger in small, bloody granules.  She had frostbite on the hand that had held the knife, skin already turning waxy, but with gloves on, it wasn’t visible yet.

All fixable.

Yeah, there were a few dangerous things that could be communicated to Callison.  A had already voiced a worry about being shot by the security ship.  Maybe that stemmed from something she’d seen before Basil was online and running.

It took them a minute to get Alysse locked away.  They shackled her improvised wrist restraints to the guy’s -Lans’s- ankle restraints.  Then A got some privacy, suited up better, and pulled on a suit over that.  She -awkwardly, with frostbitten and damaged hand- wound her hair up before twisting it into a disc-shaped bun.  Basil adjusted the nanoparticles to have hair bind to hair and stay firmly in place.  She pulled on a helmet over that, the hair forming a kind of cushion in the back half.

Life would be so much easier without that hair, but she liked it, so Basil made himself like it too.

They crossed to the other ship, broke in, and used the airlock protocol.

It was nicer than A’s ship, but that was more because A hadn’t prioritized nice, not on the inside, anyway.  Basil had never properly dug into why.

With access to the ship, Basil had information.  These void cowboys were the son of a mining corporation owner and his girlfriend, who had a dad that worked with her boyfriend’s dad.  Not so unusual, for this entitled, self-obsessed, risk taking mindset to stem from that culture and group.  To stem from money, too.

Among the things they found in the ship was a live human being.  A young man who raised his hands.

A, hurt and a bit haggard, and perhaps emotionally wounded on multiple levels, by Amber, still, but also by being targeted like this, was a dangerous figure.

“I’m their safety.  I wasn’t really a part of this.”

[Safeties are monitors and backup for these adrenaline junkies,] Basil told A.  To the safety, he said, [you weren’t flying earlier, A thinks.]

“No.  I wasn’t.  I had a bad feeling, I said I’d keep them alive but I wouldn’t help them.  I didn’t realize- I didn’t think they’d hurt you like this.”

Basil didn’t believe him.

[Can you fly this ship?  Help us handle the security ship?]

“Bas,” A managed, before the safety could reply.  She shook her head.

[Not him, then.  Alright.  I can try to access their ship.  I’ll fly this one, you fly yours?]

A nodded.

She didn’t trust anyone anymore.

➨

In the end, the security ship didn’t put up a fight.  It was a man, older than any of the other three, who had the personality of a suck-up little brother, eager to please his cousin Lans, or his cousin’s girlfriend and friend.  They’d already fallen, so he didn’t want to put up a fight.

The other ship had been shot, that was what A had seen that made her wary of the security ship and the damage it could do, but the damage was limited to the engines and when they circled back, the crew of the security ship was in an area of the ship sealed off by foam, rationing oxygen with tranquilized sleep.

They reached the belt, and the wider puzzle became clear.

Basil had painted things in terms of minority opinions within minority opinions.  Things had turned.  Some of those turns had been engineered.  Others… the public liked to dogpile.

A had enjoyed a positive favorability with eighty to ninety percent of the belt before, and the outliers were ten to twenty percent, with ten to twenty percent of those being worse and making it a major facet of their personality to hate or dislike her, and so on down the line, in meaningful degrees or milestones of escalating dislike and hatred, until narrowing things down to five million or so individuals who would do something hostile or sanction that hostility for one reason or another, and seventy five thousand worth accounting for and keeping an active eye on because they felt strongly and had opportunity or traction of some sort.

That had changed.  From a ten to fifteen percent dislike to a forty five percent. The curve had dramatically shifted, from that seven million hostile people to nearly two billion.  Seven or eight hundred million, at a quick glance, Basil would’ve wanted to keep an eye on or take measures to keep A safe from them, because they would throw things in a crowd, or de-person her enough to justify hurting her.

Within ten minutes of being back in the Belt and having access to the Belt network, A’s supporters were communicating their horror that she’d been attacked, and her detractors, in roughly equal numbers, were making hay of the fact she’d stabbed Alysse in the neck without flinching, adding it to their collected citations to paint A as a cold, dangerous monster.

Alysse, Lans, and their two cronies were four out of that seven hundred million people.

A was already reading the words that came pouring in.  Accusations, disparagement, disgust.  Some still were earmarked as key people.  People she’d met, liked, or wanted the support of, who she kept an eye out for.

“Elabre,” A said.  “Call in the teams.”

[Are you sure?  You’re still healing, you need to rest.]

She didn’t answer him.

He shifted course to take them to Elabre, instead of home.  He began reaching out to people.

“Is it an emergency?” Douglass, from Generation Wild, asked.  He was among the detractors now.  Vocally angry.  He’d talked to media at one point.  He’d, Basil noted, felt nothing when reading that A had been attacked.

[Attend.]

A kept reading through the messages.

[A, you’re legitimizing them by reading them.]

“Who are you to say they’re not legitimate?” A replied.  “I’m not an egomaniac.  I can take criticism.”

[Be careful.]

More negative messages than positive.  The people who supported A were less vocal than the ones who had criticisms to levy and complaints to make.

He could feel her mood getting worse, moment by moment.

Basil handled their end of the arrests.  Once they’d reached the regular security apparatus, they’d found that the company was embarrassed to have had this happen.  Not dismayed that it had been A, perhaps, especially after A had dropped all communication and stayed out there, but embarrassed about their reputation and the security leak.  Basil gave a report of events, handed over camera footage, and filled in some information.

A’s sadness transformed as they approached the place where Amber had died.  The ship landed, and she climbed out, finding herself unsteady on solid ground.  The flow of a g-panel or g-sail made someone stay upright just that little bit more than they would on terra firma, and the body overcompensated now that they were back.

She went to her office, flicked off the lights, and changed.  Black jacket, a white button-up shirt with no buttons from nipple height up, and a twisty collar, and a matching, long skirt.  She spent a minute on her hair, reading through messages, sorting herself out.  Basil, too, did some sorting out, hiding blemishes from frostbite damage and attending to that hair.  He made her drink a nutrition slurry.

Everyone arrived, and A turned the lights back on, before stepping outside, walking down the hall, and walking out to the patio meeting space.  A conference table under a glass awning, with a still water feature on one side and the railing on the other.

Flowers and other token offerings in orange shades and shades adjacent to orange were piled up at the back corner of the space, by the railing.  It was a jarring contrast to the image of Amber on the Belt Network, picked up as a face, identity, and even color -her orange- as imagery for other people’s ideas and causes.  Those groups included a swelling group of danger seekers, counter-culture assholes, and even the grotesques, a rising faction of people who were responding to onboards by being too vile to be looked at, both aesthetically and in action.

There were too many people present for everyone to sit, but a chair had been left for A.

As she approached, Green stepped out of the group, maybe to offer support, or a hug.  A shook her head slightly.

“You sure?”

She glanced at Bruin, and swayed slightly on the spot.  She still wanted her old, first boyfriend.

“If you do, I’ll start crying,” she told him.  After a second, where she and he didn’t speak, she raised her eyes to his and shook her head slightly.

He stepped back.

There were a lot of eyes on her.  She was no stranger to that, but it had a different weight now.

Very close to how it had been when she had done her first performance.

“I’m done,” A said.  “I’ll turn over the reins to Elabre’s new CEOs.  Not the original ones, but people I think will help take care of the Generations and do the right things.  Including for Amber.  I made such mistakes with her-”

“You didn’t-”

Floodgates opened, people talking over one another, voices raised.  Anger.

A raised her hands, both, eyes focused on the table, hair framing her face slightly.

It still took a solid ten seconds for things to calm down.

“I loved her.  I wish I’d seen the real her, even if that Amber hated me-”

“I, I, I, me me me,” Douglass said, from the sides.  “You still don’t get it.”

“Fuck off, Douglass,” Te said.

A, eyes focused on the table, head bowed slightly, reeled emotionally.  The void cowboy, Lans, had seemed to hold some warped stance that pain wasn’t real because most damage could be healed, the switch for pain could be flipped off.  That scaring the shit out of A by pushing those boundaries and applying pressure wouldn’t matter, in the grand scheme of things.  As if emotional pain didn’t count either.

As if nothing mattered.

But heartbreak could be the worst pain of all, and A wrestled with it now, standing in front of people, too many of them ungrateful, or not understanding the effort she had put in on their behalves, specifically.  Her heart felt as if it was going to rip in half.

“I won’t drag you down with me.  If any of you need anything, find me.”

“You can find us too,” Green said.  “Some of us.”

She swallowed past a lump in her throat, glanced for a long moment at the flowers and decorations by the patio, and then turned to go.

Basil started drafting up the paperwork for what she’d talked about.

There were other questions.  Some outstanding contracts.  A was technically supposed to have contributed to some projects.  She was technically supposed to have done other things during the three months she’d stayed away.  They would pay a penalty.  Not enough to hurt her.  Not enough to even dent her.  But it was one more thing on the pile.

“I know this makes it harder to manage things, handle problems before they come up.  Robert Simes and other bullshit.”

[We will find a way forward.  If I may say so?  I don’t want to bring up fresh hurt-]

“A drop of water in the fucking ocean, Bas.”

Still ‘Bas’.

[-You’ve said for a long time you wanted more of a part in the science center attack.  I tried to give that to you.]

“It’s a good thing you can learn, or we’d have to return you as a defective product.”

[You did well, all considered.]

“I fucked up, going in the first place.  You said not to go away right when I went.”

[It is your body, A, your life.  Your free will.  You needed to go, and when trouble came, you showed you were ready, you had ideas.  You hit the mark.]

“Probably a lot more to hit.  Everyone hates me and wants me dead, now.”

[Probably more to hit, but not even one percent want you dead.]

A snorted faintly.

Dangerous, still.

[Still, we’ll beef up security considerably.  And we’ll watch for trouble.  Robert Simes will try to take Alcyone away from you.]

“Try to keep it, keep me informed.  Play any card, including that nanotech you’ve apparently got in your back pocket, if, I dunno, Simes won’t back down, and we get a shot at him.”

The pause that followed was a gravid one.  Basil remained silent.

“There aren’t a lot of things I want to hold onto, after all that, but Alcyone’s one.”

[As you wish.]

“Good teamwork back there, Bas.”

It was eerie, the pivot.  That this was the first time she’d properly said that, if he discounted the times she was a child.  He’d raised her from birth to prominence, but it was now, almost ripped in half by the pain in her chest, walking away from her dream, that she finally said it.  Eerie that it came now.

Eerier that she didn’t mean it.  That, over time, she’d learned to put emotions away, and to not respond outwardly, even when having a heated argument with Basil.  People making accusations about A’s response to Amber in the moment were not wholly right, but they were not wholly wrong either.  She had not, in fact, flinched when stabbing the void cowboy Alysse in the neck.  She hadn’t blinked when plotting against Robert Simes.

With increasing frequency, she was putting emotions in a box and not taking them out again.

Perhaps, in helping her down this road, he had fostered that.  Fostered something that he’d now have to watch for.  Especially now that she was so keenly aware of the secret nanotech he held as a card up his sleeve.

[Good teamwork], he agreed.

4.2.W – ESC

Winnifred

“You’re in the news, Win,” Anide announced, as the first words she said when she came through the door.  “Also hello.”

Winnifred, her head deep in her work, extricated herself from underneath an industrial size ox box.  She had to make the physical effort, then get oriented enough to look directly at Anide.  Nikhil, who had to do neither, took almost exactly as long as Winnifred to ask, “News?”

[I’ll pull it up.  You seemed to be in your happy place, so I was postponing it,] Toby said.

Anide, meanwhile, didn’t answer the question, her eyes roving over the inside of Winnifred’s place, with one part of the ship in construction in the middle.  “Why do we say hello, anymore?  Who are we fooling?  We’ve been talking for more than a day, I can look through your eyes.  Why do we value the placement of the physical body so much?”

Toby, in the background, was supplying the news while Anide rambled.  Winnifred’s first thought had been that her role in the silence that gave A at least a little bit of relief had gotten some late attention.  It wasn’t that.  The ‘you’ referred to the Sixteen Families.

Winnifred read through it with a resigned feeling settling into her chest.  The entire fiasco with the docks had settled a few years back, but there was always something new.  Some planetary governments were imposing new laws forbidding the modding of children.  No cultural exclusions.  An existential threat to the Sixteen Families.

Winnifred might have even made arguments in defense of the Families, if there was anyone to argue with, but the family was protesting.  It was a mixed, seemingly uncoordinated effort with the Family at Genoa kidnapping random infants and babies as a highlight.  Retaliation in a ‘you take our children from us, we take your children from you’ sense.  They’d taken the kids and ducked into the bowels and industrial core of the superstructure, where the unmodded had difficulty following.

“Ugggggghhh,” Winnifred groaned.

“Having just spent time with family, I get it,” Anide said.  “Got out, went home, kissed the ring, said hi to Aunt Manet and the crew.  Thirty seconds in, they tried to rope me into some trouble.  You’ve done me a favor, giving me an excuse where I have obligations.  They respect obligations you might get stuck with while in prison.”

She said that, but she had family looking over her shoulder.  She’d just given away the show, kind of, which spurred remarks and commentary that she resolutely ignored.

Dealing with Anide was always such a strange thing, because there were blatant similarities between their experiences with family and the subcultures they came from, but pointing them out got Anide riled up.

Anide shucked off her jacket, which was an odd, stiff material that looked like brown leather up until it started to fade, when it took on a texture more like gold.  It struck Winnifred, extremely late, that it might’ve been a fashion that the ‘hidebound’ liked.  A symbol of membership, even.  The removal of the jacket exposed Anide’s arms, which like her neck, were heavily tattooed in some of the most old fashioned style.  Her hair draped over some of the tattoos, and it was bleached, fried with chemicals, greasy, and uncombed, in a way that almost became a style of its own.  She’d tied it back into a ponytail, with a length of hair serving as the tie.

“Anide’s a hidebound.  From a rougher family,” Winnifred explained to Nikhil.

“Legendary roughness,” Anide said.  “To hear auntie tell it, the Marksi’s’ve been at it since the longest distance communication humans had was a scream.  Don’t worry your pretty little heads, though, I’ll be good.”

“Please,” Winnifred said.

“If I don’t have any good left in me I’ll go,” Anide said.  She was getting bombarded with abuse from family, compounded because she’d talked about family so irreverently.  She, again, resolutely ignored it.  “I was surprised you called me and offered me this job, honestly.  I thought, hey, maybe you’re smarter than you let on.”

Winnifred drew her eyebrows together.

“You can’t just have muscle, though.”

“I’m not really…” Nikhil trailed off.  Nikhil still had the same ‘gorilla’ mods he’d had back when he had been new to the mining work, making him just over four meters tall and three and a half meters wide, all the brute power of a point drill or dozer, in a humanoid form.  The decorations he’d had when he was new to the drill site had been long stripped away, leaving it just a plain silver with some rough, marks, gouges, and edges where the decorations had broken off, with file marks suggesting he’d leveled out some ragged edges.  He kept his hair shaved at the sides and short-ish at the top, in a crown of uneven dark brown locks, and had a guileless look to him that made Winnifred think he was a kid.

Nikhil was a ‘fake gorilla’, capable of climbing out of the gorilla suit, but he did have some mods that connected to it, and from the glimpses she’d seen when he’d gotten out to rinse off and do maintenance, the fleshy parts of his body were not as well kept as Winnifred would have recommended.  Body hair was missing from stretches of his arms, legs, and chest, and there were spots that were a shiny, almost scarred pink, in contrast to the surrounding, healthy brown.  She’d have to find a moment to gracefully bring that up.

“You’re muscle,” Anide said.

“I know industrial equipment.  Did my courses.”

“Sure.  But you’re also muscle.”

“I mainly want backup,” Winnifred said.  “Give me an extra set of hands, everything else can be learned.”

“You want an enforcer, which I am,” Anide said.

“I don’t think we’ll need an enforcer on that level,” Winnifred replied.

“You might.  And I know all the tricks and scams and cheats, which I will try to impart to you so you know what to watch for, and I know what’s out there, past the communications range of the Belt.  My family’s crossed paths with them.”

“I’ve grown up working on ships coming in and out of port,” Winnifred said, prickled.

“You’ve grown up with the sorts of ships that hire people like you, who come and go, and do the resupplying thing.  I looked at your history.  Bringing me in is the smartest thing you’ve done, trust me.  You’ll see.”

Winnifred was wondering if bringing Anide in was the most regrettable thing she’d done, actually.  This seemed like a lot of bravado.

“I also take orders.  Working a job at the prison taught me that, at least,” Anide said.

“That’s what I was actually hoping for,” Winnifred said.  “Everyone learning.  Me learning what I can’t get from simulations.”

[Simulations are pretty good, if you input the right parameters,] Toby remarked.

“But it’s half of the story,” Winnifred said.  “I need to learn people, people need to learn me.”

“You need to learn the sorts of people you’ll deal with, yeah,” Anide said, absently.  She was looking up at the chunk of ship in the middle of Winnifred’s living space.  “Looking through your eyes, I was only seeing things close-up for the last couple days.  I thought it would be more done.”

“That’s, uh, it might be today’s activity,” Winnifred said.  She clambered up the side of the ox box.  “I’ve got a line on a decommissioned Wrest.  The body and the last few pieces we need should be there… or repairable, hopefully.  But to do that, we’ll need space on a dock.”

“How awesome is it that you’re in the news for stealing children, then?” Anide asked.

“I’m not in the news for stealing children.”

“Right.  That’s how everyone will see it.”

“The Families do other stuff.  Charity.  Risky work inside superstructures for free,” Winnifred said.

“Bring that up when haggling.  Maybe it’ll help.”

Winnifred frowned, feeling a little more annoyed now.  “So… anyway-”

“Anyway.”

“-You want to hang out here, Toby can give you the tour, you can relax, we’ll go-?”

“I’ll come.”

“Right.”  Winnifred remained in place for a moment, wondering if she could or should argue, and probably lose Anide’s friendship, if it could be called that, by sending her away or refusing.  After considering her options, she hopped down from the side of the central systems block.  “You two want to eat?”

“I could eat,” Nikhil said.

“Yeah,” Anide added.

“On the way, then.”  Winnifred snagged the compact blender, some tools she’d want for inspecting any ship, in case they dropped by to see the Wrest, and her repair kit for her mods, slipping them into a bag.  She felt more need to look after Nikhil’s setup than the other way around.

“Who else did you invite?” Anide asked.

“Siss.  Others from the A fan group.  Some of them have another month or another couple weeks”

“Siss doesn’t like you, after your mod family shit got brought up in the prison canteen.”

“I know.  I…”

“Reached out to the Siss you knew from before that moment?” Nikhil asked.

“Maybe,” Winnifred said.  She glanced back at the setup that was suspended and placed throughout her home, before closing the double-wide shutter she’d installed in place of a front door.  Let’s find you a home.

➨

“Each tattoo is a deed,” Anide said, her arms outstretched in front of her.  Interlinked metallic monkeys stretched down each arm, each holding onto the arm, leg, or tail of the one above it.  “Monkeys are thefts.  Gold for thefts above one hundred thousand credits, silver for thefts above twenty five thousand, copper for thefts under that.  Black if anyone else dies during the commission of the crime.  Snarling monkey is violent crime, laughing is you did it to someone who deserved it, howling is both, crying is if you got caught.”

“What do eyes covered mean?”

“Eyes covered, ears covered, or mouth covered?  That’s a secret.  Not for outsiders to know,” Anide said, eyes crinkling a bit as she smiled.  Almost a sad smile.

“Oh.”

“Gems in the eyes are the value of the best thing you got away with.  See?  Sapphire.  That’s as high as it goes. It was a three hundred year old painting.  Jewelry is specific to the planet.  Wooden ring in the left ear, that’s Earth, central super.”

“Maybe we shouldn’t talk about brazen crimes when we’re about to make a purchase?” Winnifred asked.

“I wonder what I’d get.  To mark things I’ve done,” Nikhil said.  “Four years of being kinda crap at drilling, modding myself.  Trying to find something else to do.”

“Your onboard doesn’t go that far back, you tell your parents to haul off and fuck themselves?  I don’t see them anywhere,” Anide said.

“No.  They had me, took care of me, I did well in school-”

“Good,” Anide corrected him.  “You did good in school.  That’s how you’re supposed to say it.”

“-I did well,” he insisted, which got an eye roll from Anide and a small satisfied nod from Winnifred.  It was good he wasn’t letting himself be bullied by the stronger personality.  He went on, “They were good parents.  Raising me was about status, a way of passing time.  They did it, I got top marks, had opportunities in dance, law, medicine… I asked if they had anything specific they wanted me to do.  They said no, I was free to do whatever I wanted, they gave me a stipend of money to spend, told me to reach out if I needed anything.”

“That seems fucked up somehow and I’m not sure how or why,” Anide said.

Nikhil shrugged his massive shoulders.  Metal banged as it resettled.

“Do they reach out?”

“Not really, but they were busy with some trips, and I was on mining planets that weren’t always well connected to the Belt network.  Especially just after the ships moved in to mine.  They’re fine.  It’s not a tragic story.”

“It sounds nice,” Winnifred said.  She was moving on all fours, and rose to both feet as she spotted the woman, who was doing maintenance on a fuel port.  She ran a claw through her hair.

“Not here,” the woman said, once they were in earshot.  She was a matronly woman, with a scarf tied around part of her hair.  Her bodysuit wicked off all moisture, and that included some rain, even though they were high enough in the atmosphere to be above most of that, and the fuel, which formed into beads instead of soaking into the fabric.  “Not you.”

“Me?”

“I just looked you up, my onboard says you were one of the ones who started off the war on the docks.  That situation cost me a lot of money.”

“It wasn’t exactly like that, and I’ve done my years anyway, I’ve walked away from them…”

“It’s enough like that that I’m saying no.  No and I’m busy.  So chug off.  Walk as directly out of here as you can without passing within a hundred meters of any docked ships, and if you don’t, don’t be surprised if I tell the automated security to gun down the known saboteur.”

“That’s not-” Winnifred started.

But Nikhil batted at her upper arm with a slight movement of an arm that dangled at his side.  Even the relatively light tap made her have to take a step to the side to catch herself.  She looked up at him.

“No point,” he said.

No point.

➨

“No rats.”

“But-”

“Get the fuck off my docks.  I’ll be calling some of the others on Akna, here, letting them know you might be coming.  A lot of them send me their overflow, and if they want me to keep doing that, they’re going to tell you to fuck off, too.”

Winnifred, stiff, tried to think of what to say.

“You all fucked things for us.  You fucked things for yourselves.  You’re still fucking up.  Stealing kids, now?”

“I have no part in that.”

“Fuck off.”

She backed away a bit.

“Fucking disgusting,” he said, with startling invective in his voice.

The emotion in that one final word had Winnifred reeling as she walked to the elevator that would take her off the docks.

Not on Akna, then.  That raised new questions about a possible best case scenario.  On a neighboring planet?  Only one of the two, Chryseis, was inhabited, the other was Hecale, a mining planet on its last legs.  She could theoretically set up a deal with a mining group, to park in their neck of the woods, but she’d have to tow her ship to and from the other site to her house, or permanently relocate, she’d have to account for planetary rotations – they hadn’t fully synchronized and wouldn’t before Hecale was sent on its way, like Helicon before it.

That defeated the purpose of having her place as a workshop, if interplanetary travel and shuttling things back and forth was a regular thing she’d have to do.

“Have you considered changing things up any?” Nikhil asked.

Winnifred looked up at him.

“Different…” he indicated her body from shoulder to toe with a movement of his fingers.  “…format?”

“Fidelity issues.”

“Hmm.  You can get over that, though.”

“And it’s… me.  It’s what I grew up with, it’s what I think about when I think about… me.  My body.”

“Then I guess we’ll have to find another way,” he said.  “I’ve worked on Hecale, if you want to try there.  I don’t know what my word’s worth…?”

“Let’s try Chryseis next door, before that,” she said.

➨

“Shit,” Winnifred muttered.

“Problems already?” Anide asked.  She lounged on one of the back seats of the ship that was taxiing them from their failed attempt at Chryseis to Hecale.

Winnifred nodded.  She didn’t have enough heart to bring it up.

The man at the head of the mining site was a fake gorilla, like Nihil, or had once been.  He had the jacks at his back, shoulders, and the base of his skull that the suit would fit into, to feed the signals to the rest of him.  He’d seen them come in, and stepped outside.

“Not competition,” she called out.  People could be testy about their territories on the mining planets.

“I know.  Winnifred, once of Griffey Docks.”

“Yeah.”

“Nikhil, I remember telling you not to buy the most expensive mods on the market.  Look how torn up you are.”

“Is it weird if I see it as a badge of honor?”

“Less weird if you stuck it out for longer.”

“Yeah.  I can be proud I put in enough work to destroy my body as well as I did, even if I wasn’t great at it, right?”

“I suppose.”

“Winnifred is a friend.  We got along for a few weeks, it was good.”

The man nodded.  He had a bit of swagger to how he walked, like he still had an echo of being a hundred-ton powerhouse in his muscle memory.  “Your family caught on that you’re trying to do business, Winnifred.”

“Yeah.”

“Bombarding me with messages, warnings.  Saying you have no loyalty.  Implied threats.  Saying there are docks that might not work with my people if this keeps up.  Or that ships coming out of my mining sites might run into trouble.”

“Can I change your mind?” she offered.

“I have a policy,” the man said.  “I’ve got enough little complications and engineering problems, regular personnel problems, lots to do to maximize gains on my end, minimize the things that get in the way.  If I have to dwell on something external for longer than two minutes, I get rid of it.”

Winnifred nodded.

“Your family made their pitch.  I gave it about a minute’s time before having my onboard block ’em.  You need a minute?  Convince me otherwise?”

“I’m not a salesperson.”

“I hate salespeople.  So that’s a start.”

“I- look at my record.  You already know I was in prison.  Before prison, I worked on mining sites.  It’s where I met Nikhil.  I did good, solid, hard work.”

Toby supplied the records.

“You did.”

“All I’ve really wanted was to fly.  Give me a place to park my ship, I’ll service ships that work for you, I’ll tug, haul, taxi, repair, reload, I’ll block your competitors the days they drop a new planet in, and I’ll do it with that same work ethic.  Those other people will get bored, I won’t.  You’ll have me long term.”

“Hm,” the man grunted.  “No.”

“No?” she asked.

“Hassle and a free employee, or no hassle?  Is that it, cut and dry?”

“Good employee.”

“I’d rather have neither.  Too many moving parts in consideration already.”

“Alright,” she said, barely able to bite back her disappointment.  “Thank you for your time.”

“You got more than two minutes, in the end.  That’s because of Nikhil.  Nikhil?  Drop in sometime when it’s not for a favor.  I’ll give you some spare parts.  That’s painful to look at.”

“Alright.  Thanks Dahn.”

Winnifred turned to face Nikhil and Anide, unsure what to say or do.

“Can we go grab dinner?” Anide asked.  “I could do with the greasy, meaty foods they’ve got at the mining camps.”

“Yeah.  We can grab dinner.”

➨

“…it’s fucked though,” Anide was talking to Nikhil.  All around them, miners and other laborers from Dahl’s camp were eating.  They’d had to pay for food that was otherwise free, but there had been no other objection.

Anide went on, “What’s it all about?  You talk to this guy Dahn, but he’s already vetted you, his onboard has done a deep dive, you’ve done a dive on him, skimmed him for data, right Tobes?”

[Yes,] Toby supplied.

“But we pretend we haven’t, we pretend we’re meeting for the first time, we make introductions.  You already know he’s going to say no, you make a pitch… nice try, by the way.”

“Mmf,” Winnifred grunted.  She felt grumpy enough to be nonverbal.

“He says no.  So much wasted time.  Why?”

“Niceties,” Nikhil said.

“Rich boy wants niceties.”

“I’m not rich.”

“You have a suit that cost twice what Winnifred’s did, my onboard did the math for me, and you trashed it doing hard labor as a point of pride.  You know your parents will buy you another-”

“They won’t.”

“-Or that you have the money?” Anide asked, pointing at him.  When he didn’t respond after two seconds, she said, “thought so.  You’re rich, you’re cut from the same cloth as the singer, whatshername, that Win’s so into.”

“A,” Winnifred said.

[She knows, she’s trying to provoke you,] Toby supplied.

“Yeah,” Anide said, with a note of exasperation.  “You should know I know.  That’s my point.  How long until we cut out the bullshit?  We’re only saying hello because that’s how we did it before, in the olden times, and we’re only talking about most of the stuff we talk about to have something to say, even if it’s redundant.”

“It’s lonely if we don’t,” Winnifred said, before spot-blending her portion of meat and gravy.  She’d had to buy a whole plate, they hadn’t let her get a smaller portion, so she’d given the rest to Nikhil and Anide to share.

“It’s a waste of time that we do.”

“What would you do with the time?” Nikhil asked her.

“Anything else?”

Winnifred plugged the capsule from the blender into the side of her face mask, sucking in the contents.

“You, Win.  You’ve got more problems,” Anide said, around a mouthful of food.  She held a limb of some specious, lab-grown meat.

“I don’t need more.  I’d rather focus on the problems I’ve already got,” Winnifred said.

“That you’re too much a member of the families for the people at the docks.  Not enough a member of the families for the family to play nice?” Nikhil asked.

“I guess, yeah.”

“That’s a bigger problem than you’re making it out to be,” Anide said.  “Let’s say you find a spot to dock.  What then?  Will you operate out of that spot forever?  Is that really what you want?  Having a ship to fly but you can’t go much further than a planet or two before you need to circle back to home base?”

“Can go further,” Winnifred said.

“And if you break down?  If someone fucks with you?  And no dock will have you, nobody will service you?” Anide asked.

“I can service me,” Winnifred said.

“I think you know what I mean.  Okay, nevermind.  You’ve got a home base.  Say it’s someone who isn’t selective, you’ll have other people who’ve also docked there to compete with.  Other people who might be a lot like you, desperate, grubbing for work, not a lot of friends in other docks.  People who might be racing to get the same resources as you, like choice scrap.  The same kinds of work.”

“I’m not as concerned about scrap.  There’s a lot out there.”

“Sure.  But the same sorts of people turning you down today are the same sorts of people who will turn you down when you’re looking for contracts.  If you plan to pay us well, which you said you were…”

Winnifred nodded.

“You’ve got to keep your ship afloat in the black, you’ve got to repair it.  You can stretch things with g-sails but you need fuel to properly haul someone from A to B, and nobody will want a taxi that only uses g-sails.  Any equipment you use like clamps or drills have to be maintained and stored.  Can you do that, with one tenth the contracts as the next ship owner?  Or less?”

“I don’t know.”

“No.  You can’t, you know you can’t.  Which leaves you a few options.  Nikhil raised one.”

Winnifred folded her arms on the table, leaning over them so her shoulders were directly above her elbows.  Sitting on her feet gave her the height to do it.

“Lose the tail, lose the claws.  Become a different, better Winnifred.  Get yourself a fucking mouth to chew food with,” Anide said.

“Brain plasticity.  My brain didn’t develop to… no.  I would gag and throw up.  The sensation, the texture, the mouth movements?”  Winnifred drew her shoulders together.

“The first hundred times, maybe, but then you’d just gag.  After a thousand tries, you could eat!  Right?”

“Maybe.  It’s brain plasticity, development, like I said.  It’s how my gray matter is laid out.  I might never get one hundred percent of the way to enjoying it or tasting mixed foods.”

“Lose the tail?  The claws?”

“Claws are similar.  Even changing from one high-end claw to another, it would feel uncanny.  And I don’t want to.  It’s other people who are the problem.”

“Well, sure, let’s just go and handle a whole Belt’s worth of prejudice, while the rest of the whatever number of your families are making sure people hate you all.  Your life gets easier if you change.”

“In some ways.  I wouldn’t feel comfortable in my own skin.”

“You barely have skin, you’re a machine,” Anide whispered, like it was something confidential.

“Stick with the body that works for you,” Nikhil said.  “Anide’s not totally wrong though.”

“Fuck that, I’m not even mostly wrong, or half wrong.  I’m right.”

“it’s going to be hard.  This is a big wrench in the gears of your big plan.  How do we handle that?” Nikhil asked.

“I have ideas,” Anide said.  “Ones we can’t discuss here.”

Anide glanced sideways, and from what Winnifred could see of Anide’s perspective, Anide was communicating quietly with her onboard.  Checking the planetary rotation.  Winnifred tilted her head, curious.

“If you still want to eat, let’s bring food with,” Anide said.

Nikhil collected the food.  He loped forward, walking with two legs and one fist regularly punching the floor, the other arm cradling the food.

“Are we leaving the Belt network?” Winnifred guessed.

“Yeah,” Anide said.  The area they’d been eating was made of multiple ships that had landed and interconnected, each with their own subset of services, franchises, or items for sale.  The worker’s cafeteria was located near the midpoint.  Outside was a lot with lots of ships, where people situated further away had flown in.

Dahl was outside, talking to people, and Nikhil straightened to raise a hand in a hard-to-miss wave, which got an answering nod.  Winnifred was left to wonder if part of the reason the ex-gorilla had come to stand out here was to make sure they left.

Either way, there were taxis outside.

“You good to take us outside the Belt network?  Specific coordinates?” Anide asked.

“I don’t do that.  Talk to Oller.”

Oller was an old man with a Barillas IV.  It was the kind of ship that a certain type of ship aficionado liked, because of its classic design, which was protected by law so only the Syning company could make them, and they hadn’t made many.  Someone in Generation Colors or Generation Wild could theoretically have a nice Barillas II, III, IV, or V drop them off somewhere.

Except this one was a clunker, exterior modified by necessity, ruining the whole point.  The driver was similar.  He looked like he had been situated in a lot of cockpits, flying face first into sunlight without full use of sun shielding, and his skin had baked accordingly.  Oller’s hair was wispy, white, and lightly fried, and his beard was in the old wizard style.

“Expensive,” Anide said, after checking the prices of past deals.

The man shrugged.  His voice sounded exactly like Winnifred had thought it might, a barely intelligible drawl, “Close t’a prison sentence, I fly out like I have been.”

“Pay him,” she told Winnifred.

“When I don’t know where we’re going?”

“This is why you hired me, even if you don’t realize it yet.  Pay him and trust me, or don’t, I’ll catch a ride back to Akna, and we’ll part ways.  You can figure your shit out yourself.”

Winnifred paused, and ended up looking at Nikhil.  He was a bit naive, even more than she was, but he had a good heart.  He’d stood up for her after the other people at the mining site had fucked with her stuff.  He’d kept her company, they’d talked modding.

“Hear her out, I guess?” he said.

Winnifred glanced at her money, then nodded slightly.

[Got it,] Toby replied.

They climbed into the interior, which was not large, by any means, necessitating that seats fold down into the floor so Nikhil had space to lie on one side.  As soon as the doors were shut, Oller took them out of the atmosphere.  Anide had given no coordinates, and he didn’t ask for them.

Winnifred glanced at Nikhil, worried.

If anything happened, she could imagine Nikhil having to tear the ship apart from within.  She could hold her own in space, but only for a short while.  She wasn’t sure about Nikhil.  Did he have any attachments or features that would supply him oxygen?  Liquid ox backup reserve?  Had his onboard done anything long-term in case of vacuum and radiation?

Another thing to talk to him about, if he was going to be on more flights with her.

She shifted position, using sensors and electromagnet tools in her tail to check the seat to make sure this wasn’t an elaborate trap with something mechanical ready to snare her, or an electrical charge ready to fry her.

“You alright?” Anide asked.

“Seats are molded to human shapes.  Awkward when you have a tail.  Hard to get comfortable,” Winnifred said.

“Did you see what happened to A yesterday?” Anide asked.

Not a line of questioning that made Winnifred feel better.

“She was up late last night watching,” Nikhil volunteered.

[Then up later discussing with other fans and checking on A,] Toby added.

“I should have figured.  You’re going to have to get someone on your crew who likes that shit, or you’ll go stir crazy.”

“Kinda did in prison, after moving cell blocks,” Winnifred remarked.

[There were some people,] Toby said.

“It wasn’t ideal.”

Ollie, up front in the cockpit, used an intercom to message them, “Leaving the Belt network soon, if you have any last messages to send.”

Winnifred fidgeted.

“It’s dark out there,” Anide said, looking out the little window in the door.  “I was partway wondering, if when you hired me, you had a thought about that.”

“I called you before the attack on A.”

“True.”

Another couple of minutes passed.

[We’re offline,] Toby reported.

“Alright,” Anide said.  Her onboard had reported the same thing.  The tenor of onboard-to-onboard communciation between each of them had changed.  “Onboards, time for an audit.  Same as A did.”

“That’s the sort of thing that gets you checked and interrogated,” Winnifred said.

“Fined, even,” Anide said.  “We will pay a fine.  More for me, because I’ve done it a few times recently.  You two should pay about two thousand, five hundred lux.”

That was not a tiny amount.  Winnifred frowned.

But Anide had already asked her onboard to shut down for a self-audit, after sending the encrypted coordinates she wanted to Oller.

Nikhil stared at Winnifred, and then undid a lock, and opened up the collar of his gorilla suit.  He climbed out, nearly naked, skin patchy and inconsistently bald of body hair in places there should be hair, even with a light stink of something festering.

Fuck, she really had to help him.  He didn’t seem to know how much that should not happen.  Not here, though.  Not now.

She would have rather seen him stay in the suit, even if it was so cramped he could barely move, but she could understand why he didn’t.

He was waiting for her cue, his eyes locked to hers.

“Oller,” Winnifred said.  “Can you hear?”

There was no response.  Winnifred considered her options, if they really were in danger.  She was reasonably confident in her ability to fight in close quarters, and she had what were essentially twenty knives on her, one for each finger and toe.

Anide banged on the divider.

“What?” Oller asked.

“I’m paying you, right?” Winnifred asked.

“You are.”

“Hold off on those coordinates?”

“Can’t go anywhere until I have the password, and she can’t tell me the password until you two shut off, or there’s no point,” Oller said.

“Toby?” Winnifred asked.

[You decide.  Whatever you want.]

“Hate to do this,” she murmured.

[I know.]

She glanced at the menu, opened up the option, and selected the self audit.

Nikhil did the same.  So did Oller.

“And we have privacy,” Anide said.  “Winnifred said to hold off, so give us a chance to talk before I give the password, Oller?”

“Y’r time, your money.”

“Is this where you turn the tables and kill us, then?” Winnifred asked.

“I said I’d be good, and look, do I look like a killer?” Anide asked.  She was wearing a sleeveless top with a halter collar that left shoulders and arms bare, and she extended her arms to show the interlinked monkeys that ran up and down them.

Winnifred sat forward, and extended a claw, touching one copper monkey with a hand over its mouth.  It had one eye, a coin, the other socket empty.  “That means a life snatched away, doesn’t it?  Yes, you look like a murderer.”

“Hah,” Anide murmured, and her voice had gone quiet, “Credit to you.  Where’d you learn that?”

“Like I said, I’ve been on docks all my life,” Winnifred said, glancing sideways.  No onboard.  It was eerie, not being able to check video records to check a memory for correctness as it crossed her mind.  “Some people passed through, once.  I was little.  We knew they were murderers.  I connected the dots a few months ago, while thinking of you.  The expression in your face changes a little when you talk about monkeys.  It did when you explained them to me in the prison, and it did when you explained them to Nikhil.”

Anide nodded.

“That monkey’s smaller than the rest.”

“I was a kid.”

“And the victim?”

“Also a kid.  I won’t say anything else.  Family secret.”

“I do understand those,” Winnifred said.

Anide scrunched up her nose, clearly still extremely averse to comparisons between their families, but not enough to say or do anything about it.  “Yet you still got in this ship with me.”

“I trust you.  Mostly.  I don’t think you’re armed.  While we were walking around, I waved my tail near you, the electromagnet near the tip can feel out for metals.”

“Some guns are ceramic.”

“Who carries a ceramic weapon unless they’re trying to be covert?”

“Someone with a friend with an electromagnet tail?” Anide asked.

Winnifred stared Anide down.

“I’m not going to kill you.  It’s good you’re thinking like that.  Cross my heart, swallow a thousand needles, I wanted to talk.”

Winnifred waited.

“The dumb option, I’m not even sure it would work with onboards being what they are… you give up on being the owner or being the captain,” Anide said.

“No,” Winnifred said.  “That’s not-”

“It’s not the point.  I know.  I get it.  It’s one way to go about things, depending on what you really want,” Anide said.  “Do you want to be ship owner and captain, or do you want to captain your ship?”

Winnifred drew her eyebrows together.

“In this version of events, we give up.  You go back, you sulk, you keep working on projects.  A few months pass, you sell to Nikhil.  He does some jobs, a few more months, a year, but in the end, you know the ship inside and out.  You get hired on.  Subtly, through the ship systems, you and Toby set up something so you can quietly file orders, commands, direction, buying, selling.  Nikhil is pretty, he’s wealthy, he could work as a hobbyist ship captain.  He’s the figurehead.  You?  You’d be the real captain.  Have to play it cool.  Part of the reason we came up here, is if I said this on the belt network, people doing a check could ferret it out.”

“They still could,” Winnifred said.

“Sure.  But maybe by then your family has cooled off and gotten distracted by something else.  Maybe you can segue into being an actual captain.  Maybe you decide on another career path.”

Winnifred sat forward, elbows on knees.  She looked at Nikhil.

“I can’t guarantee I’d stay forever,” he said.  “I like you but I’ve never done anything like this.”

“Option three after a physical remodel so you’re no longer a rat, or Nikhil as figurehead, is out there,” Anide said.  “Can I give the coordinates to Oller?”

Winnifred didn’t have to think for long.  She nodded.

Anide had put too much thought into that figurehead plan to be faking, as she saw it.

“Your exposure to what’s out there is limited.  A properly outfitted ship in the black can sustain itself indefinitely, you know?  Stations can.  Self-contained ecosystems, recycled matter, the net gain from sunlight and the right chemistry outweighs the shed energy.  There are a lot more people out there in the black of space than you’d think, who decided they didn’t want what the Belt had to offer.  What A dealt with was a taste of that.”

“That was a betrayal from security services.”

“Sure.  But it was a taste of the sort of thing you run into out there.  Betrayal.  People turning on you, being monstrous, with no ability to signal for help and no expectation they’d arrive in time if you could signal.”

“Where are we going?” Nikhil asked.

“We’ll know in… Oller?”

Anide had to bang.

“What?” Oller barked the word.

“How long?  I don’t have an onboard to check with.”

“A few minutes.”

“Option three, skip sheet, then,” Anide said.  “You don’t dock back there.  You dock out there.  Far outside the Belt Network.  You help them.  Ships and stations that are mostly self-sufficient.  People the Belt frowns on.”

“Hidebound?” Winnifred asked.

She was doing most of the talking.  Nikhil was wary, watching and listening.

“Some.  With scarier tattoos.  Some who checked out on Belt life.  Someone close to here, not the people we’re visiting, but a next door neighbor, bought a hundred thousand synthetic genitals and rigged them to fuck each other in interlocking, fractal configurations, has a database with everything pornographic on record, did a dozen other setups I’m not going to even guess at, wired himself up, modded his or her brain to feel it all.  Trying to transcend humanity by fucking himself across four dimensions, I don’t even know.  Ship draws enough power to keep going, keep the minimal actual flesh and mind that’s still there alive, keep the machines in motion.”

“And I’d be doing what?  Cleaning up?”

“Depends.  If you wanted to and he needed it.  Maybe something broke and he doesn’t have the capacity to fix it.  A solar panel, or the timing in the gyres in his whirling, fluid-spurting setup.”

“Not exactly the dream,” Nikhil said.

“There’d be other stuff,” Anide said.  “Some more tense.  I know these guys because I’ve flown drugs out that way.  They use substances to keep themselves going.  My family supplies, they buy.”

“How do they buy if they’re self sustaining and all the way out here?”

“They bring money when they come to stay, and spend it slow.  They also give me videos and simulations they make, as currency.  We sell it.”

“What kind?” Winnifred asked.

“We’re close.”

Ollie reached the coordinates, and after a quick check with Anide, and a video conversation Winnifred wasn’t privy to, he moved closer to the ship.

In space, lighting was hard to come by.  In the shadow of a planet, with only the trace light reflected from other directions, it was next to invisible.  The same thing A had run into.  Winnifred’s family used different light spectrums and sound spectrums for whispers and other communication, and she still had those tools.  She had to manually activate them, without Toby to help.

An ugly box of a ship.

They didn’t so much enter the airlock as move up to the edge of it.  After requisite checks, the twin doors opened.

Winnifred’s face mask filtered out a lot, but sensors and Nikhil’s reaction made it clear there was a strong odor.

The man and woman who answered were elderly, to a level Winnifred hadn’t seen before.  Hair was sparse, if it was present at all, flesh was sallow, pale, or near-translucent, veins clear on them, and flesh was wrinkled.  Teeth and fingernails were made thick and prominent by age, as if they were both two hundred years old or older.

Neither was dressed, but hanging skin protected modesty.

“Sorry to interrupt,” Anide said.  “Trying to get a friend onboard.  She has a ship mostly built, she might be coming out this way.  You’re safe, you’re known.”

The woman out of the pair made eyes at Nikhil.  A woman in the hallway behind her, also elderly, but with a full head of gray hair, noticed, and leaned over to see him better.

“And?” the man asked.  “You want to come in and watch?  Have tea?”

“Nah.  Taxi would get too expensive.  Do you need anything?  Any requests?  Systems need fixing?”

“We’re fine.  We’ve got some people who know their stuff.  They cover it when they take a break.”

“Alright.  I’ll give you a discount on your next order, for this interruption.  Trying to break her in, is all.”

“Sure.  That’s fine,” the man said.  “Tell your aunt I said hi.  She can come anytime.”

“She probably won’t.”

He smiled, then hit the button to shut the airlock door.

Winnifred settled back into her seat, a bit confused and unsettled.

“Gerontophiles.  Most of them modify themselves.  A few claim to have cracked immortality, which is…” Anide said, and trailed off without delivering the word.  “Others just partake.  A hundred and fifty billion humans across the worlds, if that number’s even close to correct-”

“You think they fake it?” Nikhil asked.

“I think they kept the official reports of the numbers artificially low to keep people from panicking about population expanding faster than they were getting planets online… and now they’re stuck with those numbers now that they’ve got things working.  They’ll explain it away with population booms.  It doesn’t matter.  There are a lot of people on all of those worlds.  Bored people who push the boundaries of art and taste.  There were enough of them who were willing to shack up together and dress up as an intentionally gross sort of old, some regular old, and go at each other until they drop dead.  They use my family’s drugs to get their energy up and go days without sleeping, so they waste no time.”

“Between the guy who turned himself into a machine and these people, is it always-?” Winnifred asked.  “-Sexual?”

“No.  No, it absolutely isn’t,” Anide said.  “I’ve always thought the Gray Frocked had some groups out there.  Maybe even now.  I know that interests you.”

Winnifred wasn’t sure how to respond to that.  She’d tried.  She’d followed official channels.  She’d reached out.  She’d even thought she would reach out through A, to do it.  Then something else had come up.

A part of her had hoped that when things settled down, that A would reach out to say thanks, or that the news would put the spotlight on her for five seconds.  Maybe then, she could say something, get attention onto the subject.  They hadn’t.  She’d been one face in the crowd, forgotten as other things took center stage.

Now she waited to see if something else came up, something that might pique Investigator Carlen Holder’s attention, so she could try again.  Or something, some sign, some movement.

Would this be a way to keep an eye on things?

“There are other cults, other groups.  One of the groups out here, they bisect brains.  Each hemisphere of the brain can run independently, with some deficits in things like speech.  They patch it a bit, grow full bodies for each.  They are fucking deranged.”

Winnifred shifted position.  Not out of fear or discomfort, but to take it all in.

“There’s a ship I know of, it had a widowed dad and his kids on board, and his cousin and his cousin’s kids.  They took a trip out into the black, left the Belt and kept going, and then never returned.  That was before my aunt was born,” Anide said.  “They’re still flying.  Still crewed.  No stasis or anything like it.  It’s been long enough, the kids had to have had kids.  There are people out there who want to be left alone, and they would shoot you for flying too close.  That’s where you’d need an enforcer.  That’s where you need muscle.”

“Would I be staying out here?”

“Probably not.  You like things like A’s music and the little things too much.  But you could do fine, making deliveries, doing all sorts of work, like tugging and hauling, repairs.  You could dock out here okay.”

“Illegal?” Winnifred asked.  “What I’d be doing?”

“Some of the deliveries would be.  But honestly?  I don’t think the belt judiciary cares.  They want some of these people staying gone.  Out of sight, out of mind,” Anide said.  “They’ll fine you occasionally, but speaking from experience, I think they go easy on us.  The money we’d make beats out the fines.  And, as a bonus, I think you could sell that you’re really just out there doing repairs and saving lives.”

“I’d have to turn off Toby.”

“For some of it.  Enough Toby’s not reading coordinates and bringing it back to the belt network for everyone to know.  There are steps that would have to be taken.  Illegal edits to Toby to keep her-”

“Him, this week.”

“-him from reading stars to calculate positions.  If you wanted his company for part of the trips.  There are people out this way that would help you with that.”

“That idea makes me uneasy.”

“Sure.  It should.  But A’s onboard, whatever its name is…”

“Basil,” Winnifred said.

“He fucked around, didn’t he?  I remember you and that group blathering about it.”

“Maybe.  Nobody knows for sure,” Winnifred said.  She considered.  Knowing Basil had done it…  She shook her head.  “And it’s dangerous.”

“Yeah.  Makes the worst parts of prison and Family-against-Dock warfare look like a fairy tale.”

“Fairy tales are pretty dark, sometimes,” Nikhil said.

“Don’t fuck with my poetry, ape.”

Nikhil sighed.

“You want to fly?  You want a place to stow your ship, when it’s too large for your house and no dock will have you?  You have three options, as I see it.  Lose the current body, make Nikhil the figurehead captain, or fly in darker seas.”

Winnifred considered.

The right answer, objectively, was a figurehead captain.

That felt so goddamn sad.

Anide startled her by banging on the divider.  “Oller!”

“What?”

“Home.  Akna.”

“Yeh.”

“Your call,” Anide said.  “Tell me you aren’t glad you reached out to me, so I could give you the rundown?”

“I’m…” Winnifred trailed off.  Glad was the wrong word.  Both of the options Anide had brought her out to talk about were so bittersweet.  Or problematic?  Difficult.  “I appreciate the ideas.”

“Good.”

Could she endure Nikhil as the acting captain, all messages relayed?  Yes.  Would it be fun?  No.  She could see herself framing it in her mind as a thing where she’d endure a few years like that, then try to run the ship herself, again.  But her entire life had been a long series of those sorts of compromises.  She’d be free, at least, piloting a ship she’d made that she technically owned, through space.  Technically captain.

On the other hand… the other option was almost the opposite.  It would be a different sort of flying.  Navigating a minefield.  Smuggling.  Trafficking.

She could keep looking out for the Gray Frocked.

She genuinely didn’t know.

“Nikhil?” she asked.  “Thoughts?”

“I have nowhere to be.  Nothing to do.  You’re the one with the ship, spending the money to get it set up, paying my wage.  I want to see more, do more.  I guess either of the second or third options count.  If I’m unhappy, I’ll leave.”

“Okay.  Glad to have you, until then.”

He smiled a bit.

It didn’t help her decide.  She knew she would have to think about it for a long while, before making a call.  It would be awkward, conveying which decision she’d made and coordinating right, with Anide and Nikhil.

“I wonder what the dipslits from the A fangroup would say,” Anide said.

“Probably not the third option,” Winnifred said.

“There’s a real chance of running into A out here, though.  Imagine if you’d been in position to rescue her.  You would, too, keeping to that area of space, paying attention?”

She would.

Winnifred toyed with the idea, and she found it hard to put fully away.

By the time they were back in the Belt Network, with Toby booting back up, she knew.  It was the only way she, as herself could actually fly her own ship.  The only way to keep the dream going.

4.3.B – ESC

Basil

A was looking at the angry, hateful, and disparaging messages up until she reached the front door of her parents’ house.

“This is a surprise,” Landon Teeg said.

It seemed very normal and casual, out of sync with how A was feeling in general- Landon’s onboard could and would inform him of A’s emotional state, and it was, in the corner of his vision, and he avoided mentioning it.  Not so different than if A had showed up covered in cuts and bruises and Landon discreetly avoided mentioning it.

Landon, like Addy, had taken to wearing a lot of white.

A’s arrival, as it always did, anywhere, came with security and permissions to screen off an area of a superstructure.  The older Teegs had acquired property on Alcyone, on a different superstructure from A.  The view of the sky was obscured by the security ships, but the clouds were swirling, shaped by the superstructures and the intake systems that drew in oxygen for interior chambers, and absorbed ambient moisture out of the air.  A grey sky with the clouds forming whorls and spirals.  A blurriness suggested rain.

Landon didn’t mention the security ships either.

“If I announced my visit, there would be a crowd,” she said.

“True,” he said.  “Come in.  I was really worried, hearing about the attack.  Can you really trust your security?”

“The company feels it has something to prove.  We’ll see if they can prove it,” A replied.

[It’s also a lot harder to target A in an environment like this.]

“Home territory,” Landon said.

[That is part of it,] Basil noted.

The Teeg’s home was open and had high ceilings and omnipresent windows, which provided a view of those security ships, black against the swirling grey and white cloudscape of the sky behind them, flying in a grid formation.  Even in cases where windows looked out at other walls or sections of the property, panels on those walls reflected more of the same sky, giving a wider sense of openness.

Along the walls leading to the sitting area was a row of advertisements from history, suspended away from the wall’s surface, going back to the first printed ads, to the modern era.  The one on the end was of A, dressed in white, biting into a crisp apple, and segued into more art around the corner that had family pictures and video clips.  That would be Addy’s touch, overall.

Landon’s touch extended along the left hand wall, through a kitchenette area, covering less ground, as it stopped where windows started.  And continued into the garden, perhaps.  A few framed images by an artist who had cultivated trees and cut them into cross sections with human figures, with a notation in fine script occupying the empty space, noting how few cuts it had taken to refine the image to what it was.  A statuette in ore with gold shot through it, of a muscular man heaving a boulder.

“Your mother is wrapping up work, but we were going to go out.  Friends will be stopping in.  You could come.”

“To?” A asked, even as Basil dug into Landon’s history and projected the art and information onto nearby walls.

“An event, some art, some music.  It’s by your friend Mechard.”

“If we’re friends and he didn’t invite me, I think showing up would be awkward,” A said.  She was barely done saying it when Mechard, apparently flagged by the fact they’d started talking about him, reached out from Earth.

“It’s a small event.  I wouldn’t want to bother you with minor things, but if you want to come, you’re very welcome.”

“Okay,” A said.  “Yeah.”

“Happy to have you.”

Basil began organizing the required security.  He watched as the people he hired got ready, changing into clothes fitting the venue, their own onboards checking how other attendees were dressing.  Of the four, two men didn’t care at all about privacy, and changed in the open.  One who hadn’t worked with A as much seemed startled when a subset of A’s followers suddenly started paying a lot of attention to him.

It was only a fraction of a percent, idly investigating everyone in her orbit, but given the scale at which A operated, even with the current state of things, it meant a ten million eyes suddenly on him.

Basil used that, as much as he used anything, not to be invasive, but to scour for all possible details in environment and body language.

He was downplaying just how hard this would be, to keep A safe in a new, more hostile dynamic.  A fraction of a percentage point could storm a superstructure and overwhelm the security blockade, if sparked to action.

“There we go,” Landon said, oblivious.  “Maybe it’s a chance to reconnect with people in the industry.”

“Given the way some people are talking, I’m a bit worried about what that would mean.”

“Connections are good,” Landon said.  “If you need any help in that regard…”

A tensed slightly, at that.  The prior meeting, in the midst of the Inui media event, how contrived it had been, when she’d been reaching out for parents and they wanted opportunity.  Landon saw that tension.  His Onboard informed him.

A wasn’t performing on a level that let her hide it.

“Can I get you anything?  Feel free to sit.”

“Water?” she asked.  Basil checked the fridge and brought up types of water.  She glanced at a glass of black water, blinking to confirm.  “And I’ll go wash my face, if that’s alright?”

“Our home is your home.”

He went to get the water, and she stepped away.

That didn’t seem especially true to Basil, but he wasn’t about to vocally object.  The Teegs were arms-length parents.  They weren’t ones to invite A over, and after their last big argument with A, early into the filming of the Inui mediascape, A hadn’t reached out either.  The closest thing to a real conversation had been them sounding her out about acquiring property on Alcyone.

Which, Basil decided, cast an odd light on ‘our home is your home’.

The bathroom itself was hyper-minimalist, barely more than a room with white marble streaked with gray on all four sides.  Basil was expected to connect to the home system and make requests for the needed features.  He did, and they emerged from the marble, seamless.

She turned off the lights of the bathroom and flicked the switch for counter-sound, and quickly used the facilities.  Basil was generally pretty efficient about waste management, reserving excess waste to be extruded from pores when A showered, and while it was possible to skip needing the facilities entirely, that was a more holistic project, in the whole body sense.  Most people who went that direction were those who stayed in deep space, or worked nonstop.

She washed her face using water that flowed down and away from the wall at an angle from a darker patch of the dark gray in the marble, and then leaned over the counter, forearms resting on the edge of the stand, a circular pedestal or tube that dropped down away into more oblivion.  Not that she saw, with the lights off.  She lowered her head to her arms, and the narrow rim of the edge of the pedestal dug into skin.

Basil started to dim her interface, in case she needed actual quiet, but stopped when she turned her attention to the menus in the corner of her field of vision and brought up more recent messages, tucked away in archives.  Invectives.  Blame for Amber’s death.  Accusations that the attack by the void cowboys had been planned.

She glanced back through the menus, blinking in the darkness, until she’d gone back to the very first days, when her career had been new.  Except she went specifically for the angry messages he’d shuffled to the bottom of the pile.

[Is there anything specific you’re looking for?] Basil asked.

“No,” A replied, quiet.  There could almost have been a question mark at the end of the statement.  Her eyes skimmed through years of the darkest angriest messages.  Ones Basil had worked to downplay and push out of sight and out of mind, because they could multiply so easily.  They represented a trap for A, where everything she did was either a response to something negative or an attempt to not respond to it.  Even if she put herself out of that frame of mind -and Basil was unsure that was possible for her- her following wouldn’t.

She straightened, putting the messages away, and dried her face.  Light flooded the room as the door opened, and the various features and furnishings gracefully dipped into the wall and floor for a silent deep cleaning, even the floor panel that had droplets of moisture on it flipping over.

Addy had stepped out of her room, and embraced A, wordless.

A took a moment before responding to the hug.

“Have I hugged you since the top of your head came up to my chin?” Addy asked.

She had, twice, and had even made the same comment the last time they had hugged, but Basil decided providing the information came second to giving A the moment.  She buried her face in her mom’s shoulder.

“I’m sorry it’s been so hard,” Addy said.

A pulled away, nodding, and swallowed with a bit more difficulty than usual..

“For what it’s worth, I think stepping down from Elabre was the right thing to do, as hard as it must have been.  Hopefully the changes you made carry forward.”

“I think it’s falling apart.  Green left.”

“Yeah.  Maybe he’ll go back.  Maybe you will, in some capacity.”

“Hah,” A huffed out the laugh with very little humor.  She opened her mouth to say something, then couldn’t.  Her mom reached out to put a hand on her shoulder, steering her in an about-face so they could walk over to where Landon was greeting their guests.

“How’s the advertising work?” A asked.  Addy had picked up a leadership role in an advertising company, ostensibly from her background watching ads, but mostly for her association with A.

“It’s interesting.  I think we’re on the cusp of something new.  That’s why we’re attending tonight’s event.  It’s research.  People keep talking about a new tone of things, to go with the second belt.”

“Interesting.”

“You should be part of that,” Addy said.  Addy raised a hand and momentarily flapped a few fingers while keeping her palm still, to greet their guests, as they entered the foyer.

“These people okay, Bas?” A asked, through the backchannel.

[They vet fine.  You’ve met Curt before.  You and Quinn interrupted him and your parents, many years ago.]

“Oh.  Right.  Ohhh.”

Basil actually didn’t have the scene in his archives, except from the perspectives of Addy, Landon, Curt, and Quinn.  It had been before the science center.  He’d been down for a routine audit, and she was at Quinn’s with Vince, trying not to be bored, while flirting a bit with Vince.  Addy and Landon hadn’t had onboards, and the pre-set measures that would have alerted them that A was incoming hadn’t caught her because the onboard was off.

An awkward moment for all.

[I’d be suspicious of these people if your parents didn’t seem so legitimately surprised you turned up.  Do you want a deeper rundown?]

“I’ll manage.  Give me the usual.”

Eula Saine and Curt Porter.  Eula was a colleague of Addy, and did most of the actual business work, with Addy taking on the face to face and interpersonal work that Eula didn’t want to do.  However awkward and transparently obvious the nature of Addy’s hiring had been, they had found something resembling a rhythm, with Eula providing about seventy percent of the labor and grace required to keep that rhythm stable.  She had dark hair in an ‘up’ style, held in place with jewelry, and wore a bodysuit that looked like a proper suit from the sternum up, with jewelry around her gloved hands and ankles that made for a seamless blend of pant and sleeve into boot and glove, respectively.

Curt, meanwhile, was an odd fellow, who had done what a lot of teenagers who were overeager to grow up did, and used his onboard to grow to about the upper edge of reasonable heights, and to help him gain a lanky musculature to fit.  The difference was that most who pushed their bodies and aesthetic in one direction or otherwise experimented walked it back later.  He hadn’t.

That might have played a part in A not placing who he was, when she was very sharp without Basil’s aid, otherwise – her memory could have been rifling through the wrong folders.  Now fifty, Curt looked more like a teenager pretending to be older, with a slight slouch from decades of ducking through doorways, long in the torso, ungainly, long in the torso, all arms and legs, and old around the eyes.  A friend of Landon and a sometime lover of both Landon and Addy.

He said he stayed like that because he loved being the big spoon when cuddling.

Basil was intentionally sparing with the information provided in the way of reminders.  By making it look like she didn’t need information, it would achieve far more.

A took the glass of black water from her dad.  Nutrient rich and loaded with materials for Basil to use, including short hydrocarbon chains he could pull apart for energy, for a quick refresher of some systems.  Sour and a bit bitter, but he could anticipate that and make it refreshing.

“Do you remember me?”

“I’m a tiny bit scarred, so yes,” she replied, pinching fingers together so they were almost touching, smiling a bit to soften the words.

“I’m going to decline to ask why or have my onboard look,” Eula murmured.

“As you should,” Addy said, the fingertips of one hand going to her forehead, head hanging.

“Sorry about that.  I hoped I’d be memorable for other reasons.”

“You-” A paused for such a small amount of time that Basil wasn’t sure other people would notice, unless they were the type to microanalyze literally everything about A.  That pause coincided with a burst of something like positivity that a lot of people would notice.  Curt did.  “-round out my parents, Curt.  You’re good for them.”

“I’m glad,” Curt said.

He was genuinely touched.  A’s parents seemed surprised.

Basil was surprised.  That touch of positivity?  Fondness?  He followed A’s every move and he hadn’t expected it.

“They’re happier and… better as people, when you’re around, or-” she paused momentarily, like she was searching for a word.  Basil would have supplied one, but he had no inkling where this was coming from.  “-in the vicinity.”

A funny word choice that didn’t clarify much.

“I think we do fine,” Landon said, acting faintly offended.

“We can always be better,” A said.  “Whatever.  I’m glad to see you, Curt.  And pleased to meet you, Eula.”

“As am I.  I’m a little awestruck, if I’m honest.”

“I’m just a person,” A replied.

Basil’s processing finally connected dots.  A was thinking of the hug from her mom.  Saying ‘when you’re around or when you’re going to be around’ would have been too blatant.

Addy Teeg started talking about the show and how she’d invited Eula for research.

Meanwhile, Basil checked, and yeah, Curt had been in the vicinity, chronologically or positionally, a few times when her parents had shown surprising affection.

[Point to you, A.  I didn’t even catch that.  He does make your parents better.]

“You’re saying that to cheer me up.”

[I’m not.  I should track these things better.]

“You know the funny thing, Bas?  I almost said ‘you fill out my parents’.  Can you imagine?  Those words, when he was filling one of them up-“

[Okay, A.]

“My audience would never let it go.”

A touch of positivity.  She’d almost laughed at her own internal joke, and maybe the joke had hit harder because of how upset she was, in general.

“I’m a titan, even now, as it all falls apart, Bas.  I trample people without even knowing it.  I could have ruined his life with a bad choice of words, or even by having my throat tighten with a laugh I don’t let out, and having enough people realize why.”

[You’re a titan, yes, but you’re also a person.  Mistakes happen.]

A might’ve responded, but Eula asked her, abrupt, “You’ve been part of some big campaigns.”

“I have,” A said.  “Some bigger ones.  I also directed a few while leading Elabre.  But it’s not a strength.”
